q: What is a risk of just-in-time inventory?

options.t: Too much unsold stock in storage
options.why: Too much unsold stock is the risk of overstocking. Just-in-time keeps stock low, so excess is not its risk.

options.t: A supply delay can stop production
options.why: With so little buffer stock, a supplier delay can halt production. That fragility is the main risk of just-in-time.

options.t: High storage costs for the stock
options.why: High storage costs come with large inventories. Just-in-time reduces them, so they are a benefit, not a risk.

options.t: Wasted materials from overproduction
options.why: Wasted materials from overproduction come from making goods ahead of demand. Just-in-time makes goods only when needed.

q: What is a purchase order?

options.t: A pay slip for an employee, listing wages paid and tax
options.why: A pay slip shows wages paid. A purchase order is a request to a supplier.

options.t: A bill sent to a customer after a sale has been made
options.why: A bill sent to a customer after a sale is an invoice. A purchase order is sent by the buyer, before delivery.

options.t: A document that requests goods or services from a supplier
options.why: A purchase order is a document that requests goods or services from a supplier. It states the items, quantities, prices and delivery terms.

options.t: A record of goods that arrived, signed by the receiving clerk
options.why: A record of goods that arrived is a receiving report. A purchase order is made before the goods come.

q: What is capacity?

options.t: The minimum price of a product that a firm will accept
options.why: The minimum price a firm will accept is a pricing floor. Capacity is about how much can be produced.

options.t: The profit per unit that a firm earns on each sale made
options.why: Profit per unit is a measure of earnings. Capacity measures output.

options.t: The maximum amount a business can produce in a period
options.why: Capacity is the maximum amount a business can produce in a period. It limits how much the firm can sell without expanding.

options.t: The number of customers served in a day by the staff
options.why: The number of customers served is a measure of demand. Capacity is about production.

q: What is lifelong learning?

options.t: Avoiding new skills once a person has a steady job
options.why: Avoiding new skills is the opposite of lifelong learning. It means learning continues throughout a career.

options.t: Learning only from books in a library or a classroom
options.why: Learning only from books is too narrow. Lifelong learning includes training, experience and practice.

options.t: Learning only in school and then stopping for good
options.why: Learning only in school and then stopping is the opposite. Lifelong learning never stops.

options.t: Continuing to learn new skills throughout a career
options.why: Lifelong learning means continuing to learn new skills throughout a career. It helps workers adapt as jobs and technology change.

q: What is a SWOT analysis?

options.t: A review of sales, wages, orders and taxes for the year
options.why: A review of sales, wages, orders and taxes describes financial reports. SWOT stands for something else.

options.t: A review of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
options.why: A SWOT analysis reviews strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. It looks inside and outside the business to guide planning.

options.t: A review of suppliers, workers, owners and traders in a market
options.why: Suppliers, workers, owners and traders are groups of people. They are not what SWOT stands for.

options.t: A review of stocks, wealth, output and trade in a nation
options.why: Stocks, wealth, output and trade of a nation are economic ideas. They are not the four parts of SWOT.

q: A new competitor opening nearby is an example of a:

options.t: Threat
options.why: A new competitor opening nearby is an external factor that could hurt the business. External negatives are called threats.

options.t: Chance
options.why: A chance, or opportunity, is an external positive. A new competitor is a negative, so it is not a chance.

options.t: Weakness
options.why: A weakness is an internal problem. A competitor is outside the business, so it is not a weakness.

options.t: Strength
options.why: A strength is an internal advantage. A new competitor is external and harmful, so it is not a strength.

q: What is a key performance indicator (KPI)?

options.t: A list of products that a firm sells to its customers
options.why: A list of products a firm sells is a catalog. A KPI measures progress toward goals.

options.t: A company's phone number and email address, on its letterhead
options.why: A phone number and email address are contact details. They are not a measure of performance.

options.t: A customer's name and address kept on file by the firm
options.why: A customer's name and address are records. They do not measure how well goals are being met.

options.t: A measurable value showing how well goals are being met
options.why: A key performance indicator is a measurable value showing how well goals are being met. Examples are sales growth and customer satisfaction scores.

q: Which is the best example of a measurable goal?

options.t: Increase online sales by 15 percent in six months
options.why: Increasing online sales by 15 percent in six months is specific, has a number and has a deadline. That makes it measurable.

options.t: Try to improve things as much as we can this year
options.why: Trying to improve as much as we can has no number or deadline. Progress cannot be measured.

options.t: Become popular soon with as many people as we can
options.why: Becoming popular with as many people as possible is vague. There is no target to check.

options.t: Do better next quarter than in the last one
options.why: Doing better than last quarter has no size of improvement. It cannot show whether a goal was met.

q: What is operations management?

options.t: Setting the prices customers see in the store each season in every town
options.why: Setting prices is a marketing decision. Operations management runs the activities that make goods or services.

options.t: Hiring new workers and handling their yearly reviews and pay
options.why: Hiring and reviewing workers is human resources. Operations management focuses on production and service delivery.

options.t: Managing the activities that turn resources into goods or services
options.why: Operations management manages the activities that turn resources into goods or services. It focuses on efficiency, quality and cost.

options.t: Choosing the advertisements that appear on television and radio
options.why: Choosing ads is a marketing task. Operations deals with how products are made and delivered.

q: What is inventory management?

options.t: Deciding which employees work weekend shifts
options.why: Scheduling shifts is workforce planning. Inventory management is about the stock a business holds.

options.t: Controlling the amount of stock a business holds
options.why: Inventory management controls the amount of stock a business holds. It aims to avoid both running out and having too much.

options.t: Counting the money in a cash register each night
options.why: Counting cash is a cash handling duty. Inventory management deals with goods, not money.

options.t: Planning how a store will be decorated for holidays
options.why: Planning holiday decorations is a visual merchandising task. It is not inventory management.

q: A store orders far more winter coats than it can sell. What is the likely result?

options.t: Higher profits because there is more to sell
options.why: More stock than can be sold does not raise profits. Unsold coats earn nothing and cost money to hold.

options.t: Lower storage costs because stock is bulk purchased
options.why: Bulk buying does not lower storage costs when the goods stay unsold. Extra stock needs more space.

options.t: Faster service for every customer who shops there
options.why: Extra stock does not speed up service. It leaves goods unsold on the shelves.

options.t: Money tied up in unsold stock and later markdowns
options.why: Overordering ties money up in unsold coats. The store may have to cut prices later, which cuts profit.

q: What is a stockout?

options.t: Receiving an item late from a supplier each month
options.why: A late delivery is a supply problem. A stockout is when an item is unavailable to customers.

options.t: Running out of an item customers want to buy
options.why: A stockout is running out of an item customers want to buy. It means lost sales and disappointed customers.

options.t: Selling an item at a deep discount on a sale day
options.why: Deep discounting is a markdown. A stockout is a shortage, not a sale.

options.t: Having far too much of an item in storage
options.why: Having far too much of an item is overstock, the opposite of a stockout.

q: What is a reorder point?

options.t: The price at which a product is sold
options.why: The selling price is a pricing decision. A reorder point is an inventory trigger.

options.t: The number of items returned by customers
options.why: Returns are customer sends back. A reorder point concerns when to restock.

options.t: The stock level that triggers a new order
options.why: A reorder point is the stock level that triggers a new order. Ordering at that point keeps shelves filled until the delivery arrives.

options.t: The date a supplier is paid by the firm
options.why: The date a supplier is paid is a payment term. A reorder point is about stock levels.

q: A shop sells 20 units a day and a supplier takes 5 days to deliver. About what reorder point avoids a stockout?

options.t: 100 units
options.why: Reorder point equals daily use times lead time. 20 units a day over 5 days is 100 units, so reordering at 100 avoids a stockout.

options.t: 25 units
options.why: 25 units would run out in about a day and a bit. Delivery takes 5 days at 20 a day.

options.t: 500 units
options.why: 500 units far exceeds what is needed. The store only needs enough for the 5 days of delivery time.

options.t: 4 units
options.why: 4 units is far too few. The store sells 20 a day, so it would run out well before delivery.

q: What is a vendor?

options.t: A business that supplies goods or services to another business
options.why: A vendor is a business that supplies goods or services to another business. Shops and factories depend on vendors for stock and materials.

options.t: A customer who buys goods from a local business each week
options.why: A customer who buys goods is on the buying side. A vendor is on the supplying side.

options.t: A rival firm that competes with the business for its sales
options.why: A rival firm is a competitor. A vendor supplies to the business instead of competing with it.

options.t: An employee who sells products in a shop for a wage and a bonus
options.why: An employee who sells in a shop is a salesperson. A vendor is an outside supplier.

q: What does lead time mean?

options.t: The time between a sale and a refund being given
options.why: The time between a sale and a refund is a refund period. Lead time is about ordering.

options.t: The time a product spends on a shelf before it sells
options.why: The time a product sits on a shelf is the holding period. Lead time is the wait for an order.

options.t: The time between placing an order and receiving it
options.why: Lead time is the time between placing an order and receiving it. Knowing it helps a business reorder before running out.

options.t: The time a leader spends in meetings with the staff
options.why: A leader's time in meetings is not what lead time means. It is a supply term.

q: Why should a business check goods when a shipment arrives?

options.t: To raise the price of the goods that arrive
options.why: Checking goods does not raise prices. It confirms what arrived.

options.t: To confirm quantity and condition match the order
options.why: Checking confirms quantity and condition match the order. It catches shortages and damage before paying.

options.t: To make deliveries take longer to reach the shop
options.why: Checking does not delay deliveries. It happens after goods arrive.

options.t: To avoid recording it so the invoice stays unpaid
options.why: Not recording a shipment would leave records wrong. Goods should be checked and recorded.

q: What is efficiency?

options.t: Working slowly to avoid mistakes of any kind at all
options.why: Working slowly to avoid mistakes is not efficiency. Efficiency also saves time.

options.t: Spending more to produce less than before at the firm
options.why: Spending more to produce less is the opposite of efficiency. Efficiency gets more from less.

options.t: Producing as much waste as possible, since scrap shows output
options.why: Producing waste is the opposite of efficiency. Efficient firms cut scrap.

options.t: Producing results with minimal waste of time and resources
options.why: Efficiency is producing results with minimal waste of time and resources. It lowers costs and raises output.

q: What is productivity?

options.t: The amount produced for the resources used
options.why: Productivity is the amount produced for the resources used. Higher productivity means more output from the same inputs.

options.t: The number of stores that a firm owns now
options.why: The number of stores is a size measure. Productivity is output per input.

options.t: The price of a finished product in the shop
options.why: The price of a product is a pricing matter. Productivity measures output.

options.t: The profit a firm makes during the year
options.why: Profit measures earnings. Productivity measures output for resources used.

q: A worker makes 40 items in 8 hours. After training the worker makes 60 items in 8 hours. What happened to productivity?

options.t: It cannot be measured, since days differ
options.why: Productivity can be measured. Output per hour is the usual measure, even when days differ.

options.t: It increased from 5 to 7.5 items per hour
options.why: Productivity rose. The worker went from 40 items in 8 hours, or 5 an hour, to 60 in 8 hours, or 7.5 an hour.

options.t: It decreased from 5 to 4 items per hour
options.why: Output rose from 40 to 60 items, so productivity increased. A decrease would need fewer items per hour.

options.t: It stayed the same at 5 items per hour
options.why: The worker made more items in the same time, so productivity did not stay the same. It rose from 5 to 7.5 items an hour.

q: What is a safety procedure for?

options.t: Increasing the speed of every task for workers
options.why: Speeding up tasks is not the purpose of safety procedures. They can slow work slightly to keep people safe.

options.t: Lowering the price of products sold in the shop
options.why: Prices are not set by safety procedures. They are rules for staying safe.

options.t: Replacing the need for training of the new staff
options.why: Safety procedures do not replace training. Training helps staff follow them.

options.t: Reducing the chance of accidents and injuries
options.why: A safety procedure reduces the chance of accidents and injuries. It sets clear steps for working safely.

q: What is preventive maintenance?

options.t: Replacing all equipment every month of the year
options.why: Replacing all equipment every month is wasteful. Preventive maintenance services what the firm already has.

options.t: Repairing equipment only after it fails and stops
options.why: Repairing equipment only after it fails is reactive maintenance. Preventive maintenance acts before failure.

options.t: Servicing equipment regularly to avoid breakdowns
options.why: Preventive maintenance is servicing equipment regularly to avoid breakdowns. It saves money and keeps work running.

options.t: Ignoring equipment problems until a machine stops
options.why: Ignoring problems until a machine stops is the opposite. Preventive maintenance fixes problems early.

q: A bakery oven is serviced every three months to avoid sudden failure. What is this?

options.t: Preventive maintenance
options.why: Servicing the oven every three months to avoid failure is preventive maintenance. It heads off problems before they happen.

options.t: Price skimming plan
options.why: Price skimming is a pricing strategy. It has nothing to do with oven upkeep.

options.t: Channel conflict risk
options.why: Channel conflict is a distribution issue. It does not describe servicing an oven.

options.t: Emergency repair work
options.why: Emergency repair work happens after a failure. The regular servicing here is done to avoid one.

q: What is customer-focused operations?

options.t: Ignoring what customer needs in order to cut cost and save money
options.why: Ignoring customer needs to cut costs is not customer-focused. It puts cost ahead of customers.

options.t: Setting rules that make buying harder, to keep away customers
options.why: Rules that make buying harder push customers away. Customer-focused operations make buying easy.

options.t: Making decisions without any feedback from the customers at all
options.why: Deciding without feedback ignores customers. A focus on customers listens to them.

options.t: Running processes to meet customer needs for quality, speed and cost
options.why: Customer-focused operations run processes to meet customer needs for quality, speed and cost. The customer's needs shape how work is done.

q: What is a soft skill?

options.t: Writing computer code, which is a technical skill
options.why: Writing computer code is a technical skill, not a soft skill. It is learned and measurable.

options.t: A personal ability such as communication or teamwork
options.why: A soft skill is a personal ability such as communication or teamwork. Soft skills help people work well with others.

options.t: Using accounting software, which is a technical skill
options.why: Using accounting software is a technical skill. It is taught as a specific tool.

options.t: Operating a machine, which is a technical skill
options.why: Operating a machine is a technical skill. Soft skills are about people.

q: Which is an example of a technical skill?

options.t: Listening well to your peers
options.why: Listening well to peers is a soft skill. It is an interpersonal ability.

options.t: Showing empathy to coworkers
options.why: Showing empathy is a soft skill. It relates to people's feelings.

options.t: Preparing a spreadsheet budget
options.why: Preparing a spreadsheet budget is a technical skill. It uses software and math know-how that can be taught and measured.

options.t: Working in a team with coworkers
options.why: Working in a team is a soft skill. It is about cooperation, not a technical ability.

q: What is a cover letter?

options.t: A list of every job you have held, with the dates and pay
options.why: A list of jobs with dates and pay is a resume or work history. A cover letter introduces you and explains why you fit the job.

options.t: A request for a bank loan to start a new business in town
options.why: A bank loan request is a financial document. A cover letter is part of a job application.

options.t: A tax document that is filed with the government each year
options.why: A tax document is filed with the government. A cover letter goes to an employer.

options.t: A letter introducing yourself and explaining why you fit a job
options.why: A cover letter introduces you and explains why you fit a job. It highlights relevant skills and shows interest in the role.

q: What is a reference?

options.t: A person who can speak about your skills and character
options.why: A reference is a person who can speak about your skills and character. Employers contact references to check what you have told them.

options.t: A list of your hobbies and interests outside of school
options.why: Hobbies and interests are details for a resume. A reference is a person, not a list.

options.t: A copy of your diploma from the last school you attended
options.why: A diploma is proof of education. It is not a reference.

options.t: A job offer letter that an employer has sent to you
options.why: A job offer is sent by an employer after hiring. It is not a reference.

q: Why should you ask before listing someone as a reference?

options.t: Because the law requires it for every job application
options.why: No law requires asking, but it is polite and wise. The main reason is to make sure they are ready to speak for you.

options.t: So they can pay your fees for school or for college
options.why: References do not pay your school fees. They speak about your abilities.

options.t: So they are prepared and willing to speak well of you
options.why: You ask first so they are prepared and willing to speak well of you. A surprised or unwilling reference can hurt your chances.

options.t: So they can write your resume and know the job well
options.why: References do not write your resume. They give an opinion of your work.

q: What is time management?

options.t: Working without breaks all day long
options.why: Working without breaks all day is not time management. It leads to tiredness and poor work.

options.t: Planning how to use time to meet goals
options.why: Time management means planning how to use time to meet goals. It involves priorities, schedules and deadlines.

options.t: Doing tasks in random order each day
options.why: Doing tasks in random order is poor planning. Good time management uses priorities.

options.t: Delaying all work until the deadline
options.why: Delaying work until the deadline is procrastination. It leaves no room for mistakes.

q: You have an urgent, important task and an unimportant, non-urgent one. Which first?

options.t: Whichever is easier to do
options.why: Doing the easier task first is not the best choice. Priority should depend on importance and urgency.

options.t: The urgent and important task
options.why: An urgent and important task should be done first, since delay carries real consequences. The unimportant one can wait.

options.t: Neither, so as to avoid stress
options.why: Neither is a poor choice. Avoiding both leaves important work undone.

options.t: The unimportant, non-urgent one
options.why: The unimportant, non-urgent task can wait. Doing it first wastes time needed for the urgent one.

q: What is workplace etiquette?

options.t: Accepted rules of polite and respectful behavior at work
options.why: Workplace etiquette is accepted rules of polite and respectful behavior at work. It includes punctuality, courtesy and professionalism.

options.t: A list of company products and prices given to the customers
options.why: A list of products and prices is a catalog. Etiquette is about behavior.

options.t: A set of tax rules that firms must follow each year
options.why: Tax rules are legal requirements. Etiquette is about manners at work.

options.t: A dress code for parties and other fun social events
options.why: A dress code for parties is not workplace etiquette. Etiquette applies to work behavior.

q: A coworker is often late for team meetings. What is the best response?

options.t: Shout at the coworker in front of everyone at the meeting
options.why: Shouting in front of everyone humiliates the coworker. It makes the problem worse.

options.t: Gossip about the coworker to others in the office
options.why: Gossip spreads rumors and breaks trust. It does not fix lateness.

options.t: Ignore it forever and hope that it just goes away
options.why: Ignoring it forever lets the problem continue. The team will keep losing time.

options.t: Politely discuss the impact and agree on expectations
options.why: Politely discussing the impact and agreeing on expectations addresses the problem respectfully. It gives the coworker a chance to change.

q: What is an internship?

options.t: A loan for students that is paid back after leaving school
options.why: A loan for students is a student loan. An internship is work experience.

options.t: A permanent management role in a company with a fixed salary
options.why: A permanent management role is a full job. An internship is short-term.

options.t: Short-term work experience that helps you learn on the job
options.why: An internship is short-term work experience that helps you learn on the job. It builds skills and contacts.

options.t: A form for taxes that workers must file with the state
options.why: A tax form is a government document. It is not an internship.

q: What is job shadowing?

options.t: Taking a worker's place permanently after watching
options.why: Taking a worker's place permanently is a job change. Job shadowing is observing.

options.t: Doing a worker's job for a month at full pay
options.why: Doing a worker's job for a month at full pay is a trial job. Shadowing is only watching.

options.t: Working in a dark room for hours on end each day
options.why: Working in a dark room has no relation to the term. Shadowing means following someone.

options.t: Following a worker to learn what a job involves
options.why: Job shadowing means following a worker to learn what a job involves. It lets students see daily tasks without doing the job.

q: Which is a good reason to join a professional organization like DECA or FBLA?

options.t: To guarantee a job after graduation
options.why: No organization can guarantee a job after graduation. DECA and FBLA build skills that help you compete.

options.t: To build skills, leadership and contacts
options.why: Professional organizations build skills, leadership and contacts. DECA and FBLA also offer competitions and networking.

options.t: To skip school requirements and get a pass
options.why: Joining does not skip school requirements. Students must still meet them.

options.t: To avoid any competition from other students
options.why: These groups involve competition, not avoiding it. Competing builds skills.

q: What is networking?

options.t: Building relationships that can offer advice and opportunities
options.why: Networking is building relationships that can offer advice and opportunities. Contacts can lead to jobs, mentors and ideas.

options.t: Selling to strangers on the street to earn a quick profit
options.why: Selling to strangers is a sales activity. Networking builds mutual relationships.

options.t: Working alone with no contact with any other people at work
options.why: Working alone with no contact is the opposite. Networking depends on connecting with people.

options.t: Connecting computers together over a wire or wireless link
options.why: Connecting computers is a technical meaning. In careers it means connecting with people.

q: What is strategic planning?

options.t: Ordering daily supplies for the kitchen and the shop
options.why: Ordering daily supplies is an operational task. Strategic planning looks far ahead.

options.t: Scheduling this week's staff shifts and who works when
options.why: Scheduling this week's shifts is short-term operational planning. Strategic planning is long-term.

options.t: Setting long-term goals and deciding how to reach them
options.why: Strategic planning means setting long-term goals and deciding how to reach them. It guides the whole organization over years.

options.t: Filing patient charts and records in the clinic office
options.why: Filing charts is routine office work. It is not planning.

q: A company wants to double its revenue in five years. Which is the most appropriate first step?

options.t: Hire many workers without a plan to bring in more sales
options.why: Hiring many workers without a plan may add cost with no sales. A plan should come first.

options.t: Cut all advertising immediately and stop all promotions
options.why: Cutting advertising would likely reduce sales. It works against doubling revenue.

options.t: Analyze the market and its own strengths and weaknesses
options.why: Analyzing the market and its own strengths and weaknesses gives the facts needed to plan growth. It is the sensible first step.

options.t: Raise prices by half and hope that sales will double
options.why: Raising prices by half could drive customers away. It would not double sales.

q: A delivery firm compares its on-time rate with the industry leader. What is this?

options.t: Market research
options.why: Market research studies customers. Comparing on-time rates with a leader is benchmarking.

options.t: Benchmarking
options.why: Benchmarking compares performance with the industry leader's. The delivery firm sees how far it is from the best.

options.t: Stock counting
options.why: Stock counting checks inventory. It is not a comparison with a leader.

options.t: Price fixing
options.why: Price fixing is an illegal agreement on prices. It is unrelated.

q: What is diversification as a growth strategy?

options.t: Closing all branches of the business
options.why: Closing all branches is the opposite of expansion. Diversification adds new products or markets.

options.t: Selling only one product for good
options.why: Selling only one product for good is the opposite. Diversification means offering more.

options.t: Cutting all prices to the lowest level
options.why: Cutting prices to the lowest is a price strategy. It is not diversification.

options.t: Expanding into new products or markets
options.why: Diversification means expanding into new products or markets. It spreads risk and creates new sources of income.

q: A shoe maker starts selling bags and belts. Which growth strategy is this?

options.t: Product diversification
options.why: A shoe maker adding bags and belts enters new product lines. That is product diversification.

options.t: Lower prices to gain share
options.why: Lowering prices to gain share is a pricing move. The shoe maker is adding products.

options.t: Cost leadership strategy
options.why: Cost leadership is about the lowest costs. The shoe maker is expanding.

options.t: Exit from the market
options.why: Exit from the market is leaving. The shoe maker is growing.

q: What is a merger?

options.t: One company splitting in two
options.why: One company splitting in two is a split or spin-off. A merger joins companies.

options.t: Two companies combining into one
options.why: A merger is two companies combining into one. It can create a larger firm with shared resources.

options.t: A company closing a small branch
options.why: Closing a small branch is a downsizing. A merger is a combination.

options.t: A company paying a big dividend
options.why: Paying a dividend shares profit with owners. It is not a merger.

q: What is customer segmentation?

options.t: Grouping customers by shared traits such as age or interests
options.why: Customer segmentation groups customers by shared traits such as age or interests. It lets a business target each group.

options.t: Treating every customer the same, whatever their age or income
options.why: Treating every customer the same is mass marketing. Segmentation tailors efforts.

options.t: Counting customers only, with no traits recorded for each
options.why: Counting customers with no traits is not segmentation. It requires grouping by traits.

options.t: Ignoring customer data when planning any marketing at all
options.why: Ignoring data is the opposite. Segmentation uses it.

q: A gym promotes student discounts to teens and wellness classes to adults over 50. What is this?

options.t: Mass marketing to everyone with the same message
options.why: Mass marketing sends one message to everyone. The gym tailors offers.

options.t: Channel conflict between a firm and its retail sellers
options.why: Channel conflict is a dispute between a firm and its sellers. It does not describe tailored offers.

options.t: Price fixing between a few rival firms in the market
options.why: Price fixing is illegal collusion. It is unrelated.

options.t: Targeting different segments with tailored offers
options.why: Student discounts for teens and wellness classes for adults over 50 target different segments with tailored offers. It fits the audience of each.

q: What is promotion?

options.t: Choosing where to sell a product, in a shop or on a website
options.why: Choosing where to sell is place. Promotion communicates.

options.t: Setting the price of a product for sale to the public
options.why: Setting the price is price. Promotion informs and persuades.

options.t: Communication that informs and persuades customers to buy
options.why: Promotion is communication that informs and persuades customers to buy. It includes ads, sales and publicity.

options.t: Designing the product so that it looks good to buyers
options.why: Designing the product is part of product development. Promotion is communication.

q: Which promotion best reaches teenagers?

options.t: Radio ads at 3 a.m. daily
options.why: Radio ads at 3 a.m. reach few teenagers. They are asleep.

options.t: Printed notices in an office
options.why: Printed notices in an office reach working adults. They miss teenagers.

options.t: Ads in a retirement newsletter
options.why: Ads in a retirement newsletter reach older readers. Teenagers do not read them.

options.t: Short videos on social media
options.why: Short videos on social media reach teens where they spend time. They suit the audience.

q: What is customer loyalty?

options.t: A customer who avoids the store and never comes back
options.why: A customer who avoids the store is not loyal. Loyalty is returning.

options.t: A customer who asks for refunds often and rarely buys again
options.why: Asking for refunds often and rarely buying again is not loyalty. It shows low engagement.

options.t: A customer's tendency to keep buying from the same business
options.why: Customer loyalty is a customer's tendency to keep buying from the same business. Loyal customers also recommend it.

options.t: A customer who buys only once and then never returns
options.why: Buying once and never returning is the opposite of loyalty. Loyal customers repeat.

q: What is a marketing mix?

options.t: The combination of product, price, place and promotion
options.why: The marketing mix is the combination of product, price, place and promotion. A business adjusts these to reach customers.

options.t: The mix of ingredients in a recipe used to bake a cake
options.why: A mix of recipe ingredients is cooking. The marketing mix is a business tool.

options.t: The combination of tax and profit for the business
options.why: Tax and profit are not the marketing mix. The mix is the four Ps.

options.t: The combination of stores and offices of the firm
options.why: Stores and offices are locations. They are not the marketing mix.

q: A phone company lowers its price to attract buyers. Which part of the marketing mix changed?

options.t: Promotion
options.why: Promotion is how a business tells customers about a product. Lowering price does not change that.

options.t: Price
options.why: Lowering the price changes the price element of the marketing mix. The company wants to attract buyers with a lower cost.

options.t: Place
options.why: Place is where products are sold. Lowering the price does not change location.

options.t: Product
options.why: Product is the item itself. Lowering price does not change the product.

q: What is a firewall?

options.t: A program that edits photos and videos for the firm's ads
options.why: A program that edits photos is design software. A firewall protects networks.

options.t: A security tool that controls traffic into and out of a network
options.why: A firewall is a security tool that controls traffic into and out of a network. It blocks unwanted connections.

options.t: A wall that stops fires in buildings, made of brick or steel
options.why: A wall that stops fires is a building feature. A firewall in computing is a security tool.

options.t: A password for a website that a new user needs to log in with
options.why: A password is a login credential. A firewall filters network traffic.

q: What is multi-factor authentication?

options.t: Requiring two or more proofs of identity to sign in
options.why: Multi-factor authentication requires two or more proofs of identity to sign in, such as a password and a code. It makes accounts much harder to break into.

options.t: Writing a password on a note stuck to the screen
options.why: Writing a password on a note is a security risk. It is not authentication.

options.t: Sharing a password with a team so all can log in
options.why: Sharing a password weakens security. Multi-factor needs more proofs.

options.t: Using one long password only, for every account
options.why: One long password is only one factor. Multi-factor needs more.

q: Which practice best protects accounts?

options.t: Sharing passwords by email with all coworkers and friends
options.why: Sharing passwords by email exposes them. It weakens security.

options.t: Reusing one password everywhere so there is less to recall
options.why: Reusing one password everywhere is risky. If one account is hacked, the rest follow.

options.t: Using easy-to-guess passwords that are short and simple
options.why: Easy passwords are guessed quickly. They offer little protection.

options.t: Using unique strong passwords with multi-factor authentication
options.why: Unique strong passwords with multi-factor authentication give layered protection. An attacker needs more than a guessed password.

q: What is data entry?

options.t: Deleting data from a system when it is old
options.why: Deleting old data is data disposal. Data entry puts information in.

options.t: Encrypting data so that others cannot read it
options.why: Encrypting data protects it. Data entry adds data.

options.t: Typing or importing information into a system
options.why: Data entry is typing or importing information into a system. It creates the records that businesses rely on.

options.t: Printing data onto paper sheets for later use
options.why: Printing data creates paper copies. Data entry adds data.

q: Why does accurate data entry matter?

options.t: Errors make reports more interesting to read
options.why: Errors do not make reports more interesting. They make them wrong.

options.t: Errors lead to wrong reports and decisions
options.why: Errors lead to wrong reports and decisions. Accurate entry keeps information reliable.

options.t: Errors improve security for the whole system
options.why: Errors do not improve security. They weaken data quality.

options.t: Errors reduce storage needs of the system
options.why: Errors do not reduce storage needs. They can add more corrections.

q: What is an email attachment risk?

options.t: It may contain malware
options.why: An unexpected attachment may contain malware that harms your device. Opening it can infect systems.

options.t: It always improves safety
options.why: Attachments do not always improve safety. They can carry viruses.

options.t: It makes email faster
options.why: Attachments do not make email faster. They make messages larger.

options.t: It deletes spam for you
options.why: Attachments do not delete spam. They can carry it.

q: You receive an unexpected attachment from an unknown sender. What should you do?

options.t: Save it to a shared drive
options.why: Saving it to a shared drive could spread malware to others. It is unsafe.

options.t: Open it to see what it is
options.why: Opening it to see what it is may infect the computer. Unknown attachments are a risk.

options.t: Not open it and report it
options.why: Not opening it and reporting it is the safe choice. IT can check it and warn others.

options.t: Forward it to coworkers
options.why: Forwarding it spreads the risk. It puts coworkers in danger.

q: What is a database used for in business?

options.t: Tracking employee shifts only and the hours each has worked
options.why: Tracking shifts only is too narrow. A database stores many kinds of records.

options.t: Printing posters to advertise the firm's sales events
options.why: Printing posters is a design job. A database holds data.

options.t: Moving products to customers by van or by truck each day
options.why: Moving products is logistics. A database stores information.

options.t: Storing organized records that can be searched and updated
options.why: A database stores organized records that can be searched and updated. Businesses use it for customers, orders and inventory.

q: What is cloud storage?

options.t: Deleting files after use to free up space on the disk
options.why: Deleting files to free space is cleanup. Cloud storage keeps files online.

options.t: Keeping files only on one computer in a locked folder
options.why: Keeping files on one computer is local storage. Cloud storage uses remote servers.

options.t: Keeping files on remote servers reached over the internet
options.why: Cloud storage keeps files on remote servers reached over the internet. Users can open them from many devices.

options.t: Keeping files on paper in a cabinet in the main office
options.why: Paper files in a cabinet are physical storage. Cloud storage is digital.

q: A small business wants employees to access files from home. Which option fits best?

options.t: A single office computer
options.why: A single office computer cannot be reached from home. It does not meet the need.

options.t: Paper files in a cabinet
options.why: Paper files cannot be accessed remotely. They must be in the office.

options.t: USB drives passed around
options.why: USB drives passed around can be lost or infected. They are not secure or convenient.

options.t: Secure cloud storage
options.why: Secure cloud storage lets employees reach files from home safely. It keeps data protected.

q: What is customer-focused marketing?

options.t: Planning marketing around rivals' logos and designs
options.why: Planning around rivals' logos is competitor-focused. Customer-focused marketing looks at customers.

options.t: Planning marketing around what customers need and value
options.why: Customer-focused marketing plans around what customers need and value. It makes the product and message fit buyers.

options.t: Planning marketing around the lowest cost only today
options.why: Planning around the lowest cost is cost-focused. It does not put customers first.

options.t: Planning marketing around what the owner likes most
options.why: Planning around what the owner likes is owner-focused. It may not suit customers.

q: What is a production schedule?

options.t: A plan showing what will be made, when and in what amount
options.why: A production schedule is a plan showing what will be made, when and in what amount. It helps match output to demand.

options.t: A report of a firm's yearly taxes for the government
options.why: A tax report is for the government. A production schedule plans output.

options.t: A list of customers who bought last year and what they spent
options.why: A list of past customers is a sales record. It does not plan production.

options.t: A chart of employee birthdays and work anniversaries
options.why: A chart of birthdays is an HR note. It is unrelated.

q: What is a personal brand at work?

options.t: A list of your favorite products and the stores that sell them in your town
options.why: Favorite products and stores are personal preferences. A personal brand is how others see you.

options.t: The impression others have of your skills, reliability and character
options.why: A personal brand is the impression others have of your skills, reliability and character. It shapes opportunities at work.

options.t: A tax form that employees must file with the government every year
options.why: A tax form is a government document. It has nothing to do with personal brand.

options.t: A logo painted on your car, advertising your own firm to all
options.why: A logo painted on a car is advertising for a firm. A personal brand is a reputation.

q: A bakery owner signs a one-year lease for a storefront. Which element makes this agreement a legally binding contract?

options.t: An offer, acceptance and something of value exchanged by both parties
options.why: A contract needs an offer, acceptance and something of value exchanged by both sides. A lease with these elements is legally binding.

options.t: A handshake and a friendly conversation between the two parties to the lease
options.why: A handshake and a friendly chat do not make a written lease. The elements of a contract are needed.

options.t: A verbal promise made in front of customers at the store itself
options.why: A verbal promise before customers is not a lease agreement. It lacks the required elements.

options.t: A signature from only the landlord, without the owner agreeing
options.why: A signature from only the landlord lacks the owner's agreement. Both sides must agree.

q: What is the purpose of a trademark for a business?

options.t: To give the government control over the company's prices
options.why: A trademark does not give the government price control. It protects a brand identity.

options.t: To guarantee that every product sold will make a profit
options.why: A trademark cannot guarantee profit. It protects a name or logo.

options.t: To protect a name, logo or slogan that identifies its products
options.why: A trademark protects a name, logo or slogan that identifies a business's products. It stops others from copying the brand.

options.t: To protect a new invention from copying for twenty years
options.why: Protecting an invention for twenty years is a patent. A trademark protects identity.

q: A song used in a store's online ad was written by a famous artist. What should the store get before using it?

options.t: A receipt showing the song was purchased as a download
options.why: A receipt for a download does not give the right to use a song in an ad. Commercial use needs a license.

options.t: Nothing, because songs on the radio are free
options.why: Songs on the radio are not free to use in ads. Copyright still applies.

options.t: A note from a customer saying they like the song
options.why: A customer's note has no legal effect. Only the owner can give permission.

options.t: Permission or a license from the copyright owner
options.why: The store should get permission or a license from the copyright owner. Using the song without it would be infringement.

q: A customer slips on a wet floor with no warning sign and is injured. Which legal concept is most likely involved?

options.t: Libel, a false statement that harms a name
options.why: Libel is a false written statement that harms a reputation. A wet floor injury is not defamation.

options.t: Fraud, a deliberate deception to gain money
options.why: Fraud is deliberate deception. The store did not deceive anyone.

options.t: Negligence, a failure to use reasonable care
options.why: Negligence is a failure to use reasonable care. Leaving a wet floor with no warning is a failure that caused injury.

options.t: Bankruptcy, a process when debts go unpaid
options.why: Bankruptcy is a process for unpaid debts. It does not apply to an injury claim.

q: What does a warranty on a product do?

options.t: Promises that the product will work or meet certain standards
options.why: A warranty promises that the product will work or meet certain standards. If it fails, the buyer can seek repair or replacement.

options.t: Lets the seller change the product after the sale is made
options.why: A warranty does not let the seller change the product afterwards. It binds the seller.

options.t: Requires the buyer to return the product within one hour of sale
options.why: A warranty does not require return within one hour. It covers a longer period.

options.t: Guarantees that the price of the product will never go up
options.why: A warranty does not guarantee a price. It covers quality.

q: Which type of business ownership gives owners limited personal liability for business debts?

options.t: A general partnership of two close friends
options.why: A general partnership gives partners unlimited personal liability. It does not limit it.

options.t: A sole proprietorship run by one person
options.why: A sole proprietorship has unlimited liability. The owner and business are the same legally.

options.t: A business with no legal registration
options.why: A business with no registration offers no protection. Liability would be personal.

options.t: A corporation or limited liability company
options.why: A corporation or LLC is a separate legal entity, so owners are not personally liable for business debts. Their risk is limited to what they invested.

q: An employer pays a 16-year-old worker less than the minimum wage and schedules a 14-hour shift on a school night. Which laws are most likely being broken?

options.t: Zoning and building laws
options.why: Zoning and building laws concern property use. They are not about pay or hours.

options.t: Wage and child labor laws
options.why: Paying below minimum wage breaks wage laws, and a 14-hour shift on a school night for a 16-year-old breaks child labor rules. Both are likely violated.

options.t: Antitrust and merger laws
options.why: Antitrust and merger laws concern competition. They are not about worker pay.

options.t: Copyright and trademark laws
options.why: Copyright and trademark laws protect creative works. They do not apply here.

q: What is the role of an agent in business law?

options.t: A person who buys goods only for his or her personal use
options.why: A person who buys only for personal use is a consumer. An agent acts for another.

options.t: A person authorized to act on behalf of another, the principal
options.why: An agent is a person authorized to act on behalf of another, the principal. The principal is bound by what the agent does within that authority.

options.t: A person who lends money to businesses and to their owners
options.why: A person who lends money is a lender. An agent represents someone.

options.t: A person who inspects a business for tax errors and reports them
options.why: A person who inspects for tax errors is an auditor. It is a different role.

q: Why do businesses use written contracts instead of relying only on spoken agreements?

options.t: Written contracts remove the need to follow the terms
options.why: Written contracts do not remove the duty to follow the terms. They make the terms clear.

options.t: Spoken agreements are always illegal in every business deal
options.why: Spoken agreements are not always illegal. They are harder to prove.

options.t: A written record shows the agreed terms and reduces disputes
options.why: A written record shows the agreed terms and reduces disputes. It is easier to prove if there is a disagreement.

options.t: Written contracts guarantee that no one will ever disagree
options.why: Written contracts cannot guarantee no disagreement. They reduce disputes.

q: A company imports electronics and fails to follow customs rules at the border. What is the most likely result?

options.t: The company earns a government subsidy
options.why: A subsidy is a payment from the government. Breaking customs rules would not earn one.

options.t: The shipment moves faster, skipping checks
options.why: Skipping checks is not allowed. Breaking rules brings problems.

options.t: The company is exempt from future import laws
options.why: A company cannot become exempt by breaking customs rules. It would face trouble.

options.t: Shipments may be delayed, seized or fined
options.why: Failing to follow customs rules may cause delays, seizure or fines. Importers must comply.

q: What does the term 'liability' mean for a business?

options.t: A legal responsibility, often for debts or harm caused
options.why: Liability is a legal responsibility, often for debts or harm caused. A business can be liable to customers, lenders or others.

options.t: The number of employees a company must hire each year
options.why: The number of employees is a staffing decision. Liability is a legal duty.

options.t: The value of a company's trademarks and its brand names
options.why: The value of trademarks is an asset. Liability is an obligation.

options.t: The total revenue a business earns in a single year
options.why: Revenue is income. Liability is a responsibility.

q: A supplier promises delivery by Friday in a signed contract but ships a week late. What is this called?

options.t: A patent infringement
options.why: A patent infringement is using an invention without permission. A late shipment breaks a delivery promise.

options.t: A tariff on imports
options.why: A tariff is a tax on imports. It does not describe a late delivery.

options.t: A breach of contract
options.why: Shipping a week late after promising Friday delivery breaks the signed contract. That is a breach of contract.

options.t: A merger of two firms
options.why: A merger combines firms. A late shipment is not a merger.

q: Which agency enforces rules that protect consumers from deceptive advertising in the United States?

options.t: The Internal Revenue Service
options.why: The IRS collects taxes. It does not police advertising.

options.t: The Federal Reserve Board
options.why: The Federal Reserve oversees the nation's money and banks. It does not enforce advertising rules.

options.t: The SEC securities agency
options.why: The SEC oversees securities markets. It does not police ads for consumers.

options.t: The Federal Trade Commission
options.why: The Federal Trade Commission enforces rules that protect consumers from deceptive advertising. It also guards fair competition.

q: What is the main purpose of environmental regulations for businesses?

options.t: To help businesses avoid paying all taxes owed
options.why: Environmental rules do not help avoid taxes. They are separate.

options.t: To limit pollution and protect natural resources
options.why: Environmental regulations limit pollution and protect natural resources. They aim to keep air, water and land healthy.

options.t: To increase the prices of all products in stores
options.why: They do not exist to raise prices. Their goal is protection.

options.t: To protect large companies from all competition
options.why: They do not protect big companies from competition. They apply to everyone.

q: Two competing firms secretly agree to set the same high prices. Which law does this most likely violate?

options.t: Antitrust law against price fixing
options.why: Antitrust law bans price fixing, where competitors secretly agree on prices. It protects consumers from artificially high prices.

options.t: Child labor law limiting teen work
options.why: Child labor law limits teen work. It does not cover price agreements.

options.t: Zoning law controlling land use
options.why: Zoning law controls how land is used. It does not apply.

options.t: Copyright law protecting written works
options.why: Copyright law protects written works. It does not cover prices.

q: Which channel is best for sharing a detailed, formal policy change with all employees?

options.t: A rumor passed from coworker to coworker
options.why: A rumor is unreliable. It is not a formal channel.

options.t: A written memo or email with clear details
options.why: A written memo or email with clear details is formal and keeps a record. It suits a detailed policy change.

options.t: A quick hallway comment to a few workers
options.why: A quick hallway comment reaches only a few people. It lacks detail.

options.t: A text message with no explanation given
options.why: A text with no explanation leaves people confused. It is not formal.

q: What is the first step in writing a clear business email?

options.t: Decide the purpose and who the reader is
options.why: The first step is to decide the purpose and who the reader is. That shapes what to write and how to say it.

options.t: Write in all capital letters for emphasis
options.why: All capital letters look like shouting. They are not professional.

options.t: Include every detail from the past year
options.why: Including every detail makes the email long and unfocused. It should be concise.

options.t: Add as many attachments as possible
options.why: Many attachments overload the reader. They should be limited.

q: A manager's words say 'I'm open to ideas' but she frowns and crosses her arms. What does this show?

options.t: She has a strong writing style in her memos
options.why: Her writing style in memos does not show in a frown and crossed arms. It concerns body language.

options.t: She is following a company policy on tone
options.why: A company tone policy does not explain contradictions in body language. It is a rule about writing.

options.t: Her nonverbal cues may contradict her message
options.why: Her nonverbal cues may contradict her message. People often trust body language over words.

options.t: She is using the most effective channel here
options.why: Channel choice is separate. The issue is mixed signals.

q: Why is it useful to adapt your communication style to your audience?

options.t: It lets you avoid giving accurate information
options.why: Adapting does not avoid accuracy. It makes accurate information clearer.

options.t: It makes your message longer and more complex
options.why: Adapting does not make messages longer. It makes them fit the audience.

options.t: It removes the need to ask any questions at all
options.why: Adapting does not remove questions. Questions help check understanding.

options.t: It helps the message be understood and accepted
options.why: Adapting your style helps the message be understood and accepted. Different audiences need different words and detail.

q: What should you do when you answer a business phone call?

options.t: Greet the caller, state your name and offer help
options.why: Greeting the caller, stating your name and offering help is professional. It tells the caller they reached the right place.

options.t: Ask the caller to call back later without explaining
options.why: Telling the caller to call back later without explanation is unhelpful. It leaves them stuck.

options.t: Talk about your personal plans while waiting
options.why: Talking about personal plans is unprofessional. It ignores the caller.

options.t: Answer quickly without saying anything useful
options.why: Answering without saying anything useful wastes the caller's time. A clear greeting helps.

q: A team's meeting runs long because no one prepared. Which action would best improve the next meeting?

options.t: Invite more people with no purpose
options.why: Inviting more people with no purpose would make meetings longer. It does not help.

options.t: Remove time limits so everyone can talk
options.why: Removing time limits lets talk run on. Meetings should have limits.

options.t: Share an agenda and goals beforehand
options.why: Sharing an agenda and goals beforehand lets everyone prepare. It keeps the meeting focused.

options.t: Cancel all of the future meetings
options.why: Cancelling all future meetings stops communication. It avoids the problem.

q: Which graphic aid is best for showing how a company's sales changed over twelve months?

options.t: A pie chart
options.why: A pie chart shows parts of a whole. It does not show change over time well.

options.t: A line graph
options.why: A line graph shows how a value changes over time. It suits sales across twelve months.

options.t: A staff list
options.why: A staff list is a list of names. It shows no sales trend.

options.t: A store photo
options.why: A store photo shows a place. It does not show data.

q: What is the purpose of an executive summary?

options.t: To hide all the bad news from the readers of the report
options.why: An executive summary does not hide bad news. It gives honest key points.

options.t: To list every employee who worked on the project each week
options.why: Listing everyone who worked on the project is credits. An executive summary gives key findings.

options.t: To replace the full report completely, for any reader
options.why: An executive summary does not replace the full report. Readers who need details still read it.

options.t: To give busy readers the key points of a longer report
options.why: An executive summary gives busy readers the key points of a longer report. They can decide whether to read the details.

q: An employee writes 'Per my last email' in an angry tone to a coworker. What is the likely effect?

options.t: It may cause conflict and hurt the working relationship
options.why: Writing 'Per my last email' in an angry tone sounds blaming and sarcastic. It can spark conflict and damage the working relationship, even when the writer was right.

options.t: It improves teamwork by showing strong leadership to the team
options.why: Sarcastic phrasing does not show leadership. It makes the coworker feel accused, which hurts cooperation and weakens teamwork instead of building it.

options.t: It ensures the coworker will always respond faster
options.why: An angry reminder does not guarantee a faster response. Hostile messages usually make people defensive or less willing to help, so replies may even slow down.

options.t: It makes the whole message sound more professional
options.why: Anger does not make writing more professional. Professional messages stay calm, specific and respectful, and this phrase read in anger comes across as passive aggressive.

q: Why should business writing use clear, simple words?

options.t: Complex words always impress customers who read it
options.why: Complex words do not always impress customers. They can confuse readers and hide the message, so clear words are usually more effective in business writing.

options.t: Simple words are not allowed in formal reports
options.why: Simple words are allowed in formal reports, and many reports prefer them. Plain language makes the writing accurate and easy for any reader to follow.

options.t: Short words take much more time to write well
options.why: Short words are not harder to write well. Plain, short wording usually takes less effort for the reader, and clear writing is a skill worth practicing.

options.t: Readers understand it faster and with fewer errors
options.why: Clear, simple words help readers understand faster with fewer errors. That saves time, avoids misunderstandings and lets the reader act on the message.

q: Which step helps you edit and revise a document effectively?

options.t: Add extra words to make it a lot longer than needed
options.why: Adding extra words makes a document longer without making it better. Editing usually cuts unneeded words so the main point is easier to find.

options.t: Review it for clarity, accuracy and errors after writing
options.why: Reviewing for clarity, accuracy and errors after writing catches mistakes you missed while drafting. A careful revision makes the document stronger and more professional.

options.t: Change the topic halfway through the whole document
options.why: Changing the topic halfway confuses readers and breaks the flow. Revising should keep the document focused on its purpose.

options.t: Send it right away without reading it again at all
options.why: Sending without rereading lets typos and mistakes through. Editing means reading the draft again and fixing problems before it goes out.

q: During a presentation, a listener asks a question you cannot answer. What is the best response?

options.t: Make up an answer so you look well prepared
options.why: Making up an answer is dishonest and can mislead the audience. If the invented answer is wrong, you lose credibility.

options.t: Ignore the question and move on to the next
options.why: Ignoring the question disrespects the listener. It makes you seem evasive and leaves the person without help.

options.t: Admit you do not know and offer to follow up
options.why: Admitting you do not know and offering to follow up is honest and professional. It keeps trust and shows you care about giving a correct answer later.

options.t: Tell the listener the question is not important
options.why: Telling the listener the question is unimportant is rude and dismissive. It discourages people from taking part and damages your credibility as a presenter.

q: What is customer relationship management (CRM)?

options.t: A rule that requires customers to buy a product every month from a firm
options.why: Requiring customers to buy every month is a contract or subscription term. CRM is about managing interactions and information, not forcing purchases.

options.t: A method for lowering prices for all customers, so as to win more of their business
options.why: Lowering prices for everyone is a pricing choice. CRM instead uses customer information to build relationships, not just to cut prices.

options.t: A way to keep customers from sharing feedback about the firm's service
options.why: CRM does not stop customers from sharing feedback. It usually collects feedback so a business can respond to what customers say.

options.t: Managing interactions and information to build lasting customer relationships
options.why: CRM means managing interactions and information to build lasting customer relationships. Software stores purchase history and contacts so staff can serve each customer better.

q: A customer is upset about a late delivery. What should an employee do first?

options.t: Listen, apologize and ask what outcome would help
options.why: Listening first calms the customer and shows respect. Apologizing and asking what outcome would help then points the conversation toward a real solution.

options.t: Say it is not the company's responsibility at all
options.why: Saying it is not the company's responsibility dismisses the complaint. It makes the customer angrier and damages trust.

options.t: Ask the customer to call back again some other day
options.why: Asking the customer to call back shifts the work onto them. The problem stays unresolved and the customer feels ignored.

options.t: Explain why the customer should have ordered earlier
options.why: Blaming the customer for ordering late is defensive and unfair. A late delivery is the company's problem to address.

q: Why does a business collect customer feedback?

options.t: To reduce the number of customers served each day by the firm
options.why: Collecting feedback is not about serving fewer customers. Businesses want more satisfied customers, and feedback helps them get there.

options.t: To learn what customers want and improve products and service
options.why: Businesses collect feedback to learn what customers want and to improve products and service. It shows strengths to keep and problems to fix.

options.t: To avoid training employees and save money for the owner
options.why: Feedback does not replace training. Employees still need training, and feedback can even show where more training is needed.

options.t: To prove to customers that the company is always right every time
options.why: Feedback is not a way to prove the company is always right. It is a way to find out where the company can do better.

q: A loyalty program gives a free item after ten purchases. How does this support customer relations?

options.t: It guarantees every customer will be satisfied
options.why: A loyalty program cannot guarantee satisfaction for every customer. It rewards repeat purchases but does not replace good products and service.

options.t: It discourages customers from returning to the store
options.why: A free item after ten purchases encourages customers to come back. It does not discourage returns, which is the opposite of its aim.

options.t: It rewards repeat business and encourages loyalty
options.why: A free item after ten purchases rewards repeat business and builds loyalty. Customers have a reason to keep returning, and the business benefits from steady sales.

options.t: It reduces the quality of service given to customers
options.why: A reward program does not lower service quality. It adds value for the customer and works best with good service.

q: What does it mean to show a customer service mindset?

options.t: Avoiding customers who ask many questions of staff
options.why: Avoiding customers who ask many questions is the opposite of a service mindset. Questions show what the customer needs.

options.t: Putting customers' needs at the center of your actions
options.why: A customer service mindset means putting customers' needs at the center of your actions. It makes staff look for ways to help rather than just follow routine.

options.t: Focusing only on closing as many sales as possible
options.why: Focusing only on closing sales treats customers as targets. A service mindset values helping them, even when no sale follows.

options.t: Following only the rules that benefit the company
options.why: Following only rules that benefit the company ignores the customer. A service mindset balances policy with the customer's needs.

q: A customer asks for a refund outside the return window. What is the best response?

options.t: Argue that the customer should have read the policy
options.why: Arguing that the customer should have read the policy is confrontational. It may be true, but it loses goodwill and rarely settles things.

options.t: Refuse and walk away without explaining why to them
options.why: Refusing and walking away without explanation is rude and leaves the customer confused. They deserve to know why.

options.t: Explain the policy kindly and offer any allowed options
options.why: Explaining the policy kindly and offering any allowed options respects the customer and the rules. It can offer store credit or an exchange to keep goodwill.

options.t: Break the policy without telling a manager first
options.why: Breaking policy without telling a manager is unfair to others and can cause problems. Exceptions should be approved by someone with authority.

q: How can employees build rapport with customers?

options.t: Greet them warmly and show genuine interest in their needs
options.why: Greeting customers warmly and showing genuine interest in their needs builds rapport. Customers feel valued and are more likely to trust and return.

options.t: Talk only about the company's profits and its growth plans
options.why: Talking about company profits is about the business, not the customer. It does nothing to build a connection.

options.t: Use technical terms that the customer cannot easily follow
options.why: Using technical terms the customer cannot follow creates distance. Plain language makes people feel respected and understood.

options.t: Avoid eye contact with them in order to seem professional
options.why: Avoiding eye contact comes across as cold or uninterested. Eye contact shows attention and helps build rapport.

q: A company's brand promise is 'fast and friendly service.' Which employee behavior best supports it?

options.t: Taking long breaks during the busy periods of the day
options.why: Taking long breaks during busy periods leaves customers waiting. It breaks the promise of fast service.

options.t: Ignoring customers until they ask three or more times
options.why: Ignoring customers until they ask several times is neither fast nor friendly. It contradicts the brand promise.

options.t: Speaking sharply to customers who ask for help twice
options.why: Speaking sharply to customers is unfriendly. It breaks the promise of friendly service.

options.t: Helping each customer quickly while staying courteous
options.why: Helping each customer quickly while staying courteous delivers both parts of the promise, fast and friendly. It makes the brand promise real for customers.

q: What is a customer touch point?

options.t: A tax that a customer pays on top of the price
options.why: A tax a customer pays is a cost. A touch point is any contact with the business.

options.t: A coupon given only to employees of the firm
options.why: A coupon for employees is an internal perk. A touch point is about customers.

options.t: A product that is out of stock in the store
options.why: An out-of-stock product is a supply problem. A touch point is an interaction.

options.t: Any interaction a customer has with a business
options.why: A customer touch point is any interaction a customer has with a business. Examples are the website, store visits, calls and ads, and each shapes the customer's impression.

q: A customer says the website was confusing but the store staff were helpful. What does this show?

options.t: Employees should avoid helping customers
options.why: Employees helping customers is a good thing, as the store staff did. The feedback suggests no change to that.

options.t: Experience can vary across touch points
options.why: A confusing website but helpful staff shows the experience can vary across touch points. A business should work to make each one equally good.

options.t: Stores should close their doors for good
options.why: Closing stores is an extreme reaction. The feedback praised the staff, so the stores are working well.

options.t: Online service is not important to customers
options.why: Online service matters to customers. The confusing website shows it needs improvement, not that it is unimportant.

q: Why is following up with a customer after a sale useful?

options.t: It shows care and can reveal problems or new needs
options.why: Following up shows care and can reveal problems or new needs. It keeps the relationship going and can lead to repeat sales.

options.t: It lets the business avoid honoring warranties
options.why: Following up does not help avoid warranties. Honoring them is part of good service.

options.t: It reduces the chance the customer returns again
options.why: Following up makes it more likely the customer will return. It shows the business cares after the sale.

options.t: It replaces the need for good products or service
options.why: Following up does not replace good products or service. It supports them.

q: Which technology helps a business keep track of customer purchase history and preferences?

options.t: A printer used for office documents
options.why: A printer is for printing documents. It cannot track purchase history or preferences.

options.t: A calculator used in the back office
options.why: A calculator does arithmetic. It does not store customer information.

options.t: A customer database or CRM system
options.why: A customer database or CRM system stores purchase history and preferences. Staff can use it to personalize service and marketing.

options.t: A security camera in the parking lot
options.why: A security camera records video. It does not track purchases.

q: A new coffee shop sells out of lattes every morning at $4. What will likely happen to the price if demand stays strong?

options.t: Price will not matter to buyers
options.why: Price matters to buyers when goods run short. A shortage at $4 means buyers want more than is supplied.

options.t: Price will tend to fall to zero
options.why: Price does not fall to zero when lattes sell out. Strong demand and limited supply push the price up.

options.t: Price will stay fixed by law
options.why: Prices in a market are not fixed by law here. The shop can raise the price when demand is strong.

options.t: The price will tend to rise
options.why: When lattes sell out each morning, demand exceeds supply at $4. The shop can raise the price until supply and demand match.

q: What does the term 'opportunity cost' mean?

options.t: The profit earned from a sale of goods to a customer
options.why: Profit from a sale is revenue minus costs. Opportunity cost is about alternatives given up.

options.t: The value of the next best alternative you give up
options.why: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative you give up. Every choice has one because resources are limited.

options.t: The tax added to a purchase made at a store or shop
options.why: A tax on a purchase is a tax. Opportunity cost is not a payment.

options.t: The price you pay for a product at checkout in the store
options.why: The price you pay at checkout is a money cost. Opportunity cost includes what else you could have done.

q: Gas prices rise sharply, and fewer people take long road trips. Which economic principle does this show?

options.t: Comparative advantage
options.why: Comparative advantage explains trade between countries. It does not explain fewer road trips when gas rises.

options.t: The law of supply
options.why: The law of supply says suppliers offer more at higher prices. The example is about buyers cutting back.

options.t: The law of demand
options.why: The law of demand says that when price rises, quantity demanded falls. Fewer people take long trips when gas gets expensive.

options.t: Diminishing returns
options.why: Diminishing returns concerns production. The example describes consumer behavior.

q: Which is an example of a service rather than a good?

options.t: A haircut
options.why: A haircut is a service, an activity performed for someone. You cannot hold or store it.

options.t: Some shoes
options.why: Shoes are a physical good. You can touch and own them.

options.t: A bicycle
options.why: A bicycle is a physical good. It is made and sold as a product.

options.t: Bottled water
options.why: Bottled water is a physical good. A service is an activity, not an item.

q: A country's unemployment rate rises from 4% to 9%. What is the most likely effect on consumer spending?

options.t: It will not change at all
options.why: Spending usually changes when many people lose jobs. A rise from 4% to 9% unemployment cuts incomes.

options.t: It will likely rise
options.why: Spending would not rise when more people are out of work. They have less income to spend.

options.t: It will become illegal
options.why: Spending does not become illegal. It simply falls when fewer people are earning.

options.t: It will probably fall
options.why: When unemployment rises, fewer people earn wages. Consumer spending probably falls because incomes drop and people feel less secure.

q: What is competition in a market?

options.t: A government rule that sets all prices of goods
options.why: A government rule that sets prices is price control. Competition is rivalry among businesses.

options.t: An agreement among businesses to share profits each year
options.why: Agreeing to share profits is collusion. It reduces real competition and is often illegal.

options.t: Rivalry among businesses that sell similar products
options.why: Competition is rivalry among businesses that sell similar products. It pushes firms to improve quality and keep prices fair.

options.t: A single business with no rivals in its whole market
options.why: A single business with no rivals is a monopoly. Competition needs several firms.

q: Why might a business specialize in one product instead of making many?

options.t: It can become more efficient and productive
options.why: Specializing lets a business become more efficient and productive. Focusing on one product builds skill and lowers costs.

options.t: It will no longer need any customers at all
options.why: A business always needs customers. Specializing does not remove that.

options.t: It avoids all competition from other firms
options.why: Specializing does not avoid competition. Other firms may sell the same product.

options.t: It must always produce less than other firms
options.why: Specializing does not force less output. It usually raises output per worker.

q: The central bank raises interest rates. What is a likely effect on business borrowing?

options.t: Borrowing becomes free for all small businesses
options.why: Higher rates do not make borrowing free. They raise the cost of loans.

options.t: Borrowing becomes more expensive and may decline
