options.why: The cost of materials used to make a product is a production cost, which affects supply, not the buyers' willingness to purchase that defines demand.

options.t: The quantity sellers make and offer for sale at various prices
options.why: The quantity sellers offer at various prices describes supply rather than demand, the other side of the market that comes from producers.

options.t: The quantity buyers are willing and able to buy at various prices
options.why: Demand is the quantity of a good that buyers are both willing and able to buy at various prices, and it generally rises as the price falls.

options.t: The price set by the government for each good that is sold in a market
options.why: A government-set price is a price control, such as a ceiling or floor, which is a policy and not what economists define as demand.

q: A new technology makes producing smartphones cheaper. What is the likely effect on the market?

options.t: Prices become fixed by the state for good
options.why: A cheaper production technology does not make the state fix prices; markets still set prices through supply and demand unless the government intervenes separately.

options.t: Supply increases and prices tend to fall
options.why: Cheaper production lowers costs, so firms can supply more at each price, shifting supply right and pushing the market price down.

options.t: Demand disappears from the whole market
options.why: Cheaper production does not make demand disappear; consumers still want smartphones, and lower prices may even increase the quantity they buy.

options.t: Supply decreases and prices rise a lot
options.why: Lower production costs make firms willing to supply more, not less, so supply increases and prices fall rather than rise.

q: What is a budget deficit?

options.t: Imports exceed exports in the whole economy
options.why: Imports exceeding exports is a trade deficit, which concerns international trade and not the government's own budget.

options.t: Government revenue is greater than spending
options.why: Revenue greater than spending is a budget surplus, the opposite of a deficit, in which the government takes in more than it spends.

options.t: Prices rise quickly across the economy
options.why: Prices rising quickly across the economy is inflation, which is a general price increase and not a government budget measure.

options.t: Government spending is greater than revenue
options.why: A budget deficit occurs when government spending is greater than revenue in a period, so it must borrow to cover the gap, adding to the national debt.

q: What is the role of the Federal Reserve?

options.t: Manage the money supply and interest rates
options.why: The Federal Reserve is the US central bank, and it manages the money supply and interest rates to promote stable prices, maximum employment and a stable financial system.

options.t: Run local businesses for their owners
options.why: The Fed does not run local businesses; private owners operate those, while the central bank oversees monetary policy and supervises banks.

options.t: Set the prices each firm charges for goods
options.why: Individual firms set their own prices based on costs and competition, and the Federal Reserve does not control what each firm charges.

options.t: Collect income taxes from every worker
options.why: The Internal Revenue Service collects income taxes from workers, while the Federal Reserve focuses on monetary policy and banking.

q: What is it called when you put yourself in another person's position to understand them?

options.t: Avoidance
options.why: Avoidance means staying away from a person or problem, so it is the opposite of putting yourself in another person's position to understand them.

options.t: Rivalry
options.why: Rivalry means competing against others, which is the opposite of trying to understand how another person feels.

options.t: Delegation
options.why: Delegation means assigning tasks to others, and it does not describe understanding another person's feelings or point of view.

options.t: Empathy
options.why: Empathy is the ability to see a situation from another person's position and understand their feelings, which builds trust and improves teamwork and communication.

q: A team member is frequently late with work. Which response best combines respect and accountability?

options.t: Do the work without telling anyone to keep the schedule
options.why: Quietly doing the late person's work hides the problem, lets the lateness continue, and does not hold them accountable or help them improve.

options.t: Publicly criticize the person in front of the whole team today
options.why: Publicly criticizing someone in front of the team humiliates them and damages trust, so it shows no respect even though it points out the problem.

options.t: Discuss the issue, ask about obstacles and set clear deadlines
options.why: Discussing the issue privately, asking about obstacles and setting clear deadlines respects the person while holding them accountable, which gives the best chance of improvement.

options.t: Ignore it and hope that the person improves on their own
options.why: Ignoring the problem and hoping it fixes itself lets the lateness continue and shows no accountability, and the team's work suffers.

q: Why is listening to different viewpoints valuable?

options.t: It wastes time, as the team knows the answer
options.why: Listening to other views does not waste time; even when the team feels sure, other viewpoints can reveal mistakes or better options.

options.t: It can lead to better ideas and decisions
options.why: Listening to different viewpoints brings in new information and options, which can lead to better ideas and more informed decisions, and it builds team trust.

options.t: It prevents making decisions in the team
options.why: Listening does not prevent decisions; it informs them, and teams can still decide after hearing the range of views.

options.t: It proves others are wrong every time
options.why: Hearing others out does not prove them wrong every time; the purpose is to learn and consider, not to win an argument.

q: What is an angel investor?

options.t: A bank that lends only to firms with ten years in business now
options.why: A bank that lends only to firms with ten years in business is a traditional lender, not an angel investor, who backs young start-ups.

options.t: A person who provides money to a start-up in exchange for ownership
options.why: An angel investor is a wealthy person who funds a start-up early, often alongside mentoring, in exchange for ownership or equity in the company.

options.t: A government agency that taxes new firms and checks their books
options.why: A government agency that taxes new firms collects revenue, while an angel investor is a private individual who provides capital.

options.t: A customer who buys products from a start-up and then tells friends
options.why: A customer who buys products is a source of revenue, not an investor, since an angel investor provides capital in exchange for ownership.

q: A small business owner must choose between buying a $5,000 machine or hiring a worker for $5,000 a year. What should she compare first?

options.t: The worker's favorite food at lunch time
options.why: A worker's favorite lunch has no bearing on whether the machine or the hire is the better business decision.

options.t: Whether competitors have the same machine only
options.why: Whether competitors have the same machine is a minor point; she should compare cost and output of each option before looking elsewhere.

options.t: Expected output, long-term costs and demand
options.why: She should compare expected output, long-term costs and demand to see which option gives the best return and fits what customers will buy.

options.t: The machine's color only, not how it works
options.why: The machine's color is unimportant; its capacity, reliability and cost determine whether it is a good investment compared with hiring a worker.

q: What is a business incubator?

options.t: An organization that helps new businesses grow with space and advice
options.why: A business incubator is an organization that helps new businesses grow by providing space, advice, networking and sometimes funding during the early stage.

options.t: A competitor's warehouse used to store goods for sale in shops
options.why: A competitor's warehouse stores goods for a rival firm and gives no support to new businesses, which is what an incubator does.

options.t: A machine that warms eggs only, so that they hatch into chicks on a farm
options.why: An egg incubator warms eggs so they hatch, but in business the term refers to a program supporting start-ups, so this answer is a literal meaning.

options.t: A tax office that collects money from new businesses and firms
options.why: A tax office collects money from businesses for the government, while an incubator helps start-ups succeed by offering resources and guidance.

q: What is a check register used for?

options.t: Hiring employees for the firm's main shop
options.why: Hiring employees is an HR function, while a check register is a record of transactions in a checking account.

options.t: Selling products to customers in the store
options.why: Selling products is a sales function, and a check register is a tool used for personal or business bookkeeping.

options.t: Printing checks only, with no record of deposits
options.why: A check register records deposits as well as checks, so it is not a tool only for printing checks without recording deposits.

options.t: Recording deposits, withdrawals and balances
options.why: A check register records deposits, withdrawals and running balances in a checking account, which helps catch errors, avoid overdrafts and reconcile with bank statements.

q: A person has $4,000 in credit card debt at 24% APR. Which action saves the most interest?

options.t: Pay more than the minimum each month
options.why: Paying more than the minimum reduces the principal faster, so less interest accrues each month at 24% APR, which saves the most interest and clears the debt sooner.

options.t: Charge more to earn more reward points
options.why: Charging more adds to the balance at 24% APR, so interest grows, and reward points are worth far less than the interest cost.

options.t: Skip payments for a few months now
options.why: Skipping payments brings late fees, penalty rates and a damaged credit score, while interest keeps accruing on the full balance.

options.t: Pay the minimum only every month
options.why: Paying only the minimum mostly covers interest, so the $4,000 balance falls slowly and the total interest paid stays high.

q: What is a tax deduction?

options.t: A refund of sales tax to the buyers
options.why: A refund of sales tax is a return of tax paid on purchases, while a deduction reduces income before income tax is calculated.

options.t: A payment to employees each month
options.why: A payment to employees each month is wages or salary, which is an expense for the employer and not a tax concept.

options.t: An amount that reduces taxable income
options.why: A tax deduction is an amount that reduces taxable income, so the tax owed is lower; for example, $1,000 deducted at a 22% rate saves $220.

options.t: A penalty for late filing of a tax return
options.why: A penalty for late filing is a fine added to taxes owed, which is the opposite of a deduction that reduces them.

q: What is retirement planning?

options.t: Planning a vacation for the whole family soon
options.why: Planning a family vacation is leisure planning, which concerns a short-term trip and does not focus on income after a person stops working.

options.t: Saving and investing to support life after work
options.why: Retirement planning means saving and investing during your working years so you have enough income to live on after you stop working.

options.t: Planning holiday sales at the store for December
options.why: Planning holiday sales is a retail business task for a store, not a personal financial plan for life after work.

options.t: Planning a business launch with the budget and staff
options.why: Planning a business launch involves budgets and staffing for a company and is a different process from planning personal finances for retirement.

q: What is a probation review?

options.t: A review of the company's taxes by the revenue agency
options.why: A review of taxes by the revenue agency is a tax audit, which examines a company's tax returns rather than a new employee's work.

options.t: A customer survey on how happy shoppers are today
options.why: A customer survey measures shopper satisfaction, while a probation review evaluates a new hire's performance early in employment.

options.t: A product test run by the design team before launch
options.why: A product test run by the design team checks goods before launch, but a probation review checks an employee.

options.t: An early evaluation of a new employee's performance
options.why: A probation review is an early evaluation of a new employee's performance, usually after 90 days, to decide whether to keep them on permanently.

q: A company wants to improve diversity. Which action helps most?

options.t: Hire only from one school near the company's main office
options.why: Hiring only from one school near the office limits the applicant pool and excludes many qualified people, so it reduces diversity.

options.t: Recruit from diverse communities and use fair hiring practices
options.why: Recruiting from diverse communities and using fair hiring practices widens the applicant pool and removes bias, which improves diversity and gives everyone an equal chance.

options.t: Avoid posting jobs publicly and hire only through managers
options.why: Avoiding public job postings and hiring only through managers keeps the pool narrow and relies on personal networks, which tends to repeat the existing makeup.

options.t: Ignore diversity goals and hire whoever applies first each time
options.why: Ignoring diversity goals and hiring the first applicant does nothing to broaden the workforce and may reinforce existing patterns.

q: Why do employers offer flexible schedules?

options.t: To avoid hiring new people for the firm at all times
options.why: Flexible schedules do not replace hiring; employers still need enough staff, so avoiding new hires is not the reason they offer flexibility.

options.t: To raise product prices for weekend shoppers
options.why: Product pricing for weekend shoppers is a marketing choice that has no connection to work-hour flexibility for employees.

options.t: To attract and keep employees with different needs
options.why: Flexible schedules help attract and keep employees who have different needs, such as family care or school, which raises satisfaction and cuts turnover costs.

options.t: To reduce all training given to new and old staff
options.why: Flexible schedules are about when and where people work, and they do not reduce training for new or experienced staff.

q: A company wants to share a large file with a customer securely. Which method is best?

options.t: Email it to everyone on the open list
options.why: Emailing to everyone on an open list exposes the file to many unintended readers, which is not secure for sensitive customer data.

options.t: Post it on a public site for anyone
options.why: Posting the file on a public site lets anyone download it, which defeats the purpose of sharing securely with one customer.

options.t: Leave it on a USB in a public place
options.why: Leaving a USB drive in a public place risks theft or loss and exposes the data to anyone who picks it up.

options.t: Use an encrypted file-sharing service
options.why: An encrypted file-sharing service scrambles the data and limits access to the intended customer, so it protects a large file in transit and storage.

q: What is the main benefit of using templates for business documents?

options.t: Consistency and time savings
options.why: Templates provide a standard layout and wording, which keeps documents consistent and saves time because staff do not start from scratch each time.

options.t: More errors in each document
options.why: Templates reduce errors because standard formats and wording are reused, so they do not cause more mistakes in each document.

options.t: Longer documents, extra pages
options.why: Templates are meant to be efficient, and do not aim to lengthen documents or add extra pages.

options.t: Less clarity in each document
options.why: Templates improve clarity through a standard structure, and they do not reduce clarity in each document.

q: What does a marketing budget cover?

options.t: Employee vacations, travel and staff benefits
options.why: Employee vacations, travel and benefits are HR or operating costs, not part of a marketing budget, which pays for promotion.

options.t: Tax payments owed to the state each year
options.why: Tax payments are a legal obligation and belong to finance or accounting, not to the marketing budget.

options.t: Rent only, and nothing else for marketing
options.why: Rent is an overhead expense, and a marketing budget covers many promotion costs beyond rent, so this answer is too narrow.

options.t: Money planned for advertising and promotion
options.why: A marketing budget is money planned for advertising and promotion, such as ads, events and samples, so spending can be tracked against sales goals.

q: A brand sees a drop in repeat purchases after changing its packaging. What is the best next step?

options.t: Stop all marketing for the product line
options.why: Stopping all marketing would reduce awareness and sales further, and it would not find out why repeat purchases dropped after the change.

options.t: Gather customer feedback about the change
options.why: Gathering customer feedback about the change shows what customers disliked, so the brand can decide whether to fix or reverse the packaging using real data.

options.t: Assume customers are wrong about the change
options.why: Assuming customers are wrong ignores the evidence of falling repeat purchases and risks losing more loyal buyers.

options.t: Keep changing the package until sales go up
options.why: Changing the package repeatedly without information is guesswork that confuses customers and costs money, and it does not find the real cause.

q: What is customer segmentation by geography?

options.t: Dividing customers by where they live
options.why: Geographic segmentation divides customers by where they live, such as region, city or climate, so marketing can match local needs and preferences.

options.t: Dividing customers by birthday month
options.why: Dividing customers by birthday month is not geographic; it is a basis for timing promotions and says nothing about location.

options.t: Dividing customers by favorite color
options.why: Favorite color is a personal preference, which is not a geographic basis for dividing customers.

options.t: Dividing customers by their shoe size
options.why: Shoe size is a physical attribute, so grouping customers by it is not geographic segmentation, which depends on location.

q: What is the purpose of preventive maintenance?

options.t: To ignore equipment until it fails or breaks down
options.why: Ignoring equipment until it fails is reactive maintenance, the opposite of preventive maintenance, which acts before problems occur.

options.t: To reduce safety training for the staff in the plant
options.why: Preventive maintenance has no connection to safety training, and cutting training would raise risk instead of preventing breakdowns.

options.t: To fix equipment problems before they cause breakdowns
options.why: Preventive maintenance involves regular inspection and servicing that fix equipment problems before they cause breakdowns, which reduces downtime and costly emergency repairs.

options.t: To replace working equipment every day in the plant
options.why: Replacing working equipment every day would waste money; preventive maintenance services equipment on a schedule to extend its life.

q: A manufacturer reduces batch size to avoid overstock. What is a possible downside?

options.t: More frequent setups and higher per-unit cost
options.why: Smaller batches mean more frequent machine setups, which add time and cost, so the per-unit cost can rise even though overstock risk falls.

options.t: Zero risk of shortages in the supply chain
options.why: Smaller batches do not remove the risk of shortages, since any production plan can fall short of demand; claiming zero risk is wrong.

options.t: Higher inventory levels held in the warehouse
options.why: Smaller batches lower inventory levels, so higher stock in the warehouse would be a result of larger batches, not smaller ones.

options.t: Unlimited storage costs as batches get larger
options.why: Storage costs fall when batches are smaller; costs rise with larger batches, and they are never unlimited in any case.

q: What does a safety audit do?

options.t: Writes ads for the products of the firm online
options.why: Writing ads is a marketing task, while a safety audit inspects the workplace for hazards and rule compliance.

options.t: Checks that workplace safety rules are followed
options.why: A safety audit checks that workplace safety rules are followed, finds hazards, and recommends fixes, which protects workers and helps avoid injuries, fines and lawsuits.

options.t: Counts the company's profits and equipment spending
options.why: Counting profits and equipment spending is an accounting task, whereas a safety audit examines safety practices and conditions.

options.t: Hires workers for the firm's open posts and jobs
options.why: Hiring workers is an HR function, and a safety audit evaluates safety conditions rather than filling open positions.

q: Why is first impression important in an interview?

options.t: It replaces your résumé in the application
options.why: A first impression does not replace a resume; the application still needs one to show your experience and qualifications.

options.t: It decides your salary alone, nothing else
options.why: A first impression does not decide salary alone, since pay depends on skills, experience, the job and negotiation.

options.t: It influences how the interviewer views you
options.why: A first impression influences how the interviewer views you, shaping early judgments about professionalism and confidence that can color the rest of the interview.

options.t: It matters only after you are hired at all
options.why: A first impression matters during the hiring process, since interviewers form opinions in the first minutes, so it matters before you are hired.

q: A coworker asks you to cover for them by lying to the manager. What should you do?

options.t: Agree to lie for your coworker today
options.why: Agreeing to lie is dishonest and could get you disciplined or fired along with your coworker, and it harms trust at work.

options.t: Quit the job right away in a rage
options.why: Quitting in a rage is an extreme overreaction that hurts your career and does not solve the problem, and a calm refusal is enough.

options.t: Lie louder and more boldly than they do
options.why: Lying more boldly makes the dishonesty worse and spreads the problem, which damages your own reputation and credibility.

options.t: Decline politely and encourage honesty
options.why: Declining politely and encouraging honesty protects your integrity and your relationship with the coworker, and it avoids being part of a deception.

q: What is outsourcing a strategic benefit of?

options.t: Focusing on core activities while others handle support tasks
options.why: Outsourcing lets a firm focus on its core activities while outside specialists handle support tasks, which can cut costs and improve efficiency.

options.t: Doing everything internally with all of the firm's own staff
options.why: Doing everything internally is the opposite of outsourcing, which hands some tasks to outside providers.

options.t: Eliminating customers who need much attention from the staff
options.why: Outsourcing hands over tasks such as payroll or IT, and it is not a way to eliminate demanding customers.

options.t: Reducing all quality to lower costs in every part of the work
options.why: Outsourcing aims to improve efficiency or cost with quality in mind, not to lower quality everywhere, which would harm the business.

q: A firm sees several competitors lower prices. Which response is most strategic?

options.t: Lower quality to save cost without warning, to match rival prices now
options.why: Secretly lowering quality to match prices risks losing customer trust and damaging the brand once buyers notice, so it is not strategic.

options.t: Ignore the market and the moves that rivals make in it, and wait it out
options.why: Ignoring the market and waiting it out gives up customers to rivals and shows no analysis, so it is not a strategic response.

options.t: Match all price cuts at once without any analysis of costs or value
options.why: Matching every price cut without analyzing costs and value can erode profit margins, and it is a reaction and not a strategy.

options.t: Analyze costs and value, then decide whether to match, differentiate or hold
options.why: Analyzing costs and value and then deciding whether to match, differentiate or hold lets the firm protect margins and respond with a plan that suits its position.

q: What is vertical integration?

options.t: A company closing one department to save a lot of money
options.why: Closing one department to save money is cost cutting, whereas vertical integration is control of several stages of the supply chain.

options.t: A company controlling several stages of its supply chain
options.why: Vertical integration means a company controls several stages of its supply chain, such as producing materials, manufacturing and distribution, which can cut costs and secure supply.

options.t: A company selling only online and never in person to anyone
options.why: Selling only online is a sales channel choice and has nothing to do with owning stages of the supply chain.

options.t: A company hiring a consultant to advise on its marketing plan
options.why: Hiring a consultant to advise on marketing is outside help and does not involve owning more stages of the supply chain.

q: What is a deposition?

options.t: A tax payment made by a firm to the state
options.why: A tax payment to the state is a payment to the government, and it has nothing to do with testimony in a legal case.

options.t: A sales talk made to a prospective customer
options.why: A sales talk to a prospective customer is a sales pitch, while a deposition is a legal procedure in which a witness gives testimony under oath.

options.t: Sworn testimony taken outside the courtroom
options.why: A deposition is sworn testimony taken outside the courtroom, usually in a lawyer's office, and recorded for later use in a lawsuit.

options.t: A trade show where firms display their products
options.why: A trade show displays products to buyers and is a marketing event, so it is not a legal proceeding.

q: What is insurance fraud?

options.t: Filing an accurate claim with an insurer
options.why: Filing an accurate claim is the proper use of insurance, so it is honest and not fraud.

options.t: Shopping for a lower premium among insurers
options.why: Shopping for a lower premium among insurers is smart comparison buying and entirely legal, so it is not fraud.

options.t: Paying an insurance premium on time each month
options.why: Paying a premium on time is what the insured is supposed to do, so it is not fraud.

options.t: Making false claims to get insurance money
options.why: Insurance fraud means making false claims, such as exaggerating a loss or faking an accident, to collect money, which is a crime that raises costs for everyone.

q: What is a press release?

options.t: A staff schedule posted in the break room each week
options.why: A staff schedule posted in the break room is an internal notice for employees, while a press release is sent outside to news outlets.

options.t: An announcement sent to the media about company news
options.why: A press release is an announcement sent to the media about company news, such as a product launch, so reporters can share the story with the public.

options.t: A private diary kept by one of the firm's owners
options.why: A private diary is personal and not meant for the public, whereas a press release is written for the media.

options.t: A product receipt given to a customer after a sale
options.why: A product receipt is proof of purchase given to a customer, unlike a press release, which announces news to the media.

q: What is the difference between fixed and variable costs?

options.t: Fixed costs change with output and variable costs stay put
options.why: This reverses the definitions: fixed costs stay the same regardless of output, and variable costs change as output changes.

options.t: Neither affects profit, since both are really the same thing
options.why: Both fixed and variable costs affect profit, and they are different kinds of costs, so claiming that they are the same is wrong.

options.t: Fixed costs stay the same while variable costs change with output
options.why: Fixed costs, such as rent, stay the same regardless of output, while variable costs, such as materials, rise and fall with the number of units produced.

options.t: Both always change in the same way with every unit of output
options.why: Variable costs change with output but fixed costs do not, so both do not change in the same way for every unit.

q: What is a mixed economy?

options.t: An economy with both private business and government involvement
options.why: A mixed economy combines private business with government involvement, as in the United States, where markets operate but government regulates and provides some services.

options.t: An economy with no money and no trade of any kind between people
options.why: An economy with no money or trade would be extremely primitive, and a mixed economy involves active markets and government.

options.t: An economy without markets where people trade goods or services
options.why: An economy without markets describes a command economy, while a mixed economy includes both markets and government direction.

options.t: An economy run only by tradition, where customs decide what is made
options.why: An economy run by custom and tradition is a traditional economy, and not a mixture of private enterprise and government.

q: What is an example of professional behavior during a disagreement?

options.t: Staying respectful and focusing on the issue
options.why: Staying respectful and focusing on the issue keeps the discussion productive, protects relationships and helps both sides reach a solution, which marks professional behavior.

options.t: Raising your voice at the other person loudly
options.why: Raising your voice escalates conflict and shows a lack of self-control, which is unprofessional and hurts working relationships.

options.t: Name-calling and insults at the other person
options.why: Name-calling and insults attack the person and not the problem, which damages trust and is unprofessional in any workplace.

options.t: Walking away mid-sentence to show disinterest
options.why: Walking away mid-sentence is dismissive and shows disrespect, which blocks the discussion and leaves the disagreement unresolved.

q: What is a franchise fee?

options.t: A salary for staff who work in the franchise's outlets
options.why: Salaries for franchise staff are wages paid by the franchisee, whereas a franchise fee is paid to the franchisor.

options.t: A refund to customers who return goods to a store
options.why: A refund to customers is a return of money for goods and has nothing to do with the franchise relationship.

options.t: A payment to the franchisor to use its brand and system
options.why: A franchise fee is a payment from the franchisee to the franchisor for the right to use its brand, products and operating system.

options.t: A tax on products that a franchise sells to the public
options.why: A tax on products is a government charge, while a franchise fee is a payment made by the franchisee to the franchisor.

q: What is a credit report?

options.t: A bank advertisement for savings and loan products
options.why: A bank advertisement promotes products and does not record a person's borrowing history, which is what a credit report does.

options.t: A tax return filed by a person each year with the state
options.why: A tax return reports income to the government and is a different document from a credit report, which tracks borrowing.

options.t: A list of grocery purchases kept in a household notebook
options.why: A list of grocery purchases is a household record that is unrelated to credit, loans or lenders.

options.t: A record of a person's borrowing and repayment history
options.why: A credit report records a person's borrowing and repayment history, including loans, cards and late payments, and lenders use it to judge whether to lend.

q: What is an exit interview?

options.t: A job interview for a new hire who just applied
options.why: A job interview for a new hire happens at the start of employment, whereas an exit interview takes place when someone leaves.

options.t: A conversation with an employee who is leaving
options.why: An exit interview is a conversation with an employee who is leaving, to learn why they are going and how the company could improve.

options.t: A customer survey on how the shop is doing
options.why: A customer survey asks shoppers about the business, but an exit interview is held with a departing employee.

options.t: A performance bonus paid to a worker each year
options.why: A performance bonus is extra pay for results, which differs from an exit interview, a conversation with a departing worker.

q: What is a software update used for?

options.t: Slowing the computer down on purpose for staff
options.why: A software update is meant to improve performance, so slowing the computer on purpose is the opposite of its purpose.

options.t: Deleting all files from the computer for good
options.why: Updates do not delete all files; they change program code, and deleting files would harm users and the business.

options.t: Fixing issues and improving security or features
options.why: A software update fixes bugs, patches security holes and adds features, which keeps systems stable and protects them from newly discovered threats.

options.t: Removing user accounts that are no longer in use
options.why: Removing user accounts is done by an administrator, while a software update changes the program itself.

q: What is an endorsement?

options.t: A printed voucher that lowers the price when a customer buys the item
options.why: A printed voucher that lowers the price is a coupon, a sales promotion, and not an endorsement, which is a statement of support.

options.t: A public statement of support for a product by a person or group
options.why: An endorsement is a public statement of support for a product by a person or group, such as a celebrity or expert, and it builds trust in the brand.

options.t: A government fee that is added to the price of a product at checkout
options.why: A government fee added to a price at checkout is a sales tax and not a marketing endorsement.

options.t: A written promise to repair or replace a product that breaks early
options.why: A written promise to repair or replace a broken product is a warranty, a separate concept from an endorsement.

q: What is batch production?

options.t: Buying finished goods from other firms
options.why: Buying finished goods from other firms is purchasing for resale, and batch production means making goods in the firm's own plant.

options.t: Making one custom item at a time to order
options.why: Making one custom item at a time to order is job production, whereas batch production makes a group of identical items together.

options.t: Making goods nonstop on an assembly line
options.why: Making goods nonstop on an assembly line is continuous or mass production, which differs from producing in separate batches.

options.t: Making a set number of items at one time
options.why: Batch production makes a set number of identical items at one time, then switches to another product or batch, which suits moderate-demand goods like bakery products.

q: What does it mean to demonstrate initiative?

options.t: Take action without waiting to be told
options.why: Taking action without waiting to be told is what initiative means, and it shows motivation and leadership that employers value.

options.t: Wait for someone else to start the task
options.why: Waiting for someone else to start the task is the opposite of initiative, which means acting first.

options.t: Wait until the last minute and then hurry
options.why: Waiting until the last minute shows poor planning and not initiative, which requires acting early and on your own.

options.t: Avoid new tasks given to you at work
options.why: Avoiding new tasks shows a lack of initiative, which means taking on work and responsibility without being asked.

q: What is the purpose of a return policy?

options.t: To set clear rules for returns and refunds
options.why: A return policy sets clear rules on time limits, condition and refund type, which protects both the store and the customer and builds trust in the business.

options.t: To discourage all returns so sales stay high
options.why: A return policy is meant to be fair and clear, not to block all returns; discouraging every return would drive customers away and hurt long-term sales.

options.t: To raise prices on all returned goods
options.why: Return policies do not set prices; raising prices on returned goods is not their function, and prices are decided separately through pricing strategy.

options.t: To hide product defects from the buyers
options.why: A return policy does not exist to conceal defects; hiding problems is deceptive and illegal, while a policy actually gives buyers a remedy for faulty goods.

q: What is purchasing power?

options.t: The profit of a business each year
options.why: Profit is what a business earns after costs; it measures business performance and has nothing to do with how much goods a consumer's money can buy.

options.t: The number of stores in a country each year
options.why: The number of stores in a country describes market size or retail presence, not the value of money, so it is unrelated to purchasing power.

options.t: The amount of goods that money can buy
options.why: Purchasing power is the quantity of goods and services a unit of money can buy; it falls when inflation raises prices and rises when prices drop.

options.t: The tax on income paid by a worker
options.why: Income tax is a government charge on earnings; it can reduce take-home pay, but it is not the definition of purchasing power.

q: What is the purpose of a business license renewal?

options.t: To hire workers for the business and all of its shops
options.why: Renewing a license has nothing to do with hiring; hiring workers is a human resources activity and is not what a license renewal accomplishes.

options.t: To confirm the business still meets legal requirements
options.why: License renewal lets the government confirm the business still meets legal requirements such as safety, tax and zoning rules, so it may keep operating lawfully.

options.t: To raise prices on the goods that the business sells
options.why: License renewal is a regulatory step and has no effect on pricing; prices are set by the business based on costs, demand and competition.

options.t: To advertise the business to the public in the local news
options.why: Advertising is a marketing activity done through media; a license renewal is a legal filing and does not promote the business to the public.

q: What is the purpose of a nondisclosure clause in an employment contract?

options.t: To limit an employee's future pay raises
options.why: Pay raises are handled by compensation policy and performance reviews; a nondisclosure clause deals with confidentiality and does not limit an employee's future pay.

options.t: To prevent employees from taking vacations
options.why: Vacation time is set by company leave policy and labor agreements; a nondisclosure clause concerns secrecy and has no power to prevent taking vacation.

options.t: To give workers ownership of the company
options.why: Ownership is gained through stock or equity plans, not a nondisclosure clause, which only restricts sharing information and gives employees no ownership stake.

options.t: To keep company secrets from being shared
options.why: A nondisclosure clause binds employees to protect trade secrets, client lists and other confidential information, which guards the firm's competitive advantage even after they leave.

q: A franchisee changes the franchisor's recipe without approval. What contract issue may result?

options.t: A zoning approval by the city
options.why: A zoning approval is a city land-use permission; it is not a contract problem and has nothing to do with changing a recipe without approval.

options.t: A trademark expiry ending its rights
options.why: A trademark expiring is an intellectual property matter caused by failing to renew; altering a recipe does not by itself end the franchisor's trademark rights.

options.t: A tax refund from the city office
options.why: A tax refund from the city is a government payment on overpaid taxes and has no link to a franchisee breaking recipe rules in the contract.

options.t: Breach of the franchise agreement
options.why: Franchise agreements require franchisees to follow the franchisor's standards, so changing the recipe without approval breaches the contract and can lead to penalties or termination.

q: What is the best way to open a presentation?

options.t: Grab attention and state the purpose
options.why: A strong opening grabs attention and states the purpose, which gets the audience interested and gives them a clear picture of what to expect from the talk.

options.t: Skip the introduction and just start
options.why: Skipping the introduction leaves the audience unsure of the topic and purpose, so they have no context and may lose interest early in the presentation.

options.t: Read the whole script aloud to them
options.why: Reading the whole script aloud is dull and breaks eye contact; good presenters speak naturally using notes, and this is not a good way to open.

options.t: Apologize for being nervous at first
options.why: Apologizing for nerves draws attention to weakness and lowers credibility; confident presenters begin with a hook or purpose rather than excuses.

q: A customer email is long and emotional. What should the employee do before replying?

options.t: Ignore the email and do not reply to the customer
options.why: Ignoring a customer email leaves the concern unresolved and damages the relationship, so staying silent is poor service and may lose the customer for good.

options.t: Reply with one word and nothing more at all to them
options.why: A one-word reply shows no effort to understand the concerns and would likely upset an already emotional customer even more, so it fails basic service standards.

options.t: Identify the main concerns and respond to each calmly
options.why: Identifying the main concerns and answering each calmly shows the customer they were heard, reduces the emotion and moves toward a solution, which is good communication practice.

options.t: Forward it to the entire staff to show how upset it is
options.why: Forwarding a customer's upset email to all staff is unprofessional, spreads private matters unnecessarily and does nothing to address the customer's actual concerns.

q: What is a service guarantee?

options.t: A fee for using the service each time it is used
options.why: A guarantee is a promise, not a usage charge; a fee paid for each use of the service is a price and is not what a guarantee means.

options.t: A promise to fix or refund if service falls short
options.why: A service guarantee promises to correct the problem or refund the customer if service falls short, which builds trust and lowers the buyer's perceived risk.

options.t: A warning that service will be late, so expect delays
options.why: A warning of delays is a notice and not a guarantee; a guarantee commits the firm to making things right, not to expecting late service.

options.t: A list of employees who provide the service to buyers
options.why: A staff roster names who performs the work but makes no promise about results, so it is not a service guarantee.

q: A store notices many customers ask the same question. What is the best response?

options.t: Raise prices on all the items sold
options.why: Raising prices does not answer customers' repeated question and may even drive away buyers, so it fails to solve the real information gap.

options.t: Hide the information from the customers
options.why: Hiding information leaves the question unanswered and frustrates customers, which hurts trust and increases the number of people asking staff directly.

options.t: Tell customers to stop asking questions
options.why: Telling customers to stop asking is rude and drives them away; questions signal an information gap the store should fix instead of silencing.

options.t: Add the answer to signs or the website
options.why: Posting answers on signs or the website resolves the common question in advance, saving staff time and customers effort while improving the shopping experience.

q: What is a price floor?

options.t: A legal minimum price
options.why: A price floor is a legal minimum price set above the market price, like a minimum wage, and it can cause surpluses when set above equilibrium.

options.t: The lowest shop price
options.why: The lowest price a shop charges is just a business pricing decision; a price floor is a government-imposed legal limit, not a store's lowest price.

options.t: A tax placed on goods
options.why: A tax is a government charge added to a good; a price floor is a legal limit on how low a price may go, not a tax.

options.t: A legal maximum price
options.why: A legal maximum price is a price ceiling, such as rent control, which is the opposite of a price floor, which sets a minimum.

q: If the minimum wage is set above the equilibrium wage, what is a likely result?

options.t: A shortage of workers in the field
options.why: A wage set above equilibrium attracts more job seekers while firms demand fewer workers, producing a surplus of labor rather than a shortage of workers.

options.t: Lower prices everywhere for all goods
options.why: A minimum wage affects labor costs for certain jobs and does not lower prices everywhere; if anything, higher labor costs may push some prices up.

options.t: Some workers may lose hours or jobs
options.why: When the minimum wage exceeds equilibrium, firms hire fewer workers or cut hours because labor costs more, so some workers may lose hours or jobs.

options.t: No effect at all on workers or firms
options.why: A binding wage floor changes pay and hiring decisions, so it has effects on both workers and firms; claiming no effect ignores basic labor market economics.

q: What is the best way to respond to praise?

options.t: Ignore the comment and say nothing to the person
options.why: Ignoring praise comes across as cold or rude and misses a chance to build goodwill with the person who took the time to give it.

options.t: Say thank you and share credit with others who helped
options.why: Thanking the person and sharing credit with those who helped shows gratitude and humility, and it strengthens teamwork and relationships, which is the mark of emotional intelligence.

options.t: Take all the credit for the work done by your team
options.why: Taking all the credit ignores the contributions of teammates, harms trust and morale, and shows poor emotional intelligence and a lack of humility.

options.t: Brag about it to everyone in the office to show your worth
options.why: Bragging to everyone in the office comes across as arrogant, damages relationships and does not show emotional intelligence, which values humility and respect for others.

q: What is a pitch in entrepreneurship?

options.t: A legal contract between a firm and a buyer of goods
options.why: A legal contract between a firm and a buyer is a sales agreement; it records terms of a deal and is not what an entrepreneur's pitch is.

options.t: A product recall issued by a firm for any unsafe goods
options.why: A product recall is a corrective action for unsafe goods; it is unrelated to presenting a business idea to investors or partners.

options.t: A short presentation to persuade people to support an idea
options.why: A pitch is a short, focused presentation used to persuade investors, partners or customers to back an idea, so it must be clear, convincing and brief.

options.t: A tax form that a small business must file each year
options.why: A tax form is a government filing a business completes each year, and it has nothing to do with presenting a business idea to supporters.

q: An entrepreneur sees that her customers are mostly parents of young kids. How should she adapt her marketing?

options.t: Target teenagers only, with ads for school life
options.why: Targeting only teenagers ignores her actual customer base of parents; marketing works best when the message matches who really buys the product.

options.t: Use messages for retirees, who have more savings
options.why: Retirees are not her main customers, and having more savings does not make them the right audience, so messages aimed at them would miss her market.

options.t: Avoid all advertising to parents and families
options.why: Avoiding advertising to parents would cut her off from her best customers; she should reach existing buyers rather than ignore them in her marketing.

options.t: Use messages and channels that fit busy parents
options.why: Adapting marketing to the target market means using messages and channels that suit busy parents, such as social media, convenience and time-saving benefits.

q: What is a net profit margin?

options.t: Net income divided by sales
options.why: Net profit margin equals net income divided by sales, shown as a percent; for example, $10,000 net income on $100,000 in sales is a 10 percent margin.

options.t: Sales divided by the units
options.why: Sales divided by units sold gives average selling price per unit, not a margin, because it does not include any costs or profit measure.

options.t: Assets divided by liabilities
options.why: Assets divided by liabilities is a solvency measure that compares what a firm owns to what it owes; it is not a profit margin.

options.t: Expenses divided by assets
options.why: Expenses divided by assets is not a standard profitability ratio; net profit margin compares net income to sales, not expenses to assets.

q: A business has $90,000 in sales, $45,000 in cost of goods sold and $20,000 in other expenses. What is its net income?

options.why: $45,000 is the cost of goods sold alone, or gross profit; it ignores the $20,000 of other expenses that must still be subtracted to find net income.
Net income = $90,000 sales - $45,000 cost of goods sold - $20,000 other expenses = $25,000, which is what remains after all costs.
$155,000 results from adding the costs to sales ($90,000 + $45,000 + $20,000); costs must be subtracted from sales, not added to them.
$65,000 comes from subtracting only the $25,000 of costs combined wrongly, instead of subtracting both $45,000 and $20,000 from $90,000, which correctly leaves $25,000.

q: What is a mentorship program in a company?

options.t: A schedule of vacations for the employees, on a calendar
options.why: A vacation schedule is a leave calendar for staff; it does not match experienced and newer employees, so it is not a mentorship program.

options.t: A list of customers and the goods that they have bought
options.why: A list of customers and their purchases is a sales or customer record, which has nothing to do with developing employees through guidance.

options.t: A pay chart showing wages for each job grade in the firm
options.why: A pay chart showing wages by job grade is a compensation structure; it sets pay levels rather than providing mentoring support to employees.

options.t: Pairing experienced employees with newer ones for guidance
options.why: A mentorship program pairs experienced employees with newer ones so that they can pass on skills, advice and company knowledge, which builds careers and improves retention.

q: What is a data privacy policy?

options.t: A sales forecast made for the next year by the firm's team
options.why: A sales forecast predicts future revenue and is a planning tool; it says nothing about how the company handles customer data.

options.t: A statement of how a company collects, uses and protects data
options.why: A data privacy policy tells customers and staff how the company collects, uses, stores and protects personal data, helping it meet laws and build trust.

options.t: A list of employees and their jobs in the company's offices
options.why: A list of employees and their jobs is an organization chart or directory, which describes roles and does not explain data handling practices.

options.t: A product warranty that comes with goods sold to the buyers
options.why: A product warranty promises repair or replacement of goods; it covers product defects and has nothing to do with how data is handled.

q: A sales manager wants to know last quarter's best-selling product. Which tool would be most efficient?

options.t: A sales report from the database
options.why: A sales report from the database quickly shows units sold by product, so the manager can identify last quarter's best seller accurately and efficiently.

options.t: Guessing from memory alone now
options.why: Guessing from memory is unreliable and can be wrong, so it is not an efficient or accurate way to identify the best seller.

options.t: Asking every customer by phone
options.why: Phoning every customer is extremely slow and costly, and customers' recollections would be less reliable than the sales data the firm already holds.

options.t: Counting receipts by hand only
options.why: Counting receipts by hand takes far too long and invites errors when a database report can give the answer in seconds.

q: What is a call to action in an advertisement?

options.t: The company's address only, shown in small print
options.why: A company address in small print may help contact, but it does not urge the audience to take a specific step, so it is not a call to action.

options.t: A list of product ingredients printed on the package
options.why: A list of ingredients is product information printed on the package; it informs buyers but does not tell them what action to take next.

options.t: A message telling the audience what to do next
options.why: A call to action tells the audience what to do next, such as "buy now" or "call today", and it turns interest into a response.

options.t: A legal warning printed at the bottom of the page
options.why: A legal warning is a disclosure required for safety or compliance; it does not prompt the audience to take a buying step.

q: A company wants to measure brand awareness. Which method is most direct?

options.t: Ask a sample of people if they recognize the brand
options.why: Surveying a sample of people about whether they recognize the brand directly measures awareness, which is the share of the market that knows the brand.

options.t: Count its employees and the hours that each works
options.why: Counting employees and their hours measures staffing and labor, which says nothing about whether the public recognizes the brand.

options.t: Review its rent costs for the last three years
options.why: Rent costs are an operating expense and reveal nothing about how many people recognize the brand, so they are not a measure of awareness.

options.t: Check its tax records to see what it paid last year
options.why: Tax records show what the company paid in taxes, which is a financial matter and not a direct measure of public brand awareness.

q: What is an inventory turnover ratio?

options.t: The number of employees working at the firm each day
options.why: The number of employees working each day is a staffing measure; inventory turnover relates to goods sold and replaced, not to workforce size.

options.t: How many times inventory is sold and replaced in a period
options.why: Inventory turnover shows how many times a firm sells and replaces its inventory in a period, calculated as cost of goods sold divided by average inventory.

options.t: The size of the warehouse where all goods are stored
options.why: Warehouse size describes storage capacity and is not a ratio of sales activity; turnover measures how fast stock moves, not how much space it uses.

options.t: The price of goods sold by the firm to its own buyers
options.why: The price of goods sold to buyers is the selling price; turnover is a ratio of how quickly inventory sells, not a price.

q: A store's inventory turnover falls from 8 to 4 times per year. What does this suggest?

options.t: Sales are totally unaffected
options.why: Turnover falling from 8 to 4 shows a major change in how fast stock moves, so sales are clearly affected rather than unchanged.

options.t: The store has no inventory
options.why: A store with no inventory would have no turnover to calculate at all, yet the ratio is still 4, so stock exists and is selling.

options.t: Stock is selling more slowly
options.why: Turnover of 4 instead of 8 means inventory is being sold and replaced half as often, so stock is selling more slowly, tying up cash and risking obsolescence.

options.t: Stock is selling twice as fast
options.why: Stock selling twice as fast would raise turnover from 8 to 16, not lower it from 8 to 4, which is the opposite direction.

q: What is the purpose of a career goal?

options.t: To avoid work and any form of effort at all times
options.why: A career goal is meant to drive effort and purpose, not to avoid work, so this option reverses its actual purpose.

options.t: To prevent learning new skills in a career for good
options.why: Career goals encourage learning new skills to reach the goal; they do not prevent skill growth, which is needed for advancement.

options.t: To limit your options so you stay in one job for life
options.why: Goals expand and guide options, they do not trap you in one job; people often change jobs and paths while working toward them.

options.t: To give direction to your education and work choices
options.why: A career goal gives direction to education and work choices, such as courses, training and jobs, so efforts stay focused on the career you want.

q: A supervisor gives you critical feedback. What is the most professional response?

options.t: Ignore the feedback and carry on exactly as you were before
options.why: Ignoring feedback shows poor professionalism and wastes a chance to improve; supervisors expect employees to act on constructive criticism.

options.t: Argue and blame others for the issues that were raised
options.why: Arguing and blaming others avoids responsibility and damages the working relationship, which makes it an unprofessional response to criticism.

options.t: Quit immediately and walk out of the office in anger
options.why: Quitting in anger is an immature reaction that harms your reputation and career and fixes none of the problems raised.

options.t: Listen, ask clarifying questions and make a plan to improve
options.why: Listening, asking clarifying questions and making an improvement plan shows maturity and a growth mindset, and it helps you correct the issue and strengthen trust with your supervisor.

q: What is a stakeholder analysis used for?

options.t: Designing a logo for the brand that the firm will sell under
options.why: Logo design is a branding task handled by designers; stakeholder analysis does not deal with artwork or brand visuals at all.

options.t: Understanding who is affected by a decision and their interests
options.why: Stakeholder analysis identifies the groups affected by a decision, such as employees, customers and investors, and weighs their interests and influence to plan communication and reduce conflict.

options.t: Setting product prices for the goods that a firm sells to buyers
options.why: Product pricing relies on cost, demand and competition analysis, not on stakeholder analysis, which examines who is affected by decisions.

options.t: Counting inventory in the warehouse at the end of every month
options.why: Counting inventory is an operations and accounting task done through stock counts, and it is unrelated to analyzing stakeholders.

q: A company enters a market with strong local competitors. Which strategy could set it apart?

options.t: Charge the same price with no real difference
options.why: Charging the same price with no difference gives buyers no reason to switch from established local competitors, so it does not set the firm apart.

options.t: Copy competitors exactly, down to their prices
options.why: Copying competitors exactly, including prices, makes the company look identical and offers customers no reason to choose the newcomer over local firms.

options.t: Differentiate with unique features or service
options.why: Differentiation means offering unique features, quality or service that rivals lack, which gives customers a reason to choose the new entrant despite strong local competition.

options.t: Hide the product from local customers and shops
options.why: Hiding the product from local customers would produce no sales at all, so it cannot be a strategy to compete in the market.

q: What does regulatory compliance mean for a business?

options.t: Setting its own industry standards for rival firms to follow
options.why: Rival firms follow their own industry practices; setting standards for them is not compliance, which is about the business obeying existing rules.

options.t: Following the laws and regulations that apply to its operations
options.why: Regulatory compliance means obeying the laws and regulations that apply to the business, such as safety, labor, tax and consumer protection rules, to avoid penalties.

options.t: Avoiding all government inspections of its premises each year
options.why: Compliance does not avoid inspections; inspectors check that a firm obeys rules, and avoiding them would suggest the firm is hiding violations.

options.t: Choosing the cheapest legal option even when it harms buyers
options.why: Picking the cheapest option that harms buyers breaks consumer protection duties; compliance requires following the law, even when a cheaper path exists.

q: A health inspector finds a restaurant storing food at unsafe temperatures. This violation falls mainly under which type of compliance?

options.t: Health and safety regulations
options.why: Food storage temperatures are governed by health and safety regulations, which exist to prevent foodborne illness, so unsafe temperatures violate this type of compliance.

options.t: Advertising regulations only
options.why: Advertising regulations cover truthful claims in promotions and do not govern food storage temperatures, so this is the wrong type of compliance.

options.t: Tax regulations on income
options.why: Tax regulations deal with reporting and paying taxes on income, and storing food too warm is not a tax issue.

options.t: Labor classification rules
options.why: Labor classification rules decide whether workers are employees or contractors; they do not address food safety or storage temperature.

q: Which U.S. agency sets and enforces workplace safety standards?

options.t: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency
options.why: The EPA protects the environment by regulating pollution and chemicals; it does not set workplace safety standards for employees.

options.t: Securities and Exchange Commission, for stocks
options.why: The SEC regulates securities markets and investor disclosure, and it has no authority over workplace safety rules.

options.t: Occupational Safety and Health Administration
options.why: OSHA, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, sets and enforces workplace safety and health standards, inspects employers and can issue fines for violations.

options.t: The Federal Trade Commission of the U.S.
options.why: The FTC enforces consumer protection and competition law, such as false advertising; it does not oversee safety in the workplace.

q: An employer must keep records of employee hours and pay for several years. What is the main reason?

options.t: To meet the legal requirements for advertising a product online
options.why: Advertising law concerns truthful claims in promotions; employee hour and pay records are kept under labor law and are not an advertising requirement.

options.t: To help set next year's prices for all of the products the company sells
options.why: Prices are set by costs, demand and competition; payroll records are kept for legal reasons and are not mainly used for pricing products.

options.t: To qualify for a discount on shipping and freight costs for goods
options.why: Shipping discounts depend on carrier agreements and shipping volume, and payroll records have no role in getting a freight discount.

options.t: To prove compliance with wage and hour laws in an audit or dispute
options.why: Wage and hour laws such as the FLSA require records, which let the employer prove compliance and defend against claims during an audit or dispute.

q: What is the main responsibility of a company's compliance officer?

options.t: Making sure policies and operations follow laws and regulations
options.why: A compliance officer makes sure company policies and operations follow applicable laws and regulations, trains staff and monitors for violations to reduce legal risk.

options.t: Setting the monthly sales targets for each member of the sales team
options.why: Setting monthly sales targets belongs to sales management, not to the compliance officer, whose role is legal and regulatory oversight.

options.t: Recruiting and hiring new employees for open positions in the company
options.why: Recruiting and hiring are human resources duties; a compliance officer checks that hiring follows laws but does not recruit workers.

options.t: Designing the packaging that products are sold in on shelves
options.why: Package design is a marketing and product task; the compliance officer would only check that packaging meets legal labeling rules.

q: Which is a likely result of failing to comply with applicable regulations?

options.t: Lower taxes for the firm too
options.why: Failing to follow regulations does not lower taxes; if anything, violations may add back taxes, interest and penalties for the firm.

options.t: Fines or other legal penalties
options.why: Noncompliance can lead to fines, lawsuits, lost licenses and damage to reputation, which is why firms invest in compliance programs.

options.t: Higher supplier discounts too
options.why: Suppliers do not reward a firm for breaking rules, and violations can damage relationships, so higher supplier discounts are not a result.

options.t: Automatic license renewals
options.why: Regulators may refuse to renew or may even revoke licenses for violations, so automatic renewals are not a likely result of noncompliance.

q: Which feature separates a project from everyday operations?

options.t: It repeats forever with the same tasks
options.why: Repeating the same tasks forever describes ongoing operations; a project is a temporary effort that ends, so this option describes operations.

options.t: It has no specific goal at any time
options.why: Every project is created to achieve a specific goal; a project with no goal would have nothing to deliver or measure.

options.t: It needs no resources of any kind
options.why: Projects always need resources such as people, money, time and materials, so a project needing none of them could not be carried out.

options.t: It has a defined beginning and end
options.why: A project is temporary, with a defined start and finish and a specific result, unlike everyday operations, which are ongoing and repetitive.

q: A project manager lists tasks, owners and due dates on a chart. What is this tool mainly used for?

options.t: Recruiting new staff for the team
options.why: Recruiting staff is a human resources process and does not rely on a chart listing tasks, owners and due dates.

options.t: Forecasting product demand for next year
options.why: Demand forecasting uses sales history and market data rather than a chart of tasks, owners and deadlines, so this is not its use.

options.t: Scheduling work and tracking progress
options.why: A chart of tasks, owners and due dates, like a Gantt chart or task tracker, schedules the work and tracks progress against deadlines.

options.t: Calculating payroll taxes owed each month
options.why: Payroll taxes are computed from wages and tax rates, not from a task chart, which has no pay data in it.

q: What is the scope of a project?

options.t: The legal structure of the company and all its owners
options.why: The legal structure and ownership of a company is a business formation matter and does not define what a project covers.

options.t: The pay of the team members who work on the project
options.why: Team pay belongs to the budget and compensation, not to scope; scope defines the work and deliverables.

options.t: The work that is included in, and left out of, the project
options.why: Scope defines the work included in the project and what is excluded, which prevents scope creep and keeps the team focused on agreed deliverables.

options.t: The number of customers served after the project launches
options.why: Customers served after launch is a result or outcome measure and does not define the work covered by the project.

q: Halfway through a website project the client asks for three new features. What should the project manager do first?

options.t: Refuse all changes regardless of how valuable they are to the client
options.why: Refusing all changes ignores valuable requests and harms the client relationship; project managers should evaluate changes instead of rejecting them outright.

options.t: Assess the effect on time and cost and agree any changes before proceeding
options.why: The first step is to assess the effect on time, cost and scope, then agree the change formally with the client, which is proper change control.

options.t: Pause the whole project until the client stops asking for any changes
options.why: Pausing the whole project delays the work and wastes resources; the correct response is to review the change request, not stop everything.

options.t: Accept every change at once without checking the effect on time or cost
options.why: Accepting changes without checking can blow the budget and schedule, which is scope creep; changes must be evaluated and approved first.

q: Which two are among the classic constraints on a project?

options.t: Price and place
options.why: Price and place are two of the four Ps of the marketing mix, not project constraints, which are mostly time, cost and scope.

options.t: Color and size
options.why: Color and size are product attributes and not classic project constraints, which relate to schedule, budget and scope.

options.t: People and brand
options.why: People and brand are not among the classic project constraints, which are time, cost and scope or quality.

options.t: Time and cost
options.why: Time and cost are two classic project constraints, along with scope and quality; changing one usually affects the others, often called the triple constraint.

q: What does a project risk register list?

options.t: Possible problems, how likely they are and planned responses
options.why: A risk register lists possible problems, the likelihood and impact of each, and planned responses, so the team can manage threats before they hurt the project.

options.t: The salaries and pay rates of all of the team members
options.why: Salaries and pay rates belong in the budget or payroll records, not in a risk register, which tracks potential problems.

options.t: The final results and deliverables of the whole project
options.why: Final results and deliverables are recorded in the project scope and completion reports, not in the risk register, which tracks possible problems.

options.t: Only the contact details of the project's suppliers and sponsors
options.why: Supplier contact details belong in a stakeholder or contact list; a risk register tracks risks, not contact information.

q: Knowledge management is the practice of:

options.t: Hiring new employees to fill vacant positions
options.why: Hiring to fill vacancies is a human resources function; it adds staff but does not capture or share what the organization knows.

options.t: Setting the prices charged for the company's products
options.why: Setting product prices is a pricing decision made on costs, demand and competition, so it is not knowledge management.

options.t: Auditing a company's financial statements each year
options.why: Auditing financial statements checks accuracy of accounts, which is an accounting task and not about managing organizational knowledge.

options.t: Capturing and sharing what an organization knows
options.why: Knowledge management is the practice of capturing, organizing and sharing what an organization knows so employees can use it, which improves decisions and avoids repeated work.

q: Which is an example of tacit knowledge?

options.t: A veteran technician's instinct for diagnosing a fault
options.why: Tacit knowledge is gained from experience and is hard to write down, like a veteran technician's instinct for diagnosing faults that is not in any manual.

options.t: A written user manual that comes with the equipment
options.why: A written user manual is explicit knowledge because it is already documented and can be easily shared with others.

options.t: A database containing the details of past customer orders
options.why: A database of past orders holds recorded data, which makes it explicit knowledge and not tacit knowledge, which is held in people's minds.

options.t: A safety checklist posted on the wall of the workshop
options.why: A posted safety checklist is written down and shared, so it is explicit knowledge rather than tacit knowledge.

q: Which tool best helps employees find answers to common questions without asking a coworker?

options.t: A paper time sheet for hourly staff
options.why: A paper time sheet records hours worked for payroll, and it contains no answers to employees' common work questions.

options.t: An internal searchable knowledge base
options.why: An internal searchable knowledge base stores answers and guides in one place, letting employees find information quickly without interrupting a coworker.

options.t: An annual report for the investors
options.why: An annual report summarizes company results for investors and does not answer employees' day-to-day how-to questions.

options.t: A supplier invoice sent for payment
options.why: A supplier invoice is a bill requesting payment and gives no help in answering employees' common questions.

q: A senior employee will retire soon. Which step best preserves their knowledge before they leave?

options.t: Rely on their old email archive alone to hold it all
options.why: Relying on an email archive alone captures messages but not judgment and know-how, and it is hard to search, so much knowledge is lost.

options.t: Delete their old files to save space on the server
options.why: Deleting the files would destroy valuable knowledge the company might need; saving server space does not justify losing what the senior employee created.

options.t: Document key processes and pair them with a successor
options.why: Documenting key processes and pairing the employee with a successor transfers both written and tacit knowledge, so the company keeps it after retirement.

options.t: Ask them to keep working without pay after they retire
options.why: Asking a retiree to work without pay is unfair and likely illegal; it does not capture knowledge for the organization.

q: Which benefit is most closely tied to sharing knowledge across a company?

options.t: Larger inventory stocks
options.why: Inventory levels are driven by demand and supply planning and are not a benefit of sharing knowledge across a company.

options.t: Fewer repeated mistakes
options.why: When employees share knowledge, lessons are not lost, so teams avoid repeating the same mistakes, saving time and money and improving quality.

options.t: Higher office rent costs
options.why: Higher rent costs result from property markets and lease terms and are not a benefit of sharing knowledge.

options.t: Longer team meetings daily
options.why: Longer meetings are a cost, not a benefit; good knowledge sharing aims to make work more efficient, not to lengthen meetings.

q: What is quality control?

options.t: Setting the prices charged for the company's products
options.why: Setting prices is a pricing function; quality control focuses on checking that products meet standards, not on setting prices.

options.t: Advertising the company to attract new customers
options.why: Advertising attracts customers and is a marketing activity; it is unrelated to inspecting output against standards, which is quality control.

options.t: Checking products or services against set standards
options.why: Quality control checks products or services against set standards to find defects before they reach customers, using inspection and testing.

options.t: Hiring temporary staff during a busy sales season
options.why: Hiring temporary staff for busy seasons is a staffing decision and is not part of quality control.

q: A factory counts the defective items found per 1,000 produced. What is this measure called?

options.t: Defect rate
options.why: The defect rate measures defective items per number produced, such as per 1,000 units, and helps track quality and spot process problems.

options.t: Staff turnover
options.why: Staff turnover measures how many employees leave a firm in a period, which has nothing to do with counting defective items.

options.t: Stock turnover
options.why: Stock turnover measures how often inventory is sold and replaced, so it relates to inventory management rather than defects per 1,000 units.

options.t: Return on sales
options.why: Return on sales is a profitability ratio of profit to sales, and it does not count defective items.

q: What does continuous improvement mean?

options.t: Leaving processes unchanged once they are approved
options.why: Leaving processes unchanged once approved is the opposite of continuous improvement, which keeps looking for better ways of working.

options.t: Replacing the whole business every single year
options.why: Replacing the whole business every year would be wasteful and disruptive; continuous improvement is about small, steady refinements rather than total replacement.

options.t: Changing only when customers complain loudly
options.why: Changing only when customers complain is reactive; continuous improvement looks for problems and chances to improve before complaints arise.

options.t: Making ongoing small changes to improve processes
