options.t: Please leave if you are not sure about it
options.why: Asking an unsure buyer to leave is rude and ends the sale. Closing techniques guide the buyer toward a purchase and do not push the customer away.

q: What is follow-up in selling?

options.t: Avoiding contact with the buyer after the sale is done and paid
options.why: Avoiding contact after the sale ignores the customer's needs and loses repeat business. Follow-up is the opposite: staying in touch to confirm the buyer is satisfied.

options.t: Contacting the customer after a sale to ensure satisfaction
options.why: Follow-up means contacting the customer after the sale to confirm satisfaction, solve problems and encourage repeat business. It builds loyalty and referrals that raise future sales.

options.t: Reducing the product's quality after the sale is made
options.why: Lowering quality after a sale would hurt customers and the company's reputation. It is unethical and has nothing to do with the follow-up step of selling.

options.t: Raising the price after the sale is made to the buyer
options.why: Raising the price after the sale would break the agreement with the buyer and destroy trust. Follow-up is about service and satisfaction, not changing terms.

q: What is suggestion selling?

options.t: Offering additional items that go with a purchase
options.why: Suggestion selling means offering extra or related items that go with the main purchase, like batteries with a toy. It adds value for the customer and raises the sale total.

options.t: Refusing to sell what the customer wants to buy
options.why: Refusing to sell what the customer wants would lose the sale and has nothing to do with suggesting add-ons. It does not describe any selling technique.

options.t: Selling only the cheapest item in the store each day
options.why: Selling only the cheapest item is a fixed pricing approach, not suggesting extra products. It ignores customer needs, which suggestion selling is meant to serve.

options.t: Selling only to customers who ask for it twice
options.why: Waiting until a customer asks twice describes passive selling. Suggestion selling is proactive, because the seller offers related items without being asked.

q: A customer buys a camera. Which suggestion is most helpful?

options.t: A kitchen blender for home use
options.why: A kitchen blender does not relate to photography, so offering it would not help the camera buyer. Suggestions should complement the main purchase.

options.t: A bicycle helmet for children
options.why: A child's bicycle helmet has no connection to using a camera. A helpful suggestion fits the item just bought, which this does not.

options.t: A bag of garden soil for planting
options.why: Garden soil is unrelated to a camera purchase and would not meet any need the buyer has. Good suggestions match how the product will be used.

options.t: A memory card and a carrying case
options.why: A memory card stores photos and a case protects the camera, so both are accessories the buyer will actually need. That makes this a helpful, relevant suggestion.

q: What is trading up?

options.t: Encouraging a customer to return a product for credit
options.why: Encouraging a return for credit is a returns procedure, not selling. Trading up aims to increase the sale value, whereas returns reduce sales for the store.

options.t: Encouraging a customer to buy a cheaper version of the item
options.why: Pushing a cheaper version is trading down, which lowers the sale amount. Trading up is the reverse: moving the buyer toward a higher-priced option.

options.t: Encouraging a customer to buy a more expensive version
options.why: Trading up means encouraging a customer to buy a more expensive, higher-quality version of an item. It benefits the customer through better features and raises the sale total.

options.t: Encouraging a customer to leave the store right now
options.why: Encouraging the customer to leave ends the sale and helps no one. Trading up is about guiding a buyer to a better, higher-priced product.

q: What is product knowledge?

options.t: Knowing a competitor's private sales data and plans
options.why: A competitor's private data is not product knowledge and may be obtained unethically. Product knowledge concerns the seller's own products and how they serve customers.

options.t: Understanding a product's features, benefits and uses
options.why: Product knowledge means understanding a product's features, benefits and uses. With it, salespeople can explain value, answer questions and match items to needs.

options.t: Knowing the store's opening hours and its address
options.why: Store hours and address are general business information. They do not tell a salesperson what the product does, so this is not product knowledge.

options.t: Knowing a customer's home address and phone number
options.why: A customer's address and phone number are personal contact details and have nothing to do with knowing the product being sold.

q: Why does a salesperson need strong product knowledge?

options.t: To hide the product's drawbacks from the law and buyers
options.why: Hiding drawbacks from buyers is dishonest and can be illegal. Strong product knowledge is used to inform customers truthfully, not to conceal problems.

options.t: To answer questions with confidence and match products to needs
options.why: Knowing the product lets a salesperson answer questions with confidence, build trust and match the right product to the customer's needs, which leads to satisfied buyers and sales.

options.t: To make the sale last as long as possible for the buyer
options.why: Extending the length of a sale does not help the customer and wastes time. Product knowledge is meant to make selling efficient and useful, not longer.

options.t: To avoid listening to the customer and what they need or want
options.why: Product knowledge should work together with listening. Ignoring what the customer wants leads to poor matches and lost sales, so this is the opposite of good practice.

q: What is relationship selling?

options.t: Building long-term trust with customers rather than focusing on one sale
options.why: Relationship selling focuses on building long-term trust and repeat business with customers. It values ongoing satisfaction and loyalty over making a single quick sale.

options.t: Selling only to family members and to close friends of the seller
options.why: Relationship selling is not limited to family and friends. It applies to all customers by building trust over time, not by selling to people the seller already knows.

options.t: Avoiding any follow-up after the sale is made and the customer pays
options.why: Avoiding follow-up is the opposite of relationship selling, which depends on staying in touch after the sale to maintain trust and encourage repeat purchases.

options.t: Making as many one-time sales as possible with no contact after the sale is made
options.why: Maximizing one-time sales with no later contact is transaction selling. Relationship selling instead keeps in touch with customers to earn their repeat business over many years.

q: Which action best shows ethical selling?

options.t: Pressuring buyers until they give in and agree to buy
options.why: Pressuring buyers until they give in is manipulative and damages trust. Ethical selling respects the customer's right to make a free and informed choice.

options.t: Hiding a product's problems to close the sale fast
options.why: Hiding a product's problems is deceptive and may violate consumer protection law. Ethical sellers disclose material information the buyer needs to decide.

options.t: Making false claims to beat a competitor in the sale
options.why: False claims about competitors or products are dishonest and can lead to legal action for false advertising. Ethical selling relies on truthful statements.

options.t: Giving honest information, including a product's limits
options.why: Honest information, including a product's limits, respects the customer and builds trust. Ethical selling avoids deception and pressure, leading to satisfied customers and repeat sales.

q: What is a sales quota?

options.t: A discount given to every customer who comes in
options.why: A discount for every customer is a pricing policy. A quota is a goal set for the salesperson, not a price reduction given to buyers.

options.t: A tax on each item that a salesperson sells
options.why: A tax on items is a government charge, such as sales tax. A quota is an internal sales goal that has nothing to do with taxing items sold.

options.t: A sales target a salesperson is expected to meet
options.why: A sales quota is a target, in dollars or units, that a salesperson is expected to reach in a period. Managers use quotas to measure and reward performance.

options.t: A limit on how many customers can enter a store
options.why: Limiting how many customers enter a store is a capacity rule. A quota concerns the sales volume a seller is expected to achieve.

q: A salesperson has a quota of $20,000 and sells $24,000. By what percent did they exceed the quota?

options.why: 120% is the sales as a share of quota ($24,000 / $20,000 = 1.20). The question asks by how much they exceeded it, which is 120% minus 100%.
4% might come from dividing $4,000 by $100,000 or a similar slip. The excess is $4,000 and the quota is $20,000, so the correct ratio is much higher.
83% results from dividing $20,000 by $24,000 (0.833), which compares quota to sales. The excess must be measured against the quota, not against the sales.
Excess is $24,000 - $20,000 = $4,000. Dividing by the quota gives $4,000 / $20,000 = 0.20, or 20%, so the salesperson beat the quota by 20 percent.

q: What is a commission?

options.t: Pay that is a fixed yearly amount for a job
options.why: A fixed yearly amount is a salary. Commission varies with performance, so a flat annual pay does not describe commission.

options.t: Pay based on a percentage of the sales made
options.why: A commission is pay based on a percentage of the sales a person makes. It rewards effort, since earnings rise as the salesperson sells more.

options.t: Pay given as a gift at the end of the year
options.why: A gift at year end is a bonus or present and is not tied to a percentage of sales, so it is not commission.

options.t: Pay that is the same every hour worked each week
options.why: Pay that is the same for every hour is a regular hourly wage. Commission changes with the sales produced, not with hours worked.

q: A salesperson earns 6% commission on $15,000 of sales. What is the commission?

options.why: $9,000 is 60% of $15,000, a misplaced decimal point. A 6% rate means 0.06, so the commission must be much smaller than this amount.
$90 is 0.6% of $15,000 and results from moving the decimal one place too far. The 6% rate should be converted to 0.06 before multiplying.
Commission equals sales times rate: $15,000 x 0.06 = $900. This is the percentage of sales the salesperson earns as pay.
$2,500 results from dividing $15,000 by 6, which is not how percent is calculated. Multiply the sales by 0.06 instead to get the commission.

q: What is customer needs assessment?

options.t: Asking questions to learn what a customer needs and wants
options.why: A needs assessment means asking questions to learn what the customer needs and wants. This lets the seller recommend the right product instead of guessing.

options.t: Showing every product in the store to the customer
options.why: Showing every product does not identify needs and may overwhelm the customer. Needs assessment comes first, so the seller can show only suitable items.

options.t: Telling the customer what they need without asking any questions
options.why: Telling customers what they need without asking skips the assessment entirely. Good selling begins with questions and listening rather than assumptions.

options.t: Printing a price list for the customer to take home
options.why: A price list does not discover the customer's needs. Needs assessment is an interactive questioning process, not handing out information.

q: A customer says they need a laptop for school and travel. What should the seller ask next?

options.t: How much they want to spend and what programs they use
options.why: Budget and intended programs are key needs questions. They help the seller choose a laptop with the right price, power and software for school and travel.

options.t: Whether they like the seller's shoes or hairstyle
options.why: The seller's shoes or hairstyle have no link to the customer's needs. Questions should focus on how the customer will use the laptop.

options.t: What their favorite food is at lunch time on school days
options.why: Lunch preferences do not help choose a laptop. The next question should clarify use, budget and features, not unrelated personal tastes.

options.t: Where they went to elementary school and which teachers
options.why: A customer's elementary school and teachers are unrelated to selecting a laptop. Relevant questions concern budget, uses and needed features.

q: What is an intermediary in a distribution channel?

options.t: A customer who buys goods directly from the factory floor
options.why: A customer who buys direct from the factory is an end buyer, not a middle link. An intermediary stands between the producer and the final buyer.

options.t: A business that sits between the producer and the final buyer
options.why: An intermediary is a business such as a wholesaler or retailer between the producer and final buyer. It helps move goods, store them and sell them, forming part of the channel.

options.t: A company that supplies raw materials to a producer firm
options.why: A raw material supplier sits before the producer in the supply chain, not between the producer and the consumer, so it is not a channel intermediary.

options.t: A government office that sets the price of imported goods
options.why: A government office that sets prices is a regulator and not part of the distribution channel. Intermediaries buy, hold or sell goods themselves.

q: What is disintermediation?

options.t: Raising the price of goods at every step of the channel of sale
options.why: Raising prices at every step describes markup layering, not channel structure. Disintermediation specifically involves removing intermediaries from the channel.

options.t: Adding more wholesalers to a distribution channel for goods
options.why: Adding wholesalers adds layers to the channel, which is the opposite of disintermediation. The term refers to cutting out middlemen.

options.t: Removing middlemen so a producer sells directly to customers
options.why: Disintermediation removes middlemen such as wholesalers or retailers so the producer sells directly to customers, often online. It can cut costs and give the producer more control.

options.t: Closing a factory to cut the cost of making all goods
options.why: Closing a factory to cut production costs is a manufacturing decision. Disintermediation is about distribution channel structure, not about production.

q: A farm starts selling vegetables through a weekly box delivered to homes instead of through grocery stores. What is this?

options.t: Channel conflict with its own retail outlets
options.why: Channel conflict is a dispute between channel members. The farm's box program may cause some, but the question asks what the direct delivery model itself is.

options.t: Intensive distribution through every store
options.why: Intensive distribution places a product in as many outlets as possible. The farm is cutting out stores to deliver itself, which is the opposite.

options.t: A reverse channel for returned goods only
options.why: A reverse channel handles returns, recycling or reuse of goods. The farm is delivering new vegetables to customers, not collecting used goods.

options.t: Disintermediation through a direct channel
options.why: Selling vegetable boxes straight to homes removes the grocery stores as intermediaries. That is disintermediation through a direct channel from producer to consumer.

q: What is omnichannel retailing?

options.t: Giving customers a smooth experience across stores, apps and websites
options.why: Omnichannel retailing integrates stores, apps and websites so customers move between them smoothly, with shared inventory, accounts and order history across all of them.

options.t: Selling only to other businesses in bulk quantities each month
options.why: Selling only to other businesses in bulk is business-to-business wholesale. Omnichannel is a retail approach that connects many customer-facing channels.

options.t: Selling only through one physical store location in a single city
options.why: Using one location in a single city is the opposite of multiple integrated channels, so it cannot be omnichannel.

options.t: Using several unrelated channels that do not share any data at all
options.why: Unrelated channels that share no data are multichannel at best. Omnichannel requires the channels to be connected so the customer experience is consistent.

q: A customer orders online and returns the item at a local store, and the store shows the order history. Which approach does this show?

options.t: Price skimming at launch
options.why: Price skimming sets a high initial price on a new product at launch. It has nothing to do with how orders and returns work across channels.

options.t: Omnichannel retailing
options.why: Ordering online, returning in a store and having the store see the order history shows linked channels. That connected experience is omnichannel retailing.

options.t: Direct mail promotion
options.why: Direct mail promotion sends printed advertising to homes. The scenario concerns channel integration for orders and returns, not mailed ads.

options.t: Exclusive distribution
options.why: Exclusive distribution gives one outlet the right to sell a product in an area. It does not describe sharing data between online and store channels.

q: What does RFID technology help with in a channel?

options.t: Setting the final price shown in advertisements and on shelves
options.why: Prices are set by management decisions, not by radio frequency tags. RFID reads tags to identify items, so it does not decide what ads or shelves show.

options.t: Choosing the color and shape of a package for the shelf
options.why: Package color and shape are design decisions. RFID tags track items but do not influence how packaging looks.

options.t: Tracking goods automatically as they move and are stored
options.why: RFID tags use radio signals so goods can be scanned and located automatically during transport and storage, which improves inventory accuracy and reduces manual counting.

options.t: Training sales staff to greet customers at the shop door
options.why: Training staff to greet customers is a human resources task, not a function of tracking technology such as RFID.

q: What is a barcode used for in retail?

options.t: Advertising a product on television and on the radio daily
options.why: Television and radio ads are promotion tools. A barcode is a printed code scanned at the register, which does not advertise anything.

options.t: Showing customers how to use a product at home with ease
options.why: Instructions for using a product are given in manuals or demos. A barcode only stores a number that identifies the item.

options.t: Protecting a product from copying through a registered design right
options.why: Protecting designs from copying is done through legal registration such as patents. A barcode does not provide legal protection.

options.t: Identifying a product quickly so it can be priced and tracked
options.why: A barcode is scanned to identify a product quickly, so the system can look up its price and update stock records. It speeds checkout and improves tracking accuracy.

q: A store scans each item at checkout and its stock levels update automatically. What is the main benefit?

options.t: Higher prices for every customer in the whole market
options.why: Scanning does not raise prices for customers. The system only records items, and prices are set by management decisions.

options.t: Removal of the need to count stock by hand ever again
options.why: Physical counts are still needed to check for theft, damage or errors. Automatic updates reduce counting work but do not remove the need entirely.

options.t: Fewer products offered to customers in every store branch
options.why: Scanning does not reduce the product range. It records what is sold, and that information can actually help a store stock the right goods.

options.t: More accurate inventory records that support reordering
options.why: Each scan subtracts the item from stock, so inventory records stay current and accurate. This supports timely reordering and helps avoid shortages or excess stock.

q: What is a cold chain?

options.t: A temperature-controlled supply chain for perishable goods
options.why: A cold chain is a supply chain that keeps perishable goods such as food and vaccines at controlled low temperatures from producer to consumer, preventing spoilage.

options.t: A group of suppliers that refuse to work together on pricing
options.why: Suppliers who refuse to cooperate on pricing is not a cold chain. The term refers to temperature control, not to supplier behavior.

options.t: A rule that sets low prices in winter for all the shops
options.why: A winter pricing rule is a pricing policy. A cold chain concerns refrigerated transport and storage, not seasonal prices.

options.t: A chain of ice cream shops spread across a large region
options.why: A chain of ice cream shops is a retail business structure. The cold chain is a logistics concept, even if ice cream shops may use one.

q: A company ships fresh fish across the country. Which channel feature matters most?

options.t: A long list of advertising slogans for the fish
options.why: Slogans are promotional content and do not keep fish fresh. For perishable goods, the logistics must protect quality during shipment.

options.t: A large selection of colors for the boxes
options.why: Box colors do not protect fresh fish from spoiling. Preserving product quality across the country is the main concern.

options.t: Temperature-controlled transport and storage
options.why: Fresh fish spoils quickly, so refrigerated transport and storage are essential. A cold chain keeps the product safe and sellable on a long trip across the country.

options.t: A high markup on each fish that is sold today
options.why: A high markup affects profit but not whether the fish arrives in good condition. Quality preservation matters most for a perishable shipment.

q: What is a distributor?

options.t: A firm that makes goods from raw materials in a large factory plant
options.why: A firm that makes goods from raw materials is a manufacturer. A distributor buys finished goods rather than producing them.

options.t: A firm that buys from producers and sells to retailers or businesses
options.why: A distributor buys goods from producers and sells them to retailers or businesses, often storing and delivering them. It connects makers with many buyers and takes on logistics.

options.t: A person who buys goods for personal use from a local retail store
options.why: A person buying for personal use is a consumer. Distributors serve retailers and businesses rather than being the end user.

options.t: A group that sets standards for an industry and gives out licenses to firms
options.why: A group that sets industry standards and issues licenses is a trade or regulatory body. It does not buy and resell goods.

q: What is a sales agent or broker in a channel?

options.t: A manufacturer who sells only through its own website and its shops
options.why: A manufacturer selling through its own channels uses a direct channel and needs no agent. Agents act as middlemen for other firms' products.

options.t: An intermediary who arranges sales for a fee without owning the goods
options.why: An agent or broker arranges sales for a fee or commission without taking ownership of the goods. This differs from wholesalers and retailers, who buy and own inventory.

options.t: A retailer who sells directly to the public from a store, mall or website
options.why: A retailer sells directly to the public and usually owns the goods it sells. An agent does not take title to the products.

options.t: A wholesaler who buys and stores large quantities of goods for resale
options.why: A wholesaler buys and stores goods in large quantities for resale, so it owns the inventory. An agent or broker does not.

q: A small craft brewer wants to reach stores in several states without hiring its own sales team. Which choice fits best?

options.t: Raise prices until the stores call and ask to buy it
options.why: Raising prices does not create demand or help reach stores. A brewer without a sales team needs a way to be sold, not a higher price.

options.t: Wait for stores to find the brewery by pure chance
options.why: Waiting for chance discovery is not a strategy and would give slow, unreliable growth across several states. The brewer needs an active channel.

options.t: Sell only at its own taproom door to walk-in guests
options.why: Selling only at its taproom limits reach to walk-in guests. The goal is stores in several states, which a taproom cannot supply.

options.t: Use a distributor that already serves those stores
options.why: A distributor already has relationships and delivery systems for those stores. Using one lets a small brewer reach many states without building its own sales force.

q: What is a franchise as a distribution model?

options.t: Independent owners sell a company's products under its brand and rules
options.why: In a franchise, independent owners sell the franchisor's products or services under its brand name and rules, in return for fees. This expands distribution with the owners' own capital.

options.t: A store owned by the producer's employees to share all the profits
options.why: A store owned by a producer's employees is an employee-owned or company store. Franchisees are independent owners, not the employees of the producer.

options.t: A government-run store that sells goods at fixed state prices only
options.why: A government-run store with fixed prices is a state enterprise. Franchises are private businesses that follow a brand's system.

options.t: A store that sells only used goods bought from the public each week
options.why: A used-goods store is a secondhand or resale shop. A franchise is defined by licensed brand use and not by selling used goods.

q: What is vendor-managed inventory?

options.t: A policy that bans reorders of stock for a whole year
options.why: Banning reorders does not describe vendor-managed inventory. In VMI the supplier replenishes stock, so reordering continues but is handled by the supplier.

options.t: A system that sets prices for rivals in the same market
options.why: Setting prices for rivals is illegal price fixing. VMI is a cooperative inventory arrangement between a supplier and its customer.

options.t: A supplier monitors and refills a customer's stock
options.why: In vendor-managed inventory the supplier monitors the customer's stock levels and refills them. This reduces stockouts and ordering work for the customer.

options.t: A customer that runs the supplier's factory floor daily
options.why: A customer running the supplier's factory reverses the VMI arrangement. In VMI, the supplier takes responsibility for the customer's inventory.

q: A snack maker's employees check a grocery store's shelves and restock them automatically. What is this?

options.t: A reverse channel plan
options.why: A reverse channel moves used goods back from customers. Here the maker is restocking new snacks, which is a forward flow.

options.t: Price fixing by competitors
options.why: Price fixing is an illegal agreement between competitors. The scenario involves a cooperative supply arrangement between a snack maker and a store.

options.t: Vendor-managed inventory
options.why: The snack maker's staff check the store's shelves and restock them, so the supplier manages the customer's inventory. That arrangement is vendor-managed inventory.

options.t: Disintermediation plan
options.why: Disintermediation means removing middlemen. The grocery store remains in the channel here, so the snack maker is only managing its stock.

q: What are shipping terms such as FOB used for?

options.t: Showing who pays for shipping and bears risk during transport
options.why: FOB and similar terms state who pays shipping costs and who bears the risk of loss or damage during transport. They show when ownership responsibility passes to the buyer.

options.t: Deciding which employees ship orders and when they pack
options.why: Choosing which employees ship orders is an internal staffing decision. Shipping terms are contract terms between buyer and seller.

options.t: Choosing advertising for a shipment of goods to a store
options.why: Advertising choices are promotion decisions. Shipping terms such as FOB only set the responsibilities for transport costs and risk.

options.t: Setting the color of a shipping box for the goods inside
options.why: Box color is a packaging design choice. Shipping terms such as FOB are about cost and risk, not appearance.

q: Under FOB shipping point, who bears the risk once goods leave the seller's dock?

options.t: The carrier
options.why: The carrier moves the goods but does not own them. Under FOB shipping point, risk transfers to the buyer, with the carrier only transporting for them.

options.t: No one
options.why: Someone always bears the risk of loss. FOB shipping point assigns it to the buyer once goods leave the seller's dock.

options.t: The seller
options.why: The seller bears the risk only until goods are loaded at the seller's dock under FOB shipping point. After that the buyer is responsible.

options.t: The buyer
options.why: Under FOB shipping point, title and risk pass to the buyer when goods leave the seller's dock. The buyer typically pays freight and handles any claims for damage in transit.

q: What is last-mile delivery?

options.t: The step of designing the product for the final buyer
options.why: Designing a product is a development step at the start, not a delivery step. Last-mile delivery concerns the final movement to the customer.

options.t: The final step of moving a product to the customer's door
options.why: Last-mile delivery is the final leg of moving a product from a local hub or store to the customer's door. It is often the most costly and visible part of shipping.

options.t: The first step of moving raw materials to a factory in the chain
options.why: Moving raw materials to a factory is early supply chain inbound logistics. Last-mile refers to the end of the delivery process.

options.t: The step of setting the retail price for the customer
options.why: Setting the retail price is a pricing decision. Last-mile delivery is a physical logistics step.

q: A retailer offers same-day delivery in a city. Which channel cost is most affected?

options.t: Cost of designing the logo
options.why: A logo is a branding cost, unaffected by delivery speed. Same-day delivery changes transport and handling expenses.

options.t: Cost of staff training only
options.why: Staff training is only a small part of costs and does not rise because of speed. Fast local delivery mainly increases transport and handling costs.

options.t: Cost of making the product
options.why: Production cost does not depend on delivery speed. Same-day delivery affects how the finished goods are brought to the customer.

options.t: Last-mile delivery cost
options.why: Same-day delivery requires quick local transport, extra drivers and often smaller loads, so last-mile delivery cost rises most. It is the final and most expensive leg of shipping.

q: What is a warehouse management system?

options.t: Software that tracks stock locations and movements in a warehouse
options.why: A warehouse management system is software that tracks stock locations and movements in a warehouse. It helps staff find items, fill orders and keep records accurate.

options.t: A system that sets customer prices for goods in a large shop
options.why: Setting customer prices is a pricing function, not warehouse software. A WMS manages inventory handling inside the warehouse.

options.t: A system that pays employees their wages each month on payday
options.why: Paying wages is handled by payroll software. A WMS concentrates on stock, locations and warehouse activity.

options.t: A system that writes advertisements and slogans for the firm
options.why: Writing advertisements is a promotion task. A warehouse management system has no role in creating slogans or ads.

q: What is cross-docking?

options.t: Returning goods to the maker for repair or a full refund of the price
options.why: Returning goods for repair or refund is reverse logistics. Cross-docking is about quickly passing goods through a facility toward customers.

options.t: Moving goods straight from incoming to outgoing trucks with little storage
options.why: In cross-docking, goods move directly from incoming trucks to outgoing trucks with little or no storage. This cuts handling, storage costs and delivery time.

options.t: Storing goods for many months before sale, in a large warehouse near the factory
options.why: Storing goods for months is the opposite of cross-docking, which is designed to avoid storage and move products through quickly.

options.t: Selling goods at a loss to clear stock from the warehouse shelves
options.why: Selling goods at a loss to clear stock is a clearance strategy. Cross-docking is a logistics method, not a pricing approach.

q: A retailer wants to shorten the time goods spend in storage. Which practice helps?

options.t: Ordering far more than needed from suppliers
options.why: Ordering far more than needed increases inventory and the time goods sit in storage, which is the opposite of the goal.

options.t: Storing goods in several buildings across town
options.why: Using more buildings spreads inventory and adds handling, so goods stay in storage no faster. It does not shorten storage time.

options.t: Cross-docking goods from arrival to shipment
options.why: Cross-docking moves goods straight from arriving trucks to outgoing shipments with little storage. That cuts the time goods spend in the warehouse.

options.t: Holding goods until prices rise again later
options.why: Holding goods until prices rise lengthens storage time and ties up money, so it does not shorten time in storage.

q: What is channel power?

options.t: The speed of a delivery truck on the highway at night time
options.why: Truck speed is a transport factor, not power. Channel power is about one member's ability to influence other members.

options.t: The ability of one channel member to influence others' decisions
options.why: Channel power is the ability of one channel member, such as a large retailer, to influence the decisions and actions of other members. It comes from size, information or control of customers.

options.t: The electricity used by a warehouse, billed to the owner each month
options.why: Electricity used by a warehouse is an operating expense. Channel power refers to influence among channel members, not energy.

options.t: The size of a store's parking lot for its customers' cars
options.why: Parking lot size is a facilities detail. It has no connection to influence in a distribution channel.

q: A giant retailer demands lower prices from a small supplier or threatens to drop it. What does this show?

options.t: Price discrimination between customers
options.why: Price discrimination means charging different customers different prices for the same product. Here a retailer pressures its supplier, which is a different situation.

options.t: Direct marketing to buyers online
options.why: Direct marketing communicates with buyers directly. The scenario shows a retailer forcing terms on a supplier, not marketing to customers.

options.t: A reverse channel for old goods
options.why: A reverse channel moves used goods back from customers. The retailer is demanding lower prices from a supplier, not returning goods.

options.t: Channel power held by the retailer
options.why: The giant retailer is able to demand lower prices and threaten to drop the supplier. This ability to influence another channel member is channel power.

q: What are channel partner incentives?

options.t: Rewards that encourage resellers to promote and stock a product
options.why: Channel partner incentives are rewards such as bonuses, discounts or prizes that motivate resellers to promote, stock and sell a product more actively.

options.t: Penalties for selling too much of a product each month by resellers
options.why: Penalties for selling too much would discourage sales, the opposite of incentives. Producers want resellers to sell more.

options.t: Fines for late deliveries made by the resellers to buyers
options.why: Fines for late deliveries are penalties, not incentives. Incentives reward good performance rather than punish poor performance.

options.t: Taxes paid by resellers on the goods that they sell each year
options.why: Taxes are charged by governments. Incentives come from producers to encourage partner effort, not from taxes on goods.

q: A maker offers a bonus to stores that display its product at eye level. What is this?

options.t: A warranty offer
options.why: A warranty offers customers repair or replacement of defective goods. A bonus for stores displaying products is paid to resellers instead.

options.t: A recall notice
options.why: A recall notice informs people of a defective product that must be returned. It has nothing to do with a bonus for display placement.

options.t: A channel incentive
options.why: A bonus paid to stores for eye-level display rewards resellers for supporting the product. That reward is a channel incentive.

options.t: A tariff on goods
options.why: A tariff is a government tax on imported goods. A maker's bonus to stores is a producer-paid incentive, not a tariff.

q: What is a trade show used for in channel management?

options.t: Printing labels for shipments sent out by the warehouse staff
options.why: Printing shipping labels is a warehouse task. A trade show is an event where companies display products to attract buyers.

options.t: Meeting buyers and resellers to show products and make deals
options.why: At a trade show, producers meet buyers and resellers to show products, build relationships and make deals. It is an efficient way to find new channel partners.

options.t: Counting the stock inside a warehouse once each year by staff
options.why: Counting warehouse stock is an inventory process. Trade shows are marketing events, not stock counts.

options.t: Setting the price of products for customers in the stores
options.why: Setting product prices is a management decision. Trade shows focus on meeting buyers and displaying products rather than setting prices.

q: What is selective distribution?

options.t: Using every possible outlet that is open in the whole region
options.why: Using every possible outlet is intensive distribution. Selective distribution limits outlets rather than using them all.

options.t: Using only one outlet in a region, so the brand controls sales
options.why: Using one outlet in a region is exclusive distribution, which gives maximum brand control. Selective distribution uses more than one.

options.t: Using a moderate number of outlets chosen for fit with the brand
options.why: Selective distribution uses a moderate number of outlets chosen for fit with the brand image and service. It balances reach with control, as with many appliance or clothing brands.

options.t: Using no outlets at all, and selling only by mail or by phone
options.why: Using no outlets and selling only by mail or phone is a direct marketing approach. Selective distribution still sells through chosen outlets.

q: A sports shoe brand sells in a limited number of specialty running stores. Which strategy is this?

options.t: Exclusive distribution
options.why: Exclusive distribution gives one outlet sole rights in an area. A brand using several specialty stores uses more than one outlet, so it is not exclusive.

options.t: Intensive distribution
options.why: Intensive distribution places a product in as many outlets as possible. A limited set of specialty stores is the opposite.

options.t: Direct online selling
options.why: Direct online selling skips retailers. The brand here uses specialty running stores, so it is selling through intermediaries.

options.t: Selective distribution
options.why: Using a limited number of specialty stores chosen for fit with the brand is selective distribution. It balances reach with image and customer service.

q: What is reverse logistics?

options.t: Moving products back from customers for return, repair or recycling
options.why: Reverse logistics moves products back from customers for return, repair, resale or recycling. It handles returns efficiently and can recover value from used goods.

options.t: Moving products forward to customers faster, using more trucks
options.why: Moving products forward to customers faster is normal forward logistics. Reverse logistics runs in the opposite direction.

options.t: Running trucks in reverse gear along the roads to the depot
options.why: Driving trucks in reverse gear is a literal misreading. The term refers to the backward flow of goods from customers to sellers.

options.t: Cutting prices to move old stock out of the warehouse quickly
options.why: Cutting prices to clear stock is a markdown strategy. Reverse logistics concerns returned goods and not price changes.

q: A company collects used printer cartridges and recycles them. What is this?

options.t: Mass distribution
options.why: Mass distribution means selling widely to the whole market. Collecting used cartridges is a flow of goods back from customers.

options.t: Price skimming
options.why: Price skimming sets a high price on a new product at launch. It is unrelated to collecting used items.

options.t: A reverse channel
options.why: Collecting used printer cartridges and recycling them moves products backward from customers to the company. That backward flow is a reverse channel.

options.t: Direct selling
options.why: Direct selling sells products straight to consumers. The scenario describes recovering used products, which is a different flow.

q: What is a service level agreement (SLA) in a channel?

options.t: A contract that sets the delivery and performance standards a partner must meet
options.why: An SLA is a contract that sets the delivery and performance standards, such as on-time rates, that a partner must meet. It makes expectations clear and measurable.

options.t: A rule about advertising colors that applies to all of the partner firms
options.why: Rules about advertising colors are brand guidelines. An SLA concerns service and performance levels that partners must meet.

options.t: A discount for large orders that a supplier gives to its regular steady buyers
options.why: A volume discount is a pricing incentive for large orders. An SLA sets service standards rather than prices.

options.t: A tax form for shipping firms, filed each year with the customs agency
options.why: A tax form for shipping firms is a government document. An SLA is a business contract between channel partners.

q: A retailer's contract says suppliers must deliver 98 percent of orders on time. What is this?

options.t: A price war in retail
options.why: A price war is competition through repeated price cuts. The contract described sets delivery performance standards instead.

options.t: A service level agreement
options.why: A contract that requires 98 percent of orders delivered on time sets a measurable standard. That is a service level agreement, which defines expected performance.

options.t: A trade show invitation
options.why: A trade show invitation asks businesses to attend an event. It does not set delivery obligations for suppliers.

options.t: A product recall notice
options.why: A product recall notice tells buyers to return defective goods. It has no connection to on-time delivery targets.

q: Why do producers evaluate channel partners regularly?

options.t: To raise the price of products for no reason each month
options.why: Raising prices for no reason would harm partners and customers. Evaluation is about checking performance, not changing prices without cause.

options.t: To avoid speaking with partners about their results
options.why: Avoiding conversations about results defeats the purpose of an evaluation. Reviews involve discussing results and fixing issues with partners.

options.t: To remove all partners from the channel right now
options.why: Removing all partners would destroy the channel. Regular evaluation aims to keep good partners and improve or replace only weak ones.

options.t: To make sure partners meet sales and service goals
options.why: Evaluating partners regularly confirms they meet sales, service and quality goals. It lets producers reward strong performers and address problems before customers are hurt.

q: A distributor often delivers late and loses orders for a producer. What should the producer do?

options.t: Raise the price paid to the distributor with no changes each year
options.why: Raising the price paid to a poorly performing distributor rewards the problem and does nothing to fix late deliveries and lost orders.

options.t: Blame the final customers for the late deliveries and losses
options.why: Blaming final customers is unfair and solves nothing. The distributor causes the late deliveries, so the producer must address the distributor's performance.

options.t: Ignore the problem to keep things simple for the firm and staff
options.why: Ignoring the problem allows lost orders to continue and hurts customer relationships. Late deliveries need action from the producer.

options.t: Review performance and fix, support or replace the distributor
options.why: The producer should review performance, then fix the problem with feedback, support or training, or replace the distributor if it fails to improve. This protects customers and sales.

q: What is observational research?

options.t: Watching how people behave without asking them questions
options.why: Observational research collects data by watching how people behave, such as which products they pick up, without asking questions. It records real actions instead of stated opinions.

options.t: Reading industry reports written by others last year
options.why: Reading industry reports is secondary research, using data that others already collected. Observation gathers fresh data directly.

options.t: Testing prices on a single product in a few stores
options.why: Testing prices in a few stores is an experiment or test market. Observational research does not change conditions, it just watches.

options.t: Asking people to fill out long written surveys about habits
options.why: Long written surveys ask people questions, which is survey research. Observation avoids asking and instead watches behavior.

q: A store records which aisles shoppers walk down and where they pause. What research method is this?

options.t: A focus group
options.why: A focus group is a guided discussion with a small group. Recording shopper movement involves watching behavior, not discussion.

options.t: Observation
options.why: Recording where shoppers walk and pause is watching behavior without asking questions. That is observation, which shows actual shopping patterns in the store.

options.t: A phone survey
options.why: A phone survey asks people questions by telephone. The store here simply records what shoppers do.

options.t: Desk research
options.why: Desk research reviews existing information. The store is gathering new data from watching shoppers, so it is primary research.

q: What is an experiment in marketing research?

options.t: Guessing which price customers prefer without any tests
options.why: Guessing without tests is not research. An experiment is a controlled test that gathers evidence about cause and effect.

options.t: Counting the number of stores in a region and writing totals
options.why: Counting stores is a simple data collection task. An experiment changes something to see how it affects results.

options.t: Testing a change in one factor to see its effect on results
options.why: An experiment tests a change in one factor, such as price or package, to see its effect on results while keeping other things the same. It shows cause and effect.

options.t: Copying a competitor's price exactly, every single week
options.why: Copying a competitor's price is an imitation tactic. It is not a test designed to measure how a change affects results.

q: A retailer shows two versions of a web page to different visitors to see which sells more. What is this?

options.t: A census
options.why: A census collects data from every member of a population. Showing two page versions to visitors is a test, not a full count.

options.t: A/B testing
options.why: A/B testing shows two versions to different visitors to see which performs better. It is a marketing experiment that compares results to guide decisions.

options.t: A focus group
options.why: A focus group is a moderated discussion. Showing different versions to different visitors is not a discussion.

options.t: A trend report
options.why: A trend report summarizes changes over time. It does not compare versions of a page by showing them to visitors.

q: What is a customer panel?

options.t: A group of employees who sell products in shops
options.why: Employees who sell products are a sales team. A customer panel is made up of customers, not staff.

options.t: A group of suppliers who set prices for goods sold
options.why: Suppliers who set prices are sellers and not a panel of customers. Customer panels provide feedback, not pricing.

options.t: A group of retailers who sign contracts with the maker
options.why: Retailers who sign contracts with a maker are channel partners. A customer panel consists of customers.

options.t: A group of customers who give feedback over time
options.why: A customer panel is a group of customers who give feedback over time. It shows how opinions and behavior change and helps test new ideas.

q: What is a census?

options.t: A study of a small group chosen at random from the population
options.why: A study of a small random group is a sample survey. A census collects data from the whole population.

options.t: A study of a single competitor in the same market area
options.why: A study of one competitor is a case study or competitive analysis. A census covers every member of a population, not a single firm.

options.t: A study that collects data from every member of a population
options.why: A census collects data from every member of a population. It is complete but can be costly and slow, which is why samples are often used.

options.t: A study of past reports only, with no new data collected
options.why: Studying past reports only uses secondary data. A census collects new data directly from all members.

q: Why do businesses usually use samples instead of a census?

options.t: Samples are faster and cheaper than studying everyone
options.why: Samples can be gathered faster and at lower cost than studying everyone. A well chosen sample gives reliable results without the expense of a census.

options.t: Samples are always more accurate than any census
options.why: Samples are not always more accurate. A census has no sampling error, but samples are chosen for speed and cost.

options.t: A census is illegal for businesses in most countries
options.why: A census is not generally illegal for businesses. Samples are used because a census is expensive and slow.

options.t: Samples avoid the need to ask any questions at all
options.why: Samples still ask questions, or observe people. A sample just uses a smaller group, so questions are still required.

q: What is a margin of error?

options.t: The number of questions on a survey that people have to fill out online
options.why: The number of questions is the survey length. Margin of error measures how much results might differ from the true population value.

options.t: The profit a company makes on each product, as a percent of its price
options.why: Profit as a percent of price is a profit margin, which is a different concept from a survey's margin of error.

options.t: The range within which a survey result is likely to vary from the true value
options.why: A margin of error gives the range within which survey results are likely to differ from the true population value. Smaller margins come from larger samples.

options.t: The cost of running a survey, including the fees paid to the staff who do it
options.why: Survey cost is a budget item. Margin of error describes the statistical accuracy of the results.

q: A poll says 52% of customers prefer a flavor with a margin of error of 5 points. What does this mean?

options.t: The true value is likely between 47% and 57%
options.why: With 52% and a 5 point margin, the true value is likely between 47% and 57% (52 - 5 and 52 + 5). The result is an estimate, not an exact figure.

options.t: Exactly 52% of all customers prefer the flavor
options.why: The poll is a sample, so 52% is an estimate. The margin of error shows that the true value may differ from 52%.

options.t: Between 40% and 60% of customers prefer it
options.why: A 5 point margin gives a range from 47% to 57%, not 40% to 60%. That range would require a margin of 12 points either way.

options.t: Nobody prefers the flavor among all customers
options.why: A result of 52% with a 5 point margin cannot mean nobody prefers the flavor. The range from 47% to 57% shows many prefer it.

q: What is a closed-ended question?

options.t: A question that allows any written answer
options.why: A question allowing any written answer is open-ended. Closed-ended questions limit the answers to fixed choices.

options.t: A question that no one can ever answer at all
options.why: Questions that no one can answer would be useless. A closed-ended question can be answered easily by choosing from options.

options.t: A question that asks for a long story in writing
options.why: Asking for a long story is an open-ended question. Closed-ended questions have simple, fixed choices.

options.t: A question with a fixed set of answer choices
options.why: A closed-ended question offers a fixed set of answer choices, such as yes or no or multiple choice. Answers are easy to tabulate and compare.

q: Which is an open-ended survey question?

options.t: Are you satisfied with us: yes or no?
options.why: Yes or no allows only two answers, so it is closed-ended. Open-ended questions let people respond in their own words.

options.t: What do you like most about our store?
options.why: 'What do you like most about our store?' has no fixed answers, so respondents reply in their own words. That makes it open-ended, giving richer detail.

options.t: Rate our service from 1 to 5 stars.
options.why: A 1 to 5 rating offers fixed choices on a scale. That makes it a closed-ended rating scale question.

options.t: Do you shop here weekly, monthly or never?
options.why: Weekly, monthly or never gives a fixed list of choices. It is a closed-ended multiple choice question.

q: What is a rating scale question?

options.t: A question that asks for a home address and a phone number
options.why: An address and phone number are contact details. A rating scale question asks for an opinion on a numeric scale.

options.t: A question that asks for a story about the customer's last visit
options.why: A story about the last visit is an open-ended question. Rating scales use numbers rather than free narratives.

options.t: A question that asks for a name only, nothing else at all
options.why: Asking for a name is a simple identification question, not a rating. Rating scale questions require choosing a point on a scale.

options.t: A question that asks respondents to choose a number on a scale
options.why: A rating scale question asks respondents to choose a number on a scale, such as 1 to 5, to show their opinion. It measures degree and is easy to analyze.

q: What is data analysis?

options.t: Collecting data without examining it, storing it for later
options.why: Collecting data without examining it is only data gathering. Analysis requires reviewing the data to learn something from it.

options.t: Deleting data to save space on the company computers
options.why: Deleting data does not produce insight. Analysis examines data to learn from it, not to remove it.

options.t: Examining data to find patterns and draw conclusions
options.why: Data analysis examines data to find patterns and draw conclusions that help make decisions. Marketers use it to understand customers and measure results.

options.t: Printing data on paper for the files in the office cabinet
options.why: Printing data for filing only stores it. Analysis requires studying the data to find meaning.

q: Sales data show most customers buy on Fridays. How should the store use this?

options.t: Schedule more staff and promotions for Fridays
options.why: If most customers buy on Fridays, scheduling more staff and promotions that day serves them and increases sales. Good analysis leads to practical action.

options.t: Stop recording sales and ignore what customers buy
options.why: Ignoring what customers buy wastes useful information. Sales data should be used to guide decisions, not discarded.

options.t: Raise prices only on Mondays, as customers shop less
options.why: Raising prices only on Mondays does not respond to Friday demand. It is also unrelated to the pattern the data revealed.

options.t: Close the store on Fridays to save on staff costs
options.why: Closing on Fridays would lose the busiest day of sales. The data shows Friday is the best day to be open.

q: What is sales forecasting?

options.t: Setting the price of products sold in the shop each day
options.why: Setting prices is a pricing decision. Sales forecasting predicts future sales and does not set what products cost.

options.t: Estimating future sales using past data and trends
options.why: Sales forecasting estimates future sales using past data, trends and market conditions. Businesses use forecasts to plan inventory, staffing and budgets.

options.t: Counting stock in a warehouse at the end of each month
options.why: Counting stock is an inventory task. Forecasting looks forward rather than recording what is on hand.

options.t: Recording sales that happened in the past quarter
options.why: Recording past sales is bookkeeping. Forecasting uses past sales to predict future sales.

q: A shop sold 800 units last December and expects 10 percent growth. What is its forecast?

options.t: 900 units
options.why: 900 units would be 12.5% growth over 800. Ten percent growth means 800 x 0.10 = 80 extra units, so the forecast is 880.

options.t: 8,000 units
options.why: 8,000 units is ten times 800, which would mean 900% growth. A 10 percent increase adds only 80 units to 800.

options.t: 810 units
options.why: 810 units adds 10 units instead of 10 percent. Ten percent of 800 is 80, so the forecast is higher.

options.t: 880 units
options.why: Growth of 10 percent on 800 units is 800 x 0.10 = 80. Adding gives 800 + 80 = 880 units as the forecast.

q: What is a key performance indicator (KPI) in marketing?

options.t: A description of a brand's colors, fonts and logo in its ads
options.why: Brand colors and fonts describe visual identity. A KPI measures progress toward a goal in numbers.

options.t: A measurable value showing how well a marketing goal is being met
options.why: A KPI is a measurable value showing how well a marketing goal is being met, such as conversion rate or sales growth. It helps teams track progress and adjust plans.

options.t: A record of employees' birthdays and their start dates at work
options.why: Employee birthdays are personnel records. They do not measure marketing results.

options.t: A list of competitors and the prices they charge for their goods
options.why: A list of competitors is market information. A KPI is a measurable value tied to an objective, and not a list of rivals.

q: What is a conversion rate?

options.t: The number of employees hired by the firm during the last year of work
options.why: Employee hiring counts are a human resources number. Conversion rate measures customers taking an action.

options.t: The rate at which a currency changes into another for a traveler
options.why: Currency exchange rates describe money changing between currencies. A marketing conversion rate measures customer actions.

options.t: The share of people reached who take the desired action, such as buying
options.why: Conversion rate is the share of people reached who take the desired action, such as buying or signing up. It shows how effective marketing is at turning interest into results.

options.t: The speed of a website when it loads on a mobile phone for a visitor
options.why: Website load speed is a performance measure. It does not describe the share of visitors who take an action.

q: 1,000 people see an offer and 50 buy. What is the conversion rate?

options.why: Conversion rate is buyers divided by people reached: 50 / 1,000 = 0.05, or 5%. This shows the share of viewers who took the desired action.
50% would mean 500 of the 1,000 people bought. Only 50 bought, which is a much smaller share.
20% would require 200 buyers out of 1,000. With 50 buyers, 50 / 1,000 gives a lower rate.
0.5% would be 5 buyers per 1,000 people. The 50 buyers make 5%, so the decimal point is misplaced.

q: What is return on marketing investment (ROMI)?

options.t: The profit gained from marketing relative to what was spent
options.why: ROMI measures profit gained from marketing relative to what was spent. A positive ROMI shows marketing creates more value than it costs.

options.t: The size of a marketing team and the pay of its staff members
options.why: Team size and pay are staffing details. ROMI compares marketing returns to marketing spending.

options.t: The cost of one advertisement placed in a local newspaper
options.why: The cost of one ad is a single expense. ROMI compares total return with total investment.

options.t: The total number of ads shown, counted by the agency
options.why: Counting ads shown is a reach or impression metric. It does not measure financial return.

q: A campaign costs $2,000 and produces $5,000 in profit. What is the net gain?

options.why: $7,000 adds the cost to the profit ($2,000 + $5,000). The net gain subtracts the cost from the return rather than adding.
Net gain is the return minus the cost: $5,000 - $2,000 = $3,000. This treats the $5,000 as the return from the campaign and subtracts what was spent.
$5,000 is the stated return before subtracting the $2,000 spent. Net gain accounts for the campaign cost, so it must be lower.
$2,500 would come from dividing $5,000 by 2, which is not how net gain is found. Subtract the $2,000 cost from the $5,000 return.

q: What is customer segmentation by behavior?

options.t: Grouping customers alphabetically by their name
options.why: Alphabetical grouping by name sorts a list but says nothing about buying behavior. Behavioral segmentation uses actions.

options.t: Grouping customers by the color of their clothes
options.why: Clothing color has no relation to how people buy or use products, so it does not form a useful segment.

options.t: Grouping customers by the day they were born only
options.why: Birth day alone is not behavior. Behavioral segmentation uses actions such as purchase frequency or loyalty.

options.t: Grouping customers by how they buy and use products
options.why: Behavioral segmentation groups customers by how they buy and use products, such as purchase frequency, brand loyalty or usage rate. It helps tailor offers to each group.

q: A store sends special offers to customers who have not bought in six months. What is this?

options.t: Channel conflict among sellers
options.why: Channel conflict is a dispute between channel members. Sending offers to lapsed customers is a marketing action, not a dispute.

options.t: Price fixing among competitors
options.why: Price fixing is an illegal agreement among competitors. A store offering deals to its own customers is not that.

options.t: Targeting a behavior-based segment
options.why: Offers aimed at customers who have not bought in six months target a segment based on buying behavior. That is behavior-based segmentation used to win them back.

options.t: Mass marketing to everyone equally
options.why: Mass marketing sends the same message to everyone. The store selected a specific group of customers, so this is targeted.

q: What is market research ethics?

options.t: Selling personal data to anyone who wants to buy it
options.why: Selling personal data to anyone is a privacy violation. Research ethics protects participants and their information.

options.t: Changing results to look better for the client who pays
options.why: Changing results to please a client is data manipulation. Ethical research reports findings honestly.

options.t: Collecting data without telling people, as is normal
options.why: Collecting data without telling people breaks the principle of informed consent. Ethical research tells participants what is collected.

options.t: Honest, fair treatment of participants and their data
options.why: Market research ethics means honest, fair treatment of participants and their data, with consent and privacy protected. It keeps trust and ensures reliable findings.

q: A researcher changes survey results to make a client happy. What is this?

options.t: A sampling technique for surveys
options.why: Sampling is a method of choosing respondents. Changing results is not a sampling technique at all.

options.t: A normal practice in research
options.why: Manipulating results is not normal practice. Professional codes of conduct forbid altering findings.

options.t: Unethical manipulation of data
options.why: Altering survey results to please a client is unethical manipulation. It misleads decision makers and violates professional research standards.

options.t: A way to protect user privacy
options.why: Changing results does not protect privacy. Privacy protection involves safeguarding participant information, which is a different matter.

q: What is a loyalty card used for in market research?

options.t: Collecting data on what members buy and how often
options.why: Loyalty cards record what members buy and how often. This purchase data helps stores understand habits and tailor offers.

options.t: Replacing all surveys, as purchases show everything
options.why: Purchase data does not replace surveys because it shows what people buy but not why. Surveys reveal opinions and motives.

options.t: Raising prices for members who have a loyalty card
options.why: A loyalty card is meant to reward customers, not to increase their prices. Raising prices for members would defeat its purpose.

options.t: Hiding what customers buy from the store owner
options.why: Loyalty card data goes to the store, which uses it to learn about customers. It does not hide purchases from the owner.

q: Loyalty card data shows a customer buys diapers and then baby food. What can the store do?

options.t: Send offers for totally unrelated items
options.why: Offers for unrelated items would waste money and miss the shopper's needs. The data points to baby products.

options.t: Send relevant offers for baby products
options.why: Buying diapers and baby food suggests a family with a baby. Sending relevant baby product offers meets real needs and is likely to produce sales.

options.t: Stop sending any offers to the shopper
options.why: Stopping offers wastes an opportunity. The data shows what the shopper wants and should be used to help them.

options.t: Share the data publicly on a website
options.why: Posting customer data publicly violates privacy and may break laws. Customer data should be kept secure and used responsibly.

q: What is syndicated data?

options.t: Data with no source that anyone can read for free in a library
options.why: Syndicated data is not free and without a source. It is collected by a research firm and sold to clients.

options.t: Market data collected by a research firm and sold to many clients
options.why: Syndicated data is market data collected by a research firm and sold to many clients. Examples include retail audits and TV ratings, which save each client the cost of collecting it.

options.t: Data that is secret and kept inside one single company only
options.why: Secret data kept in one company is proprietary internal data. Syndicated data is shared with many paying clients.

options.t: Data collected by one company for its own use only and kept private
options.why: Data collected by one company for its own use is primary research. Syndicated data is sold to multiple clients.

q: What is a competitive intelligence report?

options.t: A list of employee names and the jobs that each of them does
options.why: A list of employee names is a staff directory. A competitive intelligence report focuses on rivals.

options.t: A summary of the company's own profit and dividends paid out
options.why: A summary of the company's own profit is a financial report. Competitive intelligence studies other firms.

options.t: A report of a store's opening hours and its holiday closing days
options.why: Store hours are basic business details. A competitive report analyzes rivals' strategy.

options.t: A summary of information about rivals' products, prices and plans
options.why: A competitive intelligence report summarizes information about rivals' products, prices and plans. It helps a firm respond to competitors and spot opportunities, using legal sources.

q: A firm studies a rival's public price list and ads. What kind of information is this?

options.t: Primary survey data it gathered
options.why: Primary survey data is collected directly by the firm. A rival's public price list already exists, so this is not primary data.

options.t: Confidential data from the rival
options.why: A rival's public price list and ads are open to anyone, so the data is not confidential. Confidential data would be hidden from the public.

options.t: Secondary competitive information
options.why: Studying a rival's public price list and ads uses existing, publicly available information. That is secondary competitive information and is legal and ethical to collect.

options.t: Stolen trade secrets of the rival
options.why: Public prices and ads are not trade secrets. Trade secrets are confidential information, and taking them would be illegal.

q: What is a dealer network?

options.t: A group of independent businesses authorized to sell a maker's products
options.why: A dealer network is a group of independent businesses authorized to sell a maker's products. Car and equipment makers use dealers to reach local customers.

options.t: A group of workers who deliver a maker's products to customers' homes each day
options.why: Workers delivering products are a delivery staff. A dealer network is a group of independent sellers.

options.t: A group of competitors who set prices together for the same goods
options.why: Competitors who set prices together would be breaking antitrust laws. A dealer network is a channel structure.

options.t: A group of customers who review products for a living at stores
options.why: Customers who review products are reviewers. Dealers are businesses that sell a maker's products.

q: A car maker sells vehicles through independently owned local dealerships. What is this?

options.t: A cold chain for perishable goods
options.why: A cold chain handles perishable goods. A car maker selling through dealers is a distribution arrangement.

options.t: An indirect channel using dealers
options.why: Selling through independently owned dealerships places intermediaries between the maker and the buyer. That is an indirect channel using dealers.

options.t: A reverse channel for old cars
options.why: A reverse channel moves used goods back from customers. The car maker is selling new vehicles forward.

options.t: A direct channel selling to buyers
options.why: A direct channel sells straight to buyers. Using independent dealerships means the maker sells through intermediaries.

q: What is a stock keeping unit (SKU)?

options.t: A price tag on a shelf that shows the cost of one single item
options.why: A price tag shows cost. An SKU is a code that identifies a product variant for inventory.

options.t: A tax code for imported goods used at the border by customs
options.why: A tax code for imports is a customs classification. An SKU is used inside a business for inventory.

options.t: A slogan for a product that is used in the firm's ads and signs
options.why: A slogan is a promotional phrase. An SKU is a code and has no advertising purpose.

options.t: A unique code that identifies a specific product for inventory
options.why: An SKU is a unique code that identifies a specific product, including its size or color, for inventory tracking. It lets stores count and reorder each variation accurately.

q: A shirt comes in three sizes and four colors. How many SKUs does it have?

options.why: Each size and color combination is a separate SKU, so 3 sizes x 4 colors = 12 SKUs. This lets the store track each variation of the shirt.
34 comes from writing 3 and 4 side by side. SKUs are found by multiplying the options: 3 x 4 = 12.
7 comes from adding 3 and 4. Variants combine, so sizes and colors are multiplied to give 12.
One would only count the shirt as a single item. Each size and color combination has its own SKU, so there are 12.

q: What is safety stock?

options.t: Stock that is about to expire within the next few weeks or so
options.why: Stock about to expire is perishable inventory. Safety stock is extra inventory held as a buffer.

options.t: Stock that has been recalled by the maker for a safety issue
options.why: Recalled stock is defective and must be removed. Safety stock is good extra inventory kept as a buffer.

options.t: Extra inventory kept to avoid running out during delays or surges
options.why: Safety stock is extra inventory kept to avoid running out during supplier delays or demand surges. It protects sales and customer service at the cost of some storage.

options.t: Inventory kept for safety inspections only, which are held once each year
options.why: Safety stock is not for inspections. It serves as a buffer against shortages, and the goods are available for sale.

q: A supplier is sometimes late and demand spikes unexpectedly. What helps most?

options.t: Holding safety stock
options.why: Holding safety stock gives a buffer when the supplier is late or demand spikes. It prevents stockouts and lost sales.

options.t: Dropping the supplier
options.why: Dropping the supplier does not solve a demand spike and may create a new problem. A buffer of inventory is a better fix.

options.t: Ordering less, no buffer
options.why: Ordering less without a buffer increases the risk of running out when the supplier is late or demand rises.

options.t: Ignoring forecasts
options.why: Ignoring forecasts removes planning information and makes stockouts more likely. A safety stock covers uncertainty that forecasts cannot.

q: What is a data privacy notice for customers?

options.t: A list of customers' credit card numbers kept in a secure file
options.why: A list of card numbers is sensitive data that must be protected. A privacy notice informs customers about data use and does not publish it.

options.t: A report of a company's yearly profit that is sent to its owners
options.why: A yearly profit report is a financial document for owners. A privacy notice is addressed to customers about their data.

options.t: A statement telling customers what data is collected and how it is used
options.why: A data privacy notice tells customers what data is collected, why, and how it is used and protected. It supports transparency and legal compliance.

options.t: A discount code for loyal buyers that is sent out by email each month
options.why: A discount code is a promotion. A privacy notice explains data practices and does not offer deals.

q: A website collects visitors' emails but never explains why. What should it add?

options.t: A countdown timer for sales shown on the home page
options.why: A countdown timer is a sales gimmick. It does not explain why emails are collected.

options.t: A clear privacy notice explaining how emails are used
options.why: A clear privacy notice explains how collected emails will be used. This gives visitors transparency and helps meet legal requirements.

options.t: A larger logo at the top of the page for visitors
options.why: A larger logo changes the design. It does nothing to tell visitors why their emails are collected.

options.t: A new background color for the home page of the site
options.why: A new background color changes appearance only. The site needs a notice explaining its use of email data.

q: What is a cookie on a website?

options.t: A snack offered to site visitors who fill out a short form
options.why: A snack offered to visitors is a literal cookie. In web terms it is a data file.

options.t: A password for the site that a visitor can use to log in
options.why: A password is a login credential. A cookie is a small file that stores browsing information.

options.t: A coupon sent by email to a visitor of the site who signed up
options.why: A coupon sent by email is a promotion. A web cookie is stored on the visitor's device.

options.t: A small file stored on a visitor's device to remember activity
options.why: A cookie is a small file stored on a visitor's device to remember activity, such as logins or items in a cart. Websites use cookies to personalize and analyze visits.

q: Why do some websites ask visitors to accept cookies?

options.t: To hide the privacy policy from the people who visit the site
options.why: Cookie notices do not hide a privacy policy. They are meant to inform visitors about data collection.

options.t: To collect payment from visitors before they can view the page
options.why: Accepting cookies is not a payment. It is a consent step about data use.

options.t: To reduce the speed of the site, as each cookie slows loading
options.why: Cookies do not mainly slow the site. The prompt exists for privacy transparency, not performance.

options.t: To explain data collection and obtain consent where required
options.why: Sites explain that they collect data through cookies and obtain consent where laws such as GDPR require it. This respects visitors' privacy choices.

q: What is a dashboard in marketing analytics?

options.t: A display that shows key marketing numbers at a glance
options.why: A dashboard displays key marketing numbers at a glance, such as visits, sales and conversion rate. It helps managers see performance and make decisions quickly.

options.t: A tool that sets prices for each of the shop's products
options.why: Setting prices is a pricing task. A dashboard displays data and does not set prices.

options.t: A printed list of competitors posted on the office wall
options.why: A printed competitor list is a document. A dashboard is a live display of the company's own key metrics.
