q: What is a high-yield savings account?

options.t: A stock account used to trade shares
options.why: A stock account is a brokerage account used to trade shares, not a savings account, and it is not FDIC insured.

options.t: A checking account that pays no interest
options.why: A checking account that pays no interest is not a high yield account. High yield means a higher interest rate on savings.

options.t: A loan that charges a high interest rate
options.why: A loan that charges high interest is a borrowing product. A high yield savings account pays you interest.

options.t: A savings account paying a higher rate
options.why: A high yield savings account pays a higher interest rate than a regular savings account, often at online banks, and is typically FDIC insured.

q: What is inflation's effect on savings kept in cash?

options.t: Purchasing power declines over time
options.why: Inflation raises prices, so cash buys less over time. Cash that is not growing loses purchasing power.

options.t: The cash earns interest automatically
options.why: Cash kept as cash earns no interest. Only money in an interest paying account earns interest.

options.t: The cash doubles each year on its own
options.why: Cash does not grow on its own. It stays the same amount while prices rise, so it loses value in real terms.

options.t: Purchasing power increases over time
options.why: Inflation reduces purchasing power rather than increasing it, because the same amount buys fewer goods as prices go up.

q: A savings account pays 1% interest while inflation is 3%. What is happening to the real value of the savings?

options.t: It is doubling every year on its own with no help at all
options.why: Savings do not double every year on their own. At 1 percent interest, the balance grows very slowly.

options.t: It is staying exactly the same, as nothing has changed
options.why: The balance grows by 1 percent, but prices rise 3 percent, so the real value is not staying the same.

options.t: It is decreasing because inflation outpaces interest
options.why: Real value falls because inflation (3 percent) is higher than interest (1 percent). The real return is about 1 - 3 = negative 2 percent a year.

options.t: It is increasing because interest earned is positive
options.why: Interest is positive, but real value depends on inflation too. With prices up 3 percent and interest only 1 percent, buying power declines.

q: What is the main purpose of a college savings plan such as a 529?

options.t: To buy individual stocks only, with no other aim at all
options.why: A 529 plan is designed for education savings, not for buying individual stocks only, though funds may be invested.

options.t: To save for education expenses with tax advantages
options.why: A 529 plan is a tax advantaged account for education costs, with tax free growth and withdrawals when used for qualified expenses.

options.t: To save for family vacations only, and for nothing else
options.why: A 529 plan is meant for education, not family vacations. Using it for non education costs can bring taxes and penalties.

options.t: To pay off credit card bills each month for the family
options.why: A 529 plan is for education costs, not paying off credit cards. Credit card payments are not qualified expenses.

q: Which of these is a good reason to keep money in a savings account instead of a checking account?

options.t: Savings accounts allow unlimited checks
options.why: Savings accounts do not allow unlimited checks. Checking accounts are the ones made for frequent payments and check writing.

options.t: Savings accounts require no deposits
options.why: Deposits are needed to build savings. A savings account is not defined by requiring no deposits.

options.t: Savings accounts have no safety at all
options.why: Savings accounts are usually FDIC insured, so claiming they have no safety at all is false.

options.t: Savings accounts usually pay interest
options.why: Savings accounts usually pay interest, while many checking accounts pay little or none, which is the main reason to keep savings there.

q: What is the main reason to read a contract before signing?

options.t: To avoid having to talk with the seller in person
options.why: Contracts are about legal terms, not conversation; avoiding the seller does not protect you, and reading the document is what actually prevents costly surprises later.

options.t: To make the document last longer on a shelf for years
options.why: Reading has no effect on how long paper lasts; the purpose of reviewing a contract is to learn the terms you are legally agreeing to follow.

options.t: To understand your rights, fees and obligations
options.why: Reading shows your rights, any fees or penalties, and your obligations before you sign. A signed contract is legally binding, so surprises found afterward are usually your responsibility.

options.t: To make sure the font is easy to read on screen
options.why: Font readability is a minor formatting detail; the real reason to read is to learn the binding terms, costs and duties the contract places on you.

q: A buyer is told 'sign now or lose the deal' on a big purchase. What is the smartest reaction?

options.t: Slow down, compare options and read the terms
options.why: High-pressure deadlines are a classic sales tactic. Slowing down lets you compare competing offers, read every term, ask questions, and walk away if the deal is not truly good.

options.t: Share financial details with the seller right away
options.why: Sharing financial details such as account or Social Security numbers with a pushy seller increases fraud risk and does nothing to help you evaluate the deal.

options.t: Sign immediately to avoid missing out on the deal
options.why: Signing immediately because of pressure is exactly what high-pressure sellers want; you could miss hidden fees or poor terms and have little chance to reconsider.

options.t: Sign without reading to save time and effort today
options.why: Signing without reading means agreeing to unknown fees, penalties and obligations; a contract is binding whether or not you read it, so skipping it is risky.

q: Which payment method gives the strongest protection against unauthorized charges in many cases?

options.t: A gift card
options.why: Gift cards work like cash, so if one is lost, stolen or used by a scammer, there is generally little or no way to recover the money.

options.t: A credit card
options.why: Federal law caps cardholder liability for unauthorized charges at $50 and lets you dispute charges while the bank investigates, so you are not out your own money.

options.t: Cash on delivery
options.why: Cash on delivery means paying before you can verify the goods, and there is no automatic dispute process, so recovering money from a bad seller is difficult.

options.t: A wire transfer
options.why: Wire transfers are nearly instant and very hard to reverse, which is why scammers prefer them; they offer little consumer protection against unauthorized or fraudulent payments.

q: What is a consumer right?

options.t: The right to ignore store policies if the price is cheap
options.why: Store policies such as return rules apply regardless of price, and consumer rights do not let buyers ignore them; rights concern fair treatment, not exemption from rules.

options.t: The right to be informed and protected from deception
options.why: Core consumer rights, such as those in the Consumer Bill of Rights, include safety, being informed, choice and being heard, which protect buyers from fraud and misleading claims.

options.t: The right to avoid paying sales tax on purchases
options.why: Sales tax is a legal obligation set by state and local governments; consumer rights do not exempt buyers from it on their purchases.

options.t: The right to buy anything you want for free at all
options.why: No law gives people free goods; consumer rights protect fair treatment and honest information in the marketplace, not a right to get products without paying.

q: Which agency helps protect consumers from deceptive advertising?

options.t: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
options.why: The FTC enforces laws against unfair or deceptive practices, including false advertising, and also takes consumer complaints and shuts down scams, making it the main consumer protection agency.

options.t: The Internal Revenue Service (IRS)
options.why: The IRS collects federal taxes and enforces the tax code; it has no primary role in policing deceptive advertising claims made to consumers.

options.t: The Social Security Administration
options.why: The Social Security Administration runs retirement, disability and survivor benefit programs, not consumer protection or advertising regulation of businesses.

options.t: The Federal Reserve Board system
options.why: The Federal Reserve sets monetary policy and supervises banks to keep the financial system stable; it does not regulate advertising claims aimed at consumers.

q: What is credit?

options.t: Money that you receive as a gift from your relatives each year
options.why: A gift is money given freely with no repayment expected, so it is not credit, which always involves an obligation to repay the lender later.

options.t: Money that you earn from a regular paycheck at work
options.why: Paycheck earnings are income you have already worked for, not borrowed funds; credit is a different concept because it creates a debt that must be repaid.

options.t: Money that you deposit into a savings account each month
options.why: Deposits into savings are your own money being set aside; credit is the opposite, since you use someone else's money and owe it back.

options.t: Borrowing money or buying now with a promise to pay later
options.why: Credit lets you obtain money, goods or services now and repay later, usually with interest, based on the lender's trust that you will pay as promised.

q: What is a credit score?

options.t: A number that shows how much money you have saved up in total
options.why: Savings are shown on bank statements and are not part of a credit score, which is calculated from your borrowing and repayment behavior instead.

options.t: A number that shows how many credit cards you currently own or carry
options.why: The number of cards is only a small part of the picture; a credit score measures repayment reliability, not simply how many cards you hold.

options.t: A number that shows how likely you are to repay borrowed money
options.why: A credit score, often 300 to 850 in the FICO model, summarizes your credit report to predict how likely you are to repay debts, which lenders use to decide approvals and rates.

options.t: A number that shows how much you earn each year at work
options.why: Income is not part of a credit score calculation; lenders may ask for income separately, but the score reflects your credit history only.

q: Which factor has the largest impact on a typical credit score?

options.t: Payment history
options.why: Payment history is the largest FICO factor, about 35 percent of the score, because lenders care most about whether you pay bills on time.

options.t: Your age in years
options.why: Age in years is not a factor in credit scores, and the law prohibits using age to discriminate in credit; length of credit history is different.

options.t: Your favorite store
options.why: Your favorite store has no effect on your score; only reported credit behavior such as payments and balances is used in scoring models.

options.t: Your zip code
options.why: Zip code is not used in credit scoring, and using location to discriminate could violate fair lending laws; the score uses credit account data.

q: What is credit utilization?

options.t: The number of credit cards in your wallet
options.why: Counting cards in your wallet is not utilization; utilization compares balances to credit limits, whereas the number of accounts is a separate smaller factor.

options.t: The age of your oldest credit card account now
options.why: The age of your oldest account relates to length of credit history, a different scoring factor from utilization, which looks at how much of your limit you use.

options.t: The share of available credit you are using
options.why: Utilization is your balances divided by your credit limits, shown as a percent. Keeping it under about 30 percent helps your score, and lower is generally better.

options.t: The interest rate on your credit card balance
options.why: Interest rate (APR) is the cost of borrowing and is not what utilization measures; utilization compares the balance you carry to your available limit.

q: A card has a $2,000 limit and a $500 balance. What is the credit utilization?

options.why: 50 percent would require a $1,000 balance on a $2,000 limit; here $500 divided by $2,000 is only 0.25, so this is too high.
Utilization equals balance divided by limit: $500 / $2,000 = 0.25, or 25 percent. This is under the commonly recommended 30 percent mark for healthy credit scores.
75 percent would mean a $1,500 balance on a $2,000 limit; with a $500 balance the ratio is $500 / $2,000, which equals 25 percent, not 75.
400 percent comes from dividing limit by balance ($2,000 / $500 = 4) which inverts the formula; utilization is balance divided by limit, giving 25 percent.

q: On a loan or credit card, what is APR?

options.t: The total balance that you owe on the card this month
options.why: The balance is the amount owed right now; APR is a rate that describes the yearly cost of borrowing, not a dollar balance.

options.t: The credit limit that is set on your card by the bank
options.why: The credit limit is the maximum you can borrow on the card, set by the issuer; APR is the interest rate and is unrelated to the limit.

options.t: The amount of your required monthly payment on the account
options.why: The monthly payment is a dollar amount due each billing cycle; APR is a percentage rate and does not by itself tell you the payment.

options.t: The yearly cost of borrowing expressed as a percentage
options.why: APR, annual percentage rate, expresses the yearly cost of credit including interest and certain fees, letting you compare loans and cards on equal terms.

q: What happens if you pay only the minimum on a credit card balance?

options.t: Interest stops being charged on the balance
options.why: Interest continues on any unpaid balance, so paying only the minimum does not stop it; most of a minimum payment can go toward interest.

options.t: Your credit limit doubles right away with no review
options.why: Paying the minimum does not raise your limit; limit increases require issuer approval and are unrelated to how little you pay each month.

options.t: The balance is erased from the account immediately
options.why: The minimum payment covers only a small part of the balance, so most of the debt remains and is not erased after one payment.

options.t: Interest keeps building and the debt lasts longer
options.why: Minimum payments are mostly interest, so the balance shrinks slowly, interest compounds on what remains, and repayment can stretch for years and cost far more overall.

q: What is a grace period on a credit card?

options.t: Time when the debt is forgiven by the lender for good
options.why: A grace period does not forgive debt; the lender still expects full repayment, and it only gives you time before interest starts on new purchases.

options.t: Time during which the card cannot be used for purchases
options.why: Cards remain usable during a grace period; it refers to interest-free time on purchases, not any suspension of the card's use.

options.t: Time after the billing cycle to pay in full without interest
options.why: If you pay your statement balance in full by the due date, usually about 21 or more days after the cycle ends, you pay no interest on purchases.

options.t: Time when you owe double the normal interest rate to the bank
options.why: A grace period never doubles interest; penalty rates are a separate consequence of late payments, while a grace period is a benefit that avoids interest.

q: What is a secured credit card?

options.t: A card backed by a cash deposit as collateral
options.why: A secured card requires a refundable cash deposit that usually becomes your credit limit, so the issuer is protected, and it helps people build or rebuild credit.

options.t: A card that comes with no spending limit
options.why: Every card has a limit; a secured card's limit is typically tied to the deposit, and no card gives truly unlimited spending.

options.t: A card whose balance never needs to be repaid
options.why: Balances on secured cards must be repaid like any card; if you do not pay, the issuer can keep your deposit and you still owe interest.

options.t: A card that is issued only to businesses
options.why: Secured cards are mainly offered to individual consumers with limited or damaged credit, not restricted to businesses.

q: What is a secured loan?

options.t: A loan guaranteed by the borrower's signature alone, no property
options.why: A loan with only a signature and no property backing is unsecured; a secured loan specifically involves pledged collateral such as a car or house.

options.t: A loan backed by collateral the lender can take if you default
options.why: Collateral, such as a car or home, secures the lender, who can repossess or foreclose if you default. That lower risk usually means lower interest rates.

options.t: A loan from a friend that has no written terms or papers
options.why: A secured loan involves property pledged as collateral; informal loans with no paperwork have no collateral or legal protections and are not the definition.

options.t: A loan that carries no repayment requirement of any kind
options.why: All loans carry a repayment requirement; a secured loan is defined by collateral that the lender can claim if repayment fails, not by lack of repayment.

q: What is an unsecured loan?

options.t: A loan with no collateral, based on credit
options.why: An unsecured loan, such as a personal loan or credit card, has no collateral, so approval and rates depend on your credit score and income.

options.t: A loan that is backed by a car or a truck
options.why: A loan backed by a car or truck is a secured loan, since the vehicle is collateral the lender can repossess if you default.

options.t: A loan from a pawn shop that holds an item
options.why: Pawn loans are secured by the item you leave, so the pawn shop holds collateral; that makes them secured rather than unsecured.

options.t: A loan that is backed by a house or a flat
options.why: A loan backed by a house or flat is a mortgage, a secured loan where the property is collateral the lender can foreclose on.

q: What is a cosigner?

options.t: A person who gives the borrower extra money to spend
options.why: A cosigner does not give the borrower spending money; they pledge their own credit and take legal responsibility for the debt if the borrower does not pay.

options.t: A person who approves the loan paperwork for the bank staff
options.why: Approving paperwork is the lender's job; a cosigner is a third party who guarantees repayment, not an employee of the bank.

options.t: A person who agrees to repay a loan if the borrower fails
options.why: A cosigner signs the loan alongside the borrower and becomes legally liable for repayment if the borrower defaults. This can help a borrower with thin credit qualify.

options.t: A person who inspects collateral for the lender's bank
options.why: Inspecting or appraising collateral is done by an appraiser or lender; a cosigner's role is to guarantee repayment with their own credit.

q: What is a loan term?

options.t: The interest rate that is charged on the loan
options.why: The interest rate is the cost of borrowing as a percentage; the term is a separate feature that states how long you have to repay.

options.t: The amount of money that was first borrowed
options.why: The amount first borrowed is the principal; the term describes the repayment period, not the loan size.

options.t: The fee that is charged for a late payment
options.why: A late fee is a penalty charged for missing a due date; the term is simply the length of the repayment period.

options.t: The length of time you have to repay a loan
options.why: The loan term, such as 36 months or 30 years, is the repayment period. Longer terms lower monthly payments but usually raise total interest paid.

q: Which has the lower monthly payment: a $10,000 loan over 5 years or the same loan over 3 years (same rate)?

options.t: The 3-year loan, with lower total interest paid
options.why: The 3-year loan has the higher monthly payment because the same principal is paid off in fewer payments; it saves total interest but costs more each month.

options.t: The 5-year loan, though total interest is higher
options.why: Spreading $10,000 over 60 payments rather than 36 makes each payment smaller, but interest accrues longer, so total interest is higher on the 5-year loan.

options.t: Both have exactly the same monthly payment
options.why: Payments depend on the term: 36 payments are larger than 60 payments for the same principal and rate, so they cannot be exactly equal.

options.t: Neither one has any payment due at all each month
options.why: Any loan with a balance requires regular payments until it is repaid; neither term avoids payments, so this option makes no sense.

q: What is principal?

options.t: The extra amount charged for it
options.why: The extra amount charged for borrowing is interest, not principal; principal is the original sum before interest is added.

options.t: The original amount borrowed
options.why: Principal is the original amount borrowed or invested, which interest is calculated on. Payments reduce the principal balance over time, lowering future interest.

options.t: The monthly payment amount
options.why: The monthly payment typically combines principal and interest; it is not the same thing as principal, which is only the amount borrowed.

options.t: The fee for paying very late
options.why: A fee for paying late is a penalty charge; it is separate from the principal, which is the original amount borrowed.

q: A loan of $2,000 at 6% simple interest for 2 years accrues how much interest?

options.why: $24 would be interest on only a small base; simple interest is principal times rate times time, which is $2,000 x 0.06 x 2, not $24.
$120 is just one year of interest ($2,000 x 0.06); the loan runs two years, so the interest must be doubled to $240.
Simple interest = P x r x t = $2,000 x 0.06 x 2 = $240. Interest is figured only on the original principal, so it does not compound.
$2,240 is the total owed at the end (principal $2,000 plus $240 interest), not the interest itself, which is $240.

q: What does a credit report contain?

options.t: Your borrowing and repayment history
options.why: A credit report lists your accounts, balances, payment history, inquiries and public records, which lenders use to judge how reliably you borrow and repay.

options.t: Your shopping lists and receipts
options.why: Shopping lists and receipts are not tracked by credit bureaus; the report records credit accounts and payment behavior only.

options.t: Your bank passwords and card numbers
options.why: Credit reports do not show your passwords, and card numbers are truncated; keeping them off the report protects your private information.

options.t: Your medical history and records
options.why: Medical history is private and not part of a credit report, though unpaid medical debts sent to collections can sometimes appear as accounts.

q: How often can you get a free credit report from each major bureau?

options.t: Only after two denials
options.why: Free reports are not limited to people who have been denied credit, although a denial also gives you an additional free report.

options.t: Never once in a year
options.why: Federal law allows free reports, and weekly access has been offered through AnnualCreditReport.com, so saying never is wrong.

options.t: Once every ten years
options.why: Reports are available far more often than every ten years; that interval would make it hard to catch errors or identity theft.

options.t: At least once a year
options.why: Under federal law you may get a free report from Equifax, Experian and TransUnion at least once every 12 months at AnnualCreditReport.com, helping you catch errors early.

q: What should you do if you find an error on your credit report?

options.t: Close all your accounts right away to be safe
options.why: Closing accounts does not remove an error and can lower your score by cutting available credit and shortening your history; the mistake still needs fixing.

options.t: Ignore it because errors fix themselves over time
options.why: Errors do not fix themselves, and they may hurt loan approvals or rates meanwhile, so waiting leaves the problem unresolved.

options.t: Pay the debt even if it is not yours to pay
options.why: Paying a debt that is not yours could be mistaken for accepting responsibility; the correct step is disputing the error, not paying it.

options.t: Dispute it with the credit bureau in writing
options.why: The Fair Credit Reporting Act lets you dispute inaccurate items; the bureau must investigate, normally within 30 days, and correct or delete wrong information. Include documents as proof.

q: What is identity theft?

options.t: Using someone's personal data to commit fraud
options.why: Identity theft is the unauthorized use of someone's personal data, such as a Social Security number, to open accounts or commit fraud. Monitoring reports and freezing credit help prevent it.

options.t: Sharing a photo online with a close friend
options.why: Sharing a photo with a friend is normal sharing with consent, not stealing someone's identity or using it for fraud.

options.t: Forgetting your password to an online account
options.why: Forgetting your own password is an access problem and not a crime; identity theft requires another person misusing your identifying information.

options.t: Changing your own name through a court process
options.why: Legally changing your own name through a court is a lawful personal choice, unlike identity theft, which is the misuse of another person's data.

q: What does a credit freeze do?

options.t: Raises your credit score by a set number of points
options.why: A freeze does not change your score; it only restricts access to your report, so it cannot add points to your credit score.

options.t: Blocks access so new accounts are harder to open
options.why: A credit freeze restricts access to your report so lenders cannot check it, making it hard for thieves to open new accounts in your name. It is free to place and lift.

options.t: Cancels all of the cards that you hold today
options.why: A freeze does not close accounts; your existing cards stay open and usable, since it only affects new credit inquiries.

options.t: Erases all of the debts that you owe to others
options.why: A freeze erases nothing; your debts and history remain, and you still owe everything you borrowed.

q: What is a payday loan?

options.t: A long-term low-cost loan from a credit union
options.why: Credit unions offer low-cost loans such as payday alternative loans, but a payday loan is the opposite: short-term, high cost, and typically due within weeks.

options.t: A grant that never needs any repayment at all
options.why: Payday loans always must be repaid, usually with a large fee; grants and scholarships are the money that does not require repayment.

options.t: A short, costly loan due on the next payday
options.why: A payday loan is a small, short-term loan, usually due on the borrower's next payday, with very high fees equivalent to APRs of 400 percent or more.

options.t: A loan with no fees and no interest charged
options.why: Payday loans carry high fees and effective interest rates, often $15 per $100 borrowed for two weeks, so claiming no cost is false.

q: Why are payday loans considered risky?

options.t: High fees can trap borrowers in a cycle of repeat borrowing
options.why: Fees equivalent to triple-digit APRs, plus short due dates, push borrowers to roll over or borrow again, making debt grow instead of shrinking.

options.t: They offer some of the lowest rates for people who need cash
options.why: Payday loans have some of the highest rates, often 400 percent APR or more, not the lowest, which is why they are considered risky.

options.t: They are insured by the federal government in all cases
options.why: Payday lenders are not government-insured, and borrowers have no guarantee of protection; their high costs are the main danger.

options.t: They are slowly repaid over thirty years at low rates
options.why: Payday loans are due in weeks, not decades, and carry high rates; a thirty-year low-rate loan describes something like a mortgage.

q: What is debt consolidation?

options.t: Ignoring the debts until they somehow vanish
options.why: Ignoring debts does not make them vanish; interest, late fees and collections can grow, and missed payments harm your credit score.

options.t: Splitting one large debt into many small fixed ones
options.why: Consolidation combines debts rather than splitting them; splitting one debt into many pieces would make them harder to manage, not simpler.

options.t: Borrowing more money so you can spend freely
options.why: Taking on more borrowing for spending increases debt; consolidation is about organizing and paying off existing debts, ideally at a lower rate.

options.t: Combining several debts into one loan or payment
options.why: Debt consolidation merges several debts into one loan or payment, often at a lower rate, which simplifies repayment and may cut interest costs if the terms are better.

q: Which debt-repayment method targets the highest-interest debt first to save the most money?

options.t: The snowball method
options.why: The snowball method pays off the smallest balance first for motivation, so it does not focus on the highest interest rate and may cost more.

options.t: The avalanche method
options.why: The avalanche method pays minimums on all debts and puts extra money toward the highest interest rate first, minimizing total interest paid over time.

options.t: The random method
options.why: Paying in a random order has no strategy behind it and does not target high rates, so it is not a recognized money-saving method.

options.t: The minimum-only method
options.why: Paying only the minimums keeps debts alive longest and builds the most interest; it is not a method for targeting high-rate debt.

q: What is bankruptcy?

options.t: A program that pays out tax refunds each spring
options.why: Tax refunds are paid by the government after you file a return; bankruptcy is a court process dealing with debts, not an income payment program.

options.t: A type of savings plan for families and children
options.why: Savings plans such as 529s help families save for college; bankruptcy is a legal debt relief process, not a saving option.

options.t: A legal process for those who cannot repay debts
options.why: Bankruptcy, such as Chapter 7 or Chapter 13, is a federal court process that can discharge or restructure debts but stays on credit reports for 7 to 10 years.

options.t: A way to make sure you never owe any lender again
options.why: Bankruptcy does not guarantee you will never borrow again; it damages credit for years, and you can still take on new debt afterward.

q: What is a mortgage?

options.t: A loan that has no collateral behind it
options.why: A loan with no collateral is unsecured; a mortgage is the opposite, because the real estate itself serves as collateral for the loan.

options.t: A loan that is taken out to pay for school
options.why: A loan for education is a student loan; a mortgage specifically finances the purchase of property.

options.t: A loan that is taken out to buy a car
options.why: Auto loans finance vehicles; a mortgage is a loan used to buy real estate, with the property as collateral.

options.t: A loan to buy real estate, secured by it
options.why: A mortgage is a loan used to buy property where the home is the collateral, so the lender can foreclose if payments stop. Terms often last 15 or 30 years.

q: What does a down payment do?

options.t: Reduces the amount you must borrow for a large purchase
options.why: A down payment is cash paid upfront, which lowers the loan amount, reduces interest costs and may help avoid private mortgage insurance on home loans.

options.t: Increases the interest rate on the whole loan for five years
options.why: A bigger down payment generally lowers, not raises, the interest paid, since you borrow less; it does not increase the rate on the whole loan.

options.t: Adds fees to the loan for the whole term of years
options.why: A down payment does not add fees to the loan; it reduces the amount financed, so total interest and monthly payments usually fall.

options.t: Eliminates the need for a loan always and forever
options.why: A down payment cuts what you borrow but rarely removes the loan entirely, since it is only part of the price of a large purchase.

q: A buyer puts $4,000 down on a $20,000 car. How much needs to be financed, ignoring fees?

options.why: $24,000 adds the down payment to the price instead of subtracting it; a down payment reduces the amount financed.
$4,000 is the down payment itself, not the amount financed; the loan covers the remaining price after the down payment.
Amount financed equals price minus down payment: $20,000 - $4,000 = $16,000. A larger down payment means a smaller loan and less interest.
$20,000 is the full price, which would be financed only if nothing were paid down; with $4,000 down, less is borrowed.

q: What is a student loan?

options.t: A grant that never needs to be repaid by the student
options.why: Student loans must be repaid, usually with interest; money that does not need repayment is a grant, so this option describes a different thing.

options.t: Money borrowed for education, repaid with interest
options.why: A student loan is borrowed money for education costs that must be repaid with interest. Federal loans often have lower rates and more protections than private loans.

options.t: A scholarship that a school awards to a student
options.why: Scholarships are awards that need no repayment; a student loan is borrowed money with repayment and interest.

options.t: A free gift of money from the federal government
options.why: Student loans are borrowed and must be repaid; a free gift from the government would be a grant, such as the Pell Grant.

q: Which is generally better to apply for first when paying for college?

options.t: Private loans from big banks first of all
options.why: Private bank loans usually have fewer protections and often higher rates, so they should come after free aid and federal loans.

options.t: Grants, scholarships and federal aid first
options.why: Grants and scholarships never need repayment, and federal aid usually has lower rates and flexible repayment, so they should come before private borrowing. Start by filing the FAFSA.

options.t: Credit cards with high interest from a bank
options.why: High-interest credit cards are an expensive way to pay tuition because balances grow quickly with interest, so they are a poor first choice.

options.t: Payday loans from short-term lenders first
options.why: Payday loans have extremely high fees and short terms, making them a costly and risky way to pay for college.

q: What is a late fee?

options.t: A tax that is charged on interest earned
options.why: Taxes on interest earned are a tax matter; a late fee is a penalty for paying a bill late.

options.t: A reward that is given for paying early on
options.why: A reward for paying early is a discount or incentive; a late fee is the opposite, a penalty for paying after the due date.

options.t: A service that the bank gives to every customer
options.why: A late fee is a penalty rather than a bank service, and customers can avoid it by paying on time.

options.t: A charge for paying a bill after the due date
options.why: A late fee is a penalty charged when a payment arrives after its due date. Late payments can also hurt your credit score if they are over 30 days past due.

q: What is the best way to build a good credit history?

options.t: Pay bills on time and keep balances low
options.why: On-time payments and low balances are the biggest drivers of a score, since payment history and utilization together make up well over half of it.

options.t: Miss payments now and then to save cash
options.why: Missed payments are reported to the bureaus and can drop your score significantly, so skipping them harms your credit history rather than helping it.

options.t: Close every account that you have open
options.why: Closing accounts reduces available credit, raising utilization and shortening history, which can lower your score rather than build it.

options.t: Max out your cards every single month
options.why: Maxing out cards creates very high utilization, which lowers scores and signals risk to lenders; keeping balances low builds good credit.

q: What is a hard inquiry?

options.t: A question from a cashier at the till
options.why: A cashier's question has no connection to credit; a hard inquiry is a lender looking at your credit report after you apply.

options.t: A bank statement mailed to your home
options.why: A mailed bank statement is a regular account summary and does not count as an inquiry on your credit report.

options.t: A credit check made when you apply
options.why: A hard inquiry occurs when a lender checks your credit because you applied for credit. It can lower your score slightly for about a year and stays on your report for two years.

options.t: A check you make on your own report
options.why: Checking your own report is a soft inquiry, which does not affect your score, unlike a hard inquiry from a lender.

q: What is predatory lending?

options.t: Lending only to people who have great credit and high pay
options.why: Lending only to people with strong credit is standard prime lending, not predatory; predatory lending targets vulnerable borrowers with unfair terms.

options.t: Lending money with clear and fair terms to all
options.why: Clear and fair terms for everyone describes responsible lending; predatory lending uses hidden or deceptive terms instead.

options.t: Unfair or deceptive lending that exploits borrowers
options.why: Predatory lending uses deception, hidden fees, or excessive rates to exploit borrowers, often targeting people with low incomes or little financial knowledge. Warning signs include pressure and unclear terms.

options.t: Lending money at the lowest market rate available
options.why: Lending at the lowest market rate is fair pricing, not predatory; predatory lenders charge high or hidden costs to exploit borrowers.

q: What is a premium?

options.t: The amount you pay for an insurance policy
options.why: A premium is the regular payment, often monthly or yearly, that you make to keep insurance coverage active, and it is the price of the policy.

options.t: The amount you pay before the coverage starts
options.why: What you pay before coverage begins is the deductible, not the premium; the premium is what you pay to hold the policy.

options.t: The amount the insurer pays after a loss
options.why: The amount the insurer pays after a loss is the claim payout, not the premium, which is what you pay in.

options.t: The maximum coverage that you can claim
options.why: The maximum coverage is the policy limit, the most the insurer will pay; the premium is the price of the policy.

q: What is a deductible?

options.t: The profit that the insurer makes each year
options.why: Insurer profit is its own business result; a deductible is the portion of a covered loss you pay yourself first.

options.t: The premium that you pay each year in full
options.why: The premium is the regular price of the policy; the deductible is a separate out-of-pocket amount paid when you file a claim.

options.t: The coverage limit that is set in the policy
options.why: The coverage limit is the maximum the insurer pays; the deductible is the amount you pay first, so they are different parts of a policy.

options.t: What you pay before insurance begins to pay
options.why: A deductible is the amount you pay out of pocket on a covered loss before insurance pays the rest. Higher deductibles usually mean lower premiums.

q: Alex has a $500 deductible and a covered repair bill of $1,800. How much does the insurer pay, ignoring other terms?

options.why: $1,800 is the full bill and ignores the deductible; the insurer only pays what remains after Alex covers the first $500.
Insurer pays the bill minus the deductible: $1,800 - $500 = $1,300. Alex pays the first $500 and the insurer covers the remaining covered amount.
$500 is the deductible, which is what Alex pays, not the insurer; the insurer pays the remaining $1,300.
$2,300 adds the deductible to the bill instead of subtracting it; the insurer cannot pay more than the covered bill, which is $1,800 minus $500.

q: What does liability insurance cover?

options.t: Your own medical bills and nothing else besides those
options.why: Your own medical bills are covered by health or medical payments coverage; liability insurance pays for harm you cause to others.

options.t: Damage to your own property and nothing else besides it
options.why: Damage to your own property is covered by collision, comprehensive or property coverage; liability pays for others' losses.

options.t: Harm or damage you cause to other people or their property
options.why: Liability insurance pays for injuries or property damage you cause to others and covers legal defense costs, up to your policy limits, protecting your assets from lawsuits.

options.t: Routine maintenance and repairs on your property and vehicles
options.why: Routine maintenance is not insurable because it is a predictable expense, and liability coverage pays for harm to others, not upkeep.

q: What does collision coverage on a car policy pay for?

options.t: Oil changes and other routine upkeep for a car
options.why: Oil changes are routine maintenance costs, which are predictable and not covered by any car insurance; collision pays for accident damage.

options.t: Theft of the car and nothing else besides
options.why: Theft is covered by comprehensive coverage rather than collision, which pays for damage from hitting something or being hit.

options.t: Damage to other people's cars only, not yours
options.why: Damage to other people's cars is covered by liability coverage; collision pays to repair your own car.

options.t: Damage to your car in an accident, any fault
options.why: Collision coverage pays to repair or replace your own car after a crash with another vehicle or object, regardless of who was at fault, minus your deductible.

q: What does comprehensive car coverage pay for?

options.t: Tire wear from normal driving on public roads
options.why: Normal tire wear is routine maintenance and not an insured event; comprehensive covers sudden, non-collision losses.

options.t: Non-collision damage such as theft, fire or hail
options.why: Comprehensive covers damage not caused by a collision, such as theft, fire, vandalism, falling objects, floods and hail, usually minus your deductible.

options.t: Injuries to other drivers in a crash that you cause
options.why: Injuries to other drivers that you cause are covered by liability coverage, not comprehensive, which covers your own vehicle.

options.t: Damage from a crash that you cause yourself
options.why: Crash damage you cause is covered by collision coverage on your own car, whereas comprehensive covers non-collision events.

q: What does renters insurance cover?

options.t: A renter's belongings and liability, not the building
options.why: Renters insurance covers your belongings and your liability if you cause harm, but the building belongs to the landlord, who insures it separately.

options.t: Unpaid rent owed to the landlord by the renter now
options.why: Renters insurance does not pay unpaid rent; rent is a contractual obligation between tenant and landlord that insurance does not cover.

options.t: The building structure that the landlord owns and insures
options.why: The landlord insures the building structure with their own property policy; renters insurance covers the tenant's contents and liability.

options.t: The income that the landlord earns from tenants' rent
options.why: A landlord's rental income is protected by the landlord's own policy, not by a tenant's renters insurance.

q: Why does a young driver often pay higher car insurance premiums?

options.t: Young drivers always own pricier cars than older adults do
options.why: Premiums are based on risk, not on vehicle price alone, and many young drivers drive older, cheaper cars.

options.t: Young drivers are exempt from needing any insurance cover
options.why: Young drivers are not exempt from insurance; state laws require liability coverage for almost every driver.

options.t: Insurers simply dislike young people as their paying customers
options.why: Insurers price using data on risk, not personal dislike; age is a measurable factor tied to accident rates.

options.t: Statistics show higher accident risk for inexperienced drivers
options.why: Insurers price using claims statistics, and drivers under about 25 have more accidents per mile because of inexperience, so they pay higher premiums.

q: Which action can lower car insurance premiums?

options.t: Lowering the deductible all the way down to zero
options.why: Lowering the deductible raises the premium because the insurer takes on more cost per claim, so this raises, not lowers, premiums.

options.t: A clean driving record and a higher deductible
options.why: Insurers reward low-risk drivers with discounts, and choosing a higher deductible means you carry more risk yourself, which lowers your premium.

options.t: Driving around without any insurance cover
options.why: Driving uninsured is illegal in nearly every state and brings fines, and it does not lower premiums; it risks big personal costs.

options.t: Getting several speeding tickets each year
options.why: Speeding tickets signal risk and raise premiums, so collecting them would increase your costs, not lower them.

q: What is health insurance?

options.t: A loan that is used to pay hospital bills later
options.why: Health insurance is not a loan; it is a contract where you pay premiums and the insurer pays covered medical costs, with no repayment of claims.

options.t: A discount on memberships at local gyms and clubs
options.why: Gym discounts are a perk, not health insurance, which covers medical care such as doctor visits and hospital stays.

options.t: Coverage that pays part of the cost of medical care
options.why: Health insurance pays a share of medical costs for covered services such as doctor visits, hospital stays and prescriptions, protecting you from large bills. You still pay premiums and cost sharing.

options.t: A savings plan employers set up to help with retirement
options.why: Employer retirement savings plans like a 401(k) are about retirement, not medical care; health insurance covers medical expenses.

q: What is a copay?

options.t: A fixed amount you pay for a covered service
options.why: A copay is a set dollar amount, such as $25 for a doctor visit, that you pay when you receive a covered service, separate from the premium.

options.t: The yearly premium you pay to the insurer
options.why: The yearly cost of the policy is the premium; a copay is a small fixed fee paid at the time of care.

options.t: The total claim amount for the whole year
options.why: A claim total for the year is not a copay; a copay is a fixed payment made per service.

options.t: A fine for missing a doctor visit without notice
options.why: A fine for a missed appointment is a no-show fee, and a copay is paid for covered care you actually receive.

q: What is coinsurance?

options.t: A percentage of costs you share after the deductible
options.why: After you meet your deductible, coinsurance splits remaining costs, such as the plan paying 80 percent and you paying 20 percent, until you reach the out-of-pocket maximum.

options.t: A flat fee that you pay at every single doctor visit
options.why: A flat fee per visit is a copay; coinsurance is a percentage of the cost rather than a fixed amount.

options.t: A penalty for using out-of-network care at a hospital
options.why: Out-of-network penalties or higher costs are a separate matter; coinsurance is the percentage split of covered costs after the deductible.

options.t: The monthly premium that you pay to the insurer
options.why: The monthly premium is a fixed charge to keep the policy; coinsurance is a share of covered costs that applies when you use care.

q: What is life insurance?

options.t: Coverage that pays you money when you retire from work
options.why: Retirement income comes from pensions, annuities or savings; life insurance pays a death benefit to beneficiaries when the insured dies.

options.t: Coverage that pays for car damage and repairs
options.why: Car damage and repairs are covered by auto insurance, not by life insurance, which pays out upon the insured person's death.

options.t: Coverage that pays for medical costs and drugs
options.why: Medical costs and drugs are covered by health insurance, whereas life insurance pays a benefit after the insured dies.

options.t: Coverage paying beneficiaries when the insured dies
options.why: Life insurance pays a death benefit to named beneficiaries when the insured person dies, replacing lost income and covering debts, funeral costs and other expenses. Term and whole life are two common types.

q: Who should consider buying life insurance?

options.t: Everyone with no dependents or debts to pay
options.why: People with no dependents or debts generally have little need for it, since there is no one financially relying on their income.

options.t: Only people who never work at any job
options.why: People who do not work may still have family responsibilities, and this option is clearly too narrow to be a real guideline.

options.t: People whose income dependents rely on
options.why: Life insurance is most useful for people with dependents such as a spouse or children who would suffer financially if that income were lost.

options.t: No one at all, ever, in any situation
options.why: Life insurance is useful for those with dependents or debts, so saying no one needs it ever is false.

q: What is disability insurance?

options.t: Coverage that pays for damage to a car's body
options.why: Car body damage is covered by auto collision coverage, whereas disability insurance replaces income lost when injury or illness prevents work.

options.t: Coverage replacing income if you cannot work
options.why: Disability insurance replaces a portion of your income, often 60 percent, if illness or injury keeps you from working. It protects your paycheck, which is usually your largest asset.

options.t: Coverage that pays for a vacation trip abroad
options.why: Vacations are not covered by disability insurance; travel insurance may cover trip problems, but disability pays income when you cannot work.

options.t: Coverage that pays the taxes you owe each year
options.why: Taxes are not paid by disability insurance; it replaces lost wages when you cannot work.

q: What is homeowners insurance?

options.t: Coverage for a home, belongings and liability
options.why: Homeowners insurance usually covers the dwelling, personal belongings, liability for injuries on your property, and additional living expenses after a covered loss.

options.t: Coverage for car accidents and repairs only
options.why: Car accidents and repairs are covered by auto insurance, a separate policy; homeowners insurance protects your house and property.

options.t: Coverage that is meant for renters only today
options.why: Renters insurance is for tenants; homeowners insurance covers people who own their home, and mortgage lenders often require it.

options.t: Coverage that pays your mortgage if jobless
options.why: Homeowners insurance does not pay your mortgage if you lose your job; that would require special payment protection, whereas homeowners covers property damage and liability.

q: What is risk avoidance?

options.t: Taking safety steps to lower the chance of a loss
options.why: Safety steps that lower the chance of loss are risk reduction, which accepts the activity while making it safer, not avoidance.

options.t: Saving money to cover a loss that may occur later on
options.why: Saving money to cover a possible loss is risk retention, because you plan to absorb the cost yourself rather than avoid it.

options.t: Buying insurance for a loss that may occur later on
options.why: Buying insurance is risk transfer, shifting the cost of a possible loss to an insurer instead of avoiding the activity.

options.t: Choosing not to do something that could cause a loss
options.why: Risk avoidance means not doing the risky activity at all, such as not driving, which removes the chance of loss completely but also gives up the benefits.

q: What is risk transfer?

options.t: Accepting a risk and paying for a loss yourself
options.why: Accepting a risk and paying for losses yourself is risk retention, the opposite of transferring the risk to someone else.

options.t: Shifting the financial burden to an insurer
options.why: Risk transfer shifts the financial burden of a possible loss to another party, most commonly by buying insurance and paying premiums.

options.t: Avoiding a risk entirely by not taking part
options.why: Avoiding a risk entirely by not taking part is risk avoidance, not transfer, because no one else takes on the loss.

options.t: Reducing the chance that a loss will happen
options.why: Lowering the chance a loss happens is risk reduction, such as installing alarms; transfer moves the cost to someone else.

q: What is risk retention?

options.t: Buying insurance to cover a possible loss of money or property
options.why: Buying insurance to cover a possible loss is risk transfer, because the insurer takes on the cost rather than you.

options.t: Installing safety devices to lower the chance of loss
options.why: Installing safety devices is risk reduction because it lowers the chance of loss, but you still bear any loss that occurs.

options.t: Accepting a risk and planning to pay for a loss yourself
options.why: Risk retention means accepting the risk and paying for any loss yourself, often through savings or a high deductible, and works best for small, affordable losses.

options.t: Avoiding the risky activity altogether and for good
options.why: Avoiding the risky activity altogether is risk avoidance, which eliminates the exposure rather than accepting and paying for it.

q: A family installs smoke detectors and keeps a fire extinguisher. Which risk strategy is this?

options.t: Risk reduction
options.why: Smoke detectors and extinguishers lower the chance and size of a fire loss, which is risk reduction, also called loss control or prevention.

options.t: Risk transfer
options.why: Risk transfer would be buying insurance or otherwise shifting the cost to another party; safety equipment does not do that.

options.t: Risk retention
options.why: Risk retention means accepting the possible loss and paying yourself, whereas installing safety equipment actively tries to prevent the loss.

options.t: Risk avoidance
options.why: Risk avoidance would mean not having the exposure at all, such as not owning a home; the family keeps the exposure but reduces it.

q: What is an insurance claim?

options.t: A type of savings that earns monthly interest
options.why: A savings type that earns interest is an account; an insurance claim is a request to the insurer for payment of a covered loss.

options.t: A fee that you pay for a policy each month
options.why: The regular fee you pay for a policy is the premium, whereas a claim is something you file after a loss.

options.t: A refund of the premium you paid earlier
options.why: A refund of premiums is not a claim; a claim asks the insurer to pay for a covered loss.

options.t: A request for payment after a covered loss
options.why: A claim is a formal request to your insurer for payment after a covered loss, such as an accident or theft. The insurer investigates and pays according to policy terms, minus your deductible.

q: What is an insurance exclusion?

options.t: A discount for very good driving habits
options.why: A discount for good driving is a credit that lowers cost; an exclusion limits what the policy pays.

options.t: The monthly cost of the whole policy
options.why: The monthly cost of the policy is the premium; an exclusion is a specific loss or situation the policy does not cover.

options.t: Something the policy does not cover
options.why: An exclusion lists causes, property or situations the policy will not pay for, such as floods or earthquakes under standard homeowners policies. Reading exclusions helps you spot gaps in coverage.

options.t: The coverage limit in the policy
options.why: The coverage limit is the most the insurer will pay; an exclusion is something not covered at all.

q: After a flood damages a home, the owner learns the standard homeowners policy does not pay. What is the likely reason?

options.t: The owner is not allowed to file any claims at all
options.why: Owners are allowed to file claims on any policy; the issue is that flood damage is not a covered cause of loss in a standard policy.

options.t: Floods are usually excluded; separate coverage is needed
options.why: Standard homeowners policies exclude flood damage, so owners must buy separate flood insurance, often through the National Flood Insurance Program. Check exclusions before disasters strike.

options.t: The insurer simply made a mistake in the policy terms
options.why: The insurer did not err; the policy terms exclude floods, and the written exclusion is the reason the claim is denied.

options.t: Floods are always covered in standard policies at no extra cost
options.why: Floods are generally excluded from standard homeowners policies, and flood coverage costs extra, so this option states the opposite of the truth.

q: What is an emergency fund's role in managing risk?

options.t: It is meant only for paying for vacations
options.why: An emergency fund is meant for unexpected needs such as job loss or repairs, not planned expenses like vacations.

options.t: It replaces the need for all your insurance
options.why: An emergency fund handles smaller shocks, but it cannot replace insurance, because large losses like a house fire or major illness can far exceed savings.

options.t: It covers unexpected costs without borrowing
options.why: An emergency fund covers unexpected costs such as car repairs or lost income, so you avoid high-interest debt. Experts recommend three to six months of expenses.

options.t: It increases the amount of risk a family faces
options.why: An emergency fund reduces a family's exposure to financial risk by providing a cushion, so it does not increase risk.

q: Why compare insurance quotes from several companies?

options.t: It removes the need for coverage
options.why: Comparing quotes does not remove the need for coverage; it helps you choose among policies, not skip insurance.

options.t: Prices and coverage can vary
options.why: Insurers set prices differently using their own formulas, so the same coverage can cost very different amounts, and shopping around can save significant money.

options.t: It guarantees the lowest rate
options.why: Comparing quotes can find a lower price, but it cannot guarantee that you get the lowest rate available anywhere, as rates change.

options.t: All companies charge the same
options.why: Companies price risk differently, which is exactly why comparing quotes is worth doing; rates are not identical across insurers.

q: What is investing?

options.t: Borrowing money just to have fun
options.why: Borrowing for fun is spending financed by debt, not investing, which aims to build value over time through assets.

options.t: Hiding cash in a drawer at home daily
options.why: Hiding cash in a drawer earns nothing and loses value to inflation; investing puts money to work in assets.

options.t: Spending money on daily needs each month
options.why: Spending on daily needs is consumption, not investing, because it does not aim to grow your money.

options.t: Putting money into assets to grow it
options.why: Investing means buying assets such as stocks, bonds or real estate expecting them to grow in value or earn income over time, though returns are not guaranteed.

q: What is a stock?

options.t: A share of ownership in a company
options.why: A stock represents a share of ownership in a corporation, so shareholders may gain from price growth and dividends and often can vote on company matters.

options.t: A deposit held at a local bank
options.why: A deposit at a bank is a savings or checking account, not a stock; stocks represent ownership in a company.

options.t: A type of insurance policy for cars
options.why: Car insurance is a protection product; a stock is an ownership share in a company, so they are different things.

options.t: A loan made to a company and repaid
options.why: A loan to a company repaid with interest describes a bond; a stock gives ownership rather than lending.

q: What is a mutual fund?

options.t: A savings account at a local bank branch
options.why: A bank savings account is an insured deposit; a mutual fund pools many investors' money into securities and is not a bank deposit.

options.t: A loan that a bank makes to a single borrower
options.why: A bank loan to one borrower is lending; a mutual fund pools money from many investors rather than lending to a single borrower.

options.t: A single stock owned by one person alone
options.why: A mutual fund spreads money across many holdings, so it is not a single stock owned by one person alone.

options.t: A pool of money buying a mix of securities
options.why: A mutual fund pools money from many investors to buy a diversified mix of stocks, bonds or other securities, managed by professionals, giving small investors instant diversification.

q: What is an index fund?

options.t: A fund guaranteed to never lose any of your money ever
options.why: No investment is guaranteed against loss; an index fund can lose value whenever the market it tracks declines.

options.t: A fund that tries to beat the market through trading each year
options.why: Trying to beat the market describes an actively managed fund; an index fund simply tracks an index with low trading.

options.t: A fund that aims to match the performance of a market index
options.why: An index fund tracks a market index such as the S&P 500, so it holds the same stocks. It typically has low fees and broad diversification.

options.t: A fund that holds only one stock at a time for its owners
options.why: An index fund holds many securities in its index, which makes it diversified rather than a single stock holding.

q: What is diversification?

options.t: Spreading money across different investments to reduce risk
options.why: Diversification spreads money across different assets, industries or regions so a loss in one has less effect on the whole, lowering risk without necessarily lowering returns.

options.t: Borrowing money in order to invest it in a business firm today
options.why: Borrowing to invest is leverage, which increases risk, whereas diversification reduces risk by spreading investments.

options.t: Putting all your money in one single stock that you like
options.why: Putting everything in one stock is the opposite of diversifying and leaves you fully exposed to that company's performance.

options.t: Holding only cash and nothing else at all for many years
options.why: Holding only cash is a single asset type and gives up growth; diversification means owning a range of different investments.

q: What is the relationship between risk and return?

options.t: Risk and return are unrelated, so one tells you nothing
options.why: Risk and return are linked, because investors demand higher potential returns for taking on greater uncertainty; saying they are unrelated is wrong.

options.t: Higher potential returns usually come with higher risk
options.why: Higher expected returns generally come with higher risk, as seen with stocks versus savings accounts. Investors need to be paid for accepting the chance of loss.

options.t: Higher returns always come with no risk or cost to you
options.why: Higher returns do not come without risk; stocks may earn more over time but can fall sharply in the short term.

options.t: Low risk always guarantees high returns to everyone
options.why: Low-risk investments such as savings accounts and Treasury bills usually pay low returns, so low risk never guarantees high returns.

q: Which investment is generally expected to be riskiest?

options.t: A broad index fund of many stocks
options.why: A broad index fund holds many stocks and is diversified, so it is far less risky than one company's shares.

options.t: A federally insured savings account
options.why: Federally insured savings accounts are protected up to $250,000 by the FDIC, making them one of the safest options.

options.t: A U.S. Treasury bill held to the end
options.why: Treasury bills are backed by the U.S. government and, held to maturity, return the principal, making them very low risk.

options.t: A single start-up company's stock
options.why: A single start-up stock can lose all its value, and its price is volatile, so it carries high risk, though it also has potential for large gains.

q: What is a dividend?

options.t: A share of company profit paid to owners
options.why: A dividend is a payment to shareholders from company profits, often quarterly, which gives investors income in addition to any price growth.

options.t: A fee that is paid to a broker each time
options.why: Broker fees are commissions or charges for trades, not dividends, which are money received by owners.

options.t: Interest that is charged to each borrower
options.why: Interest charged to borrowers is a cost of loans; a dividend is a payment to stock owners, not a charge.

options.t: A tax that is charged on stock trades
options.why: Taxes on trades are a government charge, while a dividend is money that a company pays to its shareholders.

q: What is a capital gain?

options.t: Wages that are earned from a job each month of work
options.why: Wages earned from a job are ordinary income, not capital gains, which come from selling assets for more than their cost.

options.t: Profit from selling an investment for more than you paid
options.why: A capital gain is the profit when you sell an asset, such as a stock, for more than you paid. Assets held over a year get lower long-term tax rates.

options.t: A gift of money from a relative in the family each year
options.why: Gifts from relatives are not capital gains; a gain arises only from the sale of an asset at a profit.

options.t: Interest that is paid on a savings account balance daily
options.why: Interest on savings is interest income and is taxed as ordinary income, not capital gains, which arise from selling assets.

q: What is a 401(k)?

options.t: A car loan from a local bank for a new car
options.why: A car loan is borrowing to buy a vehicle; a 401(k) is a retirement account, named after a section of the tax code.

options.t: A type of health insurance plan for workers
options.why: Health insurance plans cover medical costs; a 401(k) is a retirement savings plan, so these are different products.

options.t: An employer-sponsored retirement savings plan
options.why: A 401(k) is an employer-sponsored plan where employees contribute from their paychecks, often pre-tax, and employers may match contributions. Investments grow tax-deferred until retirement.

options.t: A savings plan that is meant for college costs
options.why: Savings for college costs is described by a 529 plan, whereas a 401(k) is for retirement.

q: An employer matches 100% of contributions up to 3% of pay. If you earn $30,000 and contribute 3%, how much does the employer add?

options.why: Employer matches 100 percent of contributions up to 3 percent of pay: 3% x $30,000 = $900 from you, so the employer adds an equal $900.
$90 comes from misplacing the decimal; 3 percent of $30,000 is $900, so the match equals $900 rather than $90.
$300 is only 1 percent of $30,000; the match is 100 percent of your 3 percent, which is $900.
$9,000 would be 30 percent of pay; 3 percent of $30,000 equals $900, so the match is $900.

q: What is an IRA?

options.t: A loan that is made to retired people only
options.why: An IRA is an account, not a loan, and retirees are not its only users; people save in one while still working.

options.t: A retirement account with tax advantages
options.why: An IRA, or individual retirement arrangement, is a personal account for retirement savings that offers tax advantages, such as deductions or tax-free growth. Annual limits apply.

options.t: An insurance policy for retirees only
options.why: An IRA is an investment account and not an insurance policy; anyone with earned income can contribute, not just retirees.

options.t: A government tax form filed by retirees only
options.why: An IRA is a retirement account, not a tax form for retirees; anyone with earned income can contribute.

q: What is the main feature of a Roth IRA?

options.t: It pays a guaranteed return of ten percent each year to you
options.why: No retirement account guarantees a return; Roth IRA investments rise and fall with the market, and no fixed ten percent is promised.

options.t: Contributions are tax-deductible and withdrawals are taxed as income
options.why: That describes a traditional IRA, where contributions may be deductible and withdrawals are taxed; a Roth works the opposite way.

options.t: Contributions are after-tax and qualified withdrawals are tax-free
options.why: Roth IRA contributions come from after-tax money, so qualified withdrawals in retirement, including earnings, are tax-free. This helps if you expect higher taxes later.

options.t: Withdrawals are always free of any rules or limits at any age
options.why: Roth withdrawals follow rules, such as the age 59 and a half and five-year requirements for tax-free earnings, so they are not rule-free.

q: Why is it better to start investing early?

options.t: Fees are lower for all of the early investors
options.why: Fees are charged by funds and brokers regardless of how early you start, so starting early does not lower fees.

options.t: Taxes disappear for early investors in every year
options.why: Taxes still apply to investors of any age, so starting early does not remove them; the benefit is growth over time.

options.t: Early investors never lose any money at all
options.why: Early investors can still lose money, as markets fluctuate; time horizon helps by allowing recovery, but nothing guarantees gains.

options.t: Compounding has more time to grow your money
options.why: Compounding means earnings generate their own earnings, so more years lets small deposits grow substantially. Starting at 25 instead of 35 can mean much more by retirement.

q: What is dollar-cost averaging?

options.t: Investing a fixed amount on a regular schedule
options.why: Dollar-cost averaging means investing a set amount at regular intervals, such as $200 monthly, so you buy more shares when prices are low and fewer when high.

options.t: Waiting for the lowest price to appear again
options.why: Waiting for the lowest price is market timing, which is very hard to do and not what dollar-cost averaging involves.

options.t: Selling when prices fall by a fair amount
options.why: Selling after prices fall is a reaction to losses and not dollar-cost averaging, which involves steady, regular buying.

options.t: Investing everything at once on a hunch about prices
options.why: Investing everything at once on a hunch is lump-sum investing based on guessing, not the regular steady purchases of dollar-cost averaging.

q: What is a brokerage account?

options.t: An account that guarantees a set rate of return
options.why: No account guarantees a rate of return; a brokerage account holds investments whose value rises and falls.

options.t: An account to buy and sell stocks and funds
options.why: A brokerage account lets you buy and sell investments such as stocks, bonds and funds through a brokerage firm. Unlike retirement accounts, it has no special tax benefits.

options.t: An account that is used only for borrowing
options.why: Borrowing is done through loans or credit lines; a brokerage account is for investing, though margin accounts can borrow.

options.t: An account that is used for paying bills
options.why: Paying bills is the job of a checking account; a brokerage account is used to hold and trade investments.

q: What is the effect of fees on long-term returns?

options.t: Fees only affect investors who hold for the short term, not savers
options.why: Fees affect all long-term investors, and the effect grows with time, so they are not limited to short-term holders.

options.t: Fees actually increase returns over time for long-term savers
options.why: Fees subtract from your returns and never add to them, so claiming they increase returns is incorrect.

options.t: Fees have no effect at all on returns over the long run
options.why: Fees compound against you over decades, so even small percentages matter, meaning they do have an effect on long-term returns.

options.t: Higher fees reduce the amount that stays invested and compounds
options.why: Fees come out of your balance, so less money stays invested to compound. Even a 1 percent difference in annual fees can cost tens of thousands over decades.

q: What is a time horizon?

options.t: The time it takes to open an account
options.why: Opening an account is a quick setup task; a time horizon is the length of time you plan to invest before needing the money.

options.t: The date a company was first founded
options.why: The founding date of a company is unrelated to your own investing plans; time horizon refers to how long you expect to stay invested.

options.t: How long you expect to stay invested
options.why: A time horizon is how long you expect to keep money invested before you need it. Longer horizons can handle more stock risk, while short ones favor safer assets.

options.t: The time of day that a market opens
options.why: Market opening hours are a trading schedule, whereas a time horizon is the length of your investing plan.

q: Which investment mix is most suitable for a goal 40 years away?

options.t: A diversified portfolio weighted toward stocks
options.why: With 40 years, a portfolio weighted toward diversified stocks has time to ride out downturns and benefit from compounding, which historically offers higher long-term growth.

options.t: A single speculative bet on one company only
options.why: A single speculative bet is too risky for any goal, even a long one, because one company can fail completely.

options.t: Only a one-month Treasury bill held to maturity
options.why: A one-month Treasury bill would likely earn less than inflation over 40 years, so it is far too conservative for a long-term goal.

options.t: Only cash kept hidden under a mattress at home
options.why: Cash under a mattress earns nothing and loses buying power to inflation over four decades, so it is a poor choice.

q: Which investment mix is most suitable for a goal one year away?

options.t: All of the money in cryptocurrency coins of one type
options.why: Cryptocurrency can swing wildly in weeks, and a one-year goal cannot absorb a large drop, so it is too risky.

options.t: All of the money in a single volatile tech stock
options.why: A single volatile tech stock could fall sharply, and with only a year, there is no time to recover.

options.t: All of the money in a long-term growth fund each year
options.why: Long-term growth funds hold stocks that can fall in the short run, which is risky when you need the money in a year.

options.t: Safe, liquid options like a savings account or CD
options.why: For a one-year goal, protecting principal matters most, so savings accounts or CDs offer safety and easy access, even though returns are modest.

q: What is a Ponzi scheme?

options.t: A savings option that banks offer to savers
options.why: Savings options offered by banks are legitimate products; a Ponzi scheme is a fraud that pays returns using money from newer investors.

options.t: A bond program run by the government for savers
options.why: Government bond programs are legal and backed by the government; a Ponzi scheme is an illegal fraud.

options.t: A fraud paying early investors with new money
options.why: A Ponzi scheme pays earlier investors with money from newer investors rather than real profits, and collapses when recruits run out. Bernie Madoff ran a famous one.

options.t: A legal retirement plan for workers and firms
options.why: Legal retirement plans such as 401(k)s are regulated; a Ponzi scheme is an illegal fraud with no real investments.

q: Which is a red flag of investment fraud?

options.t: A registered adviser with a public record of past work
options.why: A registered adviser with a public record is a sign of legitimacy, since you can check their background through regulators.

options.t: Promises of guaranteed high returns with no risk
options.why: Guaranteed high returns with no risk are impossible in real markets, so this is a hallmark of fraud. Higher returns always involve higher risk.

options.t: Independent audited statements and records
options.why: Independent audited statements indicate transparency and accountability, so they are a good sign, not a red flag.

options.t: Clear disclosures of risks and fees to investors
options.why: Honest disclosure of risks and fees is expected from legitimate investments, so it is a good sign rather than a warning.

q: What is inflation risk?

options.t: The risk that tax rates will rise again for you this year
options.why: Higher tax rates are a different issue, called tax risk; inflation risk is about prices rising faster than your returns.

options.t: The risk that a bank closes its doors for good this year
options.why: A bank closing is institutional risk, which FDIC insurance covers; inflation risk concerns loss of buying power.

options.t: The risk that rising prices reduce the value of your money
options.why: Inflation risk is the chance that rising prices erode purchasing power, so money earning less than inflation buys less over time. Cash savings are especially exposed.

options.t: The risk that a company fails and cannot repay its lenders
options.why: A company failing to repay lenders is credit or default risk, whereas inflation risk is about rising prices reducing what your money can buy.

q: What is the best reason to compare savings account interest rates?

options.t: Lower rates always earn you more money each year
options.why: Lower rates earn less, not more, so comparing rates is done to find the higher one.

options.t: Rates do not affect how much you earn at all
options.why: Rates directly determine your interest earnings, so claiming they have no effect is wrong.

options.t: All accounts pay exactly the same rate to you
