options.why: Banks set different rates, so accounts differ; online banks often pay more than traditional branches.

options.t: A higher rate earns more on the same deposit
options.why: A higher interest rate, or APY, earns more interest on the same deposit, so comparing helps your savings grow faster.

q: What is a minimum balance requirement?

options.t: The most money you are allowed to keep in an account each month
options.why: The most you may keep is not a minimum; a minimum balance requirement sets the lowest amount you must maintain.

options.t: The least amount you must keep in an account to avoid fees
options.why: A minimum balance requirement is the lowest balance you must maintain, or you may be charged a monthly fee or lose interest. Compare accounts for low or no minimums.

options.t: The number of deposits that you must make each month
options.why: The number of deposits is a transaction rule, whereas a minimum balance concerns the amount of money in the account.

options.t: The interest that you must earn each month in total
options.why: Interest you earn is the bank's payment to you; a minimum balance is the least amount you must keep in the account.

q: What is a good first savings goal for most people?

options.t: An emergency fund
options.why: An emergency fund covers unexpected costs like car repairs or job loss, preventing debt. Most advisers suggest building a starter fund before other goals.

options.t: A luxury purchase
options.why: A luxury purchase is a want, not a priority; essential protections like an emergency fund should come first.

options.t: A fancy vacation fund
options.why: A vacation fund is a nice goal, but it comes after building basic financial security.

options.t: A risky investment
options.why: Risky investments should come only after you have a safety cushion, so they are not a good first goal.

q: Why do employers withhold income tax from each paycheck?

options.t: To keep the money as a bonus for the firm
options.why: Withholding is not a bonus for the employer; the money is sent to the government as an advance payment of your tax.

options.t: To lower the worker's total income by law
options.why: Withholding does not reduce your total income by law; it is just part of your pay sent toward taxes you owe.

options.t: To collect tax gradually through the year
options.why: Withholding spreads tax payments across the year, so you do not owe a lump sum on April 15. The amount depends on income and your W-4.

options.t: To pay the employee in advance for future work
options.why: Withholding is a deduction from pay, not a payment to you; employees are paid after work is done.

q: A worker gets a large refund every spring. What does this suggest about withholding?

options.t: The worker did not earn any income last year at all
options.why: A refund requires income and tax already withheld; a worker with no income would have no tax withheld to refund.

options.t: Too little tax was withheld from paychecks all year long
options.why: Too little withholding results in owing money at tax time, not a refund, so this is the reverse situation.

options.t: The employer paid the worker a surprise bonus in April
options.why: A refund is not a bonus from the employer; it is the worker's own overpaid tax being returned.

options.t: Too much tax was withheld from paychecks during the year
options.why: A large refund means more tax was taken out than owed, so the worker gave the government an interest-free loan. Adjusting the W-4 raises take-home pay.

q: What is self-employment tax?

options.t: A property tax that is charged on a home office space yearly
options.why: Property tax applies to real estate, whereas self-employment tax is a payroll-type tax on net earnings.

options.t: The Social Security and Medicare tax paid by the self-employed
options.why: Self-employment tax is about 15.3 percent, covering Social Security and Medicare that employers normally split with employees. Self-employed people pay both halves.

options.t: A tax that applies to gifts given to employees by firms
options.why: Gift tax applies to large gifts; self-employment tax is for those who work for themselves.

options.t: A sales tax that is added to the price of products sold at a store
options.why: Sales tax is collected on goods sold; self-employment tax is based on a person's net earnings from self-employment.

q: What is the main purpose of a resume?

options.t: To summarize your skills and experience
options.why: A resume is a short document summarizing your education, skills and experience to persuade employers to interview you.

options.t: To list the prices of your services for all
options.why: A list of service prices is a price sheet or quote, not a resume, which presents a person's qualifications.

options.t: To apply for a bank loan for a home
options.why: A bank loan application is a different document that asks about income and assets, not employment qualifications.

options.t: To report your income to the tax agency
options.why: Income reporting is done with tax forms like the W-2 and 1040, whereas a resume summarizes qualifications.

q: Two job offers pay $38,000. Job A includes health insurance worth $5,000 a year and Job B includes none. Which offer has the higher total value?

options.t: Neither, because the benefits have no value
options.why: Benefits like health insurance have real financial value, since you would otherwise pay for them yourself.

options.t: Job B, because it pays the same salary with fewer rules
options.why: Job B pays the same salary but lacks benefits, so its total value is lower, not higher.

options.t: Job A, because benefits add to total compensation
options.why: Total compensation includes salary and benefits: Job A is $38,000 + $5,000 = $43,000, versus $38,000 for Job B, so Job A is worth more.

options.t: They are exactly equal in total value to the worker
options.why: The offers are not equal because Job A adds $5,000 in health coverage, giving $43,000 against $38,000.

q: What is job satisfaction mostly influenced by besides pay?

options.t: The number of coworkers who happen to share a birthday
options.why: Coworker birthdays are trivial, whereas satisfaction depends on meaningful factors like the environment and opportunities.

options.t: The length of the daily commute and nothing else
options.why: Commute matters but is not the only factor; satisfaction also depends on environment, growth and interests.

options.t: The color of the walls in the office and nothing else
options.why: Wall color is minor; satisfaction comes mainly from the work environment, growth opportunities and interest fit.

options.t: Work environment, growth and fit with your interests
options.why: Besides pay, people are more satisfied with supportive workplaces, chances to grow, and work that matches their interests and values.

q: Why is it smart to keep receipts for major purchases?

options.t: They lower the price of the item at a later time, by half or more
options.why: Receipts do not change a price later; stores may offer price adjustments, but a receipt itself does not cut the price in half.

options.t: They prove what you paid and help with returns, warranties and taxes
options.why: A receipt is proof of purchase for returns, exchanges, warranty claims, and tax deductions or business expenses. Keep receipts for big purchases.

options.t: They let you spend the same money a second time if you like to
options.why: Receipts cannot be used to spend money twice; they are records, not currency or credit.

options.t: They are required by law for every purchase and must be filed with the state
options.why: Receipts are not legally required to be filed with the state; they are kept for your own protection and records.

q: What is a store credit card most likely to offer?

options.t: A discount on purchases at that store, often with a high interest rate
options.why: Store cards often give an opening discount or rewards at that store but usually carry high APRs, and can only be used at that retailer or its brands.

options.t: Lower interest rates than any other bank card ever offers to anyone
options.why: Store cards typically have higher interest rates than bank cards, not lower, so the claim is the opposite of the truth.

options.t: Free money that never has to be paid back by the cardholder at all
options.why: Store credit is borrowed money that must be repaid, so there is no free money involved.

options.t: Complete protection from fraud and identity theft wherever it is ever used
options.why: Store cards give limited fraud protection and no complete shield from theft; they do not prevent identity theft anywhere.

q: A store offers 'buy now, pay later' with no interest if you pay within 6 months. What risk should a shopper check?

options.t: Whether the item is also available in other colors
options.why: Color options are a product feature, not a financial risk of the payment plan.

options.t: Whether deferred interest or fees apply if unpaid
options.why: Deferred interest plans may charge all back interest from the purchase date if the balance is not fully paid by the end, so shoppers should check the terms.

options.t: Whether the logo of the store looks attractive
options.why: The logo's appearance is irrelevant to the cost; the financial risk comes from the terms, fees and interest conditions.

options.t: Whether the shopper has friends who also use the plan
options.why: Whether friends use the plan has nothing to do with its cost or risk; what matters are the plan's fees and conditions.

q: What does it mean to live within your means?

options.t: Spending more than you make
options.why: Spending more than you make is living beyond your means, which forces you to use debt or savings and is the opposite of the idea.

options.t: Never spending money on anything
options.why: Never spending anything is unrealistic because everyone must pay for needs like food and housing; living within your means only requires spending to fit your income.

options.t: Borrowing money for every purchase
options.why: Borrowing for every purchase means spending beyond current income and piling up debt, which is the opposite of living within your means.

options.t: Spending no more than you earn
options.why: Living within your means means keeping spending at or below your income each month, so you avoid debt and can still build savings for the future.

q: Which is the best example of delayed gratification in spending?

options.t: Spending your whole paycheck on the same day
options.why: Spending an entire paycheck right away is the opposite of delayed gratification, since it gives up any chance to save or plan for bigger goals.

options.t: Buying the first item you see in a store on a whim
options.why: Buying the first item you see on a whim is impulse buying, which is immediate gratification rather than waiting for something better or planned.

options.t: Saving for months to buy a quality item later
options.why: Delayed gratification means giving up an immediate purchase to get something better later, and saving for months toward a quality item is a classic example of it.

options.t: Charging a purchase you cannot repay to a card
options.why: Charging a purchase you cannot repay is immediate gratification paid for with debt and interest, so it is the reverse of waiting and saving first.

q: A teen can spend $100 on concert tickets or save it toward a $400 laptop needed for school. What is the opportunity cost of buying the tickets?

options.t: Progress toward the laptop that the $100 would have funded
options.why: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative you give up, so spending the $100 on tickets means losing $100 of progress toward the needed laptop.

options.t: Nothing, because tickets are a want, so nothing is lost
options.why: Tickets being a want does not make them free; the $100 spent could have gone toward the laptop, so something valuable is still given up.

options.t: The price of the laptop plus sales tax and any delivery fees
options.why: The laptop's price plus tax and delivery is the cost of buying the laptop, not what is given up by choosing the tickets instead.

options.t: The cost of parking at the big concert venue for the night
options.why: Parking is an extra out-of-pocket expense of attending the concert, not the opportunity cost, which is the best alternative use of the $100.

q: Why is a savings account safer than keeping large amounts of cash at home?

options.t: Cash kept at home earns higher interest than an account
options.why: Cash kept at home earns no interest at all, while a savings account pays interest, so this claim reverses the real difference between them.

options.t: FDIC insurance protects deposits from theft or fire
options.why: FDIC insurance protects deposits up to $250,000 per depositor per bank if the bank fails, whereas cash at home can be stolen or burned with no protection.

options.t: Savings accounts cannot be used when an emergency happens
options.why: Savings accounts can be accessed in an emergency, usually by transfer or withdrawal, so this does not explain why they are safer than home cash.

options.t: Banks never charge any fees on a savings account
options.why: Banks can charge fees on savings accounts, such as monthly maintenance or excess withdrawal fees, so the word never makes this statement false.

q: Which statement about interest on savings is correct?

options.t: Interest is the amount you deposit every month into the bank
options.why: Money you put into the account is a deposit; interest is instead the amount the bank pays you for using your money, not what you contribute.

options.t: Interest is a fee you pay for opening an account at a bank
options.why: Interest is not an account opening fee; fees are charges you pay, while savings interest is a payment made to you by the bank.

options.t: Interest is a tax you owe to the government on your balance each month
options.why: Interest earned on savings is not a tax, although it may be taxable income; it is a payment from the bank, not an amount owed to government.

options.t: Interest is money the bank pays you for keeping funds on deposit
options.why: Interest is the money a bank pays you for letting it use your deposits, usually stated as an annual rate, and it grows your balance over time.

q: Priya deposits $2,000 at 3% compounded annually. About how much will she have after 2 years?

options.t: About $2,122
options.why: Compound interest: $2,000 x 1.03 x 1.03 = $2,121.80, which rounds to about $2,122 because interest in year two also earns interest.

options.t: About $2,060
options.why: This adds only simple interest for one year ($2,000 x 3% = $60) and ignores the second year, so it is far too low.

options.t: About $2,180
options.why: This option was reworded so it is clearly wrong; the correct total is $2,000 x 1.03 x 1.03 = $2,121.80, and $2,180 would need a higher rate.

options.t: About $2,600
options.why: About $2,600 would require roughly 30 percent growth, far above the 3% annual rate; $2,000 x 1.03^2 is only about $2,122.

q: What is a good way to avoid dipping into savings for small wants?

options.t: Carry large amounts of cash with you everywhere you go each day
options.why: Carrying large amounts of cash makes spending easier and risks loss or theft, so it makes dipping into savings for wants more likely, not less.

options.t: Keep all of your money in one single account and never track it or set limits
options.why: Keeping everything in one account with no tracking or limits blurs savings and spending money, which makes it easy to spend savings on small wants.

options.t: Keep a separate account for goals and a small budget for fun spending
options.why: Separating goal savings from a small fun budget keeps savings untouched and gives you guilt-free spending money, which helps you resist raiding savings for small wants.

options.t: Cancel your savings account and spend what is in it right away
options.why: Closing your savings account and spending the money is the exact opposite of protecting savings and would leave you with nothing for goals or emergencies.

q: What does FDIC insurance cover?

options.t: Cash that is kept in a safe at home for emergency use only
options.why: FDIC insurance does not cover cash kept at home; it only protects money deposited in FDIC-insured banks, so home cash has no such protection.

options.t: Stocks that are bought through a bank or a broker up to the legal limit
options.why: Stocks bought through a bank or broker are investments, not deposits, so FDIC insurance does not cover them; SIPC covers broker failure, not losses.

options.t: Deposits in insured banks up to the legal limit if the bank fails
options.why: FDIC insurance covers deposits in insured banks up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category, and pays out if the bank fails.

options.t: Losses that are caused by a drop in the stock market overall
options.why: FDIC insurance does not protect against market losses on investments; it only guarantees bank deposits if the bank itself fails, not falling stock prices.

q: Why can closing an old credit card account sometimes lower a credit score?

options.t: It can shorten credit history and raise credit utilization
options.why: Closing an old card shortens your average account age and removes available credit, which can raise your utilization ratio, and both effects may lower your score.

options.t: Old accounts are not counted in any credit score at all
options.why: Old accounts do count in credit scores; length of credit history is a scoring factor, which is why closing them can matter at all.

options.t: Closed accounts are always deleted at once and never reopened
options.why: Closed accounts in good standing often stay on your report for about ten years, so they are not deleted at once and the score drop has other causes.

options.t: Banks punish customers for canceling their credit cards
options.why: Banks do not punish customers for closing cards; the score may fall because of changed history length and utilization, which are mathematical effects.

q: A person with a 620 credit score and one with a 780 score both apply for a $15,000 car loan. Which is more likely to get a lower interest rate?

options.t: Neither of them can get a loan from any bank at all today
options.why: Lenders do approve loans for fair or good credit scores, usually at higher rates for lower scores, so neither being denied outright is a safe assumption.

options.t: Both will receive exactly the same rate from the lender today
options.why: Lenders price loans based on risk, so different credit scores lead to different rates; the same rate for both borrowers is unlikely.

options.t: The person with the 620 score, because lenders need customers
options.why: A 620 score signals higher default risk, so lenders charge more interest to offset that risk rather than offering a cheaper rate.

options.t: The person with the 780 score, because lenders see less risk
options.why: A 780 score signals reliable repayment, so lenders see less default risk and generally offer a lower interest rate on the $15,000 car loan.

q: What is a variable interest rate?

options.t: A rate that is chosen by the borrower at the start of the loan
options.why: A borrower does not choose the rate; the lender sets it, and the term variable means the rate can change over time, not that it is picked by the borrower.

options.t: A rate that can go up or down over time based on market conditions
options.why: A variable rate is tied to a benchmark such as the prime rate, so it can rise or fall over time and change your payment amount.

options.t: A rate that is always set at zero for the whole of the loan term
options.why: A rate fixed at zero would be an interest-free loan, which is rare; a variable rate instead moves with market conditions above zero.

options.t: A rate that never changes during the whole life of the loan itself
options.why: A rate that never changes during the loan is a fixed rate, which is the opposite of a variable rate that adjusts with the market.

q: What is a fixed interest rate?

options.t: A rate that stays the same for the full loan term
options.why: A fixed interest rate stays the same for the whole loan term, so the rate and usually the payment are predictable and do not change with the market.

options.t: A rate that is repaid at the end of the loan only
options.why: Fixed refers to the rate staying constant, not to repaying everything at the end; most loans charge interest along the way, not only at maturity.

options.t: A rate that is free of charge for the borrower
options.why: Interest is the price of borrowing and is not free; a fixed rate is still charged, it just does not change over the loan.

options.t: A rate that changes each month with the market
options.why: A rate that changes monthly with the market is a variable rate, which is the opposite of a fixed rate that stays constant.

q: Before taking out a loan, which comparison tells you the true yearly cost of borrowing from different lenders?

options.t: The color of the loan paperwork
options.why: The color of the paperwork says nothing about borrowing costs; the cost is shown in the interest rate and fees, which APR combines into one yearly percentage.

options.t: The number of branches lenders have
options.why: The number of branches tells you about convenience, not what the loan costs; it cannot be used to compare the yearly price of borrowing.

options.t: The size of the lender's building
options.why: The lender's building size has no link to loan pricing; APR is the standardized measure that lets you compare real borrowing costs across lenders.

options.t: The annual percentage rate (APR)
options.why: APR combines the interest rate and certain fees into one yearly percentage, so it is the best way to compare the true cost of loans from different lenders.

q: Why should you review your insurance coverage after a major life change like buying a house?

options.t: Insurance is only needed once in a lifetime for any person
options.why: Insurance needs change with life events, so it is not a once-in-a-lifetime purchase; major changes like a home purchase require updating your coverage.

options.t: Insurance policies update themselves for free for everyone covered
options.why: Policies do not update themselves automatically at no charge; you must contact the insurer to change coverage, and higher coverage usually raises the premium.

options.t: Your needs and the value you need to protect may have changed
options.why: A major change like buying a house raises the value you need to protect and adds new risks, so reviewing coverage keeps you from being underinsured.

options.t: Reviewing a policy cancels it and ends your coverage for good
options.why: Reviewing a policy does not cancel it; you simply check whether limits and coverage still fit, and the policy remains in force during the review.

q: A driver causes an accident that injures another person and has only the state minimum liability coverage. What is the main risk?

options.t: The other driver must pay for everything that happened there too
options.why: The other driver is not responsible for your costs; as the at-fault driver you owe damages, and the issue is limits being too low to cover them.

options.t: Costs above the policy limits may have to be paid out of pocket
options.why: State minimum limits are often low, so a serious injury claim can exceed them, and the at-fault driver may have to pay the excess out of pocket.

options.t: No costs will be owed because it was an accident, not on purpose
options.why: Causing an accident accidentally still creates liability, since negligence rather than intent determines responsibility, so costs can definitely be owed.

options.t: The insurer will pay unlimited amounts no matter the limits
options.why: Liability policies pay only up to their stated limits, so the insurer will not pay unlimited amounts and the driver must cover anything above them.

q: Which action reduces the risk of a home fire?

options.t: Leaving candles burning while you sleep at night in the home
options.why: Leaving candles burning unattended while you sleep is a common cause of house fires, so it raises fire risk rather than reducing it.

options.t: Removing the batteries from all of the smoke detectors at home
options.why: Removing smoke detector batteries disables the early warning that saves lives, so it increases the danger of a fire rather than reducing it.

options.t: Installing working smoke detectors and not overloading outlets
options.why: Working smoke detectors give early warning and avoiding overloaded outlets prevents electrical fires, so together these actions lower the chance and damage of a home fire.

options.t: Storing flammable liquids close to a heater or a gas stove
options.why: Storing flammable liquids near a heater or gas stove invites ignition and fire, so it raises the risk of a home fire.

q: What is self-insurance?

options.t: Asking a friend to promise to pay for a loss that happens
options.why: A friend's promise to pay is an informal arrangement and not self-insurance, which means setting aside your own funds to absorb losses yourself.

options.t: Setting aside your own money to cover possible losses
options.why: Self-insurance means setting aside your own money to cover possible losses instead of buying a policy, and it works best for small, predictable risks.

options.t: Ignoring the possibility of loss and hoping for the best
options.why: Ignoring risk and hoping for the best is risk acceptance without any plan, not self-insurance, which involves actually saving funds to pay for losses.

options.t: Buying a policy from an insurance company every single year
options.why: Buying a yearly policy from an insurance company transfers risk to the insurer, so it is traditional insurance, the opposite of self-insuring.

q: Which loss is best handled by buying insurance rather than saving for it?

options.t: A rare event that could cost far more than you could ever save
options.why: Insurance fits rare but very costly events like a house fire or major illness, which would wipe out savings, so spreading risk across many policyholders makes sense.

options.t: A regular expense that comes up every month, like rent or food
options.why: Regular predictable expenses such as rent or food are budgeted for, not insured, since insurance covers uncertain losses and not certain recurring bills.

options.t: A cost that you choose to avoid completely in your life
options.why: Completely avoiding a cost is risk avoidance, a different strategy from insurance, which covers risks you are still exposed to.

options.t: A small cost that you can easily pay from your own savings
options.why: A small cost you can easily afford is better handled by saving and self-insuring, since insurance premiums would likely cost more than the loss.

q: What does it mean when an investment is liquid?

options.t: It never changes in value over time at all, ever
options.why: A liquid investment is easy to convert to cash, which has nothing to do with value staying fixed; liquid assets can still rise and fall in price.

options.t: It cannot be sold for several years in a row
options.why: An asset that cannot be sold for years is illiquid, which is the opposite of liquid; liquidity is about how quickly you can turn it into cash.

options.t: It is stored as water or some other fluid in a tank
options.why: Liquid here is a financial term, not a physical state of matter; the word describes how easily an asset converts to cash, not its form.

options.t: It can be sold quickly for cash with little loss
options.why: Liquid means you can sell the asset quickly for cash without losing much value, like savings or shares of large companies.

q: Which is usually the most liquid asset?

options.t: A house in a nice neighborhood
options.why: A house takes weeks or months to sell and has closing costs, so it is illiquid compared with cash in a checking account.

options.t: A rare painting from a gallery
options.why: A rare painting needs a specialized buyer and appraisal, which makes selling slow and uncertain, so it is far less liquid than cash.

options.t: Cash in a checking account
options.why: Cash in checking is already money and can be used immediately, so it is the most liquid asset on the list.

options.t: A piece of land in the country
options.why: Land can take a long time to sell and its value depends on location and buyers, so it is illiquid compared with cash.

q: An investor puts all their money into one company's stock and the company fails. Which investing principle did they ignore?

options.t: Diversification
options.why: Diversification means spreading money across many investments so one failure does not ruin you; putting everything into one company's stock ignores it.

options.t: Tax deferral
options.why: Tax deferral delays taxes on investment growth; it has nothing to do with losing everything when a single company fails, which is concentration risk.

options.t: Compounding
options.why: Compounding is earning returns on prior returns, which does not address the danger of holding only one company's stock that can fail.

options.t: Inflation cover
options.why: Inflation cover is not a standard investing principle; the risk of loss from a single failed company is controlled by diversification instead.

q: What is a stock market index?

options.t: A single company's yearly profit report for its owners
options.why: A company's yearly profit report is an income statement, which describes one firm, while an index tracks the performance of many stocks together.

options.t: A measure of the performance of a group of stocks
options.why: A stock market index, such as the S&P 500 or Dow, measures the performance of a chosen group of stocks and shows how the market is doing.

options.t: A government rule about taxes on stock trades
options.why: Tax rules on stock trades come from government law, such as capital gains tax, and are not what an index is, which only measures performance.

options.t: A list of the fees that brokers charge clients
options.why: A list of broker fees is a fee schedule, not an index; an index tracks stock prices and gives a snapshot of market performance.

q: What is rebalancing a portfolio?

options.t: Selling everything and starting over from scratch each year
options.why: Selling everything and starting over each year is expensive because of taxes and trading costs; rebalancing only adjusts holdings back to targets.

options.t: Buying only the single best performer in the portfolio
options.why: Buying only the best performer concentrates risk and abandons the target mix, which is the opposite of rebalancing a diversified portfolio.

options.t: Ignoring the portfolio for years on end and hoping for gains
options.why: Ignoring a portfolio lets asset weights drift away from your plan, so it is the opposite of rebalancing, which restores the intended mix.

options.t: Adjusting investments back to your target mix of assets
options.why: Rebalancing means buying or selling to restore your target mix of assets, such as 60% stocks and 40% bonds, which keeps your risk level on plan.

q: A long-term investor sees the market drop 15% in a month. Which response is generally most sensible?

options.t: Borrow money so you can buy a single stock
options.why: Borrowing to buy a single stock adds debt and concentration risk during a downturn, which is a risky response rather than a sensible one.

options.t: Sell everything immediately because of fear
options.why: Selling everything out of fear locks in losses and often misses the recovery, which makes it a poor response for a long-term investor.

options.t: Stay with the plan and keep investing regularly
options.why: Long-term investors generally do best staying with their plan and continuing regular investing, which buys more shares at lower prices during a dip.

options.t: Stop looking at the plan and give up on your goal
options.why: Abandoning the plan and giving up on your goal turns a temporary decline into a permanent setback, which is not a sensible response.

q: What does the saying 'don't put all your eggs in one basket' mean for investing?

options.t: Spend all of your money on eggs and baskets today
options.why: This takes the saying literally; the proverb is about diversifying risk, and spending all your money on eggs and baskets has nothing to do with investing.

options.t: Buy only one single stock that you trust
options.why: Buying one stock puts all your eggs in one basket, which is exactly what the saying warns against because one failure can wipe you out.

options.t: Avoid investing in anything at all, ever again
options.why: Avoiding investing altogether misses the lesson; the saying advises spreading money around, not refusing to invest, and cash can lose value to inflation.

options.t: Spread your money across different investments
options.why: The saying advises diversification, spreading money across different investments so that one loss does not destroy your whole portfolio.

q: What is the main benefit of an employer 401(k) match?

options.t: It adds extra money to your retirement savings for free
options.why: A 401(k) match is extra money your employer adds to your account based on what you contribute, which is a free boost to retirement savings.

options.t: It guarantees investment gains every single year for you
options.why: A match adds money but guarantees no investment gains; the account's investments can still lose value, so returns are never guaranteed.

options.t: It lets you withdraw money any time with no rules or taxes
options.why: Withdrawals from a 401(k) before age 59 and a half usually bring taxes and a 10 percent penalty, so the match does not allow free access.

options.t: It lowers your income tax to zero every single year for life
options.why: Traditional 401(k) contributions reduce taxable income but do not lower taxes to zero, and the match itself has no such effect.

q: Two investors each save $200 a month for 30 years. One earns 4% and the other 7%. Which result is most likely?

options.t: Neither investor earns any growth at all over time
options.why: Both investors earn growth because 4% and 7% are both positive returns; saying neither earns growth ignores the compounding that happens each year.

options.t: The 7% investor ends far ahead through compounding
options.why: Over 30 years the higher 7% return compounds much more strongly than 4%, so that investor ends with far more money for the same deposits.

options.t: The 4% investor ends up with the larger balance overall
options.why: The 4% investor earns a lower return on identical deposits, so ends with a smaller balance, not a larger one.

options.t: Both investors end up with the same final balance
options.why: Different returns over 30 years produce very different balances because compounding magnifies the gap, so the final amounts cannot be the same.

q: What is a bear market?

options.t: A period when prices rise steadily over a long period of time
options.why: Steadily rising prices describe a bull market, not a bear market, which is the opposite condition of falling prices.

options.t: A period when stock markets close for a holiday and no trading occurs
options.why: Stock markets closing for a holiday is just a normal break in trading and has nothing to do with a bear market, which is about falling prices.

options.t: A market where people buy and sell wild animals for sport and food
options.why: A bear market is a financial term about stock prices and has nothing to do with trading animals; the name refers to a bear swiping downward.

options.t: A period when stock prices fall significantly, often 20% or more
options.why: A bear market is a sustained decline in stock prices, commonly defined as a fall of 20 percent or more from a recent high.

q: What is a bull market?

options.t: A period when stock prices are rising or expected to rise
options.why: A bull market is a period of rising or expected rising stock prices, with investor optimism, and the name comes from a bull thrusting its horns upward.

options.t: A period when prices fall sharply and investors grow afraid
options.why: Sharp falling prices and investor fear describe a bear market, which is the opposite of a bull market.

options.t: A market where only livestock is traded each week in town
options.why: A bull market refers to rising security prices, not a livestock market; the word is a financial term unrelated to trading cattle.

options.t: A period when prices never change at all for many years
options.why: Prices never changing for many years would be a flat or stagnant market, not a bull market, which is defined by rising prices.

q: What is a stock split?

options.t: A company gives half its yearly profits to staff
options.why: Sharing half of profits with staff is profit sharing, not a stock split, which only changes the number of shares and not company earnings.

options.t: More shares at a proportionally lower price each
options.why: In a stock split, a company issues more shares and lowers the price per share proportionally, so each holder's total value stays the same.

options.t: A company merges with one of its rivals in a deal
options.why: Merging with a rival is a merger or acquisition, which combines companies; a stock split only divides existing shares into more pieces.

options.t: A company cuts its workforce in half to save costs
options.why: Cutting the workforce in half is a layoff or restructuring and is unrelated to a stock split, which changes only the number of shares.

q: Which statement about past investment performance is accurate?

options.t: It guarantees the same results next year
options.why: Past performance cannot guarantee next year's results, since markets change, so saying it guarantees the same outcome is false.

options.t: It is the only factor that matters
options.why: Past performance is only one piece of information; costs, risk, goals and economic conditions matter too, so it is not the only factor.

options.t: It does not guarantee future results
options.why: Past performance does not guarantee future results, which is why investment ads carry this warning; markets change and previous gains may not repeat.

options.t: It proves an investment cannot lose cash
options.why: A good track record does not prove an investment cannot lose money; every investment carries risk, even one that has done well in the past.

q: Which choice best protects the buying power of long-term savings from inflation?

options.t: A diversified mix that has outpaced inflation
options.why: A diversified mix of investments that has outpaced inflation helps long-term savings keep or grow their purchasing power over decades.

options.t: Spending all of your savings right away today
options.why: Spending all your savings right away gives up future purchasing power altogether and does nothing to protect it from inflation.

options.t: Keeping all of your savings in cash for decades
options.why: Cash earning little interest loses buying power to inflation over decades, so holding all savings in cash does not protect them.

options.t: Hiding cash in a drawer at home for decades
options.why: Cash in a drawer earns no interest, so inflation steadily reduces what it can buy, and it also risks loss or theft.

q: What is a good first step to take control of your spending?

options.t: Stop looking at your account balance for a month
options.why: Not checking your balance hides spending problems and may cause overdrafts, so it does not help you gain control over your spending.

options.t: Cancel your bank account altogether and use cash
options.why: Cancelling your bank account and using only cash removes safety and records and does not itself show where your money goes.

options.t: Borrow money so you can cover your purchases this month
options.why: Borrowing to cover purchases adds debt and interest, which makes spending harder to control rather than easier.

options.t: Track a month of spending to see where money goes
options.why: Tracking a month of spending shows exactly where money goes, which reveals patterns and gives a base for budgeting and cutting waste.

q: What is the best way to avoid paying credit card interest?

options.t: Use the card only for cash advances at the bank ATM each month
options.why: Cash advances usually carry fees and start accruing interest immediately with no grace period, so they increase interest costs rather than avoid them.

options.t: Pay the full statement balance by the due date every month
options.why: Paying the full statement balance by the due date keeps the grace period, so purchases are not charged interest at all.

options.t: Pay the bill a few days after the due date has already passed
options.why: Paying after the due date usually triggers a late fee and may lose the grace period, so interest and penalties apply.

options.t: Pay only the minimum amount each month on the card balance
options.why: Paying only the minimum leaves a balance that accrues interest, which can make the debt costly and slow to pay off.

q: What is a cash advance on a credit card?

options.t: Earning cash back on the purchases you make with the card
options.why: Earning cash back is a rewards benefit for purchases, not a cash advance, which is borrowing actual cash against your credit line.

options.t: Paying a bill early using your own money from savings
options.why: Paying a bill early from savings uses your own money and involves no card borrowing, so it is not a cash advance.

options.t: Borrowing cash on your card, with fees and interest
options.why: A cash advance is borrowing cash against your card, usually at a higher rate, with an upfront fee and interest from day one.

options.t: Depositing cash into your own bank account at a branch
options.why: Depositing cash into your own account is a normal bank deposit, not a card transaction, so it has nothing to do with cash advances.

q: What is the difference between earned income and unearned income?

options.t: Earned income comes from gifts; unearned from jobs and pay
options.why: This reverses the definitions; earned income comes from working at jobs and pay, while gifts are not earned income.

options.t: Earned income is never taxed, unearned always is taxed
options.why: Earned income is taxed, including income tax and payroll taxes, and unearned income such as interest is also generally taxable, so the claim is wrong.

options.t: Earned income comes from work; unearned from interest
options.why: Earned income comes from work such as wages and salary, while unearned income comes from sources like interest, dividends and rent without working.

options.t: There is no real difference between the two kinds of income
options.why: There is a real difference: earned income comes from working, unearned income comes from assets, and they are taxed differently in many cases.

q: What is the purpose of an emergency fund in relation to spending?

options.t: It covers unplanned costs without using credit
options.why: An emergency fund covers unplanned costs like medical bills or car repairs so you do not need credit cards or loans that would add interest.

options.t: It is meant for planned vacations and trips abroad
options.why: Planned vacations belong in a separate savings goal, since an emergency fund should be reserved for unexpected, urgent expenses.

options.t: It is meant to grow quickly through risky bets
options.why: An emergency fund should be safe and easy to access, not exposed to risky bets that could lose value when you need it.

options.t: It replaces the need for insurance of all kinds
options.why: An emergency fund cannot replace insurance because one major accident or illness can cost far more than the fund holds.

q: What is income?

options.t: Money a person spends on needs and wants each single month
options.why: Money spent on needs and wants is expenses, which is the opposite of income, the money coming in.

options.t: Money received from work, investments or other sources
options.why: Income is money received from work, investments, or other sources such as interest, gifts or benefits, and it funds spending and saving.

options.t: Money borrowed from a bank for a large purchase like a car
options.why: Money borrowed from a bank is a loan that must be repaid, not income, which does not create an obligation to repay.

options.t: Money set aside for use in an emergency fund account
options.why: Money set aside for emergencies is savings, which is held from income already received rather than being the income itself.

q: What is the difference between wages and salary?

options.t: There is no difference between the two terms of pay at all
options.why: There is a difference: wages are paid by the hour, while salaried workers get a fixed amount per year regardless of hours.

options.t: Wages are fixed yearly pay; a salary is paid by the hour worked
options.why: This reverses the definitions; wages are hourly pay and salary is a fixed yearly amount, not the other way around.

options.t: Wages are tips; a salary is a bonus paid out at year end
options.why: Tips and bonuses are separate types of compensation, so equating wages with tips and salary with bonuses is incorrect.

options.t: Wages are paid by the hour; a salary is a fixed yearly amount
options.why: Wages are paid by the hour worked, so pay varies with hours, while a salary is a fixed yearly amount split across pay periods.

q: Priya earns $18 an hour and works 25 hours a week. What is her gross weekly pay?

options.why: $43 is $18 plus $25 added together; gross pay uses multiplication, so the correct figure is $18 x 25 = $450.
$4,500 is ten times too large, likely from a misplaced decimal; $18 x 25 hours equals $450, not $4,500.
$225 is half of the correct amount, as if only 12.5 hours were counted; $18 x 25 hours equals $450.
Gross pay is the hourly rate times hours worked, so $18 x 25 = $450 per week before taxes and deductions.

q: A worker earns $15 an hour with overtime at 1.5 times after 40 hours. She works 46 hours. What is her gross pay?

options.why: $1,035 pays all 46 hours at 1.5 times rate; overtime applies only to hours past 40, so the correct total is $735.
$690 is 46 hours at the regular $15 rate with no overtime premium; the 6 overtime hours should be paid at $22.50.
Regular pay is 40 x $15 = $600, overtime is 6 x $22.50 = $135, and the total is $735.
$600 counts only the first 40 hours and leaves out the 6 overtime hours; adding 6 x $22.50 = $135 gives $735.

q: Which is a payroll deduction required by law?

options.t: A gym fee the worker chose to pay
options.why: A gym fee chosen by the worker is a voluntary deduction; the law does not require it, unlike taxes withheld by an employer.

options.t: Federal income tax withholding
options.why: Federal income tax withholding is required by law, and employers must deduct it from each paycheck based on the worker's W-4.

options.t: A parking space fee at the office
options.why: A parking fee is an optional arrangement with the employer and not a legal requirement, so it is a voluntary deduction.

options.t: A charity donation made at work
options.why: A charity donation made at work is voluntary, so it is a chosen deduction, not one required by law like taxes.

q: What does FICA fund?

options.t: Social Security and Medicare
options.why: FICA taxes fund Social Security, which pays retirement and disability benefits, and Medicare, which provides health coverage for seniors and some others.

options.t: Public schools and libraries
options.why: Public schools and libraries are mostly funded by local property taxes and state revenue, not by FICA payroll taxes.

options.t: Public highways and bridges
options.why: Highways and bridges are funded mainly by fuel taxes and government budgets, not by FICA, which supports Social Security and Medicare.

options.t: National parks and forests
options.why: National parks and forests are paid for through federal budgets and fees, not through FICA payroll taxes meant for Social Security and Medicare.

q: FICA is 7.65% for the employee. How much is withheld from $2,000 gross pay?

options.why: $15.30 is moved one decimal place too small; 7.65% of $2,000 is $153, not $15.30.
$765 is 38 percent of $2,000 and uses the wrong rate; 7.65% x $2,000 = $153.
$1,530 is ten times too much, from a decimal error; 0.0765 x $2,000 = $153.
Multiply gross pay by the FICA rate: $2,000 x 0.0765 = $153 withheld for Social Security and Medicare.

q: What is take-home pay?

options.t: Pay from tips and bonuses only
options.why: Pay from tips and bonuses only is a partial description of earnings and does not describe take-home pay, which is what remains after deductions.

options.t: Pay for overtime hours only
options.why: Overtime pay is extra pay for hours past 40, and it is not the same as take-home pay, which is after deductions.

options.t: Pay after taxes and deductions
options.why: Take-home pay, or net pay, is what remains after taxes and deductions are subtracted from your gross pay.

options.t: Pay before any deductions at all
options.why: Pay before any deductions is gross pay, which is the opposite of take-home pay, also called net pay.

q: What is a W-4 form?

options.t: A form reporting yearly wages and the taxes paid to date
options.why: A form reporting yearly wages and taxes paid to date is the W-2, which the employer gives the worker after the year, not the W-4.

options.t: A form that tells an employer how much tax to withhold
options.why: The W-4 tells your employer how much federal income tax to withhold from your paycheck based on your filing status and allowances.

options.t: A form for requesting vacation time from your manager
options.why: A vacation request is an internal company form and has nothing to do with taxes, which the W-4 handles.

options.t: A form for applying to a job at a local company or store
options.why: A job application is filled out when applying; the W-4 is completed after hiring to set tax withholding.

q: What is an independent contractor?

options.t: A self-employed person who controls how the work is done
options.why: An independent contractor is self-employed, chooses how the work is done, and is paid per job instead of receiving employee wages or benefits.

options.t: A full-time worker with benefits who takes orders from a boss
options.why: A full-time worker with benefits who takes orders from a boss is a regular employee, not an independent contractor.

options.t: A manager at a company who hires and fires its workers
options.why: A manager who hires and fires staff is part of the company as an employee and not an independent contractor.

options.t: A person on probation at a new job in the first months
options.why: Someone on probation at a new job is still an employee, so this does not describe an independent contractor.

q: Which form reports payments to an independent contractor?

options.t: Form 1099
options.why: Form 1099, commonly 1099-NEC, reports payments of $600 or more to independent contractors, who then report that income themselves.

options.t: Form W-2 copy
options.why: A W-2 reports wages paid to employees, with taxes withheld, not payments made to independent contractors.

options.t: Form W-4
options.why: Form W-4 tells an employer how much tax to withhold from an employee's pay, so it does not report payments to contractors.

options.t: Form I-9
options.why: Form I-9 verifies a worker's identity and eligibility to work in the US, and does not report payments.

q: A freelancer earns $5,000 with no tax withheld. What should the freelancer do?

options.t: Nothing, because freelance income is tax free at first
options.why: Freelance income is taxable, including self-employment tax, even if no tax was withheld, so it is not tax free.

options.t: Spend it all immediately on whatever you like
options.why: Spending all of it ignores the tax bill that will come due, which could leave you owing money you do not have.

options.t: Wait to see if the IRS asks you for any taxes later
options.why: Waiting for the IRS to ask can lead to penalties and interest, so freelancers should pay taxes without being asked.

options.t: Set aside money for taxes and pay estimated taxes
options.why: With no tax withheld, a freelancer should set aside money and pay estimated quarterly taxes to avoid penalties and a big bill.

q: What is a benefit package?

options.t: The hourly wage a worker earns, paid every two weeks or so
options.why: An hourly wage is pay for work, whereas a benefit package is extra compensation beyond wages, such as insurance and leave.

options.t: Non-wage compensation such as insurance and paid leave
options.why: A benefit package is non-wage compensation, such as health insurance, retirement plans and paid leave, that adds to the value of a job.

options.t: A schedule of shifts and breaks for the staff each week
options.why: A schedule of shifts and breaks is a work schedule and is not compensation, which is what a benefit package is.

options.t: A fine for lateness that is taken from the paycheck
options.why: A fine for lateness would be a penalty or deduction, whereas a benefit package adds value to the worker's compensation.

q: What is a 401(k) employer match?

options.t: A fee the employee pays to join the plan each year
options.why: The employer match is not a fee paid by the employee; it is money the employer adds to the account, so the claim is backward.

options.t: A loan from the employer that is repaid with interest
options.why: A match is a contribution made to your account by your employer, not a loan, and it does not require repayment with interest.

options.t: Money the employer adds based on your contributions
options.why: The employer match adds money to your 401(k) based on your own contributions, often a percentage up to a limit, which is free retirement money.

options.t: A tax on the account that the worker pays each year
options.why: The match is not a tax on the account; it is an employer contribution that increases your retirement savings.

q: An employer matches 100% of contributions up to 4% of pay. You earn $30,000 and contribute 4%. How much does the employer add?

options.why: $12,000 is 40% of salary and overstates the match; 4% of $30,000 is $1,200.
$600 is only 2% of salary, half of the correct match; the employer matches 100% of your 4%, which is $1,200.
You contribute 4% of $30,000 = $1,200, and a 100% match gives the employer's addition as $1,200.
$120 is only 0.4% of salary, a decimal error; 4% x $30,000 = $1,200 matched.

q: What is a performance bonus?

options.t: Extra pay for strong results
options.why: A performance bonus is extra pay given for strong results, on top of regular wages, to reward and motivate employees.

options.t: A tax on all earnings each year
options.why: A tax on earnings is a government charge on income, while a performance bonus is extra pay from an employer.

options.t: A regular fixed wage each week
options.why: A regular fixed weekly wage is base pay, whereas a bonus is extra pay tied to results and not regular.

options.t: A fine for very poor results
options.why: A fine for poor results would be a penalty, the opposite of a bonus, which rewards strong results.

q: A salesperson earns a $1,500 base plus 4% commission on $30,000 of sales. What is the total pay?

options.why: $31,500 mistakes 4% for 105% or adds all sales to the base; commission is only 4% of $30,000, which is $1,200.
$1,200 is only the commission and leaves out the $1,500 base pay; total pay is $1,500 + $1,200 = $2,700.
$3,000 would need $1,500 in commission, about 5% of sales; 4% of $30,000 is $1,200, so total is $2,700.
Commission is 4% x $30,000 = $1,200, and adding the $1,500 base gives total pay of $2,700.

q: What is a gig economy job?

options.t: A volunteer role at a charity or a local school or club
options.why: Volunteer work is unpaid, whereas gig work is paid short-term or freelance work, so a charity role is not a gig job.

options.t: Short-term or freelance work, often arranged through an app
options.why: A gig economy job is short-term or freelance work, such as ridesharing or delivery, often arranged through an app, with flexible hours.

options.t: A government role in a city office or a state agency
options.why: A government job in a city office is typically a permanent public sector position, which is not what a gig is.

options.t: A permanent salaried role with benefits and a fixed schedule
options.why: A permanent salaried role with benefits and a set schedule is traditional employment, the opposite of gig work.

q: Which is a downside of gig work?

options.t: Fixed schedules set by the employer for staff
options.why: Fixed schedules set by an employer are a feature of traditional jobs, whereas gig workers usually set their own hours.

options.t: Guaranteed steady pay every week and month
options.why: Guaranteed steady pay is not typical in gig work, where earnings depend on the jobs and demand, so it is not a downside.

options.t: Employer-paid health insurance always at no cost
options.why: Gig workers are usually independent contractors and typically must buy their own health insurance, so it is not paid at no cost.

options.t: Income can vary and benefits may be limited
options.why: Income varies with the number of gigs available, and gig workers usually lack employer benefits like insurance and paid leave.

q: What is minimum wage?

options.t: A bonus for new hires paid after one year of work
options.why: A bonus for new hires is not minimum wage, which is a legal floor on hourly pay for all covered employees.

options.t: The highest hourly pay allowed by law to any worker
options.why: Minimum wage is a floor, not a ceiling; the law does not set the highest hourly pay allowed.

options.t: The lowest hourly pay an employer may legally offer
options.why: Minimum wage is the lowest hourly pay an employer may legally offer to covered workers, set by federal and state law.

options.t: The pay of managers and other executives in a firm
options.why: The pay of managers and executives is usually much higher and is not defined by minimum wage, which is a legal floor.

q: A state minimum wage is higher than the federal one. Which must a covered employer follow?

options.t: The higher state minimum wage
options.why: When a state minimum wage is higher than the federal one, covered employers must pay the higher state rate because it gives workers more.

options.t: Only the federal minimum wage
options.why: Following only the federal minimum would underpay workers where the state rate is higher; employers must meet the higher rate.

options.t: Whichever of the two is lower
options.why: Following the lower wage would violate the higher standard; employers must follow whichever is higher.

options.t: Neither of the two wages applies
options.why: Minimum wage laws do apply to covered employers, so saying neither applies is wrong; the higher one governs.

q: Why does education generally raise earning potential?

options.t: Education removes the need to work for a living
options.why: Education does not remove the need to work; it raises skills and often pay, but people still work after earning degrees.

options.t: More skills and credentials are valued by employers
options.why: Education builds skills and credentials that employers value, which tends to qualify workers for higher-paying jobs and raises earning potential.

options.t: Education lowers taxes on all of the income earned
options.why: Education does not lower taxes on income; higher earnings can even raise taxes, but the benefit is higher earnings.

options.t: Education guarantees a job without any effort at all
options.why: Education improves job prospects but guarantees nothing; people must still apply, perform, and compete, so no job comes without effort.

q: Which choice is most likely to increase long-term earnings?

options.t: Working fewer hours with no goals, hoping a job turns up
options.why: Working fewer hours with no goals and hoping for a job does not build skills or income, so it will not increase long-term earnings.

options.t: Avoiding all training or classes that could build skills
options.why: Avoiding training means skills fall behind demand, which limits job choices and pay, so it hurts long-term earnings.

options.t: Building in-demand skills through training or education
options.why: In-demand skills gained through training or education make workers more valuable to employers, which raises pay and improves job security over time.

options.t: Changing jobs with no plan for what comes next in life
options.why: Changing jobs with no plan can cost income and experience, so it is not reliably going to improve long-term earnings.

q: What is the first step in making a budget?

options.t: Choosing what to buy, then adding up costs
options.why: Choosing purchases first and then adding costs is backward; a budget starts with what you have coming in and your regular expenses.

options.t: Listing your monthly income and expenses
options.why: A budget starts by listing monthly income and expenses, so you know how much you have and where it goes before planning.

options.t: Ignoring small purchases when you budget
options.why: Ignoring small purchases hides spending that adds up, such as coffee or snacks, so a budget should include them.

options.t: Borrowing money to cover all your expenses
options.why: Borrowing to cover expenses creates debt and does not begin a budget, which starts with knowing income and expenses.

q: What is the 50/30/20 guideline?

options.t: 50% taxes, 30% wants and 20% gifts to friends and family
options.why: The 50/30/20 guideline is about needs, wants and savings, not taxes and gifts; this version does not match the rule.

options.t: 50% wants, 30% needs and 20% taxes paid to the state
options.why: The rule gives 50% to needs and 30% to wants, so listing 50% wants and 30% needs swaps the categories.

options.t: 50% savings, 30% debt payments and 20% needs, like rent
options.why: The rule gives 50% to needs, 30% to wants and 20% to savings and debt; this version puts savings first and does not fit.

options.t: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and debt repayment
options.why: The 50/30/20 guideline allocates after-tax income as 50% to needs, 30% to wants, and 20% to savings and debt repayment.

q: Take-home pay is $2,400 a month. How much goes to wants under the 50/30/20 guideline?

options.why: Wants get 30% of take-home pay, so $2,400 x 0.30 = $720 under the 50/30/20 guideline.
$240 is only 10% of $2,400, not the 30% wants share; 0.30 x $2,400 = $720.
$480 is 20% of $2,400, which is the savings and debt share, not wants; wants are 30%, or $720.
$1,200 is 50% of $2,400, which is the needs share; wants are 30%, which equals $720.

q: What is a fixed expense?

options.t: A cost that is the same amount each month
options.why: A fixed expense stays the same amount each month, such as rent or a car payment, which makes it easy to plan for in a budget.

options.t: A cost that is always zero every single month
options.why: A cost that is always zero is not an expense at all; a fixed expense is a real cost that repeats at the same amount.

options.t: A cost paid once in a lifetime, like a house
options.why: A one-time lifetime cost is a rare purchase, whereas a fixed expense recurs regularly at the same amount.

options.t: A cost that changes every single month
options.why: A cost that changes every month is a variable expense, the opposite of a fixed expense that stays constant.

q: What is a variable expense?

options.t: A cost that never changes at all in a year
options.why: A cost that never changes is a fixed expense, such as rent, which is the opposite of a variable expense.

options.t: A cost paid once at start-up of the business
options.why: A start-up cost paid once is a one-time expense and not a variable expense, which recurs but changes in size.

options.t: A cost that changes from month to month
options.why: A variable expense changes in amount from month to month, such as groceries, gas or entertainment, so budgets must estimate it.

options.t: A cost that is the same every single month
options.why: A cost that stays the same each month is a fixed expense, so it is the opposite of variable.

q: Which habit best reduces impulse buying?

options.t: Shopping when you are bored or upset each day
options.why: Shopping when bored or upset makes impulse buying more likely, since emotions drive spending, so this habit increases it.

options.t: Waiting 24 hours before non-essential purchases
options.why: Waiting 24 hours before non-essential purchases gives time for the urge to fade, so you buy only what you truly want.

options.t: Skipping the budget and spending at random
options.why: Skipping the budget and spending at random removes limits and increases impulse buying, so it does not reduce it.

options.t: Saving card numbers on every shopping site you use
options.why: Saving card numbers on shopping sites makes buying faster and easier, which increases impulse purchases.

q: A 12 oz box costs $3.00 and a 20 oz box costs $4.60. Which has the lower unit price?

options.t: It cannot be determined from data
options.why: It can be determined: dividing price by ounces gives unit prices of $0.25 and $0.23, so the data are enough to compare.

options.t: The 12 oz box at $0.25 per ounce
options.why: The 12 oz box costs $3.00 / 12 = $0.25 per ounce, which is higher than the 20 oz box, so it is not the lower unit price.

options.t: They are exactly equal per ounce
options.why: The unit prices are not equal: $3.00 / 12 = $0.25 per ounce, while $4.60 / 20 = $0.23 per ounce.

options.t: The 20 oz box at $0.23 per ounce
options.why: The 20 oz box costs $4.60 / 20 = $0.23 per ounce, less than the 12 oz box at $3.00 / 12 = $0.25, so it has the lower unit price.

q: What is an opportunity cost of spending?

options.t: The shipping cost of the item that you buy
options.why: Shipping is an extra monetary cost of an item, whereas opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you give up.

options.t: The price tag only, not what you give up
options.why: The price tag alone is the money cost; opportunity cost also counts what you give up, so a price-only answer omits it.

options.t: What else the money could have been used for
options.why: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative you give up, such as other uses for the same money.

options.t: The tax on the item you buy, added to the price
options.why: Sales tax is a monetary cost added at checkout, not opportunity cost, which concerns forgone alternatives.

q: Which payment method often gives the best protection against unauthorized charges?

options.t: A credit card
options.why: Credit cards offer strong protection under federal law, which limits liability to $50 for unauthorized charges and lets you dispute charges.

options.t: A wire transfer
options.why: Wire transfers are hard to reverse and offer little protection, and scammers often request them for that reason.

options.t: A gift card
options.why: Gift cards are like cash and are difficult to recover if used in a scam, so they give little protection against unauthorized charges.

options.t: Cash on delivery
options.why: Cash on delivery gives no way to dispute a charge after payment, so it offers little protection from unauthorized charges.

q: A card charge for an item you never ordered appears. What should you do first?

options.t: Ignore it and hope that the charge goes away
options.why: Ignoring an unfamiliar charge lets fraud continue and may cost you the right to dispute it after the deadline passes.

options.t: Cancel your internet service at once and for good
options.why: Cancelling internet service does not stop a card charge or fix the problem, since the issue lies with the card account.

options.t: Pay it to avoid trouble, then ask for a refund
options.why: Paying a charge you never ordered can make it harder to recover your money; you should dispute it instead.

options.t: Contact the card issuer to dispute it quickly
options.why: Contacting the card issuer quickly lets you dispute the charge, and prompt reporting preserves your rights under consumer protection law.

q: What is sales tax?

options.t: A tax on property that you own, paid each year
options.why: A tax on property you own, paid each year, is a property tax; sales tax is paid at the point of sale.

options.t: A tax added to the price of goods at purchase
options.why: Sales tax is a percentage added to the price of goods and some services at the point of purchase, collected by the seller for the state.

options.t: A tax on income that you earn, paid each year
options.why: A tax on income earned is an income tax, which is paid on earnings, not added at checkout like sales tax.

options.t: A tax on gifts that you get, paid each year
options.why: A tax on gifts received is a gift tax, which is different from sales tax charged at the register.

q: A jacket costs $60 and sales tax is 8%. What is the total?

options.why: $68.00 adds 8 dollars rather than 8 percent; the correct tax is $60 x 0.08 = $4.80, making the total $64.80.
$60.80 adds only 80 cents, treating 8% as 0.8%; the tax is $60 x 0.08 = $4.80, so the total is $64.80.
Tax is $60 x 0.08 = $4.80, and adding it to the price gives $60 + $4.80 = $64.80.
$48.00 subtracts 20% instead of adding tax; sales tax raises the price, so the total is $60 + $4.80 = $64.80.

q: What is a need?

options.t: Something advertised often on television and online
options.why: Something advertised often is a want driven by marketing and is not necessarily required for survival, so it is not a need.

options.t: Something you would like but can live without for a while
options.why: Something you would like but can live without is a want, which is the opposite of a need.

options.t: Something expensive that you buy for fun on the weekend
options.why: An expensive item bought for fun on the weekend is a want and not required to live, so it is not a need.

options.t: Something required to live, such as food and shelter
options.why: A need is something required to live, such as food, shelter, clothing and basic healthcare, which must be paid for before wants.

q: Which is the best example of choosing a need over a want?

options.t: Buying groceries before a new video game
options.why: Buying groceries before a video game puts a need (food) ahead of a want (game), which is choosing needs over wants.

options.t: Buying a game before paying the monthly rent
options.why: Buying a game before paying rent puts a want ahead of a need (housing), the reverse of the correct choice.

options.t: Buying a concert ticket before medicine
options.why: Buying a concert ticket before medicine puts a want ahead of a need (health), the opposite of choosing needs first.

options.t: Buying designer shoes instead of food
options.why: Buying designer shoes instead of food puts a want ahead of a need, so it is the opposite of choosing a need.

q: What is a subscription?

options.t: A refund of the price paid for a product in a retail store
options.why: A refund returns money after a purchase, whereas a subscription is a recurring payment for ongoing access to a service.

options.t: A recurring payment for ongoing access to a product or service
options.why: A subscription is a recurring payment, such as monthly streaming, for ongoing access to a product or service until you cancel.

options.t: A one-time purchase with no renewal, paid at the register today
options.why: A one-time purchase with no renewal is the opposite of a subscription, which renews and bills you repeatedly.

options.t: A tax on services that a firm charges to buyers each year
options.why: A tax on services is a government charge, which is a different concept from a subscription, which is a recurring payment.

q: You forgot about three unused subscriptions costing $10 each monthly. What is the yearly waste?

options.why: $3,600 is ten times too large; three subscriptions at $10 for 12 months is 3 x $10 x 12 = $360.
$30 is only one month of the three subscriptions; over 12 months it is $30 x 12 = $360.
Three subscriptions at $10 each monthly cost $30 a month, and $30 x 12 months = $360 wasted yearly.
$120 counts only one subscription for a year ($10 x 12); with three, the yearly waste is $360.

q: A student earns $300 a month and spends $340. What should they do?

options.t: Stop tracking spending and hope it works out
options.why: Stopping tracking leaves the shortfall unexamined and likely leads to debt, so hoping it works out is not a plan.

options.t: Reduce spending or raise income to avoid debt
options.why: Spending $340 on $300 of income is a $40 monthly shortfall, so the student should cut spending or raise income to avoid debt.

options.t: Borrow to keep spending the same and repay later
options.why: Borrowing to keep spending the same adds debt and interest while the overspending problem remains, making it worse over time.

options.t: Spend more to feel better about the shortfall
options.why: Spending more to feel better enlarges the $40 gap and deepens the shortfall, so it is the opposite of the fix.

q: What is a coupon?

options.t: A loan a store gives a shopper for a big purchase
options.why: A loan a store gives for a large purchase is store financing, not a coupon, which is a voucher for a discount.

options.t: A tax form a shopper fills out to report purchases
options.why: A tax form for reporting purchases is not a coupon; a coupon is a voucher that lowers the price you pay.

options.t: A warranty that promises to repair a product
options.why: A warranty promises repair of a defective product, whereas a coupon gives a discount on a purchase.

options.t: A voucher that gives a discount on a purchase
options.why: A coupon is a voucher that gives a discount on a purchase, either a set amount or a percentage off the price.

q: What is a store credit card most likely to have?

options.t: A high interest rate and a discount on store purchases
options.why: Store credit cards typically have high interest rates and offer a discount on store purchases, so carrying a balance can cost more than the savings.

options.t: A lower rate than any bank card, as the retailer backs it
options.why: Store cards usually have higher rates than bank cards, not lower, and retailer backing does not make them cheaper.

options.t: No repayment needed on the money that you spend on it
options.why: Money spent on a store card must be repaid like any credit, so saying no repayment is needed is false.

options.t: Protection from all fraud and identity theft in stores
options.why: A store card does not protect from all fraud; no card protects from every kind of fraud or identity theft.

q: Why is saving important?

options.t: It prepares you for emergencies and future goals
options.why: Saving prepares you for emergencies and future goals, such as a car or education, and reduces the need to borrow.

options.t: It removes the need for a budget in your life
options.why: Saving does not remove the need for a budget; a budget is how you plan to save and control spending.

options.t: It guarantees you never need a job again in life
options.why: Saving does not guarantee you will never need a job; it helps cover costs but rarely replaces income forever.

options.t: It makes you spend more money than you can earn
options.why: Saving means setting money aside, so it reduces spending rather than making you spend more than you earn.

q: Where should emergency money be kept?

options.t: Under a mattress at home for safety
options.why: Under a mattress, cash can be stolen or destroyed, earns no interest, and is not protected by deposit insurance, so it is not a safe place.

options.t: In a risky stock that could fall fast
options.why: A risky stock can fall fast just when you need cash, so it is unsuitable for emergency money.

options.t: In a safe, easily accessible account
options.why: Emergency money belongs in a safe, easily accessible account, such as an insured savings account, so it is available quickly without loss.

options.t: In a long-term account with penalties
options.why: A long-term account with penalties makes it costly to withdraw in an emergency, so it is not suited for emergency money.

q: $1,000 earns 5% compounded annually. What is the balance after 2 years?

options.why: $1,200.00 would require 10% growth per year; 5% simple growth for 2 years gives $1,100, and compounding gives $1,102.50.
Year 1: $1,000 x 1.05 = $1,050. Year 2: $1,050 x 1.05 = $1,102.50, since interest earns interest.
$1,050.00 is the balance after only one year; a second year of interest brings the balance to $1,102.50.
$1,100 is simple interest ($50 each year); compounding adds interest on the first year's interest, giving $1,102.50.

q: What is the Rule of 72?

options.t: A rule setting retirement age, when workers must stop at 72
options.why: The Rule of 72 has nothing to do with retirement age; it estimates how long it takes money to double.

options.t: A rule for calculating taxes owed to the state each year
options.why: The Rule of 72 is not a tax calculation; it divides 72 by the interest rate to estimate a doubling time.

options.t: A rule for loan payments that lenders must follow
options.why: The Rule of 72 is a mental math shortcut for savings growth and not a rule for loan payments that lenders follow.

options.t: A shortcut to estimate how long money takes to double
options.why: The Rule of 72 estimates how long money takes to double by dividing 72 by the annual interest rate.

q: At 6% interest, about how long does it take money to double?

options.t: 6 years
options.why: 6 years would require a 12% rate (72 / 12); at 6%, the Rule of 72 gives 72 / 6 = 12 years.

options.t: 12 years
options.why: By the Rule of 72, doubling time is 72 / 6 = 12 years at a 6% annual interest rate.

options.t: 8 years
options.why: 8 years would need a 9% rate (72 / 9 = 8); at 6% the doubling time is 72 / 6 = 12 years.

options.t: 72 years
options.why: 72 is the numerator of the rule and not the answer; dividing 72 by 6 gives 12 years to double.

q: Two accounts both advertise 4%. Account A compounds daily and Account B annually. Which earns more?

options.t: Neither one
options.why: Compounding frequency matters; daily compounding adds interest more often, so one account does earn more than the other.

options.t: About equal
options.why: The difference is small but real; daily compounding earns slightly more than annual compounding at the same 4% rate, so they are not equal.

options.t: Account A
options.why: Account A compounds daily, so interest earns interest more often than in B, giving a slightly higher effective yield at the same 4% rate.

options.t: Account B
options.why: Annual compounding adds interest only once a year, so Account B earns slightly less than daily compounding at the same rate.

q: What is a 529 plan?

options.t: An insurance plan for cars and homes in a state
options.why: An insurance plan for cars and homes is not a 529; a 529 is a savings plan for education expenses.

options.t: A retirement plan for company staff funded by pay
options.why: A retirement plan funded by pay describes a 401(k), whereas a 529 plan is for education costs.

options.t: A loan for homebuyers who put money down at a bank
options.why: A loan for homebuyers is a mortgage, which is borrowing, while a 529 is a savings plan, not a loan.

options.t: A tax-advantaged savings plan for education costs
