options.why: A 529 plan is a tax-advantaged savings plan for education costs, with tax-free growth if used for qualified expenses like tuition.

q: Inflation is 3% and a savings account pays 1%. What happens to the real value of the savings?

options.t: It decreases
options.why: With inflation at 3% and interest at 1%, prices rise faster than savings grow, so the real value, or buying power, of the savings decreases.

options.t: It doubles
options.why: Real value does not double; with a 1% return below 3% inflation, buying power falls over time.

options.t: It increases
options.why: Real value would increase only if interest exceeded inflation; here 1% is below 3%, so buying power falls.

options.t: No change
options.why: There is a change because inflation outpaces the interest earned, shrinking the real purchasing power of the savings.

q: Why start saving early?

options.t: You can spend all of your income on fun
options.why: Spending all your income on fun does nothing for saving and does not explain why starting early helps.

options.t: Compound interest has more time to grow
options.why: Starting early gives compound interest more time to work, so earnings earn their own earnings and small deposits grow large.

options.t: Banks pay young savers a much higher rate
options.why: Banks do not pay young savers a higher rate; the advantage of starting early comes from more time to compound.

options.t: You never need to save again in your life
options.why: Saving early does not mean you never need to save again; regular saving is still needed for years.

q: Which factor can lower a credit score the most?

options.t: Checking your own credit report yearly
options.why: Checking your own credit report is a soft inquiry and does not affect your score, so it cannot lower it.

options.t: Keeping a card account open for years
options.why: Keeping a card open for years lengthens your credit history, which tends to help your score, not lower it.

options.t: Missing a payment by 30 or more days
options.why: Payment history is the largest factor in credit scores, and a payment 30 or more days late can sharply lower your score.

options.t: Paying the balance in full each month
options.why: Paying the balance in full each month shows responsible use and keeps utilization low, which helps your score.

q: What is a good credit utilization rate to aim for?

options.t: Exactly 100 percent at all times of the month
options.why: Using 100 percent of your limit means being maxed out, which hurts your score and shows risk to lenders.

options.t: More than your credit limit allows you to use
options.why: Using more than your limit is not normally possible, and being near or over the limit is a negative for scores.

options.t: Above 90 percent of the total available credit
options.why: Above 90 percent utilization signals heavy reliance on credit, which hurts your score; lower is better.

options.t: Below about 30 percent of available credit
options.why: Keeping utilization below about 30 percent of your available credit shows responsible use, which supports a higher credit score.

q: A card has a $4,000 limit and a $1,000 balance. What is the utilization rate?

options.why: Utilization is balance divided by limit: $1,000 / $4,000 = 0.25, which is 25%.
400% flips the ratio ($4,000 / $1,000); utilization divides the balance by the limit, giving $1,000 / $4,000 = 25%.
10% would need a $400 balance on a $4,000 limit; $1,000 / $4,000 is 25%.
75% is the unused share of the limit ($3,000 / $4,000); the utilization rate is $1,000 / $4,000 = 25%.

q: What is an installment loan?

options.t: A loan repaid in one lump sum at the lender's choice
options.why: A loan repaid in one lump sum at the lender's choice is not an installment loan, which has set scheduled payments.

options.t: A gift that never needs any repayment at all
options.why: A gift never needs repayment, whereas an installment loan must be repaid in regular payments plus interest.

options.t: A loan repaid in fixed regular payments over time
options.why: An installment loan is repaid in fixed regular payments over time, such as monthly payments on a car or student loan.

options.t: A credit line with no end date at all for you
options.why: A credit line with no end date is revolving credit, which differs from an installment loan with a set term.

q: What is revolving credit?

options.t: A loan repaid in fixed payments over set months only
options.why: A loan repaid in fixed payments over set months is an installment loan, not revolving credit.

options.t: Credit you can use, repay and use again up to a limit
options.why: Revolving credit lets you borrow up to a limit, repay it, and borrow again, as with credit cards.

options.t: A loan with no interest that you never repay in full
options.why: A loan with no interest that you never repay does not exist; revolving credit must be repaid and usually charges interest.

options.t: A one-time cash gift from a bank to a customer who asks
options.why: A cash gift from a bank is not credit; revolving credit is borrowed money that you must repay.

q: Which is an example of installment credit?

options.t: A home equity loan line
options.why: A home equity line of credit is revolving credit, which you can borrow and repay again, unlike an installment loan.

options.t: A store credit card
options.why: A store credit card is revolving credit, with a limit you can use repeatedly, not a fixed-payment installment loan.

options.t: A bank credit card
options.why: A bank credit card is revolving credit, so it is not installment credit.

options.t: A 48-month car loan
options.why: A 48-month car loan is repaid in fixed monthly installments over a set term, making it a classic installment loan.

q: What is a loan origination fee?

options.t: A charge for processing a new loan
options.why: A loan origination fee is a charge by the lender for processing and setting up a new loan, often a percentage of the loan.

options.t: A fee for using an ATM machine abroad
options.why: An ATM fee for use abroad is a foreign bank charge, unrelated to the cost of setting up a new loan.

options.t: A fee charged for paying off early
options.why: A fee for paying off early is a prepayment penalty, not an origination fee, which is charged when the loan begins.

options.t: A fee for paying a bill very late
options.why: A fee for paying a bill late is a late fee and not an origination fee, which is charged to open the loan.

q: What is a prepayment penalty?

options.t: A tax on loan interest that borrowers pay yearly
options.why: A tax on loan interest is a government charge and has nothing to do with the lender's prepayment penalty.

options.t: A fee for paying late on a loan or a credit card bill
options.why: A fee for paying late is a late fee; a prepayment penalty is charged for paying the loan off early.

options.t: A fee some lenders charge for paying off a loan early
options.why: A prepayment penalty is a fee some lenders charge for paying off a loan early, because they lose expected interest income.

options.t: A reward for paying early on a loan from a bank branch
options.why: A reward for paying early is the opposite of a penalty; a prepayment penalty is a cost for early payoff, not a prize.

q: Which loan feature should you check before signing to avoid surprise costs?

options.t: The size of the lender's main building
options.why: The size of the lender's building tells you nothing about the cost; fees, rate and terms determine the total price.

options.t: Fees, interest rate and prepayment terms
options.why: Checking fees, the interest rate and prepayment terms before signing reveals the true cost and helps you avoid surprise charges later.

options.t: The color of the loan paperwork forms
options.why: The color of the paperwork has no effect on cost, so it does not help you avoid surprises.

options.t: The name of the loan officer who helps you
options.why: The loan officer's name does not affect the cost of the loan; the terms in the contract do.

q: What is the total cost of a loan?

options.t: The monthly payment only, times the months
options.why: The monthly payment times months gives total payments, but this leaves out fees, so it is not the full cost of the loan.

options.t: The interest rate only, with no fees included
options.why: The interest rate alone does not include fees or principal, so it is not the total cost of a loan.

options.t: The principal only, with no interest or fees
options.why: The principal is only the amount borrowed and leaves out the interest and fees that make borrowing cost more.

options.t: The principal plus all interest and fees
options.why: The total cost of a loan is the principal plus all interest and fees, so it shows what you actually pay to borrow.

q: Maria borrows $5,000 and repays $5,800 in total. How much did borrowing cost her?

options.why: The cost of borrowing is total repaid minus amount borrowed: $5,800 - $5,000 = $800, which is the interest and fees.
$5,800 is the total repaid and includes the $5,000 borrowed; the cost of borrowing is $5,800 - $5,000 = $800.
$10,800 adds the borrowed amount to the repayment; the cost of borrowing is only the extra paid, $800.
$5,000 is the amount borrowed and not the cost; the extra paid beyond it is $5,800 - $5,000 = $800.

q: What is a down payment?

options.t: An upfront payment that reduces the amount you must borrow
options.why: A down payment is an upfront payment toward a purchase that reduces the amount you must borrow and can lower interest cost.

options.t: A monthly loan payment that you make to the lender each month
options.why: A monthly loan payment is an installment, not a down payment, which is paid upfront at the start.

options.t: A fee for paying late on a loan or a credit card bill
options.why: A fee for paying late is a late fee, not a down payment, which is paid at purchase to reduce the loan.

options.t: A refund the seller pays back to the buyer after the sale
options.why: A refund from the seller to the buyer is not a down payment, which is a buyer's upfront payment.

q: A $24,000 car requires a 15% down payment. How much is the down payment?

options.why: $360 is only 1.5% of $24,000, so it comes from moving the decimal one place too far; 15% of $24,000 is ten times larger.
15% of $24,000 is 0.15 x 24,000 = $3,600. A larger down payment lowers the amount financed and usually reduces the interest paid over the loan.
$2,400 is 10% of $24,000, not 15%. You would need to add another 5% ($1,200) to reach the correct 15% down payment of $3,600.
$20,400 is the amount left to finance after the down payment ($24,000 - $3,600), not the down payment itself, so it answers a different question.

q: What is leasing a car?

options.t: Buying a car outright with cash from your savings
options.why: Buying outright with cash is a purchase that transfers full ownership to you, which is the opposite of a lease, where the dealer keeps title.

options.t: Borrowing a car for free from a friend or a relative
options.why: Borrowing a car free from a friend is an informal favor with no contract or set payments, while a lease is a formal paid agreement.

options.t: Paying to use a car for a set time without owning it
options.why: Leasing means paying regular fees to use a car for a fixed term while the leasing company keeps ownership; at the end you return it or may buy it.

options.t: Selling your car to a dealer in exchange for the cash
options.why: Selling your car to a dealer for cash is a sale that ends your ownership, not a lease, where you pay to use a car you do not own.

q: What is a common drawback of leasing compared with buying?

options.t: You own the car at the start and can sell it at will
options.why: Owning the car from the start and selling at will describes buying, not leasing; a lessor keeps title, so a lessee cannot sell the vehicle.

options.t: You can never drive the car on any public roads
options.why: Leased cars are driven on public roads just like owned cars; the real limits are contract terms such as annual mileage caps, not road access.

options.t: You always pay less overall in the long run of years
options.why: Leasing often has lower monthly payments, but over many years it usually costs more because you keep paying and never build ownership or equity in the car.

options.t: You do not own the car and may face mileage limits
options.why: A lessee never builds equity, since the lessor holds title, and most leases cap annual mileage (often 10,000 to 15,000 miles) with per-mile fees if exceeded.

q: What is a fixed-rate mortgage?

options.t: A home loan whose interest rate stays the same for the life of the loan
options.why: A fixed-rate mortgage keeps the same interest rate and the same principal and interest payment for the whole term, such as 15 or 30 years, making budgeting easy.

options.t: A loan with no interest that you do not need to repay in full ever
options.why: Mortgages always charge interest and must be repaid in full; no legitimate home loan is interest-free or exempt from repayment.

options.t: A loan whose rate changes with the market, rising and falling from year to year
options.why: A rate that rises and falls with the market describes an adjustable-rate mortgage, whereas a fixed-rate loan holds its rate constant.

options.t: A loan with no repayment due for the first thirty years of its term
options.why: Standard mortgages begin repayment right away, usually the month after closing; there is no thirty-year payment holiday on a fixed-rate loan.

q: What is an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM)?

options.t: A loan only for businesses and big firms
options.why: An ARM is a consumer home loan available to individuals, not a business-only product; business borrowers use commercial loans instead.

options.t: A loan whose rate never changes for its life
options.why: A rate that never changes describes a fixed-rate mortgage, the opposite of an ARM, whose rate resets periodically.

options.t: A loan with no collateral and no interest due
options.why: A mortgage is secured by the home as collateral and always charges interest, so a no-collateral, no-interest loan is not an ARM.

options.t: A home loan whose rate can change over time
options.why: An ARM usually starts with a lower fixed introductory rate, then resets at set intervals based on a market index, so payments can rise or fall.

q: Which borrower benefits most from a fixed-rate mortgage?

options.t: Someone who wants payments to change each year over time
options.why: Someone who wants payments to change each year would prefer an adjustable-rate loan; a fixed-rate mortgage is chosen precisely to avoid payment changes.

options.t: Someone who wants predictable payments for many years
options.why: A fixed rate locks in the same principal and interest payment for decades, which suits borrowers on a steady budget who plan to stay in the home long term.

options.t: Someone who plans to move next month to a new city
options.why: A person moving next month would not benefit from a long-term fixed rate; they would not own the loan long enough to enjoy its stability.

options.t: Someone who wants no payments at all for many years
options.why: No mortgage lets you skip payments for years; every mortgage requires regular payments, so nobody benefits from a nonexistent no-payment loan.

q: What is escrow in a mortgage?

options.t: A type of interest rate that changes over all the years
options.why: A rate that changes over time describes an adjustable-rate mortgage, whereas escrow is an account the lender manages, not a type of interest rate.

options.t: A fee for opening a loan that the bank charges at the very start
options.why: A fee charged at the start of a loan is an origination fee or closing cost, not escrow, which holds money collected over time.

options.t: An account that holds money for property taxes and insurance
options.why: The lender collects part of each monthly payment into an escrow account and pays property taxes and homeowners insurance bills when they come due.

options.t: A penalty for paying early on a loan, set by the bank
options.why: A penalty for paying a loan off early is a prepayment penalty, which is a different term and does not describe an escrow account.

q: What is private mortgage insurance (PMI)?

options.t: Insurance that protects the lender when the down payment is small
options.why: PMI protects the lender, not the borrower, if you default; it is usually required when the down payment is under 20% of the home price.

options.t: Insurance that pays your monthly bills if you ever lose a job
options.why: Insurance that pays bills after job loss is credit or payment protection insurance, not PMI, which is tied to the mortgage and the lender's risk.

options.t: Insurance that covers your car if it is damaged in a crash
options.why: Insurance covering a car damaged in a crash is auto collision coverage, which has nothing to do with mortgage lending or small down payments.

options.t: Insurance that protects the borrower's furniture and possessions at home
options.why: Insurance on furniture and possessions at home is homeowners or renters personal property coverage, while PMI protects the lender against loan default.

q: What is foreclosure?

options.t: A bank approving a loan for a new home buyer in a small town
options.why: A bank approving a loan is loan origination; foreclosure happens later, only after a borrower has stopped making mortgage payments.

options.t: A tax credit for homeowners who pay their mortgage on time each year
options.why: A tax credit for on-time mortgage payments does not exist; foreclosure is a legal process, not a reward for paying.

options.t: The lender taking and selling a home after the borrower stops paying
options.why: When a borrower defaults, the lender legally takes the home and sells it to recover the unpaid loan balance, which badly damages the borrower's credit.

options.t: Selling a home by choice with no debt, to move to a bigger house
options.why: Selling a home by choice with no debt is an ordinary sale; foreclosure is involuntary and follows missed mortgage payments.

q: What is a federal student loan benefit compared with many private loans?

options.t: No need to repay any of the money you borrowed ever
options.why: Federal student loans must be repaid with interest; only specific forgiveness programs cancel debt, so having no repayment duty at all is false.

options.t: Approval based on a perfect credit score alone
options.why: Federal loans generally do not require a good credit score (many undergraduate loans have no credit check), so approval is not based on a perfect score.

options.t: Always higher interest rates than private loans
options.why: Federal student loan rates are fixed by Congress and are often lower than private rates, so they are not always higher.

options.t: Flexible repayment options and borrower protections
options.why: Federal loans offer income-driven repayment, deferment, forbearance and possible forgiveness, protections that most private lenders do not provide.

q: A student wants to limit education debt. Which step helps most?

options.t: Use high-interest cards for tuition first
options.why: High-interest credit cards for tuition cost far more than student loans and quickly grow expensive debt, so they increase rather than limit education debt.

options.t: Seek scholarships and grants before loans
options.why: Scholarships and grants are free money that need not be repaid, so using them before loans directly reduces the total debt you take on.

options.t: Borrow the maximum amount available now
options.why: Borrowing the maximum available means taking on more debt than needed, and you pay interest on every dollar, so it increases education debt.

options.t: Ignore costs until after graduation day
options.why: Ignoring costs until graduation lets interest build and prevents planning, so debt grows larger than necessary instead of being limited.

q: What is a grace period on a student loan?

options.t: A time when interest is always free on the balance
options.why: Interest is often not free during a grace period; on unsubsidized loans interest usually keeps accruing and may be added to the balance later.

options.t: A time after leaving school before repayment begins
options.why: A grace period is a set time (commonly six months) after graduating or leaving school before required payments begin, giving the borrower time to find work.

options.t: A time when the loan is forgiven in full by the school
options.why: A grace period delays payment but does not forgive anything; the school does not cancel the loan and the full balance remains owed.

options.t: A time when the lender pays you extra money to borrow
options.why: Lenders do not pay borrowers extra money during a grace period; it only postpones the first required repayment, and the borrower still owes the loan.

q: What is loan consolidation?

options.t: Borrowing more to spend freely on fun and trips
options.why: Borrowing more to spend on fun is simply new debt; consolidation replaces existing loans and is not a way to fund extra spending.

options.t: Splitting one loan into many smaller loans for later
options.why: Splitting one loan into many smaller ones is the opposite of consolidation, which merges multiple loans into a single one.

options.t: Ignoring loans until they vanish from your report
options.why: Ignoring loans does not make them vanish; unpaid loans go delinquent and hurt your credit report, and consolidation requires actively combining them.

options.t: Combining several loans into one with one payment
options.why: Consolidation merges several loans into one new loan with a single monthly payment, which can simplify repayment, though the rate or term may change.

q: When might consolidating debts be a bad idea?

options.t: If the new loan has a higher rate or extra fees
options.why: Consolidating makes sense only if it saves money or helps repayment; a higher rate or added fees makes the combined loan more expensive than the originals.

options.t: If it lowers the monthly cost and the interest rate
options.why: Lowering the monthly cost and the interest rate is a good reason to consolidate, so it would not be a bad idea in that case.

options.t: If the new loan has a lower rate and no extra fees
options.why: A lower rate with no extra fees makes consolidation beneficial because you pay less interest, so this is a good time to consolidate.

options.t: If it simplifies payments for you and lowers cost
options.why: Simplifying payments while lowering total cost is the goal of consolidating, so it is a good idea rather than a bad one.

q: What is a debt-to-income ratio?

options.t: Income divided by total savings held at a bank
options.why: Income divided by savings compares earnings with assets and says nothing about how much of your income goes toward repaying debt.

options.t: Savings divided by debt owed to lenders each year
options.why: Savings divided by debt is a coverage measure of assets against what you owe, not the ratio lenders use to judge your monthly debt burden.

options.t: Monthly debt payments divided by monthly income
options.why: DTI = total monthly debt payments / gross monthly income; lenders use it to judge whether you can afford a new loan, often preferring under about 36 to 43%.

options.t: Debt divided by the interest rate charged on loans
options.why: Dividing debt by an interest rate mixes unrelated measures and gives no meaningful number; DTI compares monthly payments with monthly income.

q: Monthly debt payments are $600 and monthly income is $2,400. What is the debt-to-income ratio?

options.why: 60% does not match the math; $600 / $2,400 is one quarter, which is 25%, not 60%.
400% comes from flipping the ratio ($2,400 / $600 = 4); DTI divides debt payments by income, not income by debt payments.
75% is the share of income left after debt payments ($1,800 / $2,400), not the debt-to-income ratio itself.
DTI = $600 / $2,400 = 0.25, or 25%. This is well below the common lender limit of about 36 to 43%, so the borrower looks manageable.

q: What risk does a co-signer take?

options.t: Being responsible for the debt if the borrower defaults
options.why: A co-signer legally promises to repay if the main borrower defaults, so missed payments can hurt the co-signer's credit and let the lender collect from them.

options.t: Earning interest from the loan if it is repaid on time
options.why: Co-signers do not earn interest; the lender earns interest, and a co-signer only takes on risk to help the borrower qualify.

options.t: No risk because they borrow none of the money themselves
options.why: A co-signer does bear risk, since they are fully liable for the debt even though they receive none of the borrowed money.

options.t: Owning the borrower's property after the loan is paid
options.why: A co-signer does not gain ownership of the borrower's property; they only guarantee repayment and receive no rights to the asset.

q: What is a credit bureau?

options.t: A store that sells credit cards to customers who need cash
options.why: A store that sells credit cards is a retailer or card issuer; credit bureaus do not issue cards, they gather and report credit data.

options.t: A bank that lends money to people who need a home
options.why: A bank lending for homes is a mortgage lender; credit bureaus do not lend, but they supply the reports lenders use to decide.

options.t: A company that collects and sells credit information
options.why: Bureaus such as Equifax, Experian and TransUnion collect your borrowing and payment history and sell reports and scores to lenders and others.

options.t: A government tax office that collects income taxes
options.why: The IRS collects income taxes; credit bureaus are private companies that track credit history and are not government tax offices.

q: What does the Fair Credit Reporting Act give consumers?

options.t: The right to delete any debt that you simply choose not to pay
options.why: The FCRA does not erase debts you simply choose not to pay; only inaccurate or outdated items can be removed from your report.

options.t: The right to see and dispute information in their credit reports
options.why: The FCRA lets you get free annual copies of your credit reports and dispute errors, requiring bureaus to investigate, typically within 30 days.

options.t: The right to a loan from any lender, whatever your credit status
options.why: No law guarantees a loan from any lender; lenders may decline based on credit, income and risk, and the FCRA governs reports, not lending.

options.t: The right to a perfect credit score at any time you ask for it
options.why: The FCRA cannot promise a perfect credit score; scores reflect your actual history, and the law only ensures reports are accurate and fair.

q: You find an account you never opened on your credit report. What should you do?

options.t: Pay it off right away to protect your credit
options.why: Paying an account you never opened can validate a fraudulent debt and costs you money for a debt that is not yours.

options.t: Close your bank account so the thief cannot use funds
options.why: Closing your bank account does not remove the fraudulent credit account, and the thief may have opened it using other information.

options.t: Dispute it and consider a fraud alert or freeze
options.why: Disputing the account with the bureaus and creditor, then adding a fraud alert or credit freeze, is the standard way to limit identity theft damage.

options.t: Ignore it and hope that the account goes away
options.why: Ignoring a fraudulent account lets it grow, damage your credit and go to collections, so it will not disappear by itself.

q: What is a fraud alert?

options.t: A bill from a lender that you must pay within about thirty days
options.why: A bill from a lender is a payment statement; a fraud alert is a flag on your file, not a charge you must pay.

options.t: A notice on your credit file asking lenders to verify your identity
options.why: A fraud alert is placed on your credit file with one bureau, who tells the others, and it asks lenders to verify your identity before opening new credit.

options.t: A reward for good credit that lenders pay out to you each year
options.why: Fraud alerts are protective notices, not rewards; lenders do not pay anyone for good credit through such an alert.

options.t: A ban on all credit use forever after one late payment is reported now
options.why: A fraud alert is temporary (typically one year, or longer for victims) and does not ban credit use; a freeze is the stronger tool that blocks access.

q: What is a debt collector?

options.t: A person or firm that tries to collect overdue debts
options.why: Debt collectors, either agencies or in-house staff, contact people to recover overdue debts, and in the US they must follow the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act.

options.t: A tax auditor who checks the returns of most local firms
options.why: A tax auditor reviews tax returns for the government; a debt collector pursues unpaid consumer debts and has nothing to do with audits.

options.t: A bank teller who handles deposits for customers daily
options.why: A bank teller handles deposits and withdrawals; a debt collector instead contacts people who owe overdue balances.

options.t: A lawyer for borrowers who negotiates the loan terms
options.why: A lawyer who negotiates for borrowers is a debt settlement or consumer attorney; collectors work for creditors, not for the borrower.

q: A collector calls at midnight and threatens arrest for a credit card debt. What is this?

options.t: A requirement of the card contract for collectors
options.why: Card contracts do not authorize collectors to threaten arrest; credit card debt is a civil matter, not a crime, so such threats are not contractual.

options.t: A protection under bankruptcy law for all debtors
options.why: Bankruptcy law protects debtors in a court process but does not make midnight threats a protection; this behavior is a violation, not a safeguard.

options.t: A normal collection step that all collectors may take
options.why: Threatening arrest for ordinary civil debt is not a normal step; the FDCPA bans such threats and bars calls at inconvenient times, generally before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m.

options.t: Likely illegal harassment under debt collection law
options.why: The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act prohibits threats of arrest and calls outside 8 a.m. to 9 p.m., so you can report the collector to the CFPB or FTC.

q: What does APR on a credit card represent?

options.t: The size of your monthly payment on the card
options.why: The monthly payment is a separate figure, often a minimum percentage of the balance; APR is an annual rate and not the payment size.

options.t: The amount of your credit limit on the card
options.why: The credit limit is the maximum you can borrow on the card, a dollar amount, not a percentage rate like APR.

options.t: The yearly cost of borrowing on the balance
options.why: APR (annual percentage rate) expresses the yearly cost of borrowing as a percentage, and carrying a balance means interest is charged at roughly APR/12 each month.

options.t: The yearly fee to own the card, no interest
options.why: An annual fee is a separate flat charge for owning a card; APR is the interest rate on borrowed balances, not a fee without interest.

q: Which action best avoids credit card interest?

options.t: Taking cash advances on your credit card often
options.why: Cash advances usually start accruing interest immediately with no grace period, and they carry fees, so they increase borrowing costs rather than avoid them.

options.t: Paying the full statement balance every month
options.why: Paying the full statement balance by the due date uses the grace period, so purchases incur no interest at all.

options.t: Paying only the minimum amount due each month
options.why: Paying only the minimum leaves most of the balance, which then accrues interest at the APR, making the debt last years and cost much more.

options.t: Paying after the due date, since it costs little
options.why: Paying late triggers late fees, possible penalty APRs and credit damage, so it costs a lot and does not avoid interest.

q: What is a balance transfer?

options.t: Moving money into savings from your paycheck each month
options.why: Moving money from a paycheck into savings is saving; a balance transfer relocates existing credit card debt rather than adding to savings.

options.t: Moving a car loan to a friend who takes over the monthly payments
options.why: Handing a car loan to a friend is a loan assumption or transfer of the debt; a balance transfer specifically involves credit card balances.

options.t: Paying a bill early using money that you have in savings
options.why: Paying a bill early from savings is just early payment; it does not transfer a debt from one lender or card to another.

options.t: Moving a debt from one card to another, often with a lower rate
options.why: A balance transfer shifts debt from one credit card to another, often to get a promotional low or 0% rate, though a fee of about 3 to 5% usually applies.

q: A balance transfer has a 3% fee and 0% interest for 12 months. You move $2,000. What is the fee?

options.why: Fee = 3% x $2,000 = 0.03 x 2,000 = $60. It is charged on top of the moved amount, so it must be weighed against interest saved.
$2,060 is the new total balance after adding the fee ($2,000 + $60), not the fee itself, which is only the $60 charge.
$600 would be 30% of $2,000, so it moves the decimal wrong; 3% of $2,000 is much smaller at $60.
$6 would be 0.3% of $2,000, a tenth of the true fee; 3% of $2,000 equals $60.

q: What is a credit limit?

options.t: The interest you pay on a loan each year
options.why: The yearly interest on a loan is its APR in cost terms; a credit limit is a dollar cap on borrowing, not an interest charge.

options.t: The date payment is due each month
options.why: The payment due date is a calendar deadline; a credit limit is the dollar ceiling on how much you may borrow.

options.t: The minimum you must pay every month
options.why: The minimum payment is the smallest amount you must pay each month, which differs from the credit limit on total borrowing.

options.t: The maximum you can borrow on a card
options.why: A credit limit is the most the issuer lets you charge to the card at once; using over about 30% of it can lower your credit score.

q: Which change would most likely lower your monthly premium?

options.t: Raising your deductible
options.why: A higher deductible means you take on more of each loss, so the insurer carries less risk and charges a lower monthly premium.

options.t: Adding more coverage
options.why: Adding coverage increases what the insurer might have to pay, which usually raises your premium rather than lowering it.

options.t: Having more accidents
options.why: More accidents label you a higher risk, so insurers charge higher premiums after claims instead of lowering them.

options.t: Lowering your deductible
options.why: Lowering your deductible shifts more of each loss to the insurer, so the premium goes up, not down.

q: After a covered accident you owe a $500 deductible and repairs cost $2,100. How much does insurance pay?

options.why: $2,100 ignores the deductible; insurance pays only the amount above your $500 deductible, which you must cover first.
$2,600 adds the deductible to the repair bill, which is backward; the deductible is subtracted from the payout, not added to it.
The insurer pays repairs minus the deductible: $2,100 - $500 = $1,600, and you pay the first $500 yourself.
$500 is the deductible that you pay yourself, not what the insurer pays; the insurer covers the remaining $1,600.

q: What is liability coverage on a car policy?

options.t: Coverage for your own car repairs only, not for others
options.why: Coverage for your own car repairs is collision or comprehensive coverage; liability coverage pays for harm you cause to other people.

options.t: Coverage for injuries and damage you cause to others
options.why: Liability coverage pays for other people's injuries and property damage when you are at fault, and most states require minimum amounts of it.

options.t: Coverage for routine oil changes and car washes
options.why: Routine oil changes and car washes are maintenance costs that insurance does not cover; liability pays for harm you cause others.

options.t: Coverage for theft only, and nothing else at all
options.why: Theft-only coverage is part of comprehensive insurance; liability coverage addresses damage and injuries to others, not theft of your car.

q: What is uninsured motorist coverage?

options.t: Coverage if you are hit by a driver without insurance
options.why: Uninsured motorist coverage pays your medical bills and sometimes car damage when an at-fault driver has no insurance or cannot be identified.

options.t: Coverage for your own accidents only, not others'
options.why: Covering only your own accidents describes collision coverage; uninsured motorist coverage applies when another driver without insurance harms you.

options.t: Coverage for rental cars only, on short trips away
options.why: Rental car coverage is a separate add-on for rented vehicles; uninsured motorist coverage protects you after crashes caused by uninsured drivers.

options.t: Coverage for drivers without licenses who are hit by cars
options.why: The coverage is not for unlicensed drivers who are hit; it protects you, the insured, when an uninsured driver causes the crash.

q: Which situation shows why uninsured motorist coverage matters?

options.t: You wash your car at home on a sunny weekend
options.why: Washing your car involves no driver at fault or loss, so no insurance coverage is triggered and the scenario shows nothing about uninsured motorists.

options.t: An uninsured driver hits your car and cannot pay
options.why: If an uninsured driver causes the crash and cannot pay, your uninsured motorist coverage pays your bills so you do not bear the cost.

options.t: You park legally in a lot and a car backs into yours
options.why: If a car backs into yours in a lot and the driver is identified and insured, their liability coverage pays, so you do not need uninsured coverage.

options.t: You get an oil change at a garage near your home
options.why: An oil change is ordinary maintenance with no accident, so no insurance claim arises and uninsured motorist coverage is irrelevant.

q: What does health insurance's out-of-pocket maximum do?

options.t: Limits what the insurer earns in profit each year
options.why: An insurer's profit is separate from the out-of-pocket maximum, which limits what the patient pays, not what the insurer earns.

options.t: Sets the minimum premium that you pay each month
options.why: The monthly premium is a fixed charge set by the plan; the out-of-pocket maximum sets a ceiling on yearly costs, not a minimum premium.

options.t: Limits what you pay in a year for covered care
options.why: After you hit the out-of-pocket maximum through deductibles, copays and coinsurance, the plan pays 100% of covered in-network care for the rest of the year.

options.t: Removes all costs forever for every covered person
options.why: The limit resets each plan year and excludes premiums and non-covered care, so it does not remove all costs forever.

q: What is a health insurance network?

options.t: A computer network at a hospital linking its wards
options.why: A hospital computer network is IT infrastructure; a health insurance network is a group of doctors and hospitals contracted with the insurer.

options.t: A group of patients who share the same insurer
options.why: A group of patients sharing an insurer is its member pool; the network refers to the providers who agree to discounted rates.

options.t: A list of medicines that a hospital pharmacy keeps
options.why: A list of medicines is a formulary, not a network; the network consists of doctors, hospitals and clinics under contract.

options.t: A group of providers that contract with an insurer
options.why: A network is the set of doctors, hospitals and clinics that contract with an insurer to accept negotiated rates, so in-network care costs you less.

q: Seeing an out-of-network provider usually results in:

options.t: Free care always and everywhere
options.why: Out-of-network care is not free; the insurer often pays less or nothing and the patient can owe the rest through balance billing.

options.t: Higher costs for the patient
options.why: Out-of-network providers have no negotiated rate, so plans cover less, deductibles are higher and you may owe the difference between billed and allowed amounts.

options.t: Lower costs for each patient
options.why: Lower costs are the result of staying in-network, where negotiated rates apply, so out-of-network care does the reverse.

options.t: No change in cost for patients
options.why: Costs usually differ sharply: in-network care has discounted rates and lower cost sharing, while out-of-network care is billed at higher patient cost.

q: What is term life insurance?

options.t: Coverage for the whole life with cash
options.why: Lifelong coverage with cash value describes whole life insurance; term life lasts only a set period and has no cash value.

options.t: Coverage for car repairs and damage
options.why: Car repair coverage is auto collision insurance; term life insurance pays a death benefit to beneficiaries, not repair bills.

options.t: Coverage for health care costs only
options.why: Health care costs are covered by health insurance; term life pays a death benefit rather than medical expenses.

options.t: Coverage for a set number of years
options.why: Term life insurance pays a death benefit only if the insured dies within a set term such as 10, 20 or 30 years, and it is usually cheaper than whole life.

q: What is whole life insurance?

options.t: Coverage for a set number of years only, which then ends
options.why: Coverage for a set number of years that then ends describes term life insurance; whole life stays in force for the insured's entire life.

options.t: Coverage for a home and all the belongings in it
options.why: Coverage for a home and its contents is homeowners insurance, which has nothing to do with life insurance on a person.

options.t: Coverage for your entire life that builds cash value
options.why: Whole life lasts the insured's lifetime if premiums are paid, pays a death benefit and builds cash value the owner can borrow against, at higher cost than term.

options.t: Coverage for medical bills of your family members
options.why: Medical bill coverage is health insurance; whole life pays a death benefit to beneficiaries rather than paying a family's medical expenses.

q: A young single person with no dependents is least likely to need:

options.t: A large life insurance policy
options.why: Life insurance replaces income for dependents, so a young single person with no dependents has little need for a large policy.

options.t: Renters insurance for the flat
options.why: Renters insurance protects belongings and liability in a rental unit, which a young single person with possessions still may need.

options.t: Auto insurance if they drive
options.why: Auto insurance is legally required in nearly all states for anyone who drives, so a young driver still needs it.

options.t: Health insurance for a young man
options.why: Health insurance is needed for everyone, since a single serious illness can cost tens of thousands of dollars even for a young person.

q: What is renters insurance?

options.t: Coverage for a renter's belongings and liability
options.why: Renters insurance covers your belongings against fire and theft and gives liability protection, usually for a low cost of around $15 to $30 a month.

options.t: Coverage for the landlord's income if a fire hits
options.why: A landlord's income loss is covered by landlord insurance, not a renter's policy, which protects the tenant's own property and liability.

options.t: Coverage for the building that the landlord owns
options.why: The landlord's building is covered by the landlord's property policy, not a renter's policy, which only covers the tenant's items.

options.t: Coverage for rent payments that you owe each month
options.why: Renters insurance does not pay your monthly rent; it covers property loss and liability, though some policies cover temporary housing after a loss.

q: A fire destroys a renter's belongings. Which policy covers them?

options.t: Health insurance
options.why: Health insurance pays medical expenses, not property losses, so it will not replace belongings destroyed by fire.

options.t: Renters insurance
options.why: Renters insurance covers personal property damaged by fire, and many policies also pay for temporary living expenses while the home is repaired.

options.t: Auto insurance
options.why: Auto insurance covers vehicles and driving liability, not household belongings destroyed in an apartment fire.

options.t: The landlord's policy
options.why: The landlord's policy covers the building structure, not tenants' personal belongings, so renters need their own policy.

q: After a flood damages a home, the owner learns the standard policy does not pay. Why?

options.t: Floods are always covered by a standard home policy
options.why: Standard homeowners policies typically exclude flood damage, so saying floods are always covered is false.

options.t: The insurer made a mistake in handling the claim
options.why: The refusal is not an insurer error; flood is a standard, written exclusion in homeowners policies, so the claim is properly denied.

options.t: The owner cannot file claims, as insurers exclude water damage
options.why: Owners can file claims for many covered losses, but water damage from floods is a standard exclusion, not a ban on filing claims.

options.t: Floods are usually excluded and need separate insurance
options.why: Standard homeowners policies exclude flooding, so owners in risk areas need separate flood insurance, often through the National Flood Insurance Program.

q: What is an umbrella policy?

options.t: Coverage for cars only, and for nothing else at all
options.why: An umbrella policy applies to liability from many incidents, not only cars; it extends liability limits on auto, home and other policies.

options.t: Coverage for rain damage only, when a storm harms the roof
options.why: Rain damage to a roof falls under homeowners property coverage; an umbrella policy provides extra liability coverage, not weather damage coverage.

options.t: Extra liability coverage beyond other policies' limits
options.why: An umbrella policy adds extra liability coverage, often $1 million or more, once the limits of your auto or home policy are exhausted.

options.t: Coverage for jewelry only, and not for other goods
options.why: Jewelry is insured by a scheduled personal property rider; an umbrella policy covers liability for lawsuits, not specific items.

q: A person decides not to ride a motorcycle because it is dangerous. Which strategy is this?

options.t: Risk retention
options.why: Risk retention means accepting the risk and paying for losses yourself, but this person avoids the activity entirely.

options.t: Risk transfer
options.why: Risk transfer shifts the risk to another party such as an insurer; the person here simply chose not to ride at all.

options.t: Risk reduction
options.why: Risk reduction lowers the chance or severity of loss, for example by wearing a helmet, but the person still engages in the activity.

options.t: Risk avoidance
options.why: Risk avoidance eliminates the risk by not taking part in the dangerous activity at all, so no motorcycle loss can occur.

q: Which loss is best handled by retention rather than insurance?

options.t: A huge medical bill too large to pay from savings
options.why: A huge medical bill beyond your savings is a severe loss that insurance is designed to cover, so retention would be unaffordable.

options.t: A house fire that destroys the whole home
options.why: A house fire can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, a catastrophic loss that needs insurance rather than retention.

options.t: A small cost you can easily pay from savings
options.why: Small, affordable losses are best retained, since you save premiums and a minor cost, paid from savings, will not create hardship.

options.t: A major lawsuit for a large amount of money
options.why: A major lawsuit could cost far more than anyone has in savings, so liability insurance is better than retention for this risk.

q: What does comparing insurance quotes help you do?

options.t: Lower your deductible to zero
options.why: Comparing quotes does not change deductibles; deductible choices are made when selecting a policy, and zero is not a result of comparison.

options.t: Find better prices and coverage
options.why: Quotes from several insurers show different prices and coverage terms for the same needs, so you can pick the best value.

options.t: Avoid ever filing a claim again
options.why: No quote comparison prevents future claims; you may still file claims whenever a covered loss happens, and comparing only affects what you buy.

options.t: Make all companies charge the same
options.why: Companies set their own rates using their own risk models, so comparing quotes cannot make them charge the same price.

q: Why might a person with a good driving record pay less for auto insurance?

options.t: They are viewed as lower risk
options.why: Insurers use driving history to estimate claims, and a clean record signals lower risk of accidents, which earns lower premiums.

options.t: They have a much longer last name
options.why: Last name length has no bearing on risk or rates; insurers price based on driving record, age, vehicle and location instead.

options.t: Insurers like their car color
options.why: Car color does not affect rates; insurers consider the vehicle's make, model, safety and repair costs, not paint color.

options.t: They live near a big bank branch
options.why: Living near a bank branch is irrelevant to risk; insurers consider the garaging ZIP code for theft and accidents, not nearby businesses.

q: What is the main purpose of an emergency fund in managing risk?

options.t: To increase risk for the whole family unit
options.why: An emergency fund reduces the financial harm of surprises, so it lowers rather than increases risk for a household.

options.t: To replace all insurance, as a fund pays all
options.why: An emergency fund does not replace insurance; a few thousand dollars cannot pay a major hospital, lawsuit or house-fire loss.

options.t: To fund vacations and trips abroad each year
options.why: Vacation spending is a discretionary goal; an emergency fund is set aside for unexpected needs like job loss or urgent repairs.

options.t: To cover unexpected costs without borrowing
options.why: An emergency fund of three to six months of expenses pays for surprises such as car repairs or medical bills so you avoid credit card debt.

q: Which is the best first step if your wallet is stolen?

options.t: Cancel cards and report the theft
options.why: Cancel cards quickly to stop charges and report the theft to police and the card issuers; consider a fraud alert or freeze for added protection.

options.t: Wait to see if anything happens
options.why: Waiting lets a thief run up charges or open accounts in your name, so delay increases your losses and recovery time.

options.t: Post about it online with details
options.why: Posting details online can expose more of your personal data and help thieves, rather than protecting you from further harm.

options.t: Share your PIN with a close friend
options.why: Sharing your PIN, even with a friend, exposes your accounts to misuse; PINs should stay private and be changed after a theft.

q: What is identity theft insurance or monitoring meant to do?

options.t: Raise your credit score by a set amount
options.why: These services cannot raise your credit score by a set amount; scores depend on your payment history, credit use and other real behavior.

options.t: Help detect and recover from identity theft
options.why: Monitoring alerts you to suspicious activity and many plans help pay recovery costs and give restoration support after identity theft.

options.t: Erase your debts from your credit file
options.why: They cannot erase valid debts from your file; only accurate corrections or disputes of fraudulent items can change your credit report.

options.t: Prevent all theft forever, so you never check
options.why: No service can prevent all theft; you still need to check statements and reports, and these products only detect problems and aid recovery.

q: What does it mean to own a share of stock?

options.t: You hold an insurance policy from it
options.why: An insurance policy gives you protection against a loss, not ownership; owning stock makes you a part-owner of the company.

options.t: You have a savings account there
options.why: A savings account is a deposit with a bank; stock is ownership in a company, with value that can rise or fall.

options.t: You own a small part of a company
options.why: A share of stock is a unit of ownership, called equity, which may entitle you to dividends and voting rights in the company.

options.t: You lent money to a firm to be repaid
options.why: Lending money to a firm to be repaid describes buying its bonds; stockholders are owners, not creditors.

q: How can a stockholder earn money?

options.t: Only by working at the company, which pays shareholders wages
options.why: Wages come from working for the company as an employee; shareholders earn from dividends and price gains, not from working there.

options.t: Through dividends and by selling shares at a higher price
options.why: Stockholders can receive dividend payments out of profits and can profit by selling shares for more than they paid (a capital gain).

options.t: Only by borrowing money from the company's own bank
options.why: Stockholders do not earn by borrowing from the company's bank; returns come from dividends and share price growth, not from borrowing.

options.t: Only by paying a monthly fee to the stock exchange
options.why: Investors do not earn from paying a monthly fee to an exchange; fees are costs of trading, while returns come from dividends and price changes.

q: You buy 10 shares at $40 and sell them at $55. Ignoring fees, what is your gain?

options.why: Gain = (sale price - purchase price) x shares = ($55 - $40) x 10 = $15 x 10 = $150, before any fees or taxes.
$400 is the original cost (10 x $40), not the gain; the gain is only what the shares earned above that cost.
$550 is the total sale proceeds (10 x $55), not the gain; subtract the $400 cost to find the $150 profit.
$15 is the gain per share ($55 - $40), but you hold 10 shares, so the total gain is 10 x $15 = $150.

q: What is a bond's maturity date?

options.t: The date interest rates change for the bond
options.why: Interest rate changes are not what maturity means; a bond's coupon is usually fixed, and maturity is when principal is returned.

options.t: The date the bond is first sold to the public
options.why: The date a bond is first sold is its issue date, which differs from the maturity date when the issuer repays what it borrowed.

options.t: The date the issuer repays the principal
options.why: At maturity the issuer repays the bond's face value (principal) to the holder, and interest payments end on that date.

options.t: The date the buyer pays taxes on the bond
options.why: Taxes on bond interest are paid when interest is earned each year; maturity is not a tax date but the date principal is repaid.

q: A $1,000 bond pays 5% interest each year. How much interest does it pay annually?

options.why: $1,050 is principal plus one year of interest ($1,000 + $50), the value after a year, not the annual interest itself.
$500 would be a 50% rate; 5% is 0.05, so the interest on $1,000 is far smaller than $500.
$5 would be 0.5% of $1,000; a 5% rate is ten times larger, giving $50, so the decimal is misplaced.
Interest = principal x rate = $1,000 x 0.05 = $50 per year, which is the bond's annual coupon payment.

q: What is a Treasury bond?

options.t: A bond issued by a small company
options.why: Bonds from small companies are corporate bonds; Treasury bonds are issued by the federal government and are backed by its full faith and credit.

options.t: A bond issued by the U.S. government
options.why: Treasury bonds are long-term debt (10 to 30 years) issued by the US government, considered very low in default risk.

options.t: A bond issued by a city's government
options.why: Bonds from a city's government are municipal bonds, which often have tax advantages but are not Treasury bonds.

options.t: A stock issued by the government
options.why: A Treasury security is a debt instrument, not a stock; stocks represent ownership in a company and governments do not issue stock.

q: What is a corporate bond?

options.t: A type of insurance that covers company assets
options.why: Insurance covering company assets is a business property policy; a corporate bond is a debt security that investors buy.

options.t: A government savings plan for company workers
options.why: A government savings plan is a different product; a corporate bond is issued by a company and not by any government.

options.t: A loan investors make to a company for interest
options.why: A corporate bond is a loan made to a company; the company pays periodic interest and returns the principal at maturity.

options.t: A share of ownership in a company with voting rights
options.why: Ownership with voting rights describes common stock; a bondholder is a lender with no ownership or voting power.

q: Which is generally riskier: a corporate bond from a struggling firm or a Treasury bond?

options.t: Neither of them has any risk at all
options.why: Every investment carries some risk; even Treasury securities have inflation and interest-rate risk, so none is risk-free.

options.t: They carry exactly the same risk
options.why: The two bonds do not carry the same risk; a struggling firm is far more likely to default than the US government.

options.t: The Treasury bond from the government
options.why: Treasury bonds are backed by the US government and have very low default risk, so they are safer, not riskier, than a weak corporation's bond.

options.t: The struggling firm's corporate bond
options.why: A struggling firm may fail to pay interest or principal, so default risk is higher, and it must offer higher yields to attract investors.

q: Why might many beginners prefer a broad index fund to picking individual stocks?

options.t: It spreads risk across many companies at low cost
options.why: An index fund holds hundreds of companies (like the S&P 500), so one failure matters little, and expense ratios are often below 0.1%.

options.t: It avoids all market ups and downs for the beginner
options.why: Index funds still rise and fall with the market; diversification reduces single-company risk but cannot avoid overall market swings.

options.t: It guarantees the highest return in every year
options.why: No fund guarantees top returns; an index fund matches the market return and can lose value in down years.

options.t: It requires no money at all to buy shares in it
options.why: Buying fund shares requires money; some brokers allow fractional shares or low minimums, but nobody can buy without paying anything.

q: What is an ETF?

options.t: A basket of securities that trades like a stock
options.why: An exchange-traded fund holds many stocks or bonds and trades on an exchange throughout the day, so it offers diversification with a single purchase.

options.t: A type of insurance for the owner of a stock
options.why: Insurance for stock owners is not an ETF; an ETF is an investment product that holds assets, not a protection policy.

options.t: A loan to a company that must be repaid in time
options.why: A loan to a company that must be repaid describes a bond; an ETF is a pooled fund and not a debt contract.

options.t: A bank savings account that pays fixed interest
options.why: A bank savings account pays a fixed interest rate and is FDIC insured, whereas an ETF's value changes with its holdings.

q: What is an expense ratio?

options.t: The interest rate on a loan, charged to the borrower yearly
options.why: The yearly interest on a loan is an APR; an expense ratio measures fund costs and not borrowing costs.

options.t: The tax rate on dividends that you receive each year
options.why: The tax rate on dividends is set by tax law; the expense ratio is a fee charged by the fund and not a tax.

options.t: The ratio of debt to income for a family each year
options.why: The ratio of debt to income is a lending measure; an expense ratio is a fund cost compared with its assets.

options.t: The yearly cost of owning a fund as a percent of assets
options.why: The expense ratio is the annual fund fee as a percent of assets; 0.5% on $10,000 costs $50 a year, taken out of the fund's returns.

q: Fund A charges 0.05% yearly and Fund B charges 1.0%. Other things equal, which likely leaves you with more over 30 years?

options.t: Neither
options.why: One of the funds likely leaves you with more, since the fee gap is large and compounds over three decades; the result is not neutral.

options.t: Both equal
options.why: The funds differ by 0.95 percentage points yearly, so outcomes are not equal; the lower fee fund keeps more of the same gross return.

options.t: Fund A
options.why: With the same gross return, Fund A's 0.05% fee versus Fund B's 1.0% leaves more compounding in your account, potentially tens of thousands of dollars after 30 years.

options.t: Fund B
options.why: Fund B charges twenty times the fee of Fund A, and that drag compounds yearly, so it likely leaves you with less.

q: What is a Roth IRA?

options.t: A savings account insured by the FDIC up to the legal limit set for each saver
options.why: A savings account insured up to a legal limit by the FDIC is a bank deposit, not a Roth IRA, which is a retirement investment account.

options.t: A retirement account funded with after-tax money with tax-free qualified withdrawals
options.why: Roth IRA contributions use after-tax dollars, and qualified withdrawals in retirement (after age 59 and a half with a five-year rule) are tax-free.

options.t: A retirement account funded with pre-tax money, with fully taxed withdrawals later in life
options.why: Pre-tax contributions with fully taxed withdrawals describe a traditional IRA, which is the opposite tax treatment from a Roth IRA.

options.t: A loan for retirees that is repaid from their yearly pension and their savings
options.why: A loan for retirees repaid from pensions is not a Roth IRA, which is an account you fund yourself and later withdraw from.

q: Who might benefit most from a Roth IRA?

options.t: Someone who needs the money next month for a new car purchase
options.why: Someone needing money next month should not use a retirement account, because early withdrawals of earnings face taxes and penalties.

options.t: Someone who wants a guaranteed return of ten percent
options.why: No IRA guarantees a return of ten percent; investments inside the account can gain or lose value depending on the markets.

options.t: Someone who expects to be in a higher tax bracket later
options.why: A Roth locks in today's tax rate on contributions, so it benefits people who expect a higher tax bracket in retirement or later in their careers.

options.t: Someone with no income now or in the near future
options.why: A Roth IRA requires earned income to contribute, so someone with no income now or soon cannot fund it.

q: What is a traditional IRA?

options.t: A retirement account with tax-free withdrawals, funded with after-tax money by its owner
options.why: Tax-free withdrawals from after-tax contributions describe a Roth IRA; a traditional IRA instead offers deductible contributions and taxable withdrawals.

options.t: An insurance policy that pays out when a person retires from work and stops working
options.why: An insurance policy paying out at retirement describes an annuity or pension; a traditional IRA is an account you invest in yourself.

options.t: A bank loan that a retiree takes out against the house to pay for their expenses
options.why: A bank loan against a house is a reverse mortgage or home equity loan, which is unrelated to an individual retirement account.

options.t: A retirement account where contributions may be tax-deductible and withdrawals are taxed
options.why: Traditional IRA contributions may be tax-deductible and grow tax-deferred, but withdrawals in retirement are taxed as ordinary income.

q: What penalty usually applies to early withdrawals from retirement accounts before age 59 and a half?

options.t: A 10% bonus paid by the IRS for any early use
options.why: The IRS does not pay bonuses for early withdrawals; instead it charges a penalty on taxable amounts taken before 59 and a half.

options.t: A 10% additional tax plus ordinary income tax
options.why: Early withdrawals typically face a 10% additional tax on top of regular income tax, with exceptions such as certain first-home or medical uses.

options.t: No penalty applies if you take the money out early
options.why: A penalty usually does apply, so saying nothing applies is wrong; the 10% additional tax exists to discourage early use of retirement money.

options.t: A free refund of tax paid by the state on money
options.why: The IRS and states do not refund tax on early withdrawals; taking money early generally adds a tax cost rather than a refund.

q: What is a pension?

options.t: A retirement plan that pays a regular benefit
options.why: A pension is an employer-sponsored plan that pays retirees a regular income, often based on salary and years of service.

options.t: A loan for retirees paid back from their pensions
options.why: A pension is not a loan; retirees receive benefits from it rather than borrowing money and paying it back from their own pensions.

options.t: A one-time bonus for new hires who stay one year
options.why: A one-time bonus for new hires is a signing or retention bonus, whereas a pension pays ongoing income after retirement.

options.t: A payment for unused vacation days at the firm
options.why: Payment for unused vacation days is a payout of accrued leave, which is separate from a pension that pays retirement income.

q: What is Social Security?

options.t: A stock market fund that pays benefits to every adult citizen of the state
options.why: Social Security is not a stock market fund; it is a government insurance program funded by payroll taxes and paid to eligible workers, not every adult.

options.t: A loan program for homes run by the government to help buyers with low pay
options.why: A government home loan program for buyers with low pay is a housing program like FHA or VA lending, not Social Security.

options.t: A government program that provides retirement, disability and survivor benefits
options.why: Social Security, funded by payroll taxes under FICA, pays retirement, disability and survivor benefits to eligible workers and their families.

options.t: A private savings account owned by each worker and paid out when they retire from work
options.why: Social Security is a federal program funded by payroll taxes and not a private savings account owned by each worker.

q: Why should most people not rely only on Social Security for retirement?

options.t: It never changes over time and always covers all living costs
options.why: Social Security benefits are adjusted for inflation and do not always cover living costs; saying it never changes and covers everything is wrong.

options.t: It is a private account that grows fast, so benefits cover costs
options.why: Social Security is not a private account that grows quickly; it is a government program funded by payroll taxes, and benefits are limited.

options.t: It pays more than most people ever earned while working
options.why: Benefits generally replace less than half of average pre-retirement earnings, so it does not pay more than most people earned.

options.t: Benefits typically replace only part of pre-retirement income
options.why: Social Security replaces roughly 40% of average pre-retirement income, so savings, 401(k)s and IRAs are needed to maintain your standard of living.

q: Which is generally taxed at a lower rate: a long-term or a short-term capital gain?

options.t: A long-term capital gain
options.why: Assets held more than a year are taxed at long-term rates of 0%, 15% or 20%, which is lower than the ordinary income rates on short-term gains.

options.t: A short-term capital gain
options.why: Short-term gains, from assets held a year or less, are taxed at ordinary income rates, which are higher, not lower.

options.t: Neither one gets taxed
options.why: Capital gains are taxable income when you sell an asset at a profit, so saying neither is taxed is incorrect.

options.t: They are taxed the same
options.why: The two are taxed differently: long-term gains get special lower rates, and short-term gains are taxed as ordinary income.

q: You invest $100 monthly. Prices are $10, $20 and $10. What happens to your average cost versus the average price?

options.t: It cannot be calculated
options.why: The average cost can be calculated by dividing total dollars invested by shares bought; dollar-cost averaging makes this simple.

options.t: Your average cost is lower
options.why: $300 buys 10 + 5 + 10 = 25 shares, so average cost = $300 / 25 = $12, below the average price of ($10 + $20 + $10) / 3 = $13.33.

options.t: It equals the highest price
options.why: Your average cost is not the highest price of $20; you buy more shares when prices are low, so your average cost stays below that.

options.t: Your average cost is higher
options.why: Your average cost is lower, not higher, since the fixed $100 buys more shares at $10 than at $20; the average price is $13.33 and your cost is $12.

q: What is rebalancing?

options.t: Buying only the winners and selling the losers each week
options.why: Buying only winners and selling losers weekly is chasing momentum, not rebalancing, which restores target percentages.

options.t: Ignoring your portfolio and letting it drift over the years
options.why: Ignoring your portfolio and letting it drift is the opposite of rebalancing, which means actively bringing allocations back to target.

options.t: Adjusting your portfolio back to your target mix of assets
options.why: Rebalancing sells assets that have grown beyond their target share and buys those that fell short, keeping risk in line with your plan.

options.t: Selling everything and then buying a new set from scratch
options.why: Selling everything and starting over is a full liquidation that creates taxes; rebalancing makes smaller adjustments to restore the target mix.

q: Your target is 60% stocks and 40% bonds, but stocks have grown to 75%. What does rebalancing involve?

options.t: Buying more stocks to restore the target
options.why: Buying more stocks would push the stock share even higher above 60%, moving away from the target instead of restoring it.

options.t: Selling all bonds and holding all stocks
options.why: Selling all bonds and holding only stocks would abandon the 40% bond target and make the portfolio far riskier.

options.t: Doing nothing at all to the portfolio
options.why: Doing nothing leaves stocks at 75%, which is 15 points over target and carries more risk than you planned.

options.t: Selling some stocks and buying bonds
options.why: Stocks grew to 75%, so you sell some stocks and buy bonds to return to 60/40, which locks in gains and restores your planned risk level.

q: What is risk tolerance?

options.t: How much a stock paid last year in dividends to holders
options.why: Last year's dividends measure an investment's income, while risk tolerance describes your willingness and ability to endure losses.

options.t: How much loss in value you can accept without panic
options.why: Risk tolerance is how much decline in value you can accept without panic selling, and it helps decide the right mix of stocks and bonds.

options.t: How much you earn from your job each year in total
options.why: Your job earnings are your income, which can affect risk capacity but are not the definition of risk tolerance.

options.t: How many accounts you hold at different banks
options.why: The number of accounts you hold has no bearing on your comfort with loss, so it does not define risk tolerance.

q: Which investor most likely holds a higher share of stocks?

options.t: A 25-year-old saving for retirement in 40 years
options.why: With 40 years until retirement, a young investor can ride out downturns, so holding a larger share of stocks, which grow more over long periods, makes sense.

options.t: A person saving for a car to buy next year
options.why: Someone saving for a car next year needs safe, liquid assets, because stocks could fall right before the money is needed.

options.t: A person with no time to wait for any growth
options.why: A person with no time to wait should avoid volatile stocks, since there is no chance to recover from a drop.

options.t: A retiree needing the money next month for bills
options.why: A retiree needing money next month needs stable cash, because a market dip could force selling at a loss.

q: What is inflation risk for investors?

options.t: The risk that rising prices erode the value of returns
options.why: Inflation risk is the chance that rising prices reduce purchasing power, so returns that do not outpace inflation lose real value.

options.t: The risk that a company fails and its shares are worthless
options.why: A company failing and shares becoming worthless is business or credit risk, not inflation risk, which concerns price levels across the economy.

options.t: The risk that taxes rise on your investment gains
options.why: Rising taxes on gains is tax risk, a separate risk from inflation reducing the real value of your returns.

options.t: The risk that a bank closes its doors for good and fails
options.why: A bank failing is institutional risk, and FDIC insurance covers deposits up to $250,000, so it differs from inflation risk.

q: What is liquidity risk?

options.t: The risk of rising taxes on income that you earn from investments
options.why: Rising taxes on income describe tax risk, which differs from liquidity risk, the difficulty of selling quickly at a fair price.

options.t: The risk that prices fall for all assets at the same time in the market
options.why: Prices falling for all assets together is market or systematic risk, while liquidity risk is about the ability to sell without a loss.

options.t: The risk of default by a borrower who cannot repay what they owe
options.why: A borrower failing to repay is default or credit risk, a different risk from not being able to sell an asset quickly.

options.t: The risk that you cannot sell an asset quickly without losing value
options.why: Liquidity risk is the chance you cannot turn an asset into cash fast without taking a price cut, as with real estate or thinly traded stocks.

q: Which asset is typically the least liquid?

options.t: A bank deposit
options.why: A bank deposit can be withdrawn at once, so it is highly liquid, not the least liquid.

options.t: Blue chip stock
options.why: Blue chip stocks trade daily on exchanges with high volume and settle in days, so they are liquid.

options.t: Real estate
options.why: Selling real estate takes weeks or months and has high transaction costs, making it one of the least liquid common assets.

options.t: Cash in hand
options.why: Cash in hand is the most liquid asset since it can be spent immediately without conversion.

q: Which portfolio is best diversified?

options.t: Five stocks from one industry that the investor follows daily
options.why: Five stocks in one industry are exposed to the same sector risks, so a downturn in that industry would hit all of them.

options.t: Stocks, bonds and cash across many companies and industries
options.why: Mixing stocks, bonds and cash across many companies and industries spreads risk, so no single event harms the whole portfolio.

options.t: One company's stock held by a single investor in a brokerage
options.why: One company's stock puts all your money in one place, the opposite of diversification, so a single failure could wipe out your savings.

options.t: Ten bonds from one issuer, all with the same maturity date
options.why: Ten bonds from one issuer share the same default risk and maturity, so they are not diversified despite the number of bonds.

q: During a bear market a long-term investor with a steady plan should generally:

options.t: Borrow to buy the single stock that has fallen most
options.why: Borrowing to buy a fallen stock adds debt and concentrates risk, which can magnify losses and is not a sound long-term approach.

options.t: Stop looking at the plan and hope for the best
options.why: Ignoring the plan and hoping is not a strategy; a long-term investor should follow the plan and review it periodically.

options.t: Sell everything immediately and keep only the cash
options.why: Selling everything in a downturn locks in losses and misses the recovery, which often hurts long-term results.

options.t: Stay with the plan and keep investing regularly
options.why: Staying invested and continuing regular contributions buys shares at lower prices, helping long-term returns when markets recover.

q: What is a market order?

options.t: An order to buy only at a set price, and wait for it to appear
options.why: Buying only at a set price and waiting describes a limit order, while a market order executes right away at the current price.

options.t: An order that triggers at a set loss, selling if price falls
options.why: An order that triggers at a set loss is a stop order, which differs from a market order that trades immediately.

options.t: An order to buy or sell immediately at the best available price
options.why: A market order executes immediately at the best available price, which gives speed but no guarantee of the exact price.

options.t: An order that cancels itself at the end of each trading day by rule
options.why: An order that expires at the end of the trading day is a day order, a duration setting rather than a market order.

q: You want to buy a stock only if the price falls to $20. Which order fits?

options.t: A market order
options.why: A market order buys immediately at the current price, so it would not wait for the price to fall to $20.

options.t: A limit order
options.why: A limit order sets the maximum price you will pay, so it buys only if the stock falls to $20 or less.

options.t: A day trade
options.why: A day trade is buying and selling a security on the same day, not an order type that waits for a target price.

options.t: A margin call
options.why: A margin call is a broker demand for more funds when a margin account falls in value, not an order to buy a stock.

q: What is margin investing?

options.t: Borrowing money from a broker to buy securities
options.why: Buying on margin means using a loan from your broker to purchase securities, which magnifies both gains and losses.

options.t: Investing only with cash that you have saved up
options.why: Investing only with saved cash is a cash account, which is the opposite of using borrowed funds.
