options.why: Cash can be lost or stolen and has no fraud protection, so it is not safe from loss anywhere.

options.t: It earns rewards like points on purchases
options.why: Cash does not earn reward points. Rewards come from credit cards or loyalty programs.

options.t: It limits spending to the money you have
options.why: Correct. Paying with cash limits spending to what you actually have, which helps prevent overspending and debt.

options.t: It builds a credit history over time for you
options.why: Paying cash does not build credit history. Credit history comes from borrowing and repaying credit.

q: A subscription costs $9.99 per month and a person forgets to cancel it for a year. How much does she waste?

options.t: About $120
options.why: Correct. $9.99 x 12 months = $119.88, which is about $120 wasted on a service she did not use.

options.t: $10 a year
options.why: $10 is roughly one month of the subscription, not the full year. It is paid every month.

options.t: $1,200 total
options.why: $1,200 is ten times too high, a decimal slip. Twelve payments of about $10 total about $120.

options.t: $12 a year
options.why: $12 is a miscalculation of the year's cost. Twelve monthly payments of $9.99 total about $120.

q: What is buyer's remorse?

options.t: A discount only for new buyers
options.why: A discount for new buyers is a promotion. Buyer's remorse is a feeling, not a price offer.

options.t: Regret after making a purchase
options.why: Correct. Buyer's remorse is the regret or doubt a person feels after making a purchase, often after an impulse buy.

options.t: A product defect found by buyers
options.why: A defect is a product fault. Buyer's remorse is an emotional response, not a fault in the item.

options.t: A credit score after a purchase
options.why: A credit score is a number that rates borrowing history. Buyer's remorse is a feeling after buying.

q: Which spending choice most likely improves long-term financial health?

options.t: Skipping insurance to save money in the short run of a year
options.why: Skipping insurance leaves you exposed to large costs from accidents or illness, which can damage long-term finances.

options.t: Taking a loan for every purchase that you make in a year
options.why: Borrowing for every purchase builds debt and interest costs, which hurt long-term financial health.

options.t: Buying the priciest car on credit, so the payments go on for years
options.why: Buying the priciest car on credit adds large, long-lasting payments and interest, which strains finances for years.

options.t: Buying a reliable used car in cash and saving the difference
options.why: Correct. Paying cash for a reliable used car avoids interest and depreciation of a new car, and saved money can go to savings.

q: What is a store credit?

options.t: A paycheck that an employer issues to a worker every two weeks
options.why: A paycheck from an employer is wages for work, not a store credit.

options.t: Value given for a return that can only be used at that store
options.why: Correct. Store credit is value issued when you return an item, which can be used only at that store, rather than a cash refund.

options.t: A tax refund that the government sends after a return
options.why: A tax refund is money returned by the government and is not issued by a store.

options.t: A bank loan that a customer repays in monthly payments
options.why: A bank loan repaid monthly is an installment loan. Store credit is a balance given for a return.

q: What is the benefit of using a shopping list?

options.t: It increases prices in the shop a lot
options.why: A shopping list does not increase prices. It helps you buy only what you planned.

options.t: It makes shopping take much longer
options.why: A list usually makes shopping faster and more focused because you know what to buy.

options.t: It helps avoid unplanned purchases
options.why: Correct. A shopping list keeps you focused on planned items, which helps you avoid unplanned purchases and stay within your budget.

options.t: It removes the need for any budget
options.why: A shopping list does not replace a budget. It supports it by guiding spending decisions.

q: What is a peer pressure effect on spending?

options.t: Buying something because friends have it
options.why: Correct. Peer pressure affects spending when people buy things just because friends have them, rather than because they need or can afford them.

options.t: Paying less because of a big sale at the till
options.why: Paying less because of a big sale reflects a price promotion, not social influence from friends.

options.t: Saving because your friends ask you to save
options.why: Saving because friends ask you to save is positive social influence on saving, not an effect on spending.

options.t: Having more income than most of your friends
options.why: Having more income than friends describes your income level, which is not a pressure effect.

q: A teen earns $120 a week. She spends $90 on entertainment and food. What share of her income does she keep?

options.why: 30% mistakes the $30 she keeps for a percent. The share kept is $30 divided by the $120 income, which is 25%, not 30%.
90% confuses $90 spent with the percent kept. She keeps only the money left after spending.
75% is the share she spends, since $90 / $120 = 75%. The share she keeps is the rest.
Correct. She keeps $120 - $90 = $30, and $30 / $120 = 0.25, so she keeps 25% of her income.

q: What does it mean to negotiate a price?

options.t: Discuss with a seller to agree on a lower or fair price
options.why: Correct. Negotiating means discussing with a seller to reach a lower or fair price, often by comparing prices and asking politely.

options.t: Argue loudly with the seller until they give in to you
options.why: Arguing loudly is not negotiation. Negotiation is a respectful discussion aimed at an agreement both sides accept.

options.t: Pay the sticker price only, without discussing terms
options.why: Paying the sticker price without discussion skips negotiation entirely.

options.t: Refuse to buy anything from the seller at all, ever again
options.why: Refusing to buy anything from the seller is not negotiation. It ends discussion rather than seeking an agreement.

q: What is a hidden fee?

options.t: A refund of the money that you spent
options.why: A refund returns money you spent. A hidden fee is an added charge you did not know about.

options.t: A discount on a coupon given by a store
options.why: A discount on a coupon lowers the price. A hidden fee raises your cost.

options.t: A charge not clearly shown at the start
options.why: Correct. A hidden fee is a charge not clearly disclosed at the start, such as a service or processing fee, which raises the final price.

options.t: A tax shown on the receipt at the bottom
options.why: A tax listed on the receipt is a disclosed sales tax, not a hidden fee.

q: Which is the best reason to wait 24 hours before a big, unplanned purchase?

options.t: The store will cancel the item that you want
options.why: The store will not usually cancel an item because you waited a day. Waiting does not cause the item to disappear.

options.t: The price always drops overnight, so waiting helps
options.why: Prices do not always fall overnight. A waiting period is meant for reflection, not a price drop.

options.t: It removes the need for money in any store
options.why: Waiting does not remove the need for money. You still need funds to buy the item.

options.t: It gives time to decide if you really need it
options.why: Correct. Waiting 24 hours gives time to judge whether you truly need the item and can afford it, which reduces impulse purchases.

q: What is the effect of spending more than you earn?

options.t: Your debts disappear all at once
options.why: Debts do not disappear. Spending more than you earn adds to what you owe.

options.t: You must borrow or use savings
options.why: Correct. If spending exceeds income, the shortfall must come from savings or borrowing, which can lead to debt.

options.t: Your savings automatically grow
options.why: Savings fall when you spend more than you earn, so they do not grow automatically.

options.t: Your taxes drop to zero this year
options.why: Taxes do not drop to zero because of overspending. Taxes depend on income and not on spending.

q: If $1,000 earns 5% compound interest annually, about how much will it be after 2 years?

options.why: Correct. Year 1: $1,000 x 1.05 = $1,050. Year 2: $1,050 x 1.05 = $1,102.50, because interest is earned on previous interest.
$1,100 is simple interest, which uses 5% of the original $1,000 each year. Compound interest also earns interest on interest.
$1,200 is far too high. A 5% rate over 2 years gives about 10% growth, not 20%.
$1,050 is the balance after only one year, so it leaves out the second year of growth.

q: Why do financial advisers recommend an emergency fund?

options.t: To pay for vacations and what the family wants
options.why: Vacations and wants are not emergencies. An emergency fund is for unexpected, necessary costs.

options.t: To invest in stocks only, for high gains
options.why: An emergency fund is kept in safe, liquid accounts, not invested in stocks for high gains.

options.t: To cover unexpected costs without borrowing
options.why: Correct. An emergency fund covers unexpected costs, such as job loss or repairs, so you do not need to borrow or use credit cards.

options.t: To avoid saving anywhere else in your life
options.why: An emergency fund does not replace other saving. Goals like retirement and large purchases still need savings.

q: A person wants $1,200 for a trip in 6 months. How much must she save each month?

options.why: $120 times 6 months is only $720. To reach $1,200 she must save more each month.
Correct. Divide the goal by the months: $1,200 / 6 = $200 per month.
$72 is $1,200 divided by about 17 months. It comes from a miscalculation and falls short of the goal.
$600 is half the goal and would be saved in just two months, not spread over six.

q: Which account is usually safest for short-term savings?

options.t: Cash kept under a mattress at home
options.why: Cash under a mattress can be stolen, lost or destroyed, and it earns no interest, so it is not safe.

options.t: A cryptocurrency coin held online
options.why: Cryptocurrency prices swing wildly and are not insured, so it is risky for short-term savings.

options.t: A single stock in one company
options.why: A single stock can lose value quickly and is not suited for short-term money.

options.t: An FDIC-insured savings account
options.why: Correct. FDIC insurance protects deposits up to $250,000 per depositor per bank, so a savings account is very safe for short-term money.

q: Which choice earns the most interest on $1,000 over one year?

options.t: 0.5% APY
options.why: 0.5% APY on $1,000 earns about $5 in a year, much less than the highest rate offered.

options.t: 1.0% APY
options.why: 1.0% APY earns about $10 in a year, which is less than 4.5%.

options.t: 4.5% APY
options.why: Correct. 4.5% APY on $1,000 earns about $45 in a year, the most of these choices because a higher rate gives more interest.

options.t: 0.1% APY
options.why: 0.1% APY earns about $1 on $1,000 in a year, the least of these options.

q: What is a CD (certificate of deposit)?

options.t: A type of loan that a bank offers to a customer
options.why: A loan is money you borrow. A CD is money you deposit, so it is a savings product.

options.t: A deposit held for a set time at a fixed rate
options.why: Correct. A certificate of deposit holds your money for a set term at a fixed rate, and early withdrawal usually brings a penalty.

options.t: A stock share in a large listed company today
options.why: A stock share is ownership in a company. A CD is a bank deposit that pays interest.

options.t: A checking account with no limits on withdrawals
options.why: A CD limits withdrawals until maturity, unlike a checking account with easy access.

q: What is the benefit of paying yourself first?

options.t: You set aside savings before spending
options.why: Correct. Paying yourself first means moving money to savings as soon as you are paid, before spending, which makes saving a habit.

options.t: It increases spending every single month
options.why: It does not increase spending. Paying yourself first reduces the money available to spend unnecessarily.

options.t: It lets you skip saving for a long while
options.why: It does the opposite of skipping saving. Savings are set aside first.

options.t: It removes the need for any budget
options.why: Paying yourself first does not remove the need for a budget. A budget still plans your spending of the remaining money.

q: Which is the best way to build savings if your income is irregular?

options.t: Spend every payment immediately on whatever you like
options.why: Spending every payment immediately leaves nothing for slow months, which makes irregular income harder to manage.

options.t: Save nothing until income is steady, then save some
options.why: Waiting for steady income may mean never saving. Irregular earners should save whenever they get paid.

options.t: Rely on credit cards instead of saving up money
options.why: Relying on credit cards creates debt and interest rather than savings.

options.t: Save a percentage of each payment when it arrives
options.why: Correct. Saving a set percentage of each payment builds savings in good months that can cover lean months.

q: What is the main reason to start saving early?

options.t: Early savers pay no taxes on gains
options.why: Savings gains can be taxed, so early savers still may owe taxes on interest.

options.t: Interest rates always rise over time
options.why: Interest rates do not always rise. They change with the economy, so this is not a reason to start early.

options.t: Saving late is simply impossible
options.why: Saving late is possible, though harder. Starting early is better because of compounding, not because late saving is impossible.

options.t: Time allows interest to compound
options.why: Correct. Starting early gives interest more time to compound, earning interest on prior interest, so small deposits grow into a larger sum.

q: A saver deposits $100 monthly into an account with no interest for 2 years. How much will she have?

options.why: $200 is only 2 months of deposits. She saves for 24 months.
Correct. $100 per month for 24 months is $100 x 24 = $2,400, with no interest added.
$1,200 is only 12 months of deposits, one year rather than two.
$2,000 counts 20 months. Two years is 24 months, so $2,400.

q: What is inflation's effect on savings?

options.t: It reduces the purchasing power of money over time
options.why: Correct. Inflation raises prices, so each dollar buys less over time, which reduces the purchasing power of savings if interest is lower.

options.t: It increases purchasing power, as prices rise
options.why: Rising prices reduce purchasing power, not increase it, because each dollar buys fewer goods.

options.t: It deletes savings accounts at banks across the country
options.why: Inflation does not delete accounts. Your balance remains, but its buying power shrinks.

options.t: It has no effect on savings or on prices over time
options.why: Inflation does affect savings by eroding buying power, and it is the same as rising prices.

q: A savings account pays 2% and inflation is 3%. What is the real change in buying power?

options.t: It rises by about 5%
options.why: Buying power does not rise by 5%. Adding the rates is wrong; you subtract inflation from the interest rate.

options.t: It stays about equal
options.why: It does not stay equal, because 2% interest is below 3% inflation, so prices rise faster than the balance.

options.t: It falls by about 1%
options.why: Correct. The real change is about 2% - 3% = -1%, so buying power falls by about 1%.

options.t: It rises by about 1%
options.why: It does not rise by 1%. Inflation of 3% beats the 2% interest, so the real change is negative.

q: What is a good use of a tax refund?

options.t: Add to savings or pay down high-interest debt
options.why: Correct. Putting a refund in savings or paying down high-interest debt improves your finances and saves you money on interest.

options.t: Ignore it and let the money sit in a drawer
options.why: Letting money sit unused in a drawer earns nothing and loses buying power to inflation.

options.t: Hide it at home in a drawer for years to come
options.why: Hiding cash at home for years earns no interest and risks theft or loss.

options.t: Spend all of it on impulse buys at the mall
options.why: Spending it all on impulse buys gives short-term enjoyment but no lasting financial benefit.

q: Why might someone choose a CD over a regular savings account?

options.t: CDs have no interest and are less safe than regular savings accounts
options.why: Certificates of deposit do pay interest, usually more than regular savings, and they are FDIC insured up to limits, so this claim is false.

options.t: CDs allow unlimited withdrawals at any time, with no penalty and no wait
options.why: Unlimited penalty-free withdrawals describe a regular savings or checking account; a CD locks money until maturity and charges a penalty for early withdrawal.

options.t: A fixed rate for a set term can pay more if the money is not needed soon
options.why: A CD locks in a fixed rate for a set term, which usually beats a regular savings rate, so it suits money you will not need until the term ends.

options.t: CDs are not insured and can be lost in full if the bank ever fails
options.why: CDs from banks are covered by FDIC insurance (or NCUA at credit unions) up to $250,000 per depositor, so a bank failure does not wipe them out.

q: What is direct deposit into savings?

options.t: Buying a gift card for a friend at a local shop each year
options.why: A gift card is a purchase made at a store; it has nothing to do with sending part of your paycheck into a savings account.

options.t: Paying cash to a cashier at the register of a local shop
options.why: Paying cash at a register is a spending transaction at a store, not a way of moving earnings into savings.

options.t: Writing a check each month to the savings account at a branch
options.why: Writing a monthly check is a manual deposit you must remember each time; direct deposit is automatic and requires no check.

options.t: Automatically sending part of your pay to a savings account
options.why: Direct deposit has an employer send part of each paycheck straight into savings, which builds the habit of paying yourself first without relying on willpower.

q: An investor buys 10 shares at $25 and sells at $32. What is her gain before costs?

options.why: $250 is the original purchase cost of 10 shares at $25 each; it is what she paid, not the profit she made.
Gain = 10 shares x ($32 - $25) = 10 x $7 = $70, the difference between the sale price and the purchase price before fees and taxes.
$7 is the gain on a single share; she owns 10 shares, so the total gain must be multiplied by 10.
$320 is the total sale proceeds (10 x $32), not the gain; the gain subtracts the $250 she originally paid.

q: Which investment typically carries the least risk?

options.t: U.S. Treasury securities
options.why: U.S. Treasury securities are backed by the full faith and credit of the federal government, so default risk is extremely low compared with other investments.

options.t: A single speculative stock
options.why: A single speculative stock can swing sharply or lose most of its value, so it carries far more risk than government-backed securities.

options.t: A start-up investment
options.why: Start-up investments often fail, and investors can lose everything, which makes them one of the riskiest places to put money.

options.t: A new cryptocurrency
options.why: A new cryptocurrency is highly volatile and mostly unregulated with no guarantee behind it, so it is among the riskiest investments available.

q: An employer matches 50% of contributions up to 6% of pay. An employee earning $50,000 contributes 6%. What is the employer match?

options.why: $750 would be a 25% match on the $3,000 contribution; the plan matches 50 cents per dollar, which is double this amount.
$6,000 is twelve percent of pay; the match is capped at 6% of $50,000 and paid at only 50 cents on the dollar.
$3,000 is the employee's own contribution (6% x $50,000); a 50% match pays half of that, not the full amount.
Employee contributes 6% x $50,000 = $3,000, and the employer matches 50% of it: 0.50 x $3,000 = $1,500 of free retirement money.

q: A 25-year-old saving for retirement in 40 years can usually take more risk than a 60-year-old. Why?

options.t: Older people never invest in the stock market
options.why: Many older investors do hold stocks, often alongside bonds, so saying they never invest in the market is simply false and unrelated to risk capacity.

options.t: More time to recover from market declines
options.why: With 40 years until retirement, a young investor has time to recover from market declines and benefit from long-term growth, so she can accept more risk.

options.t: Younger people cannot lose money in the market
options.why: Young investors can certainly lose money, since stock prices fall at any age; they simply have more time to recover before needing the money.

options.t: Retirement accounts are always fully insured
options.why: Retirement accounts are not insured against market losses; FDIC insurance covers bank deposits, not stocks or funds held inside an IRA or 401(k).

q: Which statement about diversification is true?

options.t: It means owning only one stock to focus on the best company and follow it
options.why: Owning only one stock is the opposite of diversification and leaves the whole portfolio exposed to a single company's fortunes.

options.t: It eliminates all risk from the portfolio of an investor for good
options.why: Diversification lowers risk but cannot eliminate it, since market-wide events can hurt nearly all investments at the same time.

options.t: It reduces the impact of any single investment's poor performance
options.why: Spreading money across different investments means one poor performer hurts less, so diversification reduces the impact of any single investment's decline.

options.t: It guarantees profits on every investment that you hold for a year
options.why: No strategy guarantees profits, and diversification only spreads risk; investments can still lose value even when held for a year or longer.

q: What is capital gain?

options.t: A tax refund that the state pays to a worker each spring
options.why: A tax refund is money returned by the government when too much tax was withheld; it is not a profit from selling an investment.

options.t: A bank fee charged when your account balance falls too low
options.why: A low-balance charge is an account fee, a cost to the customer, while a capital gain is a profit earned on an investment.

options.t: A regular paycheck from an employer for work done each period
options.why: A paycheck is wage income earned from working, while a capital gain comes from an asset such as a stock rising in value.

options.t: Profit from selling an investment for more than its cost
options.why: A capital gain is the profit made when you sell an asset, such as a stock or home, for more than you paid for it.

q: Why is it risky to invest money you will need in six months in the stock market?

options.t: Stocks cannot be sold at any time or at any price at all
options.why: Stocks trade on exchanges and can usually be sold on any market day, so liquidity is not the problem; the risk is the price you might get.

options.t: Stocks always rise in six months, so the investor gains
options.why: Stocks never always rise over short periods, and a six-month window has no guaranteed gain, so this claim is false.

options.t: Prices can fall and you may have to sell at a loss
options.why: Short-term prices can drop, and if you need the money in six months you may be forced to sell at a loss with no time to wait for recovery.

options.t: Stocks pay no returns to those who buy and hold them
options.why: Stocks can pay returns through dividends and price growth; the short-term risk is about price swings, not about earning nothing.

q: What does a financial adviser do?

options.t: Guarantees returns on all of your investments each year
options.why: No adviser can guarantee investment returns, and promising guaranteed gains is a warning sign of fraud rather than a duty of a legitimate adviser.

options.t: Gives guidance about money and investment decisions
options.why: A financial adviser gives guidance on saving, investing, insurance, and retirement so clients can make informed decisions about their money.

options.t: Collects taxes from clients on the money they invest
options.why: Collecting taxes is the job of government agencies such as the IRS; an adviser may help with tax planning but does not collect taxes.

options.t: Sets interest rates for the banks of a whole country
options.why: Interest rates for a nation are set by its central bank, such as the Federal Reserve in the U.S., not by a financial adviser.

q: If an investment's value falls 50%, what gain is needed to return to the original value?

options.why: After a 50% loss, $100 becomes $50, and doubling $50 back to $100 requires a 100% gain, because percent gains apply to the smaller base.
A 25% gain on $50 yields only $62.50, still well short of the original $100 value.
A 75% gain on $50 yields $87.50, which is still below the original $100, so it is not enough to break even.
A 50% gain on $50 gives only $75, so the investor would remain $25 short of the original $100 value.

q: What is an investment fee, such as an expense ratio?

options.t: A tax refund paid to investors each year
options.why: A tax refund is a payment from the government; an expense ratio is a charge investors pay, and it reduces their returns.

options.t: A yearly cost charged to manage a fund
options.why: An expense ratio is the annual percentage of fund assets charged to cover management and operating costs, which lowers the investor's return each year.

options.t: A free service offered to fund investors
options.why: Funds are not free; management, administration, and trading costs are real and are passed on to investors through the expense ratio.

options.t: A bonus paid to investors who hold a fund
options.why: Fees are costs, not rewards; investors pay them, and they are never a bonus for holding a fund.

q: What is a portfolio?

options.t: A savings account that pays a fixed rate to its owner
options.why: A savings account that pays a fixed rate is a single deposit product; a portfolio is a whole collection of different holdings.

options.t: A paycheck that an employer gives to a worker each week
options.why: A paycheck is income from an employer for work done, not a set of investments that a person owns.

options.t: A collection of investments owned by a person or group
options.why: A portfolio is the full collection of investments, such as stocks, bonds, and funds, held by an individual, family, or institution.

options.t: A bank statement listing deposits and withdrawals made
options.why: A bank statement lists deposits and withdrawals for an account; it records transactions, not the mix of investments someone owns.

q: Which is a warning sign of an investment scam?

options.t: Registered advisers with a clean public record
options.why: Registered advisers with a clean public record are a good sign; you can check an adviser's background through regulators such as FINRA or the SEC.

options.t: A clear explanation of the risks and past fund results
options.why: Honest sellers explain risks and show past results clearly, so a clear explanation is a sign of a legitimate offer, not a scam.

options.t: Written disclosures of fees, risks and past results
options.why: Written disclosures of fees, risks, and results are required for legitimate investments and signal transparency rather than fraud.

options.t: Promises of guaranteed high returns with no risk
options.why: No real investment can guarantee high returns without risk; this promise is the classic sign of a Ponzi scheme or other investment fraud.

q: At a 6% annual return, about how long does it take money to double using the Rule of 72?

options.t: 12 years
options.why: Rule of 72: years to double = 72 divided by the rate, so 72 / 6 = 12 years for money to double at a 6% annual return.

options.t: 6 years
options.why: Six years simply repeats the interest rate; dividing 72 by 6 gives 12 years, not 6.

options.t: 1 year
options.why: One year would require a 72% return to double, far above the 6% rate stated in this problem.

options.t: 72 years
options.why: Seventy-two is the numerator in the rule, not the answer; you must divide it by the 6% rate to get 12 years.

q: A card has a $2,000 limit and a $1,000 balance. What is the credit utilization?

options.why: Utilization = balance / limit = $1,000 / $2,000 = 50%, which is high; keeping it under 30% is better for a credit score.
A 100% utilization would require a $2,000 balance on a $2,000 limit, which is double the balance she actually carries.
Twenty percent would need a $400 balance on a $2,000 limit; her balance is $1,000, so utilization is higher than that.
A 200% utilization would mean owing $4,000 on a $2,000 limit; her $1,000 balance is only half of the limit.

q: What does a lender look at when deciding whether to approve a loan?

options.t: Shoe size and hair color too
options.why: Physical traits like shoe size and hair color have no bearing on whether a borrower can repay, and lenders may not use them to decide.

options.t: Social media followers and likes
options.why: Social media popularity says nothing about repayment ability, so lenders do not weigh followers or likes in a loan decision.

options.t: Credit history, income and debts
options.why: Lenders review credit history, income, and existing debts to judge how likely a borrower is to repay the loan on time.

options.t: Favorite color of the applicant
options.why: A favorite color has no connection to the ability to repay, so it plays no role in a lender's decision.

q: A loan has a 6% APR and a 4% APR offer is available from another lender for the same terms. Which is cheaper?

options.t: Neither costs
options.why: Loans always cost something, since interest is the price of borrowing; 'neither costs' ignores that both loans charge interest.

options.t: The 6% APR loan
options.why: A 6% APR charges more interest per year than 4% on identical terms, so the 6% loan is the more expensive choice.

options.t: They cost the same
options.why: The rates differ by two percentage points, so the costs differ; the 6% loan charges noticeably more interest over the same term.

options.t: The 4% APR loan
options.why: With identical terms, a lower APR means less total interest paid, so the 4% APR loan is the cheaper option.

q: A person with no credit history wants a first card. Which option is often easier to qualify for?

options.t: A big home mortgage loan
options.why: A mortgage needs good credit and a large down payment, so someone with no credit history is unlikely to qualify for one first.

options.t: A secured credit card
options.why: A secured card is backed by a cash deposit, which lowers the lender's risk and makes approval easier for people building credit for the first time.

options.t: A small business loan
options.why: Business loans typically require financial records, collateral, or a track record, which a person with no credit history lacks.

options.t: A large unsecured limit
options.why: Large unsecured limits go to borrowers with proven credit; with no history, lenders will not offer a big limit without collateral.

q: What does a hard inquiry mean?

options.t: You closed an account and the bank checked all your records
options.why: Closing an account does not create an inquiry; a hard inquiry occurs when a lender pulls your report in response to an application.

options.t: You paid a bill early and the lender thanked you for doing so today
options.why: Paying a bill early may help your record, but it does not trigger a hard inquiry; those come from credit applications.

options.t: You checked your own score and no lender looked at your file
options.why: Checking your own score is a soft inquiry that does not affect your score, which is the opposite of a hard inquiry.

options.t: A lender checked your credit report because you applied for credit
options.why: A hard inquiry happens when a lender reviews your credit report because you applied for credit, and it can lower your score slightly for a while.

q: What is the grace period on a credit card?

options.t: Time to pay the balance without being charged interest on new purchases
options.why: A grace period lets you avoid interest on new purchases if you pay the statement balance in full by the due date, usually about 21 days.

options.t: A permanent waiver of fees on every purchase you make with the card
options.why: A grace period does not waive fees permanently; fees such as annual or late fees still apply when they are charged.

options.t: A reward for late payment that the issuer gives to loyal cardholders
options.why: Late payments are penalized, not rewarded; a grace period only applies when the full balance is paid by the due date.

options.t: The time to ignore the bill without any penalty or interest being added
options.why: The grace period does not allow ignoring the bill; unpaid balances start accruing interest, and late payments bring fees and credit damage.

q: A person pays only the minimum on a $3,000 balance at 20% APR. What is the main effect?

options.t: Interest stops being charged and the whole debt is wiped out
options.why: Interest keeps accruing on the unpaid balance, so paying only the minimum never wipes out the debt or stops charges.

options.t: The credit limit is cut to zero, so the card cannot be used again
options.why: Issuers do not cut a limit to zero for paying the minimum; the real problem is that interest keeps compounding on the remaining balance.

options.t: Much of the payment goes to interest and the debt lasts longer
options.why: At 20% APR on $3,000 (about $600 a year), minimum payments mostly cover interest, so the balance shrinks slowly and the debt lasts for years.

options.t: The debt is erased quickly and the card is closed by the bank
options.why: Minimum payments pay down debt slowly, not quickly, and the bank does not close an account simply because minimums are made.

q: Why check your credit report for errors?

options.t: Credit reports are private and cannot be corrected
options.why: Credit reports can be corrected; under the Fair Credit Reporting Act you can dispute errors with the bureaus and the lender.

options.t: Errors can lower your score and cost you money
options.why: Errors such as wrong balances or accounts that are not yours can lower your score and lead to higher rates or denied credit.

options.t: Reports never contain errors of any kind at all
options.why: Reports do contain mistakes, and studies have found errors on many of them, which is why free annual checks are recommended.

options.t: Errors only help you and never cost you money
options.why: Errors usually hurt, not help; wrong late payments or accounts can raise your borrowing costs, so checking is worthwhile.

q: A teen is offered a credit card with a 29% APR. What is the best advice?

options.t: Carry a balance to build credit, as lenders like it
options.why: Carrying a balance does not build credit; it only racks up interest at 29%, and paying on time and in full is what lenders reward.

options.t: Compare lower-rate options and pay in full each month
options.why: A 29% APR is very high, so comparing lower-rate options and paying the full balance monthly avoids costly interest charges.

options.t: Ignore the APR and sign up for the card straight away
options.why: Ignoring the APR is risky because the rate determines the cost of carrying a balance, and 29% is much higher than typical cards.

options.t: Take every offer that arrives in the mail this year
options.why: Accepting every mailed offer can create many accounts and hard inquiries and tempt overspending, which can hurt a young person's finances.

q: A $300 payday loan charges a $45 fee for two weeks. What is the approximate APR?

options.t: About 15.0%
options.why: About 15% is the fee as a share of the loan for one two-week period ($45 / $300), not the annualized rate.

options.t: About 45%
options.why: 45% mistakes the $45 fee for a percentage; the fee is 15% of $300 and must be annualized to get the APR.

options.t: About 390%
options.why: $45 / $300 = 15% per two weeks; with 26 two-week periods in a year, 15% x 26 = 390% APR, which is why payday loans are so costly.

options.t: About 0%
options.why: The loan charges a $45 fee, so the APR cannot be zero; the fee on $300 works out to a very high annual rate.

q: What does it mean to default on a loan?

options.t: To fail to make required payments
options.why: Default means failing to make required payments, which can bring late fees, collections, credit damage, and possibly loss of collateral.

options.t: To refinance the loan at a lower rate
options.why: Refinancing replaces a loan with a new one at better terms; it is a deliberate action, not a failure to pay.

options.t: To pay the loan off early in full
options.why: Paying off a loan early in full is a good outcome that closes the debt; it is the opposite of defaulting.

options.t: To ask a question about your loan
options.why: Asking a question about a loan is normal customer service and has no effect on the loan or your payment record.

q: What is refinancing?

options.t: Paying a loan with a credit card, moving debt between lenders
options.why: Paying a loan with a credit card just moves the debt to a different lender and is not what refinancing means; refinancing replaces the loan itself.

options.t: Ignoring a loan and not paying it back to the lender
options.why: Ignoring a loan is a default, which damages credit and can lead to collections; refinancing is a planned change of terms.

options.t: Canceling insurance that you pay for every month to protect you
options.why: Canceling insurance is unrelated to loans; refinancing deals with replacing existing debt, not coverage payments.

options.t: Replacing a loan with a new one, often to get better terms
options.why: Refinancing replaces an existing loan with a new loan, often to get a lower rate, lower payment, or different term.

q: What is the best way to build a good credit score over time?

options.t: Pay bills on time and keep balances low
options.why: Payment history and utilization are the biggest score factors, so paying bills on time and keeping balances low builds good credit over time.

options.t: Max out your cards each month for fun
options.why: Maxing out cards drives utilization up, which hurts your score and creates large debts that cost interest.

options.t: Close all accounts that you have opened
options.why: Closing accounts shortens your credit history and cuts available credit, which can raise utilization and lower your score.

options.t: Apply for many cards at once to get credit
options.why: Applying for many cards at once creates multiple hard inquiries and signals risk, which can lower your score.

q: What is the difference between a credit card and a debit card?

options.t: They are identical in every way and in every use of them
options.why: Credit and debit cards work differently: credit borrows from the issuer, while debit takes money directly from your checking account.

options.t: Debit cards charge interest monthly on the balance, like credit
options.why: Debit cards use your own funds and do not charge interest, so describing them as charging interest monthly is wrong.

options.t: Credit cards use only your cash and never any loan from a bank
options.why: Credit cards lend you money up to a limit, so saying they use only your cash and no loan describes debit cards instead.

options.t: Credit cards borrow money and debit cards use your own funds
options.why: A credit card is a loan you repay later, often with interest, while a debit card pulls money straight from your own account.

q: A customer is offered 0% APR for 12 months followed by 22% on any balance. What should she do?

options.t: Spend as much as possible in the promotion, since the rate is low
options.why: After 12 months the rate jumps to 22%, so heavy spending without a payoff plan could leave a large balance charged that high rate.

options.t: Plan to pay the balance before the promotional period ends
options.why: Planning to pay off the balance before the 0% period ends avoids the 22% rate, so she gets the benefit of the offer without the cost.

options.t: Ignore the end date of the offer and keep on spending
options.why: Ignoring the end date risks owing a big balance at 22% APR, which can erase any benefit of the promotion.

options.t: Make no payments until the offer ends in twelve months
options.why: Not paying anything for a year wastes the 0% window, and late payments or missing minimums can cancel the promotional rate.

q: What is a credit utilization ratio?

options.t: The fee for a card that you pay each year
options.why: An annual fee is a yearly charge for holding the card, while utilization compares your balance to your credit limit.

options.t: The number of cards you own on the credit report
options.why: The number of cards you own is a different credit factor; utilization measures how much of your available limit you are using.

options.t: The share of available credit you are using
options.why: Utilization = balances divided by total credit limits, and keeping it low, ideally below 30%, helps your credit score.

options.t: The interest on a card that is charged monthly
options.why: Monthly interest is a cost of carrying a balance; the utilization ratio is a percentage of credit used, not a charge.

q: A person with a $1,000 deductible has a $4,000 covered car repair. How much does the insurer pay?

options.why: $5,000 adds the deductible to the repair cost; insurance pays the covered cost minus the deductible, so it cannot exceed the bill.
The insurer does not pay the full $4,000 because the policyholder pays the first $1,000 deductible out of pocket.
$1,000 is the deductible, which the driver pays, not the amount the insurer pays.
Insurer pays covered cost minus the deductible: $4,000 - $1,000 = $3,000, while the driver pays the $1,000 deductible.

q: Which insurance protects against losses from damage to your own car in an accident?

options.t: Life insurance
options.why: Life insurance pays a death benefit to beneficiaries and has nothing to do with repairing your car after an accident.

options.t: Collision coverage
options.why: Collision coverage pays to repair or replace your own car after a crash with another vehicle or object, regardless of who was at fault.

options.t: Health insurance
options.why: Health insurance covers medical expenses for illness or injury, not damage to a vehicle.

options.t: Renters insurance plan
options.why: Renters insurance covers belongings and liability in a rented home, not damage to your car in an accident.

q: A renter owns $15,000 of belongings. Which policy best protects them from theft or fire?

options.t: Renters insurance
options.why: Renters insurance covers a tenant's personal property against theft, fire, and other covered events, and often includes liability coverage as well.

options.t: Disability insurance
options.why: Disability insurance replaces income if you cannot work due to injury or illness; it does not cover stolen or burned possessions.

options.t: Auto insurance
options.why: Auto insurance protects a vehicle and driver liability, and a renter's household belongings inside the apartment are not covered by it.

options.t: Term life insurance
options.why: Term life insurance pays a death benefit to beneficiaries, not the replacement cost of belongings lost to theft or fire.

q: What does term life insurance provide?

options.t: Coverage for car damage and its repairs
options.why: Coverage for car damage and repairs is provided by auto insurance, not by a life insurance policy of any kind.

options.t: Income during retirement paid out each month
options.why: Retirement income comes from annuities, pensions, or Social Security; term life insurance pays only when the insured person dies.

options.t: A death benefit for a set number of years
options.why: Term life pays a death benefit to beneficiaries if the insured dies during a set term, such as 10, 20, or 30 years.

options.t: Lifetime investment growth with a cash value
options.why: Cash value and lifetime coverage belong to permanent policies such as whole life; term insurance has no cash value.

q: What is health insurance used for?

options.t: Paying property taxes owed
options.why: Property taxes are paid to local government and are not covered by health insurance, which handles medical expenses.

options.t: Paying for groceries each week
options.why: Groceries are everyday living costs; health insurance only helps pay medical bills such as doctor visits and hospital stays.

options.t: Paying part of medical costs
options.why: Health insurance pays part of medical costs, with the insured sharing costs through premiums, deductibles, and copays.

options.t: Paying all costs, no deductible
options.why: Health insurance rarely pays everything; deductibles, copays, and coinsurance mean the insured still pays a share of costs.

q: Which choice usually lowers an insurance premium?

options.t: A higher deductible
options.why: A higher deductible means you carry more of each loss, so the insurer charges a lower premium in return.

options.t: More coverage added
options.why: Adding coverage increases what the insurer might pay out, so it normally raises the premium rather than lowering it.

options.t: A lower deductible
options.why: A lower deductible shifts more cost to the insurer, which typically raises the premium rather than lowering it.

options.t: More claims filed
options.why: Filing more claims marks a driver as higher risk, which tends to raise premiums at renewal rather than lower them.

q: What is a good way to protect against identity theft?

options.t: Ignore bank statements when they arrive in the mail
options.why: Ignoring bank statements lets fraud go unnoticed; reviewing statements is how you catch unauthorized charges early.

options.t: Share your passwords with friends and with family
options.why: Sharing passwords gives others access to your accounts and raises the chance of theft or misuse, even with trusted people.

options.t: Use one simple password everywhere, so it is never lost
options.why: One simple password reused everywhere means a single breach exposes every account, so reuse is a major security weakness.

options.t: Use strong, unique passwords and monitor accounts
options.why: Strong, unique passwords plus regular monitoring of accounts and credit reports help prevent and quickly catch identity theft.

q: A text says your account is locked and asks you to click a link and enter your password. What should you do?

options.t: Reply with your card number and your PIN code at once
options.why: Sending a card number and PIN to someone who texted you hands criminals what they need to commit fraud.

options.t: Contact the company using a trusted number or app
options.why: Contact the company through a number or app you already trust; unexpected texts like this are typical phishing attempts.

options.t: Forward it to friends and ask what they think of it
options.why: Forwarding a phishing message may spread it to others and does nothing to verify whether your account is really locked.

options.t: Click the link and enter your password before it locks
options.why: Clicking the link and entering a password sends your login to scammers, who built the urgency to rush you into acting.

q: What is liability insurance?

options.t: Coverage for harm or damage you cause to others
options.why: Liability insurance pays for injury or property damage you cause to others, and covers legal defense costs if you are sued.

options.t: Coverage for your own injuries only, none for others
options.why: Covering only your own injuries describes other policies; liability insurance protects others harmed by your actions.

options.t: A warranty on a product that you have recently bought
options.why: A warranty covers repair or replacement of a defective product, while liability insurance covers harm you cause to others.

options.t: A savings account for lawsuits that a firm may face
options.why: Insurance is a risk-sharing contract with an insurer, not a savings account that a firm sets aside for lawsuits.

q: Which is an example of self-insuring?

options.t: Ignoring risk completely and hoping nothing goes wrong
options.why: Ignoring a risk hoping nothing goes wrong is not self-insuring because there is no plan or funds set aside for a loss.

options.t: Borrowing at high interest to pay for every loss that occurs
options.why: Borrowing at high interest after each loss is costly and unplanned, unlike self-insuring, which relies on money saved beforehand.

options.t: Saving an emergency fund to cover small losses yourself
options.why: Self-insuring means setting aside your own money, such as an emergency fund, to pay for small, predictable losses instead of buying insurance.

options.t: Buying a full policy for every risk, however small
options.why: Buying a policy for every small risk transfers risk to an insurer, which is the opposite of self-insuring.

q: What does it mean to avoid a risk?

options.t: Accept it and plan to pay for any loss yourself
options.why: Accepting a risk and planning to pay for any loss yourself is risk retention, not risk avoidance.

options.t: Choose not to do the activity that creates it
options.why: Avoiding a risk means not doing the activity that creates it, such as not riding a motorcycle to avoid the chance of a crash.

options.t: Reduce its effects with safety steps and training
options.why: Using safety steps and training is risk reduction, which lowers the chance or size of a loss instead of eliminating the activity.

options.t: Buy a policy for it, so an insurer pays the loss
options.why: Buying insurance transfers the financial risk to an insurer, which is risk transfer rather than avoidance.

q: A driver causes an accident injuring another person. Which coverage most directly pays that person's medical bills?

options.t: Roadside assistance plan
options.why: Roadside assistance covers towing, jump-starts, and similar services for your own car, not medical bills of an injured person.

options.t: Comprehensive insurance
options.why: Comprehensive insurance covers non-collision damage to your own car, such as theft, fire, hail, or hitting an animal.

options.t: Collision coverage plan
options.why: Collision coverage pays for damage to your own vehicle, and it does not pay medical bills for another person you injured.

options.t: Bodily injury liability
options.why: Bodily injury liability pays medical costs and related claims for people you injure when you are at fault in an accident.

q: A student can earn $15 per hour at a café or $12 per hour with a $1.50 per hour tip average at a bookstore. Which pays more per hour on average?

options.t: The bookstore at $13.50, because tips are always higher
options.why: The bookstore pays $12 + $1.50 = $13.50 per hour, but that is less than the café's $15, and tips are not always higher.

options.t: They pay exactly the same per hour of work they do
options.why: The totals differ: the café pays $15 per hour while the bookstore averages $13.50, so the two jobs do not pay the same.

options.t: The bookstore at $12 plus extra benefits only, each hour
options.why: Even if benefits were counted, the question asks about pay per hour, and the bookstore's $13.50 is already below the café's $15.

options.t: The café at $15, because $12 plus $1.50 is only $13.50
options.why: Bookstore total is $12 + $1.50 = $13.50 per hour, which is less than the café's $15, so the café pays $1.50 more per hour.

q: Which document shows a worker's earnings and taxes for the whole year?

options.t: A W-2 form
options.why: A W-2 is issued by an employer after year end and shows total wages and taxes withheld for the full year.

options.t: A W-4 form
options.why: A W-4 is filled out by the employee to tell the employer how much tax to withhold; it does not report annual earnings.

options.t: A pay stub
options.why: A pay stub shows earnings and deductions for a single pay period, not the totals for the entire year.

options.t: A bank record
options.why: A bank record lists deposits and withdrawals, but it does not show gross earnings and taxes withheld the way a W-2 does.

q: Why do employers withhold income taxes from paychecks?

options.t: To pay the company's profits out to the owners each year
options.why: Withholding is taken from employee wages and sent to the government, not used to pay company profits to the owners.

options.t: To lower the employee's wage rate, so the firm pays less
options.why: Withholding does not change the wage rate; it simply sends part of the employee's earned pay to the tax authorities.

options.t: To pay part of the employee's tax bill during the year
options.why: Employers withhold income tax so employees pay part of their tax bill gradually during the year instead of in one lump sum.

options.t: To fund the employee's vacation and sick days at the firm
options.why: Vacation and sick days are employer benefits; withheld income tax goes to the government and not to those benefits.

q: A worker is paid $52,000 a year, biweekly. What is her gross pay per paycheck?

options.why: $1,000 is the weekly amount ($52,000 / 52), but biweekly pay comes every two weeks, so each check is double that.
Biweekly means 26 pay periods a year, so gross pay per check is $52,000 / 26 = $2,000 before taxes and deductions.
$4,333 is the monthly figure ($52,000 / 12), which does not match a biweekly pay schedule.
$26,000 is half a year's pay ($52,000 / 2), as if paid twice a year, not every two weeks.

q: What is a signing bonus?

options.t: A fee for starting work, paid by the new hire
options.why: A signing bonus is paid by the employer to the new hire, not a fee the new hire pays to start working.

options.t: A yearly tax refund from the state or city
options.why: A tax refund comes from the government after filing a return, whereas a signing bonus is paid by an employer.

options.t: A one-time payment offered to a new hire
options.why: A signing bonus is a one-time payment an employer offers to attract a new hire, often with conditions such as staying a certain time.

options.t: A monthly loan paid back to the employer
options.why: A signing bonus is a payment to the worker, not a loan to be repaid monthly to the employer.

q: Which action best helps a worker earn a promotion?

options.t: Doing the minimum amount of work that is asked of you
options.why: Doing only the minimum rarely shows initiative, and managers usually promote employees who go beyond basic expectations.

options.t: Arguing with supervisors about every decision they make
options.why: Arguing with supervisors about every decision damages working relationships and makes promotion less likely.

options.t: Avoiding responsibility for any of the tasks you are given
options.why: Avoiding responsibility shows a lack of reliability, so employers are unlikely to trust such a worker with a higher position.

options.t: Consistently performing well and building new skills
options.why: Employers promote workers who consistently perform well and keep building new skills, since those workers show reliability and growth potential.

q: Two job offers pay $45,000. Offer A has a 6% employer retirement match; Offer B has none. About how much extra does A provide per year if the worker contributes 6%?

options.why: The match is 6% x $45,000 = $2,700 per year of extra compensation that Offer B does not provide to the worker.
$27,000 is ten times the correct amount; 6% of $45,000 is $2,700, not 60%.
Offer A provides a match and Offer B does not, so the difference cannot be zero when she contributes 6%.
$270 would be 0.6% of salary, a decimal slip; 6% of $45,000 is $2,700.

q: What is a union?

options.t: A government tax office that collects income tax from workers
options.why: The tax office is a government agency, while a union is an organization formed by workers themselves.

options.t: An organization of workers that bargains with employers
options.why: A union is an organization of workers that bargains collectively with employers over pay, benefits, and working conditions.

options.t: A company's marketing team that plans ads for its brands
options.why: A marketing team is a department inside a company that plans advertising, which is unrelated to workers' collective bargaining.

options.t: A type of bank that lends only to members of the public
options.why: A credit union lends to members, but a labor union is not a bank; it represents workers in negotiations with employers.

q: What does an employer's matching contribution to a 401(k) mean?

options.t: The employer deletes the account when pay is too low to match it
options.why: The employer does not delete the account; a match is extra money added when the employee contributes, not a penalty for low pay.

options.t: The employer adds money based on what the employee contributes
options.why: Employer matching means the company adds money to the employee's 401(k) based on the employee's contribution, often up to a stated percentage of pay.

options.t: The employer pays the employee's taxes for the whole year
options.why: Employer matching contributions go into the retirement account; they do not mean the employer pays the employee's yearly taxes.

options.t: The employer takes money from savings to pay its own bills
options.why: The match is added to the employee's retirement account by the employer, not taken from savings to cover the employer's bills.

q: A worker's hourly wage rises from $14 to $16. What is the percent increase?

options.t: About 2.0%
options.why: A 2% answer mistakes the $2 dollar raise for a percentage; the percent increase must be measured against the old wage.

options.t: About 20.0%
options.why: 20% would need a raise of $2.80 on $14, which is more than the actual $2 raise.

options.t: About 12.5%
options.why: 12.5% divides the $2 raise by the new wage of $16, but percent change must use the original wage as the base.

options.t: About 14.3%
options.why: Percent increase = ($16 - $14) / $14 = $2 / $14 = about 14.3%, using the original wage as the base.

q: What is a part-time job?

options.t: A job with no pay for the worker at all
options.why: A job with no pay is volunteering; part-time work is paid but involves fewer hours than a full-time job.

options.t: A job with exactly 60 hours each week of work
options.why: Sixty hours a week is more than a typical full-time schedule, so it is not part-time work.

options.t: A job with fewer hours than a full-time job
options.why: A part-time job has fewer hours than full-time work, often under 30 to 35 hours a week, and may offer fewer benefits.

options.t: A job for only one day a year, like a holiday
options.why: One day a year would be an occasional job, not part-time work, which involves regular weekly hours.

q: What does 'net income' mean for a self-employed person?

options.t: Business income left after business expenses
options.why: Net income is business revenue minus business expenses; it is the profit left for the owner before personal considerations.

options.t: Taxes paid on the business income that you earn
options.why: Taxes on business income are a cost the owner pays and do not define net income.

options.t: All sales before costs, the total money taken in
options.why: All sales before costs describes gross revenue, which is higher than net income.

options.t: Money borrowed from a bank to run the business
options.why: Borrowed money is a loan to be repaid, not income, and borrowing does not measure what the business earned.

q: A freelancer earns $60,000 in sales and has $18,000 in business expenses. What is the net business income?

options.why: $18,000 is the expense total, not what remains after expenses are subtracted from sales.
$60,000 is gross sales before expenses; net income subtracts the $18,000 of costs.
Net income = sales - expenses = $60,000 - $18,000 = $42,000 of business income before personal taxes.
$78,000 adds expenses to sales, but expenses must be subtracted to find net income.

q: What does an employer look for in a reference?

options.t: A person who can speak honestly about your work
options.why: A good reference is someone who knows your work and can speak honestly about your skills, reliability, and character to an employer.

options.t: A friend who does not know you well but is nice
options.why: A friend who barely knows you cannot give meaningful details about your work, so employers gain little from their opinion.

options.t: A stranger who has never met you or seen your work
options.why: A stranger has no knowledge of your work or character, so cannot serve as a reference to an employer.

options.t: A relative who will lie to make you look good
options.why: A relative who lies would hurt your credibility; employers want honest, informed references, usually from supervisors or teachers.

q: What is job satisfaction?

options.t: The number of coworkers on the staff team
options.why: The number of coworkers is a team-size fact and not a measure of how content a worker feels in the job.

options.t: The size of the office you work in each day
options.why: Office size describes the workplace, while job satisfaction measures how fulfilled a worker feels, regardless of space.

options.t: The distance to work from your home each day
options.why: Commute distance is a logistics factor that may influence satisfaction, but it is not what the term itself means.

options.t: How content a worker feels with their job
options.why: Job satisfaction is how content and fulfilled a worker feels about the job, influenced by pay, duties, coworkers, and growth.

q: A family spends $450 on groceries each month. They cut it by 10%. How much do they save per year?

options.why: $54 is 12% of $450, which does not match the 10% cut or the yearly total.
A 10% cut saves $45 a month ($450 x 0.10), and $45 x 12 months = $540 per year.
$450 is the entire monthly grocery bill, not the yearly savings from a 10% cut.
$45 is only the monthly savings; the question asks for the yearly figure, which is 12 times that.

q: What is a 'needs versus wants' decision about a cell phone plan?

options.t: Plans have no cost, so the choice is never a trade-off for anyone
options.why: Phone plans cost money, so choosing one always involves trade-offs between price and features.

options.t: Every plan is a want, so none of them can ever count as a need
options.why: Calling every plan a want ignores that basic phone service may be essential for work, school, or safety.

options.t: A basic plan may be a need while a premium unlimited plan may be a want
options.why: A basic plan may be a need for communication, while a premium unlimited plan with extras goes beyond what is necessary and is a want.

options.t: Every plan is a need at any price, since phones are essential to all of us
options.why: Not every plan is a need; a premium unlimited plan with extras goes beyond what is essential, so some plan features are wants.

q: Which is a variable expense?

options.t: Entertainment spending
options.why: Entertainment spending changes from month to month depending on choices, which makes it a variable expense.

options.t: Monthly rent payment
options.why: Monthly rent is usually the same amount each month, which makes it a fixed expense.

options.t: A fixed car loan payment
options.why: A fixed car loan payment is the same amount each month, so it is a fixed expense rather than variable.

options.t: Insurance premium bill
options.why: Insurance premiums are typically set amounts due on a schedule, so they are fixed rather than variable expenses.

q: A person's rent is $900, car payment $250, and insurance $100 monthly. Take-home pay is $2,400. What share of pay goes to these fixed costs?

options.t: About 25%
options.why: 25% would be about $600; fixed costs total $900 + $250 + $100 = $1,250, which is more than that.

options.t: About 100%
options.why: 100% would mean fixed costs equal all take-home pay, but they total $1,250 out of $2,400.

options.t: About 12%
options.why: 12% would be about $288, far below the $1,250 total of fixed monthly costs.

options.t: About 52%
options.why: Fixed costs are $900 + $250 + $100 = $1,250, and $1,250 / $2,400 = about 52% of take-home pay.

q: What is a bargain hunter's best approach?

options.t: Buy the most expensive item that you can find in the whole shop
options.why: The most expensive item is not necessarily the best; a smart shopper looks for value rather than the highest price.

options.t: Compare unit prices and quality, not just the sticker price
options.why: Comparing unit prices and quality lets a shopper find the best value, not just the lowest sticker price.

options.t: Buy without checking the price or the quality of the item
options.why: Buying without checking prices or quality risks overpaying and getting poor items, which is the opposite of bargain hunting.

options.t: Buy the cheapest item always, whatever its quality or use
options.why: Always buying the cheapest item can backfire if it breaks or doesn't do the job, so quality and use matter too.

q: What is the cost of 'convenience' purchases?

options.t: Always better value than anything else
options.why: Convenience items often cost more than comparable ones, so they are not always better value than other options.

options.t: Always lower than all other options
options.why: Convenience items such as pre-cut food or delivery frequently cost more than alternatives, so they are not always cheaper.

options.t: Free of any fees or extra charges at all
options.why: Convenience purchases often carry delivery or service fees and higher markups, so they are not free of extra charges.

options.t: Often a higher price for saving time
options.why: Convenience purchases, such as ready-made meals or delivery, often charge a premium for saving the buyer's time or effort.

q: A shopper pays $4.50 daily for coffee on 250 workdays. How much does she spend in a year?

options.why: $450 equals only 100 days of $4.50 coffee, far fewer than the 250 workdays in the problem.
Yearly cost = $4.50 x 250 workdays = $1,125, which shows how small daily purchases add up over time.
$11,250 is ten times the correct total; $4.50 x 250 equals $1,125.
$112 corresponds to about 25 days of coffee, not 250 workdays, so it is far too low.

q: What is a shopping 'trade-off'?

options.t: Giving up one item to be able to buy another
options.why: A trade-off means giving up one thing to get another, such as skipping a new game to afford shoes, because resources are limited.

options.t: Returning all items that you bought last month
options.why: Returning items bought last month is a refund choice, not a trade-off, which is about choosing between alternatives.

options.t: Buying everything at once on one shopping trip
options.why: Buying everything at once ignores limited money; a trade-off arises exactly because you cannot afford every item.

options.t: Trading with friends only, swapping goods
options.why: A trade-off is not limited to swapping goods with friends; it is any choice that gives up one option for another.

q: What is the best way to avoid overdraft fees?

options.t: Ignore your balance and spend all that you please
options.why: Ignoring your balance and spending freely is the quickest way to trigger overdraft fees when payments exceed your funds.

options.t: Close your bank account and keep cash at home
options.why: Closing your account and holding cash gives up banking services and safety, and does not teach balance management.

options.t: Track your balance and set low-balance alerts
options.why: Tracking your balance and setting low-balance alerts helps you avoid spending more than you have, preventing overdraft fees.

options.t: Write checks without checking your balance first
options.why: Writing checks without checking the balance risks overdrafts and fees, since checks can bounce when funds are short.

q: A person has $250 left in a monthly budget for fun. She spends $80 on a concert, $60 on a game and $70 on dining. How much remains?

options.why: $210 is the total spent ($80 + $60 + $70), not the amount left over from the $250 budget.
Zero would mean all $250 was spent, but she spent only $210 of the budget.
$140 would be left only if she had spent $110; her three purchases total $210.
Spending is $80 + $60 + $70 = $210, so the budget remaining is $250 - $210 = $40.

q: What is a store loyalty program?

options.t: A return penalty charged by the store
options.why: A return penalty is a store policy fee, whereas a loyalty program gives rewards to repeat customers.

options.t: A fee to enter a store and look around
options.why: Stores don't charge people to enter; loyalty programs offer perks to encourage customers to come back.

options.t: A program that rewards repeat shoppers
options.why: A loyalty program rewards repeat shoppers with points, discounts, or special offers to keep them buying from the store.

options.t: A tax on frequent buyers added at the till
options.why: Loyalty programs reward frequent buyers; they do not tax them at the register.

q: Why compare insurance quotes before buying?

options.t: Prices for similar coverage can differ
options.why: Prices for similar coverage vary by insurer, so comparing quotes can help you find the same protection for less money.

options.t: All quotes are always identical in price
options.why: Quotes are not identical, because insurers weigh risk differently, which is the very reason comparing them is worthwhile.

options.t: Quotes are illegal in most of the states
options.why: Insurance quotes are legal and free to request, and shopping around is a standard consumer practice.

options.t: Quotes eliminate all risk for the buyer
options.why: A quote is just a price estimate; it cannot eliminate risk, which is why insurance is bought separately.

q: A coupon takes $10 off a purchase of $50 or more. A shopper has $46 in items and adds a $4 item to reach $50. Is this smart?

options.t: Yes always, because coupons are free money for the shopper too
options.why: Coupons are not free money; spending on an item you do not need can cancel the savings from the discount.

options.t: Yes, if she wants the item, since she pays $40 instead of $46
options.why: If she wants the item, buying it brings her total to $50, and after the $10 coupon she pays $40 instead of $46.

options.t: Yes, because she saves $50 on the whole purchase total
options.why: The coupon saves $10, not $50; $50 is the minimum purchase needed to qualify, not the savings.

options.t: No, because coupons never work in any store she visits
options.why: Coupons do work when their conditions are met, including at stores she visits, so saying they never work is false.

q: What does it mean to shop with a budget?

options.t: Avoid looking at prices while you shop in a store
options.why: Avoiding prices makes it hard to stay within a budget, because you cannot compare costs to the limit you set.

options.t: Spend all your money on the first things you see there
options.why: Spending all your money on the first things you see ignores budgeting and leaves nothing for other needs.

options.t: Buy whatever looks nice to you at the time in the shop
options.why: Buying whatever looks nice is impulse shopping, which tends to lead to overspending.

options.t: Set a spending limit before shopping and stick to it
options.why: Shopping with a budget means setting a spending limit beforehand and sticking to it so you spend on priorities, not impulses.

q: What is an installment plan?

options.t: Receiving a gift from a friend on a special day
options.why: A gift is given freely and is not paid for, whereas an installment plan involves scheduled payments for a purchase.

options.t: Paying everything at once, in a single lump sum now
options.why: Paying everything at once is a lump sum purchase, which is the opposite of an installment plan.

options.t: Paying for a purchase in several scheduled payments
options.why: An installment plan splits the price of a purchase into several scheduled payments, often with interest or fees added.

options.t: Not paying at all for the goods that you took home
options.why: Taking goods without paying is theft, whereas installment plans require full payment in scheduled amounts.

q: If you save $50 a month at 3% interest compounded yearly for 3 years, which is closest to the total?

options.t: About $1,855
options.why: Deposits total $50 x 36 = $1,800; adding about $55 of compound interest at 3% gives roughly $1,855 after 3 years.

options.t: About $2,500
options.why: $2,500 is far above what $1,800 in deposits plus a few dozen dollars of interest could reach at 3%.

options.t: About $1,000
options.why: $1,000 is below even the $1,800 she deposits, so it can't be the total after three years of saving.

options.t: $1,800 exactly
options.why: Deposits alone total $1,800, and interest at 3% adds some more, so the total is slightly above $1,800 and not exactly equal.

q: What is the benefit of an automatic transfer to savings?

options.t: It removes the need for any bank accounts at all
options.why: Automatic transfers still use bank accounts; they move money between your own accounts without manual effort.

options.t: It saves consistently without relying on willpower
options.why: Automatic transfers save consistently without needing willpower each month, so saving happens before you can spend the money.

options.t: It spends your savings before you can use them
options.why: Transfers move money into savings, which preserves it for later; they do not spend savings.

options.t: It increases fees on your savings account every year
options.why: An automatic transfer does not raise account fees; many savings accounts have no fees to begin with.

q: What does APY stand for?

options.t: Average payment year
options.why: APY is not about average payments; it measures the interest earned on a deposit over a year.

options.t: Annual payment yield
options.why: APY does not stand for a payment yield; it is a savings measure that includes compounding.

options.t: Annual percentage yield
options.why: APY stands for annual percentage yield, the real yearly return on savings after compounding is included, useful for comparing accounts.

options.t: Applied profit per year
options.why: APY is a standard banking term for annual percentage yield, not profit applied per year.

q: Which account is best for $5,000 you may need within a few days?

options.t: A single volatile stock held in a brokerage
options.why: A volatile stock can lose value quickly, so it is a poor place for money you may need within days.

options.t: A 5-year CD with early withdrawal penalties
options.why: A 5-year CD charges a penalty for early withdrawal, so it is a poor fit for money needed soon.

options.t: A long-term retirement fund of stocks and bonds
options.why: Retirement funds are meant for long-term growth and carry market risk and withdrawal limits, which does not suit short-term needs.

options.t: A savings or checking account with easy access
options.why: A savings or checking account offers easy access, insured safety, and no market risk for money you may need within days.

q: What does it mean to set a savings priority?

options.t: Save for everything equally with no plan or order
options.why: Saving for everything equally with no plan ignores that some goals matter more and deserve funding first.

options.t: Decide which goals matter most and fund them first
options.why: Setting a savings priority means deciding which goals matter most, such as an emergency fund, and funding them first.

options.t: Never save anything toward any goal in life at all
options.why: Never saving toward any goal is the opposite of setting priorities, since priorities guide where saved money goes.

options.t: Spend first, save later with whatever is left over
options.why: Spending first and saving what is left usually means little gets saved, whereas priorities direct savings before spending.

q: A saver has $3,000 and her monthly expenses are $1,500. How many months of expenses does she have saved?

options.t: 2 months
options.why: Months of expenses saved = $3,000 / $1,500 = 2 months, which is below the 3 to 6 months often recommended.

options.t: 0.5 months
options.why: 0.5 months comes from flipping the division ($1,500 / $3,000); the savings are larger than one month of expenses.

options.t: 6 months
options.why: Six months would need $9,000 in savings ($1,500 x 6), but she has only $3,000.

options.t: 1 month
options.why: One month would need only $1,500 in savings, but she has $3,000, which covers two months.

q: What is a savings bond?

options.t: A checking account that you use to pay bills from the bank
options.why: A checking account is a deposit account for paying bills, and a savings bond is a government security that earns interest.

options.t: A credit card that lets you borrow money up to a limit at a bank today
options.why: A credit card lets you borrow up to a limit, whereas a savings bond is a loan you make to the government.

options.t: A government debt security sold at a set value that earns interest
options.why: A savings bond is a government debt security bought at a set value that earns interest over time and is repaid at maturity.

options.t: A share of a company that is owned by the stock holders of a firm
options.why: A share of a company is stock, which represents ownership, while a savings bond is a government loan.

q: What is a good reason to keep savings separate from a checking account?

options.t: It reduces the temptation to spend it
options.why: Keeping savings in a separate account reduces the temptation to spend it and makes it easier to reach your goals.

options.t: It removes interest from your account
options.why: Savings accounts usually pay interest, so separate accounts don't remove interest; many checking accounts pay little or none.

options.t: It prevents deposits from a paycheck
options.why: A separate account does not stop paycheck deposits; you can direct part of your pay straight into it.

options.t: It increases fees on your own account
options.why: Separate accounts do not raise fees; many savings accounts have no fees if you meet minimum balance rules.

q: Why does a longer time horizon usually allow for more risk in saving for goals?

options.t: Banks guarantee all returns on long-term stocks
options.why: Banks do not guarantee stock returns; deposit insurance covers bank accounts, not market investments.

options.t: There is more time to recover from market dips
options.why: With a longer horizon, investments have more time to recover from market dips, so savers can accept more risk for goals far away.

options.t: Risk disappears over time for long-term savers
