options.why: Receipts, invoices, bank statements and other records support each deduction and income item. Keep them at least three years after filing in case of an audit.

options.t: Only the return itself
options.why: The return alone shows the claimed amounts but does not prove them. Supporting records are needed to back each figure in an audit.

q: A business buys equipment for $12,000 with a five-year life and no salvage value, using straight-line depreciation. What is the annual depreciation?

options.why: Straight-line depreciation with no salvage value is cost divided by life: $12,000 / 5 years = $2,400 per year, the same amount each year.
$1,200 would be correct for a ten-year life ($12,000 / 10). With a five-year life, the annual amount is $2,400.
$60,000 multiplies cost by life instead of dividing. Straight-line depreciation divides, so $12,000 / 5 = $2,400.
$12,000 is the full cost, which would be deducted all in one year. Straight-line spreads it over five years at $2,400 per year.

q: Equipment cost $20,000, has a salvage value of $2,000 and a 6-year life. What is straight-line annual depreciation?

options.why: $2,000 is the salvage value, not the yearly expense. Depreciation uses cost minus salvage, divided by life.
Straight-line depreciation = (cost - salvage) / life = ($20,000 - $2,000) / 6 = $3,000 per year. Salvage is excluded because it is not depreciated.
$18,000 is the depreciable base (cost minus salvage) before dividing by the six-year life. Dividing it by 6 gives $3,000 per year.
$3,333 divides the full cost of $20,000 by 6 and ignores salvage value. The correct figure subtracts $2,000 first, giving $3,000.

q: What is a tax loss carryforward?

options.t: Moving the loss over to a different company
options.why: A loss carryforward stays with the same taxpayer. Moving a loss to a different company is not how it works.

options.t: Paying tax on a loss that occurred last year
options.why: A loss does not create tax. Paying tax on last year's loss makes no sense, since losses reduce taxable income.

options.t: Ignoring the loss entirely in the future
options.why: Ignoring the loss would waste a tax benefit. A carryforward lets the taxpayer use it, rather than disregard it.

options.t: Using a loss to cut taxable income later
options.why: A net operating loss can be carried forward to later years to offset taxable income. This lowers future tax bills after a loss year.

q: Which is a reason to keep personal and business expenses separate for tax purposes?

options.t: It makes deductions easier to prove
options.why: Separate records make it easier to show which expenses are for the business, so deductions are supported and less likely to be disallowed in an audit.

options.t: It removes the need for receipts
options.why: Receipts are still needed to support deductions. Keeping accounts separate makes records clearer but does not remove the documentation requirement.

options.t: It increases taxes owed each year
options.why: Keeping expenses separate does not raise taxes. It supports valid deductions and keeps personal costs from being claimed by mistake.

options.t: It is never allowed by the IRS at all
options.why: The IRS does not forbid separate accounts. It actually encourages them, since mixing personal and business spending causes problems.

q: What is a tax return?

options.t: A refund check from the IRS or the state
options.why: A refund check is what the government may send after a return is processed. It is the result, not the tax return itself.

options.t: A form reporting income and tax owed
options.why: A tax return is a form filed with the IRS or state reporting income, deductions, credits and tax owed. It determines refund or balance due.

options.t: A bank statement of your deposits
options.why: A bank statement lists deposits and withdrawals. A tax return reports income and tax for the year to the government.

options.t: A list of the employer's yearly costs
options.why: A list of employer costs is an expense report. A personal tax return reports individual income and tax.

q: What is the main purpose of a Schedule C on an individual return?

options.t: Reporting charitable gifts made in a year
options.why: Charitable gifts are itemized on Schedule A. Schedule C is for business activity of a sole proprietor.

options.t: Reporting stock sales made in the tax year
options.why: Stock sales are reported on Form 8949 and Schedule D. Schedule C covers business income and expenses.

options.t: Reporting wages paid by an employer to a worker
options.why: Wages paid to a worker are reported by the employer on payroll forms such as W-2. Schedule C is for the owner's own business.

options.t: Reporting sole proprietorship profit or loss
options.why: Schedule C, Profit or Loss From Business, reports a sole proprietor's income and expenses. The net result flows to Form 1040.

q: What is accounting software used for?

options.t: Playing training videos for all new staff
options.why: Training videos are played with media or learning software. Accounting software is built for financial records and reports.

options.t: Editing employee photos for the website
options.why: Photo editing uses graphics software. Accounting software handles ledgers, invoices and financial statements, not images.

options.t: Recording transactions and building reports
options.why: Accounting software records transactions in a ledger and produces reports such as the income statement and balance sheet, saving time and cutting errors.

options.t: Designing company logos and printed brochures
options.why: Logo and brochure design uses design software. Accounting software focuses on financial data rather than graphics.

q: What is a spreadsheet?

options.t: A video editing tool for short films
options.why: Video editing tools are used for films. A spreadsheet works with numbers and text in cells, not video.

options.t: A letter-writing program for memos
options.why: A letter-writing program is a word processor. A spreadsheet organizes data in cells and performs calculations.

options.t: A website builder for small shops
options.why: Building websites uses web design tools. A spreadsheet is for calculating and organizing data.

options.t: A grid of rows and columns for data
options.why: A spreadsheet, such as Excel or Google Sheets, is a grid of rows and columns where data is stored and calculated with formulas.

q: In a spreadsheet, what is a formula?

options.t: A color theme for the whole spreadsheet
options.why: A color theme changes how the sheet looks. A formula performs calculations, so appearance settings are not formulas.

options.t: A column heading at the top of the sheet
options.why: A column heading labels the data below it. It does not calculate anything, so it is not a formula.

options.t: An expression that calculates from cells
options.why: A formula begins with an equals sign and calculates from cell values or functions, such as =A1+B1. It updates when the cells change.

options.t: A printed page border around the data
options.why: A printed page border is a print setting for appearance. It has nothing to do with calculation.

q: Which spreadsheet function adds a range of numbers?

options.t: MAX
options.why: MAX returns the largest value in a range. It does not add the values, so it cannot total the numbers.

options.t: SUM
options.why: SUM adds all the numbers in a range, as in =SUM(A1:A10). It is the standard function for totals.

options.t: COUNT
options.why: COUNT tells how many cells hold numbers but does not add their values. SUM is used for totals.

options.t: AVERAGE
options.why: AVERAGE adds the values and divides by how many there are. It returns the mean, not the total.

q: Which spreadsheet function finds the average of a range?

options.t: AVERAGE
options.why: AVERAGE returns the arithmetic mean of a range, as in =AVERAGE(B2:B10). It adds the numbers and divides by how many values there are.

options.t: SUM total
options.why: SUM total adds the values but does not divide by the count. It gives a total rather than the average.

options.t: MIN
options.why: MIN finds the smallest value in a range. It does not compute an average.

options.t: IF test
options.why: IF tests a condition and returns one result or another. It does not compute averages of ranges.

q: What does the formula =B2*C2 do?

options.t: Adds the cells B2 and C2
options.why: Adding cells would use a plus sign, as in =B2+C2. The asterisk is the multiplication operator.

options.t: Joins text in the two cells
options.why: Joining text uses the ampersand or CONCAT function. The asterisk multiplies numbers.

options.t: Multiplies cells B2 and C2
options.why: The asterisk multiplies, so =B2*C2 returns the product of the values in B2 and C2, such as quantity times price.

options.t: Divides cell B2 by cell C2
options.why: Division uses a forward slash, as in =B2/C2. The asterisk means multiplication.

q: What does the dollar sign in $A$1 do?

options.t: Locks the reference when the formula is copied
options.why: The dollar signs make an absolute reference. The cell address stays fixed when the formula is copied to other cells.

options.t: Adds a dollar to the value of the cell itself
options.why: The dollar sign in a reference does not change the value. It only fixes the column and row of the address.

options.t: Hides the cell when the formula is copied
options.why: The dollar signs do not hide the cell. They keep the reference from shifting when copied elsewhere.

options.t: Formats the cell as currency with a dollar sign
options.why: Currency formatting is applied through number formats. In a formula, the dollar signs create an absolute reference.

q: What would =IF(B2>1000,"High","Low") return when B2 is 1,500?

options.t: Low
options.why: Low is returned only when B2 is 1,000 or less. Here 1,500 is greater than 1,000, so the condition is true.

options.t: High
options.why: The test B2>1000 is true because 1,500 is greater than 1,000. IF returns the first result, "High".

options.t: An error
options.why: No error occurs. The formula is written correctly, and with B2 equal to 1,500 it returns a valid result.
The IF function returns one of the two quoted texts, not the cell value itself. Since the test is true, it gives "High".

q: What does a pivot table do?

options.t: Encrypts the workbook with a secret key
options.why: Encrypting a workbook is done through the file protection settings. A pivot table summarizes data and does not encrypt.

options.t: Deletes duplicate files from the disk
options.why: Removing duplicate files is a disk utility task. A pivot table summarizes data inside the workbook.

options.t: Prints checks for the accounts staff
options.why: Printing checks is a payroll or accounts payable task. Pivot tables analyze and summarize data instead.

options.t: Summarizes data by grouping and totaling
options.why: A pivot table groups data by categories and totals or averages the values, letting users summarize large lists quickly without writing formulas.

q: What is VLOOKUP used for?

options.t: Adding a list of numbers in a column
options.why: Adding a column of numbers is done with SUM. VLOOKUP looks up values in a table.

options.t: Finding a value in a table by key
options.why: VLOOKUP searches the first column of a table for a key and returns a related value from another column, such as a price for a product code.

options.t: Counting characters in a text cell
options.why: Counting characters in text uses the LEN function. VLOOKUP is for finding values in tables.

options.t: Rounding a number to the nearest ten
options.why: Rounding is done with ROUND. VLOOKUP does not change numbers and instead retrieves matching values.

q: Which spreadsheet feature helps catch typing errors in a cell that should only hold dates?

options.t: Data validation
options.why: Data validation restricts what can be entered in a cell, for example allowing only valid dates, and rejects bad input. This prevents typing errors.

options.t: Freeze panes
options.why: Freeze panes keeps rows or columns visible while scrolling. It does not check what is typed.

options.t: Page breaks
options.why: Page breaks control where printed pages split. They have no effect on what can be entered.

options.t: Cell colors
options.why: Cell colors change appearance only. They do not stop invalid entries like text in a date cell.

q: What is cloud-based accounting software?

options.t: Software that works only on paper
options.why: Cloud software is not paper-based. It runs on computers and is used through the internet, not on paper.

options.t: Software that only works when offline
options.why: Cloud software needs an internet connection to run. It does not work only when offline.

options.t: Software stored on one office desktop
options.why: Software stored on one desktop is a desktop installation. Cloud software is hosted remotely and reached over the internet.

options.t: Software run online on remote servers
options.why: Cloud-based accounting software is hosted on remote servers and used through a browser or app, so users access their books from any device.

q: Which is a benefit of cloud accounting?

options.t: It works with no internet connection
options.why: Cloud tools need an internet connection, so working with no connection is not a benefit. Offline access is limited.

options.t: It removes the need for any passwords overall
options.why: Cloud accounting still requires passwords and security controls. Removing passwords would be a risk, not a benefit.

options.t: Automatic updates and multi-device access
options.why: Cloud accounting updates automatically and lets users sign in from many devices. This convenience is a key benefit over locally installed software.

options.t: It guarantees no errors for the users
options.why: No software can guarantee error-free results. Users still make mistakes, and cloud tools only help reduce them.

q: What is a risk of cloud accounting?

options.t: Records cannot be backed up, as the provider holds them
options.why: Cloud providers usually back up data and offer recovery. Saying records cannot be backed up is incorrect.

options.t: It cannot print reports for the owners of the firm
options.why: Cloud accounting can print and export reports easily. Printing is not a limitation of this kind of software.

options.t: Reliance on internet access and provider security
options.why: Cloud accounting depends on internet access and the provider's security. An outage or breach can block access or expose records.

options.t: It cannot handle numbers of any size or type at all
options.why: Cloud accounting handles large numbers and all common data types well. Limits on number size are not a typical risk.

q: What is a database?

options.t: A tool for drawing charts, with no data storage
options.why: A tool for drawing charts is graphics software. A database stores and retrieves data, which charting tools lack.

options.t: An organized collection of searchable data
options.why: A database is an organized collection of data that can be searched, sorted and updated, such as customer or inventory records stored in tables.

options.t: A printed filing cabinet in an office
options.why: A printed filing cabinet is a paper filing system. A database is electronic and searchable.

options.t: A type of calculator used by the office staff
options.why: A calculator performs arithmetic. A database stores and retrieves organized information.

q: What is data entry?

options.t: Typing or importing data into a system
options.why: Data entry means typing or importing data into a system, such as keying invoices into accounting software. Accuracy here is important for reliable reports.

options.t: Deleting old files from the system
options.why: Deleting old files is data removal or cleanup. Data entry adds information to a system.

options.t: Printing statements for the clients
options.why: Printing statements is output work. Data entry puts information into the system.

options.t: Encrypting information so nobody reads it
options.why: Encrypting information is a security measure. Data entry is the act of inputting data.

q: What does backup mean?

options.t: Deleting old data from the system
options.why: Deleting old data is data removal. A backup is a copy kept for safety.

options.t: Updating software on the computers
options.why: Updating software is maintenance. Backups are copies of data, not changes to programs.

options.t: Encrypting a password so nobody can read it
options.why: Encrypting passwords is a security step. A backup is a stored copy of data.

options.t: A copy of data kept in case it is lost
options.why: A backup is a copy of data stored separately so it can be restored after loss, theft, failure or a cyberattack.

q: The 3-2-1 backup rule recommends:

options.t: 3 users, 2 passwords and 1 server
options.why: Users, passwords and servers are not what the rule counts. The 3-2-1 rule is about copies, media types and off-site storage.

options.t: 3 copies, 2 media types, 1 off-site
options.why: The 3-2-1 rule means keeping 3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy stored off-site. This protects against many failures.

options.t: Backing up every 3 hours for 2 days
options.why: The rule is not a schedule of hours or days. It describes how many copies, media and locations to keep.

options.t: 1 copy on each of 3 office computers
options.why: One copy on each of 3 office computers keeps everything in one place. The rule calls for different media and an off-site copy.

q: What is encryption?

options.t: Compressing data to save space on a disk
options.why: Compressing data reduces file size and is not a security step. Encryption scrambles data to keep it private.

options.t: Copying data to another drive for safety
options.why: Copying data to another drive is a backup. It does not scramble the data to protect it from others.

options.t: Deleting data after use to save disk space overall
options.why: Deleting data after use is data disposal. Encryption keeps data stored but unreadable without a key.

options.t: Scrambling data so only approved users read it
options.why: Encryption scrambles data using an algorithm and key, so only approved users with the key can read it. It protects data stored or sent.

q: What is multi-factor authentication?

options.t: Two or more proofs of identity to sign in
options.why: Multi-factor authentication requires two or more proofs of identity, such as a password plus a code sent to a phone, making stolen passwords alone useless.

options.t: Using one very long password forever
options.why: One long password is a single factor. Multi-factor authentication requires more than one type of proof.

options.t: Writing passwords on a note by the screen
options.why: Writing passwords by the screen is a bad habit that exposes them. It is not multi-factor authentication.

options.t: Sharing a login with a coworker at work
options.why: Sharing a login is unsafe and removes accountability. Multi-factor authentication adds more proof of identity.

q: Which is an example of strong password practice?

options.t: Reusing one password everywhere you go
options.why: Reusing one password across accounts is risky because a breach of one site exposes all the others.

options.t: Sharing passwords by email with the team
options.why: Emailing passwords can expose them to anyone who reads the message. Passwords should not be shared that way.

options.t: A long, unique passphrase for each account
options.why: A long, unique passphrase for each account resists guessing and limits damage if one site is breached. A password manager can help store them.

options.t: Using the company name as every password
options.why: A company name is easy to guess. Using it as every password is weak and exposes all accounts at once.

q: What is phishing?

options.t: A fake message that tricks you into sharing data
options.why: Phishing uses fake emails or messages that look genuine to trick people into giving passwords, account numbers or other sensitive data, or into clicking harmful links.

options.t: A way of backing up files to the cloud storage
options.why: Backing up files to the cloud is a data protection step, not an attack. Phishing is a scam that tricks users.

options.t: A type of spreadsheet formula that adds numbers
options.why: A spreadsheet formula adds numbers, but phishing is a fraud technique and has nothing to do with spreadsheets.

options.t: A virus that slows down computers at the office
options.why: A virus is malicious software. Phishing is a social engineering scam delivered by messages, not a program that slows computers.

q: An email from 'your bank' asks you to click a link and confirm your password. What should you do?

options.t: Click the link and enter your password now
options.why: Clicking the link and entering a password is exactly what phishers want. It would hand your login to criminals.

options.t: Forward the email to all of your coworkers
options.why: Forwarding the email spreads the threat to others. It should be reported to the IT team or the bank instead.

options.t: Do not click; call the bank on a known number
options.why: Banks do not ask for passwords by email. Do not click, and contact the bank using a phone number you already know to be real.

options.t: Reply with your password to the sender at once
options.why: Replying with a password gives it directly to a scammer. Legitimate banks never ask for passwords this way.

q: What is malware?

options.t: Software that speeds up a computer
options.why: Software that speeds up a computer is a utility or optimizer. Malware is harmful software designed to cause trouble.

options.t: A safe backup program for your files
options.why: A safe backup program protects files. Malware is malicious code that harms them.

options.t: A kind of accounting formula used daily
options.why: An accounting formula calculates numbers. Malware is malicious software that attacks systems.

options.t: Software built to damage or break in
options.why: Malware is malicious software, such as viruses, spyware and ransomware, built to damage systems, steal data or gain unauthorized access.

q: What is ransomware?

options.t: A software license for the office computers
options.why: A software license grants permission to use a program. Ransomware is a type of malicious software that demands payment.

options.t: Malware that locks data until a ransom is paid
options.why: Ransomware is malware that encrypts or locks a victim's data and demands a ransom payment to restore access. Backups are the best protection.

options.t: A tax filing tool used by small firms each year
options.why: A tax filing tool helps prepare returns. Ransomware is an attack that holds data hostage.

options.t: A bank loan program for small firms short of cash
options.why: A bank loan program provides credit. Ransomware is criminal software that extorts payment.

q: Which action best protects a business against ransomware?

options.t: Opening all email attachments you get
options.why: Opening every attachment is a common way ransomware spreads. Attachments from unknown senders should not be opened.

options.t: Turning off the firewall at work
options.why: Turning off the firewall removes a layer of protection and makes attacks easier. It increases the risk.

options.t: Paying any ransom right away to be safe
options.why: Paying a ransom does not guarantee data return and encourages more attacks. Backups and prevention are safer choices.

options.t: Offline backups and software updates
options.why: Offline backups allow restoring data without paying, and updates patch holes malware uses. Together they are strong protection.

q: What is a firewall?

options.t: A tool that controls network traffic
options.why: A firewall monitors and filters network traffic between a trusted network and outside networks, using rules to allow or block connections.

options.t: A tool for editing spreadsheet files
options.why: Editing spreadsheet files uses spreadsheet software. A firewall guards a network instead.

options.t: A type of invoice sent to a buyer
options.why: An invoice is a bill sent to a buyer. A firewall is a security tool and has nothing to do with billing.

options.t: A backup drive for all office files
options.why: A backup drive stores copies of files. A firewall controls network traffic and does not store backups.

q: What is an audit trail in accounting software?

options.t: A list of customer birthdays and ages
options.why: Customer birthdays and ages are customer data. An audit trail records changes to accounting data.

options.t: A plan for future audits of the firm
options.why: A plan for future audits is an audit program. The audit trail is a record of past actions in the software.

options.t: A log of who changed what and when
options.why: An audit trail logs who made each entry or change, what changed and when. It supports accountability, fraud detection and audits.

options.t: A path to the server room downstairs
options.why: A path to the server room is a physical route. An audit trail is an electronic log of activity.

q: Why should access to accounting software be limited by role?

options.t: To make the software run faster for all
options.why: Role-based access is about security, not speed. Limiting access does not make software run faster.

options.t: So users see only what their job needs
options.why: Limiting access by role means each user sees and changes only what their job needs. This reduces errors and fraud and protects confidential data.

options.t: To prevent updates to the software
options.why: Role-based access is not meant to stop updates. Its purpose is to limit who can see or change data.

options.t: To avoid paying for licenses each year
options.why: Limiting access does not change license costs. It is a security control that restricts what users can do.

q: A bookkeeper can create vendors, approve invoices and print checks in the same system. What is the main weakness?

options.t: Taxes will be higher for the whole business
options.why: Taxes are not affected by this weakness. The problem is control over fraud and errors, not tax cost.

options.t: The software will run slowly for all users
options.why: System speed is unrelated to who has which permissions. The issue is control, not performance.

options.t: No separation of duties, so fraud is easier
options.why: One person who can create vendors, approve invoices and print checks lacks separation of duties. That person could create fake vendors and pay themselves without detection.

options.t: Vendors will be paid late each and every month
options.why: Payment timing is not the concern. The weakness is that one person controls the whole process, making fraud easier.

q: What is electronic funds transfer (EFT)?

options.t: A paper check mailed to a vendor
options.why: A paper check mailed to a vendor is a physical payment. EFT moves money electronically.

options.t: A type of tax form for small firms
options.why: A tax form is a document. EFT is a method of moving money between accounts.

options.t: A cash deposit made in person at a bank
options.why: A cash deposit in person is not electronic. EFT moves funds between accounts without cash or paper.

options.t: Moving money between accounts online
options.why: Electronic funds transfer moves money between bank accounts online or through networks, as in direct deposit, ACH and wire payments. It is faster than paper checks.

q: What is direct deposit?

options.t: Paying wages into an employee's bank account
options.why: Direct deposit sends an employee's pay electronically into their bank account on payday. It is faster, safer and cheaper than paper checks.

options.t: Handing employees cash on payday in an envelope
options.why: Handing out cash in envelopes is a paper cash payroll method. Direct deposit sends pay electronically.

options.t: Paying wages in goods and gifts, not money
options.why: Paying in goods is payment in kind. Direct deposit moves money to a bank account.

options.t: Mailing paper checks to each employee by post
options.why: Mailed paper checks are a different payroll method. Direct deposit sends money electronically without paper.

q: What does ACH stand for in payments?

options.t: Accounting Cash Handler
options.why: This phrase is invented. ACH stands for Automated Clearing House, the network used for electronic bank transfers.

options.t: Automated Clearing House
options.why: ACH stands for Automated Clearing House, the US electronic network that processes batch payments such as payroll, bill payments and direct deposits.

options.t: Authorized Check Holder
options.why: This phrase is not what ACH means. The acronym refers to the electronic clearing network for payments.

options.t: Annual Credit History
options.why: Annual credit history is not related. ACH is the network banks use to move money electronically.

q: What is a point-of-sale (POS) system?

options.t: A system that records sales and updates inventory
options.why: A POS system records each sale at checkout, takes payment, and updates inventory in real time. It often feeds sales data to the accounting records.

options.t: A system for scheduling meetings and events
options.why: Scheduling meetings is done with calendar software. A POS system handles sales transactions.

options.t: A system for designing buildings and site plans overall
options.why: Designing buildings uses CAD software. A POS system processes sales at the register.

options.t: A system for payroll taxes only, not for sales
options.why: Payroll taxes are handled by payroll software. A POS system is for recording sales, not payroll only.

q: What is the benefit of integrating a POS system with accounting software?

options.t: Taxes are eliminated for the whole business
options.why: Integration cannot eliminate taxes. Taxes are still owed, though integration helps record sales tax correctly.

options.t: Customers pay lower prices at the register
options.why: Integration does not change prices charged to customers. It affects bookkeeping behind the scenes.

options.t: Inventory is never counted by the staff again
options.why: Physical counts are still needed to check records. Integration updates records but does not remove inventory counts.

options.t: Sales data flows into the books automatically
options.why: Integration sends sales data straight into the accounting records, saving manual entry, reducing errors and keeping the books current.

q: What is optical character recognition (OCR) used for in accounting?

options.t: Backing up files to a cloud drive each night
options.why: Backing up files is a storage task. OCR reads text from images.

options.t: Turning scanned documents into digital text
options.why: OCR converts scanned documents or images, such as receipts and invoices, into editable digital text, reducing manual typing and speeding data entry.

options.t: Encrypting email messages sent by staff
options.why: Encrypting email is done with security tools. OCR extracts text from scanned images.

options.t: Printing checks for the vendors we pay
options.why: Printing checks is done by check-printing software. OCR reads text from scanned documents.

q: What is an application programming interface (API) used for?

options.t: Counting inventory by hand each night
options.why: Counting inventory by hand is manual work. An API connects software systems so data moves between them.

options.t: Creating tax forms by hand each year
options.why: Creating tax forms by hand is manual work. An API links programs so they can exchange data.

options.t: Letting different programs share data
options.why: An API sets rules that let different programs exchange data, such as a bank feed sending transactions into accounting software.

options.t: Printing reports for the managers
options.why: Printing reports is a different output task. An API lets programs share data with each other.

q: What does automation do best for accounting teams?

options.t: Handles routine tasks so staff can analyze
options.why: Automation handles repetitive, rules-based tasks such as data entry and reconciliations, freeing accountants to focus on analysis, judgment and advising clients.

options.t: Guarantees perfect accuracy every time
options.why: No system gives perfect accuracy. Automation can repeat errors if the data or setup is wrong, so checking is needed.

options.t: Replaces ethics requirements for staff
options.why: Automation cannot replace ethics requirements. Accountants remain bound by professional standards whatever tools are used.

options.t: Eliminates the need for any review of the work
options.why: Automated work still needs review. Controls and oversight are needed to catch errors, so review is never eliminated.

q: Which type of task is easiest to automate?

options.t: Resolving an ethics dilemma at work
options.why: Ethics dilemmas require judgment and values. They cannot be automated by following simple rules.

options.t: Judging whether an estimate is reasonable
options.why: Judging whether an estimate is reasonable requires experience and professional judgment, so it is hard to automate.

options.t: Recurring invoices for the same amount
options.why: Recurring invoices for the same amount follow fixed rules and repeat on a schedule, so they are easy to automate.

options.t: Interviewing a new client in person
options.why: Interviewing a client in person requires human interaction and judgment. It cannot be automated easily.

q: Which statement about artificial intelligence in accounting is most accurate?

options.t: It is not affected by bad data in any way
options.why: AI is affected by bad data, since it learns from and processes the data it is given. Poor data can mean poor results.

options.t: It speeds routine work, but humans must review
options.why: AI can speed up routine accounting work, such as coding transactions, but humans must review its output because errors and bias can occur.

options.t: It makes human review unnecessary at all
options.why: Human review is still necessary. AI can make mistakes, so accountants must check the work and apply judgment.

options.t: It cannot be used for any accounting tasks overall
options.why: AI can be used for many accounting tasks, including data entry and anomaly detection. Saying it cannot be used is wrong.

q: What is the main risk of relying on AI-generated entries without review?

options.t: The software is illegal
options.why: AI software is legal to use. The risk of unreviewed entries is mistakes, not illegality of the software.

options.t: Taxes become optional
options.why: Taxes remain required regardless of AI. Unreviewed entries do not change tax obligations.

options.t: Backups stop working
options.why: Backups work independently of AI entries. The risk is about accuracy, not backups.

options.t: Errors may go unnoticed
options.why: Without human review, wrong entries can slip into the books unnoticed and flow into financial statements. Review is needed to catch mistakes.

q: What is blockchain in simple terms?

options.t: A shared digital ledger that is hard to alter
options.why: Blockchain is a shared digital ledger copied across many computers, with records linked in blocks and secured so they are very hard to change later.

options.t: A tax form for the state revenue agency yearly
options.why: A tax form is a government document. Blockchain is a technology for recording transactions.

options.t: A paper ledger kept in a safe at the bank
options.why: A paper ledger in a bank safe is a physical record. Blockchain is digital and shared.

options.t: A type of spreadsheet formula for totals only
options.why: Blockchain is not a spreadsheet formula. It is a distributed ledger technology used for recording transactions.

q: What is data analytics in accounting?

options.t: Typing entries faster with a keyboard
options.why: Typing entries faster is data entry skill. Data analytics examines data for insights.

options.t: Filing documents in cabinets by letter
options.why: Filing documents in cabinets is record keeping. Analytics is the study of data to find patterns.

options.t: Printing statements on paper for clients
options.why: Printing statements is a reporting output task. Analytics studies data to support decisions.

options.t: Examining data for patterns and decisions
options.why: Data analytics examines large sets of financial data to find patterns, trends and anomalies, helping accountants detect fraud, forecast and support decisions.

q: A dashboard in accounting software is used to:

options.t: Replace the general ledger with one screen
options.why: The general ledger remains the core record of every account, and a dashboard only summarizes its data, so it cannot replace the ledger.

options.t: Shows key figures and trends at a glance
options.why: A dashboard pulls figures such as cash, revenue and expenses into charts and gauges, so managers can spot trends and problems quickly without reading full reports.

options.t: Back up files to the cloud storage nightly
options.why: Cloud backups are a data protection task handled by backup software or IT settings, not the purpose of a dashboard, which only displays summarized information.

options.t: Enter journal entries for each sale
options.why: Journal entries are keyed into the journal or transaction screens, not the dashboard, which displays summarized results rather than being used for entering transactions.

q: What is a template in a spreadsheet?

options.t: A chart type only, nothing more
options.why: A chart is just one object built from spreadsheet data, whereas a template is a whole preformatted file that includes layout, formulas and styles.

options.t: A virus scanner for the files
options.why: Virus scanners are security software and have nothing to do with how a spreadsheet is laid out, so this describes a different tool entirely.

options.t: A preformatted file for reuse
options.why: A template is a preformatted file with set layouts, labels and formulas, so users can start new invoices, budgets or reports without rebuilding them each time.

options.t: A password for the workbook
options.why: A password protects a workbook from unwanted opening or editing, but it is a security setting, not a reusable preformatted starting file like a template.

q: Which chart type best shows how a total is divided into parts?

options.t: Histogram
options.why: A histogram shows how many values fall into numeric ranges, so it displays frequency distribution rather than how a whole is split into parts.

options.t: Line chart
options.why: A line chart connects points over time to show trends, so it suits changes across months but not the share each part takes of a total.

options.t: Scatter plot
options.why: A scatter plot shows the relationship between two numeric variables as dots, which helps find correlation but does not show parts of a whole.

options.t: Pie chart
options.why: A pie chart splits a circle into slices sized by percentage, so it shows how a total, such as expenses by category, divides into parts.

q: Which chart type best shows sales over twelve months?

options.t: Org chart
options.why: An org chart shows the reporting structure of people in a company, not numeric values such as monthly sales over a period of time.

options.t: Pie chart
options.why: A pie chart shows shares of one total at a single point in time, so it cannot display how sales moved month by month.

options.t: Line chart
options.why: A line chart plots values over time, so twelve monthly sales points joined by a line show rises, dips and trends clearly across the year.

options.t: Flow chart
options.why: A flow chart diagrams the steps of a process or decision, not numeric data, so it cannot display twelve months of sales figures.

q: A formula shows #DIV/0!. What is the most likely cause?

options.t: It divides by zero or an empty cell
options.why: #DIV/0! appears when a formula divides by zero or by a blank cell, which spreadsheets treat as zero, and fixing the divisor or using IF removes the error.

options.t: The cell has too many digits in it
options.why: Too many digits in a cell usually shows as ##### or scientific notation, not #DIV/0!, which is specifically a division by zero error.

options.t: The font is too small to read it
options.why: Font size affects how text looks on screen but never triggers a formula error code such as #DIV/0!, which comes from the calculation itself.

options.t: The file was not saved to the disk
options.why: Failing to save a file does not change how formulas calculate, so unsaved work cannot cause a #DIV/0! error in a cell.

q: A circular reference in a spreadsheet means:

options.t: The file is too large to be opened
options.why: File size may slow opening but is unrelated to formulas, whereas a circular reference is a formula problem where a cell depends on itself.

options.t: A formula refers back to its own cell
options.why: A circular reference occurs when a formula refers directly or indirectly to its own cell, such as =A1+1 typed in A1, which creates an endless loop and a warning.

options.t: The sheet contains a round pie chart
options.why: A pie chart is a visual object and has nothing to do with formula logic, while circular refers to the formula loop, not chart shape.

options.t: The workbook is password protected
options.why: Password protection limits who can open or edit a workbook, but it is an access setting and does not describe a formula referencing its own cell.

q: What is the purpose of version control for important accounting files?

options.t: To remove the need for backups, as old files stay
options.why: Version control does not replace backups, because saved versions can still be lost with the device, and good practice keeps both versions and backups.

options.t: To make files larger in size on the disk
options.why: The purpose of version control is not to make files bigger, and storing sensible versions of a file is done to protect work rather than to add size.

options.t: To track changes and avoid overwriting files
options.why: Version control records who changed what and when, keeps earlier versions, and prevents staff from accidentally overwriting each other's work in accounting files.

options.t: To hide changes from the auditors of the firm
options.why: Hiding changes from auditors would defeat the purpose, since version control creates a visible trail that auditors can review to confirm accuracy and integrity.

q: Which is the best way to dispose of old paper financial records containing account numbers?

options.t: Hand to anyone
options.why: Handing records to anyone could expose account numbers and enable identity theft or fraud, so confidential documents must go only to trusted secure disposal.

options.t: Shred them
options.why: Shredding destroys paper so account numbers cannot be read or reconstructed, which protects clients and the business from identity theft and meets privacy rules.

options.t: Leave in a bin
options.why: Papers left in a bin can be picked up by anyone, which exposes account numbers and risks fraud, so a bin is not secure disposal.

options.t: Toss in trash
options.why: Putting intact records in the trash lets anyone retrieve them and misuse the account numbers, which is why sensitive documents must be shredded first.

q: What does CPA stand for?

options.t: Corporate Planning Associate
options.why: Corporate Planning Associate is an invented title; CPA is a licensed credential and the letters do not stand for a planning job within a firm.

options.t: Certified Payroll Assistant
options.why: Payroll assistants are clerks who process pay, and CPA is not a payroll title, so Certified Payroll Assistant is not what the letters mean.

options.t: Chief Profit Analyst role
options.why: There is no accounting designation called Chief Profit Analyst, and the CPA letters refer to a state licensed accountant rather than an executive role.

options.t: Certified Public Accountant
options.why: CPA stands for Certified Public Accountant, a state licensed professional who passes the CPA exam and can audit financial statements, prepare taxes and give advice.

q: What does a bookkeeper mainly do?

options.t: Records daily transactions
options.why: A bookkeeper records daily transactions such as sales, purchases and payments in the books, which provides the basic data that accountants later summarize and analyze.

options.t: Audits public companies
options.why: Auditing public companies is done by licensed CPAs at audit firms, and it is more advanced than the daily recording work that a bookkeeper does.

options.t: Designs advertising campaigns
options.why: Designing advertising campaigns is a marketing or advertising job, which is unrelated to the recordkeeping duties of a bookkeeper.

options.t: Sets national tax laws
options.why: Tax laws are set by legislatures such as Congress, not by bookkeepers, whose job is to record transactions for an employer.

q: What does a tax preparer do?

options.t: Manages a warehouse for a firm
options.why: Managing a warehouse is a logistics or operations job, whereas a tax preparer works with clients' income records and filing forms.

options.t: Hires new employees for a firm
options.why: Hiring employees is a human resources function, and a tax preparer instead handles tax filings for individuals or businesses.

options.t: Sells insurance to families in town
options.why: Selling insurance requires a separate license and is a different career, while a tax preparer concentrates on completing returns correctly.

options.t: Prepares tax returns for clients
options.why: A tax preparer gathers income and deduction information and completes federal and state returns for clients, helping them file accurately and on time.

q: What does an auditor do?

options.t: Examines records for accuracy and compliance
options.why: An auditor examines financial records and controls to judge whether statements are accurate and follow rules, giving users confidence in the reported numbers.

options.t: Designs company logos and brand marks for firms
options.why: Designing logos and brand marks is the work of graphic designers, which has nothing to do with checking financial records.

options.t: Sells accounting software to small firms
options.why: Selling software is a sales role; auditors must stay independent and examine records rather than promote products to the firms they review.

options.t: Records every daily transaction in the books
options.why: Recording daily transactions is a bookkeeper's task, whereas an auditor reviews those records afterward to check their accuracy.

q: What does a payroll clerk do?

options.t: Designs products for a large factory
options.why: Designing products is the work of engineers and designers, while payroll clerks deal with employee pay records and calculations.

options.t: Files lawsuits against a firm in court
options.why: Filing lawsuits is done by attorneys, and a payroll clerk instead handles wages and deductions for employees.

options.t: Calculates and processes employee pay
options.why: A payroll clerk calculates hours, wages, taxes and deductions, then processes paychecks or deposits so employees are paid correctly and on time.

options.t: Sets the company's strategy for the year
options.why: Setting company strategy is the job of executives and the board, while a payroll clerk carries out routine pay processing.

q: What does an accounts payable clerk do?

options.t: Prepares the audit report for firms
options.why: Audit reports are prepared by auditors, who are independent of the clerks who process the bills of the company.

options.t: Processes and pays vendor bills
options.why: An accounts payable clerk checks vendor invoices, records them and schedules payment, so the firm pays what it owes accurately and on time.

options.t: Collects money from customers
options.why: Collecting money from customers is the work of accounts receivable, which handles amounts owed to the firm and not by it.

options.t: Recruits staff for the firm
options.why: Recruiting staff is a human resources job, and accounts payable clerks only process bills owed to vendors.

q: What does an accounts receivable clerk do?

options.t: Maintains the company's computers
options.why: Maintaining computers is an information technology job, while accounts receivable deals with money customers owe the firm.

options.t: Bills customers and tracks payments
options.why: An accounts receivable clerk sends invoices, records customer payments and follows up on late accounts so the firm collects the cash it is owed.

options.t: Sets prices for products in stores
options.why: Pricing decisions are made by managers or marketing staff, and receivable clerks do not set prices; they bill and collect.

options.t: Pays vendors and suppliers weekly
options.why: Paying vendors is the job of accounts payable, which handles what the firm owes, whereas receivable concerns money coming in from customers.

q: What is a controller?

options.t: A person who sells stocks and bonds for a firm
options.why: Selling stocks and bonds is the work of a broker, while a controller oversees accounting and financial reporting inside the company.

options.t: A machine that prints checks for staff
options.why: A check printer is a device, whereas a controller is a human accounting manager who supervises the staff and the financial statements.

options.t: A person who controls inventory stock only
options.why: Controlling inventory is a narrow operations task, but a controller oversees the whole accounting function, including reports and internal controls.

options.t: A senior accountant who oversees reporting
options.why: A controller is a senior accountant who manages the accounting department and ensures accurate financial reporting, budgets and internal controls, often reporting to the CFO.

q: What does CFO stand for?

options.t: Certified Finance Official
options.why: Certified Finance Official is not a real title, and CFO is the standard abbreviation for the top financial executive of a company.

options.t: Chief Funding Operator
options.why: Chief Funding Operator is invented; CFO means Chief Financial Officer, who oversees all of the firm's finance and accounting.

options.t: Chief Financial Officer
options.why: CFO stands for Chief Financial Officer, the senior executive responsible for financial planning, reporting, budgeting and managing the company's money and risk.

options.t: Company Fiscal Overseer
options.why: Company Fiscal Overseer sounds plausible but is not the standard meaning, because the C in CFO stands for Chief, an executive level.

q: Which career focuses on investigating financial crimes and fraud?

options.t: Forensic accountant
options.why: A forensic accountant investigates fraud, embezzlement and other financial crimes, often supporting legal cases by tracing money and examining records for evidence.

options.t: Billing clerk job
options.why: A billing clerk prepares invoices for customers, which is routine work and does not involve investigating financial crimes.

options.t: Retail till cashier
options.why: A retail cashier handles sales at the till and does not investigate crimes, so this job is unrelated to financial forensics.

options.t: Payroll clerk job
options.why: A payroll clerk processes employee pay, not criminal investigations, so this job does not concentrate on fraud cases.

q: Which career helps a business plan spending and measure results against budgets?

options.t: External auditor of firms
options.why: External auditors review a company's statements independently for outsiders and are not part of the internal planning of spending against budgets.

options.t: Tax preparer for firms
options.why: A tax preparer completes tax returns, which is a compliance task and not the work of planning spending against a budget.

options.t: Management accountant
options.why: A management accountant gathers cost and budget data for internal managers and compares actual results to plans, helping the business plan spending and control costs.

options.t: Bank teller at a branch
options.why: A bank teller handles customer deposits and withdrawals at a branch, which is unrelated to planning business spending or budgets.

q: What is the difference between a bookkeeper and an accountant?

options.t: Bookkeepers always earn more than accountants
options.why: Pay depends on experience, credentials and role, and bookkeepers generally earn less than accountants, so this claim is incorrect.

options.t: Accountants analyze data; bookkeepers record it
options.why: Bookkeepers record transactions day to day, while accountants analyze, interpret and report on that data and give advice, and so have broader duties.

options.t: Accountants only enter receipts into the books
options.why: Entering receipts is typical bookkeeper work, but accountants do more, such as analysis, tax planning and preparing statements.

options.t: There is no difference between them at all
options.why: The jobs overlap but differ in training, scope and responsibility, with accountants doing analysis and advice beyond the recording that bookkeepers do.

q: Which requirement is typically needed to become a licensed CPA?

options.t: Passing the CPA Examination
options.why: A state requires candidates to pass the Uniform CPA Examination, along with education and experience requirements, before it grants a CPA license.

options.t: Working as a bank teller
options.why: Working as a bank teller is not a licensing requirement, and CPA candidates need specific accounting education and supervised experience instead.

options.t: Owning a business for a year
options.why: Owning a business is not required for a CPA license, as states ask for coursework, an exam and supervised accounting experience.

options.t: Winning an election in a state
options.why: Winning an election has nothing to do with professional licensing, which a state board of accountancy grants after exam and education requirements are met.

q: Which exam do CPA candidates take?

options.t: The SAT college test
options.why: The SAT is a college admission test taken in high school and is not used for professional accounting licensure.

options.t: The law bar exam
options.why: The bar exam licenses lawyers, not accountants, so CPA candidates do not take it.

options.t: The Series 7 exam
options.why: The Series 7 exam licenses securities representatives who sell investments, which is a different field from public accounting.

options.t: The CPA Examination
options.why: CPA candidates take the Uniform CPA Examination, a multi-section test of auditing, business concepts, financial accounting and regulation that is required for licensure.

q: What does an Enrolled Agent (EA) specialize in?

options.t: Selling real estate to home buyers
options.why: Selling real estate requires a real estate license, which is a separate field from the tax work of an enrolled agent.

options.t: Auditing public companies for investors
options.why: Auditing public companies is done by CPAs, whereas enrolled agents focus on taxes and are not audit professionals.

options.t: Representing taxpayers before the IRS
options.why: An Enrolled Agent is a tax professional licensed by the IRS who can represent taxpayers in audits, appeals and collection matters before the IRS.

options.t: Managing payroll software for firms
options.why: Managing payroll software is an administrative or technical function, while the EA credential is about tax representation, not software.

q: What does CMA stand for in accounting?

options.t: Certified Management Accountant
options.why: CMA stands for Certified Management Accountant, a credential for professionals in internal accounting, budgeting, cost analysis and strategic planning inside organizations.

options.t: Certified Market Analyst title
options.why: Certified Market Analyst is not the accounting meaning, as the A in CMA refers to Accountant in management accounting.

options.t: Corporate Marketing Associate
options.why: Corporate Marketing Associate is a marketing term, and in accounting the CMA letters refer to a management accounting certification.

options.t: Chief Money Advisor at a bank
options.why: Chief Money Advisor is not a real credential, and CMA in accounting refers to a certification earned by passing an exam.

q: What does CIA stand for as an auditing credential?

options.t: Central Intelligence Agency
options.why: The Central Intelligence Agency is a government spy agency, but in auditing the CIA letters refer to a professional certification.

options.t: Certified Internal Auditor
options.why: CIA stands for Certified Internal Auditor, a credential from the Institute of Internal Auditors showing skill in risk, controls and internal audit work.

options.t: Chartered Investment Analyst
options.why: Chartered Investment Analyst is not the auditing credential, since the investment credential is the CFA and CIA is about auditors.

options.t: Certified Insurance Adjuster
options.why: Insurance adjusters evaluate claims, and the term certified insurance adjuster has nothing to do with auditing credentials.

q: Which workplace skill helps accountants explain results to non-accountants?

options.t: Using complex jargon
options.why: Heavy jargon confuses people without accounting training, so it makes results harder to understand, which is the opposite of what is needed.

options.t: Speaking quickly
options.why: Speaking quickly makes information harder to follow, and does nothing to help explain results clearly to non-accountants.

options.t: Keeping data secret
options.why: Keeping data secret blocks understanding, while accountants must share needed information appropriately, even though they protect confidential details.

options.t: Clear communication
options.why: Clear communication lets accountants turn numbers into plain explanations managers and clients can act on, so results and risks are understood and used.

q: Which of these is a typical entry-level accounting job?

options.t: Accounting clerk
options.why: An accounting clerk records transactions and handles basic tasks such as filing and data entry, which makes it a common entry-level position.

options.t: Finance chief
options.why: Finance chief is a top executive position that requires many years of experience, so it is not an entry-level job.

options.t: Controller of a firm
options.why: A controller is a senior manager over the accounting function, which takes years of experience to reach and is not an entry job.

options.t: Partner at a firm
options.why: Becoming a partner at a firm comes after many years of experience and advancement, so it is a senior position, not entry level.

q: What is continuing professional education (CPE)?

options.t: A school for retirees and older seniors
options.why: CPE is not a school for retirees; it is training that working professionals complete regularly to keep their knowledge up to date.

options.t: The first course taken in a college degree
options.why: The first course in a degree is introductory coursework, whereas CPE is taken after becoming licensed to stay current.

options.t: Ongoing training to keep a license current
options.why: CPE is ongoing training, often a required number of hours each year or period, that keeps a CPA license and skills current with changing rules.

options.t: A tax return filed by a person each year
options.why: A yearly tax return is a filing to the government and is not training, so it has nothing to do with continuing education.

q: Why do accountants need to keep up with changes in tax law?

options.t: Laws never change over the long years
options.why: Tax laws change often through new legislation, rulings and court decisions, so the claim that they never change is false.

options.t: Only clients need to know the rules
options.why: Accountants prepare and advise on returns, so they themselves must know the rules, because clients rely on their expertise.

options.t: It affects only large companies and owners
options.why: Tax rules affect individuals, small businesses and large companies alike, so this limits the reason to large firms wrongly.

options.t: Rules change and affect client returns
options.why: Tax rules are revised regularly, and accountants must follow current law to prepare correct returns, avoid penalties and give clients sound advice.

q: Which type of firm is known as one of the 'Big Four' accounting firms?

options.t: Walmart
options.why: Walmart is a retail chain, not an accounting firm, so it is not among the Big Four.

options.t: Deloitte
options.why: Deloitte is one of the Big Four, along with PwC, EY and KPMG, the largest professional services firms that audit most big companies.

options.t: Nike
options.why: Nike is a sportswear company and not a public accounting firm, so it is not one of the Big Four.

options.t: Apple
options.why: Apple makes electronics and is a client of auditors, rather than being an accounting firm itself.

q: What does an accounting career in government typically involve?

options.t: Only working for private firms
options.why: Government accountants work for public agencies, so saying they work only for private firms is the opposite of the actual situation.

options.t: Managing public funds and budgets
options.why: Government accountants track and report how public funds are collected and spent, prepare budgets and help keep agencies accountable to taxpayers.

options.t: Writing novels for a publisher
options.why: Writing novels is a publishing and writing career, and has nothing to do with accounting in a government agency.

options.t: Selling products to the public
options.why: Selling products to the public is a sales function, whereas government accountants oversee funds, budgets and financial reports.

q: What does a not-for-profit accountant focus on?

options.t: Avoiding all reports to donors and the state
options.why: Not-for-profits must report to donors, boards and the government, such as through IRS Form 990, so avoiding reports is not appropriate.

options.t: Selling shares of stock to investors
options.why: Not-for-profits do not sell shares of stock to investors, because they have no owners who receive profits.

options.t: Maximizing owner profits for dividends
options.why: Maximizing owner profits and dividends is a goal of for-profit firms, whereas nonprofits aim to serve a mission, not pay owners.

options.t: Tracking donations and how funds are used
options.why: A not-for-profit accountant records donations and grants and tracks how funds are spent, helping show donors and regulators that money supports the mission.

q: Which career path involves advising companies on mergers and valuing businesses?

options.t: Janitor of a large office building complex
options.why: A janitor cleans and maintains buildings, which is unrelated to advising on mergers or valuing businesses.

options.t: Mail clerk for a company's main offices
options.why: A mail clerk sorts and delivers mail, a routine clerical task, and does not advise on mergers or business valuation.

options.t: Financial analyst or valuation specialist
options.why: Financial analysts and valuation specialists study financial data to value firms and advise on mergers and acquisitions, using models and market information.

options.t: Cashier at a large retail store chain
options.why: A retail cashier processes customer sales at a register, which is not related to valuing companies or advising on mergers.

q: What is an internship?

options.t: Short-term work experience for learning
options.why: An internship is short-term work experience, often for students, that lets them learn on the job, build skills and make professional contacts.

options.t: A type of loan for students and interns
options.why: An internship is not a loan, since interns may earn pay or credit rather than borrow money, and it is unrelated to student financing.

options.t: A permanent management role with a salary
options.why: Internships are temporary and learning focused, not permanent management positions with a regular salary and long-term duties.

options.t: A tax form that interns must file each year
options.why: Interns generally receive standard wage forms like any employee, so an internship is not itself a tax form.

q: Why is networking important for a career in accounting?

options.t: It can lead to openings and advice
options.why: Networking builds relationships with professionals who may share job openings, advice and referrals, which can help in finding positions in accounting.

options.t: It guarantees promotion at once
options.why: Networking helps open doors but promotion depends on performance and opportunities, so it cannot guarantee a promotion.

options.t: It avoids the need for a resume
options.why: Employers still expect a resume even with connections, so networking does not remove the need to submit one.

options.t: It replaces the need for skills
options.why: Skills are needed for success, and networking can only lead to openings, so it cannot substitute for real ability.

q: Which document lists your education, skills and work experience for employers?

options.t: Ledger
options.why: A ledger is a book of accounts that records financial transactions, not a document describing a person's work history.

options.t: Budget
options.why: A budget is a plan for income and spending, and it does not list education or work experience for employers.

options.t: Resume
options.why: A resume summarizes your education, skills and work experience in a concise document to show employers why you qualify for a position.

options.t: Invoice
options.why: An invoice is a bill for goods or services sold, which has no role in presenting a job applicant's background.

q: What is the main purpose of a cover letter?

options.t: To list every job you had, with dates and bosses
options.why: Listing every job with dates and bosses is more like a work history or resume detail, and a cover letter is not meant to be a list.

options.t: To introduce yourself and show fit for the job
options.why: A cover letter introduces you, explains your interest and shows how your skills fit the specific job, and it supports your resume.

options.t: To request a loan from a local bank branch
options.why: Loan requests are made in a loan application with a lender, so this is not the purpose of a cover letter.

options.t: To report taxes to the state revenue office
options.why: Tax reports go to a government agency using tax forms, which has no connection to a job application cover letter.

q: During an interview, which behavior is most professional?

options.t: Checking your phone during the interview
options.why: Checking a phone during an interview shows a lack of attention and respect, so it makes a poor impression on an employer.

options.t: Interrupting the interviewer often
options.why: Interrupting an interviewer is rude and shows poor listening, so it harms your chances rather than showing professionalism.

options.t: Arriving late and only apologizing
options.why: Arriving late is unprofessional, and apologizing alone does not erase the poor impression that lateness makes on an employer.

options.t: Arriving on time and answering honestly
options.why: Arriving on time and answering honestly shows respect, reliability and integrity, which are qualities employers want, especially in accounting.

q: Which factor most often leads to higher accounting pay over time?

options.t: Avoiding training courses at work
options.why: Avoiding training holds back skills and growth, so it tends to limit pay rather than raise it over time.

options.t: Changing careers every year or two
options.why: Frequent career changes prevent building expertise and seniority, so they rarely produce steady increases in accounting pay.

options.t: Experience, credentials and specialty
options.why: More experience, advanced credentials like the CPA, and a valued specialty increase an accountant's skills and market value, which tends to raise pay over time.

options.t: Working fewer hours with no growth
options.why: Working fewer hours with no growth limits experience and advancement, so it does not usually lead to higher pay.

q: Which technology skill is most useful for modern accountants?

options.t: Spreadsheet and accounting software skill
options.why: Accountants use spreadsheets and accounting software every day to record, analyze and report data, so these skills are very useful in modern practice.

options.t: Photography and video editing skills
options.why: Photography and video editing are creative skills that may help in media jobs but are not central to accounting tasks.

options.t: Typing speed alone, as accountants type
options.why: Typing speed helps a little, but accountants need analysis and software skills, so typing alone is not the most useful skill.

options.t: Video game design and level building
options.why: Game design and level building are for the game industry and have little to do with accounting work.

q: Which factor best explains why accounting remains a stable career?

options.t: Software has removed all accounting needs for firms
options.why: Software automates routine tasks, but organizations still need accountants to interpret results, give advice and ensure compliance, so needs have not vanished.

options.t: Every organization keeps records and follows tax rules
options.why: Every organization needs financial records and must follow tax rules, so accountants are needed in good and bad economies, which makes the career stable.

options.t: Tax laws never change from one year to the next at all
options.why: Tax laws change often, and this creates ongoing demand for accountants to interpret them, so the claim that they never change is false.

options.t: Businesses no longer need any financial records to run
options.why: Businesses need financial records for taxes, lenders and decisions, so saying they no longer need records is incorrect.

q: A student likes solving puzzles and examining details to find mistakes. Which accounting career might fit best?

options.t: Delivery driver for a courier
options.why: A courier driver delivers packages and does not examine detailed records, so this job does not match a liking for finding mistakes.

options.t: Cashier at a shop checkout
options.why: A cashier handles customer payments at a checkout and does little detailed examination, so it does not match this interest.

options.t: Event planner for weddings
options.why: An event planner organizes social events, which is a creative and logistical job unrelated to finding errors in records.

options.t: Auditor or forensic accountant
options.why: Auditors and forensic accountants examine records closely to find errors or fraud, which suits someone who enjoys solving puzzles and noticing details.

q: A student enjoys helping families with their money and filing returns each spring. Which role fits best?

options.t: Tax preparer
options.why: A tax preparer helps families by gathering income information and filing their returns, which fits someone who enjoys helping with money in tax season.

options.t: External auditor
options.why: External auditors examine company statements for outsiders and do not usually help families file their individual returns.

options.t: Finance chief
options.why: Finance chief is a top executive role at a company, not a job that helps families file their yearly returns.

options.t: Cost accountant
options.why: Cost accountants study production costs inside a firm, which is not the same as helping individual families file returns.

q: What does a cost accountant analyze?

options.t: Customer satisfaction surveys from sales
options.why: Customer satisfaction surveys are marketing research data, whereas cost accountants study what it costs to make products and deliver services.

options.t: Employee birthdays and work start dates
options.why: Employee birthdays and start dates are human resources records and are not cost data for a cost accountant.

options.t: Public opinion polls on local politics
options.why: Public opinion polls measure political views, which are unrelated to analyzing costs inside a business.

options.t: The costs of producing goods or services
options.why: A cost accountant studies materials, labor and overhead to find what goods or services cost to produce, helping managers set prices and control spending.

q: What does a budget analyst do?

options.t: Sells insurance to families
options.why: Selling insurance is a separate licensed career, whereas a budget analyst works on an organization's spending plans.

options.t: Repairs plant equipment
options.why: Repairing equipment is a maintenance job, and budget analysts work with financial plans instead of machinery.

options.t: Plans and monitors spending
options.why: A budget analyst helps prepare budgets and monitors actual spending against them, so managers can control costs and meet financial goals.

options.t: Prints checks for vendors
options.why: Printing checks for vendors is an accounts payable task, which is unrelated to planning and monitoring budgets.

q: What does a credit analyst do?

options.t: Sets rates on savings accounts
options.why: Setting savings rates is a decision of bank management, and credit analysts study borrowers' ability to repay loans, not deposit rates.

options.t: Judges whether borrowers can repay
options.why: A credit analyst reviews financial statements and credit history to judge whether a person or business can repay a loan, helping lenders manage risk.

options.t: Prepares tax returns for clients
options.why: Preparing returns is the work of tax preparers, which is different from analyzing borrowers' ability to repay debts.

options.t: Audits public companies' books
options.why: Auditing public companies is the work of CPA auditors, while credit analysts evaluate the risk of lending.

q: What does a financial planner help clients do?

options.t: Run a school for young children in town
options.why: Running a school is an education career, which is unrelated to helping people manage their money and plan finances.

options.t: Operate factory machinery and train others
options.why: Operating machines and training others is an industrial job, and financial planners do not do this work for clients.

options.t: File lawsuits against banks and firms
options.why: Filing lawsuits is the work of attorneys, whereas financial planners give advice on managing money.

options.t: Plan savings, investing and retirement
options.why: A financial planner reviews a client's income, goals and risk, then helps plan savings, investments, insurance and retirement to reach long-term goals.

q: What is a resume reference?

options.t: A tax form that you file each year
options.why: A tax form is a government filing and has no connection to a reference that supports a job applicant.

options.t: Your grade report from your school
options.why: A grade report is an academic record, and it is different from a reference, who is a person.

options.t: A person who vouches for your skills
options.why: A reference is a person such as a former boss or teacher who can vouch for your skills, character and work habits when employers call.

options.t: A list of your hobbies and school clubs
options.why: A list of hobbies and clubs describes interests or activities, but a reference is a person who speaks about your abilities.

q: Why should you ask permission before listing someone as a reference?

options.t: Because the law requires it in every state
options.why: No law in every state requires you to ask permission, so this is not the reason; it is a matter of courtesy and good practice.

options.t: So they are ready to speak well of you
options.why: Asking permission means the person agrees and can prepare to give a positive, informed recommendation when an employer calls.

options.t: So they can write your resume for you
options.why: A reference does not write your resume, and the person only speaks about your skills and character when asked.

options.t: So they can pay your school fees for you
options.why: A reference has no duty to pay your school fees, because the role is only to vouch for your abilities.

q: Which professional organization could a high school student join to learn about business careers?

options.t: Future Business Leaders of America
options.why: FBLA, Future Business Leaders of America, helps students learn about business careers through competitions, leadership training and networking with professionals.

options.t: A fantasy sports league for students
options.why: A fantasy sports league is for entertainment and does not offer business career education or professional networking for students.

options.t: A video game clan for students online
options.why: A video game clan is a recreational group and is not a professional organization that teaches students about business careers.

options.t: A fan club for a sports team at school
options.why: A sports fan club supports a team and offers fun, but it does not teach students about business careers.

q: What is job shadowing?

options.t: Applying for a loan from a local bank
options.why: Applying for a loan is a banking transaction and has nothing to do with observing someone at their job.

options.t: Taking a test about the job itself
options.why: Job shadowing is observing a professional at work, and not a test, so it is not an assessment of knowledge.

options.t: Taking over the job for a whole week
options.why: Taking over a job is working it, whereas shadowing is only watching a professional for a short time to learn.

options.t: Following a professional to see the job
options.why: Job shadowing means following a professional at work for a day or more to see their tasks, so you can decide if the career fits.

q: Which is an example of a soft skill valued in accounting?

options.t: Teamwork
options.why: Teamwork is a soft skill, a personal ability for working well with others, which employers value in accounting where staff collaborate.

options.t: Reconciling
options.why: Reconciling is a technical accounting task of comparing records to find differences, not a soft skill about personal qualities.

options.t: Depreciation
options.why: Depreciation is a technical accounting method for spreading an asset's cost over its life, not a soft skill.

options.t: Formatting
options.why: Formatting is a technical task of arranging reports and spreadsheets, so it is a technical skill, not a soft skill.

q: Which is an example of a technical skill in accounting?

options.t: Listening to clients closely
options.why: Listening to clients is a soft interpersonal skill rather than a technical skill specific to accounting procedures.

options.t: Preparing a bank reconciliation
options.why: Preparing a bank reconciliation is a technical skill because it applies accounting procedures to compare the cash book with the bank statement.

options.t: Showing empathy, a soft skill
options.why: Empathy is explicitly a soft skill involving understanding people's feelings, so it is not a technical accounting skill.

options.t: Time management and teamwork
options.why: Time management and teamwork are soft skills that help in any job, rather than technical accounting procedures.

q: A new accountant notices a coworker repeatedly altering numbers. What is the most professional response?

options.t: Ignore it to avoid any trouble at all
options.why: Ignoring altered numbers allows possible fraud to continue and may make you complicit, which is unethical and unprofessional behavior.
