options.t: Post about it on social media online
options.why: Posting on social media exposes confidential information and harms people before facts are known, which is not the proper response.

options.t: Report it through the proper channel
options.why: Reporting through the proper channel, such as a supervisor, compliance office or hotline, follows ethics standards and protects the firm and its users.

options.t: Copy the practice yourself at work
options.why: Copying the practice would be unethical and possibly illegal, because altering records is falsification and fraud.

q: A client asks an accountant to hide income from the tax authority. The accountant should:

options.t: Help if the client pays you more money for it
options.why: Extra payment does not make hiding income lawful, and helping would be tax evasion, which exposes the accountant to penalties and loss of license.

options.t: Hide it but not tell anyone at the firm
options.why: Hiding income is illegal tax evasion whether or not coworkers know, and secrecy does not make it acceptable.

options.t: Refuse and explain the duty to report income
options.why: The accountant should refuse and explain that income must be reported, since professional ethics and law require honest returns.

options.t: Do it just this once and never again after
options.why: Even one instance of hiding income is tax fraud, so doing it once and stopping does not make it acceptable.

q: What is lifelong learning, and why does it matter in accounting?

options.t: Learning only when forced to by a boss or client
options.why: Learning only when forced is not lifelong learning, which is a voluntary habit of continuing to build skills throughout a career.

options.t: Stopping education after college is done
options.why: Stopping education after college leaves skills outdated, whereas accounting needs constant learning as rules and technology change.

options.t: Memorizing one set of rules forever and a day
options.why: Rules and standards change, so memorizing one set forever becomes outdated, whereas lifelong learning means continually updating knowledge.

options.t: Updating skills as rules and technology change
options.why: Lifelong learning means continually updating skills and knowledge, which matters in accounting because tax laws, standards and software keep changing.

q: Which career offers the chance to run your own accounting practice?

options.t: Self-employed accountant or preparer
options.why: Self-employed accountants and preparers can open their own practice, serve clients directly and set their own hours, fees and services.

options.t: Lifeguard at a large public pool
options.why: A lifeguard watches over swimmers at a pool, which is not a path to owning an accounting practice.

options.t: Mail carrier for the post office
options.why: A mail carrier works for the postal service, which is unrelated to starting an accounting business.

options.t: Assembly line worker building parts
options.why: An assembly line worker builds parts in a factory, which is a different field and not a way to run an accounting practice.

q: What does the monetary unit assumption say?

options.t: Money is the only thing that matters to a business owner
options.why: The assumption concerns how activity is measured in money, not whether money is the most important thing to a business owner.

options.t: Business activity can be measured and recorded in money terms
options.why: The monetary unit assumption says business activity can be expressed and recorded in money, such as US dollars, which lets different items be added together.

options.t: Every item must be recorded at its current market price each day
options.why: Recording items at current market value each day is not what this assumption says; the cost principle covers recording at original cost.

options.t: Currencies of countries may be added with no conversion
options.why: Adding different currencies without conversion would mix units, so statements must state amounts in a single currency, and this contradicts the assumption.

q: A firm values a loyal workforce highly, but no dollar amount can be measured. How is it treated in the accounts?

options.t: It is recorded as a large asset
options.why: A loyal workforce cannot be measured in dollars reliably, so it is not recorded as an asset on the balance sheet.

options.t: It is recorded as a liability
options.why: A liability is a debt owed, and loyal workers are not a debt, so recording them as a liability would be wrong.

options.t: It is recorded as revenue earned
options.why: Revenue comes from selling goods or services, and an item like worker loyalty does not earn revenue in itself.

options.t: It is not recorded as an asset
options.why: Because it cannot be measured objectively in money, workforce loyalty is not recorded as an asset, which follows the monetary unit assumption.

q: What is the time period assumption?

options.t: Each period must be exactly ten years long, and no period may be shorter
options.why: Reporting periods are usually a month, quarter or year, not ten years, and shorter periods are common so users can get timely information.

options.t: A business must report only once at closing, when the owner sells the firm
options.why: Reporting only at closing would deprive owners and lenders of timely information, so this contradicts the assumption.

options.t: A business's life is divided into periods such as months or years for reporting
options.why: The time period assumption divides the life of a business into artificial periods like months, quarters or years so results and position can be reported regularly.

options.t: All transactions are recorded on the same day each year, at the close of business
options.why: Transactions are recorded when they occur, not all on one date each year, so this is not what the assumption says.

q: What is the historical cost principle also called?

options.t: The cost principle
options.why: The historical cost principle is also called the cost principle, which says assets are recorded at the price paid when acquired.

options.t: Going concern idea
options.why: Going concern is the assumption that a business will keep operating, which is a different concept from recording at original cost.

options.t: The materiality idea
options.why: Materiality concerns whether an item is important enough to affect decisions, which is separate from recording assets at original cost.

options.t: The matching principle
options.why: The matching principle links expenses to the revenues they help earn in the same period, which is a different idea from cost.

q: A business buys a building for $200,000 and its market value later reaches $260,000. What is the building's recorded value under the cost principle?

options.why: The $230,000 figure is a made-up midpoint, and under the cost principle no averaging between cost and market value is used.
Under the cost principle, the building stays at its original purchase price of $200,000, and market increases are not recorded because they are not objective.
Market value of $260,000 is not recorded because the cost principle uses original cost, so unrealized increases in value are ignored in the accounts.
The $60,000 is the difference between market value ($260,000) and cost ($200,000), a gain that is not recorded, and it is not the building's value.

q: What is owner's capital?

options.t: Money the business owes to banks and other lenders
options.why: Money owed to banks and other lenders is a liability, a creditor claim, which is not owner's capital.

options.t: The value of sales for the year, as shown on the income report
options.why: Sales for the year are revenue shown on the income statement, which is a flow of income and not the owner's investment.

options.t: The cash held in a business bank account, not capital
options.why: Cash in a bank account is an asset, and the question asks about capital, which is the owner's claim on assets.

options.t: The owner's investment in the business plus earnings kept
options.why: Owner's capital is the owner's investment in the business plus profits kept in the business, which is the owner's claim on the assets.

q: What is drawing (withdrawals)?

options.t: Money borrowed from a bank by the business owner for use as a rule
options.why: Money borrowed from a bank is a liability, whereas drawing is something the owner takes out and reduces equity.

options.t: Money earned from customers for goods and services sold
options.why: Money earned from customers is revenue, which increases equity, but drawing is a withdrawal that reduces it.

options.t: Assets the owner takes out of the business for personal use
options.why: Drawing is when an owner takes cash or other assets out of the business for personal use, which reduces owner's equity and is not an expense.

options.t: Equipment bought by the business and added to assets
options.why: Equipment bought by the business is an asset purchase, and drawing is instead an owner withdrawal of assets.

q: The owner withdraws $500 in cash. What is the effect on the accounting equation?

options.t: Assets increase and liabilities increase by $500 each
options.why: A withdrawal reduces assets, and liabilities do not increase, so assets and liabilities do not rise by $500 each.

options.t: Assets and owner's equity both decrease by $500
options.why: A $500 cash withdrawal lowers cash, an asset, by $500 and lowers owner's equity by $500, so the accounting equation stays in balance.

options.t: Only expenses increase by $500 in the period
options.why: Drawings are not an expense, so expenses do not increase; the withdrawal reduces owner's equity directly through the drawing account.

options.t: Liabilities decrease by $500 in the same period
options.why: A withdrawal by the owner does not change what the business owes, so liabilities are unaffected by the $500 withdrawal.

q: What is a proprietorship's income statement item called 'cost of goods sold'?

options.t: The cost of merchandise that was sold
options.why: Cost of goods sold is the cost of the merchandise that was sold during the period, deducted from sales to compute gross profit.

options.t: The cost of rent for the whole year
options.why: Rent is an operating expense and is not part of cost of goods sold, which concerns the cost of items sold.

options.t: The price customers paid at checkout
options.why: What customers paid at checkout is the selling price, recorded as sales revenue, not the cost to the business.

options.t: The money owed to suppliers for goods
options.why: Money owed to suppliers is accounts payable, a liability, and is not the same as cost of goods sold.

q: What is merchandise inventory?

options.t: Money owed by customers for sales
options.why: Money owed by customers is accounts receivable, a separate asset from the goods held for sale.

options.t: Supplies used in an office daily
options.why: Supplies used in an office are consumed in operations rather than held for resale, so they are not merchandise inventory.

options.t: Goods a business holds for resale
options.why: Merchandise inventory is the goods a business holds to sell to customers, and it is a current asset on the balance sheet.

options.t: Equipment used in daily production
options.why: Equipment used in production is a long-term asset, and it is not held for resale, so it is not merchandise inventory.

q: Under the periodic inventory system, when is inventory updated in the records?

options.t: After every single sale that is made in the shop
options.why: Updating after every sale describes the perpetual system, whereas the periodic system updates inventory only after a count.

options.t: Only when the owner decides, whenever it suits them
options.why: Records follow set accounting policy, not the owner's whim, so updating whenever it suits does not describe the periodic system.

options.t: Never, because no physical count is made at all
options.why: The periodic system does rely on a physical count, so saying no count is made is false.

options.t: At the end of the period after a physical count
options.why: Under the periodic system, inventory is updated only at the end of the period after a physical count, which is then used to find cost of goods sold.

q: What is the perpetual inventory system?

options.t: A system that updates inventory records with each purchase and sale
options.why: The perpetual system updates inventory records continuously with each purchase and sale, so the balance is always current, usually through scanners and software.

options.t: A system that ignores purchases and only tracks the sales made
options.why: Ignoring purchases would leave inventory records incomplete, so tracking only sales does not describe a perpetual system.

options.t: A system that updates inventory records only once a year, after a count
options.why: Updating only once a year after a count describes the periodic system, which is the opposite of perpetual.

options.t: A system that records only cash sales made in stores each day
options.why: The perpetual system tracks all inventory movements, not just cash sales, so recording only cash sales does not describe it.

q: A store scans every sale and its stock records adjust instantly. Which system is this?

options.t: Cash basis accounting
options.why: Cash basis accounting records items when cash moves and has no relation to how inventory is tracked.

options.t: Perpetual inventory
options.why: Scanning each sale and updating stock records instantly is perpetual inventory, because the records are adjusted continuously with each transaction.

options.t: Double taxation
options.why: Double taxation refers to corporate profits taxed twice, which has no relation to tracking inventory.

options.t: Periodic inventory
options.why: The periodic system updates inventory only after a physical count at period end, so it does not adjust instantly with each sale.

q: What does FIFO stand for?

options.t: First income of owners
options.why: First income of owners is not an accounting term, because FIFO is an inventory costing method and has nothing to do with owner income.

options.t: First-in, first-out
options.why: FIFO stands for first-in, first-out, an inventory method that assumes the oldest goods bought are the first ones sold.

options.t: Fixed inventory, output
options.why: Fixed inventory, output is not a real phrase, and FIFO refers to the order in which inventory costs flow.

options.t: Final stock for owners
options.why: Final stock for owners is not an accounting term, because FIFO describes the assumed flow of inventory costs.

q: What does LIFO stand for?

options.t: Long-term stock order
options.why: Long-term stock order is not what LIFO means, which is an inventory costing assumption about which units are sold.

options.t: Lowest stock output
options.why: Lowest stock output is not an accounting term, because LIFO is about the order in which costs leave inventory.

options.t: Last-in, first-out
options.why: LIFO stands for last-in, first-out, an inventory method that assumes the newest goods purchased are the first ones sold.

options.t: Latest owner income
options.why: Latest owner income is not an accounting term, since LIFO is an inventory costing method, not a measure of income.

q: Purchases were 10 units at $5 then 10 units at $7. Ten units are sold. Under FIFO, what is cost of goods sold?

options.why: Under FIFO the oldest units are sold first, so the 10 units sold cost 10 x $5 = $50 as cost of goods sold.
$70 is 10 x $7, the cost of the newest units, which would be the LIFO cost of goods sold and not the FIFO cost.
$60 would be an average of $5 and $7 across 10 units, but FIFO uses the actual oldest cost of $5 per unit.
$120 is the total cost of all 20 units (10 x $5 + 10 x $7), but only 10 units were sold.

q: In a period of rising prices, which method usually reports the higher net income?

options.t: Equal
options.why: Methods do not produce equal income when prices rise, because they assign different costs to goods sold and so give different profits.

options.t: Neither
options.why: The methods differ in net income when prices rise, so one of them reports higher income, and saying neither does is not accurate.

options.t: LIFO
options.why: With rising prices LIFO charges the newest, higher costs to cost of goods sold, so it reports lower net income than FIFO.

options.t: FIFO
options.why: FIFO charges the oldest, lower costs to cost of goods sold when prices rise, which leaves higher gross profit and net income than LIFO.

q: What is the purpose of the adjusted trial balance?

options.t: To record daily sales in the general journal book
options.why: Daily sales are recorded in the journal, whereas the adjusted trial balance is prepared after the adjusting entries to test equality.

options.t: To list customers and their contact details too
options.why: Customer contact details are kept in a customer list or subsidiary records, not in a trial balance, which lists ledger accounts and balances.

options.t: To close temporary accounts at the end of the year overall
options.why: Closing temporary accounts is done by closing entries after the adjusted trial balance, so it is not the purpose of the trial balance itself.

options.t: To check that debits equal credits after adjustments
options.why: The adjusted trial balance lists all account balances after adjusting entries and confirms total debits equal total credits before financial statements are prepared.

q: Supplies on hand at year end are $300 and the supplies account shows $900. What adjustment amount is needed?

options.t: $1,200 to Supplies Expense
options.why: $1,200 is the total of $300 plus $900, but the adjustment is only the supplies used, so adding the two figures is wrong.

options.t: $300 to Supplies Expense
options.why: $300 is the supplies still on hand, which stays as an asset, so it is not the amount to expense.

options.t: $600 to Supplies Expense
options.why: The supplies account shows $900 and $300 remains, so $900 - $300 = $600 of supplies were used and is debited to Supplies Expense.

options.t: $900 to Supplies Expense
options.why: Expensing $900 would write off all supplies, but $300 is still on hand, so only the used portion is expensed.

q: What is accrued interest receivable?

options.t: Interest earned but not yet received
options.why: Accrued interest receivable is interest that has been earned but not yet received in cash, and it is recorded as an asset at period end.

options.t: Interest paid in advance by a firm
options.why: Interest paid in advance by a firm is a prepaid expense, which is the opposite of interest earned and not yet collected.

options.t: Interest that is never earned at all
options.why: Interest that is never earned would not be recorded, whereas accrued interest receivable has been earned and is expected to be collected.

options.t: Interest owed to a lender by a firm
options.why: Interest owed to a lender is interest payable, a liability, while receivable refers to interest the firm is owed.

q: A $6,000 note at 8% was held for 3 months by year end with no interest received. What interest should be accrued?

options.why: $12 is far too small, because interest = $6,000 x 8% x 3/12 = $120, and $12 mislocates a decimal point.
Interest is $6,000 x 8% x 3/12 = $120, which is recorded as accrued interest receivable and interest revenue.
$1,440 would use 3 months as 3 years or similar, which is wrong because the period is only a quarter of a year.
$480 is a full year of interest ($6,000 x 8%), but the note was held for only 3 months, so only one fourth applies.

q: What is the purpose of a post-closing trial balance?

options.t: To prepare reversing entries for the next period before closing
options.why: Reversing entries are optional and prepared after closing, at the start of the next period, so a post-closing trial balance is not a tool for preparing them.

options.t: To show net income for the full year of trading and sales
options.why: Net income is shown on the income statement, and the post-closing trial balance has only permanent accounts with no income figures.

options.t: To prove debits equal credits after closing entries are posted
options.why: The post-closing trial balance proves debits equal credits after closing entries, and it lists only permanent accounts with balances carried to the next period.

options.t: To record new sales made after the year end in the books
options.why: New sales after year end belong in the next period's journal, and the trial balance does not record transactions.

q: What is a bad debt expense adjustment?

options.t: An entry that records a cash sale at the counter
options.why: Recording a cash sale is a normal revenue entry and has nothing to do with estimating losses on uncollectible accounts.

options.t: An entry that pays a supplier in cash on time
options.why: Paying a supplier in cash reduces payables and cash, which is unrelated to adjusting for customers who will not pay.

options.t: An entry that closes revenue at the year end
options.why: Closing revenue is a closing entry made at period end, and a bad debt adjustment is a different type of entry.

options.t: An entry that estimates uncollectible receivables
options.why: A bad debt adjustment estimates the receivables that will not be collected, recording bad debts expense and an allowance so receivables and income are not overstated.

q: Which accounts are closed at the end of the period?

options.t: Accounts payable and the equipment
options.why: Accounts payable and equipment are permanent accounts, so they are kept open and carry their balances forward.

options.t: Revenue, expense and drawing accounts
options.why: Revenue, expense and drawing accounts are temporary accounts closed at period end so each new period starts at zero and the balances move into owner's equity.

options.t: Owner's capital and supplies accounts
options.why: Owner's capital and supplies are permanent accounts carried forward; capital is updated by closing but is not itself closed.

options.t: Cash and accounts receivable balances
options.why: Cash and accounts receivable are asset accounts that continue into the next period, so they are not closed.

q: What is a trade discount?

options.t: A reduction from a list price given to a buyer
options.why: A trade discount is a reduction from a list price given to a buyer, such as for volume or dealers, and is deducted before the invoice price is set.

options.t: A tax on trade between two countries each year
options.why: A tax on trade between countries is a tariff, which is a government charge and not a seller's price reduction.

options.t: A fee for shipping goods to a buyer by truck
options.why: Shipping fees are freight charges, which are separate from discounts that reduce the price.

options.t: A discount for paying early, taken off the invoice
options.why: A discount for early payment is a cash or sales discount, which differs from a trade discount applied to the list price.

q: An item lists at $400 with a 25% trade discount. What is the invoice price?

options.why: $100 is the amount of the discount (25% of $400), not the price the buyer pays after the discount.
$425 would add 25% to the price, but a discount reduces the price, so the invoice is lower than $400.
$375 subtracts only $25, which is not a 25% discount; 25% of $400 is $100, not $25.
The discount is $400 x 25% = $100, so the invoice price is $400 - $100 = $300.

q: What is a purchases return?

options.t: Goods sent back to a supplier for credit
options.why: A purchases return is goods sent back to a supplier for credit or refund, which reduces what the buyer owes.

options.t: Goods sent back by a customer to the seller
options.why: Goods sent back by a customer are a sales return from the seller's viewpoint, not a purchases return.

options.t: Goods sold at a discount to loyal buyers
options.why: Selling goods at a discount is a sales transaction, which is not a return of purchased goods.

options.t: Goods ordered from a supplier by a firm
options.why: Ordering goods from a supplier is a purchase order, not a return, which sends goods back.

q: What is a debit memorandum?

options.t: A tax form that a firm files with the government every year
options.why: A tax form filed with the government is unrelated to a debit memorandum, which is a notice between buyer and seller.

options.t: A notice from a buyer to a seller that a payable is being reduced
options.why: A debit memorandum is a notice from a buyer telling a seller that the buyer is reducing the payable, for example because of returned goods.

options.t: A receipt for payment that a seller gives to a buyer in a shop
options.why: A receipt confirms payment received, and a debit memo is instead a notice reducing an amount owed.

options.t: A bill sent by a seller to a buyer for goods that were delivered overall
options.why: A bill sent by a seller for goods delivered is an invoice, and a debit memorandum is a notice from the buyer.

q: A credit memorandum issued by a seller to a customer does what to the customer's balance?

options.t: It has no effect at all
options.why: A credit memorandum does have an effect, because it lowers the customer's balance for returns or allowances.

options.t: It cancels the account
options.why: A credit memo reduces the balance but does not cancel the whole account, unless the credit equals the full amount owed.

options.t: It reduces the amount owed
options.why: A credit memorandum from a seller reduces the amount the customer owes, such as for returned or damaged goods, and it reduces accounts receivable.

options.t: It increases the amount owed
options.why: A credit memo lowers the balance, so saying it increases the amount owed is the opposite of its effect.

q: What is days sales outstanding (DSO)?

options.t: The average number of days to collect receivables
options.why: Days sales outstanding measures the average number of days it takes to collect receivables after a credit sale, and a lower number shows faster collection.

options.t: The number of days in a fiscal year of trade
options.why: The number of days in a fiscal year is a calendar length, and DSO is a collection measure, not a count of days in a year.

options.t: The number of days a supplier waits to be paid overall
options.why: The days a supplier waits to be paid describes payables, but DSO is about how long customers take to pay the firm.

options.t: The number of days goods stay in stock there
options.why: Days goods remain in stock is days sales in inventory, which differs from DSO, a measure for receivables.

q: Receivables turnover is 12. About how many days does collection take using 360 days?

options.t: 60 days
options.why: 60 days would result from a turnover of 6 (360 / 6), not 12, so this uses the wrong number of turns.

options.t: 4,320 days
options.why: 4,320 is 12 x 360, which multiplies instead of dividing, while the collection period is 360 divided by turnover.

options.t: 30 days
options.why: Average collection days = 360 / 12 = 30 days, so receivables are collected about every 30 days.

options.t: 12 days
options.why: 12 is the turnover number itself (times per year), not days, so it does not convert to a number of days.

q: What is the allowance method's balance sheet effect?

options.t: Receivables are shown at double their value
options.why: The allowance method does not double receivables, since it subtracts expected losses to give a lower value.

options.t: Receivables are shown net of expected losses
options.why: The allowance method shows receivables net of expected uncollectible amounts, so the balance sheet reports the amount the firm expects to collect.

options.t: Receivables are shown only in cash form
options.why: Receivables are shown as amounts owed by customers, not just cash, and the allowance method does not change them into cash.

options.t: Receivables are removed entirely from the sheet
options.why: The allowance method reduces receivables by an estimate, but does not remove all receivables from the balance sheet.

q: What is retained earnings?

options.t: Cash held in a bank account by the business owner for use
options.why: Cash in a bank is an asset, whereas retained earnings is an equity account showing profits kept, and it may not exist as cash.

options.t: Money owed to creditors by the firm after the year end
options.why: Money owed to creditors is a liability, so it is not retained earnings, which belongs to owners' equity.

options.t: Total sales for the year, shown at the top of the statement overall
options.why: Total sales are revenue on the income statement, not retained earnings, which accumulate net income after dividends over time.

options.t: Accumulated profits kept in the business instead of paid out
options.why: Retained earnings are accumulated profits kept in the business rather than paid out as dividends, and they increase owners' equity over time.

q: A corporation starts with $50,000 retained earnings, earns $20,000 and pays $5,000 in dividends. What is the ending balance?

options.why: $35,000 incorrectly subtracts the earnings and adds nothing; the correct calculation adds net income, then subtracts dividends.
Ending retained earnings = $50,000 + $20,000 - $5,000 = $65,000, because net income increases it and dividends decrease it.
$75,000 ignores the dividends, since $50,000 + $20,000 = $70,000, and it still does not subtract $5,000.
$25,000 results from subtracting earnings and dividends from the starting balance, but earnings add to retained earnings.

q: What is a classified balance sheet?

options.t: A balance sheet printed in a special font, so that it is easy to read by the board
options.why: A classified balance sheet is about grouping accounts into categories, not font style or appearance.

options.t: A balance sheet with only assets and nothing about debts or owner equity
options.why: A balance sheet must show assets, liabilities and equity, so leaving out debts and owner equity does not describe a classified balance sheet.

options.t: A balance sheet that is kept secret from the owners and banks of the firm
options.why: Balance sheets are shared with owners, lenders and others, so keeping it secret is not what classified means.

options.t: A balance sheet that groups items into categories such as current and long-term
options.why: A classified balance sheet groups items into categories such as current assets, long-term assets, current liabilities and equity, which makes analysis easier.

q: What are intangible assets?

options.t: Money owed by customers for goods that were sold on credit
options.why: Money owed by customers is accounts receivable, a current asset, which is not an intangible asset.

options.t: Assets you can touch, such as machinery and delivery vehicles
options.why: Assets you can touch, such as machinery and vehicles, are tangible, so they are the opposite of intangible assets.

options.t: Assets without physical form, such as patents and trademarks
options.why: Intangible assets have no physical form but have value, such as patents, trademarks, copyrights and goodwill, and are usually amortized.

options.t: Cash in the bank, which is a current asset held by the firm
options.why: Cash is a current asset and a tangible financial asset, not an intangible one.

q: Which is an intangible asset?

options.t: A patent
options.why: A patent is an intangible asset, because it is a legal right to an invention and has no physical form.

options.t: Furniture
options.why: Furniture is a physical item and a long-term tangible asset, which makes it not intangible.

options.t: Inventory
options.why: Inventory is physical merchandise held for sale and is a current asset, not an intangible.

options.t: The truck
options.why: A truck is a physical long-term asset, so it is a tangible asset.

q: What is goodwill?

options.t: A fee paid to a bank for keeping the accounts of the whole firm in order
options.why: A fee paid to a bank for keeping accounts is a bank service charge, which is an expense and not goodwill.

options.t: The extra amount paid for a business above the value of its identifiable assets
options.why: Goodwill is the amount paid for a business above the fair value of its identifiable net assets, reflecting reputation, customer base and other intangible advantages.

options.t: The cash left after paying all the bills and debts of the firm at year end in the end
options.why: Cash left after paying bills is simply a cash balance, and it has no connection to the premium paid for a business.

options.t: A discount from a supplier for paying early on an invoice, off the price
options.why: A discount from a supplier for early payment is a purchase discount, which differs from goodwill, an asset.

q: What is earnings per share?

options.t: Total assets divided by liabilities, to show debt cover
options.why: Total assets divided by liabilities is a solvency ratio, but earnings per share concerns profit per share.

options.t: Sales divided by the costs for the whole year of trading
options.why: Sales divided by costs is a ratio of revenue to cost, not earnings per share, which is based on net income and share count.

options.t: Dividends divided by the price paid by the investors
options.why: Dividends divided by price is the dividend yield, which differs from earnings per share.

options.t: Net income divided by the number of shares outstanding
options.why: Earnings per share is net income divided by shares outstanding, showing how much profit is attributed to each share of common stock.

q: A company earns $600,000 and has 200,000 shares outstanding. What is its EPS?

options.why: $120,000 is not found by any valid calculation, and EPS is net income divided by shares, not a total.
$400,000 results from subtracting 200,000 from 600,000, but EPS divides net income by the number of shares.
EPS = $600,000 / 200,000 shares = $3.00 per share, which shows the profit that belongs to each share outstanding.
$0.33 is shares divided by income (200,000 / 600,000), which inverts the formula; EPS divides income by shares.

q: What does return on assets (ROA) measure?

options.t: How efficiently a company uses its assets to earn profit
options.why: ROA measures how efficiently a company uses its assets to produce profit, calculated as net income divided by total assets.

options.t: How much debt a company owes compared with owner capital
options.why: Debt compared with owner capital is the debt to equity ratio, which differs from ROA, a profitability measure.

options.t: How much cash a company has in the bank on each day
options.why: Cash on hand is measured by the cash balance or current ratio, and ROA is a profitability measure of assets.

options.t: How many shares exist in the market for the company
options.why: The number of shares in the market is a share count, and has no connection to return on assets.

q: Net income is $90,000 and total assets are $900,000. What is ROA?

options.why: 90% would use $90,000 over $100,000 or similar; the correct figure is $90,000 divided by $900,000, which is far smaller.
1,000% inverts the ratio ($900,000 / $90,000 = 10 times), but ROA is net income divided by assets.
1% comes from misplacing the decimal point, as $90,000 / $900,000 = 0.10, which is 10%, not 1%.
ROA = net income / total assets = $90,000 / $900,000 = 0.10, which is 10%, meaning each asset dollar earned ten cents.

q: What is revenue recognition's five-step idea based on?

options.t: Recording revenue when the check is printed by the accounting staff
options.why: Printing a check is an internal action and does not shift control of goods or services to the customer, so it does not trigger revenue.

options.t: Recording revenue only at year end, once all of the sales are known
options.why: Waiting until year end ignores when sales were earned, because revenue is recognized as obligations are satisfied during the period.

options.t: Recording revenue when control of goods or services passes to the customer
options.why: The five-step model recognizes revenue when control of promised goods or services passes to the customer, in the amount the company expects to receive.

options.t: Recording revenue when the order is first discussed with the customer every time
options.why: Discussing an order does not create revenue, because the company has not yet transferred goods or services to the customer.

q: What is a material misstatement?

options.t: A tiny typo with no effect on any reader's decision
options.why: A trivial typo that would not sway any reader is the definition of an immaterial item, which auditors and preparers can safely leave uncorrected.

options.t: An error large enough to change a reader's decisions
options.why: A misstatement is material when it is large enough that it could change the economic decisions of investors, lenders, or other users relying on the statements.

options.t: A late filing fee charged by the tax authority only
options.why: A late filing fee is a penalty assessed by a tax authority, not an error in the financial statements, so it says nothing about materiality.

options.t: A correct entry made on the right date and amount
options.why: A correct entry with the right date and amount is simply accurate bookkeeping, not a misstatement of any kind, material or otherwise.

q: A $5 rounding error in a $10 million statement is most likely:

options.t: Immaterial
options.why: A $5 error is only 0.00005% of $10 million, far too small to change any reader's decision, so it is immaterial and needs no correction.

options.t: Material
options.why: Material errors are large enough to influence decisions, often judged against a percentage of income or assets, and $5 against $10 million is nowhere near that.

options.t: Fraud case
options.why: Fraud requires intentional deception by someone, and a tiny rounding difference is a normal arithmetic artifact, not evidence of any deliberate wrongdoing.

options.t: A restatement
options.why: A restatement reissues prior statements to fix material errors, and a $5 rounding difference would never justify redoing a $10 million set of statements.

q: What is an internal audit?

options.t: A review by company staff of controls and records
options.why: An internal audit is performed by the company's own staff or department to evaluate internal controls, accuracy of records, and compliance, then report to management.

options.t: A review of competitors by the company staff
options.why: Studying competitors is market or competitive analysis done by marketing or strategy teams, and it has nothing to do with testing controls or records.

options.t: A review by the tax agency only, done every few years
options.why: A tax agency review is an external IRS or state audit; internal audits are performed by the company itself and are ongoing rather than occasional.

options.t: A review by customers of the products they bought
options.why: Customers reviewing products they bought is a satisfaction survey or product review, not an audit of the company's controls, records, or financial reporting.

q: What does separation of duties help prevent?

options.t: Interest costs
options.why: Interest costs come from borrowing money and the terms of debt, and splitting tasks among employees does nothing to lower or prevent them.

options.t: Fraud and errors
options.why: Dividing authorization, custody, and recordkeeping among different people means no single employee can hide theft or mistakes, so fraud and errors are prevented or caught.

options.t: Sales growth
options.why: Sales growth depends on marketing, pricing, and demand; separating duties is an internal control and does not directly influence how fast sales increase.

options.t: Tax bills owed
options.why: Tax bills depend on income and tax law, and assigning duties to different employees has no effect on how much tax the firm owes.

q: Which situation violates separation of duties?

options.t: One person orders and another pays, both checked
options.why: Having one person order and a different person pay, with both checked, is actually separation of duties working as intended, so it is not a violation.

options.t: Two people count the cash together each day at close
options.why: Two people counting cash together is dual control, a strong safeguard where each person checks the other, so it supports separation of duties rather than violating it.

options.t: A manager reviews all payments made each month
options.why: A manager reviewing all payments each month is an independent review, which strengthens controls and does not break separation of duties.

options.t: One person orders, receives and pays for supplies
options.why: When one person orders, receives, and pays for supplies, nobody checks that work, so they could order fake items and pay themselves, which is the core violation.

q: What is the Fair Credit Reporting Act's concern?

options.t: Stock prices on the exchange for all listed firms
options.why: Stock prices on the exchange are overseen by the SEC under securities laws, not by the FCRA, which concerns consumer credit reporting agencies.

options.t: Business tax rates set by the state for all firms
options.why: Business tax rates are set by state and federal tax law, while the Fair Credit Reporting Act regulates how consumer credit information is handled.

options.t: Accuracy and privacy of consumer credit information
options.why: The FCRA governs credit bureaus and users of credit reports, requiring accuracy, privacy, and giving consumers the right to dispute errors and see their reports.

options.t: Interest rates on savings offered by banks to depositors
options.why: Savings interest rates are set by banks and influenced by the Federal Reserve; the FCRA deals with consumer credit reports rather than deposit rates.

q: What is an EIN?

options.t: A tax refund code that the IRS gives to each filer who asks
options.why: Refunds are issued after a return is processed and have no special code assigned to filers by request; an EIN is a business identifier, not a refund code.

options.t: A customer ID number that a store gives to its regular buyers
options.why: A store's customer ID or loyalty number is a private marketing tool, whereas an EIN is a nine-digit tax identifier issued by the federal government.

options.t: A bank account number that is issued to the firm by its bank
options.why: Bank account numbers are assigned by banks to identify deposit accounts, while an EIN is assigned by the IRS and is used for tax reporting.

options.t: A federal Employer Identification Number issued to a business
options.why: An Employer Identification Number is a nine-digit number the IRS issues to identify a business for tax filing, payroll reporting, and opening business bank accounts.

q: Which business is most likely to need an EIN?

options.t: One that hires employees
options.why: Businesses with employees need an EIN to report payroll taxes, withhold income tax, and file employment forms such as Form 941 with the IRS.

options.t: A hobby with no income
options.why: A hobby with no income has no business tax filings, no employees, and no need for a separate federal employer number.

options.t: A person washing a car
options.why: A person occasionally washing a car as a casual sole proprietor with no employees can generally use their Social Security number, so no EIN is required.

options.t: A child selling lemonade
options.why: A child selling lemonade is a small casual activity without employees or formal tax reporting duties, so no EIN is needed for it.

q: What is Form 941 used for?

options.t: Reporting contractor payments to the IRS
options.why: Contractor payments are reported on Form 1099-NEC, while Form 941 covers wages and payroll tax withholding for employees, not independent contractors.

options.t: Individuals filing their yearly returns
options.why: Individuals file annual income tax returns on Form 1040; Form 941 is filed by employers rather than by individual taxpayers.

options.t: Employers reporting quarterly payroll taxes
options.why: Form 941 is the Employer's Quarterly Federal Tax Return, reporting wages paid, income tax withheld, and the Social Security and Medicare taxes owed each quarter.

options.t: Applying for a license to operate in a state
options.why: Licenses to operate come from state or local agencies, while Form 941 is a federal IRS payroll tax return filed by employers each quarter.

q: What is a W-9 form?

options.t: A form employees use to set withholding, given to payroll when hired
options.why: Employees use Form W-4 to tell payroll how much income tax to withhold, whereas Form W-9 is for independent contractors and vendors.

options.t: A form a contractor gives a business with their taxpayer information
options.why: Form W-9 is completed by a contractor or vendor to give the business their name, address, and taxpayer ID so a 1099 can be issued later.

options.t: A form for filing a return, used by each person who pays tax
options.why: Individual income tax returns are filed on Form 1040, while Form W-9 is only an information request and is never filed as a tax return.

options.t: A form showing yearly wages and all the taxes already withheld
options.why: Form W-2 shows an employee's annual wages and taxes withheld, issued by the employer, whereas W-9 collects taxpayer information from contractors.

q: A business pays a freelancer $4,000 in a year. Which form does it generally send the freelancer?

options.t: Form W-2 copy
options.why: Form W-2 is for employees who receive wages with taxes withheld, but a freelancer is an independent contractor who is not on payroll.

options.t: Form W-4 copy
options.why: Form W-4 is filled out by employees to set their withholding; a business does not send it to a freelancer.

options.t: Form 1099-NEC
options.why: Businesses generally send Form 1099-NEC to contractors paid $600 or more in a year, so a $4,000 payment to a freelancer triggers it.

options.t: Form 941 copy
options.why: Form 941 is the employer's quarterly payroll tax return filed with the IRS, not a form sent to a freelancer.

q: What is an estimated tax payment?

options.t: A guess about next year's tax law made by the revenue agency itself in the end
options.why: Tax agencies do not guess next year's law; estimated tax is a payment made by taxpayers themselves based on income they expect to earn.

options.t: A refund sent by the government to people who overpaid in the year
options.why: A refund returns overpaid tax to a taxpayer, which is the opposite of an estimated payment where a taxpayer sends money in advance.

options.t: A tax on estimates made by people who file their yearly returns
options.why: Estimated tax is not a separate tax on estimates; it is a way to prepay regular income and self-employment tax during the year.

options.t: A quarterly payment of expected income tax by people without withholding
options.why: Self-employed people and others without enough withholding pay expected income and self-employment tax in quarterly installments to the IRS to avoid underpayment penalties.

q: What is a sales tax permit?

options.t: Government permission for a seller to collect sales tax
options.why: A sales tax permit is issued by the state and lets a seller legally collect sales tax from customers and remit it to the government.

options.t: A refund of sales tax to the buyers who shop at the store
options.why: Sales tax permits do not produce refunds to shoppers; they authorize the seller to collect tax, which is then sent to the state.

options.t: A discount on sales tax for buyers who pay in cash
options.why: A permit does not discount tax for cash payers; buyers pay the legal rate whatever payment method they use.

options.t: A tax on permits that firms must pay each year to the state
options.why: A permit is not a tax on permits; it is an authorization, though some states charge a small fee to obtain one.

q: What is electronic invoicing?

options.t: Mailing invoices by post only, never online
options.why: Mailing paper invoices only is the traditional method that electronic invoicing replaces, so it is the opposite of sending digital invoices.

options.t: Sending and receiving invoices digitally
options.why: Electronic invoicing delivers invoices by email, portal, or software, which speeds delivery, lowers printing and postage costs, and makes tracking payments easier.

options.t: Printing invoices on colored paper sheets
options.why: Printing invoices on colored paper is a stationery choice and has no connection to creating or delivering invoices in digital form.

options.t: Hiding invoices from customers who owe us
options.why: Hiding invoices from customers would stop them from paying and is unethical; e-invoicing does the reverse by delivering bills promptly and visibly.

q: Which is a benefit of automated invoicing?

options.t: Fewer manual errors and faster collection
options.why: Automation reduces typing mistakes and sends invoices instantly with payment reminders, which speeds collection and improves cash flow for the business.

options.t: No record of invoices kept anywhere at all
options.why: Keeping no invoice records would break tax and audit requirements; automated systems actually store invoices electronically and make them easy to retrieve.

options.t: Slower payments from every single customer
options.why: Automation is designed to speed up billing and payment, so slower payments from every customer would be the opposite of its benefit.

options.t: More paperwork, as each invoice is printed
options.why: Automated invoicing cuts paper use by creating and sending invoices digitally, so adding printing and paperwork is the reverse of its benefit.

q: What is a digital signature?

options.t: A scanned drawing of a pet kept on a file server
options.why: A scanned drawing of a pet is just an image file; it cannot identify a signer or show that a document is authentic.

options.t: An electronic way to verify who signed a document
options.why: A digital signature uses encryption to verify the signer's identity and that the document was not altered, and it is legally recognized under laws like the ESIGN Act.

options.t: A printed name on a letter from a firm to a client
options.why: A printed name is only typed text on paper and does not authenticate who signed or prove the document is unchanged.

options.t: A password written on paper and kept in a safe
options.why: A written password on paper is a login credential, not a signature, and storing it in a safe does not verify any document.

q: What is data analytics software used for in accounting?

options.t: Typing letters and memos for the office staff each week
options.why: Typing letters and memos is word processing, a different task from analyzing financial data for patterns and risks.

options.t: Designing logos and brand materials for the firm each year overall
options.why: Designing logos and brand materials is graphic design work done with design tools, not data analytics software used by accountants.

options.t: Printing checks only, for the vendors that a firm pays
options.why: Printing checks is a payment function of accounting systems and is not what data analytics software is mainly built to do.

options.t: Finding patterns, trends and unusual items in financial data
options.why: Data analytics tools scan large sets of financial data for trends, patterns, and outliers, helping accountants detect fraud, forecast results, and support decisions.

q: An auditor uses software to scan all transactions for duplicate payments. What is this?

options.t: Inventory counting by hand each week
options.why: Counting inventory by hand is a physical, manual procedure and does not use software to scan every transaction for duplicates.

options.t: Price discrimination by sellers
options.why: Price discrimination is a pricing practice of charging different customers different prices and has nothing to do with auditing payments.

options.t: Data analytics for fraud detection
options.why: Scanning all transactions with software to find duplicate payments is data analytics used for fraud detection, covering the whole population rather than a small sample.

options.t: Manual sampling of a few items
options.why: Manual sampling checks only a few items by hand, which is the opposite of software that tests every transaction.

q: What is the CPA exam known for?

options.t: Testing typing speed and keyboard skills for office work
options.why: Typing speed is tested in clerical or office skills assessments, while the CPA exam tests accounting, auditing, tax, and business knowledge.

options.t: Testing accounting knowledge as part of becoming licensed
options.why: The Uniform CPA Exam tests accounting, auditing, taxation, and business concepts, and passing it is one step toward earning the CPA license.

options.t: Testing artistic talent and the ability to draw and paint
options.why: Artistic talent is judged in portfolios and art programs, which have no connection to the technical content of the CPA exam.

options.t: Testing sales skills and the ability to persuade shoppers
options.why: Sales and persuasion skills are tested in sales certifications and role-plays, not in the CPA exam, which is about accounting expertise.

q: A student likes analyzing budgets and advising managers on spending. Which role fits best?

options.t: Receptionist at a hotel front desk as a rule
options.why: A hotel receptionist greets guests, books rooms, and answers calls, which does not involve analyzing budgets or advising managers on spending.

options.t: Delivery driver for a courier firm
options.why: A delivery driver transports packages and follows routes, which does not involve budgets, financial analysis, or advice to managers.

options.t: Management accountant or budget analyst
options.why: Management accountants and budget analysts study spending, prepare budgets and forecasts, and advise managers on cost control, matching the student's interests exactly.

options.t: Retail cashier at a clothing store
options.why: A retail cashier processes sales and handles payments at the register, which does not involve analyzing budgets or advising managers.

q: A business buys office supplies for $300 cash. Which journal entry is correct?

options.t: Debit Cash $300; credit Supplies $300
options.why: This entry reverses the transaction by increasing Cash and decreasing Supplies, but paying cash for supplies lowers Cash and raises Supplies.

options.t: Debit Expense $300; credit Capital $300
options.why: Buying supplies is not an expense of capital; this entry wrongly credits Capital, which would imply the owner invested $300 rather than cash being spent.

options.t: Debit Payable $300; credit Cash $300
options.why: Debiting Payable would reduce a liability, but nothing was owed here because the purchase was paid for in cash on the spot.

options.t: Debit Supplies $300; credit Cash $300
options.why: Supplies is an asset that increases with a debit, and Cash is an asset that decreases with a credit, so both sides of the entry balance.

q: Which account type normally has a credit balance?

options.t: Revenue
options.why: Revenue accounts increase with credits, so they normally carry credit balances, which matches the equation where revenue raises owner's equity.

options.t: Expense
options.why: Expenses increase with debits and normally have debit balances because they reduce owner's equity.

options.t: Asset
options.why: Assets increase with debits, so they normally have debit balances, which is the opposite of a credit balance.

options.t: Drawing
options.why: The owner's drawing account reduces equity and increases with debits, so it has a normal debit balance.

q: A trial balance shows total debits of $48,500 and total credits of $47,900. What does this indicate?

options.t: Revenue exceeds expenses by about $1,000 net
options.why: The $600 gap is a mismatch in the trial balance, not a measure of net income, and revenue and expenses are not what is being compared.

options.t: An error exists that must be found and corrected
options.why: Debits must equal credits, so the $600 difference signals an error such as a transposition or omitted entry that must be located and corrected.

options.t: The business is profitable, as credits are near debits
options.why: Close totals do not show profit; a trial balance only checks that debits equal credits, and a $600 difference means something is wrong.

options.t: The books are in balance and all is well here
options.why: Debits of $48,500 and credits of $47,900 are not equal, so the books are not in balance and need correcting.

q: What is the purpose of posting from the journal to the ledger?

options.t: To prepare tax returns for the owners of the firm
options.why: Tax returns are prepared from the finished financial records; posting is an earlier bookkeeping step with no direct link to the owners' tax filings.

options.t: To record bank interest earned on the cash account overall
options.why: Bank interest earned is recorded as a transaction in the journal and posted to accounts; it is not the purpose of the posting step.

options.t: To sort transaction amounts into individual accounts
options.why: Posting copies journal entry amounts into the ledger accounts, grouping transactions by account so each account's balance can be determined.

options.t: To close the revenue accounts at the period end
options.why: Closing revenue accounts is done through closing entries at period end, which is a separate step from posting the journal to the ledger.

q: On December 31, a company has used $1,400 of prepaid insurance that was recorded as an asset. What adjusting entry is needed?

options.t: No entry is needed because the insurance was prepaid in advance
options.why: An adjusting entry is needed because part of the prepaid asset has been used up and must be recognized as an expense in the period.

options.t: Debit Cash $1,400 and credit Prepaid Insurance for $1,400
options.why: The prepaid insurance was already paid, so no Cash is received; debiting Cash would incorrectly increase the cash balance.

options.t: Debit Prepaid Insurance $1,400; credit Insurance Expense $1,400
options.why: This entry reverses the correct one, raising Prepaid Insurance and lowering expense, when used-up insurance should become an expense.

options.t: Debit Insurance Expense $1,400; credit Prepaid Insurance $1,400
options.why: As coverage is used, the asset becomes an expense: debit Insurance Expense and credit Prepaid Insurance for $1,400, matching expense to the period.

q: Which account is closed to Income Summary at the end of the period?

options.t: Service Revenue
options.why: Service Revenue is a temporary account that is closed to Income Summary at period end so its balance can be transferred to owner's equity.

options.t: Accounts Payable
options.why: Accounts Payable is a liability and a permanent account, so it carries its balance forward and is not closed to Income Summary.

options.t: Cash on hand
options.why: Cash is an asset and a permanent account; its balance carries into the next period rather than being closed out.

options.t: Equipment asset
options.why: Equipment is a permanent asset account that remains on the balance sheet, so it is not closed to Income Summary.

q: Revenues for the year are $82,000 and expenses are $61,500. What is the net income?

options.why: The $61,500 figure is the expense total only; net income subtracts expenses from revenue instead of reporting expenses alone.
Net income equals revenues minus expenses, so $82,000 - $61,500 = $20,500.
Adding revenue and expenses, $82,000 + $61,500 = $143,500, is incorrect because expenses must be subtracted from revenue to find income.
The $82,000 figure is total revenue before expenses are deducted, so it is not the net income.

q: What is accrual-basis accounting?

options.t: Recording only when cash changes hands, whatever the date
options.why: Recording only when cash changes hands describes cash-basis accounting, which is the opposite of the accrual method.

options.t: Recording only expenses and never any revenue at all
options.why: Accrual accounting records both revenues and expenses, not expenses alone, and it uses the matching principle to place them in the right period.

options.t: Recording revenue when earned and expenses when incurred
options.why: Under the accrual basis, revenue is recorded when earned and expenses when incurred, whatever the timing of cash, which matches income with the related costs.

options.t: Recording once per decade for each business year ahead
options.why: Accounting is done in regular periods like months, quarters, and years, and recording once per decade would provide no useful timely information.

q: A company earned $2,000 in service revenue in December but will not be paid until January. Under accrual accounting, when is the revenue recorded?

options.t: January cash
options.why: Cash timing does not drive accrual accounting, so waiting for the January cash receipt would mean using the cash basis rather than accrual.

options.t: Never
options.why: Earned revenue is always recorded in accrual accounting even if payment is delayed; it is booked as Accounts Receivable.

options.t: February
options.why: February has no tie to the service; revenue is recognized when it is earned, which was December when the work was done.

options.t: December
options.why: Under accrual accounting revenue is recorded when earned, so the $2,000 is recognized in December with a debit to Accounts Receivable and a credit to Service Revenue.

q: Which is the correct order of steps in the accounting cycle?

options.t: Journalize, post, trial balance, adjust, statements, close
options.why: The cycle runs from journalizing transactions, posting, preparing a trial balance, adjusting, preparing statements, and finally closing to prepare for the next period.

options.t: Close, journalize, post, adjust, then prepare statements overall
options.why: Closing cannot come first because closing entries need adjusted balances and finished statements, and transactions must be journalized before anything else.

options.t: Adjust, journalize, close, post, then prepare statements
options.why: Adjusting before journalizing makes no sense because there would be no recorded transactions to adjust, so this order is incorrect.

options.t: Statements, journalize, post, close, the reverse order
options.why: Starting with statements is impossible because statements are the output of the cycle and need journalized and posted data first.

q: What is a contra-asset account?

options.t: An account with a credit balance that reduces an asset
options.why: A contra-asset such as Accumulated Depreciation or Allowance for Doubtful Accounts has a credit balance and reduces the book value of a related asset.

options.t: An account used only for revenue items and sales
options.why: Revenue accounts record sales and income, while a contra-asset is paired with an asset to reduce it, such as accumulated depreciation.

options.t: An account with a debit balance that increases an asset
options.why: A debit balance that increases an asset describes an ordinary asset account; a contra-asset does the opposite with a credit balance.

options.t: An account that is always zero or has no activity
options.why: A contra-asset account has activity and a balance, such as the accumulated depreciation that grows each period, so it is not always zero.

q: Equipment cost $12,000 with a $2,000 salvage value and a 5-year life. What is annual straight-line depreciation?

options.why: The $12,000 figure is the original cost and ignores both salvage value and the five-year life, so it cannot be annual depreciation.
The $10,000 figure is the depreciable cost ($12,000 - $2,000), not yet divided by the five-year useful life.
The $2,400 figure divides the full cost without subtracting salvage value ($12,000 / 5), but straight-line uses cost minus salvage.
Straight-line depreciation is (cost - salvage) / life, so ($12,000 - $2,000) / 5 years = $2,000 per year.

q: Why are adjusting entries needed?

options.t: To increase the taxes owed by the firm and its owners at the year end
options.why: Adjusting entries match income and expenses to the right period, not to raise taxes, though accurate income may affect taxes.

options.t: To hide errors from the owners and the auditors of the firm for good
options.why: Adjusting entries correct period accounts openly for accuracy; hiding errors from owners or auditors would be fraud rather than proper accounting.

options.t: To update accounts so revenues and expenses are recorded in the proper period
options.why: Adjusting entries update accounts for accruals, deferrals, and depreciation so revenues and expenses appear in the period they belong to, following the matching principle.

options.t: To change prior years' books after the statements have all been issued as a rule
options.why: Prior-year books are not altered after statements are issued; adjusting entries are made at the end of the current period before the statements are prepared.

q: Wages of $900 have been earned by employees but will be paid next period. Which adjustment is needed?

options.t: Debit Cash $900 and credit Wages Expense $900
options.why: This entry wrongly debits Cash and credits Wages Expense, but no cash was paid and expense should be increased, not reduced.

options.t: Debit Wages Expense $900; credit Wages Payable $900
options.why: Earned but unpaid wages are an accrued expense, so debit Wages Expense $900 to record the cost and credit Wages Payable $900 for the liability.

options.t: Debit Wages Payable $900; credit Cash $900 next period
options.why: Debiting Wages Payable and crediting Cash is the entry made when the wages are paid next period, not the adjusting entry now.

options.t: No adjustment because no cash was paid out yet
options.why: Accrual accounting requires recording expenses when incurred, even if no cash has been paid, so an adjustment is needed here.

q: What does the post-closing trial balance contain?

options.t: Only the owner's name
options.why: The post-closing trial balance lists account balances, not names of owners, and it checks that debits equal credits after closing entries.

options.t: Only permanent accounts
options.why: After closing, temporary accounts have zero balances, so only permanent accounts such as assets, liabilities, and owner's capital remain on the post-closing trial balance.

options.t: No accounts at all remain
options.why: Permanent accounts still carry balances after closing, so the post-closing trial balance does contain accounts such as cash and equipment.

options.t: Only revenue accounts
options.why: Revenue accounts are temporary and are closed to zero, so they do not appear on the post-closing trial balance.

q: What is a work sheet used for in accounting?

options.t: To bill customers for the goods and services that the firm sold
options.why: Customers are billed with invoices; a work sheet is an internal accounting tool and is not sent to customers.

options.t: To file taxes with the state revenue office for the firm each year
options.why: State taxes are filed on tax forms and returns, whereas a work sheet is an informal tool and is not filed with the state.

options.t: To organize trial balance and adjustments before preparing statements
options.why: A work sheet lays out the trial balance, adjustments, and adjusted balances in columns, helping prepare the financial statements accurately and spot errors.

options.t: To record daily sales in the journal of the firm each day for the year
options.why: Daily sales are recorded in the journal as source documents come in, while the work sheet is only a period-end planning tool.

q: Total owner's equity at the start of the year was $50,000. Net income was $18,000 and the owner withdrew $6,000. What is ending equity?

options.why: Ending equity equals beginning equity plus net income minus withdrawals: $50,000 + $18,000 - $6,000 = $62,000.
The $26,000 figure does not start from the $50,000 beginning equity, so it ignores the owner's existing investment that carries forward into ending equity.
The $68,000 figure adds net income to beginning equity but forgets to subtract the $6,000 withdrawal, which reduces equity.
The $74,000 figure adds both net income and withdrawals to $50,000, but withdrawals reduce equity and must be subtracted.

q: A business sells $6,000 of goods on account with terms 2/10, n/30. What payment settles the invoice if paid on day 8?

options.why: The $6,120 figure adds the discount to the price instead of subtracting it, but a 2% discount lowers the amount the buyer owes.
The $6,000 figure is the full invoice and would be paid after the discount period; paying on day 8 earns the 2% discount.
The $5,400 figure takes a 10% reduction, but terms 2/10 mean 2% off, not 10%.
Paying within 10 days earns a 2% discount: $6,000 x 0.02 = $120, so the payment is $6,000 - $120 = $5,880.

q: Receivables total $80,000 and the company estimates 3% will be uncollectible. What is the bad debt estimate?

options.why: The $24,000 figure uses 30% rather than 3% of $80,000, so it overstates the estimate by a factor of ten.
Bad debt estimate = $80,000 x 3% = $2,400, the amount expected to be uncollectible and recorded in the allowance.
The $77,600 figure is receivables minus the estimate ($80,000 - $2,400), which is net realizable value rather than the bad debt estimate itself.
The $240 figure uses 0.3% instead of 3% of $80,000, putting the decimal in the wrong place.

q: What does an aging schedule show?

options.t: Product shelf life, how long it keeps fresh
options.why: Shelf life concerns how long goods stay fresh, which is a product feature and has no connection to accounts receivable aging reports.

options.t: Equipment age in years of use by the firm
options.why: Equipment age is tracked through depreciation records and asset registers rather than an aging schedule of customer accounts.

options.t: Employee ages in years on the payroll
options.why: Employee ages belong in human resources records, and an aging schedule lists customer balances rather than payroll data.

options.t: How long receivables have been outstanding
options.why: An aging schedule groups customer balances by how long they have been unpaid, such as 30, 60, or 90 days, helping estimate bad debts and guide collections.

q: What is the purpose of a purchase order?

options.t: To prove payment was made by the buyer to the vendor firm on time overall
options.why: Proof of payment comes from a receipt or canceled check, while a purchase order is issued before delivery to request goods.

options.t: To bill the buyer for goods after they have been delivered to it
options.why: Billing the buyer is done with a sales invoice from the vendor, and a purchase order is created by the buyer, not the seller.

options.t: To authorize a vendor to deliver goods or services at stated terms
options.why: A purchase order is issued by the buyer to a vendor, listing items, quantities, prices, and terms, and it authorizes the purchase before delivery.

options.t: To record wages paid to the staff members of the firm each month
options.why: Wages are recorded through payroll records and journal entries, while a purchase order concerns buying goods or services from vendors.

q: A customer's $500 account is written off under the allowance method. What is the effect on net accounts receivable?

options.t: No change
options.why: Under the allowance method, the write-off debits Allowance and credits Accounts Receivable, so net receivables stay the same because both fall by $500.

options.t: Falls by $500
options.why: Net receivables would fall only if expense were recorded at write-off; under the allowance method the estimate was already expensed earlier.

options.t: Rises by $500
options.why: A write-off removes an uncollectible account, so net receivables cannot rise from it.

options.t: Falls $1,000
options.why: The write-off is $500, not $1,000, and it leaves net accounts receivable unchanged since the allowance falls by the same amount.

q: What is a three-way match in accounts payable?

options.t: Matching three customers with three bills on the same day overall
options.why: Matching customers to bills on one day is not an accounts payable control; the three-way match deals with vendor documents.

options.t: Splitting a bill three ways among friends at a restaurant
options.why: Splitting a restaurant bill is a casual social arrangement and has nothing to do with accounts payable controls.

options.t: Comparing the purchase order, receiving report and invoice
options.why: A three-way match compares the purchase order, the receiving report, and the vendor invoice before payment to confirm what was ordered, received, and billed.

options.t: Paying three invoices at once with one single payment
options.why: Paying several invoices with one payment is a batch payment and does not describe the three document comparison called a three-way match.

q: A company has $40,000 in credit sales and collects $32,000 during the period. What is the ending change in accounts receivable?

options.t: An increase of $8,000
options.why: Receivables rise by credit sales and fall by collections, so $40,000 - $32,000 = an $8,000 increase in accounts receivable.

options.t: An increase of $72,000
options.why: The $72,000 figure adds sales and collections together, but collections reduce receivables and must be subtracted from credit sales.

options.t: A decrease of $8,000
options.why: A decrease would occur only if collections exceeded credit sales, but here $40,000 of sales exceeded $32,000 collected.

options.t: No change in sales
options.why: Sales and collections differ by $8,000, so receivables did change, even though the credit sales were not changed by the collections.

q: What is a credit memo from a seller?

options.t: A bill for new goods ordered by a customer
options.why: A bill for new goods is an invoice, whereas a credit memo lowers what a customer owes the seller.

options.t: A document reducing the amount a customer owes
options.why: A credit memo is issued by the seller to reduce a customer's balance, such as for returned or damaged goods or a pricing error.

options.t: A payment receipt issued by a seller to a buyer
options.why: A payment receipt confirms money received, while a credit memo reduces the amount owed without a payment being made.

options.t: A tax form that a seller files with the state
options.why: Sales tax returns are filed with the state, but a credit memo is a business document sent to a customer.

q: Which statement shows revenues and expenses for a period?

options.t: The cash flow statement
options.why: The cash flow statement shows cash inflows and outflows from operating, investing, and financing activities, not revenues and expenses.

options.t: The balance sheet
options.why: The balance sheet reports assets, liabilities, and equity at a single date rather than revenues and expenses over a period.

options.t: The trial balance
options.why: A trial balance lists account balances to check that debits equal credits and is not a formal financial statement of results.

options.t: The income statement
options.why: The income statement lists revenues and expenses for a period and shows net income or loss, measuring profitability.

q: Assets total $120,000 and liabilities total $45,000. What is owner's equity?

options.why: The $165,000 figure adds liabilities to assets, but equity is found by subtracting liabilities from assets.
The $45,000 figure is the liabilities total, which is the creditors' claim on assets and not the owner's claim.
The $120,000 figure is total assets, which equals liabilities plus equity, so it is not equity alone.
Using Assets = Liabilities + Equity, equity = $120,000 - $45,000 = $75,000.

q: On a classified balance sheet, which is a current asset?

options.t: Land and buildings
options.why: Land and buildings are long-term assets used for years, so they are reported as property, plant, and equipment rather than current assets.

options.t: A 10-year bank loan
options.why: A 10-year bank loan is a long-term liability, not an asset at all, and certainly not a current asset.

options.t: Accounts receivable
options.why: Accounts receivable are amounts owed by customers expected to be collected within a year, so they are a current asset.

options.t: Owner's capital stake
options.why: Owner's capital is an equity item on the balance sheet, not an asset, so it cannot be a current asset.

q: What does gross profit equal?

options.t: Net sales plus cost of goods sold
options.why: Adding cost of goods sold to sales would raise the number; gross profit is found by subtracting costs from sales.

options.t: Net sales minus cost of goods sold
options.why: Gross profit equals net sales minus cost of goods sold, showing what remains after paying for the goods to cover operating expenses.

options.t: Cost of goods sold minus expenses
options.why: Subtracting expenses from cost of goods sold does not produce any profit measure, since gross profit starts with net sales.

options.t: Net sales minus all the expenses
options.why: Net sales minus all expenses is closer to net income; gross profit subtracts only cost of goods sold.

q: Net sales are $200,000 and gross profit is $80,000. What is the cost of goods sold?

options.why: Gross profit = net sales - COGS, so COGS = $200,000 - $80,000 = $120,000.
The $80,000 figure is the gross profit, which is what remains after cost of goods sold is subtracted from sales.
The $280,000 figure adds gross profit to sales, but COGS is found by subtracting gross profit from sales.
The $200,000 figure is net sales, which is the starting point from which cost of goods sold is subtracted.

q: What is the current ratio?

options.t: Total assets divided by total sales for the year
options.why: Total assets divided by sales is an asset turnover type measure, not a liquidity ratio like the current ratio.

options.t: Current assets divided by current liabilities
options.why: The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities, measuring whether a firm can pay obligations due within a year.

options.t: Net income divided by the total owner equity
options.why: Net income divided by owner equity is return on equity, a profitability measure, not the current ratio.

options.t: Debt divided by total assets of the whole firm
options.why: Debt divided by total assets is the debt ratio, which measures leverage rather than short-term liquidity.

q: Current assets are $90,000 and current liabilities are $60,000. What is the current ratio?

options.why: The 150,000 figure adds the two amounts, but the current ratio divides current assets by current liabilities, producing a small ratio.
The 0.67 figure flips the fraction ($60,000 / $90,000), but current assets belong on top.
The 30,000 figure is the difference between the amounts, which is working capital, not a ratio.
Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities = $90,000 / $60,000 = 1.5, meaning $1.50 of liquid assets for each $1 owed.

q: Which statement explains changes in owner's equity during a period?

options.t: The monthly bank statement list
options.why: A bank statement lists deposits and withdrawals in the bank account and does not explain changes in owner's equity.

options.t: The payroll register of wages paid
options.why: A payroll register lists employee wages and withholdings and does not explain changes in owner's equity.
