options.t: The statement of owner's equity
options.why: The statement of owner's equity shows beginning capital plus investments and net income minus withdrawals, ending with the ending capital balance.

options.t: The aging schedule of accounts
options.why: An aging schedule groups unpaid customer balances by age and does not explain changes in owner's equity.

q: What does the statement of cash flows divide activities into?

options.t: Operating, investing and financing
options.why: The cash flow statement sorts cash receipts and payments into operating, investing, and financing activities to show where cash came from and where it went.

options.t: Assets, liabilities and equity
options.why: Assets, liabilities, and equity are the balance sheet categories, not the sections of the cash flow statement.

options.t: Buying, selling and storing goods
options.why: Buying, selling, and storing goods describe business operations in general and are not the three standard cash flow sections.

options.t: Revenue, cost and profit centers
options.why: Revenue, cost, and profit centers are responsibility accounting units inside a company, not cash flow statement categories.

q: Which is an example of a financing activity?

options.t: Selling products to customers
options.why: Selling products to customers produces cash from daily operations, so it is an operating activity.

options.t: Paying wages to the staff
options.why: Paying wages is a regular expense of running the business, so it is an operating activity.

options.t: Buying equipment for cash
options.why: Buying equipment for cash is an investing activity because it involves acquiring a long-term asset.

options.t: Borrowing money from a bank
options.why: Financing activities involve raising or repaying funds from lenders and owners, and borrowing from a bank brings in cash through debt.

q: What does return on equity measure?

options.t: Net income relative to owners' investment
options.why: Return on equity equals net income divided by owners' equity, showing how much profit is earned on the money owners have invested.

options.t: Sales relative to total assets owned
options.why: Sales relative to total assets is asset turnover, an efficiency measure that is different from return on equity.

options.t: Cash relative to the debts of the firm
options.why: Cash relative to debts relates to liquidity measures such as the cash ratio, not to return on equity.

options.t: Expenses relative to sales for the year
options.why: Expenses relative to sales is an expense ratio or margin measure, not return on equity, which compares profit with equity.

q: Net income is $30,000 and average equity is $200,000. What is return on equity?

options.why: The 30% figure would result from dividing by $100,000, but average equity here is $200,000, so the result is lower.
The 150% figure is not possible here, because $30,000 divided by $200,000 is well below 1, so the return must be under 100%.
ROE = net income / average equity = $30,000 / $200,000 = 0.15, or 15%.
The 6.7% figure flips the fraction ($200,000 / $30,000 = 6.67), but net income belongs in the numerator.

q: A company has current assets of $55,000 and current liabilities of $38,000. What is its working capital?

options.why: The $38,000 figure is the current liabilities alone, one component of the working capital calculation.
Working capital = current assets - current liabilities = $55,000 - $38,000 = $17,000, the cushion available for short-term needs.
The $93,000 figure adds the two amounts, but working capital subtracts current liabilities from current assets.
The $55,000 figure is the current assets alone, before subtracting the current liabilities owed.

q: What is the role of the FASB?

options.t: Regulating banks in the United States today
options.why: Regulating banks is the work of agencies like the Federal Reserve, FDIC, and OCC, not the FASB.

options.t: Setting accounting standards in the United States
options.why: The Financial Accounting Standards Board is the private body that sets US GAAP, the standards companies follow when preparing financial statements.

options.t: Setting interest rates in the United States
options.why: Interest rates are influenced by the Federal Reserve through monetary policy, not by the FASB.

options.t: Collecting income taxes from firms and people as a rule
options.why: Collecting income taxes is the job of the IRS and state tax agencies, not the FASB, which writes accounting standards.

q: A company records a sale before the goods ship and before the customer is obligated. Which principle is likely violated?

options.t: The cost principle
options.why: The cost principle says to record assets at original cost, so it does not govern when a sale is recorded.

options.t: Materiality idea
options.why: Materiality concerns whether an amount is big enough to matter to users, not when a sale should be recognized.

options.t: Going concern idea
options.why: Going concern assumes a business will keep operating, which has nothing to do with the timing of a sale.

options.t: Revenue recognition
options.why: Revenue is recognized when earned, such as when goods are delivered and the customer is obligated, so recording a sale earlier violates revenue recognition.

q: What is the going concern assumption?

options.t: A business will continue operating for the foreseeable future
options.why: The going concern assumption presumes a business will operate long enough to carry out its plans, which justifies recording assets at cost and not at liquidation value.

options.t: A business will close next year and stop all operating
options.why: Assuming the business will close next year would require liquidation accounting, which is the opposite of the going concern assumption.

options.t: A business will never lose money, as owners cover losses as a rule
options.why: Businesses can and do lose money; going concern does not guarantee profits or owners covering losses.

options.t: A business will merge soon with another firm in the town
options.why: A merger is a specific event, and the going concern assumption makes no prediction about merging with another firm.

q: What is the purpose of an audit?

options.t: To create the company's budget for the coming year ahead of all the owners
options.why: Budgets are prepared by management and owners, and an audit does not create a budget for the coming year.

options.t: To sell products to customers and earn a profit for the owners each single year as a rule
options.why: Selling products and earning profit is the work of operations, whereas an audit is an independent review of the statements.

options.t: To give an independent opinion on whether financial statements are fairly presented
options.why: An audit gives an independent expert opinion on whether financial statements are fairly presented under GAAP, which builds trust for investors and lenders.

options.t: To prepare the daily journal entries for each of the transactions of the firm
options.why: Daily journal entries are made by company bookkeepers, while auditors review the records independently after they are prepared.

q: An auditor issues an unqualified opinion. What does this mean?

options.t: The auditor refused to give an opinion on the records
options.why: Refusing to give an opinion is a disclaimer of opinion, which is different from an unqualified opinion.

options.t: The statements contain fraud and material errors in them
options.why: Statements containing fraud and material errors would draw a qualified or adverse opinion, not an unqualified one.

options.t: The statements are fairly presented in all material respects
options.why: An unqualified, or clean, opinion means the auditor concludes the statements are fairly presented in all material respects under GAAP.

options.t: The company will never fail and will always make a profit overall
options.why: An unqualified opinion does not guarantee future success, as auditors give no promise that the company will not fail.

q: What does the Sarbanes-Oxley Act focus on?

options.t: Taxing imports from other countries and trading partners
options.why: Taxing imports is handled through tariffs and trade law, not the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, which concerns corporate reporting.

options.t: Improving corporate financial reporting and internal controls
options.why: Sarbanes-Oxley of 2002 followed scandals like Enron, requiring stronger internal controls, executive certification of reports, and an oversight board for auditors.

options.t: Regulating farm subsidies and crop prices set by the state overall
options.why: Farm subsidies and crop prices are agriculture policy matters unrelated to Sarbanes-Oxley, which regulates public company financial reporting.

options.t: Setting minimum wage rates for workers across the country
options.why: Minimum wage is set by federal and state labor laws such as the Fair Labor Standards Act, not Sarbanes-Oxley.

q: What is internal control?

options.t: An employee dress code that sets the clothes staff wear to work each day
options.why: A dress code is a workplace policy about appearance and not a system for protecting assets or making records accurate.

options.t: A tax planning method used by owners to cut the tax they pay each year
options.why: Tax planning aims to lower taxes legally and is separate from internal controls, which safeguard assets and promote reliable records.

options.t: A marketing strategy used to win more customers for the firm's products
options.why: A marketing strategy focuses on winning customers and does not protect assets or ensure record accuracy.

options.t: Policies and procedures that protect assets and ensure accurate records
options.why: Internal control is the set of policies and procedures that safeguard assets, ensure accurate records, promote efficiency, and encourage compliance with laws.

q: Which is an example of a strong internal control?

options.t: Requiring two signatures on checks over $5,000
options.why: Requiring two signatures on large checks adds a second approval, making it harder for one person to misuse funds, which is strong control.

options.t: Letting one clerk record and approve all payments
options.why: Letting one clerk record and approve all payments breaks separation of duties, because nobody else checks that person's work.

options.t: Leaving cash unlocked overnight in a drawer
options.why: Leaving cash unlocked overnight invites theft, so it is a weak control and not a safeguard.

options.t: Sharing computer passwords with other staff
options.why: Sharing passwords removes accountability, since actions cannot be traced to one user, making it a weak control.

q: What does the cost principle say about recording assets?

options.t: Record assets at current market value only
options.why: Recording assets only at current market value goes against the cost principle, which keeps records objective and verifiable.

options.t: Record assets at their original purchase cost
options.why: The cost principle says assets are recorded at the price paid when acquired, since original cost is objective and verifiable by documents.

options.t: Do not record assets that the firm owns at all
options.why: Assets owned by the business must be recorded, so leaving them out contradicts the cost principle and accounting standards.

options.t: Record assets at the owner's estimate of value
options.why: An owner's estimate is subjective and not verifiable, so the cost principle uses actual purchase cost instead.

q: A company wants to capitalize $50 for a stapler. Which concept allows expensing it immediately?

options.t: Consistency
options.why: Consistency means using the same accounting methods from period to period and does not decide whether a small purchase is expensed.

options.t: Conservatism
options.why: Conservatism says to choose the lower asset value or higher expense when uncertain; it does not allow a small purchase to be expensed.

options.t: Going concern
options.why: Going concern assumes the firm continues operating and does not explain expensing a small purchase.

options.t: Materiality
options.why: Materiality allows tiny amounts like a $50 stapler to be expensed immediately, because capitalizing and depreciating it would not change any decision.

q: What is conflict of interest in accounting?

options.t: A tax audit of a company's records by the revenue agency each year
options.why: A tax audit is an examination by the revenue agency, not a situation where personal interests affect professional judgment.

options.t: A disagreement about lunch between two staff members of the firm over a meal
options.why: A lunch disagreement is a minor workplace matter and does not involve personal interest influencing professional judgment.

options.t: A situation where personal interests may affect professional judgment
options.why: A conflict of interest arises when personal interests, such as a financial stake in a client, could compromise an accountant's objectivity and professional judgment.

options.t: A budget approval given by the board for the following year's plans
options.why: Budget approval is a normal board governance function, not a situation involving personal interests that compromise judgment.

q: An employee earns $1,000 gross. FICA is 7.65%. How much FICA tax is withheld?

options.why: FICA withholding = $1,000 x 7.65% = $76.50, made up of 6.2% Social Security and 1.45% Medicare.
The $765 figure is off by a factor of ten, since 7.65% of $1,000 is $76.50.
The $7.65 figure moves the decimal two places too far, since 7.65% of $1,000 is $76.50.
The $150 figure would be 15% of $1,000, which is not the FICA rate of 7.65%.

q: What does FICA fund?

options.t: Highway and road repair work
options.why: Highway and road repair is funded by fuel taxes, tolls, and other government revenues, not by FICA payroll taxes.

options.t: State parks and state forests
options.why: State parks and forests are funded by state budgets and fees, not by FICA payroll taxes.

options.t: Public libraries and museums
options.why: Libraries and museums are funded by local taxes, donations, and fees rather than FICA payroll contributions.

options.t: Social Security and Medicare
options.why: FICA taxes fund Social Security retirement and disability benefits and Medicare health coverage, split between employee and employer.

q: What is Form 1099-NEC used for?

options.t: Reporting wages to employees at year end
options.why: Wages paid to employees are reported to them on Form W-2, while the 1099-NEC is for non-employee compensation.

options.t: Reporting payments to independent contractors
options.why: Form 1099-NEC reports non-employee compensation, so businesses use it for payments of $600 or more to independent contractors.

options.t: Applying for a license to run a firm in town
options.why: Operating licenses come from state or local governments, and Form 1099-NEC is an IRS information return, not an application.

options.t: Filing a corporate return for the whole year
options.why: Corporations file annual returns such as Form 1120, whereas Form 1099-NEC reports payments made to contractors.

q: A business pays a freelance designer $3,500 in a year. Which form does it generally issue?

options.t: Form 1099-NEC
options.why: A business pays a freelancer designer as an independent contractor, and payments of $600 or more require Form 1099-NEC.

options.t: Form W-2 copy
options.why: Form W-2 reports wages to employees, but a freelance designer is an independent contractor, not an employee.

options.t: Form 941 copy
options.why: Form 941 is the employer's quarterly payroll tax return, filed with the IRS rather than issued to a freelancer.

options.t: Form W-4 copy
options.why: Form W-4 is completed by employees to set withholding, so it would not be issued to a freelance designer.

q: A taxpayer in the 22% bracket has a $1,000 deduction and a different taxpayer has a $1,000 credit. Who saves more?

options.t: They save the same amount in tax for the taxpayer
options.why: The two do not save the same amount, since a credit reduces tax dollar for dollar while a deduction only reduces taxable income.

options.t: The deduction saves $1,000 while the credit saves $220
options.why: This reverses the effects: the credit saves the full $1,000, while the deduction saves only the tax rate times $1,000, or $220.

options.t: The credit saves $1,000 and the deduction saves $220
options.why: A credit cuts tax by $1,000, and a deduction cuts taxable income by $1,000, saving $1,000 x 22% = $220.

options.t: Neither saves anything at all for the taxpayer
options.why: Both a deduction and a credit reduce tax, so each taxpayer saves something instead of nothing.

q: What is a sales tax permit used for?

options.t: Allowing a seller to collect and report sales tax
options.why: A sales tax permit authorizes a seller to collect sales tax from customers and report and send it to the state.

options.t: Getting a loan from a bank for the shop owner
options.why: Bank loans are granted by lenders based on credit and finances, not by a sales tax permit.

options.t: Hiring workers for the sales floor of the shop overall
options.why: Hiring workers requires payroll registration and employment paperwork, which is separate from a sales tax permit.

options.t: Reducing property tax on the shop's building
options.why: Property tax is assessed by local government on real estate, and a sales tax permit does not reduce it.

q: What is a payroll tax liability?

options.t: The employee's bonus paid out at year end by the firm to its staff
options.why: An employee bonus is compensation expense and not a payroll tax liability, though taxes may be withheld on it.

options.t: A bank fee charged to a business for keeping its accounts open
options.why: A bank fee is a service charge expense and is unrelated to taxes owed on employee wages.

options.t: Taxes withheld or owed on wages that must be paid to the government
options.why: A payroll tax liability is the amount of employee withholdings and employer taxes owed to the government but not yet paid, such as FICA and income tax.

options.t: A customer's refund of the price paid for returned goods bought earlier
options.why: A customer refund for returned goods reduces sales and is not a tax owed on wages.

q: A business collects $2,400 in sales tax during the month. Until it pays the state, how should this be recorded?

options.t: As revenue for the whole firm
options.why: Sales tax collected belongs to the state, not the business, so counting it as revenue would overstate income.

options.t: As Sales Tax Payable, a liability
options.why: Sales tax collected for the state is a liability, so it is credited to Sales Tax Payable until it is paid to the state.

options.t: As owner's capital, not a liability
options.why: Owner's capital reflects the owner's investment, not money collected from customers for the state, so this misclassifies the tax.

options.t: As an expense of the firm each year
options.why: The business has not spent anything, so recording collected tax as an expense would be incorrect; it is a liability.

q: What is cloud accounting software?

options.t: A paper ledger kept in a cabinet at the office of the firm
options.why: A paper ledger in a cabinet is the manual system that cloud software replaces, so it is not cloud accounting.

options.t: Software that predicts the weather from satellite data feeds overall
options.why: Predicting the weather from satellite data is meteorology and does not describe accounting programs run over the internet.

options.t: A calculator that adds numbers on a desk at the main office
options.why: A desk calculator adds numbers locally and is not software that stores accounting data online.

options.t: Accounting programs accessed online instead of on one computer
options.why: Cloud accounting runs on remote servers and is reached through a web browser or app, letting users work from any device with updates handled by the provider.

q: What is a key control risk of cloud-based accounting?

options.t: Software requires paper only, so records must be printed
options.why: Cloud software stores records digitally, so claiming it needs paper only is false, and printing is optional.

options.t: Unauthorized access if passwords or permissions are weak
options.why: Cloud systems depend on user access settings, so weak passwords or permissions can let unauthorized people view or change financial data.

options.t: Data can never be backed up in the cloud or on a drive
options.why: Cloud data can be backed up, and providers usually run automatic backups, so saying it never can is false.

options.t: It cannot calculate sums or totals for the accounts of a firm
options.why: Cloud accounting software calculates sums and totals easily, which is a core function, so this claim is false.

q: What does an electronic spreadsheet do well in accounting?

options.t: Sign contracts legally for a firm with no name
options.why: A spreadsheet is a calculation tool and cannot sign contracts, which require a person's legal signature or an authorized digital signature.

options.t: Eliminate all errors made by the staff in the books
options.why: Spreadsheets reduce arithmetic mistakes but cannot eliminate all errors, because formulas and data entry still depend on people.

options.t: Replace all audits done by outside auditors each year
options.why: Outside auditors give an independent opinion, which a spreadsheet cannot replace.

options.t: Perform calculations and organize data automatically
options.why: Spreadsheets use formulas to calculate totals and organize data into rows and columns, making analysis, budgeting, and reports faster and more accurate.

q: What is optical character recognition used for in accounting?

options.t: Reading printed documents and turning them into digital data
options.why: OCR scans printed or handwritten documents like receipts and invoices and converts them to editable data, reducing manual typing in accounting.

options.t: Printing checks only, with no other use in an office or a bank
options.why: Printing checks is done by accounting software printing features, and OCR is for reading documents rather than printing them.

options.t: Playing audio files through speakers in the office all day
options.why: Playing audio is a media function unrelated to reading text from documents into digital data.

options.t: Editing photos for use in the ads of the firm each season
options.why: Editing photos is graphic software work, whereas OCR extracts text from images or scans.

q: A company automates invoice approval with software. What is a likely benefit?

options.t: No controls needed, since the software checks
options.why: Software does not remove the need for controls; approval limits and review are still required to prevent errors and fraud.

options.t: Slower payments to the vendors and staff
options.why: Automation is meant to speed up processing, so slower payments would be a drawback, not a benefit.

options.t: Faster processing and fewer manual errors
options.why: Automated approval routes invoices quickly and applies consistent rules, which speeds processing and reduces manual data entry mistakes.

options.t: More paperwork for the accounts staff
options.why: Automation reduces paper by using electronic routing and approvals, so more paperwork would be the opposite of the benefit.

q: Why should accounting data be backed up regularly?

options.t: To increase storage costs only, with no benefit
options.why: Backups have a modest cost but a major benefit, because they let a business recover data after a loss.

options.t: To make data harder to read for the staff
options.why: Backups copy data safely and do not make it harder to read; the copy can be restored for use.

options.t: To delete old records of the firm for good
options.why: Backups preserve records, while deleting old records is a separate retention decision and not the purpose of backing up.

options.t: To recover records if data is lost or damaged
options.why: Regular backups create copies so records can be restored after hardware failure, cyberattack, or accidental deletion, protecting financial history and operations.

q: What is blockchain's possible use in accounting?

options.t: A tax form for the state revenue office
options.why: A tax form is issued by a revenue agency, whereas blockchain is a technology for recording data.

options.t: A way to print checks signed by hand
options.why: Printing checks signed by hand is an unrelated manual task, and blockchain is not a check printing method.

options.t: A secure shared ledger of transactions
options.why: A blockchain is a distributed ledger whose records are linked and hard to alter, which can make transactions more transparent and easier to verify.

options.t: A type of calculator for the office staff
options.why: A calculator is a computing device, whereas blockchain is a way of storing transaction records.

q: What does a certified public accountant (CPA) do?

options.t: Designs buildings and draws plans for the builders of a new site in the city as a rule
options.why: Designing buildings is the work of architects and engineers, not CPAs, who focus on accounting, audit, and tax.

options.t: Provides accounting, audit and tax services after meeting licensing requirements
options.why: A CPA is a licensed professional who provides accounting, auditing, and tax services after passing the exam and meeting education and experience requirements.

options.t: Sells insurance only, to families and firms that wish to protect their goods
options.why: Selling insurance is done by licensed insurance agents, not CPAs, whose work centers on financial records and taxes.

options.t: Repairs computers and keeps the office machines running smoothly for staff
options.why: Repairing computers is IT support work, whereas CPAs prepare and audit financial information.

q: A student enjoys finding errors and checking details. Which accounting career might fit best?

options.t: Auditor
options.why: Auditors examine records for errors and compliance, so someone who enjoys finding mistakes and checking details fits this role well.

options.t: Chef
options.why: A chef prepares food and manages a kitchen, which is not an accounting career and does not focus on checking financial details.

options.t: Designer
options.why: A designer creates visual products and does not examine financial records for errors.

options.t: Sales boss
options.why: Sales roles focus on persuading customers rather than checking records for errors, so they do not match this student's interests.

q: What does a bookkeeper typically do?

options.t: Records daily financial transactions
options.why: A bookkeeper records daily transactions such as sales, purchases, and payments, keeping the books accurate and up to date.

options.t: Sets national tax laws for the country
options.why: Tax laws are written by Congress, not by bookkeepers, who record transactions and maintain records.

options.t: Designs advertising for the firm
options.why: Designing advertising is the job of marketing and creative staff, not a bookkeeper, who maintains financial records.

options.t: Builds software only, for large firms
options.why: A bookkeeper keeps financial records and does not build software, which is the work of programmers and developers.

q: What is a forensic accountant?

options.t: A tax preparer only, who fills in forms for clients each spring
options.why: Preparing tax forms is the role of a tax preparer, and a forensic accountant instead examines evidence of fraud or disputes.

options.t: A specialist who investigates financial fraud and disputes
options.why: A forensic accountant analyzes financial records to investigate fraud, embezzlement, and disputes, often providing evidence or testimony in legal cases.

options.t: A store clerk who sells goods to shoppers at a retail shop
options.why: A store clerk sells goods at retail and does not investigate financial records for fraud.

options.t: A person who prepares meals in a restaurant kitchen for guests
options.why: Preparing meals is a culinary job, which has nothing to do with investigating financial records.

q: Which skill is most important for a staff accountant?

options.t: Avoiding teamwork at the firm
options.why: Teamwork is essential in accounting because staff share data and work with others, so avoiding it would hurt performance.

options.t: Ignoring deadlines to spend time
options.why: Deadlines such as month-end close and tax filings are critical, so ignoring them would harm the firm.

options.t: Accuracy and attention to detail
options.why: Staff accountants handle numbers that others rely on, so accuracy and attention to detail are the most important skills.

options.t: Guessing numbers in the books
options.why: Guessing numbers leads to inaccurate records and misleading statements, which is unacceptable in accounting.

q: What does a management accountant do?

options.t: Audits other companies for the public and for investors
options.why: Auditing other companies for the public is the work of external auditors, while management accountants work inside a company.

options.t: Files only external tax returns for the company
options.why: External tax returns are prepared by tax accountants, while management accountants focus on internal information for decisions.

options.t: Sells stock in a firm to the public and to investors
options.why: Selling stock is the job of investment bankers and brokers, not management accountants.

options.t: Prepares information to help managers make decisions
options.why: A management accountant prepares budgets, cost analyses, and reports for internal managers to help them plan, control, and make decisions.

q: What is the accounting equation?

options.t: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity
options.why: The accounting equation states Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity, meaning everything the business owns is financed by creditors or by the owner.

options.t: Assets = Liabilities - Owner's Equity
options.why: Subtracting owner's equity from liabilities does not match the equation, since assets are funded by liabilities plus equity.

options.t: Assets + Liabilities = Owner's Equity
options.why: Adding assets and liabilities to equal equity misplaces assets, which must be on one side with liabilities and equity on the other.

options.t: Revenue = Assets + Expenses + Equity
options.why: Revenue is part of the income statement, so equating it with assets, expenses, and equity misstates the accounting equation.

q: A business pays $2,000 of its accounts payable with cash. What is the effect on the accounting equation?

options.t: Assets increase and liabilities decrease by $2,000
options.why: Paying a liability with cash lowers assets, so assets cannot increase while liabilities decrease.

options.t: Equity decreases by $2,000 on the balance sheet
options.why: Paying off accounts payable does not change owner's equity, because only assets and liabilities are affected.

options.t: Assets and liabilities both decrease by $2,000
options.why: Cash (an asset) falls by $2,000 and Accounts Payable (a liability) falls by $2,000, so the equation stays balanced with total assets and liabilities lower.

options.t: There is no effect on the accounting equation
options.why: The transaction does change the equation, since assets and liabilities each fall by $2,000, though it stays in balance.

q: What does double-entry bookkeeping mean?

options.t: Two people must sign every entry in the books
options.why: Double-entry means each transaction affects at least two accounts, not that two people sign; signature rules are a control matter.

options.t: Only large transactions are recorded in the books
options.why: Every transaction, large or small, is recorded in double-entry, so it does not apply only to large items.

options.t: Every transaction is recorded twice in one account
options.why: Double-entry records the transaction in at least two accounts, not twice in one account, with total debits equaling total credits.

options.t: Every transaction affects at least two accounts
options.why: In double-entry bookkeeping, each transaction has at least one debit and one credit, so the accounting equation always stays in balance.

q: Which is an example of a liability?

options.t: Cash on hand
options.why: Cash on hand is something the business owns, making it an asset, not a liability.

options.t: Notes payable
options.why: Notes payable are written promises to pay a lender, so they are amounts the business owes and are liabilities.

options.t: Supplies stock
options.why: Supplies on hand are owned resources, so they are assets, not liabilities.

options.t: Owned equipment
options.why: Equipment the business owns is a long-term asset, not an obligation to pay anyone.

q: An owner invests $15,000 cash in a new business. How is the transaction recorded?

options.t: Debit Expense $15,000 and credit Cash $15,000
options.why: Debiting an expense and crediting cash would record spending, whereas an owner's investment brings cash into the business.

options.t: Debit Revenue $15,000 and credit Cash $15,000
options.why: Debiting Revenue and crediting Cash would record a revenue reduction, but an investment is not revenue and increases cash.

options.t: Debit Cash $15,000; credit Owner's Capital $15,000
options.why: The owner's investment increases Cash, an asset, with a debit, and increases Owner's Capital, equity, with a credit, keeping the equation balanced.

options.t: Debit Owner's Capital $15,000; credit Cash $15,000
options.why: This entry reduces Cash and Capital, which reverses an investment and would be the entry for the owner withdrawing money.

q: What is a source document?

options.t: A record that proves a transaction occurred
options.why: A source document, like a receipt, invoice, or check stub, provides evidence that a transaction took place and supports the journal entry.

options.t: A final statement prepared for the owners
options.why: Statements for owners are prepared from the ledger at the end of the cycle and are not source documents.

options.t: A tax return only, filed once each year
options.why: A tax return is a yearly compliance filing, whereas source documents support individual transactions throughout the year.

options.t: A budget plan for the next fiscal year ahead
options.why: A budget is a plan for future income and spending, whereas a source document proves a transaction already occurred.

q: What is the business entity concept?

options.t: Only corporations keep records, and sole owners do not need to keep any
options.why: Sole proprietors also need records, and the business entity concept applies to all forms of business, not just corporations.

options.t: A business's records are kept separate from its owner's personal records
options.why: The business entity concept treats the business as separate from its owner, so personal transactions are kept out of the business books.

options.t: Records are kept only for customers and not for the owner or the firm
options.why: Records are kept for the owner's business as well as for customers, so this misstates the concept.

options.t: The owner and the business are one, so money is kept in one set of books
options.why: This blends owner and business, which is the reverse of the entity concept that requires separate records.

q: An owner pays a personal electric bill from the business checking account. How should it be recorded?

options.t: As a normal utilities expense of the firm
options.why: Paying a personal bill with business funds is not a business expense, and recording it as one would overstate costs.

options.t: As revenue of the business each month
options.why: Paying a bill does not produce revenue for the business, since revenue comes from selling goods or services.

options.t: As an asset purchase for the business
options.why: A personal electric bill gives no asset to the business, so recording it as an asset purchase would be incorrect.

options.t: As owner's drawing, not a business expense
options.why: Personal use of business funds is a withdrawal, so it is recorded as a debit to Owner's Drawing and a credit to Cash.

q: What is the normal balance of the owner's drawing account?

options.t: Either
options.why: An account has one normal balance side, not either, and drawing is fixed on the debit side.

options.t: Zero only
options.why: Drawing usually has a balance until it is closed, but its normal balance is debit, not zero.

options.t: Credit
options.why: A credit balance would increase equity, whereas drawing reduces equity, so its normal balance is not credit.

options.t: Debit
options.why: Drawing reduces owner's equity, which has a credit balance, so the drawing account increases with debits and has a normal debit balance.

q: What is a chart of accounts?

options.t: A graph of sales over the months of a whole trading year
options.why: A graph of sales is a chart in a report, whereas a chart of accounts lists the accounts used in the books.

options.t: A list of all accounts a business uses, with account numbers
options.why: A chart of accounts lists every account the business uses with its number, usually organized as assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, and expenses.

options.t: A list of customers only, with their addresses and balances
options.why: A customer list with addresses and balances is a subsidiary ledger or contact list, not the chart of accounts.

options.t: A schedule of employees and their shifts for each week of the year
options.why: Employee shift schedules are workforce planning documents, and the chart of accounts is a list of accounting records.

q: Which account number range typically represents assets in a chart of accounts?

options.t: The 1000 series
options.why: Assets conventionally sit in the 1000 series of a chart of accounts, with liabilities in 2000, equity in 3000, revenue in 4000 and expenses in 5000.

options.t: The 5000 series
options.why: The 5000 series is normally reserved for expenses such as rent and wages, not for assets, which are numbered in the 1000 range.

options.t: The 4000 series
options.why: The 4000 series usually holds revenue accounts such as sales and service fees, which increase equity rather than represent items the business owns.

options.t: The 3000 series
options.why: The 3000 series is conventionally used for owner's equity accounts such as capital and drawings, not for the resources a business owns.

q: A company buys a $24,000 van with a 4-year life and no salvage value. What is annual depreciation under straight-line?

options.why: $96,000 multiplies the cost by the 4-year life instead of dividing, which is the wrong operation and gives an amount far above the van's price.
$4,000 would result from dividing the cost by 6 rather than by the 4-year life, so it does not match straight-line depreciation here.
Straight-line depreciation is (cost minus salvage) divided by useful life: ($24,000 - $0) / 4 years = $6,000 of expense each year, spread evenly over the van's life.
$24,000 is the full cost of the van, which would be expensed all at once; depreciation spreads that cost over the four years of use.

q: Using double-declining-balance, what is year-one depreciation on a $20,000 asset with a 5-year life?

options.why: $4,000 is the straight-line amount ($20,000 / 5 years); double-declining-balance uses twice the straight-line rate, so first-year expense must be larger than this.
$20,000 is the entire cost of the asset, which would be written off in one year; depreciation only allocates a fraction of cost each year.
Straight-line rate is 1/5 = 20%, doubled to 40%; applied to the full $20,000 book value (salvage ignored), year-one depreciation is $20,000 x 40% = $8,000.
$2,000 would come from applying only 10% to the cost, half the straight-line rate, instead of doubling the 20% rate to 40%.

q: What is accumulated depreciation?

options.t: The total depreciation recorded on an asset to date
options.why: Accumulated depreciation is a contra-asset account that adds up all depreciation expense recorded on an asset since purchase; subtracting it from cost gives book value.

options.t: The yearly expense only, shown on the income statement
options.why: The yearly expense on the income statement is depreciation expense; accumulated depreciation is the running total of all years on the balance sheet.

options.t: The resale price of the asset when sold in a later year
options.why: Resale price is market value, which can differ from book value; accumulated depreciation is an accounting allocation of cost, not an estimate of what the asset would sell for.

options.t: The cost of the asset when it was first bought by us
options.why: The original purchase price is the asset's historical cost; accumulated depreciation is the portion of that cost already written off, not the cost itself.

q: Equipment cost $15,000 and has $9,000 of accumulated depreciation. What is its book value?

options.why: $15,000 is the original cost; book value is cost minus accumulated depreciation, so it must be lower once depreciation has been recorded.
$24,000 adds the accumulated depreciation to the cost, but accumulated depreciation is subtracted from cost to find book value, never added.
$9,000 is only the accumulated depreciation; book value is what remains after subtracting it from the $15,000 cost.
Book value equals cost minus accumulated depreciation: $15,000 - $9,000 = $6,000, the portion of the asset's cost not yet expensed.

q: A company receives $3,600 for a one-year service contract in advance. After 3 months, how much revenue has been earned?

options.why: $3,600 is the whole contract amount; only a portion is earned after 3 months, and the rest remains unearned revenue, a liability until services are performed.
Revenue is earned evenly: $3,600 / 12 months = $300 per month, and 3 months x $300 = $900 earned, leaving $2,700 as unearned revenue.
$1,200 would be four months of service ($300 x 4) or a third of the contract; only 3 of 12 months have passed, so the fraction is one quarter.
$300 is the revenue for just one month; three months have passed, so earned revenue is $300 x 3 = $900.

q: What does closing entries accomplish?

options.t: Reset temporary accounts to zero and move results to owner's equity
options.why: Closing entries zero out temporary accounts (revenue, expenses, drawings) and transfer the net result to owner's equity, so the next period starts with fresh balances.

options.t: Increase revenue by recording extra sales that never took place at all
options.why: Closing entries record no new sales; they only transfer balances already recorded, and inventing revenue would be fraud rather than an accounting procedure.

options.t: Cancel the business and send all the staff home for good at year end
options.why: Closing entries are a bookkeeping step at the end of a period; they have nothing to do with ending the business or dismissing employees.

options.t: Delete all assets from the books so that the firm owns nothing at all
options.why: Closing entries never remove assets; permanent accounts like assets, liabilities and capital carry their balances forward into the next accounting period.

q: After closing, the Income Summary account has a credit balance of $14,000. What does this show?

options.t: Drawings of $14,000
options.why: Drawings are a debit-balance owner withdrawal account closed to capital; a credit balance in Income Summary instead reflects revenues exceeding expenses.

options.t: Net loss of $14,000
options.why: A net loss shows as a debit balance in Income Summary because expenses exceed revenues; a credit balance signals the opposite result.

options.t: Net income of $14,000
options.why: Income Summary collects revenues (credits) and expenses (debits); a $14,000 credit balance means revenues exceeded expenses, so net income of $14,000 transfers to capital.

options.t: Total assets of $14,000
options.why: Total assets are a balance sheet item and are not measured in Income Summary, which is a temporary account used only to compute profit or loss.

q: What is a subsidiary ledger?

options.t: A ledger kept by a rival firm to check the business sales
options.why: A rival firm's records have nothing to do with the business's own books; a subsidiary ledger is an internal detail ledger supporting a control account.

options.t: A ledger with no entries in it, kept by the head accountant
options.why: A subsidiary ledger is full of detailed entries, one account per customer or vendor, so describing it as empty misses its entire purpose.

options.t: A tax calendar that shows the filing dates for each year
options.why: A tax calendar is a scheduling tool for filing deadlines, not a ledger; it holds no debit or credit account balances at all.

options.t: A detailed ledger for accounts such as customers or vendors
options.why: A subsidiary ledger holds detailed accounts, such as individual customers or vendors, whose total must equal the related control account in the general ledger.

q: The Accounts Receivable control account shows $18,500, but customer subsidiary accounts total $18,200. What should an accountant do?

options.t: Ignore the difference and close the books at once
options.why: Ignoring a difference between the control account and subsidiary total leaves an error uncorrected, which undermines the reliability of the receivables balance.

options.t: Investigate the $300 difference and correct the error
options.why: The $300 gap (18,500 - 18,200) signals a posting or addition error somewhere; the accountant should trace entries to find and correct it so both agree.

options.t: Adjust revenue by $300 at once, so the accounts agree
options.why: Adjusting revenue merely to make accounts agree would hide the true error and could misstate income; the actual mistake has to be found and fixed.

options.t: Delete the subsidiary ledger and start a new one
options.why: Deleting the subsidiary ledger would destroy the customer detail needed to collect payments; a $300 variance is fixed by investigation, not by discarding records.

q: Which entry records the collection of $500 from a customer on account?

options.t: Debit Revenue $500 and credit Cash $500 in full
options.why: This entry reverses the effect: it credits cash and debits revenue, but collecting a receivable brings cash in and does not involve revenue at all.

options.t: Debit Cash $500; credit Accounts Receivable $500
options.why: Collecting on account increases Cash (debit) and decreases Accounts Receivable (credit); revenue was already recorded when the sale was made on credit.

options.t: Debit Cash $500 and credit Revenue $500 in full
options.why: Crediting Revenue would count the sale twice, since revenue was recognized at the time of the credit sale; collection only converts the receivable into cash.

options.t: Debit Accounts Receivable $500; credit Cash $500
options.why: This reverses the real entry: it would increase receivables and reduce cash, which is what happens when granting credit, not collecting from a customer.

q: A company pays $1,200 for a one-year insurance policy on April 1. How much insurance expense is recorded by December 31?

options.why: The policy runs April 1 to March 31, so 9 months have passed by December 31: $1,200 / 12 = $100 per month x 9 = $900 insurance expense.
$1,200 is the full annual premium; only 9 of the 12 months have elapsed by December 31, so the remaining 3 months stay as prepaid insurance.
$300 is the portion left unexpired (3 months x $100) at December 31, which remains in Prepaid Insurance rather than being expensed.
$100 is the cost of just one month of coverage; nine months from April through December have been used up.

q: A $5,000 note at 6% interest is held for 90 days (360-day year). How much interest is earned?

options.why: $750 would result from using 10 percent for a full year or a longer time; the 6 percent rate over 90 days produces much less interest.
$7.50 is off by a factor of ten, likely a misplaced decimal when applying 6% and 90/360 to the $5,000 principal.
Interest = principal x rate x time: $5,000 x 0.06 x (90/360) = $5,000 x 0.06 x 0.25 = $75 earned over the 90 days.
$300 is the interest for a full year (5,000 x 6%); the note is only held for 90 days, a quarter of a year, so interest is smaller.

q: What does it mean when a customer's check is returned for insufficient funds (NSF)?

options.t: The check was a gift from the customer to the seller and has no value
options.why: A returned check is not a gift; it is a failed payment, so the customer still owes the seller the amount of the check.

options.t: The check was paid in full by the bank to the seller on the due day
options.why: NSF means the opposite of being paid in full: the bank refused payment because funds were lacking, so the seller has not been paid.

options.t: The check was approved twice by the bank and paid two times
options.why: Banks pay a check only once; NSF means it bounced and was returned unpaid, and nothing was paid even one time.

options.t: The customer's account did not have enough money to cover the check
options.why: NSF stands for non-sufficient funds: the drawer's balance was too low to cover the check, so the bank returns it and the seller must collect another way.

q: An item lists at $800 with a 20% trade discount. What is the invoice price?

options.why: $160 is the discount amount itself (20% of $800), not the price; the invoice price is the list price minus that discount.
Trade discount is 20% x $800 = $160, so the invoice price is $800 - $160 = $640, the amount the buyer actually owes before any cash discount.
$960 adds the discount to the list price instead of subtracting it; a trade discount lowers what the buyer pays.
$780 subtracts only $20, as if the discount were a flat dollar amount; a 20% trade discount takes off $160 from the $800 list price.

q: What is freight-in?

options.t: A discount for early payment of the invoice to the seller
options.why: A discount for early payment is a purchase or cash discount, which lowers what the buyer pays; freight-in is a delivery cost that adds to cost.

options.t: A tax on imports charged at the border by the customs office
options.why: An import tax charged at the border is a customs duty or tariff, a different cost from the transportation charge called freight-in.

options.t: Shipping paid by the seller to customers who buy goods
options.why: Shipping the seller pays to deliver goods to customers is freight-out, a selling expense of the seller, not freight-in.

options.t: The shipping cost paid by the buyer on goods purchased
options.why: Freight-in is the transportation cost the buyer pays to get purchased goods delivered, and it is added to the cost of inventory purchased.

q: A buyer pays $400 freight on a $5,000 purchase. What is the total cost of the goods?

options.why: $400 is only the freight; total cost of goods includes both the purchase price and the transportation paid by the buyer to receive them.
$4,600 subtracts the freight from the price, but freight-in is added to the cost of the goods, not deducted from it.
Freight-in is part of inventory cost: $5,000 purchase price + $400 freight = $5,400 total cost of the goods bought.
$5,000 leaves out the $400 freight; the buyer's cost of goods includes the shipping needed to bring the goods to its location.

q: Which account is increased by a credit purchase from a supplier?

options.t: Accounts Payable
options.why: A credit purchase creates a liability to the supplier, so Accounts Payable increases with a credit while Inventory or Purchases is debited.

options.t: Accounts Receivable
options.why: Accounts Receivable is an asset for money owed by customers; buying from a supplier creates an amount the business owes, not one it is owed.

options.t: Owner's Capital
options.why: Owner's Capital changes with investments, profits and drawings; a purchase on credit from a supplier does not directly change the owner's investment.

options.t: Cash account
options.why: Cash would be affected only if the purchase were paid immediately; a credit purchase delays payment, so the liability rises while cash stays unchanged.

q: What is a cash discount from a supplier's point of view?

options.t: A trade discount from the price list of the maker
options.why: A trade discount reduces the list price before the invoice is prepared; a cash discount is a separate reduction offered for prompt payment of the invoice.

options.t: A reduction for paying an invoice within a short period
options.why: A cash discount, such as 2/10 n/30, is a reduction offered for paying an invoice early, which gives the supplier faster access to its money.

options.t: A late fee charged when an invoice is paid after its due date
options.why: A charge added for paying after the due date is a late fee or finance charge, the opposite of a discount for paying early.

options.t: A tax added to the invoice by the state on the goods sold
options.why: A tax added by the state is a sales tax collected for government; it is not a reduction the supplier offers to speed up payment.

q: A $2,500 invoice has terms 1/15, n/45. A buyer pays on day 12. How much should be paid?

options.why: $2,525 adds 1% to the invoice, but a discount reduces the amount paid; the buyer who pays early owes less than the invoice total.
$2,250 takes off 10% rather than 1%; the terms 1/15 allow only a 1% discount ($25) when paid within 15 days.
Day 12 is within the 15-day discount period, so the buyer takes 1% of $2,500 = $25 off and pays $2,500 - $25 = $2,475.
$2,500 is the full invoice amount; the terms 1/15 let the buyer subtract 1% for paying within 15 days, and day 12 qualifies.

q: Which section of the balance sheet lists amounts owed to creditors?

options.t: Liabilities
options.why: The liabilities section of the balance sheet lists amounts the business owes to creditors, such as accounts payable, notes payable and accrued expenses.

options.t: Owner equity
options.why: Owner's equity shows the owner's claim on the business (assets minus liabilities), not amounts owed to outside creditors.

options.t: Revenue
options.why: Revenue appears on the income statement, not the balance sheet, and it describes earnings rather than debts owed to others.

options.t: Asset list
options.why: Assets list what the business owns, such as cash and equipment; the debts owed to creditors appear on the other side of the equation as liabilities.

q: A company's debt ratio is total liabilities divided by total assets. With $60,000 in liabilities and $150,000 in assets, what is the ratio?

options.why: 250% inverts the fraction (150,000 / 60,000); the debt ratio puts liabilities in the numerator over assets in the denominator, so it cannot exceed 100% here.
90% is not what the data produce; $60,000 of liabilities is well below $150,000 of assets, so most assets are not financed by debt.
60% uses the liabilities figure ($60,000) as a percent, but the ratio must divide liabilities by assets before converting to percent.
Debt ratio = total liabilities / total assets = $60,000 / $150,000 = 0.40 = 40%, meaning creditors fund 40 cents of each asset dollar.

q: A corporation starts with $40,000 retained earnings, earns $25,000 and pays $5,000 dividends. What is the ending balance?

options.why: $20,000 subtracts earnings from the starting balance; retained earnings grow by net income and shrink by dividends, so it should not drop that far.
$70,000 adds the $25,000 income but then ignores the $5,000 dividends, which reduce retained earnings when paid out to shareholders.
$65,000 equals the beginning balance plus income minus nothing else, but it fails to subtract dividends correctly: 40,000 + 25,000 = 65,000 less 5,000 still must be applied.
Ending retained earnings = beginning + net income - dividends = $40,000 + $25,000 - $5,000 = $60,000, the profit kept in the business.

q: What is a comparative financial statement?

options.t: A statement showing data for two or more periods side by side
options.why: A comparative statement presents figures for two or more periods side by side, so readers can see changes and trends in sales, expenses and assets.

options.t: A statement with no numbers, only words about the firm and its plans
options.why: A statement with only words and no numbers is not a financial statement; comparative statements are numeric and show multiple periods together.

options.t: A statement comparing the owner to the workers on pay and hours
options.why: Comparative statements compare financial results over time, not the pay and hours of owners and employees, which is a labor matter.

options.t: A statement printed in color on glossy paper for the owners to read
options.why: Color and glossy paper are matters of presentation; what makes a statement comparative is multi-period data, not how it is printed.

q: Sales were $400,000 last year and $460,000 this year. What is the percent increase?

options.why: 1.5% results from misplacing the decimal point; the change of $60,000 on a base of $400,000 gives a much larger percent increase.
13% divides the $60,000 increase by the new figure ($460,000) instead of the earlier year's $400,000; the base must be the prior period.
60% treats the $60,000 dollar change as a percent; it must be divided by the $400,000 starting sales amount to get 15%.

q: What does horizontal analysis compare?

options.t: Only cash items in the books of a firm
options.why: Horizontal analysis is not limited to cash items; it can be applied to any line of a statement across periods.

options.t: Items within one period as percentages
options.why: Expressing items within one period as percentages of a base is vertical (common-size) analysis, not horizontal analysis.

options.t: The same item across several periods
options.why: Horizontal analysis compares the same line item across several periods, showing dollar and percent changes, which reveals trends over time.

options.t: Different companies only, in one year
options.why: Comparing different companies in one year is cross-company benchmarking; horizontal analysis follows one company's items through time.

q: What does vertical analysis do?

options.t: Compare one item over many years, as it has changed since founding
options.why: Comparing one item over many years is horizontal (trend) analysis; vertical analysis looks within a single period instead.

options.t: Remove expenses from the income statement of a firm each year
options.why: Vertical analysis removes nothing from the statements; it keeps all expenses and restates each as a percentage of a base amount.

options.t: Print statements vertically on the page of the report
options.why: Vertical has nothing to do with page orientation; it refers to analyzing each item as a percent of a base within one statement.

options.t: Express each item as a percent of a base such as total sales
options.why: Vertical analysis expresses each item as a percent of a base, such as net sales on the income statement or total assets on the balance sheet.

q: On an income statement, cost of goods sold is $120,000 and net sales are $300,000. What percent of sales is cost of goods sold?

options.why: COGS % of sales = $120,000 / $300,000 = 0.40 = 40%, so 40 cents of each sales dollar goes to the cost of the goods sold.
60% is the remainder, the gross profit margin ($180,000 / $300,000); the question asks for cost of goods sold as a percent of sales.
12% results from a decimal slip; $120,000 divided by $300,000 is 0.40, not 0.12.
250% flips the fraction ($300,000 / $120,000); the cost of goods sold must be the numerator over net sales to get a percent of sales.

q: A company earns $360,000 and has 120,000 shares outstanding. What is its EPS?

options.why: $30.00 is off by a factor of ten; $360,000 divided by 120,000 shares is $3.00, not $30.00 per share.
Earnings per share = net income / shares outstanding = $360,000 / 120,000 = $3.00 earned for each share held.
$0.33 flips the division (120,000 / 360,000); EPS puts earnings in the numerator and shares outstanding in the denominator.
$240,000 is the difference between earnings and shares (360,000 - 120,000), a meaningless subtraction; EPS is a per-share ratio found by dividing.

q: Why do lenders look at a company's financial statements?

options.t: To set its advertising plans each year
options.why: Advertising plans are set by the company's managers and marketing staff; lenders read statements to judge credit risk, not to plan promotions.

options.t: To choose its logo and its colors
options.why: A company's logo and colors are branding choices unrelated to its finances; lenders want evidence that debts will be repaid.

options.t: To judge its ability to repay a loan
options.why: Lenders review income, cash flow, assets and debts to judge whether the company can repay a loan with interest on time.

options.t: To count its employees and its offices
options.why: Headcount and office locations are operating details; lenders focus on profitability, liquidity and leverage reported in the financial statements.

q: What is the purpose of notes to the financial statements?

options.t: To explain accounting methods and give extra detail
options.why: Notes to the financial statements explain accounting methods, assumptions and contingencies and give details behind the numbers, which readers need to interpret statements fully.

options.t: To replace the statements, so readers skip the tables
options.why: Notes supplement the statements and cannot replace them; readers still need the balance sheet, income statement and cash flow figures.

options.t: To advertise products to customers and the public
options.why: Notes are about accounting disclosure and are not advertising; publicity for products belongs in marketing materials, not in audited statements.

options.t: To hide losses from the owners and from investors
options.why: Notes exist to disclose information fully, not to conceal losses; hiding losses would violate full disclosure and may be fraud.

q: A company shows strong net income but negative cash flow from operations. What might this suggest?

options.t: Cash is guaranteed to grow in the coming year without any further action
options.why: Negative operating cash flow does not guarantee future growth in cash; if anything, it signals a problem that needs management action.

options.t: Net income is always wrong because the books of a firm cannot be trusted
options.why: Net income is not always wrong; accrual accounting can legitimately differ from cash flow when revenue is earned but cash is not yet collected.

options.t: Profits may not be turning into cash, for example from slow collections
options.why: When income is high but operating cash is negative, profits may be tied up in receivables or inventory, a sign of weak collections.

options.t: The company has no customers and makes no sales to anyone at all
options.why: A company with strong net income clearly has customers and sales; the problem is converting those sales to cash, not an absence of sales.

q: What is the consistency principle?

options.t: A business must hide changes in methods from the readers of statements as a rule
options.why: The consistency principle requires methods to be applied the same way and changes disclosed, so concealing changes would violate it.

options.t: A business should use the same accounting methods from period to period
options.why: Consistency means using the same accounting methods from period to period so results are comparable, and any necessary change is disclosed in the notes.

options.t: A business must change methods each year to show the newest ideas
options.why: Changing methods every year would make statements incomparable; consistency requires stable methods unless a change is justified and explained.

options.t: A business must use cash basis only and may never use accrual rules
options.why: Consistency does not restrict a company to cash basis; most businesses use accrual accounting, applied consistently each period.

q: A company switches inventory methods and does not disclose it. Which principle is most affected?

options.t: Time period assumption rule
options.why: The time period assumption splits operations into periods like months and years; switching inventory methods secretly is a different issue.

options.t: Business entity, firm is separate
options.why: The business entity concept separates the owner's finances from the firm's; it does not concern changing inventory methods.

options.t: Monetary unit assumption rule
options.why: The monetary unit assumption says transactions are measured in money; it does not address switching inventory costing methods.

options.t: Consistency and full disclosure
options.why: Changing inventory methods without disclosure breaks consistency (same methods over time) and full disclosure (telling readers about material changes affecting comparability).

q: What is the conservatism principle?

options.t: Hide risks from the owners and the public so that the firm looks very strong
options.why: Conservatism does not mean hiding risks; it means reporting uncertainty cautiously, not concealing facts from owners or the public.

options.t: Never report losses in the statements, so that the firm always looks profitable in most cases
options.why: Conservatism does not prohibit reporting losses; probable losses should be recorded, not hidden so the firm looks profitable.

options.t: When uncertain, choose the option that is less likely to overstate assets or income
options.why: Conservatism says that when uncertain, accountants choose the option that does not overstate assets or income, such as lower of cost or market for inventory.

options.t: Always report the highest profit possible, whatever the facts and the rules say
options.why: Reporting the highest profit regardless of facts is the opposite of conservatism, which counsels caution about gains and anticipating possible losses.

q: An accountant is asked by her manager to hide a $50,000 loss. What is the best action?

options.t: Refuse and report the request through proper channels
options.why: Hiding losses is unethical and may be illegal, so the accountant should refuse and use proper channels, such as the audit committee or compliance office.

options.t: Hide it and tell nobody about the loss at all, ever
options.why: Concealing a loss is dishonest and misleads users of the statements; it could expose the accountant to legal and professional penalties.

options.t: Comply to keep the job and avoid any argument at all
options.why: Complying to keep a job violates professional ethics; accountants must put honest reporting ahead of pressure from a manager.

options.t: Alter the numbers slightly, so the loss looks smaller
options.why: Altering numbers to shrink a loss is still falsifying records, which is fraud; the accountant should report the true figure.

q: What does the IRS do?

options.t: Sets accounting standards and publishes rules
options.why: Setting accounting standards is the job of the FASB (and the SEC for public companies), not the IRS, which administers tax law.

options.t: Collects federal taxes and enforces tax laws
options.why: The IRS is the federal agency that collects income and other federal taxes and enforces the Internal Revenue Code through audits and penalties.

options.t: Regulates stock markets and company reports
options.why: Regulating stock markets and the reports of public companies is the job of the SEC, a separate agency from the IRS.

options.t: Insures bank deposits up to a legal limit
options.why: Insuring bank deposits up to a legal limit is the role of the FDIC, not the IRS.

q: What is the role of the SEC regarding public company statements?

options.t: Hires accountants for public companies to keep their books
options.why: Public companies hire their own accountants and auditors; the SEC does not keep their books but oversees what they disclose.

options.t: Prints annual reports for the shareholders of firms it watches
options.why: The SEC does not print annual reports; companies prepare them and file required reports like the 10-K and 10-Q with the SEC.

options.t: Sets sales prices for goods sold by public companies to buyers
options.why: The SEC does not set sales prices; its role is investor protection and fair, orderly markets, not pricing of products.

options.t: Requires public companies to file accurate, timely reports
options.why: The SEC requires public companies to file accurate and timely financial reports, such as 10-K and 10-Q forms, so investors can make informed decisions.

q: Which situation violates the principle of separation of duties?

options.t: One person orders and another pays, both checked by a third
options.why: Having one person order and another pay, with a third reviewing, is separation of duties working properly, as it limits chances for fraud.

options.t: One person orders supplies, receives them and approves payment
options.why: When one person orders, receives and approves payment, no one checks that person's work, which makes fraud and undetected errors easy; duties should be divided.

options.t: Two people count cash together at the close of each business day
options.why: Two people counting cash together is a dual control that supports separation of duties by letting each check the other.

options.t: A manager reviews all payments made by the firm each month
options.why: A manager reviewing payments is an independent check, which strengthens internal control rather than violating separation of duties.

q: What is an audit trail?

options.t: A hiking path through the hills and woods near the city of the firm
options.why: A hiking path has nothing to do with accounting; an audit trail is a documented sequence of records that lets reviewers follow transactions.

options.t: A budget plan for the next year that the manager has prepared for staff
options.why: A budget plan is a forecast of future income and spending, not a record of past transactions that can be traced back.

options.t: A record that lets someone trace a transaction from source to report
options.why: An audit trail lets an auditor trace a transaction from the source document through journals and ledgers to the financial statements, or the reverse.

options.t: A list of employees and the hours that they worked in each pay period
options.why: A list of employees and hours is a payroll or time record; it may support an audit but is not itself the audit trail.

q: What is gross income for tax purposes?

options.t: Only gifts received by a person in a year
options.why: Gifts are only one possible item and are often excluded; gross income covers all income sources such as wages, interest and business earnings.

options.t: Only wages earned from a regular job
options.why: Wages are just one source; gross income also includes interest, dividends, business profit and other income received during the year.

options.t: Income left after all deductions apply
options.why: Income remaining after deductions is taxable income, not gross income, which is measured before any deductions are subtracted.

options.t: All income received before deductions
options.why: Gross income is the total income from all sources before deductions or adjustments, and it is the starting point for computing taxable income.

q: A taxpayer has $50,000 in gross income and a $12,000 standard deduction. What is taxable income (before other adjustments)?

options.why: Taxable income = gross income - deductions = $50,000 - $12,000 = $38,000, the amount to which tax rates are applied.
$50,000 is the gross income before the standard deduction is subtracted; taxable income is lower once the deduction is applied.
$12,000 is only the standard deduction; taxable income is what remains after subtracting it from gross income.
$62,000 adds the deduction to income, but deductions reduce taxable income and are never added to it.

q: What is a progressive tax system?

options.t: Lower incomes pay higher rates than the rich
options.why: Lower incomes paying higher rates describes a regressive tax, the opposite of progressive.

options.t: Higher incomes are taxed at higher rates
options.why: A progressive tax applies higher rates as income rises, so wealthier taxpayers pay a larger percentage, as in the US federal income tax brackets.

options.t: Everyone pays the same rate of tax on income
options.why: The same rate for everyone is a flat (proportional) tax, not a progressive system that raises rates with income.

options.t: No one pays tax at all in the country
options.why: A system where nobody pays tax is not a tax system; progressive taxes raise revenue by taxing higher incomes at higher rates.

q: What is a flat tax?

options.t: A tax that rises as income moves higher
options.why: A tax that rises as income rises is a progressive tax; a flat tax holds the rate constant at all income levels.

options.t: A tax only on sales of goods in shops
options.why: A tax only on sales is a sales tax, which is collected on purchases; a flat tax is an income tax with one rate.

options.t: A tax with the same rate for everyone
options.why: A flat tax applies one single rate to every taxpayer's income, regardless of how much the person earns.

options.t: A tax on property such as land and homes
options.why: A tax on land and homes is a property tax; flat tax describes a single rate on income, not the type of asset taxed.

q: Which is generally a deductible business expense?

options.t: A vacation trip
options.why: A vacation trip is a personal expense, which the IRS does not allow as a business deduction unless it is a legitimate business trip.

options.t: A parking fine
options.why: Parking fines are penalties for breaking the law and are not deductible, even when incurred while doing business.

options.t: Owner's food
options.why: Personal meals for the owner are generally personal living costs, not deductible business expenses, apart from limited business meals.

options.t: Office rent
options.why: Rent paid for office space is an ordinary and necessary cost of operating a business, so it is generally deductible.

q: What is estimated tax?

options.t: Quarterly payments made by people who do not have enough tax withheld
options.why: Estimated tax consists of quarterly payments by people, such as self-employed taxpayers, whose income has no or too little tax withheld.

options.t: A guess about next year's tax law made by the revenue agency in its report
options.why: Estimated tax is paid by the taxpayer, not a forecast of tax law by the revenue agency.

options.t: A tax on estimates made by people who file their yearly returns
options.why: Estimated tax is not a tax on guesses; it is a payment of expected income tax made in installments during the year.

options.t: A refund from the IRS paid to people who overpaid their taxes in the year
options.why: A refund is money returned for overpaying; estimated tax is a payment made in advance, the reverse of a refund.

q: What is the deadline for most individual federal returns?

options.t: January 1 each year
options.why: January 1 is New Year's Day and the start of the tax year, not the filing deadline for individual returns.

options.t: April 15 in most years
options.why: Most individual federal returns are due April 15 (or the next business day if it falls on a weekend or holiday).

options.t: July 4 of each year
options.why: July 4 is Independence Day, a federal holiday, and is not the deadline for filing individual tax returns.

options.t: December 31 of the year
options.why: December 31 ends the tax year for most individuals, but the return for that year is not due until the following April.

q: A business owes $1,200 in payroll taxes and does not pay by the deadline. What is the likely result?

options.t: Penalties and interest
options.why: Missing the deadline for payroll taxes leads to penalties and interest on the amount owed, because employers hold those taxes in trust for the government.

options.t: A discount on the tax owed
options.why: Late payment never earns a discount; the IRS adds charges rather than reducing the tax owed.

options.t: No consequence at all
options.why: Failing to pay payroll taxes has real consequences, including penalties and interest, and serious cases can bring personal liability.

options.t: A tax refund check
options.why: A refund check comes from overpaying taxes, not from underpaying; an unpaid balance leads to charges instead.

q: What is a depreciation deduction?

options.t: A deduction for salaries paid to workers in the year
options.why: Salaries are a separate deductible expense; a depreciation deduction covers the cost of using up assets, not wages.

options.t: A deduction for interest paid on a loan by the firm
options.why: Interest paid on loans is a separate deduction; depreciation relates to the wearing out of long-lived property.

options.t: A tax deduction for the wear of business assets over time
options.why: A depreciation deduction lets a business deduct the cost of an asset over its useful life, reflecting wear and tear over time.

options.t: A deduction for gifts given to friends and family by the owner
options.why: Gifts to friends and family are personal and not deductible as depreciation; depreciation applies to business assets only.

q: An auditor uses software to scan every payment for duplicates. What is this an example of?

options.t: Price discrimination by sellers
options.why: Price discrimination is a pricing strategy by sellers charging different customers different prices, unrelated to auditing payments.

options.t: Manual sampling of a few items by hand
options.why: Manual sampling examines a few items by hand; scanning every payment with software is automated and covers the whole population.

options.t: Inventory counting by hand weekly
options.why: Counting inventory by hand is a physical process; scanning payment records for duplicates uses software to examine transactions.

options.t: Data analytics for fraud detection
options.why: Using software to examine every payment for duplicates is data analytics, a tool that helps detect fraud and errors faster than manual checks.

q: What is a benefit of recurring invoices in accounting software?

options.t: They bill regular customers automatically on schedule
options.why: Recurring invoices automatically bill regular customers on a set schedule, saving time, reducing errors and speeding cash collection.

options.t: They remove the need for any customers at all in the market
options.why: Invoices cannot replace customers; recurring invoices only automate billing for customers who already exist.

options.t: They raise prices for the customers who get the invoices
options.why: Recurring invoices repeat the agreed amount on schedule; they do not raise prices unless the business changes the template.

options.t: They create duplicate payments to the vendors each month
options.why: Recurring invoices bill customers, not vendors; creating duplicate vendor payments would be a control weakness, not a benefit.

q: Why is it important to limit user access in accounting software?

options.t: To avoid backups of the data kept in the system
options.why: Backups protect data from loss, so limiting access does not avoid backups; both are controls that protect information.

options.t: To slow the system down for all users of the program
options.why: Limiting access has no purpose of slowing the system; permissions work in the background and are meant to protect data.
