options.t: To increase errors made by the staff in the system
options.why: Restricting user access reduces errors and fraud because only authorized people can change records; it is not intended to increase mistakes.

options.t: To prevent unauthorized changes and protect data
options.why: Limiting user access prevents unauthorized changes and protects sensitive data, which is a key internal control in accounting software.

q: What does a payroll specialist do?

options.t: Repairs equipment in the factory and plant of the firm
options.why: Repairing equipment is the work of a maintenance technician, not a payroll specialist who works with employee pay records.

options.t: Sells insurance to individuals and firms that wish cover
options.why: Selling insurance is the work of an insurance agent; payroll specialists handle pay, not policies.

options.t: Calculates pay, taxes and deductions for employees
options.why: A payroll specialist calculates employee pay, withholds taxes and deductions, and makes sure paychecks and payroll reports are accurate.

options.t: Designs logos and brochures for the marketing team
options.why: Designing logos and brochures is a graphic design and marketing role, not a payroll accounting task.

q: A person who enjoys planning and forecasting budgets might choose which career?

options.t: Lifeguard at a large public pool
options.why: A lifeguard watches swimmers for safety and does not use budgeting or forecasting skills.

options.t: Financial analyst or budget analyst
options.why: Financial and budget analysts plan, forecast and analyze budgets, which suits someone who enjoys numbers and projections.

options.t: Delivery driver for a courier firm
options.why: A delivery driver's work focuses on transporting packages, not on planning or forecasting budgets.

options.t: Warehouse loader moving boxes and stock
options.why: A warehouse loader moves boxes and stock, which is physical work that does not involve financial planning.

q: Which credential is common for management accountants?

options.t: CPR certificate for giving first aid
options.why: A CPR certificate shows first aid training and is unrelated to accounting careers.

options.t: CMA (Certified Management Accountant)
options.why: The CMA (Certified Management Accountant) credential is common for management accountants who work with budgeting, cost analysis and decision support.

options.t: CDL license for truck drivers only
options.why: A CDL is a commercial driver's license for truck drivers, which has nothing to do with accounting.

options.t: EMT license for medical staff only
options.why: An EMT license is for emergency medical technicians, a healthcare credential, not a credential for accountants.

q: What is the monetary unit assumption?

options.t: Currencies of countries may be added without conversion
options.why: Currencies cannot be added without conversion; the monetary unit assumption says to measure in a stable currency, such as the US dollar.

options.t: Money is the only thing that matters to a business owner
options.why: The assumption does not say money is all that matters; it says only that transactions measurable in money are recorded.

options.t: Business activity can be measured and recorded in money terms
options.why: The monetary unit assumption says business activity can be measured and recorded in money terms, such as US dollars, which allows amounts to be added.

options.t: Every item must be recorded at its current market price each day
options.why: Daily market-price recording is not required; assets are recorded at historical cost under the cost principle, not marked to market each day.

q: A building is bought for $200,000 and its market value later reaches $260,000. What is its recorded value under the cost principle?

options.why: Under the cost principle, assets stay on the books at original purchase price, so the building is carried at $200,000 despite the higher market value.
$260,000 is the market value, but the cost principle records assets at original cost, not at changing market values.
$230,000 is an invented midpoint; the cost principle uses actual purchase cost, not an average or estimate of value.
$60,000 is the unrecorded increase in market value; the cost principle ignores that gain and keeps the asset at its $200,000 purchase price.

q: What is the periodic inventory system?

options.t: Inventory updates after every sale, so records show the stock
options.why: Updating inventory after every sale describes the perpetual system; the periodic system updates only after a physical count.

options.t: Inventory is never counted by the staff or by the owners of the firm
options.why: Under the periodic system, inventory is counted physically, so saying it is never counted is wrong.

options.t: Inventory is guessed by the owners from the sales made each year
options.why: Inventory under any system must be based on counts or records, not guesses from sales totals.

options.t: Inventory is updated at the end of the period after a physical count
options.why: In the periodic system, inventory records are updated at the end of the period after a physical count, and cost of goods sold is computed then.

q: In a period of rising prices, which inventory method usually reports the higher net income?

options.t: FIFO
options.why: In rising prices FIFO assigns older, lower costs to cost of goods sold, giving lower COGS and therefore higher net income than LIFO.

options.t: Equal
options.why: The methods give different results when prices change, so net income is not equal under FIFO and LIFO in a rising-price period.

options.t: LIFO
options.why: LIFO charges the newest, higher costs to cost of goods sold, which lowers net income during rising prices, so it reports less.

options.t: Neither
options.why: The two methods do not give the same result when prices change; one reports clearly higher income than the other.

q: What is weighted-average inventory costing?

options.t: Ignoring costs when valuing the stock and working out the cost of goods sold each year every time
options.why: Weighted-average costing does not ignore costs; it uses them all, averaging the costs of all units available for sale.

options.t: Using the cost of the oldest unit only to value all the stock and the goods sold
options.why: Using the oldest unit's cost is FIFO, not weighted average, which blends all unit costs together.

options.t: Using the average cost of all units available to value inventory and cost of goods sold
options.why: Weighted average divides the total cost of goods available by total units to get an average cost used for both inventory and cost of goods sold.

options.t: Using the cost of the latest unit only, to value the stock and the goods sold
options.why: Using the cost of the latest units describes LIFO, not weighted average, which spreads cost across all units.

q: Which account type has a normal debit balance?

options.t: Liability
options.why: Liabilities have a normal credit balance, since they increase with credits and decrease with debits.

options.t: Capital
options.why: Capital is an equity account with a normal credit balance, increasing when the owner invests or profits are earned.

options.t: Revenue
options.why: Revenue accounts have a normal credit balance because revenue increases owner's equity, which grows with credits.

options.t: Asset
options.why: Assets have a normal debit balance: debits increase them and credits decrease them, matching the left side of the accounting equation.

q: Which account type has a normal credit balance?

options.t: Drawings
options.why: Drawings reduce owner's equity, so they have a normal debit balance, not a credit balance.

options.t: Liability
options.why: Liabilities have a normal credit balance, because they sit on the right side of the accounting equation and increase with credits.

options.t: Expense
options.why: Expenses reduce equity, so they carry a normal debit balance and increase with debits.

options.t: Asset
options.why: Assets sit on the left of the accounting equation and have a normal debit balance, not a credit balance.

q: What is the effect of a debit on an expense account?

options.t: It increases revenue
options.why: A debit to an expense account does not touch revenue; it increases the expense itself, as expenses sit on the debit side.

options.t: It decreases the expense
options.why: Decreasing an expense requires a credit; a debit increases it, because expense accounts have normal debit balances.

options.t: It has no effect at all
options.why: Every debit has an effect: on an expense account it raises the balance and, with the offsetting credit, records the transaction.

options.t: It increases the expense
options.why: Expense accounts have normal debit balances, so a debit increases the expense, such as debiting Rent Expense when rent is paid.

q: What is the effect of a credit on a revenue account?

options.t: It increases revenue
options.why: Revenue accounts have normal credit balances, so a credit increases revenue, which in turn increases owner's equity.

options.t: It has no effect
options.why: A credit always changes the account's balance; for revenue it raises the balance rather than doing nothing.

options.t: It increases assets
options.why: Revenue does not itself increase assets; a credit to revenue is matched by a debit to cash or receivables, which increases assets.

options.t: It decreases revenue
options.why: A debit, not a credit, decreases revenue, since revenue accounts normally carry credit balances.

q: A company pays $900 cash for rent. Which entry is correct?

options.t: Debit Rent Expense, credit Payable
options.why: Crediting a payable would mean the rent is still owed; the question says $900 was paid in cash, so Cash must be credited.

options.t: Debit Prepaid Rent, credit Revenue
options.why: Prepaid Rent and Revenue do not apply: paying rent as it comes due is an expense, and paying cash does not create revenue.

options.t: Debit Rent Expense, credit Cash
options.why: Paying rent increases Rent Expense (debit) and decreases Cash (credit), so the entry is Debit Rent Expense $900, Credit Cash $900.

options.t: Debit Cash, credit Rent Expense
options.why: This reverses the entry: debiting Cash would show cash increasing and crediting Rent Expense would reduce an expense, the opposite of paying rent.

q: A company receives $500 cash from a customer for services performed. Which entry is correct?

options.t: Debit Service Revenue, credit Cash
options.why: Debiting Revenue and crediting Cash reverses the entry; receiving cash for services increases both cash and revenue.

options.t: Debit Cash, credit Service Revenue
options.why: Cash comes in (debit Cash) and the service revenue is earned (credit Service Revenue), so Debit Cash $500, Credit Service Revenue $500.

options.t: Debit Cash, credit Accounts Payable
options.why: Accounts Payable is a liability for money owed; services performed for cash earn revenue and do not create a payable.

options.t: Debit Accounts Receivable, credit Cash
options.why: Debiting Accounts Receivable and crediting Cash would mean the customer owes money and cash goes out, which is not what happened.

q: An owner invests $10,000 cash in the business. Which entry is correct?

options.t: Debit Owner's Capital, credit Cash
options.why: This reverses the entry; an owner investment increases cash and capital, rather than reducing them.

options.t: Debit Drawings and credit Cash
options.why: Drawings record withdrawals by the owner, which reduce equity; an investment is the opposite and increases cash and capital.

options.t: Debit Cash, credit Owner's Capital
options.why: An investment increases Cash (debit) and the owner's equity (credit Owner's Capital), so Debit Cash $10,000, Credit Owner's Capital $10,000.

options.t: Debit Cash and credit the Revenue
options.why: An owner investment is not revenue; crediting Revenue would overstate income, while capital is the proper equity account.

q: An owner withdraws $1,200 cash for personal use. Which entry is correct?

options.t: Debit Capital and credit Revenue
options.why: Capital and revenue are not involved in a personal withdrawal; revenue comes from earning income, not from owner withdrawals.

options.t: Debit Owner's Drawings, credit Cash
options.why: Withdrawals reduce owner's equity through the Drawings account (debit) and reduce cash (credit): Debit Owner's Drawings $1,200, Credit Cash $1,200.

options.t: Debit Salaries Expense, credit Cash
options.why: Salaries Expense is for wages paid to employees; an owner's personal withdrawal is recorded as drawings, not as an expense.

options.t: Debit Cash and credit the Drawings
options.why: Debiting Cash and crediting Drawings reverses the entry; a withdrawal takes cash out of the business.

q: A company buys equipment for $5,000, paying $2,000 cash and owing the rest. What is credited to Accounts Payable?

options.why: $5,000 is the whole cost of the equipment; part was paid in cash, so only the unpaid portion goes to Accounts Payable.
$7,000 adds the cash payment to the cost, which makes no sense; the payable cannot exceed the $5,000 purchase price.
$2,000 is the cash paid, which is credited to Cash; the payable covers the rest of the cost.
The unpaid portion is $5,000 - $2,000 = $3,000, which is credited to Accounts Payable, with $2,000 credited to Cash and $5,000 debited to Equipment.

q: What is the purpose of a trial balance?

options.t: To verify total debits equal total credits
options.why: A trial balance lists all ledger account balances to verify that total debits equal total credits, which checks the mathematical accuracy of posting.

options.t: To list the customers and their details
options.why: A list of customers and details is a customer or receivables ledger, not a trial balance, which lists account balances.

options.t: To show the net income for the whole year
options.why: Net income is shown on the income statement, not the trial balance, although the trial balance helps prepare it.

options.t: To prove the ledger has no errors in it
options.why: A trial balance cannot prove there are no errors, because errors like wrong accounts or omitted entries keep debits and credits equal.

q: Can a trial balance be in balance yet contain errors?

options.t: Yes, such as posting the right amount to the wrong account
options.why: Yes: posting the right amount to the wrong account, or omitting a whole transaction, leaves debits equal to credits even though errors exist.

options.t: Only for assets, never for any other type of account
options.why: Errors that leave a trial balance in balance can occur in any account type, not just assets.

options.t: Only for expenses, never for any other type of account
options.why: Errors that leave a trial balance in balance can occur in any account type, not just expenses.

options.t: No, never, because debits always equal credits in total overall
options.why: Equal debits and credits only prove mathematical equality; they do not prove the entries are correct, so a balanced trial balance may hide errors.

q: A trial balance shows debits of $50,000 and credits of $48,500. What is a likely cause?

options.t: Taxes are due on the $1,500 gap between the two totals
options.why: Taxes due are unrelated to a trial balance difference; the $1,500 gap signals a bookkeeping error rather than a tax issue.

options.t: The business earned $1,500, as debits exceed the credits
options.why: A business earning money does not cause debits to exceed credits in the trial balance; double-entry always records equal amounts.

options.t: Nothing is wrong, as the two totals are close enough to count
options.why: A trial balance must balance exactly; even a small difference signals an error that must be found, however close the totals look.

options.t: A $1,500 error such as an omitted credit or a posting mistake
options.why: Debits exceeding credits by $1,500 suggests a $1,500 error, such as an omitted credit, a one-sided entry or a posting mistake.

q: What is a transposition error?

options.t: Adding the numbers wrongly in a column of the ledger
options.why: Adding numbers wrongly is a mathematical or addition error; a transposition error specifically reverses digits.

options.t: Reversing digits in a number, such as writing 54 as 45
options.why: A transposition error is reversing digits in a number, such as writing 54 as 45, which makes a difference divisible by 9.

options.t: Posting to the wrong account, such as the purchases ledger
options.why: Posting to a wrong account is an error of principle or commission; it differs from reversing the digits of a number.

options.t: Omitting an entry from the books by mistake or by design
options.why: Leaving out an entry is an error of omission, not a transposition of digits.

q: A trial balance differs by $36. Which error is most likely?

options.t: A change in tax laws
options.why: Changes in tax laws do not affect whether debits and credits equal; they do not explain a small trial balance difference.

options.t: A depreciation change
options.why: A change in depreciation method affects expense amounts but is recorded with equal debits and credits, so it would not cause a trial balance difference.

options.t: A transposition error
options.why: A difference divisible by 9, such as $36, strongly suggests digits were reversed, like writing 54 as 45 (a $9 difference per swap), which is a transposition error.

options.t: A missing sales entry
options.why: A missing sales entry omits both debit and credit, so the trial balance would still balance; it would not create a $36 difference.

q: What is the normal balance of Accumulated Depreciation?

options.t: Credit
options.why: Accumulated Depreciation is a contra-asset account, so it has a normal credit balance, which reduces the related asset's book value.

options.t: Debit
options.why: A debit balance is normal for assets; accumulated depreciation is a contra-asset with the opposite, credit, balance.

options.t: Zero
options.why: Accumulated Depreciation grows each period as depreciation is recorded, so it normally carries a balance rather than zero.

options.t: Either
options.why: Every account has a normal balance; accumulated depreciation normally carries a credit balance, not either one.

q: What is the normal balance of Sales Returns and Allowances?

options.t: Either
options.why: Every account has a normal side; Sales Returns and Allowances is a contra-revenue account with a normal debit balance, not either.

options.t: Credit
options.why: A credit balance is normal for revenue, but this is a contra-revenue account, so it carries the opposite, debit, balance.

options.t: Debit
options.why: Sales Returns and Allowances is a contra-revenue account, so it has a normal debit balance that reduces gross sales to net sales.

options.t: Zero
options.why: It builds up as customers return goods or receive allowances, so it normally has a balance and is not zero.

q: What is the matching principle?

options.t: Debits match credits in every entry that is made in the books of a firm
options.why: Debits matching credits is double-entry bookkeeping, not the matching principle, which concerns timing of expenses.

options.t: Expenses are recorded in the same period as the revenues they help earn
options.why: The matching principle records expenses in the same period as the revenues they help earn, so profit is measured accurately for the period.

options.t: Revenue is recorded when cash is received, whatever the sale date
options.why: Recording revenue when cash is received describes cash-basis accounting, which differs from the matching principle.

options.t: Assets match liabilities in total on the balance sheet at the year end
options.why: Assets equaling liabilities plus equity is the accounting equation, not the matching principle, which links expenses to revenues.

q: What is the cost principle?

options.t: Assets are recorded at market value each year
options.why: Recording assets at market value each year contradicts the cost principle, which keeps them at original cost.

options.t: Assets are not recorded in the books of the firm
options.why: Assets are recorded in the books; the cost principle just says how they are valued.

options.t: Assets are recorded at replacement cost on the issue date
options.why: Replacement cost is a different valuation approach; the cost principle uses what was actually paid when the asset was acquired.

options.t: Assets are recorded at their original purchase cost
options.why: The cost principle records assets at their original purchase cost, which is objective and verifiable, and keeps them at that cost despite market changes.

q: What is the monetary unit concept?

options.t: Employee morale is recorded in the books of the firm
options.why: Employee morale cannot be measured in money, so the monetary unit concept excludes it from the books.

options.t: All events are recorded in the books of the firm
options.why: Not all events are recorded; the monetary unit concept limits records to events measurable in money.

options.t: Only transactions measurable in money are recorded
options.why: The monetary unit concept says only transactions that can be measured in money terms are recorded in the accounting records.

options.t: Customer opinions are recorded as soon as they are given
options.why: Customer opinions cannot be reliably measured in money, so the monetary unit concept leaves them out.

q: What is the revenue recognition principle?

options.t: Revenue is recorded when earned, not necessarily when cash is received
options.why: The revenue recognition principle records revenue when it is earned, usually when goods or services are delivered, not necessarily when cash arrives.

options.t: Revenue is never recorded in the books until the firm closes down overall
options.why: Revenue is recorded as it is earned during operations, not only when the firm closes down.

options.t: Revenue is recorded when cash is paid, whatever the sale date is
options.why: Revenue is recognized when earned, not when cash is paid; the payment date does not decide timing.

options.t: Revenue is recorded at year end only, when the books are closed
options.why: Revenue is recorded throughout the year as earned, not just at year end when books are closed.

q: What is cash-basis accounting?

options.t: Recording revenue when earned and expenses when they are incurred
options.why: Recording revenue when earned and expenses when incurred describes accrual accounting, the opposite of the cash basis.

options.t: Recording revenue and expenses only when cash is received or paid
options.why: Cash-basis accounting records revenue only when cash is received and expenses only when cash is paid, regardless of when they were earned or incurred.

options.t: Recording only the credits from every entry in the ledger
options.why: Recording only the credits of an entry is not an accounting method; double-entry records both debits and credits.

options.t: Recording estimates of revenue and expenses before they have taken place
options.why: Recording estimates before events take place is not cash basis; it involves anticipating transactions rather than actual cash flow.

q: A consultant completes a job in December but is paid in January. Under accrual accounting, when is the revenue recorded?

options.t: Both months
options.why: Revenue is recorded once, when earned, not in both months; counting it twice would overstate revenue.

options.t: Neither
options.why: The job was completed, so the revenue is earned and must be recorded in some period, not skipped.

options.t: January
options.why: January is when cash is received, which is the cash basis; accrual accounting records revenue when earned.

options.t: December
options.why: Under accrual accounting, revenue is recorded when earned, so December is correct since the job was completed then; the January payment just collects a receivable.

q: A business receives its December electric bill in January. Under accrual accounting, when is the expense recorded?

options.t: Both months
options.why: The expense is recorded once, in the period it was incurred, not in two months.

options.t: December
options.why: Under accrual accounting, the expense is recorded when incurred; December's electricity was used in December, so the bill is accrued as an expense then.

options.t: January
options.why: January is when the bill is received or paid, which reflects cash-basis timing; accrual records the expense in December.

options.t: Neither
options.why: The electricity was used, so an expense exists and must be recorded in some period.

q: What is a check stub used for?

options.t: Closing the books at the end of the fiscal year
options.why: Closing the books is done with closing entries, not with a check stub.

options.t: Opening an account at a local bank for the firm
options.why: Opening a bank account uses signature cards and deposit forms, not check stubs.

options.t: Recording check details for later reference
options.why: A check stub records details of a check, such as date, payee and amount, for later reference in reconciling the account.

options.t: Paying employees only, with the stub handed over
options.why: Check stubs are not limited to paying employees; they record details of any check issued by the firm.

q: What is the owner's equity formula?

options.t: Assets minus liabilities
options.why: Owner's equity equals assets minus liabilities, the residual claim of the owner after creditors are paid.

options.t: Liabilities minus assets
options.why: Liabilities minus assets reverses the formula, which would produce a negative amount for a solvent business.

options.t: Assets plus liabilities
options.why: Assets plus liabilities double counts; the accounting equation sets assets equal to liabilities plus owner's equity.

options.t: Revenue minus assets
options.why: Revenue minus assets mixes an income statement item with a balance sheet item and has no meaning as an equity formula.

q: Assets are $80,000 and owner's equity is $50,000. What are liabilities?

options.why: $50,000 is the owner's equity, not liabilities; liabilities are assets minus equity.
$130,000 adds equity to assets, but the equation requires subtracting: assets = liabilities + equity.
$80,000 is the total of assets; liabilities are only the part not funded by the owner.
Liabilities = assets - owner's equity = $80,000 - $50,000 = $30,000, from the equation assets = liabilities + equity.

q: A business has liabilities of $25,000 and owner's equity of $40,000. What are total assets?

options.why: Assets = liabilities + owner's equity = $25,000 + $40,000 = $65,000, since the equation requires both sides to be equal.
$25,000 is only the liabilities; total assets include the owner's equity funding as well.
$15,000 subtracts equity from liabilities, but the equation adds them to get assets.
$40,000 is only the owner's equity; total assets equal liabilities plus equity.

q: Paying a $600 account payable has what effect?

options.t: Increases assets and liabilities by the same
options.why: Paying a payable does not increase assets; cash goes out, so assets fall as liabilities fall.

options.t: Decreases equity by the same amount paid
options.why: Paying a payable that was already recorded does not reduce equity; the expense was recognized earlier, and only cash and liabilities change.

options.t: Decreases assets and decreases liabilities
options.why: Paying $600 reduces Cash (an asset) and reduces Accounts Payable (a liability) by the same amount, leaving equity unchanged.

options.t: Increases assets only, by the amount paid
options.why: Paying a debt does not increase assets; cash decreases, and the liability also decreases.

q: Buying supplies on account has what effect?

options.t: Decreases assets by the cost of supplies
options.why: Buying supplies on account increases assets (supplies) rather than decreasing them; cash is not paid yet.

options.t: Increases assets and increases liabilities
options.why: Supplies (an asset) increase, and Accounts Payable (a liability) increases by the same amount, so the equation stays balanced.

options.t: Increases equity by the cost of supplies
options.why: Buying on credit does not change equity; the asset rises and an equal liability is recorded.

options.t: Decreases liabilities as supplies get paid
options.why: Liabilities increase when supplies are bought on account, and they decrease only when the bill is later paid.

q: Earning service revenue on credit has what effect?

options.t: Increases liabilities and decreases owner's equity
options.why: Earning revenue on credit increases assets (receivables) and increases equity, not liabilities.

options.t: Decreases assets by the full amount earned
options.why: Assets increase because a receivable is created, so decreasing them is wrong.

options.t: Decreases equity by the full amount earned
options.why: Revenue increases owner's equity; it does not reduce it.

options.t: Increases assets and increases owner's equity
options.why: A credit sale raises Accounts Receivable (an asset) and Service Revenue, which increases owner's equity, so both sides rise equally.

q: Paying wages in cash has what effect?

options.t: Decreases assets and decreases owner's equity
options.why: Paying wages in cash reduces Cash (an asset) and raises Wages Expense, which reduces owner's equity.

options.t: No effect on assets or on owner's equity
options.why: Paying wages does affect the books: cash goes out and an expense reduces equity.

options.t: Increases assets by the total amount of wages
options.why: Paying wages reduces cash, so assets decrease rather than increase.

options.t: Increases liabilities and increases owner's equity
options.why: Paying wages does not create a liability or add to equity; cash is paid out and an expense reduces equity.

q: What is the first step in the accounting cycle?

options.t: Prepare financial statements for the owners
options.why: Preparing financial statements comes late in the cycle, after the ledger, trial balance and adjustments are done.

options.t: Close the books at the end of the year
options.why: Closing the books comes near the end of the cycle, after statements are prepared.

options.t: Post to the ledger accounts of the firm
options.why: Posting to the ledger follows journalizing, so it cannot be the first step.

options.t: Analyze transactions from source documents
options.why: The accounting cycle begins by analyzing transactions from source documents such as invoices and receipts, and then they are journalized.

q: What follows journalizing in the accounting cycle?

options.t: Financial statements
options.why: Financial statements come near the end of the cycle, after posting, trial balance and adjusting entries.

options.t: Adjusting entries
options.why: Adjusting entries come after the trial balance is prepared, not immediately after journalizing.

options.t: Posting to the ledger
options.why: After transactions are journalized, they are posted to the ledger accounts, which sorts the information by account.

options.t: Closing the entries
options.why: Closing entries come near the end of the cycle, after statements are prepared.

q: What is the purpose of the worksheet?

options.t: To replace the ledger accounts of the firm
options.why: The worksheet is a working tool and does not replace the ledger accounts, which remain the permanent records.

options.t: To organize data for adjustments and statements
options.why: The worksheet organizes trial balance data, adjustments and balances to help prepare the financial statements.

options.t: To pay bills owed by the firm to its suppliers
options.why: Bills are paid through payment procedures, not the worksheet, which is only an analysis tool.

options.t: To record source documents such as invoices
options.why: Source documents such as invoices are the starting records of transactions, not the worksheet, which is prepared later.

q: What are adjusting entries?

options.t: Entries for budgets that managers prepare for the next year of trading
options.why: Budgets for next year are planning tools, not adjusting entries, which update accounts at period end.

options.t: Entries at period end to update accounts for accruals and deferrals
options.why: Adjusting entries made at period end update accounts for accruals and deferrals so revenues and expenses are in the correct period.

options.t: Entries for new customers who sign up with the firm during the year
options.why: New customers are handled through sales and credit procedures, not by adjusting entries.

options.t: Entries that correct spelling mistakes in the customer names list
options.why: Correcting customer names is a data cleanup; adjusting entries are accounting entries tied to timing of revenues and expenses.

q: A company has $1,200 of supplies on hand at year end. It started with $2,000 and bought none. What adjusting entry is needed?

options.t: Debit Supplies Expense $800, credit Supplies $800
options.why: Supplies used = $2,000 - $1,200 = $800, so debit Supplies Expense $800 and credit Supplies $800 to reduce the asset to the $1,200 on hand.

options.t: Debit Cash $800 and credit Supplies for $800
options.why: Cash is not involved in this adjustment since the supplies were already paid for; the entry moves cost from asset to expense.

options.t: Debit Supplies $800, credit Expense for the leftover
options.why: This entry is reversed and vague: the asset is reduced by a credit to Supplies and the expense is increased by a debit.

options.t: No entry is needed for the supplies used up
options.why: An entry is needed; without it, assets would be overstated and expenses understated by the $800 of supplies used.

q: A business paid $3,600 on January 1 for a 12-month insurance policy. What is the monthly insurance expense?

options.why: $30 would be a monthly figure for a tiny policy, but $3,600 over 12 months is $300 per month.
$1,200 is the cost for four months, not one; spread across 12 months the cost is much smaller.
$3,600 is the total premium for the whole year, not the monthly expense.
Monthly insurance expense = $3,600 / 12 months = $300, which is moved from Prepaid Insurance to expense each month.

q: Using the same policy, what is the prepaid insurance balance after 3 months?

options.why: $300 is the monthly expense, not the balance; after 3 months the unexpired portion is much larger.
$900 is the expense used after 3 months, not the remaining balance of prepaid insurance.
After 3 months $900 has expired ($300 x 3), so Prepaid Insurance = $3,600 - $900 = $2,700 for the remaining 9 months.
$3,600 is the original premium; after 3 months some has expired, so the balance is lower.

q: Wages of $2,000 earned by employees at year end are unpaid. What adjusting entry is needed?

options.t: Debit Cash and credit Wages Expense $2,000
options.why: Cash is not paid yet, so crediting Cash would be wrong; the wages are owed, not paid.

options.t: Debit Wages Payable, credit Wages Expense
options.why: Debiting Wages Payable and crediting Wages Expense reverses the entry and would reduce a liability and expense instead of recording them.

options.t: Debit Wages Expense, credit Wages Payable
options.why: Unpaid but earned wages require Debit Wages Expense $2,000 and Credit Wages Payable $2,000, matching the expense to the period it was incurred.

options.t: No entry is needed for the unpaid wages
options.why: An entry is required; skipping it would understate expenses and liabilities, violating the matching principle.

q: A business earned $1,500 of interest not yet received at year end. What adjusting entry is needed?

options.t: Debit Interest Revenue $1,500, credit Receivable overall
options.why: Interest Revenue should be credited, not debited, and the debit should be to a receivable; this wording reverses the entry.

options.t: No entry is needed until the cash is received
options.why: Under accrual accounting, earned revenue must be recorded in the period earned, even without cash.

options.t: Debit Cash and credit Interest Revenue $1,500
options.why: Cash has not been received, so debiting Cash would be wrong; a receivable should be recorded instead.

options.t: Debit Interest Receivable, credit Interest Revenue
options.why: Accrued interest earned but not received requires Debit Interest Receivable $1,500 and Credit Interest Revenue $1,500, so income is reported in the right period.

q: A customer prepaid $4,000 for a 4-month service, and 1 month has been performed. What revenue is recognized?

options.why: This $3,000 figure is the revenue still unearned after one month, not the amount recognized; the remaining 3 of 4 months stay as a liability until performed.
Revenue is earned as service is performed: $4,000 / 4 months = $1,000 per month, so $1,000 is recognized now and $3,000 stays in Unearned Revenue.
This is the full prepayment of $4,000, but revenue cannot be recognized all at once when only 1 of the 4 months of service has been performed.
Zero would be right only if no service had been performed yet; here one month is complete, so $1,000 of the prepayment has been earned as revenue.

q: Which accounts are closed at period end?

options.t: Revenue, expense and drawings accounts
options.why: Temporary accounts (revenue, expenses and drawings) are closed at period end so they start the next period at zero, and their balances move into capital.

options.t: Asset accounts such as cash and land
options.why: Assets like cash and land are permanent (real) accounts; their balances carry forward to the next period and are never closed to zero at period end.

options.t: Capital account balance, which carries over
options.why: The capital account is permanent: it receives the closing entries and carries its balance into the next period, so it is not itself closed.

options.t: Liability accounts such as payables
options.why: Liabilities such as accounts payable are permanent balance sheet accounts; they keep their balances into the next period and are not closed.

q: After closing, net income of $12,000 was transferred to which account?

options.t: Revenue sales
options.why: Revenue is a temporary account that is itself closed out at period end; it feeds net income but does not receive the net income transfer.

options.t: Accounts Payable
options.why: Accounts Payable is a liability showing what the business owes suppliers; net income increases owner's equity, not a liability balance.

options.t: Owner's Capital
options.why: In closing, Income Summary is closed to the owner's Capital account, so $12,000 of net income increases Owner's Capital, which is permanent equity.

options.t: Cash on hand
options.why: Cash is an asset that is not affected by the closing entries; profit is recorded in equity, not moved into the cash account.

q: What is the post-closing trial balance?

options.t: A budget that managers use to plan spending in the next period
options.why: A budget is a forward-looking plan for spending, while a post-closing trial balance is a backward-looking check of ledger balances after closing.

options.t: A trial balance of permanent accounts after closing entries
options.why: After closing entries, only permanent accounts (assets, liabilities, capital) have balances, so this trial balance confirms debits equal credits before the next period.

options.t: A list of expenses that the firm has paid out during the year
options.why: Listing expenses paid describes an expense report; a post-closing trial balance contains no expenses because those accounts were closed to zero.

options.t: A trial balance before adjustments, prepared to check the accounts
options.why: That describes an unadjusted trial balance, taken before adjusting entries; the post-closing version is prepared after closing and lists only permanent accounts.

q: What is an unadjusted trial balance?

options.t: Never prepared by any accountant in the firm at all
options.why: Accountants routinely prepare an unadjusted trial balance as a check on the ledger before making adjusting entries, so it is a normal step.

options.t: After adjusting entries are all posted to the ledger
options.why: A trial balance after adjusting entries is the adjusted trial balance, a later step; the unadjusted one comes before those entries are posted.

options.t: After closing entries are all posted to the ledger
options.why: A trial balance taken after closing entries is the post-closing trial balance, which includes only permanent accounts; it is not the unadjusted version.

options.t: A trial balance prepared before adjusting entries
options.why: The unadjusted trial balance lists ledger balances before adjusting entries, proving debits equal credits and showing which accruals and deferrals still need adjustment.

q: What is an adjusted trial balance?

options.t: A trial balance prepared after adjusting entries are posted
options.why: The adjusted trial balance is prepared after adjusting entries are posted, and it is the source for preparing the financial statements.

options.t: A trial balance prepared before the adjusting entries
options.why: A trial balance prepared before adjusting entries is the unadjusted trial balance, the earlier step; the adjusted version reflects accruals and deferrals.

options.t: A budget that managers use to plan spending in the next period
options.why: A budget is a spending plan for the future; the adjusted trial balance is a list of account balances after adjustments, used to build statements.

options.t: After closing entries are posted to the ledger accounts
options.why: A trial balance after closing entries is the post-closing trial balance, which has only permanent accounts; the adjusted trial balance comes before closing.

q: In what order are the main statements prepared?

options.t: Any order that the accountant likes best at the time of closing
options.why: Statements must follow a set order because each feeds the next; letting the accountant choose freely would break the flow of net income into equity.

options.t: Income statement, statement of owner's equity, balance sheet
options.why: Net income from the income statement goes to the statement of owner's equity, whose ending capital goes on the balance sheet, so this order is required.

options.t: Equity statement first, then the balance sheet and income
options.why: Starting with the equity statement fails because it needs net income, which the income statement has not yet produced.

options.t: Balance sheet first, then the income and equity statements
options.why: The balance sheet needs ending capital from the equity statement, which needs net income from the income statement, so the balance sheet comes last.

q: What is a calendar year?

options.t: Any 12 months in a row
options.why: Any 12 months in a row can describe a fiscal year, which may start in any month; a calendar year has fixed start and end dates.

options.t: July 1 to June 30 each year
options.why: July 1 to June 30 is a common fiscal year (used by many governments and schools), not a calendar year, which runs January through December.

options.t: January 1 to December 31
options.why: A calendar year runs January 1 to December 31; businesses using it have a fiscal year that matches the calendar, which simplifies tax reporting.

options.t: A quarter of the whole year
options.why: A quarter is only three months, one fourth of a year, so it cannot be the whole 12-month calendar year.

q: What does posting a debit to the ledger do?

options.t: Creates a statement for the customer and mails it
options.why: Mailing a statement to a customer is billing, not posting; posting is the internal step of moving journal amounts into the ledger accounts.

options.t: Deletes the entry from the journal of the firm
options.why: Posting does not delete journal entries; the journal remains the permanent original record, and posting just copies amounts into the ledger.

options.t: Pays the bill that the firm owes to its supplier
options.why: Paying a supplier is a separate cash transaction; posting is a bookkeeping step that records amounts and does not itself move any money.

options.t: Copies the debit amount to the correct account
options.why: Posting copies each journal debit to the matching ledger account on the debit side, so the ledger shows the running balance of every account.

q: What is a T account?

options.t: A simple form showing debits on the left and credits on the right
options.why: A T account is a simplified ledger form shaped like a T, with debits on the left and credits on the right, used to see an account's activity.

options.t: A tax account that is used to track a firm's yearly payments to the IRS
options.why: A T account has nothing to do with taxes owed to the IRS; the T refers to the shape of the form used to show debits and credits.

options.t: A time record that shows the hours each employee has worked this week
options.why: Hours worked by employees are tracked on timesheets or time cards, not in a T account, which records debits and credits for one account.

options.t: A trial form that lists every account balance before reports are made
options.why: A list of every account balance is a trial balance; a T account shows only one account, and the T is the form's shape.

q: In a T account, Cash has debits of $9,000 and credits of $6,500. What is the balance?

options.t: $0 balance
options.why: A zero balance would require debits equal to credits; here debits of $9,000 exceed credits of $6,500, so the account has a balance left over.

options.t: $2,500 debit
options.why: Cash is an asset with a normal debit balance: $9,000 debits - $6,500 credits = $2,500, which is a debit balance.

options.t: $15,500 debit
options.why: This adds the debits and credits together ($9,000 + $6,500); a T account balance is the difference between the two sides, not the sum.

options.t: $2,500 credit
options.why: The $2,500 amount is right, but debits are larger than credits, so the balance falls on the debit side and cannot be a credit.

q: Accounts Payable has debits of $3,000 and credits of $7,500. What is the balance?

options.t: $0 balance
options.why: A zero balance would need debits equal to credits; here the two sides differ ($3,000 versus $7,500), so a balance remains.

options.t: $4,500 debit
options.why: The amount is correct, but credits ($7,500) exceed debits ($3,000), so the balance sits on the credit side and cannot be a debit.

options.t: $4,500 credit
options.why: Accounts Payable is a liability with a normal credit balance: $7,500 credits - $3,000 debits = $4,500 credit, still owed to suppliers.

options.t: $10,500 credit
options.why: This adds the two sides ($3,000 + $7,500); the balance is the difference between debits and credits, which is $4,500, not the sum.

q: A business sells $1,500 of goods on account. Which entry is correct?

options.t: Debit Accounts Receivable, credit Sales
options.why: A sale on account means the customer has not paid yet, so Accounts Receivable is debited for the $1,500 owed and Sales revenue is credited.

options.t: Debit Cash and credit the Receivable
options.why: Debiting Cash is wrong because no cash was received in an on-account sale, and crediting the Receivable would reduce what customers owe.

options.t: Debit Payable and credit the Sales
options.why: Accounts Payable is a liability for money the business owes others; a sale creates a receivable, an asset, so debiting Payable is wrong.

options.t: Debit Sales and credit Receivable for it
options.why: Debiting Sales and crediting Receivable reverses the sale (it would be a return or cancelled sale), rather than recording a new sale of $1,500.

q: A customer pays $1,500 on account. Which entry is correct?

options.t: Debit Cash and credit Sales Revenue
options.why: Crediting Sales Revenue would count the sale a second time; revenue was recorded when the sale was made, and this payment only collects the receivable.

options.t: Debit Sales and credit Cash received
options.why: Debiting Sales would reduce revenue; collecting a customer's payment does not change revenue, only the form of the asset from receivable to cash.

options.t: Debit Receivable and credit Cash in full
options.why: This is reversed: debiting Receivable would increase what customers owe, while a collection should decrease the Receivable with a credit.

options.t: Debit Cash, credit Accounts Receivable
options.why: Cash increases (debit) and Accounts Receivable decreases (credit) by $1,500; one asset is swapped for another, so total assets and revenue are unchanged.

q: A business buys $800 of inventory on account. Which entry is correct?

options.t: Debit Merchandise Inventory, credit Cash for $800
options.why: Crediting Cash would be right for a cash purchase, but the question says on account, so no cash leaves the business yet.

options.t: Debit Merchandise Inventory, credit Accounts Payable
options.why: Inventory (an asset) increases with a debit, and Accounts Payable (a liability) increases with a credit of $800 because the business owes the supplier.

options.t: Debit Payable, credit Inventory, as if paid in cash
options.why: This is reversed and treats the purchase as paid: it would reduce inventory and payable, but buying on account raises both inventory and the payable.

options.t: Debit Cash, credit Merchandise Inventory for $800
options.why: Debiting Cash would increase cash, which is the opposite of a purchase; buying inventory raises inventory with a debit and does not bring in cash.

q: A business pays a supplier $800 owed. Which entry is correct?

options.t: Debit Inventory, credit Receivable
options.why: Debiting Inventory is wrong because paying a bill does not buy goods, and a Receivable is money owed to the business, not by it.

options.t: Debit Cash and credit the Payable
options.why: Crediting the Payable would increase what is owed; paying a supplier should reduce the liability with a debit and reduce Cash with a credit.

options.t: Debit Expense and credit the Cash
options.why: Debiting an Expense would record a new cost; the expense or inventory was recorded when purchased, so payment only settles the existing payable.

options.t: Debit Accounts Payable, credit Cash
options.why: Paying the supplier decreases the liability, so Accounts Payable is debited $800, and Cash is credited because the asset decreases by the same amount.

q: What do the terms 2/10, n/30 mean?

options.t: A 10% discount if paid in 2 days, with net due in 10 days
options.why: The terms are 2/10, so the discount is 2%, not 10%, and the 10 refers to the discount period, not the due date; the net is due in 30 days.

options.t: 2 days discount within 10 months, with all due in 30 months as a rule
options.why: This misreads days as months; credit terms use days, so 10 and 30 refer to days after the invoice date, not months.

options.t: 2% discount if paid within 10 days; full amount due in 30 days
options.why: 2/10, n/30 means a 2% discount if paid within 10 days; otherwise the full (net) amount is due within 30 days of the invoice date.

options.t: Net amount due in full after 2 days from the invoice date
options.why: The net amount is due in 30 days, not 2 days; the 2 in the terms is the discount percentage, which applies if paid within 10 days.

q: An invoice for $2,000 has terms 2/10, n/30. What is the amount due if paid on day 8?

options.why: Day 8 is within the 10-day discount period, so the discount is 2% x $2,000 = $40, and the amount due is $2,000 - $40 = $1,960.
This adds the discount ($2,000 + $40) instead of subtracting it; paying early earns a discount, so the payment is lower than the invoice.
This subtracts a 10% discount ($200); the terms give 2% (the 10 is the number of days), so the discount is $40, not $200.
Paying the full $2,000 would be due only after the discount period ends (day 11 to 30); on day 8 the 2% discount is available.

q: An invoice for $5,000 has terms 3/10, n/30. What discount is earned if paid on day 10?

options.why: This is 10% of $5,000 ($500); the discount rate is 3%, and the 10 in the terms is the number of days to qualify for it.
This is 0.3% of $5,000 ($15), a misplaced decimal; the 3% rate gives $5,000 x 0.03 = $150.
This is 30% of $5,000; the 30 in the terms is the due date in days, not the discount percentage, which is 3%.
Day 10 is the last day of the discount period, so the discount is 3% x $5,000 = $150, and the payment would be $4,850.

q: What is a debit memo?

options.t: A receipt for payment that a seller gives to a buyer after a cash sale in a shop
options.why: A receipt for payment is given to a buyer after a cash sale; it is not a debit memo, which adjusts an amount owed on account.

options.t: A check written by a firm to pay a supplier for goods that were bought on credit
options.why: A check written to pay a supplier is a payment (a cash disbursement); a debit memo is a document that reduces a payable rather than paying it.

options.t: A document reducing a payable, such as for returned goods, issued by the buyer
options.why: The buyer issues a debit memo to reduce the amount owed to the seller, such as for returned or damaged goods, which debits Accounts Payable.

options.t: A bill increasing amounts owed, which a seller sends to a buyer for goods supplied
options.why: A bill increasing what the buyer owes is an invoice or a credit memo from the seller's view; a debit memo reduces what the buyer owes.

q: What is the allowance method for bad debts?

options.t: Writing off a debt only when a customer defaults, as a cost of that period as a rule
options.why: That is the direct write-off method, which expenses a debt only when it proves uncollectible; the allowance method estimates the loss in advance instead.

options.t: Estimating uncollectible accounts and recording expense in the period of sale
options.why: The allowance method estimates uncollectible accounts and records bad debt expense in the same period as the sales, which matches expenses to revenues.

options.t: Charging customers more to cover the debts that some of them may not pay
options.why: Raising prices is a pricing decision and is not an accounting method for recording bad debts; the allowance method estimates and records the expected loss.

options.t: Ignoring bad debts and leaving them out of the accounts of the whole firm
options.why: Ignoring bad debts would overstate receivables and income; GAAP requires recognizing the expected loss, which the allowance method does by estimate.

q: What is the direct write-off method?

options.t: Recording bad debt expense only when an account is deemed uncollectible
options.why: Under direct write-off, bad debt expense is recorded only when a specific account is deemed uncollectible, which can fall in a later period than the sale.

options.t: Ignoring bad debts and leaving them out of the accounts of the whole firm
options.why: Ignoring bad debts is not an accepted method; the direct write-off method does record the loss, but only once an account is actually written off.

options.t: Charging customers more to cover the debts that some of them may not pay
options.why: Charging customers more is a pricing decision, not an accounting method; direct write-off records an expense when a specific account proves uncollectible.

options.t: Estimating in advance the amount of debts that will never be paid in a period
options.why: Estimating in advance describes the allowance method; the direct write-off method waits until an account is actually deemed uncollectible.

q: Credit sales are $200,000 and the company estimates 1.5% will be uncollectible. What is bad debt expense?

options.why: Bad debt expense is the estimated percentage of credit sales: $200,000 x 1.5% = $3,000.
This uses 15% ($200,000 x 0.15 = $30,000); the rate is 1.5%, so the decimal is 0.015, not 0.15.
This uses 0.15% ($200,000 x 0.0015 = $300); 1.5% is 0.015 as a decimal, which gives $3,000.
This is half the correct amount, as if the rate were 0.75%; the 1.5% rate applied to $200,000 gives $3,000.

q: What is the entry for estimated bad debts under the allowance method?

options.t: Debit Receivable, credit Expense, for the expected loss
options.why: Debiting Receivable would increase what customers owe; the estimate of bad debts reduces receivables through an allowance, with the expense debited instead.

options.t: Debit Cash and credit the Allowance for Doubtful Accounts in the end
options.why: Debiting Cash would imply cash was collected; recording the estimate involves no cash, only an expense debit and an allowance credit.

options.t: Debit Bad Debt Expense, credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts
options.why: The adjusting entry debits Bad Debt Expense (recognizing the loss) and credits Allowance for Doubtful Accounts, a contra-asset reducing receivables.

options.t: Debit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts and credit Expense
options.why: This is reversed: debiting the Allowance reduces it, as when writing off a specific account, and crediting Expense would lower expense instead of recording it.

q: Accounts receivable is $60,000 and the allowance is $2,500. What is net realizable value?

options.why: $60,000 is the gross accounts receivable; net realizable value is gross receivables less the allowance for doubtful accounts, so it must be lower.
Net realizable value = gross receivables - allowance = $60,000 - $2,500 = $57,500, the amount the company expects to actually collect.
This adds the allowance to receivables; the allowance is a contra-asset, which is subtracted, so net realizable value is $57,500.
$2,500 is just the allowance for doubtful accounts, the amount expected to be uncollectible, not the net amount expected to be collected.

q: What is the receivables turnover ratio?

options.t: Cash divided by sales for the whole year of trading
options.why: Cash divided by sales does not measure collection of credit sales; receivables turnover relates net credit sales to the average accounts receivable.

options.t: Sales divided by inventory held at the end of the year
options.why: Sales divided by inventory is related to inventory turnover, which measures how fast stock sells, not how fast receivables are collected.

options.t: Assets divided by liabilities, to show if debts can be met
options.why: Assets divided by liabilities is a solvency measure of whether debts can be met; it has nothing to do with collecting receivables.

options.t: Net credit sales divided by average accounts receivable
options.why: Receivables turnover = net credit sales / average accounts receivable, showing how many times a year the company collects its receivables.

q: Net credit sales are $600,000 and average receivables are $100,000. What is receivables turnover?

options.why: $500,000 is the difference between the sales and receivables ($600,000 - $100,000); a turnover ratio is a division, not a subtraction.

options.t: 60 times
options.why: This shifts the decimal; $600,000 / $100,000 = 6, not 60, so receivables turn over 6 times a year.

options.t: 0.17 times
options.why: This inverts the ratio ($100,000 / $600,000 = 0.17); turnover divides sales by receivables, giving $600,000 / $100,000 = 6 times.

options.t: 6 times
options.why: Receivables turnover = net credit sales / average receivables = $600,000 / $100,000 = 6 times, meaning receivables are collected about six times a year.

q: Using 365 days, what is the average collection period if receivables turnover is 6?

options.t: About 61 days
options.why: Average collection period = 365 / turnover = 365 / 6 = about 60.8, or roughly 61 days, the average time to collect a credit sale.

options.t: About 2,190 days
options.why: This multiplies instead of dividing (365 x 6 = 2,190); the collection period is 365 divided by turnover, which gives about 61 days.

options.t: About 365 days
options.why: 365 days is the whole year; dividing it by a turnover of 6 gives about 61 days, so the collection period is much shorter than a year.

options.t: About 6 days
options.why: This is just the turnover figure restated as days; the collection period divides 365 by 6, giving about 61 days.

q: What is a control account?

options.t: An account for tax that the firm pays to the state each year
options.why: An account for state tax payments is not a control account; a control account is a general ledger account that summarizes a subsidiary ledger.

options.t: An account for budgets that the managers prepare each year
options.why: A budget account is not a control account; control accounts like Accounts Receivable are summaries whose balance equals the total of the subsidiary ledger.

options.t: A general ledger account summarizing a subsidiary ledger
options.why: A control account in the general ledger summarizes a subsidiary ledger, such as Accounts Receivable summarizing each customer's individual account balance.

options.t: An account for cash held by the firm in a bank or in a till
options.why: Cash held in a bank or till is just a cash account; a control account must summarize the detail in a subsidiary ledger.

q: What is a promissory note?

options.t: A check written to a supplier by a firm to pay for goods bought
options.why: A check is an order to a bank to pay money; a promissory note is the maker's own written promise to pay and is not a check.

options.t: A written promise to pay a specified amount on a certain date
options.why: A promissory note is a written promise by the maker to pay a specified sum on a specified date, and it may bear interest.

options.t: A purchase order sent to a supplier to ask for goods to be delivered
options.why: A purchase order is a buyer's request to a supplier for goods, not a promise to pay money on a set date.

options.t: A receipt for cash paid that a seller hands to a buyer in a shop
options.why: A receipt acknowledges cash already paid, whereas a promissory note is a promise to pay in the future.

q: A $5,000 note bears 6% annual interest for 3 months. What is the interest?

options.why: $25 would be the interest for one month at 6% on a smaller base or for one month at 1%; 3 months at 6% on $5,000 is $75.
Interest = principal x rate x time = $5,000 x 0.06 x 3/12 = $75, because 3 months is one quarter of a year.
This is a full year of interest at 6% ($5,000 x 0.06 = $300); the note runs only 3 months, which is 1/4 of a year, so $75.
This is 18% of $5,000 (6% for 3 full years); the rate is annual and the time is only 3 months, so $75.

q: What is dishonoring a note?

options.t: The maker fails to pay the note at maturity
options.why: Dishonoring a note means the maker fails to pay at maturity; the holder then usually transfers the note and interest to Accounts Receivable.

options.t: Selling the note to a bank before it matures
options.why: Selling a note to a bank before it matures is called discounting a note receivable, not dishonoring it.

options.t: Renewing the note for a further period of time
options.why: Renewing a note for a further period extends its term by agreement; it is not a default, so it is not dishonoring.

options.t: Paying early, before the note falls due at all
options.why: Paying early is not a default; dishonor happens only when the maker fails to pay at maturity.

q: Using the same figures, what is working capital?

options.why: This is likely one of the component balances (such as current liabilities) rather than the difference between current assets and current liabilities, which is working capital.
This figure is not the difference between current assets and current liabilities; working capital subtracts liabilities from assets rather than adding or scaling them.
A value of 1.5 is a ratio, which fits the current ratio (current assets / current liabilities), not working capital, which is stated in dollars.
Working capital = current assets - current liabilities = $30,000; it shows the liquid funds available to meet short-term obligations (a 1.5 current ratio supports it).

q: What is the quick (acid-test) ratio?

options.t: Net income over owner equity for the year
options.why: Net income over owner equity is return on equity, a profitability ratio, not the quick ratio, which measures short-term liquidity.

options.t: Sales over assets owned at the end of the year
options.why: Sales over assets is asset turnover, an efficiency measure; the quick ratio compares liquid assets to current liabilities.

options.t: Quick assets divided by current liabilities
options.why: The quick (acid-test) ratio = quick assets (cash, marketable securities, receivables) divided by current liabilities, excluding inventory because it is harder to convert to cash.

options.t: All assets over liabilities including stock
options.why: All assets over liabilities including stock is a broad solvency measure; the quick ratio uses only liquid assets and excludes inventory.

q: Cash is $10,000, receivables $20,000, inventory $30,000 and current liabilities $30,000. What is the quick ratio?

options.why: 0.5 would result from using only cash ($10,000 / $30,000 = 0.33) or a similar mistake; the quick assets here include both cash and receivables.
2.0 would need $60,000 of quick assets; counting inventory ($10,000 + $20,000 + $30,000 = $60,000) is wrong because inventory is excluded.
3.0 would require $90,000 of quick assets; the quick ratio excludes inventory and uses only cash and receivables, so it cannot be this high.
Quick assets = cash + receivables = $10,000 + $20,000 = $30,000; divided by current liabilities of $30,000 gives 1.0, excluding inventory.

q: What is the debt ratio?

options.t: Equity divided by total assets of the firm
options.why: Equity divided by total assets is the equity ratio; the debt ratio uses liabilities, and the two add up to 100% of assets.

options.t: Assets divided by liabilities, as on the sheet
options.why: Assets divided by liabilities flips the ratio; the debt ratio divides total liabilities by total assets to show the share of assets financed by debt.

options.t: Total liabilities divided by total assets
options.why: The debt ratio = total liabilities / total assets, showing the proportion of assets financed by creditors; a higher ratio means greater financial risk.

options.t: Net income divided by debt owed by the firm
options.why: Net income divided by debt is not the standard debt ratio; it would mix a profit measure with a balance sheet item.

q: What is gross profit margin?

options.t: Sales divided by total assets owned
options.why: Sales divided by total assets is asset turnover, an efficiency ratio; gross profit margin measures profit after cost of goods sold.

options.t: Gross profit divided by net sales
options.why: Gross profit margin = gross profit / net sales, showing the percent of each sales dollar left after cost of goods sold.

options.t: Net income over sales for the year
options.why: Net income over sales is net profit margin, which also subtracts operating expenses, interest and taxes; gross margin stops at cost of goods sold.

options.t: Profit divided by the owner equity
options.why: Profit divided by owner equity is return on equity, which measures return to the owners, not the share of sales left after production costs.

q: Net sales are $500,000 and cost of goods sold is $300,000. What is the gross profit margin?

options.why: Gross profit = $500,000 - $300,000 = $200,000, and $200,000 / $500,000 = 40%, the share of sales left after cost of goods sold.
200% wrongly treats the $200,000 gross profit as a percent; margin divides gross profit by net sales ($200,000 / $500,000), which is 40%.
60% is cost of goods sold as a share of sales ($300,000 / $500,000); gross margin is the remainder, 40%, after subtracting that cost.
0.4% mistakes the decimal 0.4 for a percentage; $200,000 / $500,000 = 0.4, which must be multiplied by 100 to give 40%.

q: What is net profit margin?

options.t: Net income over owner equity
options.why: Net income over owner equity is return on equity, which measures return to owners; net profit margin compares net income to net sales.

options.t: Sales over the total assets owned
options.why: Sales over total assets is asset turnover, an efficiency ratio, and does not show how much of each sales dollar becomes profit.

options.t: Net income divided by net sales
options.why: Net profit margin = net income / net sales, showing how many cents of each sales dollar remain as profit after all expenses.

options.t: Gross profit divided over sales
options.why: Gross profit over sales is the gross profit margin, which ignores operating expenses, interest and taxes that net profit margin includes.

q: What is return on assets (ROA)?

options.t: Net income divided by average total assets
options.why: ROA = net income / average total assets, measuring how efficiently a company uses its assets to generate profit.

options.t: Net income over owner equity at the year end
options.why: Net income over owner equity is return on equity (ROE), which uses equity instead of total assets as the base.

options.t: Sales over assets owned by the firm at year end
options.why: Sales over assets is asset turnover, which measures sales generated per dollar of assets rather than profit generated.

options.t: Assets over liabilities, a ratio of solvency
options.why: Assets over liabilities is a solvency ratio showing coverage of debts; it does not measure profitability from assets.

q: Net income is $24,000 and average total assets are $240,000. What is ROA?

options.why: 1% mistakes the decimal; $24,000 / $240,000 = 0.10, which is 10%, not 1%, so the decimal point was misplaced.
1,000% is far too large; dividing $24,000 by $240,000 gives 0.10, and a profit of one tenth of assets is 10%.
25% would require average assets of $96,000 ($24,000 / 0.25); with $240,000 of assets, the return is lower.
ROA = net income / average total assets = $24,000 / $240,000 = 0.10, or 10%, meaning each dollar of assets earned ten cents.

q: What is asset turnover?

options.t: Cash over total assets held by the firm
options.why: Cash over total assets is a liquidity-type ratio; asset turnover measures how many sales dollars each dollar of assets produces.

options.t: Net sales divided by average total assets
options.why: Asset turnover = net sales / average total assets, showing how efficiently the firm uses its assets to generate sales.

options.t: Assets over sales made in the year by the firm
options.why: This inverts the ratio (assets over sales); asset turnover puts sales on top, so a higher number means assets are used more efficiently.

options.t: Net income over assets, as a percent
options.why: Net income over assets is return on assets (ROA), a profitability ratio; asset turnover is based on sales, not net income.

q: What is earnings per share (EPS)?

options.t: Assets per share, which is the total assets of the firm divided by the shares
options.why: Total assets divided by shares is not EPS; EPS measures profit per share, not the book value of assets per share.

options.t: Price per share, which is the market price that a single share trades at today
options.why: Market price per share is what a share sells for today; EPS measures the profit earned per share instead.

options.t: Net income available to common shareholders divided by weighted average shares
options.why: EPS = (net income - preferred dividends) / weighted average common shares outstanding, showing profit attributable to each common share.

options.t: Dividends per share, which is the cash paid to each holder for every share owned
options.why: Dividends per share is the cash paid to each holder; EPS is the earnings per share, which may be larger or smaller than dividends.

q: Net income is $600,000 and there are 200,000 shares. What is EPS?

options.why: $0.33 inverts the division ($200,000 / $600,000); EPS divides net income by shares, so $600,000 / 200,000 = $3.00.
$30 would result from moving the decimal point; $600,000 divided by 200,000 shares is $3, not $30.
$120 multiplies the numbers incorrectly; EPS divides net income by shares outstanding, which gives $3.00.
EPS = net income / shares outstanding = $600,000 / 200,000 = $3.00 per share (assuming no preferred dividends).

q: What is the times interest earned ratio?

options.t: Operating income divided by interest expense
options.why: Times interest earned = operating income (EBIT) / interest expense, showing how many times earnings cover interest payments to lenders.

options.t: Sales over interest expense for the year
options.why: Sales over interest expense is not the standard formula; interest coverage uses operating income, since sales do not show the profit available to pay interest.

options.t: Debt over equity at the end of the year
options.why: Debt over equity is the debt-to-equity ratio, a leverage measure, not a measure of how well earnings cover interest.

options.t: Net income over sales, shown as a percent overall
options.why: Net income over sales is net profit margin; it measures profit per sales dollar, not interest coverage.

q: Operating income is $90,000 and interest expense is $15,000. What is times interest earned?

options.t: 0.17 times
options.why: 0.17 inverts the fraction ($15,000 / $90,000); times interest earned puts operating income on top, giving $90,000 / $15,000 = 6.

options.t: 6 times
options.why: Times interest earned = operating income / interest expense = $90,000 / $15,000 = 6 times, meaning earnings cover interest six times over.
$75,000 is the difference ($90,000 - $15,000); the ratio is a division, and the result is a number of times, not dollars.

options.t: 105 times
options.why: 105 adds the two figures in thousands ($90 + $15); the ratio divides operating income by interest expense and equals 6.

q: Sales were $200,000 last year and $230,000 this year. What is the percentage change?

options.t: 13% increase
options.why: 13% is a miscalculation; the change is $30,000 on a base of $200,000, which is 15%, not 13%.

options.t: 15% decrease
options.why: The sales rose from $200,000 to $230,000, so the change is an increase, not a decrease; a decrease would mean sales fell.

options.t: 30% increase
options.why: 30% uses the dollar change in thousands ($30) as the percent; percent change = $30,000 / $200,000 = 15%, not 30%.

options.t: 15% increase
options.why: Percent change = (new - old) / old = ($230,000 - $200,000) / $200,000 = 0.15, a 15% increase in sales.

q: What are the three sections of a statement of cash flows?

options.t: Revenue, expense and net profit
options.why: Revenue, expense and net profit are items on the income statement, not the three sections of the statement of cash flows.

options.t: Operating, investing and financing
options.why: The statement of cash flows reports cash from operating, investing and financing activities, which together explain the change in cash.

options.t: Debit, credit and balance totals
options.why: Debit, credit and balance are accounting terms used in the ledger, not the categories on the cash flow statement.

options.t: Assets, liabilities and equity
options.why: Assets, liabilities and equity are the three parts of the balance sheet, not the sections of the statement of cash flows.

q: Which activity is an investing cash flow?

options.t: Taking a loan
options.why: Taking a loan is a financing activity because it raises money from creditors, not an investing activity.

options.t: Customer receipts
options.why: Customer receipts are an operating cash flow from selling goods or services, not an investing activity.

options.t: Buying equipment
options.why: Buying equipment is an investing cash flow because it is a purchase of a long-term asset, along with buying land or investments.

options.t: Paying wages
options.why: Paying wages is an operating cash flow, because it is a normal expense of running the business, not investing.

q: Which activity is a financing cash flow?

options.t: Issuing stock
options.why: Issuing stock raises money from owners, which makes it a financing cash flow, along with borrowing and paying dividends or debt.

options.t: Customer receipts
options.why: Customer receipts are an operating cash flow from daily sales, not a financing activity involving owners or lenders.

options.t: Buying land
options.why: Buying land is an investing cash flow, since land is a long-term asset; financing involves debt and equity.

options.t: Buying inventory
options.why: Buying inventory is an operating cash flow, since inventory is part of daily business, not a financing activity.

q: Which activity is an operating cash flow?

options.t: Paying dividends to owners
options.why: Paying dividends is a financing cash flow because it returns money to owners; operating flows relate to day-to-day sales and expenses.

options.t: Buying a building for investing
options.why: Buying a building is an investing cash flow since it purchases a long-term asset; it is not part of day-to-day operations.

options.t: Selling stock to investors
options.why: Selling stock to investors raises capital from owners, which is a financing cash flow rather than an operating one.

options.t: Collecting cash from customers
options.why: Collecting cash from customers is an operating cash flow, since it comes from the normal sales activity of the business.

q: Beginning retained earnings are $50,000, net income is $20,000 and dividends are $8,000. What are ending retained earnings?

options.why: Ending retained earnings = beginning + net income - dividends = $50,000 + $20,000 - $8,000 = $62,000.
$70,000 adds net income but forgets to subtract the $8,000 of dividends, which reduce retained earnings.
$78,000 adds the dividends ($50,000 + $20,000 + $8,000) instead of subtracting them; dividends reduce retained earnings.
$38,000 subtracts net income and dividends ($50,000 - $20,000 - $8,000); net income increases retained earnings, so it must be added.

q: What is the audit opinion that says statements are fairly presented?

options.t: An adverse opinion on the firm
options.why: An adverse opinion says the statements are not fairly presented; it is the opposite of the clean opinion that says they are fair.

options.t: A disclaimer of opinion given
options.why: A disclaimer means the auditor could not form an opinion, such as when access was limited; it does not say statements are fair.

options.t: An unqualified (clean) opinion
options.why: An unqualified (clean) opinion says the statements fairly present the company's position in all material respects, the best result for a company.

options.t: A qualified opinion on one item
options.why: A qualified opinion says the statements are fair except for one specific item or limitation, so it is not a fully clean opinion.

q: What does an adverse audit opinion mean?

options.t: The auditor disagrees with the company on one item and says so in a note
options.why: Disagreeing on one item, with a note, describes a qualified opinion; an adverse opinion is broader and covers the statements as a whole.

options.t: The financial statements do not fairly present the company's position
options.why: An adverse opinion means the statements do not fairly present the company's financial position because of material misstatements, the most negative audit result.

options.t: The statements are fair in all material respects to every reader
options.why: Statements that are fair in all material respects describe an unqualified (clean) opinion, which is the opposite of an adverse opinion.

options.t: The audit was not done because the company would not allow access
options.why: An audit that cannot be done because of denied access leads to a disclaimer of opinion, not an adverse opinion.
