q: Who sets GAAP in the United States?

options.t: The Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB)
options.why: The FASB sets U.S. GAAP as a private nonprofit board, and the SEC recognizes and enforces its standards for public companies.

options.t: The SEC alone, for all companies and banks
options.why: The SEC has legal authority over public company reporting but relies on the FASB to set the standards; it does not set GAAP alone.

options.t: The IRS, which collects taxes in the United States
options.why: The IRS administers tax law; tax rules differ from GAAP, which is set by the FASB for financial reporting.

options.t: The Federal Reserve, which sets bank rates
options.why: The Federal Reserve is the central bank that sets monetary policy and bank rates; it does not write accounting standards.

q: What does the SEC require of public companies?

options.t: Only marketing plans and sales forecasts
options.why: Marketing plans and sales forecasts are internal documents; the SEC requires public companies to disclose audited financial results to investors.

options.t: Only tax returns for the owners of the firm
options.why: Tax returns of the owners are filed with the IRS; the SEC focuses on disclosure of the company's financial information for investors.

options.t: Regular filing of audited financial reports
options.why: The SEC requires public companies to file regular reports, such as the audited annual 10-K and quarterly 10-Q, so investors can make informed decisions.

options.t: No reports of any kind to the public at large
options.why: The SEC exists to require public disclosure for investors, so public companies must file reports, not avoid reporting.

q: What is Form 10-K?

options.t: A tax form that businesses file with the state revenue agency
options.why: A tax form filed with a state revenue agency is not Form 10-K, which is filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

options.t: A quarterly report filed with the SEC by public companies
options.why: A quarterly report filed with the SEC is Form 10-Q, not 10-K; the 10-K is filed once a year.

options.t: A loan application made by a firm to a bank for a new loan
options.why: A loan application to a bank is a private credit document; Form 10-K is a public disclosure filed with the SEC.

options.t: An annual report filed with the SEC by public companies
options.why: Form 10-K is the annual report with audited financial statements that public companies file with the SEC, including business and risk disclosures.

q: What is Form 10-Q?

options.t: A loan application made to a bank
options.why: A loan application to a bank is a private credit request; Form 10-Q is a public report filed with the SEC.

options.t: A quarterly report filed with the SEC
options.why: Form 10-Q is the quarterly report with unaudited financial statements that public companies file with the SEC for each of the first three quarters.

options.t: An annual report filed with the SEC
options.why: An annual report with audited statements is Form 10-K, filed once a year; the 10-Q covers each of the first three quarters.

options.t: A tax form that firms file each year
options.why: A tax form for a yearly return is filed with a tax agency; Form 10-Q is an SEC filing about a company's quarterly results.

q: What is the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX)?

options.t: A law that set up deposit insurance and capital rules for commercial banks and thrifts
options.why: Deposit insurance and bank capital rules came from banking laws such as the FDIC legislation, not from Sarbanes-Oxley, which targets public company reporting.

options.t: A law that raised federal income tax rates on large public corporations and owners each year as a rule
options.why: SOX did not raise federal income tax rates on large corporations; it concerns financial reporting, audits and internal controls at public companies.

options.t: A law improving corporate financial reporting and internal controls after accounting scandals
options.why: Passed in 2002 after Enron and WorldCom, SOX strengthened financial reporting, internal controls, auditor independence and executive accountability for public companies.

options.t: A law that gave workers the right to bargain collectively with their employers and unions
options.why: The right of workers to bargain collectively comes from labor law such as the National Labor Relations Act, not from Sarbanes-Oxley.

q: What is the PCAOB?

options.t: A tax agency that collects income taxes from firms
options.why: The IRS collects income taxes; the PCAOB is a nonprofit board created by Sarbanes-Oxley to oversee auditors, not to collect taxes.

options.t: The board that oversees audits of public companies
options.why: The PCAOB, created by Sarbanes-Oxley, oversees audits of public companies, setting auditing standards and inspecting accounting firms that audit them.

options.t: A stock exchange where shares of firms are traded daily
options.why: A stock exchange, such as the NYSE, is where shares trade; the PCAOB does not trade shares and instead oversees auditors.

options.t: A bank regulator that sets reserve rules for lenders
options.why: Bank reserve rules are set by the Federal Reserve; the PCAOB oversees auditors of public companies, not banks.

q: What is segregation of duties?

options.t: Dividing tasks among different people so one person cannot control all parts of a transaction
options.why: Segregation of duties splits tasks like authorizing, recording and custody among different people so no single person can commit and hide fraud.

options.t: Keeping offices in separate buildings so that staff work in different places of the city in this case
options.why: Segregation of duties is about dividing tasks between people, not about where offices are located in a city.

options.t: Segregating customers by region so that each group is served by its own separate staff
options.why: Separating customers by region is a sales organization choice and is not the internal control of dividing transaction duties among employees.

options.t: One person doing everything alone, from approving to recording to holding all the cash
options.why: One person doing everything is the opposite of segregation of duties and a major fraud risk because nobody checks the work.

q: What are the elements of the fraud triangle?

options.t: Profit, loss and cash, as in a ledger book
options.why: Profit, loss and cash are financial terms, not the three elements of the fraud triangle that explain why people commit fraud.

options.t: Audit, tax and law, as in a firm's office
options.why: Audit, tax and law are accounting and legal fields, not the fraud triangle, which describes the conditions behind fraud.

options.t: Debit, credit and balance, the ledger terms
options.why: Debit, credit and balance are bookkeeping terms; the fraud triangle instead looks at the motive, chance and justification of the fraudster.

options.t: Pressure, opportunity and rationalization
options.why: The fraud triangle says fraud occurs when a person has pressure (motive), opportunity (weak controls) and rationalization (justifying the act).

q: What is embezzlement?

options.t: A tax strategy used to cut yearly bills
options.why: A tax strategy to cut bills can be legal tax planning; embezzlement is a crime of stealing funds that were entrusted to a person.

options.t: Theft of funds entrusted to one's care
options.why: Embezzlement is theft of money or property by someone entrusted with it, such as an employee or officer, and it is a form of fraud.

options.t: A legal fee paid to a lawyer for advice
options.why: A legal fee paid to a lawyer is a normal business expense, not embezzlement, which is a crime.

options.t: A loan made by a bank to a firm in need
options.why: A bank loan to a firm in need is a lawful financing arrangement; embezzlement is theft by someone trusted with the funds.

q: What is the AICPA code of conduct principle of integrity?

options.t: Being honest and straightforward in professional dealings
options.why: Integrity under the AICPA code means being honest and straightforward, so CPAs deal truthfully with clients, employers and the public.

options.t: Serving only some clients so the accountant stays focused
options.why: Serving only some clients to stay focused is a business choice and is not integrity, which concerns honesty and straightforward dealing.

options.t: Maximizing fees by charging clients as much as possible
options.why: Maximizing fees by overcharging is not integrity; the code requires honest dealing and putting public trust ahead of personal gain.

options.t: Hiding errors from the clients and from the public
options.why: Hiding errors from clients or the public is dishonest and violates integrity, which requires being honest and straightforward.

q: What is objectivity for an accountant?

options.t: Favoring clients who pay the largest fees to the firm
options.why: Favoring clients who pay the largest fees is bias; objectivity requires impartial judgment that is not swayed by payment.

options.t: Following rumors heard from friends and coworkers
options.why: Following rumors is not objectivity; accountants must base conclusions on facts and evidence, not on gossip from friends.

options.t: Being impartial and free of conflicts of interest
options.why: Objectivity means being impartial and free of conflicts of interest, so professional judgment is not compromised by bias or outside influence.

options.t: Ignoring facts that do not suit the client's wishes
options.why: Ignoring facts that do not suit the client is the opposite of objectivity, which requires weighing all facts impartially.

q: What is independence in auditing?

options.t: The auditor owning shares of stock in the client company being audited
options.why: An auditor owning shares in the client has a financial interest that impairs independence, so it breaks the rule rather than defining it.

options.t: The auditor working alone, with no other staff to check the work done
options.why: Working alone is about staffing, not independence, which concerns freedom from financial or personal ties to the client.

options.t: The auditor working for the client as an employee on the payroll
options.why: An auditor employed by the client is not independent because the client's pay and control could bias the audit.

options.t: The auditor having no financial or personal ties that impair judgment
options.why: Independence means an auditor has no financial or personal ties to the client that would impair judgment, so the opinion is trusted by the public.

q: Gross income is $70,000 and deductions are $14,000. What is taxable income?

options.why: $70,000 is gross income before deductions; taxable income is what remains after subtracting deductions from gross income.
$14,000 is only the amount of deductions; taxable income is gross income minus deductions, not the deduction alone.
$84,000 adds the deductions to gross income ($70,000 + $14,000); deductions reduce taxable income, so they are subtracted.
Taxable income = gross income - deductions = $70,000 - $14,000 = $56,000, the amount on which tax is calculated.

q: What is the difference between a tax deduction and a tax credit?

options.t: A credit reduces taxable income while a deduction reduces tax owed
options.why: This reverses the definitions; a deduction, not a credit, reduces taxable income, while a credit reduces the tax owed.

options.t: They are the same thing and both cut the tax by the same amount
options.why: A deduction and a credit are different; a $1,000 credit saves $1,000 of tax, while a $1,000 deduction saves only that amount times your tax rate.

options.t: A deduction reduces taxable income while a credit reduces tax owed
options.why: A deduction lowers taxable income, saving tax at your rate, while a credit reduces the tax owed dollar for dollar, so credits are generally more valuable.

options.t: A deduction cuts tax owed dollar for dollar; a credit cuts taxable income
options.why: This is reversed; credits cut tax owed dollar for dollar, while deductions reduce the taxable income to which the rates are applied.

q: What is the marginal tax rate?

options.t: The average rate on all income earned
options.why: The average rate on all income is the effective tax rate; the marginal rate applies only to the last (highest) dollars earned.

options.t: The rate on the last dollar of income
options.why: The marginal tax rate is the rate on the next or last dollar of income, the bracket rate that applies to an additional dollar earned.

options.t: The lowest rate on any income earned
options.why: The lowest rate on any income is the bottom bracket rate; the marginal rate is the rate on the last dollar, usually higher.

options.t: The sales tax rate on goods you buy
options.why: A sales tax on purchases is a different tax; the marginal rate refers to income tax brackets.

q: What is the effective tax rate?

options.t: Total tax divided by total income
options.why: The effective tax rate = total tax divided by total income, the average share of income actually paid in tax.

options.t: The lowest rate in the tax table
options.why: The lowest rate in the tax table is the bottom bracket rate; the effective rate is an overall average, usually above it.

options.t: The top rate paid on the last dollar
options.why: The top rate paid on the last dollar is the marginal rate; the effective rate averages over all income.

options.t: The sales tax rate on purchases
options.why: A sales tax rate on purchases applies to spending; the effective tax rate refers to income tax paid compared with income.

q: A person pays $9,000 in tax on $60,000 of income. What is the effective tax rate?

options.why: 9% is a misreading of the $9,000 tax; the effective rate = $9,000 / $60,000 = 0.15, which is 15%.
6.7% results from inverting the numbers incorrectly ($4,000 / $60,000); the correct calculation is $9,000 / $60,000 = 15%.
Effective tax rate = total tax / total income = $9,000 / $60,000 = 0.15, or 15%.
150% mistakes the decimal; a rate above 100% would mean paying more tax than the income earned, and $9,000 / $60,000 is 15%.

q: What is payroll tax?

options.t: A tax on gifts that are given from one person to another overall
options.why: A tax on gifts is a gift tax, separate from payroll tax, which is levied on wages paid to employees.

options.t: Tax on wages paid, including Social Security and Medicare
options.why: Payroll taxes are taxes on wages paid, including Social Security and Medicare (FICA), and are shared by employer and employee.

options.t: A tax on property such as land and homes owned by people
options.why: A tax on land and homes is a property tax, not a payroll tax, which is based on wages paid.

options.t: A tax on sales of goods at the till in shops and stores
options.why: A tax on sales of goods in shops is a sales tax, not a payroll tax, which is based on wages paid.

q: An employee earns $4,000 gross in a month. Social Security is 6.2% and Medicare is 1.45%. What is the total FICA withheld?

options.why: $248 is only the Social Security part ($4,000 x 6.2%); Medicare must be added, so the total is higher.
$3,694 is the pay left after FICA ($4,000 - $306), not the amount withheld; FICA is the withholding itself.
$58 is only the Medicare part ($4,000 x 1.45%); Social Security of $248 must be added to get the total FICA.
FICA = 6.2% + 1.45% = 7.65% of $4,000 = $248 + $58 = $306 withheld for Social Security and Medicare.

q: What is a Form 1099-NEC used for?

options.t: Reporting payments to independent contractors
options.why: Form 1099-NEC reports nonemployee compensation, which means payments made to independent contractors of $600 or more.

options.t: Reporting interest paid by banks to savers
options.why: Interest paid by banks to savers is reported on Form 1099-INT, not the 1099-NEC.

options.t: Reporting wages paid to employees at year end
options.why: Wages paid to employees are reported on Form W-2, not on the 1099-NEC, which is for contractors.

options.t: Applying for a license to run a small business
options.why: A business license application is filed with the state or city, not reported on the 1099-NEC.

q: What is a Form W-2 used for?

options.t: Reporting wages and taxes withheld for an employee
options.why: Form W-2 reports an employee's annual wages and the taxes withheld, which the employer gives to the employee and the government.

options.t: Applying for credit at a bank or with a lender
options.why: Applying for credit uses a loan application; Form W-2 is a tax reporting form, not a credit form.

options.t: Reporting payments made to contractors in the year
options.why: Payments to contractors are reported on Form 1099-NEC, not on the W-2, which is for employees.

options.t: Reporting sales tax collected from the shoppers
options.why: Sales tax collected is reported on sales tax returns to the state, not on the Form W-2.

q: What is the difference between an employee and an independent contractor for tax purposes?

options.t: There is no difference in how taxes are handled for the two groups
options.why: There are major differences; employers withhold and pay payroll taxes for employees, while contractors handle their own taxes.

options.t: Employers withhold taxes for employees but not for contractors
options.why: Employers withhold income and payroll taxes from employees' pay, while independent contractors receive a 1099 and pay their own taxes, including self-employment tax.

options.t: Contractors have taxes withheld by the hirer as employees do
options.why: Contractors are not subject to withholding by the hirer like employees; they receive full payment and pay their own taxes.

options.t: Employees pay no taxes on the wages they earn at their work
options.why: Employees do pay taxes on their wages, with income and payroll taxes usually withheld from each paycheck.

q: What is self-employment tax?

options.t: An import tax that is charged on goods that enter the whole country
options.why: An import tax is a tariff on goods entering the country, not a tax on self-employed individuals.

options.t: A sales tax that shoppers pay on goods when they buy them at a store
options.why: A sales tax is paid by shoppers on purchases; self-employment tax is based on net earnings from self-employment.

options.t: A property tax that owners pay on land and buildings every single year
options.why: A property tax is paid on land and buildings; self-employment tax is not related to property ownership.

options.t: The Social Security and Medicare tax paid by self-employed individuals
options.why: Self-employment tax is the Social Security and Medicare tax paid by self-employed people, who pay both the employer and employee halves (15.3%).

q: What is a straight-line depreciation formula?

options.t: Salvage value divided by cost of asset
options.why: Salvage value divided by cost does not give yearly depreciation; it would give a ratio rather than an annual expense amount.

options.t: Cost times the useful life of the asset
options.why: Cost times useful life would give a number far larger than the asset's cost; depreciation spreads cost over the life instead.

options.t: (Cost − salvage value) ÷ useful life
options.why: Straight-line depreciation = (cost - salvage value) / useful life, which spreads the depreciable amount evenly over each year of the asset's life.

options.t: Cost plus salvage value of the asset
options.why: Adding salvage value to cost would overstate the depreciable amount; salvage value is subtracted because it will be recovered at the end.

q: A machine costs $30,000, has a $3,000 salvage value and a 9-year life. What is annual straight-line depreciation?

options.why: $3,333 divides the full cost of $30,000 by 9 years and ignores salvage value; the depreciable amount is cost less salvage value.
($30,000 - $3,000) / 9 years = $27,000 / 9 = $3,000 of depreciation per year.
$30,000 is the machine's full cost; annual depreciation spreads the depreciable amount over 9 years rather than expensing it all at once.
$27,000 is the total depreciable amount ($30,000 - $3,000), not annual; dividing by 9 years gives $3,000 per year.

q: What is MACRS?

options.t: The tax depreciation system used in the U.S., with accelerated recovery periods
options.why: MACRS (Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System) is the U.S. tax depreciation system using set recovery periods and accelerated deductions.

options.t: A payroll rule that tells employers how to withhold tax from each paycheck
options.why: Payroll withholding rules come from IRS withholding tables; MACRS covers depreciation of business assets for tax purposes.

options.t: A sales tax rule that tells stores how to charge tax on each purchase made
options.why: Sales tax collection rules are set by states; MACRS is a federal income tax depreciation method.

options.t: A banking rule that tells banks how much money to keep in reserve at all times as a rule
options.why: Bank reserve requirements are set by the Federal Reserve; MACRS is a tax depreciation method for business property.

q: What is a tax lien?

options.t: A tax deduction that lowers taxable pay
options.why: A tax deduction lowers taxable income; a tax lien is a legal claim on property, not a deduction.

options.t: A tax credit that cuts the tax bill owed
options.why: A tax credit cuts the tax bill; a tax lien is a legal claim placed on property when taxes are unpaid.

options.t: A legal claim on property for unpaid taxes
options.why: A tax lien is the government's legal claim on a taxpayer's property to secure payment of unpaid taxes, and it can affect credit and sale of the property.

options.t: A tax refund paid back to the taxpayer in cash
options.why: A tax refund is money returned to a taxpayer who overpaid; a lien is a claim against property for unpaid taxes.

q: What is a use tax?

options.t: A tax on property that is owned by people and firms in the same state
options.why: A tax on property owned is a property tax; a use tax applies to goods bought out of state and used in the buyer's state.

options.t: A tax on gifts that one person gives to another person in a single year every time
options.why: A tax on gifts is a gift tax; a use tax is on goods bought elsewhere and used in your state.

options.t: A tax on income that workers and firms earn in the course of a year
options.why: A tax on income is an income tax; a use tax is related to purchases, not earnings.

options.t: A tax on items bought out of state for use in your state without sales tax
options.why: A use tax applies to goods bought out of state, where no sales tax was charged, for use in your own state, so the state does not lose the tax.

q: What is an excise tax?

options.t: A tax on payroll paid by employers on wages
options.why: A tax on payroll is a payroll tax; an excise tax applies to specific goods and services.

options.t: A tax on all income earned by workers and firms
options.why: A tax on all income is an income tax; an excise tax applies to specific products and not to all earnings.

options.t: A tax on specific goods such as fuel or tobacco
options.why: An excise tax is placed on specific goods or activities such as fuel, tobacco, alcohol or airline tickets and is often included in the price.

options.t: A tax on property such as land and homes owned
options.why: A tax on land and homes is a property tax; an excise tax targets specific goods or services.

q: What is accounting software?

options.t: Programs for music players, used to play songs and albums
options.why: Music player programs are entertainment software; accounting software handles financial transactions and records.

options.t: Programs that record, process and report financial transactions
options.why: Accounting software records, processes and reports financial transactions, such as invoices and payroll, with programs like QuickBooks.

options.t: Programs for editing photos and drawing posters for the team in the end
options.why: Photo editing and poster design programs are graphics software; accounting software deals with financial records.

options.t: Programs for games, built for play and fun on a computer
options.why: Game programs are entertainment software; accounting software is a business tool for financial recordkeeping.

q: What is an ERP system?

options.t: A tax form that businesses use to report their yearly income to the IRS
options.why: A tax form is filed with the IRS; ERP is business software that integrates operations, not a tax form.

options.t: A spreadsheet used only by accountants to track just one account at a time
options.why: ERP is not a one-account spreadsheet; it is a large integrated system used by many departments.

options.t: A hardware part inside a computer that stores a company's files and programs overall
options.why: A hardware part storing files is a hard drive; ERP is software, not a hardware component.

options.t: Enterprise resource planning software that links accounting, HR and supply chain
options.why: ERP (enterprise resource planning) software links accounting, HR, supply chain and other functions in one system, so departments share the same data.

q: What is the cloud in accounting?

options.t: Software and data stored on internet servers rather than local machines
options.why: Cloud accounting uses software and data stored on internet servers instead of local machines, allowing access from anywhere and automatic updates.

options.t: Weather reports that show how many clouds will cover a city today or this week
options.why: Weather clouds are not related to cloud accounting, which refers to internet-based software and storage.

options.t: A calculator that adds numbers for an accountant sitting at a desk
options.why: A calculator is a local device; cloud accounting runs on internet servers and handles far more than addition.

options.t: A paper file that stores records in a drawer inside the office
options.why: A paper file in a drawer is a physical record; the cloud means digital storage on internet servers.

q: What is blockchain in accounting?

options.t: A secure distributed ledger that records transactions permanently
options.why: Blockchain is a secure distributed ledger that records transactions permanently, so entries are hard to alter and can be verified by many parties.

options.t: A calculator that totals a column of numbers as an accountant types
options.why: A calculator totals numbers; blockchain is a shared digital ledger of transactions, not a calculating device.

options.t: A paper ledger that is kept in a locked office by the head bookkeeper
options.why: A paper ledger in a locked office is a traditional record; blockchain is a digital ledger shared across a network.

options.t: A tax form that businesses fill out and send to the IRS each year
options.why: A tax form is filed with the IRS; blockchain is a technology for recording transactions, not a tax document.

q: What is robotic process automation (RPA)?

options.t: A tax rule that sets the rates for firms each year
options.why: A tax rule sets rates; RPA is software that automates tasks, not a tax rule.

options.t: Software bots that perform repetitive rule-based tasks
options.why: RPA uses software bots to perform repetitive, rule-based tasks, such as data entry and invoice matching, freeing accountants for higher-value work.

options.t: A spreadsheet formula that adds up a column of numbers
options.why: A spreadsheet formula adds numbers within a sheet; RPA bots work across applications to perform whole tasks.

options.t: Physical robots that work in offices and move paper around
options.why: RPA bots are software, not physical robots, so they do not move paper around offices.

q: What is cybersecurity?

options.t: Selling computers and other devices to customers
options.why: Selling computers and devices is a retail business; cybersecurity is the practice of protecting systems and data.

options.t: Writing code for websites and phone apps for clients
options.why: Writing code for websites and apps is software development, not cybersecurity, which protects systems.

options.t: Protecting systems and data from unauthorized access
options.why: Cybersecurity means protecting systems, networks and data from unauthorized access and attacks, which is vital for firms handling financial records.

options.t: Printing documents and reports on paper for the office
options.why: Printing documents is an office task, not cybersecurity, which protects digital systems and data.

q: Which spreadsheet function adds a range of cells?

options.t: MAX
options.why: MAX returns the largest value in a range; it does not total the cells.

options.t: COUNT
options.why: COUNT returns how many cells contain numbers; it does not add their values.

options.t: AVERAGE
options.why: AVERAGE adds the cells and then divides by how many there are; it returns the mean, not the total.

options.t: SUM
options.why: SUM adds all the numbers in a range of cells, as in =SUM(A1:A10).

q: Which spreadsheet function finds the largest value in a range?

options.t: COUNT
options.why: COUNT tells how many cells contain numbers, not which value is the largest.

options.t: SUM
options.why: SUM adds a range to a total; it does not find the largest value.

options.t: MIN
options.why: MIN finds the smallest value in a range, the opposite of what is asked.

options.t: MAX
options.why: MAX returns the largest value in a range of cells, as in =MAX(A1:A10).

q: Which spreadsheet function counts cells containing numbers?

options.t: AVERAGE
options.why: AVERAGE returns the mean of the numbers in a range; it does not count how many cells contain numbers.

options.t: SUM
options.why: SUM adds the numbers in a range; it does not count how many cells have numbers.

options.t: COUNT
options.why: COUNT returns the number of cells in a range that contain numbers, as in =COUNT(A1:A10).

options.t: MAX
options.why: MAX returns the largest value in a range; it does not count cells.

q: What does an absolute cell reference ($A$1) do?

options.t: Stays fixed when the formula is copied
options.why: An absolute reference with dollar signs ($A$1) stays fixed on the same cell when the formula is copied, which is useful for constants like a tax rate.

options.t: Changes when copied to the next cell down
options.why: Changing when copied is the behavior of a relative reference like A1, not an absolute reference with dollar signs.

options.t: Hides the cell from view on the sheet
options.why: Hiding cells is done with formatting commands; absolute references only control how a formula's cell address behaves when copied.

options.t: Deletes the cell and all the data in it
options.why: Deleting a cell is a separate editing action; an absolute reference only locks the cell address in a formula.

q: What does a relative cell reference (A1) do when copied?

options.t: Stays fixed when it is copied
options.why: Staying fixed when copied is the behavior of an absolute reference ($A$1), not a relative reference like A1.

options.t: Adjusts to the new location
options.why: A relative reference like A1 adjusts to the new location when copied, so copying down a row changes A1 to A2.

options.t: Deletes the cell and its data
options.why: Copying a formula does not delete a cell or its data; a relative reference simply shifts to the new position.

options.t: Hides the cell from the view
options.why: Hiding a cell is a formatting action; a relative reference only changes its address when copied.

q: What does a bookkeeper do?

options.t: Files lawsuits for the company in court
options.why: Filing lawsuits is done by attorneys, not by bookkeepers who handle financial records.

options.t: Records daily financial transactions
options.why: A bookkeeper records daily financial transactions, such as sales, purchases, payments and receipts, and keeps the books accurate.

options.t: Designs products for sale to customers
options.why: Designing products is the job of designers and engineers, not bookkeepers.

options.t: Sets strategy for the next ten years
options.why: Setting long-term strategy is a job for executives, not bookkeepers, who record transactions.

q: What does a financial analyst do?

options.t: Prepares payroll only, and handles nothing else in the whole firm overall
options.why: Payroll preparation is a narrow clerical task; a financial analyst evaluates data to guide investment and business decisions.

options.t: Records every sale made in the shop during each day of trade
options.why: Recording daily sales is done by a bookkeeper or cashier; a financial analyst studies data and makes recommendations.

options.t: Evaluates financial data to guide investment or business decisions
options.why: A financial analyst evaluates financial data, trends and statements to guide investment or business decisions, often with forecasts and reports.

options.t: Audits tax returns for the revenue agency and for the public
options.why: Auditing tax returns is the work of tax agency auditors, not financial analysts, who advise on investments and strategy.

q: What does a cost accountant do?

options.t: Analyzes production costs to help control expenses
options.why: A cost accountant analyzes production costs, budgets and variances to help management control expenses and set prices.

options.t: Prepares personal taxes for people who visit the office
options.why: Preparing personal taxes is the work of a tax preparer; cost accountants work on internal costs.

options.t: Audits public firms for the stock market and investors
options.why: Auditing public firms is done by external auditors; cost accountants work inside a company on costs.

options.t: Sells software to firms that need new systems and tools
options.why: Selling software is a sales role; cost accountants analyze production costs.

q: What does a controller do?

options.t: Manages the warehouse and the stock of goods held for sale
options.why: Managing the warehouse and stock is an operations or inventory manager's job, not a controller's.

options.t: Leads the sales team and sets monthly targets for sellers
options.why: Leading the sales team is the sales manager's job; a controller oversees accounting.

options.t: Runs marketing campaigns and plans ads for new products
options.why: Running marketing campaigns is the marketing manager's job; a controller oversees accounting.

options.t: Oversees a company's accounting operations and reporting
options.why: A controller oversees a company's accounting operations, financial reporting, internal controls and budgeting, usually reporting to the CFO.

q: What does a chief financial officer (CFO) do?

options.t: Records daily entries in the books of the firm
options.why: Recording daily entries is a bookkeeper's job; a CFO is a top executive who leads financial strategy.

options.t: Handles customer service and complaints for the firm
options.why: Customer service is handled by service managers; a CFO leads the company's financial function.

options.t: Leads a company's financial strategy and reporting
options.why: A CFO is a top executive who leads financial strategy, reporting, capital raising and risk management and advises the CEO.

options.t: Runs production lines and plans factory output weekly
options.why: Running production lines is an operations job, not the CFO's.

q: What is the CMA certification?

options.t: A tax license that allows people to prepare tax returns for clients
options.why: A tax license for preparing returns relates to credentials like the EA or CPA, not the CMA, which focuses on management accounting.

options.t: A sales license that allows people to run a retail shop in the town
options.why: Running a retail shop is a business license matter, not an accounting certification like the CMA.

options.t: A banking license that allows firms to take deposits from the public in the end
options.why: A banking license to take deposits is granted to banks by regulators; the CMA is a professional accounting credential.

options.t: Certified Management Accountant, focused on internal management accounting
options.why: The Certified Management Accountant (CMA) credential focuses on internal management accounting, covering planning, budgeting, cost analysis and performance management.

q: What is the CIA certification?

options.t: Certified Internal Auditor, focused on internal auditing
options.why: CIA stands for Certified Internal Auditor, the main global credential for internal audit professionals, awarded by the Institute of Internal Auditors after exams and experience requirements.

options.t: A tax license for people who prepare returns for others overall
options.why: This is a different certification, not the CIA. A tax license for return preparers is something like an enrolled agent or CPA credential, not the CIA designation.

options.t: A sales license for people who run shops and stores
options.why: The CIA is not a license for shop owners. Retail businesses need local business licenses and sales tax permits, while CIA is an auditing credential for internal auditors.

options.t: A spy agency that gathers secrets for the government
options.why: This describes the Central Intelligence Agency, a federal spy agency, not the professional certification. In accounting and business exams, CIA means Certified Internal Auditor.

q: Which branch of the U.S. government makes laws?

options.t: Executive branch
options.why: The executive branch, led by the President, enforces and carries out laws rather than writing them. It includes federal agencies and the cabinet departments.

options.t: Legislative branch
options.why: Congress, made up of the Senate and House of Representatives, is the legislative branch. Article I of the Constitution gives it the power to make federal laws.

options.t: Judicial branch
options.why: The judicial branch, headed by the Supreme Court, interprets laws and decides cases. It does not write laws, though its rulings can shape how they apply.

options.t: Military branch
options.why: The military is not one of the three constitutional branches of government. The branches are legislative, executive and judicial, with checks and balances among them.

q: Laws passed by a legislature are called:

options.t: Common law
options.why: Common law comes from judges' decisions in past cases rather than from a legislature. It is built on precedent, so it is not the name for passed laws.

options.t: Regulatory law
options.why: Regulatory law consists of rules written by government agencies under authority granted by legislatures. It is not laws passed directly by the legislature itself.

options.t: Natural law
options.why: Natural law is a philosophy that some rights come from nature or morality. It is not a body of laws enacted by a legislature.

options.t: Statutory law
options.why: Statutory law is written law enacted by a legislature, such as Congress or a state legislature. Examples include the Fair Labor Standards Act and the UCC as adopted by states.

q: How does a civil case differ from a criminal case?

options.t: The government must always be the party that files a civil lawsuit
options.why: Civil lawsuits are filed by private parties such as people or businesses. The government files criminal charges, so it is not always the civil plaintiff.

options.t: A civil judgment always results in a long jail sentence for the losing party
options.why: Civil cases usually end in money damages or court orders, not jail. Jail sentences are a criminal penalty for crimes, so a civil judgment does not bring them.

options.t: In a civil case a private party usually sues to get a remedy such as money
options.why: In civil cases a private party sues for a remedy like money damages or a court order. Criminal cases are brought by the government to punish crimes and may lead to prison.

options.t: Guilt has to be proven beyond a reasonable doubt in every civil case
options.why: Beyond a reasonable doubt is the criminal standard. Civil cases use the lower preponderance of the evidence standard, meaning it is more likely than not that the claim is true.

q: Which court usually hears a case for the first time?

options.t: A trial court
options.why: A trial court, such as a district or state trial court, hears a case first. It takes evidence, listens to witnesses and decides the facts and the law.

options.t: The Supreme Court
options.why: The Supreme Court mostly reviews cases already decided by lower courts and has limited original jurisdiction. It is usually the last court to act, not the first.

options.t: A review court
options.why: A review court is an appeals court that checks whether lower courts applied the law properly. It reviews existing records rather than hearing a case for the first time.

options.t: A jury of peers
options.why: A jury of peers is a group of citizens who decide facts inside a trial. It is not a court, and the trial court is what hears the case first.

q: Two companies agree to let a neutral third party hear their dispute and make a binding decision. This process is called:

options.t: Mediation
options.why: Mediation uses a neutral person to help the parties reach their own agreement, but the mediator cannot impose a binding decision on them.

options.t: Litigation
options.why: Litigation means resolving a dispute through a lawsuit in court before a judge or jury. It is not a private process with a neutral third party chosen by the sides.

options.t: Deposition
options.why: A deposition is sworn out-of-court testimony taken from a witness during discovery before trial. It is not a method for settling a whole dispute.

options.t: Arbitration
options.why: In arbitration, the parties agree to let a neutral arbitrator hear the dispute and issue a decision that is usually binding. It is faster and more private than court.

q: What do we call the practice of courts following earlier decisions on similar cases?

options.t: Damages
options.why: Damages are money awarded to a party who was harmed. They are a remedy a court gives, not the practice of following earlier court decisions.

options.t: Precedent
options.why: Precedent means courts follow earlier decisions on similar cases, which keeps the law consistent and predictable. The related Latin phrase is stare decisis.

options.t: Discovery
options.why: Discovery is the pretrial stage where each side obtains evidence and information from the other. It does not describe courts following earlier rulings.

options.t: Jurisdiction
options.why: Jurisdiction is a court's authority to hear a particular type of case or cases from a certain area. It is not about following earlier decisions.

q: Which best describes a tort?

options.t: A civil wrong, other than breach of contract, that causes harm to someone
options.why: A tort is a civil wrong, other than breach of contract, that causes harm. Examples include negligence, defamation and trespass, and the victim can sue for damages.

options.t: A crime that the government prosecutes and punishes in a criminal court as a rule
options.why: A crime prosecuted by the government is a criminal offense, not a tort. Torts are private civil wrongs, though one act can sometimes be both a crime and a tort.

options.t: A written agreement between two parties that a court can enforce
options.why: A written agreement a court can enforce is a contract. Breach of contract is handled separately from torts, which cover harms outside of agreements.

options.t: A type of business license that a government agency issues to owners
options.why: A business license is permission from a government agency to operate. It has nothing to do with wrongful acts that harm people, which is what a tort is.

q: Which element is required for a valid contract?

options.t: Equal bargaining power held by both of the sides
options.why: Equal bargaining power is not required for a valid contract. Courts enforce agreements between parties of unequal strength unless there is fraud, duress or unconscionable terms.

options.t: A written document signed in every single case
options.why: Many contracts are valid when oral. Only certain types, such as real estate sales, must be written under the statute of frauds, so writing is not always required.

options.t: Mutual agreement through an offer and acceptance
options.why: A valid contract requires mutual agreement, shown by an offer and an acceptance, plus consideration, capacity and legality. Without a meeting of the minds there is no contract.

options.t: A notary's seal placed on each page of the deal
options.why: A notary's seal is not required for most contracts. Notarization only helps verify identity or signatures for specific documents like deeds, not for every deal.

q: A seller offers a laptop for $500. The buyer replies, 'I'll pay $450.' Legally, the buyer's reply is:

options.t: An acceptance of the seller's price of $500
options.why: The buyer did not agree to the $500 price. Accepting means agreeing to the terms exactly, and a different price shows the buyer did not accept.

options.t: A revocation of the buyer's earlier interest in it
options.why: A revocation is when the person who made an offer withdraws it. Here the buyer is responding to the seller's offer, not withdrawing one of their own.

options.t: A counteroffer that rejects the original offer
options.why: A counteroffer changes the terms and rejects the original offer, ending the seller's offer. The seller can then accept or reject the new $450 proposal.

options.t: A binding agreement on the original price of $500
options.why: No binding agreement exists yet at $500. The buyer proposed a different price, so there is no meeting of the minds until someone accepts the new terms.

q: The Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) Article 2 governs:

options.t: Patent filings
options.why: Patent filings are governed by federal patent law, handled through the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office. The UCC does not cover intellectual property registration.

options.t: Sales of land
options.why: Sales of land fall under real property law and the statute of frauds, not the UCC. UCC Article 2 applies to goods, which are movable items.

options.t: Job contracts
options.why: Employment and job contracts are governed by common law and labor and employment statutes. UCC Article 2 deals with sales of goods, not services or jobs.

options.t: Sales of goods
options.why: UCC Article 2 governs sales of goods, meaning movable tangible items. It sets rules for contract formation, warranties, delivery and remedies in commercial sales.

q: What does the implied warranty of merchantability mean?

options.t: The seller guarantees the lowest price anywhere in town
options.why: The implied warranty of merchantability does not promise the lowest price. It concerns product quality, not price, and sellers are free to set their own prices.

options.t: Goods sold by a merchant are fit for their ordinary purpose
options.why: Merchantability means goods sold by a merchant are fit for the ordinary purpose they are used for and of average acceptable quality. The UCC implies it automatically in sales.

options.t: The buyer must test every single item before paying for it
options.why: The warranty protects buyers who expect usable goods. It does not require the buyer to test every item, since the seller guarantees ordinary quality.

options.t: The goods that are sold can never be returned for any reason
options.why: The warranty has nothing to do with banning returns. Return policies are set separately by the seller, and the warranty actually gives buyers rights if goods are defective.

q: A contract was signed because one party threatened the other. It may be voidable because of:

options.t: Duress
options.why: Duress means a party was forced into a contract by threats, so the agreement was not voluntary. A contract signed under duress is voidable by the threatened party.

options.t: Mistake
options.why: Mistake involves a misunderstanding about a fact in the contract. It does not involve a threat, so it is not the ground for avoiding a contract signed under pressure.

options.t: Capacity
options.why: Capacity means a party can legally understand and enter a contract. Lack of capacity involves minors or the mentally incompetent, not threats against a competent adult.

options.t: Illegality
options.why: Illegality means the contract's purpose breaks the law, making it void. A threat against one party concerns voluntariness, not whether the subject matter is lawful.

q: Which contract generally must be in writing to be enforceable under the statute of frauds?

options.t: A contract to buy a candy bar today
options.why: A contract to buy a candy bar today is a small sale completed immediately, so no writing is required. The statute of frauds covers larger or longer-term deals.

options.t: An oral agreement to lend a pencil to a pal
options.why: Lending a pencil is a minor informal arrangement that does not fall under the statute of frauds. Oral agreements like this are generally enforceable if proved.

options.t: A contract for the sale of real estate
options.why: The statute of frauds requires contracts for the sale of real estate to be in writing and signed. It also covers goods of $500 or more under the UCC.

options.t: A one-time babysitting deal for a night
options.why: A one-time babysitting deal is a short service that can be completed within a year, so an oral agreement is generally enforceable and no writing is required.

q: A seller fails to deliver goods as promised in a valid contract. This is a:

options.t: Breach of contract
options.why: When a party fails to perform what a valid contract requires, such as not delivering goods as promised, that is a breach of contract. The other party may seek remedies.

options.t: Assignment of rights
options.why: An assignment of rights transfers a party's contract rights to a third person. It does not describe failing to perform promised duties.

options.t: Novation of parties
options.why: A novation replaces one party in a contract with a new party, with everyone's consent. It is not a failure to perform and does not describe nondelivery.

options.t: Ratification of terms
options.why: Ratification means approving a contract or act that was not originally binding, such as a minor confirming a deal after turning 18. It is not nonperformance.

q: Which federal law sets minimum wage and overtime standards?

options.t: Occupational Safety Act
options.why: The Occupational Safety and Health Act sets workplace safety rules enforced by OSHA. It does not set minimum wage or overtime standards.

options.t: Fair Labor Standards Act
options.why: The Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 sets the federal minimum wage, overtime pay at 1.5 times the regular rate over 40 hours, recordkeeping rules and child labor limits.

options.t: Family and Medical Leave Act
options.why: The Family and Medical Leave Act gives eligible employees up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for family and medical reasons. It does not address wages.

options.t: Civil Rights Act of 1964
options.why: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 bans employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex and national origin. It does not set minimum wage or overtime pay.

q: What does at-will employment generally mean?

options.t: Employees must give a full year of notice before leaving
options.why: At-will employment does not require a year of notice. Either side can generally end the relationship at any time without advance notice, unless a contract says otherwise.

options.t: The employer can fire for any reason, including discrimination
options.why: At-will employment does not allow firing for discriminatory reasons. Federal and state laws still ban firing based on race, sex, religion, age, disability and other protected traits.

options.t: Employees may only be fired with a union's approval in advance
options.why: Union approval is not needed under at-will employment. Union contracts often require just cause for firing, which is the opposite of the at-will rule.

options.t: Either side may end the job at any time for a lawful reason
options.why: Under at-will employment either the employer or employee may end the job at any time, with or without notice, as long as the reason is lawful and not discriminatory or retaliatory.

q: The Americans with Disabilities Act requires employers to provide:

options.t: Higher pay for each worker with a disability
options.why: The ADA does not require higher pay for workers with disabilities. Disabled employees must be paid under the same standards as others doing the same job.

options.t: Reasonable accommodations for disabled workers
options.why: The ADA requires employers to provide reasonable accommodations, such as modified equipment or schedules, to qualified workers with disabilities unless it creates undue hardship for the business.

options.t: A guaranteed promotion after one year on the job
options.why: The ADA bans discrimination in promotions but does not guarantee promotions. Advancement still depends on qualifications and performance like for any other employee.

options.t: Free housing near the workplace for all staff
options.why: The ADA does not require employers to provide free housing. Its duties focus on equal access and reasonable accommodations in the workplace.

q: An employee works 46 hours in a week at $12 an hour. Overtime is paid at 1.5 times the regular rate for hours over 40. What is the gross pay?

options.why: $828 comes from paying all 46 hours at 1.5 times the rate: 46 x $18 = $828. Overtime applies only to the 6 hours beyond 40, so this overstates pay.
$480 is only the regular pay for 40 hours: 40 x $12 = $480. It leaves out the 6 overtime hours, so the gross pay is higher than this.
$552 pays all 46 hours at the regular rate: 46 x $12 = $552. It ignores that the 6 hours over 40 must be paid at time and a half.
Regular pay is 40 x $12 = $480. Overtime rate is $12 x 1.5 = $18, and 6 overtime hours are 6 x $18 = $108. Gross pay is $480 + $108 = $588.

q: Which agency enforces federal laws against workplace discrimination?

options.t: Securities and Exchange Commission
options.why: The SEC regulates securities markets and investor protection. It does not enforce laws against workplace discrimination, which is handled by a different agency.

options.t: Internal Revenue Service of the U.S.
options.why: The IRS collects federal taxes and enforces the tax code. It does not investigate discrimination complaints against employers.

options.t: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission
options.why: The EEOC enforces federal laws against workplace discrimination, including Title VII, the ADA and the ADEA. Employees file charges with it before suing in many cases.

options.t: Federal Reserve Board of Governors
options.why: The Federal Reserve Board oversees monetary policy and the banking system. It has no role in investigating workplace discrimination.

q: What does workers' compensation provide?

options.t: Benefits for employees injured on the job
options.why: Workers' compensation is insurance that pays medical costs and lost wages for employees hurt or made ill on the job, generally without proving fault, and limits employer lawsuits.

options.t: A bonus paid out at the end of the year
options.why: A year-end bonus is extra pay decided by the employer. Workers' compensation is a mandatory insurance program for job-related injuries, not a bonus.

options.t: Retirement income for older staff members
options.why: Retirement income comes from pensions, 401(k) plans and Social Security. Workers' compensation covers on-the-job injuries and illness, not retirement.

options.t: Higher pay for experienced employees each year
options.why: Raises for experience are set by employers through pay scales and reviews. Workers' compensation is insurance coverage for injured employees and does not increase pay.

q: Which is typically true of an independent contractor?

options.t: They follow a daily work schedule that the company sets for them each week
options.why: A company-set daily schedule is typical of an employee, not a contractor. Independent contractors decide their own hours and work methods under the agreement.

options.t: They receive employee benefits such as paid time off and health cover
options.why: Employee benefits like paid time off and health coverage are usually provided to employees. Independent contractors generally must arrange their own benefits.

options.t: The business withholds income taxes from each of their payments
options.why: Businesses withhold income taxes from employees' paychecks. Independent contractors are paid in full and must pay their own income and self-employment taxes.

options.t: They control how and when the work is done and handle their own taxes
options.why: Independent contractors control how and when the work is done and pay their own taxes. The business controls only the result, which separates contractors from employees.

q: What does business ethics refer to?

options.t: Rules that explain how businesses must file their taxes
options.why: Rules for filing taxes belong to tax law, not ethics. Business ethics deals with moral principles about what is right and wrong in how companies behave.

options.t: Principles of right and wrong that guide business behavior
options.why: Business ethics means principles of right and wrong that guide behavior in business, such as honesty, fairness and respect, going beyond what the law minimally requires.

options.t: Methods that businesses use to advertise to their customers
options.why: Methods of advertising belong to marketing and promotion. Ethics concerns moral standards, though advertising itself should also follow ethical standards such as honesty.

options.t: Laws that apply only to very large public corporations
options.why: Ethics applies to all businesses of every size, not only large public corporations. Laws for public companies, like Sarbanes-Oxley, are a separate subject.

q: A manager discovers a coworker is falsifying sales reports. What is the best first response?

options.t: Report it through the proper company channel
options.why: Reporting falsified sales reports through the proper company channel, such as a supervisor, compliance office or ethics hotline, handles the problem fairly and follows company policy.

options.t: Ignore it so that no conflict arises in the team
options.why: Ignoring falsified reports lets fraud continue and can hurt the company and investors. Staying silent may also make the manager part of the problem.

options.t: Copy the same practice to keep up with them
options.why: Copying a dishonest practice is unethical and could be illegal fraud. Two wrongs do not make a right, and it spreads the problem.

options.t: Post about it on social media for everyone to see
options.why: Posting accusations on social media can harm reputations unfairly and break confidentiality rules. Concerns should first go through proper internal channels so they can be investigated.

q: Which is an example of a conflict of interest?

options.t: A sales rep meets the monthly target that was set by the manager
options.why: Meeting a sales target set by a manager is normal job performance and does not involve personal interests competing with the employer's interests.

options.t: An employee takes a vacation that was approved in advance
options.why: Taking approved vacation is an ordinary workplace benefit. It does not create any clash between personal interests and job duties.

options.t: A buyer awards a contract to a company owned by their sibling
options.why: A buyer giving a contract to a sibling's company is a conflict of interest because personal ties could bias a decision that should serve the employer. It should be disclosed.

options.t: A manager thanks the whole team for finishing a project
options.why: Thanking a team is normal good management. It does not create a clash between a manager's personal gain and duty to the company.

q: What is the main purpose of whistleblower protections?

options.t: To reward employees who spread gossip about their coworkers at the office in practice
options.why: Whistleblower laws do not exist to reward gossip. They protect workers who report real legal or ethical violations through proper channels in good faith.

options.t: To stop any employee from making a report about the company to outsiders
options.why: Whistleblower laws do the opposite of stopping reports. They encourage employees to speak up about wrongdoing and shield them from punishment for doing so.

options.t: To limit which people are allowed to hold a particular job at the firm
options.why: Whistleblower laws have nothing to do with limiting who can hold a job. They protect reporting employees from retaliation like firing, demotion or harassment.

options.t: To protect employees who report illegal or unethical conduct from retaliation
options.why: Whistleblower protections shield employees who report illegal or unethical conduct from retaliation such as firing or demotion. Laws like Sarbanes-Oxley and Dodd-Frank include such protections.

q: What is a code of ethics?

options.t: A written set of standards for behavior in an organization
options.why: A code of ethics is a written set of standards that tells employees what behavior is expected, such as honesty and fairness. It guides decisions and shows company values.

options.t: A tax form that businesses file with the government each spring
options.why: A tax form filed with the government is a tax return. A code of ethics is an internal document about conduct, not a government filing.

options.t: A list of the prices that the company charges for its products
options.why: A price list shows what products cost. A code of ethics describes behavior standards, not prices charged to customers.

options.t: A schedule that lists the work shifts of every employee
options.why: A work shift schedule is an operations document that assigns hours. A code of ethics describes expected behavior and principles for employees.

q: Which action is an example of corporate social responsibility?

options.t: Hiding product safety problems from buyers
options.why: Hiding product safety problems is unethical and often illegal. Corporate social responsibility means acting for the good of society, which is the opposite of concealment.

options.t: A company reducing its packaging waste
options.why: Reducing packaging waste shows corporate social responsibility because the company voluntarily acts to protect the environment and benefit society beyond what profit alone requires.

options.t: Avoiding all community involvement
options.why: Avoiding all community involvement is the opposite of social responsibility, which includes giving back through donations, volunteering and community support.

options.t: Raising prices as much as it can each year
options.why: Raising prices as much as possible each year focuses only on profit. It does not show concern for customers or society as social responsibility requires.

q: Which is an example of insider trading?

options.t: Holding a stock for ten years before selling it for a good profit
options.why: Holding a stock for ten years is legal long-term investing. Insider trading requires using material nonpublic information, which is not present here.

options.t: Buying stock after reading a public news report about it in the paper
options.why: Buying after reading a public news report uses public information, which is legal. Insider trading involves confidential information not available to the general public.

options.t: Buying stock based on confidential information that is not yet public
options.why: Insider trading is buying or selling securities using material nonpublic information. It is illegal under securities laws enforced by the SEC and can bring fines and prison.

options.t: Selling some stock in order to pay for a new car and a new house
options.why: Selling stock to pay for personal expenses is a normal reason to sell. It does not involve confidential company information, so it is not insider trading.

q: Which U.S. agency collects federal income taxes?

options.t: Securities Exchange Agency
options.why: No agency called the Securities Exchange Agency exists for collecting taxes. The Securities and Exchange Commission regulates markets and does not collect income taxes.

options.t: Federal Trade Commission
options.why: The Federal Trade Commission protects consumers and enforces competition laws. It does not collect federal income taxes.

options.t: Internal Revenue Service
options.why: The Internal Revenue Service, part of the Treasury Department, collects federal income taxes and enforces the Internal Revenue Code, including processing returns and refunds.

options.t: Federal Reserve Bank
options.why: The Federal Reserve is the central bank that sets monetary policy. It does not collect income taxes from individuals or businesses.

q: Under Chapter 7 bankruptcy, a business typically:

options.t: Reorganizes debts and keeps going
options.why: Reorganizing debts and continuing operations is Chapter 11 bankruptcy. Chapter 7 is liquidation, so the business generally ends rather than continuing.

options.t: Sells its assets to pay creditors
options.why: Chapter 7 is liquidation: a trustee sells the business's nonexempt assets and uses the money to pay creditors, and the business usually closes.

options.t: Receives a government bailout
options.why: A government bailout is a rescue with public funds, which is not part of the Chapter 7 process. Chapter 7 is a court proceeding handled by a trustee.

options.t: Transfers its debts to its owners
options.why: Transferring debts to owners is not how Chapter 7 works. Debts are paid from asset sales, and remaining unpaid debts of a corporation are typically discharged.

q: The Truth in Lending Act requires lenders to:

options.t: Clearly disclose the costs and terms of credit
options.why: The Truth in Lending Act requires lenders to clearly disclose the cost and terms of credit, including the APR and finance charges, so borrowers can compare offers.

options.t: Keep the interest rates secret until the closing day
options.why: The law requires lenders to disclose interest rates up front, not hide them until closing. Transparency is its main purpose.

options.t: Charge no interest on any loan made at all
options.why: The law does not ban interest charges. Lenders may charge interest as long as the rate and costs are properly disclosed to the borrower.

options.t: Lend money to everyone who happens to apply
options.why: The law does not force lenders to approve every applicant. Lenders can still deny credit based on creditworthiness, within other anti-discrimination rules.

q: How is the profit of a sole proprietorship usually taxed?

options.t: On a separate corporate tax return only
options.why: A sole proprietorship is not a separate taxable entity, so it has no separate corporate return. Business income flows to the owner's personal return.

options.t: It is not taxed at all by any government
options.why: Sole proprietorship profits are taxable income. The owner pays income tax and self-employment tax on the profit each year.

options.t: Only by the state, not the federal government
options.why: Sole proprietorship profit is taxed at the federal level as well as by most states. It is not limited to state taxes.

options.t: On the owner's personal income tax return
options.why: A sole proprietorship's profit is taxed on the owner's personal income tax return, usually using Schedule C with Form 1040. The owner also pays self-employment tax.

q: Who generally collects sales tax from customers?

options.t: The local post office staff
options.why: Post office staff do not collect sales tax from customers. Sales tax is collected by sellers of taxable goods and services.

options.t: The seller at the time of sale
options.why: The seller collects sales tax from the customer at the time of sale and then sends it to the state or local tax authority.

options.t: The customer's bank or lender
options.why: Banks and lenders do not collect sales tax on purchases. The seller adds it to the price at checkout and remits it.

options.t: The product's manufacturer only
options.why: Manufacturers do not collect sales tax from final customers in a retail sale. The retail seller usually collects it, and some manufacturers collect it only on direct sales.

q: A lender holds a security interest in a borrower's car. What can the lender do if the borrower defaults?

options.t: Sell their house
options.why: A security interest covers only the specific collateral, here the car. The lender cannot take the borrower's house just because the car loan is in default.

options.t: Keep their wages
options.why: A lender cannot simply keep a borrower's wages. Wage garnishment requires a court judgment, and a security interest applies only to the pledged collateral.

options.t: Cancel other debts
options.why: A default does not cancel the borrower's other debts. Each debt stays in force, and the security interest affects only the car.

options.t: Repossess the car
options.why: When a borrower defaults, a lender with a security interest in the car can repossess it and sell it to recover the unpaid loan balance, following UCC rules.

q: What is a tariff?

options.t: A tax on imported goods
options.why: A tariff is a tax placed on imported goods. It raises their price, protects domestic producers and generates government revenue.

options.t: A ban on all exports
options.why: A ban on all exports is an export embargo, not a tariff. Tariffs are taxes on imports, not prohibitions on sending goods out.

options.t: A payment to exporters
options.why: A payment to exporters is a subsidy, which helps domestic sellers. A tariff is instead a tax charged on imports.

options.t: A cap on import amounts
options.why: A cap on import amounts is a quota. A tariff taxes imports rather than limiting how many units may enter.

q: What does a quota do?

options.t: Taxes goods that are brought in from other countries
options.why: Taxing imported goods describes a tariff, not a quota. A quota limits quantity instead of adding a tax to the price.

options.t: Bans all trade with a particular foreign country
options.why: Banning all trade with a particular country is an embargo. A quota only limits quantities and still allows some trade.

options.t: Limits the quantity of a good that may be imported
options.why: A quota limits the quantity of a good that can be imported during a period. It restricts supply, which can raise domestic prices and protect local producers.

options.t: Pays companies a subsidy to export their goods
options.why: Paying companies to export is a subsidy. A quota limits imports and does not pay businesses to sell abroad.

q: What is an embargo?

options.t: A trade deal that lowers duties for nations
options.why: A trade deal that lowers duties is a free trade agreement. An embargo does the opposite by blocking trade.

options.t: A limit on import quantities allowed
options.why: A limit on import quantities is a quota. An embargo is a full ban on trade, not a partial cap on units.

options.t: A tax on imports charged at the border
options.why: A tax on imports charged at the border is a tariff. An embargo bans trade rather than taxing it.

options.t: A government ban on trade with a country
options.why: An embargo is a government ban on trade with a particular country, often used as a political or security tool. The long-running US embargo on Cuba is an example.

q: The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act prohibits:

options.t: Advertising products in other countries abroad
options.why: The FCPA does not stop companies from advertising abroad. Marketing in foreign countries is legal and common for international businesses.

options.t: Bribing foreign officials to win business
options.why: The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act bans bribing foreign officials to win or keep business. It also requires accurate books and records for companies that report to the SEC.

options.t: Selling products to customers overseas
options.why: Selling products overseas is legal and encouraged. The FCPA targets bribery of officials, not ordinary export sales.

options.t: Paying foreign employees their regular wages
options.why: Paying foreign employees regular wages is legal. The FCPA bans bribes to foreign officials, not normal compensation for workers.

q: What does exporting mean?

options.t: Taxing goods at the border post
options.why: Taxing goods at the border is a tariff or duty. Exporting is the act of sending goods out to another country.

options.t: Buying goods from another country
options.why: Buying goods from another country is importing. Exporting is the opposite, moving goods out of the home country.

options.t: Selling goods to another country
options.why: Exporting means selling goods or services to customers in another country. It brings money into the home economy and expands the market.

options.t: Producing goods for the home market
options.why: Producing goods for the home market is domestic production. Exporting involves selling products to buyers in foreign countries.

q: Which organization sets rules for trade among its member nations?

options.t: World Trade Organization
options.why: The World Trade Organization sets and enforces rules for trade among member nations and settles trade disputes between them. It is based in Geneva, Switzerland.

options.t: International Red Cross
options.why: The International Red Cross provides humanitarian aid during disasters and war. It does not set trade rules between nations.

options.t: International Sports Body
options.why: An international sports body governs athletic competition. It does not set trade rules for member countries.

options.t: World Health Organization
options.why: The World Health Organization coordinates global public health. It does not make trade rules, which are the work of the WTO.

q: Which source of law is the highest in the United States?

options.t: Local city ordinances
options.why: Local ordinances are the lowest level of government law. They must follow state and federal law and cannot override the Constitution.

options.t: Agency rules and orders
options.why: Agency rules get their power from statutes passed by legislatures. They rank below laws and the Constitution and must stay within granted authority.

options.t: The U.S. Constitution
options.why: The U.S. Constitution is the supreme law of the land. All federal and state laws must follow it, and conflicting laws can be struck down.

options.t: Company handbook rules
options.why: Company handbooks are private rules that employers set. They have no legal power over federal, state or local law.

q: What is statutory law?

options.t: Laws written and passed by legislatures
options.why: Statutory law is written and passed by legislatures such as Congress and state legislatures. Examples include the Civil Rights Act and the Uniform Commercial Code as enacted.

options.t: Customs followed by a community group
options.why: Community customs are social habits, not laws. Statutory law is formally enacted by lawmakers.

options.t: Rules a business sets for its staff
options.why: Rules that a business sets for staff are company policies. Statutory law is made by legislatures and applies to the public.

options.t: Laws created only by judges in court
options.why: Laws created only by judges describe common law. Statutory law instead comes from legislatures.

q: What is common law?

options.t: Law adopted only by treaty with other nations
options.why: Law adopted by treaty is international law. Common law is not formed by agreements with other nations.

options.t: Law developed from judges' decisions in past cases
options.why: Common law develops from judges' decisions in past cases, which become precedent for later similar cases. It is the basis of much contract and tort law.

options.t: Law written by a legislature as written statutes
options.why: Laws written by a legislature are statutes. Common law is created by courts rather than enacted legislation.

options.t: Law set by agency regulators and government boards
options.why: Rules set by agency regulators are administrative law. Common law grows from court decisions instead.

q: What is administrative law?

options.t: Laws that apply only to licensed attorneys
options.why: Administrative law is not limited to attorneys. Rules of professional conduct for lawyers are a different, narrow set of rules.

options.t: Rules that are written inside a private company
options.why: Private company rules are internal policies. Administrative law comes from government agencies and has the force of law.

options.t: Laws that are passed only by a state senate
options.why: Laws passed by a state senate are statutes. Administrative law instead comes from agencies, not legislatures.

options.t: Rules and decisions made by government agencies
options.why: Administrative law consists of rules, regulations and decisions made by government agencies such as the EPA or SEC, under authority granted by legislatures.

q: What is the difference between civil law and criminal law?

options.t: Civil law settles disputes between parties; criminal law punishes offenses against society
options.why: Civil law settles disputes between parties, often with money damages, while criminal law punishes offenses against society with fines or prison. The government prosecutes crimes.

options.t: Civil law deals only with crimes, while criminal law deals only with contract disputes
options.why: This reverses the two. Criminal law deals with crimes, while civil law handles disputes such as contracts and torts.

options.t: There is no real difference between the two kinds of law, as both handle the same cases every time
options.why: There is a real difference. Civil and criminal cases have different parties, standards of proof and outcomes, though one act can lead to both.

options.t: Civil law applies only to businesses, while criminal law applies only to individuals
options.why: Civil law is not limited to businesses and criminal law is not limited to individuals. Both can involve people or companies, so this split is wrong.

q: Who has the burden of proof in a criminal trial?

options.t: The jury alone
options.why: The jury decides the verdict based on the evidence, but it does not carry the burden of proof. The prosecution must prove guilt.

options.t: The judge decides
options.why: The judge manages the trial and rules on law, but does not hold the burden of proof. The prosecution must prove its case.

options.t: The defendant alone
options.why: The defendant is presumed innocent and does not have to prove anything. Placing the burden on the defendant would reverse that presumption.

options.t: The prosecution
options.why: The prosecution carries the burden of proof in a criminal trial and must prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The defendant is presumed innocent until then.

q: What standard of proof is used in most civil cases?

options.t: Clear and convincing proof
options.why: Clear and convincing evidence is a higher standard used in some civil matters like fraud or termination of parental rights, but not most civil cases.

options.t: Beyond a reasonable doubt
options.why: Beyond a reasonable doubt is the criminal standard, the highest level of proof. Most civil cases use a lower standard.

options.t: Preponderance of the evidence
options.why: Most civil cases use preponderance of the evidence, meaning the claim is more likely true than not, often described as greater than 50 percent.

options.t: Absolute certainty of guilt
