options.why: A yearly income statement is an accounting report of revenues and expenses, and it has nothing to do with filing notice of a lender's claim.

options.t: A bank statement showing deposits to an account
options.why: A bank statement lists deposits and withdrawals on an account, whereas a UCC-1 is a public notice of a security interest in the debtor's property.

q: What can a secured lender do if the borrower defaults?

options.t: Repossess the collateral according to the law
options.why: Upon default a secured lender may repossess the collateral and usually sell it, following the law, to apply the proceeds to the unpaid debt.

options.t: Take all of the borrower's other property too
options.why: A secured lender's rights are generally limited to the pledged collateral, so the lender cannot just take the borrower's other unrelated property.

options.t: Ignore the debt and simply wait for payment
options.why: Simply ignoring the debt is not a required response, since the lender has remedies, and a secured creditor can act on its security interest.

options.t: Destroy the borrower's records and files
options.why: Destroying a borrower's records is unlawful and is no remedy at all, because a secured lender must follow legal procedures when it enforces its rights.

q: What is employment at will?

options.t: Either side may end the job at any time for any lawful reason
options.why: Employment at will means either the employer or the employee can end the job at any time for any lawful reason, with or without notice, in most states.

options.t: Employers must give a reason and a year's notice to workers overall
options.why: At will employment does not require a stated reason or a year's notice, because the arrangement lets either side end it freely, within legal limits.

options.t: Employees must stay for a minimum of one year in the job
options.why: There is no minimum stay required of employees, since an at will worker may resign at any time, and only a contract could set a term.

options.t: Employees can only be fired after a written warning notice
options.why: At will employees do not need a written warning before dismissal, since the employer may end the job without a progressive discipline process, unless a contract says otherwise.

q: What does the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) establish?

options.t: Taxes that are charged on business profits each year
options.why: Business profit taxes are set by tax laws such as the Internal Revenue Code, while the FLSA covers wages, hours and child labor.

options.t: Rules for owning and running a franchise business
options.why: Franchise rules come from franchise regulations and contract law, but the FLSA is a labor law about wages and hours of employees.

options.t: Standards for how products are packaged and labeled
options.why: Packaging and labeling standards are covered by consumer protection and product safety laws, not by the FLSA, which regulates pay and employment conditions.

options.t: Minimum wage, overtime pay and child labor rules
options.why: The FLSA sets the federal minimum wage, requires overtime pay for covered employees working over 40 hours a week, and restricts child labor.

q: What is overtime pay?

options.t: Pay that is given for training sessions only
options.why: Training pay may be due under wage rules, but overtime pay specifically means higher pay for hours beyond the weekly limit.

options.t: Extra pay, often 1.5 times, for hours over 40
options.why: Overtime pay is extra pay, often 1.5 times the regular rate, owed to non-exempt employees for hours worked beyond 40 in a week.

options.t: Pay that is given for sick days taken at work
options.why: Sick day pay is a benefit set by employer policy or state law, and it is different from overtime pay for hours beyond 40.

options.t: A bonus that is paid once every year to staff
options.why: An annual bonus is extra compensation paid once a year at the employer's choice, which is not tied to hours worked over 40.

q: What is the difference between exempt and non-exempt employees?

options.t: Exempt employees must work overtime for free, but non-exempt ones may not
options.why: Exempt employees are not forced to work overtime for free; they simply are not entitled to overtime pay, which is paid to non-exempt workers.

options.t: Exempt employees pay no taxes on their wages at all, unlike the others
options.why: Both exempt and non-exempt employees must pay taxes on wages, so exempt status refers to overtime rules and not to tax treatment.

options.t: Exempt employees are not entitled to overtime; non-exempt employees are
options.why: Exempt employees, often salaried executives or professionals, are not entitled to overtime pay, while non-exempt employees must receive it for hours beyond 40.

options.t: There is no difference between the two groups of employees at work
options.why: There is a real legal difference, because exemption decides whether the FLSA overtime rules apply, so the two groups are treated differently.

q: A non-exempt worker earns $14 per hour and works 45 hours in a week. How much overtime pay is owed for the extra hours?

options.t: $70 for the 5 extra hours at $14 per hour
options.why: This pays the extra hours at straight time of $14, which is wrong because overtime must be paid at 1.5 times the regular rate.

options.t: $0 because the job is hourly, not salaried
options.why: Hourly workers who are non-exempt are owed overtime, so the job being hourly does not remove the right to overtime pay at all.

options.t: $140 for the 5 extra hours at $28 per hour
options.why: This uses double the regular rate, $28, but the FLSA requires time and a half, so 5 hours at $28 equals $140, which is too high.

options.t: $105 for the 5 extra hours at $21 per hour
options.why: Overtime is 1.5 times $14, which is $21 per hour, and the 5 hours over 40 are paid at $21, so 5 times $21 equals $105.

q: What does the Equal Pay Act prohibit?

options.t: Paying men and women differently for equal work
options.why: The Equal Pay Act prohibits paying men and women different wages for equal work in jobs requiring equal skill, effort and responsibility at the same place.

options.t: Paying any worker more than the minimum wage overall
options.why: The act does not limit how much a worker can earn above minimum wage, and it targets pay differences based on sex.

options.t: Paying bonuses to high-performing workers
options.why: The Equal Pay Act does not ban bonuses for strong performers, since pay differences based on merit are allowed, but not those based on sex.

options.t: Paying workers on a weekly pay schedule only
options.why: The Equal Pay Act does not cover pay schedules, as employers can choose weekly or other pay periods, and it focuses on equal pay.

q: What does Title VII of the Civil Rights Act prohibit?

options.t: Requiring all employees to wear company uniforms to work
options.why: Requiring uniforms is a normal workplace policy and not discrimination, so Title VII does not prohibit employers from setting dress rules.

options.t: Job discrimination by race, color, religion, sex or origin
options.why: Title VII bans job discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin, and it covers hiring, firing, pay and other employment terms.

options.t: Offering paid vacation days to employees of the firm each year
options.why: Offering paid vacation is a lawful employee benefit, and Title VII does not prohibit it, though it does require benefits to be offered without discrimination.

options.t: Hiring workers only if they are under the age of 40
options.why: Hiring only people under 40 would be age discrimination, which another law, the ADEA, prohibits, and it is not what Title VII bans.

q: What does the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) protect?

options.t: Only government employees
options.why: The ADEA covers private employers and others, not only government employees, so limiting it to public workers misstates its reach.

options.t: Only retired workers
options.why: The ADEA is not limited to retirees, since it protects people who are still working or applying for jobs, as long as they are old enough.

options.t: Workers age 40 and older
options.why: The ADEA protects workers and applicants age 40 and older from age-based discrimination in hiring, firing, pay and other terms of employment.

options.t: Workers under 18 only
options.why: Workers under 18 are covered by child labor rules, while the ADEA protects older workers, which means those age 40 and above.

q: What does the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) require employers to provide?

options.t: Reasonable accommodations for disabled workers
options.why: The ADA requires employers to provide reasonable accommodations, such as modified equipment or schedules, so qualified workers with disabilities can do essential job duties.

options.t: Lower standards for every task in the job
options.why: The ADA does not lower standards for tasks, since employees must still perform the essential functions of the job, with or without accommodation.

options.t: A guaranteed promotion for every disabled worker
options.why: The ADA does not guarantee promotions, because disabled workers are treated like others and must be qualified for advancement just as any worker is.

options.t: Free housing for all of the disabled workers
options.why: Employers are not required to provide housing, because accommodations relate to doing the job, such as adjusted equipment or schedules, not living arrangements.

q: Which is an example of a reasonable accommodation?

options.t: Paying a special bonus because of the disability status
options.why: A special bonus tied to disability is not an accommodation, because accommodations help an employee perform the job and are not extra pay.

options.t: Providing a screen reader for an employee with low vision
options.why: A screen reader helps an employee with low vision do the essential job duties, which makes it a typical reasonable accommodation under the ADA.

options.t: Removing all of the employee's required job duties from the role
options.why: Removing all required duties would eliminate the job itself, and the ADA does not require employers to remove essential functions of the position.

options.t: Lowering the employee's pay to cover the cost of it
options.why: Cutting pay to cover accommodation costs is illegal, since employers must pay the cost of reasonable accommodations and cannot pass it to the worker.

q: What does the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) provide?

options.t: A guaranteed raise after the leave ends for all
options.why: The FMLA does not promise a raise after leave, though it does protect the employee's right to return to the same or an equivalent job.

options.t: Unlimited paid leave for every single worker
options.why: The FMLA does not give unlimited paid leave, since it provides a limited amount of leave that is unpaid, though employees may use paid leave if available.

options.t: Up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave
options.why: The FMLA gives eligible employees up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave per year for family and medical reasons, like childbirth or serious illness.

options.t: Paid leave lasting a full year for every worker
options.why: The FMLA does not provide a full year of paid leave, because the maximum is generally 12 weeks of unpaid leave.

q: What is sexual harassment?

options.t: Giving honest feedback about someone's work to them overall
options.why: Honest feedback about work is a normal part of management and is not harassment, since harassment involves unwelcome sexual conduct or sex-based hostility.

options.t: Wearing a company uniform to the office each day
options.why: Wearing a company uniform is a dress policy and is not harassment, because harassment involves unwelcome behavior, which a uniform rule is not.

options.t: Friendly teamwork on a shared group project at work
options.why: Friendly teamwork on a group project is welcome and professional conduct, so it differs from the unwelcome behavior that defines sexual harassment.

options.t: Unwelcome sexual conduct creating a hostile workplace
options.why: Sexual harassment is unwelcome sexual conduct, including advances or comments, that creates a hostile work environment or is tied to employment decisions.

q: What should an employee do first if they experience harassment at work?

options.t: Ignore it and simply hope that it all stops soon
options.why: Ignoring the problem usually lets it continue and can weaken a later complaint, so employees are advised to act rather than hope it stops.

options.t: Report it through the employer's complaint process
options.why: Reporting harassment through the employer's complaint process puts the company on notice and starts an investigation, and it also helps protect the employee legally.

options.t: Retaliate against the person harassing them in kind
options.why: Retaliating against the harasser can create problems for the victim, who might face discipline, and it does not follow proper reporting procedures.

options.t: Quit the job without telling anyone why you left
options.why: Quitting without telling anyone gives the employer no chance to fix the problem, and it can hurt later legal claims or benefits.

q: What is retaliation?

options.t: Reviewing an employee's work performance honestly
options.why: An honest performance review is a legitimate management activity and is not retaliation unless it is a punishment for protected activity.

options.t: Training new staff members on procedures
options.why: Training new staff on procedures is a normal duty of employers and has nothing to do with punishing someone for protected actions.

options.t: Punishing an employee for reporting wrongdoing
options.why: Retaliation is punishing an employee, through firing, demotion or other harm, for reporting wrongdoing or exercising legal rights, and it is illegal.

options.t: Giving an employee a fair raise for good work
options.why: A fair raise for good work is a reward based on merit, so it is the opposite of punishing someone for protected activity.

q: What does OSHA do?

options.t: Regulates how the stock market operates each day
options.why: Stock market operation is overseen by the Securities and Exchange Commission, not OSHA, which deals with workplace safety and health.

options.t: Collects the income taxes owed by workers each year
options.why: Collecting income taxes is the job of the Internal Revenue Service, whereas OSHA concerns workplace safety and does not handle taxes.

options.t: Sets the minimum wages that all employers must pay to workers
options.why: Minimum wage rules are set by the Fair Labor Standards Act and the Department of Labor's wage division, not by OSHA.

options.t: Sets and enforces workplace safety and health standards
options.why: OSHA, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, sets and enforces workplace safety and health standards through inspections, training and penalties.

q: What does OSHA require employers to do?

options.t: Keep the workplace free from recognized hazards
options.why: OSHA requires employers to keep the workplace free from recognized hazards that could cause death or serious harm, under the General Duty Clause.

options.t: Offer free meals to every worker on the staff
options.why: OSHA does not require meals for workers, because it is a safety agency whose rules deal with hazards and not with perks.

options.t: Give all of its workers a company car to drive
options.why: Employers are not required by OSHA to give cars to workers, since its rules cover safe workplaces and not company benefits.

options.t: Pay all of its employees exactly equal salaries
options.why: OSHA does not require equal salaries for all employees, because pay is regulated by wage laws, and its role is about safe working conditions.

q: What is workers' compensation?

options.t: Insurance for medical care and lost pay after injury
options.why: Workers' compensation is insurance that pays medical costs and part of lost wages for employees hurt or made ill on the job, no matter who was at fault.

options.t: A tax that is charged on employee wages each year
options.why: A tax on wages is a payroll tax, but workers' compensation is an insurance system funded by employers for injured workers.

options.t: A bonus that rewards high performance at the firm
options.why: A performance bonus is extra pay for results, while workers' compensation provides benefits to workers injured on the job.

options.t: A retirement account that is funded by the worker alone
options.why: A retirement account funded by the worker alone is a savings plan like an IRA, which is not injury insurance paid for by employers.

q: A warehouse worker slips on spilled oil and breaks an arm. Which system most likely pays for treatment and lost wages?

options.t: Unemployment insurance
options.why: Unemployment insurance pays people who lose jobs through no fault of their own, and it does not cover injuries that occur at work.

options.t: A sales tax refund
options.why: A sales tax refund returns tax paid on purchases and has no link to paying medical bills or wages after a workplace injury.

options.t: Workers' compensation
options.why: Workers' compensation covers medical treatment and part of lost wages for employees hurt on the job, like the warehouse worker who broke an arm.

options.t: Social Security pay
options.why: Social Security pay mainly covers retirement, long-term disability and survivor benefits, and it is not the first system for a workplace injury.

q: What is unemployment insurance?

options.t: Pay for workers who quit their jobs without notice each year
options.why: Workers who quit without notice generally do not qualify, because unemployment insurance is meant for people who lose their jobs through no fault of their own.

options.t: A bonus that rewards a worker for finding a new job
options.why: A bonus for finding a new job is not unemployment insurance, which pays temporary income while a worker is out of work.

options.t: A loan that helps someone start a company of their own
options.why: A loan to start a company is business financing, but unemployment insurance gives money to people who lost jobs and are looking for work.

options.t: Temporary income for those who lose jobs through no fault
options.why: Unemployment insurance gives temporary income to people who lose their jobs through no fault of their own, like a layoff, while they look for new work.

q: What does the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) protect?

options.t: The right to own a share of the company's stock and profits
options.why: The NLRA does not guarantee a stake in company stock or profits, because it protects the right to organize and bargain, not to own shares.

options.t: Employees' rights to organize and bargain collectively
options.why: The NLRA protects employees' rights to organize, join unions, and bargain collectively with employers, and it bars employers from interfering with these rights.

options.t: A guaranteed salary for every worker in the firm
options.why: The NLRA does not guarantee any salary, because pay is negotiated or set by the employer, and the law protects the bargaining process.

options.t: The right to work a shorter four-day week on full pay
options.why: The NLRA does not guarantee a shorter work week on full pay, since hours and pay are decided through bargaining, not set by the law.

q: What is a labor union?

options.t: Workers' group bargaining over pay and conditions
options.why: A labor union is an organized group of workers who bargain together with employers over pay, benefits, hours and working conditions.

options.t: A group of company owners who meet regularly
options.why: A group of company owners who meet regularly is a trade association or board, whereas a union is made up of workers.

options.t: A type of insurance company for workers and firms
options.why: A union is not an insurance company, as it is a group representing workers, though some unions may offer benefits to members.

options.t: A government agency that hires workers directly
options.why: A union is a private organization of workers and not a government agency, and it does not hire workers directly.

q: What is collective bargaining?

options.t: A vote by shareholders to choose a new CEO for the whole company
options.why: A shareholder vote to choose a CEO is corporate governance, which is a different process from negotiating employment terms with a union.

options.t: Negotiation between employers and a union over terms of employment
options.why: Collective bargaining is the negotiation between an employer and a union representing workers over wages, hours, benefits and other terms of employment.

options.t: Negotiation between two competing companies over prices and market share
options.why: Competing companies negotiating prices would be price fixing, which is illegal under antitrust laws, and it is not collective bargaining.

options.t: A customer haggling with a seller over a price in a shop or market
options.why: A customer haggling over a price is ordinary bargaining between individuals, but collective bargaining involves a union negotiating for a group of workers.

q: What is a strike?

options.t: A hiring event held by an employer each year
options.why: A hiring event is a recruiting activity by the employer, whereas a strike is employees refusing to work to press their demands.

options.t: An annual evaluation of an employee's work
options.why: An annual evaluation is a performance review by management, but a strike is a collective work stoppage organized by employees.

options.t: A work stoppage by employees to press demands
options.why: A strike is a work stoppage by employees, usually union members, used to press demands for better pay, benefits or conditions.

options.t: A short company shutdown ordered by the owners
options.why: A short company shutdown ordered by owners would be a lockout or closure, since a strike is started by the workers.

q: What is a lockout?

options.t: A paid day off for all of the staff members
options.why: A paid day off for all staff is a holiday or company benefit, but a lockout means the employer stops the work.

options.t: A secure entry system for the doors of a shop
options.why: A secure entry system is a physical security device, which is a different meaning from the labor term lockout.

options.t: A worker who suddenly quits the job and leaves
options.why: A worker who quits is resigning, while a lockout is an action taken by the employer, not by the worker.

options.t: An employer blocking work during a dispute
options.why: A lockout is when an employer keeps workers out of the workplace and blocks work during a labor dispute, as pressure in negotiations.

q: What is a right-to-work law?

options.t: A law that bans all unions in the whole state
options.why: Right-to-work laws do not ban unions, because workers can still organize, but they bar contracts that force workers to join or pay a union.

options.t: A law that guarantees each person a state job
options.why: A right-to-work law does not guarantee anyone a state job, because the name refers to freedom from compulsory union membership.

options.t: A law that requires unions at every firm
options.why: Right-to-work laws do the opposite of requiring unions, since they limit union security agreements so that membership cannot be required.

options.t: A state law barring required union membership
options.why: A right-to-work law is a state law that forbids requiring employees to join a union or pay union dues as a condition of keeping a job.

q: What does the Immigration Reform and Control Act require employers to do?

options.t: Hire only people who are full citizens of the country
options.why: IRCA does not require hiring only citizens, because it prohibits knowingly hiring unauthorized workers while also banning discrimination based on citizenship status or origin.

options.t: Reject any applicants who have accents or other speech traits
options.why: Rejecting applicants because of accents would be discrimination, which IRCA forbids, since it bans national origin discrimination in hiring.

options.t: Verify each new hire's identity and eligibility to work
options.why: IRCA requires employers to verify each new hire's identity and eligibility to work in the United States by completing Form I-9 for every new employee.

options.t: Ask for the tax returns of every applicant before hiring
options.why: Employers are not required to ask for tax returns, as IRCA focuses on documents proving identity and work authorization on Form I-9.

q: What is E-Verify?

options.t: A background check on credit scores and past addresses
options.why: A credit score and address check is a background screening, which is different from E-Verify, a system that checks work authorization.

options.t: An online system for checking work eligibility of new hires
options.why: E-Verify is an online system that lets employers confirm a new hire's eligibility to work in the United States by comparing Form I-9 data to government records.

options.t: A system that sets the pay rates for all jobs in the firm overall
options.why: E-Verify does not set pay rates, because it is a government work eligibility tool, and pay is set by employers and wage laws.

options.t: A tool that businesses use for filing taxes every year
options.why: Filing taxes is handled through IRS systems, and E-Verify is for checking whether new hires are authorized to work.

q: What is an independent contractor?

options.t: A self-employed person who controls the work
options.why: An independent contractor is self-employed and controls how the work is done, and is paid per job instead of receiving wages as an employee.

options.t: A full-time worker who receives benefits
options.why: A full-time worker with benefits is the usual description of an employee, and an independent contractor generally does not get employer benefits.

options.t: A person serving a four-week probation period
options.why: A probation period is a trial stage for a new employee and has no link to being a self-employed contractor.

options.t: A manager who works inside a company office
options.why: A manager working inside a company office is typically an employee, whereas an independent contractor is in business for themself.

q: Which factor most suggests a worker is an employee rather than an independent contractor?

options.t: The company controls when, where and how the work is done
options.why: Control over when, where and how the work is done points to an employee, because employers direct employees, but contractors direct themselves.

options.t: The worker uses their own tools and sets their own hours
options.why: Using their own tools and setting their own hours suggests an independent contractor, since employees typically use the employer's tools and follow its schedule.

options.t: The worker serves many different clients at the same time
options.why: Serving many clients at once suggests a contractor who runs their own business, while employees usually work for one employer.

options.t: The worker sends invoices for each project they finish
options.why: Sending invoices for each project is typical of contractors, who are paid per job, whereas employees are paid wages on payroll.

q: What is a non-compete agreement?

options.t: A rule that sets the number of vacation days each year
options.why: Vacation days are a benefit and policy matter, and a non-compete agreement is instead a contract restricting competition after the job ends.

options.t: A contract limiting work for competitors afterward
options.why: A non-compete agreement is a contract in which an employee agrees not to work for competitors or start a rival business for a set time after leaving.

options.t: A promise that the employee will never quit the job
options.why: A non-compete does not promise the employee will never quit, because it limits where they may work afterward, not whether they may leave.

options.t: A guarantee that the employee gets a raise each year
options.why: A guarantee of yearly raises is a pay term, and a non-compete agreement instead deals with working for competitors after leaving.

q: What is a non-disclosure agreement (NDA)?

options.t: A contract for a loan from a bank to a small firm
options.why: A bank loan contract involves borrowing and repayment, which is unrelated to an NDA, a contract used to protect secret information.

options.t: A promise to work overtime when asked by the boss
options.why: A promise to work overtime is a scheduling agreement and not an NDA, which deals with keeping certain information secret.

options.t: A contract to share all company data with the public
options.why: Sharing all company data with the public is the opposite of an NDA, which restricts disclosure of confidential information.

options.t: A contract to keep certain information confidential
options.why: An NDA is a contract in which a person agrees to keep certain information, such as trade secrets or client lists, confidential and not to share it.

q: What is a probationary period?

options.t: A period when the employee pays the company a fee each month
options.why: Employees do not pay the company to be on probation, and the period is simply a trial time when a new hire is evaluated.

options.t: A period when the company is unable to fire anyone for any reason
options.why: Probation does not stop the company from firing anyone, and in many cases it is easier for an employer to end employment during it.

options.t: An initial time to evaluate a new employee's fit for the job
options.why: A probationary period is an initial time when an employer evaluates a new employee's performance and fit for the job before making the position permanent.

options.t: A guaranteed contract that runs for five years in total
options.why: A guaranteed five-year contract is a fixed-term employment contract, and probation is instead a short initial evaluation period.

q: What is wrongful termination?

options.t: Laying off workers due to budget cuts
options.why: Layoffs due to budget cuts are legal business decisions based on economic conditions, not unlawful terminations, if done without discrimination.

options.t: Firing for repeated lateness and no excuse
options.why: Firing for repeated lateness with no excuse is a legitimate, lawful reason related to job performance, so it is not wrongful termination.

options.t: Ending a probationary period for poor work
options.why: Ending a probationary period for poor work is a lawful decision based on performance, so it does not count as wrongful termination.

options.t: Firing an employee for an illegal reason
options.why: Wrongful termination is firing an employee for an illegal reason, such as discrimination, retaliation, or breach of contract, which can lead to a lawsuit.

q: An employee is fired a week after reporting a safety violation to OSHA. Which claim is most likely?

options.t: Retaliation
options.why: Firing a worker soon after a safety report to OSHA suggests retaliation, an illegal punishment for protected activity, and the timing supports that claim.

options.t: Defamation
options.why: Defamation involves false statements that harm someone's reputation, which does not fit a firing that came right after a safety complaint.

options.t: Breach of duty
options.why: Breach of duty is a negligence concept, while the key fact here is the firing right after a protected report, which points to retaliation.

options.t: Price fixing
options.why: Price fixing is an antitrust violation involving competitors agreeing on prices, and it has no connection to firing an employee.

q: What is a layoff?

options.t: A promotion to a higher position in the firm
options.why: A promotion to a higher position is an advancement, while a layoff is the opposite, a loss of a job.

options.t: A termination due to business conditions
options.why: A layoff is a termination caused by business conditions such as budget cuts or reduced demand, not by the employee's own misconduct or performance.

options.t: A firing done because of a worker's theft
options.why: Firing because of theft is a termination for cause, based on the employee's own misconduct, unlike a layoff, which is not about conduct.

options.t: A paid vacation given to all workers
options.why: A paid vacation is time off with pay, which is a benefit, and a layoff is a permanent or temporary end to employment.

q: What does the WARN Act generally require for large layoffs?

options.t: A court hearing before any layoffs
options.why: The WARN Act does not require a court hearing before layoffs, and its main protection is advance notice to the affected workers and officials.

options.t: A full year of paid leave for staff
options.why: The WARN Act does not give a year of paid leave, because it only requires notice before large layoffs and plant closings.

options.t: Advance notice, typically 60 days
options.why: The WARN Act generally requires covered employers to give 60 days' advance written notice before mass layoffs or plant closings, so workers can prepare.

options.t: Same-day notice given at shift end
options.why: Same-day notice at shift end is exactly what the law is meant to prevent, because it requires 60 days of warning for large layoffs.

q: What is a hostile work environment?

options.t: A busy office during a tight monthly deadline
options.why: A busy office during a deadline is ordinary workplace stress and does not involve harassment based on a protected trait.

options.t: A strict manager who is still fair to all
options.why: A strict manager who treats everyone fairly is not creating a hostile environment, which requires severe or pervasive harassment or discrimination.

options.t: A noisy lunch room at midday for all staff
options.why: A noisy lunch room is only an annoyance and has nothing to do with discriminatory conduct that makes a workplace hostile.

options.t: Conduct so severe it interferes with work
options.why: A hostile work environment exists when harassing or discriminatory conduct is so severe or pervasive that it interferes with an employee's ability to work.

q: Which is an example of lawful hiring practice?

options.t: Asking applicants about their age or plans to have children
options.why: Asking about age or plans for children can lead to discrimination, so such questions are generally improper and unlawful in hiring.

options.t: Choosing the applicant with the best qualifications for the job
options.why: Choosing the applicant with the best qualifications for the job is a lawful, merit-based hiring practice that does not rely on protected traits.

options.t: Rejecting applicants because of their national origin or race overall
options.why: Rejecting applicants based on national origin or race is illegal discrimination under Title VII, so it is not a lawful hiring practice.

options.t: Refusing to hire someone because of their religion or faith
options.why: Refusing to hire someone because of religion is unlawful discrimination under Title VII, unless an exception such as a BFOQ applies.

q: What is a bona fide occupational qualification (BFOQ)?

options.t: A job requirement based on a characteristic that is truly necessary
options.why: A BFOQ is a job requirement based on a characteristic, like sex or religion, that is truly necessary to the business, and it is allowed only in rare cases.

options.t: A requirement that any manager is free to invent at will each year
options.why: A BFOQ is not a requirement managers can invent, since courts treat it as a narrow exception that must be reasonably necessary to the job.

options.t: A way for employers to refuse to hire people from some groups at will
options.why: A BFOQ is not a loophole for refusing groups at will, because it is allowed only when the trait is essential to the work.

options.t: A preference for hiring friends and family members of the owners
options.why: Hiring friends and family is nepotism, which is a preference and not a BFOQ, which must be necessary to the job.

q: What is affirmative action in employment?

options.t: A requirement to hire only the relatives of owners overall
options.why: Affirmative action does not require hiring only relatives of owners, which would be nepotism, and its goal is wider opportunity.

options.t: A tax that is charged to large employers each year
options.why: Affirmative action is not a tax, because it is an employment policy for expanding opportunity, not a charge on large employers.

options.t: Efforts to widen opportunity for disadvantaged groups
options.why: Affirmative action means efforts, such as outreach and recruiting, to widen opportunity for groups that have faced discrimination, within legal limits.

options.t: A ban on hiring people from certain groups at all
options.why: Affirmative action does the opposite of banning groups, since its aim is to open doors, not to exclude people from jobs.

q: What does the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) require before an employer uses a background check?

options.t: Written notice and the applicant's permission
options.why: Under the FCRA, an employer must give the applicant written notice and get their permission before using a third-party background check report.

options.t: A court order that is signed by a federal judge
options.why: A court order is not needed, since the FCRA requires notice and written permission, but no judge has to sign anything for a background check.

options.t: Nothing, as background checks are always allowed
options.why: Background checks are not allowed without conditions, because the FCRA requires disclosure and consent, and further steps if the report leads to a denial.

options.t: Paying the applicant a fee for the full report
options.why: The employer does not pay the applicant a fee for the report, and the FCRA instead requires clear notice and the applicant's consent.

q: What is a payroll deduction?

options.t: A fine that the employer must pay to the state
options.why: A fine paid by the employer to the state is a penalty and not a deduction, which is an amount taken out of an employee's pay.

options.t: An extra bonus that is added to the pay of staff
options.why: A bonus adds to pay, while a deduction subtracts from it, so an extra bonus is the opposite of a payroll deduction.

options.t: An amount withheld from pay for taxes or benefits
options.why: A payroll deduction is an amount withheld from an employee's gross pay for items such as taxes, insurance premiums or retirement contributions.

options.t: A gift that the company gives to its staff each year
options.why: A gift from the company is not withheld from pay, so it does not fit a deduction, which reduces take-home pay.

q: Which is a mandatory payroll deduction?

options.t: A voluntary retirement plan
options.why: A voluntary retirement plan is a deduction the employee chooses, so it is not mandatory, unlike withholding required by law.

options.t: Federal income tax withholding
options.why: Federal income tax withholding is mandatory, because employers are legally required to withhold taxes from wages and send them to the government.

options.t: A charity donation to a cause
options.why: A charity donation is a deduction the employee chooses to give, so it is voluntary, not required by law.

options.t: A gym membership at a local club
options.why: A gym membership is an optional benefit the employee may pick, so it is a voluntary deduction rather than a mandatory one.

q: What is a minimum wage?

options.t: The highest hourly pay allowed by law
options.why: The highest hourly pay allowed by law would be a wage ceiling, but a minimum wage is the lowest pay allowed.

options.t: The wage that is paid to all managers
options.why: Managers are usually paid salaries that are set by employers, so the minimum wage is not a pay level for managers only.

options.t: A bonus that is given to new hires
options.why: A bonus for new hires is an incentive set by the employer, and it is not related to the legal wage floor.

options.t: The lowest hourly pay legally allowed
options.why: A minimum wage is the lowest hourly pay that employers may legally pay covered workers, set by federal and state law to protect workers.

q: A state minimum wage is higher than the federal minimum. Which must a covered employer follow?

options.t: Whichever one is the lower
options.why: Following the lower rate would mean paying below the state minimum, which would violate the law, so it is not allowed.

options.t: Only the federal minimum rate
options.why: Following only the federal minimum would break state law, because employers must follow whichever minimum wage law is more protective for workers.

options.t: Neither, as wages are negotiable
options.why: Wages are not simply negotiable below the legal minimum, since minimum wage laws set a floor that agreements cannot waive.

options.t: The higher state minimum wage
options.why: When the state minimum is higher than the federal one, the employer must pay the higher state minimum, since the law more protective of workers applies.

q: What is child labor law mainly designed to do?

options.t: Set the salaries that adults must be paid in factories overall
options.why: Child labor laws do not set adult salaries, because those are covered by minimum wage laws, and child labor laws focus on minors.

options.t: Ban all employment for teenagers of every single age
options.why: Child labor law does not ban all work by teenagers, since it allows age-appropriate jobs with limits on hours and hazards.

options.t: Protect minors from unsafe work and keep them in school
options.why: Child labor law protects minors from unsafe work and limits their hours so that they can stay in school and stay healthy.

options.t: Require teenagers to work after school every day
options.why: Child labor law does not force teenagers to work after school, because it limits work rather than requiring any teenager to work.

q: Under federal law, what are limits for 14- and 15-year-olds working during school weeks?

options.t: Limited hours outside school; no hazardous jobs
options.why: Fourteen and fifteen year olds may work only limited hours outside school, such as 3 hours on a school day, and are barred from hazardous jobs.

options.t: Unlimited hours at any time of day or night
options.why: Federal rules do not allow unlimited hours at any time, since they limit the hours and times of day that young teens may work.

options.t: They may operate dangerous machinery if trained
options.why: Young teens cannot run dangerous machinery even with training, since federal hazardous occupation rules bar work of that kind for minors.

options.t: They are not allowed to work at all in any job
options.why: Fourteen and fifteen year olds are allowed to work in certain jobs under limits, so they are not barred from all employment.

q: What is a worker's right under the Fair Labor Standards Act regarding breaks?

options.t: Federal law requires a one-hour lunch break
options.why: Federal law does not require a one-hour lunch break, because the FLSA does not require meal periods for most workers.

options.t: Federal law requires no breaks; some states do
options.why: The FLSA does not require meal or rest breaks for adults, though some states require them, and short rest breaks are paid if offered.

options.t: Federal law requires paid vacations for workers
options.why: The FLSA does not require paid vacations, because vacation is a benefit that employers choose to offer, unless a contract provides it.

options.t: Federal law bans all breaks during a shift
options.why: Federal law does not ban breaks, since employers are free to give them, and some state laws actually require them.

q: What is a whistleblower protection law meant to do?

options.t: Stop employees from reporting their concerns
options.why: Whistleblower laws do the opposite of stopping reports, since they protect employees who report problems so that they can speak up safely.

options.t: Shield employees who report illegal activity
options.why: Whistleblower protection laws shield employees who report illegal activity from retaliation, such as firing or demotion, and encourage reporting of wrongdoing.

options.t: Reward employees who gossip about others
options.why: Whistleblower laws do not reward gossip, since they protect good-faith reports of legal violations, and they are not meant for rumors.

options.t: Replace the need for the police entirely
options.why: Whistleblower laws do not replace police, as they protect people who report wrongdoing, and the authorities still investigate it.

q: What is vested in a retirement plan?

options.t: A tax charged on money put in each year
options.why: A tax on money put in is not vesting, which instead refers to how much of the employer's contributions an employee has earned.

options.t: A fee that is charged by the plan each year
options.why: A plan fee is a cost of running the account, whereas vesting is about when employer contributions become the employee's own.

options.t: A loan that is taken against the plan
options.why: A loan against the plan is a borrowing feature, while vesting refers to ownership of the employer's contributions.

options.t: The right to keep employer contributions
options.why: Being vested means the employee has earned the right to keep the employer's contributions to a retirement plan, usually after a set number of years.

q: What law sets standards for private retirement and health plans?

options.t: ERISA
options.why: ERISA, the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, sets minimum standards for most private retirement and health plans, covering reporting, funding and fiduciary duties.

options.t: FLSA
options.why: The FLSA governs minimum wage, overtime and child labor, so it does not set standards for private retirement and health plans.

options.t: HIPAA
options.why: HIPAA protects the privacy and security of health information, and it does not set the broader standards for private retirement plans.

options.t: FICA
options.why: FICA is the payroll tax that funds Social Security and Medicare, so it is not the law that regulates private plan standards.

q: What is a credit report?

options.t: A list of monthly grocery purchases from the store
options.why: A list of grocery purchases is a spending record from stores, and it does not show borrowing and repayment history.

options.t: A tax return filed with the government each year
options.why: A tax return reports income and taxes owed to the government, and it is not a record of credit use.

options.t: A record of a person's borrowing and repayment history
options.why: A credit report is a record of a person's borrowing and repayment history, including accounts, balances and late payments, which lenders use to judge risk.

options.t: A statement of the person's employer's profits for the year
options.why: A statement of an employer's profits is a business financial report, which has nothing to do with a person's credit history.

q: What does the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) do?

options.t: Guarantees every consumer a perfect credit score on request as a rule
options.why: The FCRA does not give anyone a perfect credit score, since it only gives consumers rights over the accuracy of their reports.

options.t: Protects the accuracy and privacy of consumer credit information
options.why: The FCRA protects the accuracy and privacy of consumer credit information and lets consumers see their reports and dispute errors with the credit bureaus.

options.t: Sets the interest rates that banks must charge on all loans
options.why: The FCRA does not set interest rates for loans, because banks and the market set rates, and the act deals with credit reporting.

options.t: Bans the use of credit cards for travel costs while abroad
options.why: The FCRA does not ban credit cards for travel, since it regulates credit reports and not where cards may be used.

q: How often can a consumer get a free copy of their credit report from each major bureau?

options.t: At least once a year
options.why: Under federal law, consumers can get a free credit report from each major bureau at least once a year at annualcreditreport.com.

options.t: Only after two denials
options.why: Free reports are not limited to those who were denied credit, because every consumer can get one each year, and denials give extra rights.

options.t: Once every ten years
options.why: Waiting ten years is far longer than the law requires, since consumers can request a free report once a year, or more often in some cases.

options.t: Never; each costs money
options.why: Credit reports are not always sold, since federal law gives every consumer a free copy at least once a year from each bureau.

q: What does the Truth in Lending Act (TILA) require lenders to disclose?

options.t: The credit scores of the borrower's friends and family
options.why: TILA does not require disclosure of the credit scores of the borrower's friends or family, because it deals with the lender's terms.

options.t: The salaries that the lender pays its employees and executives
options.why: Lender employee salaries are internal business information, and TILA does not require them to be disclosed to borrowers.

options.t: The lender's own internal profit goals for the year
options.why: A lender's internal profit goals are private business plans, while TILA requires clear disclosure of the loan's costs to the borrower.

options.t: The cost of credit, including the APR and finance charges
options.why: TILA requires lenders to disclose the cost of credit, including the APR and finance charges, so borrowers can compare loan offers and understand the total cost.

q: What is the annual percentage rate (APR)?

options.t: The amount of the first monthly payment due
options.why: The first monthly payment is a dollar amount set by the loan terms, while APR is an annual percentage rate that expresses yearly borrowing cost.

options.t: The length of the loan measured in years and months
options.why: The loan term in years and months tells how long repayment lasts, but APR is a rate that measures the yearly cost of credit, not a time length.

options.t: The yearly cost of borrowing with certain fees
options.why: APR is the yearly cost of borrowing expressed as a percentage, including the interest rate plus certain fees, so shoppers can compare loan offers fairly under the Truth in Lending Act.

options.t: The total amount that was borrowed by the buyer
options.why: The total amount borrowed is the principal of the loan, which is a dollar figure; APR is instead a percentage showing the annual cost of that credit.

q: What does the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) prohibit?

options.t: Requiring borrowers to repay their loans on time
options.why: Requiring on-time repayment is a normal and legal part of any loan agreement, and the ECOA does not prohibit lenders from expecting borrowers to pay as promised.

options.t: Lending bias by race, sex, age or marital status
options.why: The ECOA prohibits credit discrimination based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age or receipt of public assistance, so lenders must judge applicants on creditworthiness.

options.t: Charging any amount of interest at all to borrowers
options.why: Charging interest is legal and is how lenders earn income; the ECOA bans discrimination, not interest, though usury laws and other rules may cap how high rates go.

options.t: Checking a borrower's credit reports before a loan
options.why: Lenders are allowed and expected to check credit reports before lending, since that is how they judge risk; the ECOA only prohibits using protected traits to decide.

q: What does the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) restrict?

options.t: The ability of banks to open new accounts
options.why: The FDCPA does not control how banks open accounts; it is a consumer protection law aimed at the behavior of third-party debt collectors, not at bank account opening.

options.t: The ability of retailers to advertise goods
options.why: Retail advertising is governed by other laws such as FTC rules on deceptive ads; the FDCPA deals only with how debt collectors contact and treat people who owe money.

options.t: Abusive or deceptive acts by debt collectors
options.why: The FDCPA bans abusive, deceptive and unfair practices by third-party debt collectors, such as harassing calls, threats, false statements and contacting people at unreasonable hours or places.

options.t: A borrower's right to repay a debt in full
options.why: Borrowers always keep the right to repay a debt in full; the FDCPA protects consumers from collector abuse and does not limit anyone's ability to pay off what they owe.

q: A debt collector calls a borrower at 11 p.m. and threatens arrest for an unpaid credit card bill. What is the best description?

options.t: A protection under bankruptcy law
options.why: Bankruptcy law gives debtors an automatic stay that stops collection, but it does not authorize a collector to threaten arrest or call late at night.

options.t: A needed part of the contract
options.why: A lawful contract does not allow a collector to harass or threaten the borrower, so harassment is never a needed part of a credit card agreement.

options.t: A legal and normal collection step
options.why: Collectors may lawfully call and send letters, but threatening arrest for unpaid consumer debt and calling at odd hours are not legal or normal collection steps.

options.t: A likely violation of the FDCPA
options.why: The FDCPA bars collectors from calling before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m. and from threatening arrest or other action they cannot lawfully take, so this likely violates it.

q: What is bankruptcy?

options.t: A legal process for those who cannot repay debts
options.why: Bankruptcy is a federal court process that lets people or businesses who cannot repay their debts either discharge many of them or set up a court-approved repayment plan.

options.t: A tax paid only by wealthy individuals each year
options.why: Bankruptcy is not a tax; it is a court proceeding about debts, and the wealthy are not the only ones who file, as most filers are ordinary consumers.

options.t: A method of avoiding every kind of tax owed
options.why: Bankruptcy does not erase every tax owed, and many recent income taxes are not discharged, so it is not a method for avoiding all taxes.

options.t: A type of loan that businesses often take out
options.why: Bankruptcy is a legal proceeding rather than a loan; businesses may borrow money, but filing bankruptcy is what happens when debts cannot be repaid.

q: What is Chapter 7 bankruptcy?

options.t: A program that offers a tax reduction to all small filers each year
options.why: Chapter 7 is not a tax reduction program; it is a court liquidation process, and it offers no yearly tax break to small filers.

options.t: A repayment plan that lasts three to five years for earners
options.why: A three to five year repayment plan describes Chapter 13 for people with regular income, not Chapter 7, which ends quickly through a liquidation of assets.

options.t: Liquidation, where non-exempt assets are sold to pay creditors
options.why: In Chapter 7 a trustee sells the debtor's non-exempt assets to pay creditors, and remaining eligible debts are then discharged, which is why it is called liquidation bankruptcy.

options.t: A reorganization plan that is meant only for very large businesses
options.why: Reorganization for businesses is the purpose of Chapter 11, and Chapter 7 is not limited to large firms because individuals and small businesses file it too.

q: What is Chapter 11 bankruptcy mainly used for?

options.t: Reorganizing a business so it can keep operating
options.why: Chapter 11 lets a business keep operating while it restructures debts under a court-approved plan, and it is commonly used by companies that hope to return to profitability.

options.t: Reducing the taxes owed by the business owner overall
options.why: Chapter 11 is a restructuring of business debts under court supervision, not a way to cut the owner's tax bill; taxes are handled separately.

options.t: Closing a business down immediately for good
options.why: Immediately closing a business and selling its assets describes Chapter 7 liquidation, whereas Chapter 11 is meant to keep the business running while debts are reorganized.

options.t: A repayment plan meant for wage earners only
options.why: A repayment plan for wage earners describes Chapter 13, while Chapter 11 is mainly used by businesses, though some individuals with large debts also use it.

q: What is Chapter 13 bankruptcy?

options.t: A sale of all of a business's assets at once
options.why: Selling all of a business's assets at once is liquidation, which describes Chapter 7 rather than Chapter 13, where the debtor generally keeps property while repaying.

options.t: A tax audit process run by the IRS each year
options.why: Chapter 13 is a bankruptcy proceeding in federal court and has nothing to do with an IRS tax audit, which is a review of a tax return.

options.t: A reorganization meant for corporations
options.why: Corporations reorganize under Chapter 11, while Chapter 13 is limited to individuals with regular income and debts below set limits, so this does not describe it.

options.t: A court-approved repayment plan for earners
options.why: Chapter 13 lets individuals with regular income keep their property while repaying some or all debts through a three to five year plan approved by the bankruptcy court.

q: What does an automatic stay do in bankruptcy?

options.t: Forces creditors to lend the debtor more money to keep going
options.why: An automatic stay protects the debtor from collection efforts; it does not force creditors to make new loans or extend more credit to the debtor.

options.t: Temporarily stops most collection actions against the debtor
options.why: The automatic stay temporarily halts most collection actions such as lawsuits, wage garnishment and foreclosure once a bankruptcy petition is filed, giving the debtor breathing room.

options.t: Prevents the debtor from filing any taxes at all this year
options.why: Bankruptcy has no rule stopping the debtor from filing tax returns, and the stay deals with creditor collection actions rather than tax filing duties.

options.t: Cancels all of the debtor's debts instantly and for good
options.why: The stay only pauses collection; debts are not canceled instantly or permanently, and cancellation of eligible debts comes later through a discharge order.

q: What is a discharge in bankruptcy?

options.t: A fine that is paid to the court clerk
options.why: A fine paid to the court clerk is a penalty, whereas a discharge is a court order that releases the debtor from personal liability for certain debts.

options.t: A list of all of the creditors in a case
options.why: A list of creditors is filed in the case schedules, but a discharge is the court order that actually releases the debtor from certain listed debts.

options.t: A court order releasing certain debts
options.why: A discharge is the court order that releases the debtor from personal liability for certain debts, so creditors can no longer try to collect them.

options.t: A new loan the court gives the borrower
options.why: A discharge is not a new loan; the court does not lend money, it simply relieves the debtor of obligation to pay certain debts.

q: Which debt is generally NOT discharged in bankruptcy?

options.t: Medical bills from a hospital stay
options.why: Medical bills are unsecured debts that are generally dischargeable in bankruptcy, so they are not among the debts that typically survive a discharge.

options.t: Most student loans and recent taxes
options.why: Most student loans and recent income taxes are generally not discharged, along with child support and alimony, so the debtor still owes them after bankruptcy.

options.t: Credit card balances owed to a bank
options.why: Credit card balances are unsecured debts that are generally dischargeable, so bankruptcy can usually erase them, with limited exceptions for recent fraud or luxury purchases.

options.t: Personal loans taken from a bank
options.why: Unsecured personal loans from a bank are generally dischargeable, so they typically are wiped out in bankruptcy unlike student loans or support obligations.

q: What is a lien?

options.t: A legal claim on property for a debt
options.why: A lien is a legal claim against property that secures payment of a debt, and the creditor can enforce it, for example by forcing a sale if the debt goes unpaid.

options.t: A tax refund sent by the government
options.why: A tax refund is money returned to a taxpayer, whereas a lien is a claim a creditor places on property until a debt is paid.

options.t: A written will that lists the heirs
options.why: A will is a document that lists heirs and directs distribution of property after death, while a lien is a creditor's claim against property for an unpaid debt.

options.t: A free gift of property to a friend
options.why: Giving property to a friend freely is a gift, and a lien is the opposite because it attaches a creditor's claim to property.

q: What is a mechanic's lien?

options.t: A claim by a car owner on a mechanic
options.why: A car owner does not hold a mechanic's lien; the mechanic does, as a claim on the property they worked on when they are not paid.

options.t: A warranty that comes with a car
options.why: A warranty is a promise about repair quality or coverage, while a mechanic's lien is a legal claim to secure payment for work that was done.

options.t: A tax that is charged on repair shops
options.why: A mechanic's lien is not a tax on repair shops; it is a claim filed by a worker or supplier, not collected by a government.

options.t: A claim on property for unpaid work
options.why: A mechanic's lien is a legal claim on property filed by a contractor or supplier who has not been paid for labor or materials used on it.

q: What is garnishment?

options.t: Court-ordered pay withholding to settle a debt
options.why: Garnishment is a court-ordered process where an employer withholds part of wages and sends it to a creditor, such as for unpaid debts, child support or taxes.

options.t: A voluntary savings plan the worker chooses overall
options.why: Garnishment is not voluntary; the worker does not choose it, and it is ordered by a court or agency to repay a debt rather than to build savings.

options.t: A tax refund the worker receives each year
options.why: A tax refund is money returned to a taxpayer, whereas garnishment takes money out of the worker's pay to satisfy a debt.

options.t: A bonus that is paid to employees each year
options.why: A bonus adds to pay, but garnishment reduces take-home pay because a court orders part of wages to be sent to a creditor.

q: What is a mortgage?

options.t: A type of insurance policy
options.why: Insurance is a contract paying for losses, while a mortgage is a loan; though lenders may require homeowner's insurance, the mortgage itself is a loan secured by property.

options.t: An unsecured loan from a bank
options.why: A mortgage is a secured loan because the property is collateral, so it is not an unsecured loan, which has no collateral behind it.

options.t: A loan secured by a car title
options.why: A loan secured by a car title is an auto loan, whereas a mortgage uses real estate as collateral for the money borrowed.

options.t: A loan secured by real estate
options.why: A mortgage is a loan secured by real estate, so the lender can foreclose and sell the property if the borrower stops making payments.

q: What is foreclosure?

options.t: A bank's approval of a new loan to a home buyer
options.why: Approving a new loan is underwriting, and foreclosure happens later when a borrower defaults, so it is not a loan approval.

options.t: The sale of a home by choice with no debt owed
options.why: A voluntary sale with no debt owed is an ordinary home sale, while foreclosure is forced by the lender because the borrower failed to pay.

options.t: The lender's legal process to sell after default
options.why: Foreclosure is the legal process a lender uses to take and sell a property after the borrower defaults on a mortgage, using sale proceeds to repay the debt.

options.t: A tax credit that is given to homeowners each year
options.why: A tax credit reduces taxes owed and has nothing to do with foreclosure, which is how a lender takes a home after missed payments.

q: What does the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA) mainly do?

options.t: Bans every kind of closing fee at all
options.why: RESPA does not ban closing fees; it requires lenders to disclose them and prohibits kickbacks, while fees themselves remain a normal part of buying a home.

options.t: Requires disclosure of closing costs
options.why: RESPA requires lenders to disclose closing costs and settlement services to home buyers and bans kickbacks and referral fees, helping buyers compare offers and avoid hidden charges.

options.t: Guarantees that a buyer gets a mortgage
options.why: RESPA does not guarantee a buyer approval; lenders still decide whether to lend based on credit, income and other qualifications of the borrower.

options.t: Sets the prices that homes may sell for
options.why: Home prices are set by the market of buyers and sellers, and RESPA does not regulate what price a house can sell for.

q: What is a usury law?

options.t: A law that requires banks to lend more at high rates as a rule
options.why: Usury laws restrict lending rates and do not require banks to lend more; they limit how much interest a lender can charge, not how much they must lend.

options.t: A law that sets minimum interest rates for lenders
options.why: Usury laws cap the highest rate allowed rather than set a minimum rate, so they protect borrowers and do not set a floor for lenders.

options.t: A law limiting the maximum interest a lender may charge
options.why: Usury laws set a legal maximum interest rate that lenders may charge, protecting borrowers from excessively high or predatory rates, and the limits vary by state.

options.t: A law that bans savings accounts at all local banks
options.why: Usury laws concern the interest rates charged on loans and do not ban savings accounts, which banks are free to offer.

q: What is the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)?

options.t: An agency that regulates stocks and bonds in the market
options.why: Regulating the stock and bond markets is the job of the Securities and Exchange Commission, not the FDIC, whose focus is insuring bank deposits.

options.t: An agency that insures bank deposits up to a set limit
options.why: The FDIC is an independent federal agency created in 1933 that insures bank deposits up to a set limit, which protects customers if a bank fails.

options.t: An agency that collects the income taxes owed by workers
options.why: The IRS collects federal income taxes owed by workers, while the FDIC has nothing to do with taxes and instead insures bank deposits.

options.t: A private lender that makes loans to firms and homes
options.why: The FDIC is a government agency, not a private lender, and it does not make loans to firms and homes; it insures bank deposits.

q: What is the standard FDIC insurance amount per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category?

options.why: The standard FDIC insurance amount is $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category, so deposits above that at one bank in one category may be at risk.
One million dollars is not the standard limit; coverage can reach more only by using different ownership categories or banks, since the base limit is $250,000.
The $25,000 amount is far below the actual coverage limit, which was raised over time and now stands at $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per category.
One hundred dollars is not an FDIC insurance limit at all; the actual standard coverage amount is $250,000 for each depositor, bank and ownership category.

q: What does the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) regulate?

options.t: Highway traffic and road safety for drivers
options.why: Highway traffic and driver safety are handled by agencies such as the Department of Transportation, while the SEC regulates securities markets and company disclosures.

options.t: Workplace safety inside factories and plants
options.why: Workplace safety in factories is overseen by OSHA, a different agency, while the SEC concerns itself with securities and investor protection.

options.t: Public schools and their funding sources
options.why: Public schools are funded and run by state and local governments and the Department of Education, not by the SEC, which regulates securities markets.

options.t: Securities markets and company disclosures
options.why: The SEC regulates securities markets, enforces laws against fraud and insider trading, and requires public companies to disclose financial information so investors can make informed choices.

q: What is insider trading?

options.t: A broker placing a customer's trade order on the market
options.why: A broker placing a customer's order is ordinary legal market activity, whereas insider trading involves using material non-public information to trade securities.

options.t: Trading securities based on material non-public information
options.why: Insider trading is buying or selling securities using material non-public information, which is illegal because it gives some traders an unfair advantage over other investors.

options.t: Trading stock using only public information from the news
options.why: Trading on public information from the news is legal, since everyone has access to it, whereas insider trading depends on information the public does not have.

options.t: Employees buying their own company's products at a discount
options.why: Employees buying products at a discount is a normal workplace benefit and has nothing to do with trading securities based on confidential information.

q: A manager learns privately that her company will be acquired next week and buys its stock before the announcement. What is this?

options.t: Illegal insider trading
options.why: Trading stock on confidential knowledge of an upcoming acquisition is illegal insider trading, because the information is material and not yet public, and it is punishable by the SEC.

options.t: Legal diversification
options.why: Diversification means spreading investments across assets to reduce risk, not buying one stock based on secret information about a pending deal.

options.t: Normal market research
options.why: Market research relies on public information, whereas buying stock because of a private tip about an acquisition is not research but an unfair advantage.

options.t: A permitted benefit
options.why: Employees are not permitted to trade on confidential company news, so this is not a benefit but rather a violation of securities laws.

q: What does the Sarbanes-Oxley Act require of public companies?

options.t: Lower tax rates for public companies
options.why: Sarbanes-Oxley does not change tax rates; it was passed in 2002 after accounting scandals to improve corporate governance and financial reporting.

options.t: Paying dividends to investors every year
options.why: Public companies are not required by Sarbanes-Oxley to pay dividends; dividends are a board decision, while the Act focuses on financial controls and accuracy.

options.t: Free stock for every employee of the firm
options.why: Giving every employee free stock is not something Sarbanes-Oxley requires, as the law concerns reporting accuracy, internal controls and auditor independence.

options.t: Stronger controls and accurate reporting
options.why: Sarbanes-Oxley requires public companies to keep stronger internal controls and report accurately, with executives certifying financial statements, after scandals like Enron and WorldCom.

q: In law, what exactly is a tax?

options.t: A loan that is made to the government
options.why: A loan to the government is lending money that gets repaid, such as buying a bond, while a tax is a required payment that does not have to be repaid.

options.t: A fee for a private service from a company
options.why: A fee for a private service from a company is a price paid in the marketplace, while a tax is imposed by government and funds public services.

options.t: A required payment funding public services
options.why: A tax is a mandatory payment to government, imposed by law, that funds public services such as roads, schools and defense, whether or not the payer uses them directly.

options.t: A voluntary donation to a charity by a citizen
options.why: Taxes are mandatory, not voluntary, so a voluntary donation to charity does not fit the legal definition of a tax.

q: What is a progressive tax system?

options.t: Higher incomes are taxed at higher rates
options.why: A progressive tax system charges higher rates as income rises, so people with more income pay a larger percentage, as in the US federal income tax brackets.

options.t: Lower incomes are taxed at higher rates
options.why: Taxing lower incomes at higher rates describes a regressive pattern, which is the reverse of a progressive system where the rate rises with income.

options.t: All incomes are taxed at the same rate
options.why: Taxing all incomes at the same rate describes a flat or proportional tax, not a progressive one, in which rates increase with income.

options.t: Only corporations pay any tax at all
options.why: In a progressive system individuals pay tax too; it is not limited to corporations, and progressive refers to rates rising with income.

q: What is a regressive tax?

options.t: A tax that no one pays, as it was abolished long ago in law overall
options.why: A regressive tax is still collected, so a tax that was abolished and that no one pays is not a regressive tax at all.

options.t: A tax that is the same percent of income for everyone
options.why: Taking the same percentage of income from everyone describes a proportional or flat tax, not a regressive tax, which takes a larger share from lower earners.

options.t: A tax that takes a larger share of income from lower earners
options.why: A regressive tax takes a larger share of income from lower earners than from higher earners, as with sales taxes that weigh more heavily on those with low incomes.

options.t: A tax that takes more from higher earners in each year
options.why: Taking more from higher earners describes a progressive tax, which is the opposite of a regressive tax that falls harder on low-income people.

q: Who collects federal income taxes?

options.t: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
options.why: The Federal Trade Commission handles consumer protection and competition issues, not federal income tax collection, which belongs to the IRS.

options.t: The Securities and Exchange Commission
options.why: The Securities and Exchange Commission regulates securities markets and does not collect income taxes from workers or businesses.

options.t: The Federal Reserve Board of Governors
options.why: The Federal Reserve sets monetary policy and supervises banks, but it does not collect income taxes from the public.

options.t: The Internal Revenue Service (IRS)
options.why: The Internal Revenue Service, part of the Treasury Department, collects federal income taxes and administers the tax code, including processing returns and refunds.

q: What is tax withholding?

options.t: A business keeping its tax money until year end
options.why: Withholding is not a business holding tax money until year end; employers must send withheld taxes to the government regularly, often every pay period or monthly.

options.t: Deducting income tax from pay and sending it in
options.why: Tax withholding means an employer deducts income tax from each paycheck and sends it to the government, so taxes are paid gradually throughout the year.

options.t: A penalty for lateness in filing a tax return
options.why: A penalty for filing late is a separate charge; withholding is an ordinary pay deduction, not a punishment for lateness.

options.t: A bonus given to employees at the end of the year
options.why: Withholding reduces take-home pay rather than adding to it, so it is the opposite of a year-end bonus given to employees.

q: What is the penalty risk of filing taxes late without an extension?

options.t: Lower taxes next year for filing late
options.why: Filing late does not lower taxes next year; late filers without an extension face penalties and interest that increase what they owe.

options.t: A tax refund bonus for filing late
options.why: Filing late does not earn a refund bonus; any refund is only what was overpaid, and late filing may even forfeit it after three years.

options.t: No consequence at all for late filers
options.why: Late filers do face consequences, because the IRS charges penalties and interest on unpaid tax, so claiming no consequence is wrong.

options.t: Late-filing and late-payment penalties
options.why: Filing late without an extension can bring a failure-to-file penalty and a failure-to-pay penalty plus interest, so the cost grows the longer the return and payment are late.

q: What is tax evasion?

options.t: Using legal deductions to cut a tax bill
options.why: Using legal deductions to cut a tax bill is tax avoidance, which is lawful, whereas evasion means deliberately breaking the law to pay less.

options.t: Filing a correct return right on time
options.why: Filing a correct return on time is honest compliance, which is the opposite of evasion, where income is hidden or falsified.

options.t: Illegally hiding income to cut taxes
options.why: Tax evasion is the illegal act of hiding income or lying on a return to cut taxes owed, and it can bring fines and prison.

options.t: Paying estimated taxes each quarter
options.why: Paying estimated taxes each quarter is lawful and often required for the self-employed, so it is compliance rather than evasion.

q: What is a sales tax?

options.t: A tax added to prices at purchase
options.why: A sales tax is a percentage added to the price of goods and some services at the time of purchase and collected by the seller for the state or locality.

options.t: A tax on houses and other land
options.why: A tax on houses and land is a property tax, which is based on assessed value rather than on a purchase at checkout.

options.t: A tax on inherited property at death
options.why: A tax on inherited property at death is an estate or inheritance tax, which is different from the tax added to purchases.

options.t: A tax on wages and other salaries
options.why: A tax on wages and salaries is an income or payroll tax, not a sales tax, which applies when buying goods.

q: What is a use tax?

options.t: A tax on using a bank or a credit union
options.why: There is no standard tax on using a bank or credit union; a use tax applies to goods bought without sales tax and then used in the state.

options.t: A tax on out-of-state goods used at home
options.why: A use tax is owed on goods bought out of state, such as online without sales tax, then used in your home state, so it matches the sales tax you would have paid.

options.t: A tax on using public roads, paid on fuel
options.why: A tax on fuel for using public roads is a fuel or excise tax, which is different from a use tax on purchased goods.

options.t: A tax on leased cars only, not bought ones
