options.t: They become illegal to sell to buyers abroad
options.why: A stronger dollar does not make exports illegal. It only changes prices, and sales may continue though buyers abroad may purchase fewer U.S. goods.

options.t: They become more expensive for European buyers
options.why: When the dollar strengthens, a euro buys fewer dollars, so U.S. goods cost more in euros. Higher prices usually lower European demand for U.S. exports.

q: A weaker dollar generally makes U.S. exports:

options.t: Free of all tariffs
options.why: A weaker dollar has no link to tariffs. Tariffs are taxes set by governments, and exchange rates do not remove them from exports.

options.t: More competitive abroad
options.why: A weaker dollar lowers the foreign-currency price of U.S. goods, making exports more competitive abroad. Foreign buyers get more dollars per unit of their own money, so demand tends to rise.

options.t: Less competitive abroad
options.why: Less competitive abroad is the effect of a stronger dollar. A weaker dollar makes U.S. goods cheaper for foreign buyers, which helps exporters.

options.t: Impossible to sell abroad
options.why: A weaker dollar does not make exports impossible to sell. It actually lowers prices for foreign buyers, so it generally helps sales abroad.

q: What is comparative advantage?

options.t: A country's largest army and its biggest navy fleet
options.why: A country's largest army and navy are military strengths. Comparative advantage is an economic idea about opportunity cost in producing goods.

options.t: A country's ability to make everything at lower cost overall
options.why: Making everything at lower cost describes absolute advantage in all goods. Comparative advantage can still exist when a country is less efficient at everything.

options.t: Producing a good at lower opportunity cost than others
options.why: Comparative advantage means producing a good at a lower opportunity cost than others. Countries gain by specializing in these goods and trading for the rest.

options.t: A country's ban on all imports from many other lands
options.why: A ban on all imports is extreme protectionism. Comparative advantage explains why trade is beneficial, so it supports trade rather than banning it.

q: What is absolute advantage?

options.t: The right to tax all imports from other nations
options.why: The right to tax imports is a government power of tariff. Absolute advantage is an ability to produce a good more efficiently.

options.t: The ban on all trade with every foreign nation
options.why: A ban on trade is an embargo. Absolute advantage is an economic term for efficiency in production and has nothing to do with banning trade.

options.t: The ability to produce at a lower cost than any nation
options.why: Producing at a lower cost than any nation overstates the idea. Absolute advantage only needs to be compared with another producer, and not with every nation.

options.t: Producing more with the same resources than another
options.why: Absolute advantage is the ability to produce more output with the same resources than another producer. It differs from comparative advantage, which is based on opportunity cost.

q: What is a joint venture in international business?

options.t: A trade embargo against a country
options.why: A trade embargo against a country is a government ban on trade. A joint venture is a voluntary business partnership between companies.

options.t: Firms sharing ownership of a project
options.why: A joint venture is an arrangement in which two or more firms share ownership, costs, risks, and profits of a project. Firms often use it to enter foreign markets.

options.t: A government takeover of the firm
options.why: A government takeover of a firm is nationalization or expropriation. A joint venture is a partnership created by agreement between companies.

options.t: A single firm acting alone abroad
options.why: A single firm acting alone abroad would be a wholly owned subsidiary or direct export. A joint venture involves sharing with partners.

q: What is foreign direct investment (FDI)?

options.t: A firm investing in operations abroad
options.why: FDI is when a firm invests in operations in another country, such as building a factory or buying a foreign company. It gives the investor lasting control and a presence abroad.

options.t: A tariff paid at the border crossing
options.why: A tariff paid at the border is a customs duty. FDI is a business investment in foreign operations, not a tax payment.

options.t: A bank loan from abroad to a firm
options.why: A bank loan from abroad to a firm is cross-border lending. FDI means owning or controlling business operations in a foreign country.

options.t: A person buying a souvenir abroad
options.why: A person buying a souvenir abroad is simple consumer spending. FDI refers to firms making long-term investments in operations in other countries.

q: What is a multinational corporation?

options.t: A union of workers from many different countries
options.why: A union of workers from many countries is a labor federation. A multinational corporation is a company, not an organization of workers.

options.t: A company that sells goods only at home
options.why: A company selling goods only at home is a domestic firm. A multinational corporation has operations in more than one country.

options.t: A company that operates in several countries
options.why: A multinational corporation is a company that operates in several countries, with offices, factories, or stores abroad. Examples include Coca-Cola, Toyota, and Apple.

options.t: A government agency in charge of foreign trade
options.why: A government agency in charge of foreign trade is a trade ministry or office. A multinational corporation is a private business operating across borders.

q: What is outsourcing?

options.t: Opening a new branch in the same city
options.why: Opening a new branch in the same city is local expansion. Outsourcing means hiring an outside firm to do work, rather than growing your own operations.

options.t: Contracting work to an outside firm
options.why: Outsourcing is contracting work such as customer service or manufacturing to an outside firm. Companies use it to cut costs and focus on core activities.

options.t: Selling shares of stock to investors
options.why: Selling shares of stock to investors is a way to raise capital. Outsourcing concerns who performs the work, not how a firm raises funds.

options.t: Doing all work in-house, never outside
options.why: Doing all work in-house is the opposite of outsourcing. Outsourcing moves tasks to outside companies, either at home or in another country.

q: What is a cultural consideration when doing business abroad?

options.t: Ignoring local holidays and religious traditions
options.why: Ignoring local holidays and religious traditions can offend partners and hurt a deal. Good global business respects them as part of local culture.

options.t: Using only casual slang in all of the meetings
options.why: Using only casual slang in every meeting can confuse or offend people in cultures that expect formality. Communication style should fit the local setting.

options.t: Learning local customs and communication styles
options.why: Learning local customs and communication styles, such as greetings, gift giving, and meeting etiquette, builds trust. It helps avoid misunderstandings in international business.

options.t: Assuming all cultures are identical in manners
options.why: Assuming all cultures are identical in manners is a common mistake. Customs for greetings, time, and negotiation vary widely, so assumptions can cause offense.

q: What is intellectual property protection abroad?

options.t: Selling the IP to a competitor for a small fee
options.why: Selling the IP to a competitor for a small fee gives away the asset instead of protecting it. Protection means securing legal rights abroad.

options.t: Avoiding all registration in other countries
options.why: Avoiding all registration in other countries leaves ideas unprotected. Most IP rights are territorial, so firms must register where they want protection.

options.t: Assuming U.S. protection works everywhere in the world
options.why: Assuming U.S. protection works everywhere is wrong. Patents and trademarks are generally territorial, so U.S. rights do not automatically apply in other countries.

options.t: Registering patents and trademarks in each country
options.why: IP rights are generally territorial, so firms register patents and trademarks in each country where they want protection. This helps them stop copying and counterfeiting abroad.

q: What does the WIPO treaty system help with?

options.t: Protecting intellectual property across countries
options.why: WIPO, the World Intellectual Property Organization, administers treaties like the Patent Cooperation Treaty and the Madrid system. These help protect patents, trademarks, and copyrights across countries.

options.t: Fixing tariffs between countries on all goods
options.why: Fixing tariffs between countries is the work of the WTO and trade agreements. WIPO treaties deal with intellectual property, not with duties on goods.

options.t: Setting currency values between many nations
options.why: Setting currency values between nations is a matter for markets and bodies such as the IMF. WIPO deals with patents, trademarks, and copyrights.

options.t: Regulating stock exchanges in signing countries overall
options.why: Regulating stock exchanges is a job for securities regulators in each country. WIPO treaties cover intellectual property rights and not securities markets.

q: What is the CISG?

options.t: A shipping route used by cargo vessels
options.why: A shipping route used by cargo vessels would be a trade lane. The CISG is a legal treaty about contracts for the sale of goods.

options.t: A bank holiday observed by many nations
options.why: A bank holiday observed by many nations is a day when banks are closed. The CISG is a legal convention and not a holiday.

options.t: A U.S. tax form filed by small firms
options.why: A U.S. tax form filed by small firms would be an IRS form. The CISG is an international treaty and not a U.S. tax document.

options.t: A UN convention on international sales
options.why: The CISG is the UN Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods. It provides uniform rules for sales between businesses in member countries, including the United States.

q: Two businesses in different countries disagree over a contract. Which clause helps decide which country's law applies?

options.t: A non-compete clause
options.why: A non-compete clause limits an employee or seller from competing after leaving a business. It does not decide which country's law governs a dispute.

options.t: A choice-of-law clause
options.why: A choice-of-law clause states which jurisdiction's law will govern the contract and its disputes. It brings certainty when parties are in different countries.

options.t: A force-majeure clause
options.why: A force-majeure clause excuses performance when extraordinary events like war or natural disaster occur. It does not select which law applies.

options.t: A severability clause
options.why: A severability clause keeps the rest of a contract valid if one part is struck down. It does not choose which country's law governs.

q: What does a force majeure clause do?

options.t: Increases prices when demand rises across a market
options.why: Increasing prices when demand rises is not what force majeure does. It is about unforeseeable events that prevent performance, not about pricing.

options.t: Forces a party to perform despite events outside control
options.why: Forcing a party to perform despite events outside control is the opposite of force majeure. The clause relieves parties when such events make performance impossible.

options.t: Excuses performance when extraordinary events strike
options.why: A force majeure clause excuses a party from performing when extraordinary events, such as war, floods, or pandemics, prevent it. It protects parties from liability for things beyond their control.

options.t: Requires arbitration in all cases of any dispute
options.why: Requiring arbitration in disputes is an arbitration clause. Force majeure is a separate clause dealing with excused performance during extraordinary events.

q: What is an international arbitration clause?

options.t: A term sending disputes to arbitration
options.why: An international arbitration clause sends contract disputes to a private arbitrator or panel instead of a court. It is popular because awards are easier to enforce across borders.

options.t: A term banning arbitration in any dispute
options.why: Banning arbitration would be the opposite of the clause. An arbitration clause requires the parties to settle disputes through arbitration rather than avoiding it.

options.t: A term setting delivery dates for goods
options.why: A term setting delivery dates for goods is a delivery clause. An arbitration clause deals with how disputes get resolved.

options.t: A term lowering prices for later orders
options.why: A term lowering prices for later orders is a volume discount provision. An arbitration clause is about resolving disputes outside courts.

q: What treaty helps enforce foreign arbitration awards in many countries?

options.t: The Geneva Convention
options.why: The Geneva Conventions set rules for the humane treatment of people in war. They have nothing to do with enforcing commercial arbitration awards.

options.t: The Treaty of Versailles
options.why: The Treaty of Versailles ended World War I in 1919. It is a peace treaty and not a commercial arbitration agreement.

options.t: The Paris Agreement
options.why: The Paris Agreement is a 2015 climate change treaty. It has no role in enforcing arbitration awards.

options.t: The New York Convention
options.why: The New York Convention of 1958 requires courts in member countries to recognize and enforce foreign arbitration awards. Over 160 countries have joined, which makes arbitration attractive for international deals.

q: What is a trade sanction?

options.t: A discount on exports for some nations
options.why: A discount on exports for some nations would be a trade benefit. A sanction is a penalty, which restricts rather than rewards.

options.t: A reward for partners that follow the rules
options.why: A reward for partners following the rules is an incentive. Sanctions punish a country, group, or person, usually to change behavior.

options.t: A penalty restricting trade or finance
options.why: A trade sanction is a penalty that restricts trade or financial dealings with a country, entity, or person. Governments use them to pressure targets over policy or security concerns.

options.t: A new trade agreement between nations
options.why: A new trade agreement opens trade between nations. A sanction does the reverse, because it limits or blocks trade and finance.

q: Which U.S. office administers many economic sanctions?

options.t: The National Weather Service for storms
options.why: The National Weather Service forecasts storms and weather. It has no role in administering economic sanctions.

options.t: The Office of Foreign Assets Control
options.why: The Office of Foreign Assets Control, part of the Treasury Department, administers and enforces many U.S. economic and trade sanctions. It publishes lists of blocked persons and countries.

options.t: The Peace Corps and its volunteers
options.why: The Peace Corps sends volunteers abroad for development work. It does not administer sanctions on other nations.

options.t: The Library of Congress in Washington
options.why: The Library of Congress holds books and records for lawmakers and the public. It does not run sanctions programs.

q: What is a free trade zone?

options.t: An area where goods move with reduced duties
options.why: A free trade zone is a designated area where goods may be imported, stored, or processed with reduced duties or none. It encourages trade and manufacturing.

options.t: An area with no government oversight at all
options.why: A zone with no government oversight at all is not accurate. Free trade zones are regulated by customs authorities, though duties are reduced or waived.

options.t: An area where goods are given away free to all
options.why: Goods are not given away free in these zones. Businesses still buy and sell at normal prices, but with lower duties or tax advantages.

options.t: An area where trade is forbidden by law
options.why: An area where trade is forbidden would be an embargoed area. A free trade zone is created to encourage trade and not to prohibit it.

q: What does 'Made in USA' labeling law require?

options.t: Only foreign goods can use the label, not U.S. goods
options.why: Only foreign goods using the label is wrong. The label is about U.S. origin, so it is meant for goods made in the United States.

options.t: Any product can use the label whatever its origin
options.why: Any product using the label regardless of origin would mislead buyers. FTC rules require that a Made in USA claim be truthful and supportable.

options.t: The label is always optional and false claims are fine overall
options.why: The label is not freely optional to falsify. False claims are deceptive practices and the FTC can take action and impose penalties.

options.t: The claim must be truthful: all or nearly all U.S.-made
options.why: The FTC requires that a Made in USA claim be truthful, meaning the product is all or virtually all made in the United States. False claims are treated as deceptive advertising.

q: What is an offer in contract law?

options.t: A request for the other side to make a proposal to the buyer
options.why: A request for the other side to make a proposal is an invitation to negotiate. An offer itself states terms that can be accepted to form a contract.

options.t: A final payment made to the worker after the work is done
options.why: A final payment made to a worker is wages for completed work. An offer is a proposal that begins the process of forming an agreement.

options.t: A clear proposal to enter an agreement on stated terms
options.why: An offer is a clear, definite proposal to enter an agreement on stated terms. The other party can accept it, and that acceptance creates a binding contract.

options.t: A casual remark about a possible future deal at lunch
options.why: A casual remark about a future deal is not definite enough to be an offer. An offer must show clear intent and include terms that can be accepted.

q: Sam offers to sell a bike for $100. Lee replies, 'I'll pay $80.' What is Lee's reply?

options.t: An acceptance that forms a binding contract
options.why: Lee's reply changes the price, so it is not an acceptance. Acceptance must match the offer's terms exactly under the mirror image rule.

options.t: A counteroffer that ends the original offer
options.why: Replying with a different price is a counteroffer. It rejects Sam's original offer and creates a new one, which Sam is free to accept or refuse.

options.t: A promise that needs no response from Sam
options.why: Lee's reply is a new proposal, so Sam must respond. A counteroffer needs a response before any contract can form, so it is not a promise needing none.

options.t: A revocation by Sam of the first offer
options.why: A revocation is made by the person who made the offer, to withdraw it. Lee is the offeree, so Lee cannot revoke Sam's offer.

q: What is consideration?

options.t: Something of value that each party gives in a contract
options.why: Consideration is something of legal value, such as money, goods, services, or a promise, that each party gives. It is required for most contracts to be enforceable.

options.t: The time a party takes to think about the deal terms overall
options.why: The time a party takes to think about a deal is a consideration period in everyday language only. In law, consideration means value exchanged.

options.t: A polite thank-you note sent after a deal is made
options.why: A thank-you note sent after a deal is a courtesy. Consideration is value bargained for as part of forming the contract.

options.t: A court's review of the contract and all its terms
options.why: A court's review of a contract is judicial review. Consideration is an element that must exist when the contract is formed.

q: Ann promises to give Ben a gift with nothing asked in return. Why is this usually not an enforceable contract?

options.t: It lacks consideration from Ben
options.why: A promise to make a gift with nothing asked in return lacks consideration from Ben. Without a bargained-for exchange of value, the promise is generally not enforceable.

options.t: It was made in the same state
options.why: Being made in the same state has no effect on enforceability. Contracts between people in the same state can be valid if all elements exist.

options.t: It was written down and signed
options.why: Being written down and signed does not fix a missing element. A signed promise without consideration remains generally unenforceable, with limited exceptions.

options.t: It involves two adults of legal age
options.why: Two adults of legal age have capacity to contract, so this does not cause a problem. The gift fails because nothing of value is given in return.

q: What does capacity to contract mean?

options.t: The maximum amount that a deal can cost the buyer
options.why: The maximum amount a deal can cost is not what capacity means. Capacity concerns whether a person has the legal ability to enter a contract.

options.t: The legal ability to understand and enter an agreement
options.why: Capacity is the legal ability to understand and enter an agreement. Minors, people with serious mental impairment, and intoxicated people may lack it.

options.t: The number of copies of a contract that must exist
options.why: The number of contract copies has no bearing on capacity. It is a matter of paperwork, whereas capacity is about a person's legal competence.

options.t: The size of the room where the deal is signed by both sides
options.why: The size of the room where the deal is signed is irrelevant. Capacity is about whether a party is legally able to enter a contract.

q: What does it mean when a contract is voidable by a minor?

options.t: The other party alone may cancel it
options.why: Voidable by a minor means the minor can cancel, not just the other party. Contracts with minors are generally voidable only at the minor's option.

options.t: The contract is automatically binding
options.why: A voidable contract is not automatically binding on a minor. The minor may choose to disaffirm it, which is the very point of the rule.

options.t: The contract was never formed at all
options.why: A contract that was never formed is a void contract or no contract at all. A voidable contract exists but may be canceled by one party.

options.t: The minor may choose to cancel it
options.why: Voidable by a minor means the minor can choose to cancel, or disaffirm, the contract. The adult party generally remains bound, which protects young people from unfair deals.

q: What is a void contract?

options.t: An agreement made orally by both of the parties
options.why: An oral agreement can be valid and enforceable, except for certain contracts needing writing. Being oral does not make a contract void.

options.t: An agreement that one party may choose to cancel later on
options.why: An agreement one party may cancel later is voidable, not void. A void contract has no effect for either party from the beginning.

options.t: An agreement that has no legal effect from the start
options.why: A void contract has no legal effect from the start, as if it never existed. Examples include agreements for illegal purposes, and neither party can enforce it.

options.t: An agreement that is fully performed by both parties
options.why: An agreement fully performed by both parties is an executed contract. It was valid and has been completed, so it is not void.

q: Two people agree to commit a crime for pay. What is the legal status of their agreement?

options.t: Enforceable if it is put in writing
options.why: An agreement to commit a crime is not made enforceable by putting it in writing. Courts will not enforce contracts with an illegal purpose.

options.t: Valid because both agreed freely
options.why: Free agreement by both sides is not enough. A valid contract also needs a legal purpose, and a deal to commit a crime lacks one.

options.t: Voidable by either of the two parties
options.why: A voidable contract can be canceled by a party but is valid until then. An illegal agreement is void from the start for everyone.

options.t: Void because the purpose is illegal
options.why: An agreement with an illegal purpose is void and unenforceable. Courts will not help either party enforce a contract to commit a crime.

q: What is fraud in contract law?

options.t: An honest mistake made by both parties to the deal in good faith
options.why: An honest mistake made by both parties in good faith is a mutual mistake. Fraud needs a knowing false statement made to deceive.

options.t: A change of heart after signing the contract, with nothing false
options.why: A change of heart after signing with nothing false said is not fraud. It is simply regret, and it does not allow cancellation.

options.t: A knowing false statement of material fact that induces agreement
options.why: Fraud is a knowing false statement of material fact made to induce agreement, on which the other party reasonably relies. The victim may rescind the contract or seek damages.

options.t: A sales opinion like 'best deal in town' that buyers know is a boast
options.why: A sales opinion like best deal in town is puffery. Buyers know it is a boast and not a statement of fact, so it is not fraud.

q: A seller says a used car has never been in an accident, knowing it was wrecked. The buyer relies on this. What is this?

options.t: Fraudulent misrepresentation
options.why: Knowingly lying that a car was never in an accident, when the buyer relies on it, is fraudulent misrepresentation. The buyer may rescind the sale or sue for damages.

options.t: A mutual mistake by both
options.why: A mutual mistake requires both parties to be wrong. Here the seller knew the truth and lied, which makes it fraud and not a shared error.

options.t: Harmless sales puffery only
options.why: Puffery is vague sales opinion, such as best car around. Saying there was never an accident is a specific, false statement of fact.

options.t: A valid written disclaimer
options.why: A written disclaimer cannot protect a knowing lie about a material fact. Fraud generally defeats such protections, so it is not a valid defense here.

q: What is the statute of frauds?

options.t: A list of crimes involving money and theft that are punished by law
options.why: A list of crimes involving money and theft would be a criminal statute. The statute of frauds is a civil contract rule about writing requirements.

options.t: A rule requiring certain contracts to be in writing to be enforceable
options.why: The statute of frauds requires certain contracts, such as land sales and deals that cannot be performed within one year, to be in writing. Otherwise they may not be enforceable.

options.t: A tax on written contracts that are signed and filed in the state each year
options.why: A tax on written contracts is not what the statute of frauds is. It sets writing rules for validity and does not impose any tax on contracts.

options.t: A law that bans all oral agreements, so every contract must be written
options.why: The statute of frauds does not ban all oral agreements. Many oral contracts are valid, and the writing rule applies only to specific kinds of contracts.

q: Which contract generally must be in writing under the statute of frauds?

options.t: A contract for the sale of land
options.why: A contract for the sale of land must generally be in writing under the statute of frauds. Real estate deals are among the main categories covered by this rule.

options.t: An agreement to walk a friend's dog
options.why: An agreement to walk a friend's dog is a small, informal service. It is not among the contract types the statute of frauds requires in writing.

options.t: A casual loan of a pencil to a pal
options.why: A casual loan of a pencil is trivial and informal. The statute of frauds applies to larger transactions like land sales, not everyday favors.

options.t: A promise to buy a sandwich
options.why: A promise to buy a sandwich involves a tiny sum for goods. Under the UCC, writing is required only for goods priced at $500 or more.

q: A seller breaches a contract to sell a one-of-a-kind painting. Which remedy fits best?

options.t: Nominal damages only
options.why: Nominal damages only is a small symbolic award. For a one-of-a-kind painting, money cannot replace the item, so a stronger remedy fits.

options.t: No remedy exists
options.why: No remedy exists is wrong. A breach of contract gives the injured party legal remedies, and courts can order something for unique goods.

options.t: Specific performance
options.why: Specific performance is a court order requiring the seller to carry out the contract. It is used when the subject matter is unique, like art or land, and money cannot substitute.

options.t: A refund for lost time
options.why: A refund for lost time does not make up for losing a unique painting. Courts allow specific performance when money damages are inadequate.

q: What is an assignment of a contract?

options.t: Canceling the contract entirely and for good, by mutual consent
options.why: Canceling the contract entirely by mutual consent is a rescission or discharge. An assignment transfers rights and keeps the contract alive.

options.t: Transferring one's rights under a contract to another person
options.why: An assignment is the transfer of one's rights under a contract to another person, called the assignee. The assignor generally remains responsible unless released.

options.t: Suing the other party for breach of contract in a civil court
options.why: Suing the other party for breach is a legal claim for a remedy. An assignment is a transfer of rights and does not involve suing.

options.t: Writing the contract in new words so it is easier to understand
options.why: Rewriting a contract in plain words is a redrafting. An assignment instead hands a party's rights over to a third person.

q: What is a limited partnership?

options.t: A business owned by one person who also runs it alone
options.why: A business owned and run by one person is a sole proprietorship. A limited partnership has at least two partners with different roles.

options.t: A partnership in which every partner is fully liable
options.why: A partnership in which every partner is fully liable is a general partnership. A limited partnership adds partners whose liability is limited.

options.t: A group of corporations that work together under one name
options.why: A group of corporations working together is a conglomerate or alliance. A limited partnership is made up of partners and not of corporations.

options.t: A partnership with general partners and limited partners
options.why: A limited partnership has at least one general partner who manages and is fully liable, and limited partners who invest. Limited partners risk only their investment.

q: A limited partner invests $10,000 and does not manage the firm. What is the most the partner can lose?

options.t: The $10,000 invested
options.why: A limited partner who does not manage the firm can lose at most the $10,000 invested. Liability is limited to the amount put into the business.

options.t: Nothing beyond the stake
options.why: Nothing beyond the stake is accurate, but the stake itself can be lost. The most the partner can lose is the $10,000 invested, so losing nothing is wrong.

options.t: All personal assets
options.why: Losing all personal assets is the risk of a general partner. A limited partner who does not manage is shielded from personal liability beyond the investment.

options.t: Double the investment
options.why: Doubling the investment is not how limited liability works. A limited partner's loss is capped at the amount invested, which is $10,000.

q: What is an S corporation?

options.t: A corporation owned by the government with no private shareholders overall
options.why: A corporation owned by the government is a state-owned enterprise. An S corporation is a private company with up to 100 shareholders.

options.t: A corporation taxed like a pass-through with income taxed to owners
options.why: An S corporation passes income, losses, and credits through to shareholders, who report them on personal returns. This avoids the double taxation of C corporations.

options.t: A nonprofit group with no owners but with many private donors
options.why: A nonprofit group has no owners and is tax-exempt. An S corporation is a for-profit business with shareholders who own it.

options.t: A sole proprietorship that has simply been given a new trade name
options.why: A sole proprietorship given a new trade name is just a rebranded one-owner business. An S corporation is a distinct legal entity elected for tax purposes.

q: What are articles of incorporation?

options.t: A tax return for the firm filed each year with the state
options.why: A tax return filed each year with the state is a franchise tax or annual report. Articles of incorporation create the company in the first place.

options.t: A contract with employees that sets pay and hours
options.why: A contract with employees that sets pay and hours is an employment agreement. Articles of incorporation establish the corporation as a legal entity.

options.t: Internal rules for daily operations, adopted by the board
options.why: Internal rules for daily operations adopted by the board are bylaws. Articles of incorporation are filed with the state and are not internal rules.

options.t: A document filed with the state to create a corporation
options.why: Articles of incorporation are the document filed with the state to create a corporation. They state its name, purpose, registered agent, and stock details.

q: What are bylaws?

options.t: Laws passed by the federal government that bind all firms
options.why: Laws passed by the federal government that bind all firms are statutes. Bylaws are made inside one corporation and apply only to that company.

options.t: Public records of stock prices set by the exchange
options.why: Public records of stock prices are set by market trading on the exchange. Bylaws are internal rules written by the corporation itself.

options.t: Rules that govern a corporation's internal operations
options.why: Bylaws are the rules that govern a corporation's internal operations, such as board meetings, officer duties, and voting procedures. The board adopts them after incorporation.

options.t: Contracts with customers who buy goods from the firm
options.why: Contracts with customers who buy goods are sales agreements. Bylaws are internal governance rules and do not involve customers.

q: Who elects a corporation's board of directors?

options.t: The customers
options.why: Customers buy products, but they do not vote for a corporation's directors. Only owners of the company's stock have that right.

options.t: The state government
options.why: The state government approves a corporation's charter but does not elect its directors. Directors are chosen by those who own the company.

options.t: The shareholders
options.why: Shareholders elect the board of directors, usually at the annual meeting, with votes tied to shares owned. The board then appoints officers to run daily operations.

options.t: The employees alone
options.why: Employees do not elect the board by virtue of their jobs alone. Voting rights belong to shareholders, though employees may own stock.

q: A director secretly sells company secrets to a rival for personal gain. What duty is broken?

options.t: The duty to advertise
options.why: The duty to advertise is not a recognized fiduciary duty of directors. Selling secrets harms the company, so a duty of loyalty is the issue.

options.t: The duty of loyalty
options.why: The duty of loyalty requires directors to put the corporation's interests ahead of their own. Selling company secrets to a rival for personal gain is a clear breach.

options.t: The duty to repay loans
options.why: The duty to repay loans is a debtor's obligation under a loan contract. Directors' fiduciary duties concern care and loyalty to the corporation.

options.t: The duty to hire staff
options.why: The duty to hire staff is not a fiduciary duty. Directors owe care and loyalty, and revealing secrets for gain breaks the duty of loyalty.

q: What is an agent?

options.t: A customer who buys goods from the firm each week
options.why: A customer who buys goods each week is a buyer, not someone acting for another. An agent acts on behalf of a principal.

options.t: A person who runs only personal errands for one family
options.why: A person who only runs personal errands for one family is a household helper, which is too narrow. An agent is authorized to act for another in dealings.

options.t: A government inspector who checks the books of firms
options.why: A government inspector who checks the books is an auditor or regulator. An agent represents the principal and does not inspect for the state.

options.t: A person authorized to act for another, the principal
options.why: An agent is a person authorized to act for another, called the principal, in dealings with third parties. Acts within authority bind the principal.

q: A store manager signs a supply contract within her authority. Who is bound?

options.t: The store owner, as principal
options.why: When a manager signs within her authority, the store owner as principal is bound. The agent acts for the principal, who gets the benefits and duties of the contract.

options.t: Only the manager personally
options.why: The manager is not personally bound when she acts within authority for a disclosed principal. The principal is the party bound by the contract.

options.t: Neither party would be bound
options.why: Saying neither party is bound is wrong. A contract made by an authorized agent creates binding duties on the principal and the supplier.

options.t: The supplier alone is bound
options.why: The supplier is not alone in being bound. A contract binds both sides, so the store owner as principal must also perform.

q: What is respondeat superior?

options.t: An employee's right to a raise after each full year of service
options.why: An employee's right to a raise after a year is a pay matter. Respondeat superior is a rule about employer liability for employees' acts.

options.t: A rule about the timing of contracts and the delivery dates set every time
options.why: A rule about timing of contracts and delivery dates is a performance term. Respondeat superior concerns who is liable for harm caused by workers.

options.t: An employer's liability for employees' acts within the scope of work
options.why: Respondeat superior means the employer is liable for torts committed by employees within the scope of employment. It lets injured people collect from the business.

options.t: A tax on payroll paid by the employer to the state each year
options.why: A tax on payroll paid by the employer is a payroll tax. Respondeat superior is a liability doctrine, not a tax.

q: What is at-will employment?

options.t: Either side may end the job at any time for a lawful reason
options.why: At-will employment means either the employer or the employee may end the job at any time, with or without notice. It excludes illegal reasons such as discrimination or retaliation.

options.t: The employer may fire a worker only with a court order
options.why: Firing only with a court order is not at-will employment. At-will lets the employer end the job without needing court approval.

options.t: The employee must stay for life with the same firm or boss overall
options.why: Requiring an employee to stay for life is not at-will. Employees are free to quit at any time, since the arrangement is not a lifetime commitment.

options.t: The job lasts a fixed number of years, agreed in advance
options.why: A job lasting a fixed number of years is a fixed-term contract. At-will employment has no set end date and either side may end it.

q: A warehouse worker is hurt while lifting boxes at work. Which program may pay medical costs?

options.t: Unemployment insurance
options.why: Unemployment insurance pays income to people who lost jobs through no fault of their own. It does not pay medical bills for work injuries.

options.t: Social Security pay
options.why: Social Security pay provides retirement and disability income through payroll taxes. A workplace injury is typically handled through workers' compensation instead.

options.t: Sales tax relief pay
options.why: Sales tax relief pay is not a real program. Injured workers get benefits from state workers' compensation systems.

options.t: Workers' compensation
options.why: Workers' compensation is state-regulated insurance that pays medical costs and part of lost wages for job-related injuries. Employees receive it without having to prove fault by the employer.

q: What is negligence?

options.t: Intentional harm done to another person in a fight
options.why: Intentional harm done to another in a fight is an intentional tort, such as battery. Negligence involves carelessness rather than intent.

options.t: Failure to use reasonable care that causes harm
options.why: Negligence is failure to use reasonable care that causes harm to another person. A plaintiff must show duty, breach, causation, and damages to win.

options.t: Harm that no one could foresee, from an accident
options.why: Harm that no one could foresee is generally an unavoidable accident. Negligence requires harm that a reasonable person would have been able to prevent.

options.t: A voluntary gift made to another person for free
options.why: A voluntary gift made for free is a donation or gift under property law. It is not a tort and does not involve causing harm.

q: A shop owner ignores a wet floor and a customer slips. What tort is most likely?

options.t: Trespass
options.why: Trespass is entering someone's land without permission. The customer here was an invited guest hurt by a hazard, so trespass does not fit.

options.t: Defamation
options.why: Defamation is a false statement that harms a reputation. A slip on a wet floor involves physical injury and carelessness, not words.

options.t: Fraud claim
options.why: Fraud requires a deliberate false statement meant to deceive. The owner simply failed to take care, which is the core of negligence rather than fraud.

options.t: Negligence
options.why: Ignoring a known hazard like a wet floor breaches the duty of care owed to customers. The injury it caused makes the owner liable for negligence.

q: What is defamation?

options.t: A true but unflattering remark about a person
options.why: A true but unflattering remark is not defamation, because truth is a defense. Defamation requires a false statement of fact.

options.t: A private opinion kept to oneself and never shared
options.why: A private opinion kept to oneself is not published to anyone. Defamation requires a statement communicated to a third party.

options.t: A false statement that harms someone's reputation
options.why: Defamation is a false statement communicated to others that harms someone's reputation. Spoken defamation is slander, and written defamation is libel.

options.t: A polite complaint made to the manager in person
options.why: A polite complaint to a manager in person is not defamation if it is true or an honest opinion. Defamation needs a harmful false statement.

q: Which protects a company's brand name and logo?

options.t: A trademark
options.why: A trademark protects words, names, symbols, or logos that identify a company's goods and distinguish them from others. It can last indefinitely if used and renewed.

options.t: A patent
options.why: A patent protects inventions for a limited term. It does not protect a brand name or logo, which are identifiers of source.

options.t: A copyright
options.why: A copyright protects original creative works such as books, music, and art. A brand name and logo identify a business, which is trademark territory.

options.t: A warranty
options.why: A warranty is a promise about the quality of a product. It does not protect a company's brand name or logo from copying.

q: How long does a utility patent generally last?

options.t: For the owner's whole life
options.why: A utility patent does not last for the owner's whole life. Its term is fixed by law and ends regardless of how long the inventor lives.

options.t: About 20 years from filing
options.why: A utility patent generally lasts about 20 years from the filing date. After that the invention enters the public domain, and anyone may use it.

options.t: One year from the filing
options.why: One year from filing is too short for a utility patent. Some provisional filings have a one-year window, but full patent terms last longer.

options.t: Five days after filing
options.why: Five days after filing is far too short. Patent terms are measured in years, giving inventors time to profit from their inventions.

q: Under the UCC, goods sold by a merchant are presumed fit for ordinary use. What is this?

options.t: The implied warranty of merchantability
options.why: The implied warranty of merchantability is the UCC's automatic promise that goods sold by a merchant are fit for ordinary use. It applies unless properly disclaimed.

options.t: A written service contract for repairs
options.why: A written service contract for repairs is a separate paid agreement. The implied warranty is automatic and does not need to be written.

options.t: A trade discount offered to buyers
options.why: A trade discount is a price reduction offered to buyers. The implied warranty concerns the quality of goods, not their price.

options.t: An express warranty of title from the seller
options.why: An express warranty of title is a seller's stated promise about ownership. The presumption of fitness for ordinary use is the implied warranty of merchantability.

q: What does the Federal Trade Commission do?

options.t: Prints currency and coins for the banks of the nation
options.why: Printing currency and coins is done by the Bureau of Engraving and Printing and the U.S. Mint. The FTC does not produce money.

options.t: Sets interest rates for banks and buys government bonds
options.why: Setting interest rates and buying government bonds are functions of the Federal Reserve. The FTC deals with consumer protection and competition.

options.t: Protects consumers from unfair or deceptive practices
options.why: The Federal Trade Commission protects consumers from unfair or deceptive practices and enforces antitrust laws. It handles false advertising, scams, and identity theft complaints.

options.t: Runs local schools and sets the school budgets each year
options.why: Running local schools is done by school boards and state education agencies. The FTC is a federal agency focused on commerce and consumers.

q: What is a bailment?

options.t: A sale of goods for cash to a buyer at the shop counter
options.why: A sale of goods for cash transfers ownership to the buyer. A bailment transfers only possession temporarily, with ownership staying with the owner.

options.t: A seizure of property by a court to pay debts owed by the holder
options.why: A seizure of property by a court to pay debts is a levy or garnishment. A bailment is a voluntary temporary delivery of property.

options.t: A permanent gift of property made to another person for good
options.why: A permanent gift of property transfers ownership forever. In a bailment the owner keeps ownership and the property must be returned.

options.t: Temporary delivery of property to another who must return it
options.why: A bailment is the temporary delivery of property to another, the bailee, who must return it. Examples include valet parking, coat checks, and leaving a car for repair.

q: You leave your coat at a restaurant coat check. What legal relationship is formed?

options.t: A coat sale
options.why: A coat sale would transfer ownership to the restaurant. At a coat check you intend to take the coat back, so ownership does not change.

options.t: A bailment
options.why: Leaving a coat at a coat check creates a bailment. The restaurant, as bailee, takes temporary possession and must use reasonable care and return the coat.

options.t: A partnership
options.why: A partnership is a business owned by two or more people. Leaving a coat with a restaurant creates no shared business relationship.

options.t: A land lease
options.why: A land lease gives rights to use real estate. A coat is personal property, so the relationship is a bailment and not a lease of land.

q: Which of these is a negotiable instrument?

options.t: A flyer
options.why: A flyer is advertising material. It does not contain an unconditional promise to pay money, so it is not a negotiable instrument.

options.t: A menu
options.why: A menu lists food and prices. It is not a written, signed promise or order to pay a sum, so it is not negotiable.

options.t: A receipt
options.why: A receipt is only proof of a payment or purchase. It does not promise to pay money, so it cannot be a negotiable instrument.

options.t: A check
options.why: A check is a negotiable instrument, a written order to a bank to pay a sum to the payee. It can be transferred by endorsement to another person.

q: What is an implied contract?

options.t: An agreement with no consideration from either of the parties
options.why: An agreement with no consideration from either party would not be an enforceable contract. An implied contract still needs mutual exchange, shown by conduct.

options.t: An agreement that is illegal under state law and void
options.why: An illegal agreement under state law is void. An implied contract can be fully legal, since it only means the agreement comes from conduct.

options.t: An agreement shown by the parties' conduct rather than words
options.why: An implied contract is shown by the parties' conduct instead of spoken or written words. Getting a haircut and paying for it is an example.

options.t: An agreement written and signed by both sides, with terms set out
options.why: An agreement written and signed by both sides is an express written contract. An implied contract is not stated in words.

q: What is a unilateral contract?

options.t: A contract where both sides exchange promises to each other in turn
options.why: A contract where both sides exchange promises is a bilateral contract. A unilateral contract has a promise from only one side.

options.t: A contract where one party promises and the other performs to accept
options.why: In a unilateral contract, one party makes a promise that is accepted by performance. A reward offer is an example, since finding the lost dog completes acceptance.

options.t: A contract made by one person with no other party involved in any way at all
options.why: A contract with only one person is not possible, since a contract needs at least two parties. Unilateral means only one party makes a promise.

options.t: A contract that is made orally only, with no writing at all in it
options.why: Oral-only contracts can be bilateral or unilateral. The word unilateral refers to who makes promises, not to whether the contract is written.

q: What is a bilateral contract?

options.t: A contract in which both parties exchange promises
options.why: A bilateral contract is one in which both parties exchange promises. Each side is both promisor and promisee, such as a promise to deliver goods for a promise to pay.

options.t: A contract signed by a minor alone without a parent
options.why: A contract signed by a minor alone is a voidable contract. Bilateral refers to promises made by both sides, not to the age of a signer.

options.t: A contract with no promises made by either side
options.why: A contract with no promises made by either side would not form a contract. A bilateral contract has promises from both parties.

options.t: A contract where one side makes a promise to the other
options.why: A contract where one side makes a promise to the other is a unilateral contract. A bilateral contract needs promises from both sides.

q: A buyer and seller each promise: one to deliver goods, the other to pay. Which type of contract is this?

options.t: Void deal
options.why: A void deal has no legal effect. This agreement is a valid exchange of promises, so it is not void and creates real duties.

options.t: Bilateral
options.why: Each party makes a promise, one to deliver and one to pay, so the contract is bilateral. A bilateral contract is an exchange of promises between two parties.

options.t: Unilateral
options.why: In a unilateral contract only one side promises, and the other accepts by acting. Here both sides promise, so it is bilateral instead.

options.t: Implied
options.why: An implied contract arises from conduct and not from spoken or written promises. Here the parties made express promises to each other.

q: A sports shop emails a customer: 'We will sell you the 2027 limited-edition bike for $900. Reply to accept.' The customer replies 'Accepted.' What has been formed?

options.t: A promise, no price
options.why: The email states a price and a bike, so it is a definite proposal. The deal is not just a promise with no price, since it names $900.

options.t: A void agreement
options.why: A void agreement has no legal effect. This agreement meets every element, including offer, acceptance, and consideration, so it is not void.

options.t: A binding contract
options.why: The shop made an offer with definite terms, and the customer accepted. Offer, acceptance, and consideration of $900 for a bike create a binding contract.

options.t: An invitation to bid
options.why: An invitation to bid asks others to make offers. The shop's email was a specific offer capable of acceptance, and the customer's reply concluded the deal.

q: A buyer offers to buy a car for $8,000, and the seller replies, 'I will sell it for $8,500.' What is the seller's reply legally?

options.t: An acceptance that forms a contract at the price
options.why: The seller's reply changes the price, so it is not an acceptance. Acceptance must match the terms of the offer, and this one does not.

options.t: A ratification of the offer made by the buyer
options.why: Ratification is approving an act done earlier without authority. Here the seller is replying to an offer with new terms, which is something else.

options.t: A revocation by the buyer of the earlier offer
options.why: A revocation is the offeror taking back an offer. The seller is the offeree, so the seller cannot revoke the buyer's offer.

options.t: A counteroffer that rejects the original offer
options.why: A different price is a counteroffer. It rejects the buyer's $8,000 offer and makes a new offer at $8,500, which the buyer may accept or refuse.

q: What does it mean when a contract is described as executory?

options.t: Some or all of the parties' duties have not yet been performed
options.why: An executory contract is one in which some or all of the parties' duties have not yet been performed. A signed contract for future delivery is an example.

options.t: The contract was never formed between the two parties at all
options.why: A contract that was never formed is not a contract at all. An executory contract is valid, but performance is still to come.

options.t: The contract has been canceled by both of the parties in writing
options.why: A contract canceled by both parties in writing has been discharged by mutual agreement. An executory contract is still alive and awaiting performance.

options.t: All duties are fully performed by both parties, so nothing remains
options.why: A contract with all duties fully performed is an executed contract. Executory means that something remains to be done by at least one party.

q: What is an executed contract?

options.t: One made orally only, with nothing in writing
options.why: A contract made orally only is an oral contract. Executed refers to performance, not to whether the agreement was written.

options.t: One voided by a court for mistake or fraud
options.why: A contract voided by a court is invalid. An executed contract is a valid agreement that has been completed.

options.t: One in which all parties have fully performed
options.why: An executed contract is one in which all parties have fully performed their duties. Nothing remains to be done, so the contract has been completed.

options.t: One signed but not yet performed by the parties
options.why: A contract signed but not yet performed is an executory contract. Executed means performance is complete, which is the opposite situation.

q: A 17-year-old buys a laptop on credit and later returns it, refusing to pay. Why can the minor usually do this?

options.t: Minors cannot own property or goods of their own at all
options.why: Minors can own property and goods. Their special protection involves contracts, which they may cancel, and not an inability to own things.

options.t: Contracts with minors are generally voidable by the minor
options.why: Contracts with minors are generally voidable at the minor's option, so a 17-year-old may disaffirm the laptop purchase. This rule protects young people from bad deals.

options.t: The contract is void for every party who signed it
options.why: The contract is not void for everyone. It is valid unless the minor chooses to cancel, and the adult party remains bound to the contract.

options.t: The seller may cancel the contract but the minor may not overall
options.why: The rule works the other way. The minor may cancel the contract, but the seller usually may not, since the protection benefits the minor.

q: What is a necessity in contract law involving a minor?

options.t: Basic items such as food, shelter or clothing that a minor may be bound to pay for
options.why: Necessities are basic items such as food, shelter, clothing, and medical care. A minor who cancels such a contract may still owe the reasonable value of what was received.

options.t: Any luxury item such as a sports car, a boat or a yacht that a minor wants
options.why: Luxury items such as sports cars and yachts are not necessities. A minor may generally cancel those contracts and return the goods.

options.t: Any gift received from a friend or a relative on a birthday or other holiday
options.why: A gift received from a friend or relative is not a contract. It involves no bargained exchange, so it is not a necessity in contract law.

options.t: Entertainment tickets for concerts, sports and movies that the minor buys for fun in the end
options.why: Entertainment tickets bought for fun are not necessities. They are optional spending, so a minor may usually disaffirm such contracts.

q: Two parties agree to a contract in which one will deliver illegal goods. What is the legal result?

options.t: It is voidable by the buyer only, who may choose to go on
options.why: An agreement to deliver illegal goods is void and not merely voidable by the buyer. Neither side may choose to continue it in court.

options.t: It becomes valid after delivery of the goods to the buyer
options.why: Delivery does not make the agreement valid. An illegal purpose makes a contract void from the start, and later performance cannot cure that.

options.t: It is enforceable if signed by both of the parties
options.why: Signatures by both parties do not make an illegal contract enforceable. Courts will not enforce agreements with unlawful purposes.

options.t: The agreement is void because its purpose is illegal
options.why: A contract to deliver illegal goods has an unlawful purpose, so it is void. Courts will not enforce it for either party.

q: What is a mutual mistake in contract law?

options.t: One party lies about the price of the goods being sold to it
options.why: One party lying about the price is fraud or misrepresentation. A mutual mistake requires both parties to be wrong about a fact.

options.t: One party signs under a threat from the other party
options.why: Signing under a threat is duress. A mutual mistake is not about force but about a shared false belief on a basic fact.

options.t: Both parties are wrong about a basic fact of the agreement
options.why: A mutual mistake occurs when both parties are wrong about a basic fact of the agreement. The contract may be voidable by the harmed party, as with a sale of a nonexistent item.

options.t: Both parties dislike the deal and agree to cancel it later
options.why: Both parties disliking the deal and cancelling later is a mutual rescission. A mutual mistake concerns a wrong belief about a fact at formation.

q: A seller knowingly hides termite damage in a house sale. What is the buyer's likely claim?

options.t: Fraudulent concealment that may allow rescission or damages
options.why: Hiding known termite damage is fraudulent concealment. The buyer may rescind the contract or recover damages, since the seller knowingly kept a material fact from them.

options.t: Mutual mistake only, with no hidden fact involved in it
options.why: A mutual mistake requires both parties to be unaware of the fact. Here the seller knew and hid it, so mutual mistake does not fit.

options.t: Nothing, because the buyer is bound once the contract is signed
options.why: The buyer is not stuck with the contract. Fraud lets the deceived party cancel it or seek damages, even after signing.

options.t: A trademark claim against the seller of the house and land
options.why: A trademark claim involves brand names and logos. The issue here is deception about a material defect in a house, not a brand.

q: What is a liquidated damages clause?

options.t: A clause that cancels the whole contract if either party breaches as a rule
options.why: A clause that cancels the contract if either party breaches is a termination clause. Liquidated damages set an amount payable, not an automatic cancellation.

options.t: A clause that sets in advance the amount payable if a party breaches
options.why: A liquidated damages clause sets in advance the amount that a breaching party must pay. Courts enforce it if the amount is a reasonable estimate and not a penalty.

options.t: A clause that sets interest on late payments made by the buyer
options.why: A clause that sets interest on late payments is a late fee or interest provision. Liquidated damages are a preset amount for breach of the contract.

options.t: A clause that moves the contract to a third party when one wishes
options.why: A clause that moves the contract to a third party is an assignment or delegation provision. Liquidated damages deal with the cost of a breach.

q: A contractor misses a deadline, and the contract states $500 per day in liquidated damages. The project is 6 days late. What does the owner recover?

options.why: $30,000 would result from multiplying $500 by 60 days. The project is only 6 days late, so the correct math is 6 times $500, not 60.
$500 is the amount for just one day late. The project was 6 days late, so the owner recovers six days of damages, not one.
$300 does not match any calculation of $500 per day over 6 days. Six days at $500 each is more than that amount.
Liquidated damages of $500 per day for 6 days late equals 6 x $500 = $3,000. The owner recovers this preset amount without proving actual loss.

q: What is promissory estoppel?

options.t: A doctrine that cancels all promises made without a signed contract by either party
options.why: Canceling promises without a signed contract is not what promissory estoppel does. The doctrine actually enforces some promises that lack a formal contract.

options.t: A rule on interest rates that banks may charge to borrowers on any loan
options.why: A rule on interest rates banks may charge is usury or lending law. Promissory estoppel is a contract doctrine about relied-on promises.

options.t: A tax rule on the income of firms that is earned in a given year abroad
options.why: A tax rule on firms' income earned abroad is a tax law matter. Promissory estoppel is a contract doctrine and has no connection with taxes.

options.t: A doctrine that can enforce a promise someone reasonably relied on to their harm
options.why: Promissory estoppel allows a court to enforce a promise, even without consideration, when the other party reasonably relied on it and would be harmed otherwise.

q: A person quits a job after a company promises a bigger job that is later withdrawn. Which doctrine might help?

options.t: Antitrust law claim
options.why: Antitrust law targets monopolies and price fixing. It does not help a worker who relied on a broken promise of a bigger job.

options.t: Promissory estoppel
options.why: Promissory estoppel may help because the worker reasonably relied on the company's promise by quitting. If the reliance caused harm, a court may enforce the promise or award damages.

options.t: Statute of limitations
options.why: A statute of limitations sets a deadline for filing a lawsuit. It does not create a claim based on a broken promise that was relied on.

options.t: Eminent domain claim
options.why: Eminent domain lets the government take private property for public use with payment. It has nothing to do with an employer's broken promise.

q: What is a third-party beneficiary?

options.t: A witness to a contract who watches both sides sign it in person
options.why: A witness who watches both sides sign is not a party and does not benefit from the contract. A third-party beneficiary is intended to gain from it.

options.t: A person who disagrees with the contract and has it cancelled by a court
options.why: A person who disagrees with the contract and has it cancelled by a court does not fit the term. A beneficiary is someone the parties meant to benefit.

options.t: A person who is not a party but is intended to benefit from a contract
options.why: A third-party beneficiary is not a party to the contract but is intended to benefit from it. An example is the person named on a life insurance policy.

options.t: The party who drafts the contract and sends it to the other side
options.why: The party who drafts the contract and sends it to the other side is one of the contracting parties. A third-party beneficiary is outside the agreement.

q: What does 'time is of the essence' mean in a contract?

options.t: Meeting deadlines is critical and late performance may be a breach
options.why: This clause makes timely performance a material term, so a late delivery or completion can count as a breach and let the other party cancel or claim damages.

options.t: The contract has no price set out anywhere in its written terms in the end
options.why: That describes a missing price term, which is a different gap in a contract and has nothing to do with deadlines or the timing of performance.

options.t: The contract lasts forever and can never be ended by anyone
options.why: A contract does not last forever because of this phrase, and the phrase says nothing about duration; it concerns the importance of meeting the stated deadlines.

options.t: Deadlines are optional and late work is always fully acceptable
options.why: The phrase means the opposite: deadlines are strict, so late performance is not automatically acceptable and may expose the late party to liability for breach.

q: A caterer is hired for a wedding on June 12 and arrives June 13. Which clause makes this a clear breach?

options.t: Choice of law clause
options.why: A choice of law clause only picks which state's law governs the contract, so it says nothing about a caterer who arrives a day late.

options.t: Severability clause
options.why: A severability clause keeps the rest of a contract alive if one provision is struck down, and it has no bearing on missed dates or deadlines.

options.t: Force majeure clause
options.why: Force majeure excuses performance for events beyond a party's control, such as storms, and a caterer simply arriving a day late would not usually qualify.

options.t: Time is of the essence
options.why: A time is of the essence clause makes the date a material term, so arriving June 13 for a June 12 wedding is a clear breach allowing cancellation and damages.

q: What is a force majeure clause?

options.t: A clause that doubles the price if the goods arrive on a public holiday
options.why: A holiday price increase would be an ordinary pricing term; force majeure is not about changing prices but about excusing performance after unforeseeable outside events.

options.t: A clause that assigns ownership of the goods to the buyer
options.why: Transferring ownership of goods is handled by title and delivery terms, not by force majeure, which concerns excuses for events like floods, wars or strikes.

options.t: A clause excusing performance for events beyond a party's control
options.why: Force majeure, French for superior force, frees a party from liability when events such as natural disasters, war or government orders make performance impossible or impractical.

options.t: A clause that adds interest to late payments by the buyer
options.why: Interest on late payments is a separate financial term in a contract; force majeure does not add charges but relieves a party of duties in extraordinary events.

q: What is a general partnership?

options.t: A government agency that regulates the trade of goods between states and sets national tax rates
options.why: That describes a federal regulatory body, not a business; a general partnership is a private business formed by owners and it does not set taxes or regulate trade.

options.t: A business owned by two or more people who share profits and unlimited personal liability
options.why: A general partnership is owned by two or more people who share profits and management, and each partner is personally liable without limit for the firm's debts.

options.t: A business owned by shareholders with limited liability for the debts of the company
options.why: That describes a corporation, where shareholders own the company and their personal assets are protected, unlike partners in a general partnership who face unlimited liability.

options.t: A business with a single owner who keeps all the profits and bears all the risk
options.why: That describes a sole proprietorship, which has just one owner; a partnership by definition requires at least two owners who share profits, control and risk.

q: Partner A signs a supply contract within the partnership's normal business without telling Partner B. What is the general result?

options.t: The partnership is bound
options.why: Each partner is an agent of the partnership, so a contract made within the ordinary course of business binds the partnership even if the other partner was never told.

options.t: Only Partner B is bound
options.why: Partner B did not sign or know of the deal, and a partnership contract does not bind only the partner who stayed uninvolved; the firm itself is bound.

options.t: No one at all is bound
options.why: The contract is valid and enforceable against the partnership because the supplier dealt with an agent acting within normal business, so someone is clearly bound.

options.t: Only Partner A is bound
options.why: Partner A is personally liable too, but the contract does not stop there; the partnership and so all partners are bound since A acted within normal business.

q: What is double taxation in a C corporation?

options.t: Profits are taxed twice at the same rate, once by the state and once by the nation
options.why: Corporate profits are taxed at the corporate rate and later as shareholder dividends; double taxation is not about the state and nation both taxing at the same rate.

options.t: Employees pay taxes twice on their wages, once to the state and once to the nation
options.why: Wages are taxed once as employee income; double taxation concerns corporate profits taxed at the company level and again when distributed, not an employee's pay being taxed twice.

options.t: Shareholders are taxed twice, once on their salaries and once on their dividends
options.why: Shareholders are not taxed on salaries as part of double taxation; the second tax falls on dividends paid out of profits that the corporation already paid tax on.

options.t: Profits are taxed at the corporate level and again as dividends to shareholders
options.why: A C corporation pays corporate income tax on its profits, and shareholders then pay personal tax on dividends paid from what is left, so the same earnings are taxed twice.

q: What is a pass-through tax entity?

options.t: A business owned by a state government and run by public officials across the state
options.why: A state-owned enterprise is government property and says nothing about how taxes flow; pass-through status concerns owners reporting profits on personal returns, not public ownership.

options.t: A business whose profits are taxed on owners' personal returns, not at the entity level
options.why: A pass-through entity, such as an LLC, partnership or S corporation, pays no entity-level income tax; profits and losses pass to owners who report them on personal returns.

options.t: A business that pays no taxes ever, whatever its income or its size in the market
options.why: Pass-through entities still generate taxable income for their owners; the profits are taxed once on personal returns, so the claim of paying no taxes at all is false.

options.t: A business taxed twice, once as a firm and again on dividends paid to its shareholders in general
options.why: That is a C corporation, which is taxed on profits at the corporate level and again on dividends; a pass-through entity avoids this second layer of tax.

q: Which entity gives owners limited liability and pass-through taxation?

options.t: Sole owner
options.why: A sole proprietorship has pass-through taxation but the owner has unlimited personal liability for business debts, so it lacks the liability protection the question requires.

options.t: C corp
options.why: A C corporation gives owners limited liability but its profits face double taxation, so it does not offer pass-through treatment as the question asks.

options.t: An LLC
options.why: An LLC protects owners' personal assets from business debts and by default passes profits through to the owners' personal returns, combining both features.

options.t: A GP firm
options.why: A general partnership has pass-through taxation, but each partner faces unlimited personal liability for the firm's debts, so it fails the limited liability requirement.

q: Who owns a corporation?

options.t: Its shareholders
options.why: A corporation is owned by its shareholders, who hold shares of stock and elect the board of directors to oversee the business on their behalf.

options.t: Its employees
options.why: Employees work for the corporation and may hold stock, but employment alone gives no ownership; ownership comes only from holding shares of the company's stock.

options.t: Its customers
options.why: Customers buy the corporation's products and services but have no ownership claim on the company unless they separately buy its shares as investors.

options.t: Its suppliers
options.why: Suppliers sell materials and services to the corporation as business partners, but supplying goods creates no ownership; only holding shares of stock does.

q: What is a board of directors?

options.t: A group of employees chosen by managers to run the firm
options.why: Managers answer to the board, not the reverse; directors are elected by shareholders rather than chosen by managers, and they oversee the firm instead of running daily operations.

options.t: A group elected by shareholders to oversee a corporation
options.why: Shareholders elect directors to oversee the corporation, set major policy, appoint senior officers and protect shareholder interests, while officers handle day-to-day operations of the business.

options.t: A group of lenders that fund the firm with their large loans
options.why: Lenders are creditors who are repaid under loan terms; they do not form the board, which is elected by shareholders to oversee the corporation.

options.t: A group of customers who vote on the firm's major decisions
options.why: Customers do not vote on major decisions; the board is elected by shareholders, who are the owners, and it guides the corporation on their behalf.

q: A corporation's officer approves a sale that benefits the officer's own company at the expense of the corporation. Which duty is violated?

options.t: The duty to advertise the sale
options.why: Advertising has nothing to do with the officer's self-dealing; the problem is putting personal gain ahead of the corporation, not a missing promotional duty.

options.t: The duty to hire more staff
options.why: Hiring staff is an operational choice and unrelated to the conflict of interest; the officer's wrong lies in favoring a personal company over the corporation.

options.t: The duty to audit the books
options.why: Auditing books relates to financial controls and oversight, not to the self-dealing here, where the officer put personal interests ahead of the corporation's.

options.t: The fiduciary duty of loyalty
options.why: Officers and directors owe a fiduciary duty of loyalty, which requires putting the corporation's interests ahead of their own, so a self-serving sale at its expense violates it.

q: What is piercing the corporate veil?

options.t: Raising capital by selling new shares of stock to the public in a big offering
options.why: Selling new shares to the public is an initial or secondary public offering, a way to raise capital, and has nothing to do with disregarding corporate limited liability.

options.t: Protecting owners from all liability in every case, whatever they did
options.why: Piercing the veil is the opposite of protecting owners from all liability; it is the exception where courts remove that protection when owners abuse the corporate form.

options.t: A court holds owners personally liable for corporate debts in certain abuses
options.why: Courts may pierce the corporate veil and hold owners personally liable when they commingle funds, ignore formalities, undercapitalize the firm or use it to commit fraud.

options.t: Merging two companies into one larger firm under a single shared name
options.why: Combining two companies is a merger or acquisition and does not involve piercing the veil, which concerns removing owners' limited liability protection after abuse.

q: What is a franchise agreement?

options.t: A contract allowing use of a brand and system in exchange for fees
options.why: A franchise agreement lets the franchisee operate under the franchisor's brand, trademarks and business system in exchange for fees and royalties, subject to standards and control.

options.t: A loan agreement between a bank and a business owner for funds overall
options.why: A bank loan is a financing contract that creates debt; a franchise agreement is about licensing a brand and system rather than lending money to a business owner.

options.t: A contract to buy stock in a company from its current owners
