options.why: Buying stock transfers a share of company ownership, while a franchise gives only the right to use a brand and system, not ownership of the franchisor.

options.t: A lease for land only, with no brand or system included in it
options.why: A franchise includes the brand and operating system, so a plain land lease with neither does not qualify as a franchise agreement.

q: A franchisee wants to change the menu without approval. Why might the franchisor object?

options.t: Brand consistency is part of the franchise agreement
options.why: Franchise agreements require uniform menus, quality and branding so customers get the same experience everywhere, so the franchisor can object when a franchisee changes the menu alone.

options.t: Menus are not part of the business under the agreement
options.why: Menus are generally part of the business and its brand standards, which the agreement controls, so claiming they fall outside the agreement is not a sound reason.

options.t: Franchise law forbids all menus from being altered
options.why: Franchise law does not forbid all menu changes; it is the franchise contract and brand standards that restrict changes without approval, and approved changes are allowed.

options.t: Franchisees own the trademark and the brand name
options.why: The franchisor owns the trademark and brand name and licenses them to the franchisee, who does not own them, which is why the franchisor can enforce standards.

q: What is a limited partner?

options.t: A creditor of the firm who lent money to the company and is repaid before all the owners
options.why: That describes a creditor, who lends money and is repaid under loan terms; a limited partner is an owner-investor who shares profits rather than a lender.

options.t: An investor whose liability is limited to the amount invested and who does not manage the firm
options.why: A limited partner invests capital, shares in profits and risks losing only the amount invested, but cannot take part in management without risking losing that limited liability.

options.t: A person who owns no part of the firm and has no right to its profits or to its decisions in the end
options.why: A limited partner does own part of the firm and shares in its profits, so a person with no ownership or profit right would not be a partner.

options.t: A partner with unlimited liability who manages the firm and makes every decision each day
options.why: That describes a general partner, who manages the firm and has unlimited personal liability; a limited partner has capped liability and no management role.

q: What does an operating agreement govern in an LLC?

options.t: How products are shipped to customers each week
options.why: Shipping logistics are day-to-day operations handled by managers and are not the subject of an operating agreement, which sets internal rules for owners.

options.t: How customers pay for goods and services in cash
options.why: Customer payment methods are business operations and sales policy, not governance; the operating agreement covers owners' rights, management structure and profit sharing in the LLC.

options.t: How the LLC is managed and how profits are shared
options.why: An operating agreement sets out how an LLC is managed, each member's ownership share, voting rights, how profits and losses are divided and what happens when members leave.

options.t: How taxes are filed by customers who buy goods
options.why: Customers file their own taxes; an operating agreement governs the LLC's internal affairs among members and has nothing to do with tax filings by buyers.

q: Which formation document must usually be filed with the state to create a corporation?

options.t: A trademark application form
options.why: A trademark application protects a brand name or logo with the federal trademark office and does not create a corporation or give it legal existence.

options.t: A warranty card for buyers
options.why: A warranty card records a product guarantee for buyers and has no role in forming a corporation, which requires a filing with the state.

options.t: An invoice for the goods
options.why: An invoice is a bill for goods sold, a routine business document, and plays no part in creating a corporation as a legal entity.

options.t: Articles of incorporation
options.why: Articles of incorporation, filed with the state, create the corporation as a separate legal entity and set out basics such as its name, purpose, registered agent and authorized shares.

q: What is apparent authority?

options.t: When a third party reasonably believes an agent has authority because of the principal's conduct
options.why: Apparent authority arises when a principal's words or conduct lead a third party to reasonably believe an agent is authorized, so the principal may be bound even without actual permission.

options.t: Authority held by a court of law over the parties to a lawsuit that is brought before it
options.why: That describes jurisdiction, a court's power over a case and its parties, which is a procedural concept and not a form of authority held by an agent.

options.t: No authority at all to act for anyone in a contract, a lease or a sale of any kind of goods
options.why: Apparent authority is not the absence of authority; it is the appearance of authority created by the principal, which can bind the principal to contracts the agent signs.

options.t: Authority written in a contract only, never shown by the conduct of the principal or by any words
options.why: That describes express authority, which can be written, while apparent authority comes from the principal's conduct and need not be written anywhere in a contract.

q: A store lets a new clerk wear a manager's badge. The clerk signs a large order with a supplier. What may be the result?

options.t: The supplier must pay the store, as the clerk lacked leave
options.why: The clerk's lack of leave to sign does not release the supplier or the store; the supplier is entitled to rely on appearances, and the supplier would not owe the store payment.

options.t: No contract is possible with the store or its staff
options.why: A contract is possible here because the store's conduct gave the clerk the look of authority, so the claim that no contract can exist with the store is wrong.

options.t: The store may be bound because of apparent authority
options.why: Letting the clerk wear a manager's badge made the supplier reasonably believe the clerk had authority, so the store may be bound by apparent authority even without actual permission.

options.t: Only the clerk is bound by the supply contract signed
options.why: The clerk acted as an agent for the store, so the store can be bound rather than only the clerk, because the store's own conduct created the appearance of authority.

q: What is a principal in agency law?

options.t: The person who inspects the agent's work
options.why: An inspector or supervisor checks work quality but does not authorize the agent; the principal is the person on whose behalf, and with whose authority, the agent acts.

options.t: The person who authorizes an agent to act
options.why: The principal is the person who authorizes an agent to act on their behalf, and the principal is bound by the agent's actions within that authority.

options.t: The person who drafts the agent's contract
options.why: Drafting a contract is a lawyer's or manager's task; the principal is defined by authorizing the agent to act for them, not by writing the agent's contract.

options.t: The school leader in charge of the staff
options.why: In agency law the principal is not a school head; the word here means the party who gives an agent authority to act for them in dealings with third parties.

q: Which fact most suggests a worker is an employee rather than a contractor?

options.t: She uses her own tools and sets her own schedule, working for many clients
options.why: Using her own tools, setting her own schedule and working for many clients are marks of an independent contractor, not an employee, because she controls the work.

options.t: She works for several clients at the same time during the year
options.why: Serving several clients at once suggests independence and a contractor relationship, since employees usually work for one employer who controls their time and work.

options.t: She sends invoices for each project and pays her own taxes each year
options.why: Sending invoices and paying her own taxes are typical of independent contractors, while employers withhold taxes and pay employees through payroll.

options.t: The company sets her hours and tells her exactly how to do the work
options.why: When a company controls hours and how the work is done, the worker is likely an employee, because the right to control the manner of work is the key test.

q: A delivery driver causes a crash while making a delivery. Who may be liable?

options.t: Only the other driver is paid
options.why: The other driver is not the only party who matters; the question asks who may be liable for the crash, and payment of the other driver is not a legal rule.

options.t: The employer and the driver
options.why: Under respondeat superior an employer can be liable for torts committed by an employee within the scope of employment, and the driver is also personally liable for the crash.

options.t: Only the police are liable
options.why: Police do not become liable for a delivery crash; liability falls on the people who caused the harm, here the driver and the employer under agency law.

options.t: No one is liable at all
options.why: A crash that causes harm can create liability, so saying no one is liable ignores negligence law and the employer's responsibility for employees acting within their job.

q: What is an at-will employment relationship?

options.t: Either side may end employment at any time for a lawful reason
options.why: At-will employment lets either the employer or the employee end the relationship at any time, with or without notice, so long as the reason is not illegal.

options.t: Employment that always needs a reason and ends only by court order
options.why: At-will employment does not need any reason and does not need a court order to end; requiring cause is what a contract or union agreement typically provides.

options.t: Employment with no pay for the person who does the work
options.why: At-will describes the right to end the job and says nothing about pay; employees under it are still entitled to lawful wages for the work done.

options.t: Employment for a fixed term agreed by both sides in advance
options.why: A fixed term is the opposite of at-will employment, where either side may end the job at any time and no set length of service is promised.

q: An employee is fired a week after reporting safety violations to a government agency. Which claim is most likely?

options.t: Trade dilution
options.why: Trade dilution is a trademark concept about weakening a famous brand, so it has no relevance to firing a worker who reported safety problems to a government agency.

options.t: Price fixing
options.why: Price fixing is an antitrust violation where competitors agree on prices, which has nothing to do with discipline or termination after an employee's safety report.

options.t: Retaliation
options.why: Firing someone soon after they report safety violations suggests retaliation, which laws such as OSHA and whistleblower statutes prohibit, and the close timing supports that claim.

options.t: Breach of terms
options.why: Breach of terms relates to contract duties, but the facts here, a firing right after a protected safety report, point most directly to a retaliation claim instead.

q: What is real property?

options.t: Stock certificates and bonds held by investors
options.why: Stocks and bonds are personal property, specifically intangible financial assets, because they are not land and are not permanently attached to land.

options.t: Furniture and other movable household items
options.why: Furniture and movable household items are personal property since they can be moved and are not permanently attached to land or buildings.

options.t: A car, a truck or any other motor vehicle
options.why: Vehicles are movable and so count as personal property, even though they are valuable; they are not land or permanent fixtures.

options.t: Land and things permanently attached to it
options.why: Real property includes land and anything permanently attached to it, such as buildings, trees and fixtures, together with the rights that come with owning them.

q: What is personal property?

options.t: Movable items such as vehicles and equipment
options.why: Personal property is anything movable and not attached to land, such as vehicles, equipment, furniture and inventory, as opposed to land and permanent fixtures.

options.t: Mineral rights beneath land, real property
options.why: Mineral rights beneath land are interests in real property, because they belong to the land itself and are not movable items.

options.t: A permanent building on a piece of land
options.why: A permanent building on land is real property, since it is attached to the land and not movable like personal property.

options.t: Land, houses and other fixed objects on it
options.why: Land, houses and fixed objects on land are all real property, the opposite of personal property, which consists of movable items.

q: A tenant installs a movable bookshelf. At move-out, who owns it?

options.t: The landlord, because it is real property
options.why: A movable bookshelf is not attached to the building, so it is not real property, and the landlord has no claim to it based on that label.

options.t: No one may keep it after the tenant moves
options.why: The tenant may keep the bookshelf at move-out; the claim that no one may keep it has no basis in property law for a movable item.

options.t: The bank, because it holds the tenant's lease
options.why: A bank holding a lease has no ownership of a tenant's movable furniture; leases give rights to use the premises, not title to the tenant's belongings.

options.t: The tenant, because it is personal property
options.why: A movable bookshelf is personal property and not a fixture, so it stays the tenant's and the tenant may remove it when moving out.

q: What is a lease?

options.t: A contract to buy property permanently from the owner at a price agreed in advance in the end
options.why: That describes a purchase agreement, which transfers ownership permanently; a lease only gives the right to use property for a limited time in exchange for rent.

options.t: A loan on property from a bank, repaid in monthly installments over many years
options.why: A loan on property from a bank is a mortgage, which is a financing agreement; a lease is a contract between a landlord and a tenant.

options.t: A contract giving someone the right to use property for a time in exchange for rent
options.why: A lease is a contract in which an owner gives another party the right to use property for a set time, usually in exchange for rent, while keeping ownership.

options.t: A tax on property paid by the owner to the local government every single year
options.why: A tax paid on property to local government is a property tax, a levy and not a contract; a lease is an agreement between landlord and tenant.

q: What is eminent domain?

options.t: A buyer's right to cancel a purchase within a few days of buying a house
options.why: A right to cancel a purchase within days of buying a home describes a rescission or cooling-off right, not eminent domain, which is a government power.

options.t: The government's power to take private property for public use with fair payment
options.why: Eminent domain lets the government take private property for public use, such as roads or schools, as long as the owner receives just compensation under the Fifth Amendment.

options.t: A landlord's right to evict a tenant who has not paid the rent on time
options.why: A landlord's right to evict a nonpaying tenant is an eviction remedy under landlord-tenant law and has no connection to the government's eminent domain power.

options.t: A bank's right to foreclose on a home when the borrower stops paying the loan in the end
options.why: A bank's right to foreclose on a home after nonpayment is a lender's remedy under a mortgage, while eminent domain is the government's power to take property.

q: A city needs a strip of private land for a new road. What must it generally provide to the owner?

options.t: Just compensation
options.why: The Fifth Amendment requires just compensation, meaning fair market value, when the government takes private property for public use, such as a new road.

options.t: Nothing at all
options.why: The Constitution does not allow the government to take property for nothing; the Takings Clause requires fair payment to the owner, so offering nothing at all is wrong.

options.t: A permit to build
options.why: A building permit allows construction and is not payment for land taken; the owner is entitled to just compensation, not a permit for a new project.

options.t: A tax credit only
options.why: A tax credit alone does not satisfy the Takings Clause, which requires just compensation, usually fair market value paid in money for the land taken.

q: What is an intentional tort?

options.t: A tax dispute between a firm and the revenue agency over taxes
options.why: A tax dispute between a firm and the revenue agency is an administrative or tax law matter, not a tort, which is a civil wrong that harms another person.

options.t: A wrong committed deliberately, such as assault or defamation
options.why: An intentional tort is a civil wrong committed on purpose, such as assault, battery, false imprisonment or defamation, where the person meant to act, and it can bring damages.

options.t: A contract breach by one side that fails to perform its part
options.why: A contract breach is a failure to perform a promise, which is a separate area of law from torts, which are wrongs that do not depend on a contract.

options.t: A careless act with no intent to cause harm to another person
options.why: Careless acts without intent to harm are negligence, not intentional torts, because an intentional tort requires that the wrongdoer meant to commit the act.

q: A manager publicly accuses an employee of stealing, knowing the claim is false. Which tort is most likely?

options.t: Trespass
options.why: Trespass is unauthorized entry onto someone's land and has nothing to do with a false public accusation of theft made about an employee.

options.t: Negligence
options.why: Negligence involves carelessness, but here the manager knowingly made a false statement, so the better fit is the intentional tort of defamation rather than negligence.

options.t: Conversion
options.why: Conversion is the wrongful taking or use of another's property and does not describe a false statement harming an employee's reputation.

options.t: Defamation
options.why: Defamation is a false statement of fact that harms someone's reputation; a knowing false public accusation of theft is a classic example of this intentional tort.

q: A blender sold with a defective motor injures a user. A claim that does not require proving negligence is based on:

options.t: Statute of frauds rule
options.why: The statute of frauds requires certain contracts to be in writing and has no bearing on a claim for injury caused by a defective product.

options.t: Liquidated damages term
options.why: Liquidated damages is a contract term that fixes damages in advance, not a basis for a claim by an injured user against a seller.

options.t: Strict product liability
options.why: Strict product liability holds sellers and manufacturers liable for injuries from defective, unreasonably dangerous products without the plaintiff proving negligence, only that a defect caused harm.

options.t: Adverse possession of land
options.why: Adverse possession is a way to gain title to land by long, open use, and has nothing to do with injuries from defective products.

q: What is a copyright?

options.t: Protection for trade secrets such as recipes and secret formulas kept by firms
options.why: Trade secrets such as recipes and formulas are protected by trade secret law, which depends on keeping them confidential, not by copyright protection.

options.t: Legal protection for original creative works such as books, music and software
options.why: Copyright protects original works of authorship fixed in a tangible form, such as books, music, art and software, and arises automatically when the work is created.

options.t: Protection for brand names, logos and slogans used by a company in sales
options.why: Brand names, logos and slogans are protected by trademark law, not copyright, which protects creative expression rather than words used to identify a source of goods.

options.t: Protection for inventions such as new machines and processes that work
options.why: Inventions such as machines and processes are protected by patents, which require an application, while copyright covers expressive works instead of functional inventions.

q: What is fair use?

options.t: Renting copyrighted work to other people for a fee, without ever asking the owner first as a rule
options.why: Renting copyrighted work to others for a fee without permission is not fair use; it would infringe the owner's rights, which include control over distribution.

options.t: Copying any work for free, forever, whatever the creator or the owner may say about it
options.why: Fair use does not allow copying any work for free forever; it is a limited defense that courts weigh by factors, regardless of what creators say.

options.t: Unlimited copying for profit, with no credit given to the original creators or owners
options.why: Unlimited copying for profit without credit is infringement; fair use is limited, and commercial copying of a whole work weighs strongly against it.

options.t: Limited use of copyrighted material without permission for purposes like criticism or education
options.why: Fair use permits limited use of copyrighted material without permission for purposes like criticism, commentary, news reporting, teaching and research, judged by four factors.

q: A business copies an entire popular song for its commercial ad without permission. Is this likely fair use?

options.t: Yes, because it is advertising and ads may use any song
options.why: Advertising is commercial use, and ads cannot freely use any song; using music in an ad without permission usually requires a license from the copyright holder.

options.t: Yes, because it was short and only a part of the song
options.why: The question states the business copied the entire song, so the claim that it was short and only a part contradicts the facts and weakens the fair use argument.

options.t: No, because it is a commercial use of a whole work
options.why: Copying a whole popular song for a commercial ad weighs against fair use on the purpose, amount used and market effect factors, so it likely infringes.

options.t: Yes, because songs are public property and free to all
options.why: Songs are protected by copyright and are not public property, so using one in an ad without permission generally requires a license from the owner.

q: How long does a trademark generally last?

options.t: As long as it is used and renewed
options.why: A trademark can last indefinitely as long as the owner keeps using it in commerce and files the required maintenance renewals with the trademark office.

options.t: Exactly 20 years from the filing
options.why: Twenty years is the term of a utility patent from filing, not a trademark, which can last as long as it is used and renewed.

options.t: Until the owner retires or sells up
options.why: Trademark rights do not end when the owner retires or sells; they can be sold with the business and continue as long as the mark is used.

options.t: One year only, then it must end
options.why: A trademark is not limited to one year; protection continues as long as the mark remains in use and the owner makes required renewals.

q: What is the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) Article 2 about?

options.t: The sale of land
options.why: The sale of land is governed by real property law, not the UCC, which covers movable goods and not interests in real estate.

options.t: Tax filing rules
options.why: Tax filing rules are found in tax law, not the UCC, which is a uniform set of state commercial laws.

options.t: The sale of goods
options.why: UCC Article 2 governs contracts for the sale of goods, meaning movable tangible items, and it covers formation, warranties, delivery, risk of loss and remedies for breach.

options.t: Employment rules
options.why: Employment rules are found in labor and employment statutes, not in the UCC, which regulates commercial transactions like sales of goods.

q: Under the UCC, a contract for the sale of goods priced at $600 or more generally must be:

options.t: In writing to be enforceable
options.why: The UCC statute of frauds requires a signed writing for sales of goods priced at $500 or more under the original code, and a writing is generally required to enforce larger sales.

options.t: Notarized by a public notary
options.why: Notarization is not required for goods contracts; a signed writing is what the UCC statute of frauds asks for, not a notary public's certificate.

options.t: Oral only, with no writing
options.why: An oral-only agreement for goods at this price generally cannot be enforced under the statute of frauds, so a contract resting on no writing is the weak choice here.

options.t: Recorded on video and stored
options.why: Video recording does not satisfy the writing requirement and is not required; the law asks for a signed written record showing the contract's key terms.

q: A buyer tells a clerk she needs a mattress for a bad back, and the clerk recommends a specific model that worsens her pain. Which warranty may apply?

options.t: Merchantability, for ordinary use
options.why: Merchantability is a general warranty that goods are fit for ordinary use, but here the buyer told the seller a specific need, which points to a different warranty.

options.t: No warranty applies to the sale
options.why: Implied warranties arise automatically in sales unless properly disclaimed, so saying that no warranty applies ignores the clerk's recommendation after the buyer stated her need.

options.t: Title to the goods being sold
options.why: The warranty of title promises the seller owns the goods and can transfer them; it does not address whether the mattress suits the buyer's back problem.

options.t: Fitness for a particular purpose
options.why: An implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose arises when a seller knows the buyer's special need and the buyer relies on the seller's advice to select suitable goods.

q: What is a 'lemon law'?

options.t: A law on car insurance that sets minimum cover for drivers
options.why: Car insurance minimums are set by separate state insurance laws, not by lemon laws, which protect buyers of defective vehicles rather than set insurance cover.

options.t: A state law protecting buyers of defective new vehicles
options.why: Lemon laws give buyers of new vehicles with substantial defects that the maker cannot fix after reasonable attempts a remedy such as a refund or replacement.

options.t: A law on sales tax charged in each state to shoppers
options.why: Sales tax is a separate state revenue law, whereas lemon laws deal with defective vehicles rather than taxes charged to shoppers.

options.t: A law about fruit sold in stores and sold at markets
options.why: Despite the name, a lemon law has nothing to do with fruit sales and instead protects consumers who buy defective new cars from the manufacturer.

q: What does the Truth in Lending Act require?

options.t: Lenders to waive all interest on their loans
options.why: The Truth in Lending Act does not require interest waivers; it requires clear disclosure of credit terms so borrowers can compare loan costs.

options.t: Lenders to disclose credit costs, including APR
options.why: TILA requires lenders to disclose the cost of credit, including the annual percentage rate and finance charges, in a standard form so consumers can compare offers.

options.t: Banks to lend to everyone who asks for a loan
options.why: TILA does not force banks to lend to everyone; lenders may still decide whom to approve, subject to other laws against discrimination.

options.t: Borrowers to repay within 24 hours of the loan
options.why: TILA does not require repayment within 24 hours; it concerns disclosure of loan terms, and repayment schedules are set by the loan contract.

q: A lender advertises a 'low payment' loan but hides a high APR. Which law is most directly implicated?

options.t: The Sherman Act of 1890
options.why: The Sherman Act of 1890 is an antitrust law against monopolies and price fixing and does not address disclosure of loan costs.

options.t: The Fair Labor Standards Act
options.why: The Fair Labor Standards Act sets minimum wage and overtime rules for workers and does not regulate how lenders advertise loan costs.

options.t: The Clean Air Act of 1970
options.why: The Clean Air Act of 1970 addresses air pollution and environmental standards and has nothing to do with loan advertising or disclosure.

options.t: The Truth in Lending Act
options.why: The Truth in Lending Act requires lenders to disclose the APR and other credit costs clearly, so hiding a high APR behind a low payment ad implicates it.

q: What does the Fair Credit Reporting Act protect?

options.t: Stock prices set on the major exchanges each day
options.why: Stock prices are set by trading and overseen by securities laws, not by the Fair Credit Reporting Act, which concerns consumer credit reports.

options.t: Business tax rates set by the state and the nation
options.why: Business tax rates are set by tax law and legislatures, not the Fair Credit Reporting Act, which covers how credit information is collected and used.

options.t: Accuracy and privacy of consumer credit information
options.why: The FCRA promotes the accuracy, fairness and privacy of consumer credit information held by credit bureaus and gives consumers the right to see and dispute their reports.

options.t: Interest rates on savings, as offered by banks
options.why: Savings interest rates are set by banks and market conditions; the FCRA is about credit report accuracy and privacy rather than rates on deposits.

q: What does the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act prohibit?

options.t: Abusive, deceptive or harassing debt collection practices
options.why: The FDCPA bans abusive, deceptive and harassing debt collection practices, such as repeated threatening calls, false statements and contact at inconvenient times or places.

options.t: Opening a savings account at a bank with a small deposit
options.why: Opening a savings account is a normal banking activity and is not prohibited by any law, much less the debt collection law.

options.t: Paying debts on time and in full each month to lenders
options.why: Paying debts on time is encouraged and legal; the FDCPA restricts how collectors behave, not how consumers pay what they owe.

options.t: Any debt repayment plan made between a debtor and creditor
options.why: The FDCPA does not forbid repayment plans; voluntary arrangements between debtor and creditor are common and lawful, while the law targets collectors' abusive tactics.

q: A debt collector calls a consumer at work after being told not to and threatens arrest. What is this?

options.t: A likely violation of debt collection law
options.why: Calling a consumer at work after being told to stop and threatening arrest are practices the FDCPA bans, so this is a likely violation of the law.

options.t: A credit report update sent to the borrower
options.why: A credit report update is a bureau action and not a collector's phone call, so it does not describe the harassing conduct in the question.

options.t: A normal collection step in the process
options.why: Debt collection law limits what collectors may do, and calling a workplace after a request to stop plus threatening arrest is not a normal permitted step.

options.t: A required notice about the debt owed
options.why: A validation notice is a written statement about the debt that collectors must send; threatening arrest by phone at work is not such a notice.

q: What is the FTC's Cooling-Off Rule for door-to-door sales?

options.t: Buyers must wait a year before they can cancel
options.why: The Cooling-Off Rule gives buyers three days to cancel, not a year, and a year-long wait would defeat its purpose of protecting against pressure sales.

options.t: Sellers can cancel at any time, whatever they promised
options.why: The rule protects buyers, not sellers; a seller cannot cancel whenever it likes after making a promise, since that would undermine the sale contract.

options.t: Buyers can cancel certain sales within three days
options.why: The FTC rule lets buyers cancel certain door-to-door and off-premises sales of $25 or more within three business days, helping them escape high-pressure sales.

options.t: Buyers must pay twice for each sale made at the door
options.why: The rule does not require double payment; it gives buyers a right to cancel and get a refund, and it does not add costs to buyers.

q: Which is a requirement of a negotiable instrument?

options.t: It must promise services only, never money, and must be spoken aloud to the buyer first
options.why: A negotiable instrument must be a written promise or order to pay money, not services, and it cannot be merely spoken aloud as a verbal promise.

options.t: It must be unsigned and may be left blank until the day of payment arrives for the holder overall
options.why: A negotiable instrument must be signed by the maker or drawer, so an unsigned and blank instrument fails the UCC Article 3 requirements.

options.t: It must be spoken aloud before two witnesses and need not be put in writing at all, ever
options.why: Negotiable instruments must be in writing under the UCC, so an oral promise made before witnesses cannot qualify as a negotiable instrument.

options.t: It must be in writing, signed and contain an unconditional promise or order to pay a fixed amount
options.why: Under UCC Article 3 a negotiable instrument must be a signed writing with an unconditional promise or order to pay a fixed amount of money, payable on demand or at a definite time.

q: What is endorsement of a check?

options.t: Printing the front of the check with the amount
options.why: Printing on the front of the check with the amount is filling in the check by the drawer, not endorsement, which happens on the back by the payee.

options.t: Signing the back to transfer or deposit it
options.why: Endorsement is the payee signing the back of a check, which lets the payee transfer it to another person or deposit it at a bank.

options.t: Raising the amount shown on the check
options.why: Raising the amount is alteration, a form of forgery that is illegal, and has no connection to the lawful act of endorsing a check.

options.t: Voiding the check and then tearing it up
options.why: Voiding and tearing up a check cancels it, whereas endorsement is a signature on the back that allows transfer or deposit.

q: A worker signs her name on the back of a paycheck and loses it. What is the risk?

options.t: It cannot be lost or stolen by anyone
options.why: Checks can be lost or stolen like any other item, so claiming that no one can take it ignores the risk created by a blank endorsement.

options.t: Only the employer can cash it as it names them
options.why: A paycheck names the worker as payee, not the employer, so the employer cannot cash it; the risk comes from the worker's own signature on the back.

options.t: Anyone who finds it may be able to cash it
options.why: A signature alone on the back is a blank endorsement, making the check payable to the bearer, so anyone who finds it may be able to cash or deposit it.

options.t: It is automatically void and worthless
options.why: Losing a signed check does not void it; the check stays valid, and the employer can stop payment and reissue it if the worker acts quickly.

q: What is perfection of a security interest?

options.t: Making a product perfect so that it meets every quality standard set by the maker and the buyers
options.why: Perfection is a legal term from secured transactions and has nothing to do with product quality standards set by makers and buyers.

options.t: Cancelling a loan so that the borrower no longer owes the lender any money, often after a final settlement talk
options.why: Cancelling a loan is a release or discharge of debt, whereas perfection is the step a lender takes to make its security interest effective against third parties.

options.t: Paying a debt early so that the lender cannot charge any more interest on the loan or the fees
options.why: Paying a debt early is prepayment of the loan, a borrower's act, and not a lender's step to protect a security interest in collateral.

options.t: The steps, such as filing a financing statement, that make a security interest effective against others
options.why: Perfection is the set of steps, usually filing a financing statement or taking possession of the collateral, that make a security interest effective against other creditors.

q: Two lenders both claim the same collateral. Who generally has priority?

options.t: The lender who perfected first
options.why: Under UCC priority rules, the secured party who first files or perfects generally has priority in the collateral over later claimants, so the earlier perfected lender wins.

options.t: The lender who lent last of all
options.why: Lending last gives a lender no advantage; priority generally goes to whoever perfected first, and a later lender usually ranks behind earlier perfected ones.

options.t: The lender with the larger loan
options.why: The size of the loan does not decide priority; the order of filing or perfection controls, so a larger loan gives no better claim by itself.

options.t: Neither lender has any claim
options.why: Both lenders may have valid security interests, so neither lacking a claim is wrong; priority rules decide which one is paid first from the collateral.

q: What is the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA)?

options.t: A law on imports and duties on goods coming from other countries as a rule
options.why: Imports and duties on foreign goods are covered by customs and tariff laws, not the FLSA, which regulates pay and working conditions for workers.

options.t: A federal law setting minimum wage, overtime and child labor rules
options.why: The FLSA is the federal law that sets the minimum wage, overtime pay at one and a half times the regular rate over 40 hours a week, and child labor limits.

options.t: A law on stock sales and share prices on the major exchanges
options.why: Stock sales and share prices are regulated by securities laws such as the Securities Exchange Act, not by the FLSA, which concerns wages and hours.

options.t: A law on trademarks and brand names used in the retail market
options.why: Trademarks and brand names are protected under the Lanham Act, and the FLSA addresses minimum wage, overtime and child labor instead.

q: A nonexempt employee works 46 hours in a week at $20 per hour. Under the FLSA, what is the minimum total pay?

options.why: $800 equals only 40 hours at $20 and ignores the 6 overtime hours, which must be paid at least one and a half times the regular rate.
$1,100 overstates the pay; the correct total is 40 times $20 plus 6 overtime hours at $30, which comes to less than $1,100.
The first 40 hours pay 40 times $20, or $800. The 6 overtime hours pay 1.5 times $20, or $30 each, for $180. The total is $980.
$920 is 46 hours times $20 at the straight rate, but the FLSA requires time and a half for the 6 hours over 40, so the minimum is higher.

q: What is Title VII of the Civil Rights Act?

options.t: A law on retirement accounts and the pensions that are paid to workers by firms after they leave
options.why: Retirement accounts and pensions are governed by ERISA, not Title VII, which is a civil rights law about discrimination in employment.

options.t: A law that prohibits employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin
options.why: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibits employers from discriminating in hiring, firing, pay and conditions because of race, color, religion, sex or national origin.

options.t: A law on workplace safety standards and the inspections of factories by federal agents each year
options.why: Workplace safety standards come from OSHA, not Title VII, which deals with discrimination and not factory inspections.

options.t: A law on minimum wage rates and the pay of workers in shops and factories nationwide for each hour worked
options.why: Minimum wage and hourly pay come from the Fair Labor Standards Act, while Title VII prohibits discrimination based on protected characteristics.

q: What does the Americans with Disabilities Act require employers to do?

options.t: Provide reasonable accommodations for qualified employees with disabilities
options.why: The ADA requires employers to provide reasonable accommodations to qualified employees with disabilities, such as modified equipment or schedules, unless doing so causes undue hardship.

options.t: Hire staff without holding any interviews or tests for the applicants
options.why: The ADA does not ban interviews or tests; employers may use job-related screening, though they cannot discriminate against qualified people because of a disability.

options.t: Pay everyone the same wage whatever their job or their level of skill
options.why: The ADA does not require equal pay for all jobs; it prohibits discrimination and requires accommodation rather than setting identical wages for everyone.

options.t: Ignore disabilities when the job tasks are set out for the workers in a team
options.why: The ADA does not tell employers to ignore disabilities; it requires considering reasonable accommodations so qualified people can perform the essential functions of the job.

q: An employee in a wheelchair asks for a desk adjusted to a lower height. What should the employer generally do?

options.t: Fire the employee because she asked for a new desk to be installed
options.why: Firing an employee for asking for an accommodation is unlawful discrimination and retaliation under the ADA, so it is never the right response.

options.t: Deny the request because the desk is far too costly for the firm to buy
options.why: An employer cannot simply deny the request by calling it costly; a lower desk is a modest accommodation, and denial requires proof of undue hardship.

options.t: Ignore the request until someone else raises it again with the firm
options.why: Ignoring the request fails the interactive process the ADA expects, in which employer and employee discuss a possible accommodation promptly and in good faith.

options.t: Consider and provide the accommodation unless it creates undue hardship
options.why: The ADA requires employers to consider and provide reasonable accommodations, such as an adjustable desk, unless they can show that doing so would create undue hardship.

q: What is the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA)?

options.t: A law on pensions and the retirement plans that firms set up for staff and managers
options.why: Pensions and retirement plans fall under ERISA, not the FMLA, which provides leave rather than retirement benefits.

options.t: A law banning all leave for workers who are ill or have a new baby in the family at home in this case
options.why: The FMLA does not ban leave; it does the opposite by guaranteeing eligible workers time off for illness or the birth of a child.

options.t: A law giving eligible employees unpaid, job-protected leave for family and medical reasons
options.why: The FMLA lets eligible employees take up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave a year for family and medical reasons, such as a newborn or serious illness.

options.t: A law giving paid vacation to all workers after one year of work, with full pay
options.why: The FMLA leave is unpaid, not paid, and it does not grant vacation; paid vacation is a matter of employer policy rather than this law.

q: An eligible employee takes 8 weeks of FMLA leave. What must the employer generally do when she returns?

options.t: Fire her a few days after her return from leave
options.why: Firing an employee after FMLA leave would violate the law, which protects the job, so the employer cannot end her employment for taking leave.

options.t: Demote her to a lower role after her return
options.why: Demoting her after leave would be interference with FMLA rights, since the law requires return to the same or an equivalent role.

options.t: Reduce her pay by half for the weeks she was on leave
options.why: FMLA leave is unpaid and cannot be penalized by a pay cut; returning employees must get equivalent pay, benefits and terms, not half pay.

options.t: Restore her to the same or an equivalent position
options.why: The FMLA requires restoring a returning employee to the same or an equivalent position with the same pay, benefits and working conditions.

q: What is the purpose of Form I-9?

options.t: Applying for a license to work in a regulated field in the U.S.
options.why: Work licenses for regulated fields are issued by state boards, not through Form I-9, which employers use to check identity and work eligibility.

options.t: Verifying an employee's identity and eligibility to work in the U.S.
options.why: Form I-9 is completed by employers and new hires to verify identity and authorization to work in the United States, with supporting documents examined within three business days.

options.t: Reporting wages and tax withheld to the revenue agency each quarter overall
options.why: Wages and tax withheld are reported on payroll tax forms such as Form 941 and W-2, not on Form I-9, which concerns work eligibility.

options.t: Setting the rate of tax withholding on each employee's pay stub
options.why: Withholding rates are set through Form W-4, which the employee fills in, while Form I-9 verifies identity and employment eligibility instead.

q: A company discourages employees from discussing pay with each other. What is the likely legal concern?

options.t: Employees generally have a right to discuss wages
options.why: Under the National Labor Relations Act, most employees have a protected right to discuss wages and working conditions, so discouraging such talk may be unlawful.

options.t: Only managers may speak about pay with other staff
options.why: The law does not limit pay discussions to managers; most nonsupervisory employees have a protected right to talk about wages with coworkers.

options.t: Employees may never discuss pay, since wages are secret
options.why: Wages are not secret by law, and employees generally may discuss pay, so a rule forbidding all pay talk creates the legal concern here.

options.t: Pay is always secret by law in every state and firm
options.why: Pay is not automatically secret by law; many states and the NLRA protect pay discussions, so a blanket secrecy rule can violate employee rights.

q: What is the purpose of the Securities Act of 1933?

options.t: To regulate shipping routes and ports used by cargo vessels
options.why: Shipping routes and ports are governed by maritime and transport law, not the Securities Act of 1933, which deals with securities offerings.

options.t: To require disclosure when securities are first sold to the public
options.why: The Securities Act of 1933 requires companies selling securities to the public for the first time to register them and disclose accurate financial information to investors.

options.t: To ban stock trading by all firms and all investors in the nation
options.why: The Act does not ban stock trading; it regulates new offerings through disclosure, while trading in existing shares continues and is regulated by other laws.

options.t: To set the minimum wage for all of the workers in the stock market
options.why: Minimum wage is set by the Fair Labor Standards Act and has nothing to do with the Securities Act of 1933 and its disclosure rules.

q: What does the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 do?

options.t: Sets interest on mortgages and fixes lenders' rates
options.why: Mortgage rates are not set by the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, which regulates securities trading, brokers and exchanges.

options.t: Regulates farm prices and the sale of crops in markets
options.why: Farm prices and crop sales are covered by agricultural law, whereas the 1934 Act regulates trading in securities on exchanges.

options.t: Regulates imports and the duties paid at the border
options.why: Imports and border duties are governed by customs and trade law, and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 concerns securities markets.

options.t: Regulates trading of securities and created the SEC
options.why: The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 regulates trading of securities on the secondary market and created the Securities and Exchange Commission to enforce the securities laws.

q: A company executive buys stock after learning confidential merger news before the public does. What law is most likely violated?

options.t: Antidiscrimination laws that protect workers
options.why: Antidiscrimination laws protect workers from unfair treatment and do not address trading on confidential merger news learned as an executive.

options.t: Zoning laws about the use of land in cities
options.why: Zoning laws control how land is used in cities and have nothing to do with trading stocks on confidential information.

options.t: Securities laws against insider trading
options.why: Trading on material nonpublic information, like secret merger news, is insider trading, which the Securities Exchange Act and SEC Rule 10b-5 prohibit and punish.

options.t: Child labor laws about work by minors
options.why: Child labor laws limit work by minors, so they are unrelated to an executive using confidential merger news to buy stock early.

q: What is a bankruptcy trustee?

options.t: A person appointed to manage and distribute a debtor's assets
options.why: A bankruptcy trustee is appointed to collect and manage the debtor's assets and distribute proceeds to creditors according to bankruptcy law.

options.t: A judge who presides over the bankruptcy case and decides it overall
options.why: The judge presides over the case and issues rulings, while the trustee is a separate administrator who handles the debtor's estate and payments to creditors.

options.t: A debtor's friend who offers to lend them money in need
options.why: A trustee is a neutral court-supervised officer, not the debtor's friend, and does not lend the debtor money in times of need.

options.t: A tax collector who works for the revenue agency in town
options.why: A tax collector works for a revenue agency, whereas a bankruptcy trustee administers the debtor's estate on behalf of the court and the creditors.

q: What is the difference between Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 bankruptcy?

options.t: Chapter 7 is for businesses only, and Chapter 13 is for people only
options.why: Both chapters are available to individuals; Chapter 7 is not limited to businesses and Chapter 13 is limited to individuals with regular income, not all people.

options.t: They are identical in every respect and differ only in the name used
options.why: The two chapters differ greatly: one liquidates assets while the other reorganizes debts through a plan, so they are not identical beyond the name.

options.t: Chapter 13 erases all debt immediately, while Chapter 7 requires a plan for repayment
options.why: This reverses the chapters: Chapter 13 does not erase debts immediately but requires a repayment plan, while Chapter 7 liquidates assets and discharges eligible debts.

options.t: Chapter 7 liquidates nonexempt assets while Chapter 13 sets a repayment plan
options.why: Chapter 7 liquidates nonexempt assets to pay creditors and then discharges many debts, while Chapter 13 lets an individual with regular income keep property and repay under a three to five year plan.

q: A person with a steady income wants to keep her house while repaying debts over five years. Which bankruptcy chapter best fits?

options.t: Chapter 7
options.why: Chapter 7 liquidates nonexempt assets and could put her house at risk, and it does not provide a multiyear repayment plan.

options.t: Chapter 11
options.why: Chapter 11 is a reorganization used mainly by businesses with complex finances, and it is too costly and complex for an individual repaying debts over five years.

options.t: Chapter 13
options.why: Chapter 13 lets an individual with a steady income keep her property, such as a house, while repaying debts under a court-approved plan lasting three to five years.

options.t: No such plan
options.why: A plan like this does exist: Chapter 13 provides exactly this arrangement for individuals with regular income who wish to keep their home while repaying debts.

q: What is tax avoidance?

options.t: Legally reducing taxes by using deductions and credits
options.why: Tax avoidance is the lawful reduction of taxes using deductions, credits, retirement plans and other legal strategies that the tax code allows.

options.t: Hiding income from the tax agency to pay less tax
options.why: Hiding income from the tax agency is tax evasion, which is illegal, not tax avoidance, which remains within the law.

options.t: Falsifying records to reduce the tax a person owes
options.why: Falsifying records to cut a tax bill is fraud and tax evasion, a crime that can bring fines and prison, unlike lawful avoidance.

options.t: Not filing a return at all for several years in a row
options.why: Failing to file for years is unlawful noncompliance, with penalties and possible prosecution, rather than a legal strategy to reduce taxes.

q: A business owner hides $50,000 in cash sales from the IRS. What is this?

options.t: A deduction
options.why: A deduction is a lawful reduction of taxable income for allowed expenses; hiding cash sales is not a deduction but an unlawful omission of income.

options.t: Tax evasion
options.why: Deliberately hiding cash sales from the IRS to pay less tax is tax evasion, a federal crime involving fraud that can lead to penalties and prison.

options.t: Tax avoidance
options.why: Tax avoidance is lawful planning that reduces taxes within the rules, whereas concealing $50,000 of income is illegal and not avoidance.

options.t: A tax credit
options.why: A tax credit directly reduces tax owed for qualifying items, so it is a lawful benefit and not the concealment of income described here.

q: A government bans all imports from a specific country for political reasons. This is an:

options.t: Embargo
options.why: An embargo is a government ban on trade with a specific country, here imports, usually for political reasons, and it can be a form of sanction.

options.t: Subsidy
options.why: A subsidy is government financial support for a business or industry, not a ban on trade with another country.

options.t: Merger
options.why: A merger combines two companies into one, which has nothing to do with a government banning imports from a country.

options.t: Tax cut
options.why: A tax cut lowers taxes for people or businesses, so it is not a trade ban on goods from a specific country.

q: What does the WTO do?

options.t: Sets national tax rates and collects income taxes for the nation
options.why: National tax rates are set by governments and legislatures, not by the WTO, which deals with international trade rules between member countries.

options.t: Prints currency and coins for use across the whole nation
options.why: Printing currency and coins is done by national governments and central banks, and the WTO has no role in making money.

options.t: Sets rules for trade between nations and helps resolve disputes
options.why: The World Trade Organization sets rules for trade between nations, runs trade negotiations and helps settle disputes among its member countries.

options.t: Runs world airlines and sets the fares that passengers pay
options.why: The WTO does not run airlines or set fares; airlines are private or state firms, and the WTO focuses on trade rules among countries.

q: What is the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA)?

options.t: A law on tariffs and duties on goods crossing a border
options.why: Tariffs and duties are governed by customs and trade laws, not the FCPA, which targets bribery of foreign officials.

options.t: A law that bans exports to foreign states without license
options.why: Export controls and licensing are covered by separate export laws, while the FCPA concerns improper payments to foreign government officials.

options.t: A law on minimum wage for workers in factories
options.why: Minimum wage is set by the Fair Labor Standards Act, so it is unrelated to the FCPA, which deals with international corruption.

options.t: A U.S. law that prohibits bribing foreign officials
options.why: The FCPA is a U.S. law that makes it illegal for U.S. companies and individuals to bribe foreign officials to win or keep business, and it requires accurate accounting records.

q: A U.S. company pays a foreign official to speed up a permit. Which law may be violated?

options.t: The ADA
options.why: The ADA protects people with disabilities and does not address payments to foreign officials, so it is not the law violated here.

options.t: The FCPA
options.why: The FCPA prohibits U.S. companies from paying foreign officials to gain business advantages, and paying to speed up a permit may violate it unless it is a narrow routine facilitation payment.

options.t: The CAA
options.why: The CAA, the Clean Air Act, concerns pollution and air quality, so it does not apply to a payment made to a foreign official.

options.t: The FLSA
options.why: The FLSA sets wage and hour standards for workers and has no connection to payments to foreign officials for permits.

q: Why do exporters use standard shipping terms such as FOB or CIF?

options.t: To clarify who pays freight and bears risk during transit
options.why: Incoterms like FOB and CIF state who pays for freight and insurance and when risk of loss passes from seller to buyer, avoiding disputes in international sales.

options.t: To set tax rates for all of the exporters in the country
options.why: Shipping terms do not set tax rates; governments set taxes and customs duties, whereas FOB and CIF allocate cost and risk between buyer and seller.

options.t: To avoid contracts with buyers in all other countries
options.why: Exporters use shipping terms to define duties within a sale, not to avoid foreign buyers, and they help make international contracts clearer.

options.t: To eliminate shipping costs for the buyer and the seller alike
options.why: Shipping terms do not eliminate costs; they only decide who pays freight and insurance, so some party still bears these shipping expenses.

q: In a civil case, the plaintiff generally must prove the claim by:

options.t: A unanimous vote of the public
options.why: Civil cases are decided by a judge or jury applying a legal standard, not by a public vote, which has no place in court.

options.t: A signed confession by the party
options.why: A confession by the defendant is not required in a civil case, and plaintiffs usually prove claims with evidence, testimony and documents instead.

options.t: Proof beyond any reasonable doubt
options.why: Beyond a reasonable doubt is the higher standard used in criminal cases, whereas civil plaintiffs only need to meet a lower burden.

options.t: A preponderance of the evidence
options.why: In civil cases the plaintiff must show the claim is more likely true than not, called a preponderance of the evidence, which is a lower standard than in criminal cases.

q: What is precedent?

options.t: A contract term fixing the price of goods
options.why: Fixing the price of goods is a contract term and not a precedent, which is a legal principle from earlier court rulings.

options.t: A prior court decision that guides later cases
options.why: Precedent is a prior court decision that courts follow when deciding later cases with similar facts, under the doctrine of stare decisis, which promotes consistency.

options.t: A new law from Congress that ends past rulings
options.why: A new law from Congress is a statute, and it may change court rules, but it is not a precedent set by earlier court decisions.

options.t: A tax rule applied to the sale of goods in states
options.why: Tax rules on the sale of goods are set by statutes and regulations, not by precedent, which is based on earlier judicial opinions.

q: What is a statute?

options.t: A company policy on staff pay
options.why: A company policy on pay is an internal rule set by an employer, not a statute, which is a law passed by a government legislature.

options.t: A private contract by two parties
options.why: A private contract between two parties binds only those parties and is not a statute, which is a public law made by a legislature.

options.t: A law passed by a legislature
options.why: A statute is a written law passed by a legislature, such as Congress or a state legislature, and it applies to the public within its jurisdiction.

options.t: A judge's written opinion
options.why: A judge's written opinion is case law, which applies and interprets statutes, but it is not itself a statute passed by a legislature.

q: A federal law conflicts with a state law on the same subject. Under the Supremacy Clause, which generally prevails?

options.t: The federal law
options.why: Under the Supremacy Clause of the Constitution, valid federal law overrides conflicting state law, so the federal law generally prevails when the two conflict.

options.t: The older law
options.why: The age of a law does not decide a conflict between federal and state law; the Supremacy Clause says federal law takes priority regardless of date.

options.t: The state law
options.why: The state law does not win a conflict with a valid federal law on the same subject, because the Supremacy Clause makes federal law supreme.

options.t: Neither law
options.why: One of the laws does prevail; the Supremacy Clause establishes that valid federal law controls over conflicting state law, so neither law winning is wrong.

q: What does the plaintiff do in a lawsuit?

options.t: Defends against the claim in court
options.why: The party who defends against the claim in court is the defendant, not the plaintiff, who is the person who starts the case.

options.t: Writes the statute for the whole court
options.why: Statutes are written by legislatures, not by plaintiffs, who only bring a case to court asking for a remedy.

options.t: Decides the case for both of the parties
options.why: The judge or jury decides the case, not the plaintiff, who is simply one of the parties asking the court to decide.

options.t: Brings the claim against the defendant
options.why: The plaintiff is the party who starts a lawsuit by filing a complaint, bringing a claim against the defendant and seeking a remedy such as damages.

q: Small claims courts are typically used for:

options.t: Federal crimes tried before a jury of twelve people at a trial
options.why: Federal crimes are tried in federal district courts, often before juries, and small claims courts do not hear criminal cases.

options.t: Constitutional appeals heard by the highest court in the land
options.why: Constitutional appeals go to appellate courts and ultimately the Supreme Court, not small claims courts that handle minor money disputes.

options.t: Disputes involving limited dollar amounts, often without lawyers
options.why: Small claims courts handle disputes involving limited amounts of money, with simple procedures and often no lawyers, so ordinary people can resolve minor claims quickly and cheaply.

options.t: Billion-dollar mergers between large companies in several industries
options.why: Billion-dollar mergers involve large complex transactions that belong in regulatory review or major courts, not small claims courts with low dollar limits.

q: A salesperson knows a product has a safety defect but continues to sell it to meet quotas. What best describes this?

options.t: A required legal practice by firms
options.why: No law requires selling a product known to be defective; selling one is a legal risk, not a required practice for firms.

options.t: An unethical and likely illegal act
options.why: Knowingly selling a defective, unsafe product to meet quotas puts profit over safety and is unethical and likely illegal, exposing the firm to product liability.

options.t: Good salesmanship by the seller
options.why: Good salesmanship is honest and does not hide dangers, so knowingly selling a defective product is deceptive rather than skilled selling.

options.t: A neutral business choice by the seller
options.why: Selling a known unsafe product is not neutral, because it risks harming customers and breaches duties of honesty and safety that businesses owe.

q: What is corporate social responsibility?

options.t: A legal requirement for every product sold in the country, enforced by the government
options.why: Corporate social responsibility is generally voluntary, not a legal requirement for every product, even though some laws do impose specific obligations.

options.t: A company's commitment to act in ways that benefit society and the environment
options.why: Corporate social responsibility is a company's commitment to act ethically and to benefit society and the environment, beyond simply maximizing profit or following the law.

options.t: A sales tactic used only by the largest retail firms in the whole country
options.why: CSR is practiced by firms of all sizes, not only the largest retailers, and it is a business approach rather than only a sales tactic.

options.t: A tax loophole used by large firms to cut their yearly tax bills in the nation
options.why: CSR is not a tax loophole; it concerns ethical and social commitments, while tax loopholes are legal gaps used to reduce a tax bill.

q: A company has two options: one legal but harmful to the community, one legal and beneficial. Which choice reflects strong ethics?

options.t: The cheaper option always
options.why: Always choosing the cheaper option puts cost above community welfare, and it does not reflect strong ethics when a beneficial legal option exists.

options.t: Neither option works
options.why: Refusing both options is not reasonable here, because a legal and beneficial option exists and a company can choose it to act ethically.

options.t: The harmful legal option
options.why: Choosing a legal but harmful option puts profit ahead of the community, so it meets the law but fails the test of strong ethics.

options.t: The beneficial option
options.why: Strong business ethics go beyond legality, so choosing the option that benefits the community, even if both are legal, shows responsibility toward stakeholders.

q: Why is it important for companies to be transparent with customers?

options.t: It builds trust and reduces the risk of deception claims
options.why: Transparency builds customer trust and loyalty and reduces the risk of deception or false advertising claims by giving customers accurate information.

options.t: It increases secrecy and cuts trust among the staff
options.why: Transparency reduces secrecy and builds trust, so saying it increases secrecy and cuts trust among staff reverses its actual effect.

options.t: It lowers quality and weakens the loyalty of customers
options.why: Transparency tends to raise trust and loyalty rather than lower quality or weaken customer loyalty, because honest dealing strengthens relationships.

options.t: It avoids all laws and all rules in every state and city
options.why: Transparency does not let companies avoid laws; businesses must follow all applicable laws, and being open with customers is simply good practice.

q: An accountant is asked to backdate a document so a deal looks compliant. What should she do?

options.t: Backdate it to keep the job
options.why: Backdating a document to look compliant is fraud and an ethical breach, and keeping a job is no excuse for falsifying records.

options.t: Wait and see what happens next
options.why: Waiting and doing nothing allows a falsified record to stand and leaves the accountant exposed to professional and legal consequences.

options.t: Decline and report the request
options.why: An accountant should decline to backdate the document and report the request to a supervisor, compliance officer or authority, because honesty and professional standards come first.

options.t: Backdate it but tell no one
options.why: Backdating secretly is still falsification, and hiding it makes the accountant complicit in fraud, which violates professional ethics and the law.

q: A contract says 'the entire agreement is contained in this writing.' A party later claims a prior oral promise adds a term. Under the parol evidence rule, what will a court likely do?

options.t: Void the entire contract automatically, as it has a merger clause as a rule
options.why: A merger clause does not void the contract; it states the writing is the complete agreement, which is why earlier oral promises are usually excluded.

options.t: Exclude the earlier oral promise that contradicts the final writing
options.why: The parol evidence rule bars evidence of prior oral agreements that contradict or add to a fully integrated written contract, so the court will likely exclude the oral promise.

options.t: Add the oral promise to the contract as an extra binding term
options.why: Adding the oral promise would defeat the merger clause and the parol evidence rule, which keep earlier oral terms out of a final written agreement.

options.t: Require the parties to restart negotiations from the beginning
options.why: Courts enforce the written agreement as is, so they do not usually send the parties back to renegotiate when a merger clause covers the whole deal.

q: What is anticipatory repudiation?

options.t: Assigning the contract to someone else, who then takes over the duties
options.why: Assigning a contract transfers rights or duties to another person, which is different from refusing in advance to perform the contract.

options.t: Asking to renegotiate the terms of the contract politely with the other side
options.why: Politely asking to renegotiate is not repudiation, because the party has not clearly stated that it will not perform its obligations.

options.t: One party clearly states before performance is due that it will not perform
options.why: Anticipatory repudiation occurs when a party clearly states or shows before performance is due that it will not perform, allowing the other side to treat it as a breach.

options.t: Performing the contract early, before the due date arrives for the other party
options.why: Early performance is not repudiation, because the party is carrying out its duties rather than refusing to perform them.

q: A builder tells a homeowner in March that she will not build the June project at all. What may the homeowner do?

options.t: Sue for the builder's profits only, in court
options.why: The homeowner's remedy is not limited to the builder's profits; she may recover damages for the breach, such as extra cost to hire a replacement builder.

options.t: Wait silently until June, then ask for a refund
options.why: She need not wait silently until June, because after a clear repudiation the other party may treat the contract as breached right away and mitigate damages.

options.t: Do nothing because no breach occurred yet at all
options.why: A breach can occur before the due date through anticipatory repudiation, so the claim that no breach has happened yet at all is wrong.

options.t: Treat it as a breach now and seek another builder
options.why: Because the builder clearly repudiated in March, the homeowner may treat it as a breach now, hire another builder and seek damages for any extra cost.

q: What is substantial performance?

options.t: Performance that meets the essential purpose of a contract even with minor flaws
options.why: Substantial performance means the party has met the essential purpose of the contract despite minor defects, so the other side must pay, less the cost of fixing the flaws.

options.t: Doing exactly what was promised in every detail, with no flaws or delays at all as a rule
options.why: Doing everything exactly is perfect or full performance, which is stricter than substantial performance, where minor flaws are tolerated.

options.t: Delaying a decade before starting the work promised in the written contract
options.why: Waiting a decade to start work is a material delay and does not meet the essential purpose, so it is not substantial performance.

options.t: Doing none of the work that the contract calls for, from start to finish
options.why: Doing none of the work is total nonperformance and a breach, which is the opposite of substantial performance.

q: A painter finishes a house but misses one small closet wall. The owner refuses to pay. What does substantial performance generally allow?

options.t: No payment at all for the work done on the house
options.why: Under substantial performance the painter who finished nearly all of the job can still be paid, so no payment at all would be unfair.

options.t: Payment less the cost to fix the small defect
options.why: Substantial performance lets the painter recover the contract price minus the cost of repairing the small unfinished defect, which balances both sides' interests.

options.t: Cancellation of all duties, so no one owes a thing
options.why: One minor defect does not cancel all duties; substantial performance keeps the contract alive, so the owner must still pay after the deduction.

options.t: Double payment for the work done on the house
options.why: Double payment would give the painter more than the contract price, while substantial performance gives full price less a deduction for the defect.

q: What is an accord and satisfaction?

options.t: An agreement to accept a different performance in place of the original duty, then carrying it out
options.why: In an accord and satisfaction the parties agree to accept different performance (the accord) in place of the original duty, and carrying it out (the satisfaction) discharges the duty.

options.t: A contract that is never signed by the parties and has no legal effect at all in a court
options.why: A contract that is never signed does not describe an accord and satisfaction, which is an agreement to substitute performance, not an invalid agreement.

options.t: A court order that forces one side to pay the other for the harm done to it, plus all legal costs in this case
options.why: A court order requiring payment for harm describes a judgment awarding damages, not an accord and satisfaction, which parties create by agreement themselves.

options.t: A contract with no terms at all, written as a blank sheet of paper with a signature on it
options.why: A contract with no terms and just a signature has no content, whereas an accord and satisfaction has a clear substitute performance that both sides accept.

q: What is a novation?

options.t: A contract signed by one party only, which binds the other side without its consent
options.why: A contract binding the other side without its consent is invalid, whereas a novation requires the consent of everyone involved.

options.t: A late fee charged by a landlord when the rent is paid after the due date
options.why: A late fee is a penalty on rent paid after the due date and has nothing to do with replacing a party to a contract.

options.t: A written warning sent by an employer to a worker who is late for work
options.why: A written warning from an employer to a late worker is discipline and not a novation, which changes the parties or terms of a contract.

options.t: Replacing a party or contract with a new one, with the consent of all involved
options.why: A novation replaces an original party or contract with a new one, with the consent of all parties, and releases the original party from its obligations.

q: A supplier and a buyer agree that a new company will take over the supplier's contract and the original supplier is released. What is this?

options.t: A rescission
options.why: Rescission cancels a contract and returns the parties to their positions before it, but here a new company takes over the duties, which is a different arrangement.

options.t: A breach
options.why: A breach is a failure to perform, whereas here the parties agreed to a substitution, so nothing was breached.

options.t: A novation
options.why: A novation substitutes a new party for the original one with everyone's agreement and releases the original supplier from the contract, as the facts describe.

options.t: An assignment
options.why: An assignment transfers rights but usually does not release the original party from liability; the release of the original supplier points to a novation.

q: What is the duty to mitigate damages?

options.t: The injured party must increase its losses to raise the claim in the end
options.why: The duty to mitigate is the opposite of increasing losses; the injured party must act reasonably to reduce them, not raise them to inflate a claim.

options.t: The breaching party must pay double the damages to the other
options.why: The duty to mitigate rests on the injured party, not the breaching party, and it does not require anyone to pay double damages.

options.t: The court must reduce all claims brought by injured parties
options.why: Courts do not cut all claims by default; the duty to mitigate limits recovery only for losses that the injured party could reasonably have avoided.

options.t: The injured party must take reasonable steps to reduce its losses
options.why: The duty to mitigate requires the injured party to take reasonable steps to avoid or reduce its losses after a breach, and damages may be reduced if it fails to do so.

q: A landlord's tenant leaves early. The landlord leaves the apartment empty for a year without trying to rent it. What principle may limit recovery?

options.t: The duty to mitigate damages
options.why: A landlord must make reasonable efforts to re-rent after a tenant leaves early, so leaving the unit empty for a year without trying can limit recovery under the duty to mitigate.

options.t: The statute of frauds rule
options.why: The statute of frauds concerns whether certain contracts must be in writing, not whether the landlord tried to reduce its losses by re-renting.

options.t: The parol evidence rule here
options.why: The parol evidence rule limits use of earlier oral statements to change a written contract, so it does not address the landlord's failure to re-rent.

options.t: Respondeat superior doctrine
options.why: Respondeat superior makes employers liable for employees' acts, so it has nothing to do with a landlord's duty to reduce losses after a tenant leaves.

q: What is an unconscionable contract?

options.t: A contract with a low price agreed by both of the parties
options.why: A low price agreed by both parties is not unconscionable on its own; courts look for gross unfairness and lack of real choice, not just a low price.
