options.t: One so one-sided and unfair that a court may refuse to enforce it
options.why: An unconscionable contract is so one-sided and unfair, often because of unequal bargaining power, that a court may refuse to enforce it or strike the offending terms.

options.t: A contract that is long and has a great many pages of terms
options.why: Length and the number of pages do not make a contract unconscionable; courts look at fairness and bargaining power, not how long the document is.

options.t: A contract signed on Monday that cannot be changed later by either party
options.why: Signing on a particular day and being unable to change terms later describes an ordinary binding contract, not an unconscionable one.

q: What is a contract of adhesion?

options.t: A negotiated deal between equals, where each side can change terms
options.why: A negotiated deal between equals is the opposite of an adhesion contract, which offers the weaker party no chance to bargain over terms.

options.t: A contract made orally only, with no writing involved at all
options.why: Oral contracts are valid in many cases but have nothing to do with adhesion, which concerns a standard form drafted by one party and imposed on the other.

options.t: A standard take-it-or-leave-it contract drafted by one party
options.why: A contract of adhesion is a standardized form drafted by the stronger party and offered take-it-or-leave-it, with the other party unable to negotiate, and courts may scrutinize it closely.

options.t: A contract signed by sticking notes onto a shared document
options.why: Sticking notes onto a document is not how contracts are formed, and adhesion refers to unequal bargaining power rather than the physical way a document is signed.

q: A phone company's service contract allows it to change any term at any time without notice. A court might find it:

options.t: Void because it is printed in small type on the back
options.why: Small print on the back does not void a contract by itself; the concern here is the unfairly one-sided power to change any term without notice.

options.t: A gift that the company gives to every customer
options.why: A service contract is not a gift, because customers pay for the service, and the issue is whether the one-sided change terms are fair.

options.t: Always enforceable, since customers agree to every term
options.why: Contracts are not always enforceable just because customers agree, because courts may refuse to enforce terms that are unconscionable or illusory, such as unlimited unilateral changes.

options.t: Possibly unconscionable or unenforceable in parts
options.why: A term letting a company change any term at any time without notice is very one-sided, so a court may find it unconscionable or unenforceable in part.

q: What is a click-wrap agreement?

options.t: A contract with no terms, only a blank page for both sides to sign
options.why: A contract with no terms and a blank page lacks content, whereas a click-wrap agreement presents actual terms that a user accepts online.

options.t: A contract written on paper only and signed with a pen by both sides
options.why: Paper contracts signed with a pen are traditional agreements, whereas a click-wrap agreement is formed electronically when a user clicks to accept.

options.t: An online contract in which a user clicks 'I agree' to accept terms
options.why: A click-wrap agreement is an online contract that a user accepts by clicking I agree or a similar button, and courts generally enforce it when terms are clearly presented.

options.t: A contract made only by phone, with no writing or online click at all
options.why: Phone-only contracts are oral agreements, and click-wrap involves an online click on a written set of terms, so they are not the same.

q: What does the E-SIGN Act do?

options.t: Requires every contract to be notarized before it takes effect in any court of the country
options.why: The E-SIGN Act does not require notarization; it makes electronic signatures and records valid, and many contracts do not need a notary.

options.t: Gives electronic signatures and records the same legal effect as paper in many cases
options.why: The E-SIGN Act of 2000 gives electronic signatures and records the same legal effect as paper and handwritten ones in many transactions, supporting online contracts.

options.t: Bans electronic signatures on any contract, whatever its size or type, in any state
options.why: The E-SIGN Act does the opposite of banning electronic signatures; it recognizes them as legally valid for most contracts across the states.

options.t: Sets interest rates that banks may charge on consumer loans across the country
options.why: Interest rates on consumer loans are regulated by lending and usury laws, not by E-SIGN, which concerns the validity of electronic signatures.

q: A customer signs a service contract using a typed name and a tablet. Is it likely valid?

options.t: Yes, electronic signatures are generally valid under E-SIGN
options.why: The federal E-SIGN Act and state UETA give electronic signatures, including typed names and tablet signatures, the same legal effect as ink if the parties intended to sign electronically.

options.t: No, tablets are illegal for signing contracts of any kind
options.why: Tablets and other devices are routinely used to sign contracts, and E-SIGN specifically allows electronic signing, so no general ban on tablet signatures exists in contract law.

options.t: No, only ink signatures count, so a typed name has no effect
options.why: This is outdated, since E-SIGN and UETA say a signature cannot be denied legal effect only because it is electronic, so a typed name can bind the signer.

options.t: Only if notarized by a public notary and two witnesses
options.why: Notarization and witnesses are required only for certain documents such as deeds or wills, not for an ordinary service contract, which can be validly formed without either.

q: What is the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing?

options.t: A duty to sign a second contract with the same party as soon as the first one ends
options.why: Nothing in the implied covenant forces parties to sign a second contract; it only governs how each side performs and enforces the existing agreement, not future dealings.

options.t: A duty not to act to destroy the other party's right to the benefits of the contract
options.why: The implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, found in every contract, bars a party from acting to deprive the other of the benefits it reasonably expected, even without a written term.

options.t: A duty to lower prices for customers who buy in large amounts every month of the year
options.why: Volume discounts are a matter of negotiated price terms; the implied covenant does not require sellers to cut prices for large buyers or set any pricing at all.

options.t: A duty to give gifts to the other side after the contract has been fully signed
options.why: The covenant concerns honest performance of the contract, not gifts; no party owes the other side presents after signing unless the contract itself says so.

q: What is the 'mirror image rule'?

options.t: An acceptance must match the offer's terms exactly under common law
options.why: Under the common law mirror image rule, an acceptance must match the offer's terms exactly; any change is treated as a rejection and counteroffer, which UCC 2-207 relaxes for goods.

options.t: Two contracts must be identical in every word, line and detail
options.why: The rule concerns whether the acceptance matches the offer, not whether two separate contracts are word-for-word identical, so it does not demand identical documents.

options.t: An offer must be written in mirrors, so the other party can read it back
options.why: The name is only a metaphor for matching terms; offers need not be written, and nothing about the rule involves mirrors or reading an offer back.

options.t: A seller must copy the buyer's logo onto the written contract
options.why: The rule has nothing to do with logos or branding; it only compares the terms of the acceptance with the terms of the offer to decide if a contract formed.

q: Under UCC 2-207 between merchants, an acceptance with additional minor terms generally:

options.t: Voids the offer permanently, so no contract can ever be formed
options.why: Under UCC 2-207, a definite acceptance with extra terms does not destroy the offer; the contract can still form, so the offer is not voided permanently.

options.t: Never forms a contract between merchants under any rule of law
options.why: This is wrong because 2-207 was written to abandon the strict mirror image rule for goods, so an acceptance with added terms often does form a contract between merchants.

options.t: Always replaces the original offer, whatever terms the other side adds
options.why: The additional terms do not automatically replace the offer; they are only proposals, and between merchants they join the contract only if they are not material and the offeror does not object.

options.t: Can form a contract, with the additional terms treated as proposals
options.why: Under 2-207(2), a contract forms despite the added terms, which are treated as proposals that become part of the deal only if not material and not objected to by the offeror.

q: What is a firm offer under the UCC?

options.t: An offer made by a minor under the age of eighteen, which can be legally avoided by that minor later
options.why: This describes a minor's voidable offer, which is about capacity to contract; a firm offer under UCC 2-205 concerns merchants and keeping an offer open for a stated time.

options.t: An offer that expires instantly when the other party hears it, even if the terms clearly say otherwise in this case
options.why: A firm offer does the opposite of expiring instantly; it is designed to stay open for the stated time, which is the purpose of UCC 2-205.

options.t: A merchant's signed written offer to buy or sell goods that stays open without consideration for a stated time
options.why: UCC 2-205 makes a merchant's signed written offer irrevocable for the stated time, up to three months, without consideration, so the offeree can rely on it while shopping around.

options.t: An offer with no price, no goods and no date set out in the paperwork it was made on by the seller
options.why: A valid offer needs reasonably definite terms, and a firm offer must state its assurance of staying open; one missing price, goods and date would not even be a valid offer.

q: What is an option contract?

options.t: A contract to sell stock only, at a fixed price on a future date set by both
options.why: An option contract is not limited to stock; it can cover real estate, goods or business sales, and its defining feature is keeping an offer open, not a stock sale date.

options.t: A contract with no end date and no set time for the work to be done
options.why: An option contract does have a defined period during which the offer stays open, so the missing end date described here is the opposite of how options work.

options.t: An agreement, supported by payment, to keep an offer open for a set time
options.why: An option contract is a separate agreement, supported by consideration such as a fee, to keep an offer open for a set time so the offeror cannot revoke it meanwhile.

options.t: A contract about taxes owed by the buyer and the seller to the state
options.why: Tax obligations between buyer and seller are governed by tax law and sale terms, and have no connection to an option contract, which concerns keeping an offer open.

q: A buyer pays $500 for the right to buy a property for $200,000 within 60 days. The seller cannot sell to others during that time. What is this?

options.t: A rental lease
options.why: A lease gives temporary possession of property in exchange for rent, but here the buyer pays for the right to buy later, which is purchase rights, not occupancy.

options.t: An option contract
options.why: The $500 payment is consideration for holding the offer open for 60 days, making this an option contract; the seller cannot revoke or sell to others during that period.

options.t: A gift of money
options.why: A gift involves no payment or exchange, but here the buyer pays $500 as consideration for the option, so the transaction is a bargained-for contract, not a gift.

options.t: A void agreement
options.why: A void agreement has no legal effect, but this one has consideration and definite terms, so it is a valid, enforceable option contract.

q: When can an offer be revoked?

options.t: Generally at any time before acceptance, unless it is an option or firm offer
options.why: Under common law, an offeror may revoke at any time before acceptance, but options and UCC firm offers are exceptions because they are supported by consideration or statute.

options.t: Only after acceptance has been given and the contract is formed by both
options.why: Once an offer is accepted, a contract has already formed and revocation is no longer possible; the question is about revoking before acceptance, so this is backwards.

options.t: Only by a court order after both sides have gone to a formal court hearing
options.why: An offeror can revoke by simply notifying the offeree before acceptance; no court order or hearing is needed, because revocation is a private act of the offeror.

options.t: Never, because an offer once made must stay open forever to the other party in general
options.why: Offers do not stay open forever; they end by lapse of time, rejection, revocation or death, and the offeror can generally withdraw before acceptance unless an option or firm offer applies.

q: When does silence generally operate as acceptance?

options.t: Always, since silence is a clear sign of agreement in law
options.why: Silence does not normally accept an offer, because an offeree has no duty to respond; treating all silence as agreement would let anyone force contracts on others.

options.t: Never, since silence has no effect on an offer in any case
options.why: This is too absolute because exceptions exist, such as prior dealings, an offeree who takes the benefit of services knowingly, or when the offeror's terms say silence means acceptance.

options.t: Only on weekends, when the offer is open to the whole public in general
options.why: Weekends and public offers have no special rule about silence; the exceptions depend on prior dealings, accepted benefits or agreed terms, not on the day of the week.

options.t: Rarely, such as when the parties have a prior course of dealing
options.why: Silence can operate as acceptance only in limited cases, such as an established course of dealing between the parties or when the offeree accepts the benefit of services knowing payment is expected.

q: What is the perfect tender rule?

options.t: A buyer must accept all goods delivered, whatever their condition or quality
options.why: The perfect tender rule says the opposite: a buyer is not forced to accept goods that fail to conform, and may reject any delivery that does not match the contract.

options.t: A seller may deliver any goods at all, whatever the contract says about them
options.why: The perfect tender rule protects the buyer, not the seller; a seller must deliver goods that conform to the contract rather than whatever it chooses.

options.t: A seller may never deliver late, whatever the cause of the delay in the shipment
options.why: Late delivery is only one possible defect, and the rule is about nonconforming goods generally; sellers can sometimes cure a late or defective delivery within the contract time.

options.t: A buyer may reject goods that fail in any respect to conform to the contract
options.why: Under UCC 2-601, the buyer may reject goods that fail in any respect to conform to the contract, though sellers often get a right to cure that softens the rule.

q: A seller delivers 100 blue mugs when the contract specified 100 red mugs. Under the perfect tender rule, the buyer may:

options.t: Keep them and pay nothing at all
options.why: The buyer is not entitled to keep nonconforming goods without paying; if the buyer accepts them, the price is owed, perhaps reduced by damages for the defect.

options.t: Reject the nonconforming goods
options.why: Under the perfect tender rule, wrong-color mugs are nonconforming, so the buyer may reject the delivery, subject to the seller's right to cure within the time for performance.

options.t: Sue the delivery driver for it
options.why: The driver is only a carrier and not a party to the sale; the buyer's rights run against the seller, usually rejection, not a suit against the delivery driver.

options.t: Force the seller to paint them
options.why: The buyer cannot force the seller to repaint the goods; the remedies are rejection, acceptance with damages or cover, while the seller may choose to cure by delivering red mugs.

q: What is the seller's right to cure under the UCC?

options.t: The chance to fix a defective delivery within the contract time
options.why: Under UCC 2-508, a seller who delivers nonconforming goods may notify the buyer and cure by replacing or fixing them within the original contract time, or sometimes longer.

options.t: A right to double the price of the goods when they arrive late
options.why: Right to cure gives the seller a chance to fix the problem, not a right to raise prices; a late delivery does not let the seller charge double.

options.t: A right to refuse payment for the goods the seller sent
options.why: Right to cure does not let a seller refuse payment; it protects the seller by letting them correct a defective delivery so the buyer must still accept and pay.

options.t: A right to cancel the contract if the goods are found to be late
options.why: Cure is the opposite of cancellation; it lets the seller repair or replace a bad delivery to save the contract, not end the contract because goods are late.

q: What is 'cover' as a buyer's remedy?

options.t: A late fee charged to a buyer who pays the seller after the due date in the contract
options.why: A late fee is a charge for slow payment, not a buyer's remedy; cover is what a buyer does after the seller fails to deliver.

options.t: Hiding a defect from the buyer so that it cannot be found before the sale is made
options.why: Concealing a defect is fraud or misrepresentation, not a remedy; cover is a lawful remedy the buyer uses after the seller breaches by not delivering.

options.t: Buying substitute goods after the seller fails to deliver and recovering the extra cost
options.why: Under UCC 2-712, the buyer may buy substitute goods in good faith after a seller's breach and recover the difference between the cover price and the contract price, plus incidental damages.

options.t: Covering the goods with plastic sheets to keep them dry in the warehouse before they ship
options.why: Physically covering goods is unrelated to the legal term; cover as a buyer's remedy means buying replacement goods when the seller fails to deliver or delivers goods that were rejected.

q: A seller fails to deliver 200 units at $10 each. The buyer buys 200 substitutes at $13 each. What may the buyer recover as cover damages?

options.why: This is the original contract price of 200 x $10 = $2,000, which the buyer would have paid anyway, and not the extra cost of buying substitutes.
This figure does not match any step of the calculation; the extra cost per unit is $3, and multiplying by 200 units gives a much larger amount.
This is the total substitute purchase cost of 200 x $13 = $2,600, but cover damages only recover the difference over the contract price, not the whole price.
Cover damages equal the cover price minus the contract price: ($13 - $10) x 200 units = $3 x 200 = $600, plus any incidental damages, if any.

q: What is revocation of acceptance?

options.t: A refund of shipping only, with no refund of the price paid for the goods that were sent to the buyer
options.why: Revocation of acceptance is not a shipping refund; it lets the buyer undo an acceptance of goods and recover the price paid, not just delivery costs.

options.t: A tax form that the buyer must file with the state when goods are returned to the seller after a sale
options.why: Revocation of acceptance is a contract remedy under UCC 2-608, not a tax filing; the state does not require a form when goods are returned.

options.t: A buyer's right to cancel acceptance when a substantial defect was hidden or could not reasonably be found
options.why: Under UCC 2-608, a buyer who accepted goods may revoke acceptance when a defect substantially impairs their value and was hidden or the buyer reasonably relied on the seller's assurances.

options.t: A seller's right to cancel a sale after the goods have been delivered and accepted by the buyer for use in most cases
options.why: Revocation of acceptance belongs to the buyer, not the seller; a seller cannot cancel a completed sale after delivery just because the buyer has accepted the goods.

q: What is a warehouse receipt?

options.t: A receipt for a rent payment made to a landlord by a tenant
options.why: Rent payments to a landlord are acknowledged by a rent receipt; a warehouse receipt concerns stored goods, not leases or payments of rent.

options.t: A document issued by a warehouse acknowledging stored goods
options.why: Under UCC Article 7, a warehouse receipt is a document of title issued by a warehouse, confirming it holds the stated goods, and it can be transferred to pass ownership.

options.t: A tax invoice for goods stored in a warehouse for the owner
options.why: A tax invoice records a sale and amounts owed; a warehouse receipt is a document of title that proves goods are stored, and it does not bill the owner for tax.

options.t: A letter to customers about goods held in a warehouse
options.why: A warehouse receipt is not a letter to customers; it is a formal document of title that can be negotiated and transferred to give the holder rights to the stored goods.

q: A seller learns before delivery that a buyer is insolvent. What right may the seller have?

options.t: To stop delivery or demand cash
options.why: Under UCC 2-702 and 2-705, a seller who discovers a buyer is insolvent before delivery may refuse to deliver except for cash and may stop goods in transit.

options.t: To cancel without notice always
options.why: The seller cannot always cancel without notice; the UCC lets the seller refuse credit terms or stop delivery, but other rules and notice requirements still apply.

options.t: To demand twice the price paid
options.why: Twice the price would be a windfall; remedies for an insolvent buyer protect the seller from nonpayment and do not give damages beyond the actual contract price.

options.t: To sue the carrier for the loss
options.why: The carrier did not cause the loss; the seller's protection comes from refusing credit or stopping delivery, not from suing a carrier that merely transports the goods.

q: What does the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act regulate?

options.t: Zoning rules for land used by shops
options.why: Zoning is regulated by local governments under land use law, and the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act has nothing to do with where shops may be located.

options.t: Stock offerings made by small firms
options.why: Securities offerings by small firms are regulated by the SEC under securities laws, not by the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act, which covers consumer warranties.

options.t: Employment contracts on pay and hours
options.why: Employment pay and hours are covered by laws such as the Fair Labor Standards Act, while Magnuson-Moss deals only with consumer product warranties.

options.t: Written warranties on consumer products
options.why: The Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act of 1975 governs written warranties on consumer products, requiring clear disclosure of terms and labeling warranties as full or limited.

q: What is the difference between a 'full' and a 'limited' warranty under Magnuson-Moss?

options.t: A limited warranty has no terms and gives the buyer no rights or remedies against the seller at all under the law every time
options.why: A limited warranty still has terms and remedies; the Act only requires that a limited warranty be clearly labeled, so saying it gives the buyer no rights is wrong.

options.t: A full warranty gives stronger remedies such as repair or replacement without charge, while a limited warranty offers less
options.why: Under Magnuson-Moss, a full warranty must provide repair or replacement without charge within a reasonable time, while a limited warranty gives less and must be clearly labeled limited.

options.t: They are identical in every way and give the buyer exactly the same remedies in all cases without exception
options.why: The two are not identical; a full warranty carries minimum federal standards, such as free repair, that a limited warranty need not meet.

options.t: A full warranty lasts only one day, while a limited warranty lasts for the entire life of the whole product
options.why: Full and limited do not refer to how long a warranty lasts; the labels describe the strength of the remedies, and either type can last for different periods.

q: An advertisement calls a product 'guaranteed for life,' but the written warranty excludes most defects. What legal concern arises?

options.t: A zoning issue concerning where the business is located
options.why: Zoning concerns land use, and location of the business has no bearing on whether a warranty is advertised accurately or fully disclosed to consumers.

options.t: An antitrust issue concerning competition between two firms
options.why: Antitrust law concerns competition and monopolies, but the issue here is the gap between an advertised guarantee and the actual written warranty, which affects consumers.

options.t: Misleading or deceptive advertising and warranty disclosure
options.why: Advertising a lifetime guarantee while the written warranty excludes most defects can mislead consumers, raising deceptive advertising concerns under FTC rules and the Magnuson-Moss Act.

options.t: A trademark issue only, with no effect on the consumers at all
options.why: Trademark law protects brand identity, and the misleading guarantee here deceives consumers, so the issue is not trademark only and consumers are clearly affected.

q: What does the CAN-SPAM Act require of commercial emails?

options.t: A clear way to opt out, accurate sender and subject information
options.why: The CAN-SPAM Act requires commercial emails to include a working opt-out method, accurate header and sender information, truthful subject lines, and a valid physical postal address for the sender.

options.t: That emails contain no links to any other outside websites
options.why: CAN-SPAM does not ban links; legitimate marketing emails routinely include links, and the law targets deceptive headers, missing opt-outs and misleading subject lines.

options.t: That all emails be encrypted before they are sent out to people
options.why: Encryption is not required by CAN-SPAM; the law is about honesty and opt-out rights, not about the technical security of messages in transit.

options.t: That emails be sent only at night, when most people are asleep
options.why: CAN-SPAM sets no time of day restriction on email; its rules cover truthful content and opt-out handling, unlike some telemarketing rules that limit calling hours.

q: What does COPPA protect?

options.t: Imports of goods from other countries
options.why: Imports are regulated by customs and trade law, and COPPA, the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, has nothing to do with goods from other countries.

options.t: The online privacy of children under 13
options.why: COPPA requires websites and apps directed at children under 13 to get verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information, and the FTC enforces it.

options.t: Pets kept as animals in homes and farms
options.why: Animals and pets are covered by animal welfare and property laws, while COPPA concerns the online collection of personal information from young children.

options.t: Employees' wages and hours under labor laws
options.why: Employee pay and hours are governed by labor laws such as the FLSA, but COPPA protects children's personal information online, not worker wages.

q: A game app collects names and locations of 9-year-olds without parental consent. Which law is most likely violated?

options.t: OSHA
options.why: OSHA covers workplace safety and health, and it has no role in how a game app collects personal data from children online.

options.t: FLSA
options.why: The FLSA governs minimum wage, overtime and child labor in employment, not the collection of children's personal information by an online game.

options.t: COPPA
options.why: COPPA bars collecting personal information, such as names and locations, from children under 13 without verifiable parental consent, which the app violated by collecting data from 9-year-olds.

options.t: TILA
options.why: TILA, the Truth in Lending Act, requires credit cost disclosures and has no connection to a game app collecting data from children.

q: What is the Do Not Call Registry intended to do?

options.t: Let consumers limit unwanted telemarketing calls
options.why: The National Do Not Call Registry, run by the FTC, lets consumers opt out of most telemarketing calls, and businesses must stop calling numbers listed on it.

options.t: Register businesses that sell goods by phone
options.why: The registry lists consumer phone numbers that telemarketers should not call, not businesses that sell by phone, so it works in the opposite direction.

options.t: Raise phone prices charged to the consumers
options.why: The registry has no effect on phone prices; it only restricts telemarketing calls to registered numbers, and it does not regulate carrier rates.

options.t: Ban all phone calls made by any business to anyone
options.why: The registry does not ban all calls; exemptions exist for political calls, charities, surveys and companies with an existing business relationship with the consumer.

q: What is the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's role?

options.t: Prints money and coins for use by banks in the nation
options.why: The U.S. Mint and the Bureau of Engraving and Printing produce coins and paper money, while the CFPB supervises financial products such as loans, cards and mortgages.

options.t: Sets the federal budget and how much the state spends
options.why: The federal budget is set by Congress and the President; the CFPB regulates consumer financial products and has no role in setting state or federal spending.

options.t: Runs the stock market and sets prices for shares
options.why: The SEC regulates securities markets and the exchanges set share prices through trading, while the CFPB focuses on consumer lending and financial services.

options.t: Protects consumers in financial products and services
options.why: Created by the Dodd-Frank Act in 2010, the CFPB protects consumers in financial products and services such as mortgages, credit cards, student loans and debt collection.

q: Under federal law, a cardholder reports an unauthorized charge on a credit card within 60 days. What is the typical maximum liability?

options.why: A $500 cap is not the typical limit for reported credit card fraud; it resembles older rules for certain unreported debit card losses, not this timely credit card report.
Under the Fair Credit Billing Act, a cardholder's liability for unauthorized credit card use is capped at $50, and many issuers even offer zero liability policies.
$2,500 does not match any federal liability cap; the law limits credit card losses far below this amount when fraud is reported promptly.
$5,000 is not a federal cap on credit card fraud liability; the law limits the cardholder's loss to $50 at most for unauthorized charges.

q: Who is a holder in due course?

options.t: A person who steals the instrument and then tries to cash it at a bank somewhere in town
options.why: A thief took the instrument unlawfully and did not give value in good faith, so a thief cannot be a holder in due course regardless of cashing it.

options.t: A person who receives it as a gift from a friend and gives nothing of value in return for it as a rule
options.why: Taking an instrument as a gift involves no value given, and value is required, so a donee does not qualify as a holder in due course.

options.t: A person who takes a negotiable instrument for value, in good faith and without notice of defects
options.why: A holder in due course takes a negotiable instrument for value, in good faith and without notice of defects or dishonor, and gets stronger rights than ordinary holders.

options.t: A person who knows it is forged but takes it anyway, in the hope of being paid by someone
options.why: Knowledge that an instrument is forged defeats good faith and the no-notice requirement, so someone who takes it knowingly cannot be a holder in due course.

q: A buyer pays a seller with a note, and the seller sells the note to a bank that took it in good faith for value. The buyer claims the goods were defective. Against the bank, the buyer's defense is generally:

options.t: Limited, because the bank is a holder in due course
options.why: A holder in due course takes free of most personal defenses such as breach of warranty or defective goods, so the buyer must still pay the bank and pursue the seller instead.

options.t: Required to be paid twice, to the seller and to the bank
options.why: The buyer is not required to pay twice; the buyer pays the holder in due course and then claims against the seller for the defective goods.

options.t: Fully valid against the bank, whatever the buyer says
options.why: Personal defenses like defective goods are generally not valid against a holder in due course, so saying they are fully valid against the bank is wrong.

options.t: Automatic cancellation of the note for the buyer
options.why: A defense of defective goods does not automatically cancel the note, especially once a holder in due course owns it; the buyer's remedy lies against the seller.

q: What is a real defense against a holder in due course?

options.t: A late delivery of the goods to the buyer by the seller after the due date
options.why: Late delivery of goods is a personal defense, such as breach of contract, which a holder in due course takes free of, so it does not defeat payment.

options.t: A dislike of the product shown by the buyer after he has used it for a week in this case
options.why: Dislike of a product is a personal complaint and not a legal defense at all; real defenses involve serious problems like forgery or incapacity.

options.t: A complaint about the price paid by the buyer to the seller for the goods
options.why: A complaint about price is a personal defense, such as failure of consideration or a bad bargain, and cannot be raised against a holder in due course.

options.t: A defense that works even against a HDC, such as forgery or fraud in the factum
options.why: Real defenses, such as forgery, fraud in the factum, infancy, duress and bankruptcy discharge, are valid against everyone including a holder in due course.

q: What is a stop-payment order?

options.t: An order to raise a limit on the amount of money a customer can spend
options.why: Raising a spending limit is a different banking instruction; a stop-payment order cancels payment of a specific check and does not alter limits on spending.

options.t: An order to print a statement for a customer who asked for one
options.why: Requests for statements are routine account services, while a stop-payment order is an instruction to the bank not to pay a particular check.

options.t: An order to close an account and send the remaining funds to the owner
options.why: Closing an account and withdrawing funds is a different instruction; a stop-payment order only stops payment of one particular check, without closing anything.

options.t: A customer's instruction to a bank not to pay a particular check
options.why: Under UCC 4-403, a customer may order the bank not to pay a particular check before it is paid, usually in writing or by phone, and may owe a fee.

q: A customer writes a check, then learns the goods were not delivered. What can she do if the check has not yet cleared?

options.t: Place a stop-payment order with the bank
options.why: A stop-payment order tells the bank not to pay the check, which protects the customer if goods never arrived, as long as it is placed before the check clears.

options.t: Do nothing and hope the problem goes away
options.why: Doing nothing lets the check clear and the funds leave the account, leaving the customer to recover money from the store later with more difficulty.

options.t: Mail the check back to the store only
options.why: Mailing the check back to the store does not stop it from being cashed or deposited, and the bank may still pay it if it is presented.

options.t: Pay twice to be safe with the store
options.why: Paying twice only multiplies the customer's loss; a stop-payment order is the proper step to prevent payment on an uncleared check for undelivered goods.

q: What is a cashier's check?

options.t: A personal check on a closed bank account
options.why: A check on a closed account is a worthless personal check that will be dishonored, while a cashier's check is backed by the bank's own funds.

options.t: A check with no signature on its face
options.why: An unsigned check is not valid, since a negotiable instrument requires a signature; a cashier's check is signed by a bank officer and drawn on the bank.

options.t: A check drawn by a bank on its own funds
options.why: A cashier's check is drawn by the bank on its own funds, with the bank as both drawer and drawee, so it is considered nearly as good as cash.

options.t: A check written by a store clerk by hand
options.why: A cashier's check is issued by a bank, not written by hand by a store clerk, and the purchaser pays the bank for the amount first.

q: What is a certified check?

options.t: A check with a certificate of origin attached by a foreign bank in the end
options.why: A certified check is certified by the bank on which it is drawn, not by a foreign bank, and no certificate of origin is involved.

options.t: A personal check the bank has guaranteed by setting aside the funds
options.why: A certified check is a customer's check that the drawee bank has guaranteed by marking it certified and setting aside the funds, so the bank becomes primarily liable on it.

options.t: A rubber check that bounces when the bank refuses to pay it
options.why: A bounced check is called a dishonored or bad check, and a certified check is the reverse since the bank has promised to pay it.

options.t: A check approved by a customer before it is sent to the store
options.why: Customer approval does not make a check certified; the bank itself must accept and certify the check, which guarantees that funds are held to pay it.

q: Which is generally safer for a seller receiving a large payment from an unknown buyer?

options.t: A personal check from an unknown buyer
options.why: A personal check from an unknown buyer may bounce, and the seller bears that risk, so it offers little security for a large payment.

options.t: An unsigned note from an unknown buyer
options.why: An unsigned note is not even a valid negotiable instrument and gives the seller no enforceable promise from an unknown buyer.

options.t: A promise to pay later, signed by the buyer
options.why: A promise to pay later carries the buyer's credit risk, so the seller may not be paid if the unknown buyer fails to pay.

options.t: A cashier's check from a verified bank
options.why: A cashier's check is drawn on the bank's own funds, so payment depends on the bank rather than the unknown buyer, though verifying the bank avoids counterfeit risk.

q: What is forgery in the context of checks?

options.t: Depositing a check that is made out to you
options.why: Depositing a check made out to you is a proper, lawful act, with no signature falsified, so it is not forgery in any sense.

options.t: Signing another person's name without authority
options.why: Forgery means signing another person's name, or altering an instrument, without authority, and a forged signature generally has no effect as that person's signature.

options.t: Endorsing your own check by signing the back
options.why: Endorsing your own check by signing the back is the normal, lawful way to cash or deposit it, and it involves no false signature.

options.t: Voiding a check before it is cashed by the bank
options.why: Voiding a check means canceling it before payment, which the drawer may lawfully do, and it does not involve falsely signing someone's name.

q: What does the Electronic Fund Transfer Act protect?

options.t: Consumers using electronic payments such as debit cards and ATMs
options.why: The Electronic Fund Transfer Act protects consumers using electronic transfers such as debit cards, ATMs and direct deposits, and limits their liability for unauthorized use.

options.t: Patents and trademarks held by firms and individual inventors
options.why: Patents and trademarks are protected by intellectual property laws, while the Electronic Fund Transfer Act concerns consumers' electronic banking transactions.

options.t: Employees' wages and the overtime hours that they work each week
options.why: Employee wages and overtime fall under the Fair Labor Standards Act, whereas the Electronic Fund Transfer Act covers electronic payments by consumers.

options.t: Imports and the duties that are charged on foreign goods at ports
options.why: Imports and duties are handled by customs and tariff laws, while the Electronic Fund Transfer Act governs consumer electronic payments such as debit card and ATM use.

q: A consumer reports a lost debit card within two business days. Under the EFTA, her liability for unauthorized use is generally capped at:

options.why: $500 is the cap when a consumer reports a lost debit card after two business days but within sixty days, not when it is reported promptly.
$250 is not a limit set by the EFTA; the law uses $50, $500 or unlimited liability depending on how quickly the consumer reports the loss.
Under the EFTA, reporting a lost or stolen debit card within two business days caps the consumer's liability for unauthorized use at $50.
$5,000 is not an EFTA liability cap; the statute limits prompt reporters to $50, with larger exposure only if the consumer waits much longer.

q: What is the business judgment rule?

options.t: A rule on employee pay and the benefits that firms must give to all staff members
options.why: Employee pay and benefits are covered by employment law, while the business judgment rule shields directors from liability for informed, good-faith business decisions.

options.t: A rule that directors must always profit, whatever the cost to the company's owners
options.why: Directors owe duties of care and loyalty to the corporation; they are not guaranteed profit, and the rule protects reasonable decisions even if they lose money.

options.t: A rule banning directors from taking any business risks on behalf of owners
options.why: The rule does not ban risk; directors may take reasonable business risks, and courts defer to their informed, good-faith judgment rather than penalize losses.

options.t: Courts generally will not second-guess directors' good-faith, informed decisions
options.why: The business judgment rule presumes directors acted informed, in good faith and in the company's interest, so courts generally will not second-guess their decisions absent fraud or conflicts.

q: A board makes an informed, good-faith decision to enter a new market that loses money. Shareholders sue. Under the business judgment rule, the directors are likely:

options.t: Removed by the court
options.why: Courts do not remove directors merely because a good-faith, informed decision lost money; removal requires misconduct such as breach of loyalty or fraud.

options.t: Required to repay all losses
options.why: The directors are not required to repay losses from an honest business decision, because the rule protects reasonable choices, even those that turn out badly.

options.t: Protected from liability
options.why: An informed, good-faith decision made in the company's interest is protected by the business judgment rule, even though the new market lost money for the corporation.

options.t: Automatically liable
options.why: Directors are not automatically liable for bad outcomes; liability needs a breach of duty, such as bad faith or lack of information, not merely a loss.

q: What is a derivative lawsuit?

options.t: A suit on a derivative stock held by a trader on the open market of securities each year
options.why: Derivative securities such as options relate to financial trading, while a derivative lawsuit is a shareholder suit brought on behalf of the corporation.

options.t: A suit by a shareholder on behalf of the corporation against insiders or others who harmed it
options.why: In a derivative suit, a shareholder sues on the corporation's behalf against insiders or third parties who harmed it, and any recovery goes to the corporation.

options.t: A suit by employees for unpaid wages, brought against the company that employs them
options.why: Unpaid wage claims belong to employees under labor law and are not derivative suits, which are brought by shareholders for the corporation's benefit.

options.t: A suit by a customer against a store over a faulty product that was sold to them last year as a rule
options.why: A customer suing over a faulty product brings a product liability claim for personal injury or loss, not a shareholder derivative suit on the corporation's behalf.

q: What is a proxy in corporate voting?

options.t: Authority given to another person to vote a shareholder's shares
options.why: A proxy lets a shareholder authorize another person to vote her shares at a meeting, which is common when owners cannot attend in person.

options.t: A fee paid to attend meetings of the shareholders, charged at the door
options.why: Shareholders are not charged to attend meetings, and a proxy is a grant of voting authority, not an admission fee paid at the door.

options.t: A type of stock split that gives each holder additional shares for free
options.why: A stock split increases the number of shares without changing ownership value, while a proxy is a delegation of voting authority to another person.

options.t: A legal fine imposed on a firm by the state for late reports
options.why: A fine imposed by the state would be a penalty, while a proxy is a voluntary authorization for another person to vote the shares.

q: What is cumulative voting?

options.t: A system for officers only, where shareholders cannot cast any votes at all
options.why: In cumulative voting shareholders do vote for directors, and the system exists to help minority holders, so saying they cannot vote is wrong.

options.t: A system letting shareholders concentrate their votes on fewer director candidates
options.why: Cumulative voting lets a shareholder multiply shares by open seats and put all votes on one or a few candidates, helping minority shareholders win board representation.

options.t: A system banning voting for shareholders at annual meetings of the corporation
options.why: Cumulative voting is a way of voting at meetings, not a ban on voting, and it is intended to give small shareholders more influence.

options.t: A system of one vote per director, so that votes cannot be pooled behind one person
options.why: That describes the opposite, since cumulative voting allows votes to be pooled behind one person, while straight voting restricts votes to one per share per seat.

q: A shareholder with 100 shares can elect 3 directors under cumulative voting. How many votes can she cast for one candidate?

options.why: 3 would be the number of seats and not the number of votes; votes equal shares times seats, so the total is much larger.
33 does not fit; dividing 100 shares by 3 seats has no role in the formula, since votes are multiplied by the seats rather than divided.
Under cumulative voting, total votes equal shares times seats: 100 x 3 = 300, and she may cast all 300 for a single candidate.
100 is her share count, but cumulative voting gives her 100 x 3 seats = 300 votes, all of which she may cast for one candidate.

q: What is a merger?

options.t: The combination of two corporations in which one survives
options.why: In a merger, two corporations combine and one survives, absorbing the other's assets and liabilities, while the other corporation ceases to exist.

options.t: A tax audit of a firm carried out by the revenue agency
options.why: A tax audit is a government review of a firm's returns and has nothing to do with the legal combination of two corporations.

options.t: A split of one company into many smaller firms, each sold off
options.why: Splitting one company into many smaller firms is a breakup, divestiture or spinoff, which is the opposite of a merger.

options.t: A loan between firms to cover short-term costs of trading
options.why: A loan between firms is a financing arrangement and does not combine the companies, which is what a merger does.

q: What is a hostile takeover?

options.t: A strike by workers who stop work in order to press their demands
options.why: A strike is a labor action by workers, and a hostile takeover is a corporate acquisition, so the two concepts are unrelated.

options.t: A friendly merger agreed by the boards of both of the firms involved
options.why: A friendly merger approved by both boards is the opposite of hostile; a takeover is hostile when the target's management resists the acquirer.

options.t: A product recall ordered by a regulator after a safety defect is found
options.why: A product recall is a safety action ordered by a regulator or firm, and it has nothing to do with acquiring control of a company.

options.t: An attempt to acquire a company against the wishes of its management
options.why: In a hostile takeover the acquirer goes around management, often by a tender offer to shareholders or a proxy fight, to gain control against its wishes.

q: What is dissolution of a corporation?

options.t: A change of logo and of the company name
options.why: A rebrand changes a logo or name but the corporation continues to exist, while dissolution ends its legal existence completely.

options.t: A stock split of shares into more units
options.why: A stock split divides shares into more units without ending the company, so it does not dissolve the corporation in any way.

options.t: The start of a corporation by its founders
options.why: Forming a corporation is incorporation, the opposite of dissolution, which closes the corporation down and ends its legal existence.

options.t: The legal end of a corporation's existence
options.why: Dissolution is the legal end of a corporation's existence, followed by winding up its affairs, paying debts and distributing remaining assets to shareholders.

q: On dissolution, who is generally paid first from a corporation's assets?

options.t: Creditors
options.why: On dissolution, creditors are paid first from the corporation's assets, and only what remains goes to shareholders, with preferred stockholders ahead of common stockholders.

options.t: The founders
options.why: Founders have no special claim at dissolution unless they are also creditors or shareholders, and they are paid after debts are settled.

options.t: Executives
options.why: Executives are paid as employees or creditors only for amounts owed, and they have no priority claim over creditors on dissolution.

options.t: Stockholders
options.why: Stockholders are residual owners and are paid last, after all creditors, because they bear the risk of the business; only leftover assets go to them.

q: What is a registered agent?

options.t: A stock broker who buys and sells shares for the owners of a firm
options.why: A stockbroker buys and sells securities for clients and has no role in receiving legal papers for the business.

options.t: A tax auditor who checks a company's books for the government agency
options.why: A tax auditor reviews financial records for a government agency, which differs from a registered agent who receives service of process for the company.

options.t: A person or company designated to receive legal documents for a business
options.why: A registered agent is a person or company designated to receive legal documents, such as service of process and official notices, on behalf of a business entity.

options.t: A shareholder who owns part of a company and votes on its decisions  each year
options.why: A shareholder owns part of the company and votes on its decisions, which is a different role from the registered agent who receives legal papers.

q: What is a DBA ('doing business as') filing?

options.t: A bank loan taken out by the owner to start up a new firm
options.why: A bank loan is financing and not a registration; a DBA filing simply records a business name that differs from the owner's legal name.

options.t: Registering a trade name different from the owner's legal name
options.why: A DBA, or assumed name, filing registers a trade name different from the owner's legal name, so the public can identify the real person behind the business.

options.t: A product license that lets a firm sell goods under another brand
options.why: A license to sell under another brand is a trademark or franchise arrangement, while a DBA filing only registers a business name.

options.t: A tax deduction claimed by a business for the cost of goods sold
options.why: A cost of goods sold deduction is a tax accounting item, which has no connection to registering a trade name as a DBA.

q: Maria runs 'Sunrise Landscaping' as a sole proprietor. What may she be required to file?

options.t: Articles of incorporation filed to form a company
options.why: Articles of incorporation are filed to form a corporation, but Maria runs a sole proprietorship under an assumed name and does not need one.

options.t: A trade secret filing with the patent office
options.why: Trade secrets are protected by keeping information confidential and are not filed with the patent office, so this does not apply to Maria's business name.

options.t: A DBA or fictitious business name registration
options.why: A sole proprietor using a name other than her legal name usually must register a DBA or fictitious business name with the state or county.

options.t: A patent application filed for an invention
options.why: A patent protects an invention, while Maria is using a business name, so a patent application is unrelated to her situation.

q: What is a benefit corporation?

options.t: A union of workers who bargain with the employer over pay and conditions
options.why: A union is an organization of workers who bargain with employers, whereas a benefit corporation is a for-profit company with a stated public benefit purpose.

options.t: A corporation that pays no taxes of any kind because it serves the public good
options.why: Benefit corporations still pay taxes like other for-profit corporations; their public purpose does not exempt them from taxation, unlike some nonprofits.

options.t: A government agency that regulates the trade of goods between states
options.why: A government agency regulates commerce, but a benefit corporation is a private company that voluntarily commits to social goals alongside profit.

options.t: A corporation that commits to public benefit goals in addition to profit
options.why: A benefit corporation is a for-profit company that must also pursue a stated public benefit, and directors weigh the effects on society and stakeholders as well as shareholders.

q: What is a cooperative?

options.t: A business owned by the government that provides services to citizens
options.why: A government-owned business is a public enterprise, while a cooperative is owned and controlled democratically by its member users.

options.t: A business owned and controlled by its members who use its services
options.why: A cooperative is owned and democratically controlled by its members, who use its services or buy its goods, and profits are shared among members.

options.t: A business owned by one person who also keeps all of the profits
options.why: A business owned by one person who keeps all profits describes a sole proprietorship, not a cooperative, which has many member owners.

options.t: A business with no members that is run only by a hired manager
options.why: A cooperative has members who own it and vote, so a business with no members run only by a hired manager does not fit.

q: What duties does an agent owe a principal?

options.t: Loyalty, obedience, care and accounting
options.why: Agents owe principals fiduciary duties of loyalty, obedience, reasonable care and accounting, meaning they must act in the principal's interest and report on money handled.

options.t: No duties at all owed to the principal
options.why: Agents owe several fiduciary duties because they act for the principal, so saying they owe none contradicts basic agency law.

options.t: A duty to compete with the principal
options.why: An agent must avoid conflicts of interest and not compete with the principal, which is the opposite of owing a duty to compete.

options.t: Only the duty to be paid, nothing else
options.why: Beyond being paid, an agent owes loyalty, obedience, care and accounting; pay is a right of the agent, not the agent's only duty.

q: A real estate agent secretly buys a property she was hired to find for a client at a lower price and resells it to the client at a markup. What duty is violated?

options.t: Loyalty
options.why: Secretly buying and reselling to the client at a markup puts her own interest ahead of the client's, which breaches the fiduciary duty of loyalty.

options.t: Advertising
options.why: Advertising is not a standard fiduciary duty of agents; the issue is her secret self-dealing, which conflicts with the duty of loyalty.

options.t: Tax duty
options.why: Tax duty is not an agent's core duty here; the misconduct is secret self-dealing and profit at the client's expense, which violates loyalty.

options.t: Obedience
options.why: Obedience means following the principal's lawful instructions, but the problem here is self-dealing and secret profit, which is a breach of loyalty.

q: What duties does a principal owe an agent?

options.t: No duties at all owed to the agent by the principal
options.why: A principal owes the agent duties such as compensation and reimbursement, so claiming there are no duties ignores the principal's obligations in agency law.

options.t: Compensation, reimbursement and a safe working environment
options.why: A principal must pay agreed compensation, reimburse the agent's expenses, indemnify for losses and generally provide a reasonably safe working environment.

options.t: A duty to give company stock to the agent each year
options.why: Giving stock is not a standard duty; stock is given only if the parties agreed to it in the contract.

options.t: A duty to sell the business to the agent at the end of the term
options.why: Selling the business to the agent is not a legal duty; the principal owes pay, reimbursement and safe conditions, not a transfer of ownership.

q: What is an undisclosed principal?

options.t: A principal who hides money from the agent and from the third party involved in practice
options.why: An undisclosed principal's concealment concerns the third party not knowing the principal exists, not hiding money from the agent or anyone else.

options.t: A principal who cannot be sued by any third party over the agent's acts
options.why: An undisclosed principal can be sued; once discovered, the third party may sue either the principal or the agent on the contract.

options.t: A principal with no agent working for them and no authority to act for them
options.why: An undisclosed principal does have an agent acting on his behalf with authority, but the third party simply does not know the principal exists.

options.t: A principal whose existence is unknown to the third party dealing with the agent
options.why: With an undisclosed principal, the third party does not know a principal exists and thinks the agent is acting for herself, though the principal can often still be bound.

q: How can an agency relationship be terminated?

options.t: Only by a tax filing made with the revenue agency of the state each year
options.why: Agency does not end through a tax filing; it ends through agreement, completion of the task, revocation, renunciation or the death or incapacity of a party.

options.t: Only by lawsuit brought in a court of law by one party or the other
options.why: A lawsuit is not required to end an agency; either party can usually end it by notice, completion or other events without going to court.

options.t: By agreement, completion of the task, revocation or the death of a party
options.why: An agency ends by mutual agreement, completion of the purpose, revocation by the principal, renunciation by the agent, or the death or incapacity of a party.

options.t: It can never end once it begins, whatever the principal or agent wants
options.why: Agency can always be ended by the principal's revocation or the agent's renunciation, though the party who ends it wrongly may owe damages.

q: A principal tells an agent to stop acting for her, but the agent still signs a contract with a vendor who had dealt with him before and was not told. The principal may still be bound by:

options.t: Lingering apparent authority
options.why: Apparent authority can linger when the principal fails to notify third parties who relied on past dealings, so the principal may still be bound by the agent's contract.

options.t: The statute of frauds rule
options.why: The statute of frauds concerns which contracts must be in writing and does not decide whether a former agent can bind the principal.

options.t: Express authority alone applies
options.why: Express authority was withdrawn when she told the agent to stop, so only the lingering appearance of authority to the unaware vendor can bind her.

options.t: Nothing, as notice is not needed
options.why: Notice matters because third parties who dealt with the agent before may reasonably rely on apparent authority until told otherwise, so the principal can still be bound.

q: What is the 'scope of employment'?

options.t: The company's total revenue earned during the fiscal year across divisions
options.why: Total revenue is a financial figure for the company, whereas scope of employment is about which activities an employee is authorized to perform.

options.t: The range of activities an employee is hired or authorized to perform
options.why: The scope of employment is the range of activities an employee is hired or authorized to do, and employers are liable for torts committed within it.

options.t: The employee's home address on file with the payroll office of the firm
options.why: The employee's home address is a payroll record that has no bearing on which activities fall within the job or on employer liability.

options.t: The employee's pay raise at the end of each year of service to the firm
options.why: A pay raise is a compensation matter, not a measure of the activities the employee is authorized to perform in the job.

q: An employee takes a personal day trip in a company car and causes a crash. Is the employer likely liable?

options.t: Liable only for tickets and parking fines that the driver incurs
options.why: Fines and tickets may be personal to the driver, but employer liability for a crash depends on scope of employment, not on a narrow category of charges.

options.t: Liable only if the car is red, whatever the use of the vehicle
options.why: The color of the vehicle has no legal relevance; the employer's liability depends on whether the employee was acting within the scope of employment.

options.t: Probably not, if the trip was outside the scope of employment
options.why: A personal day trip is typically outside the scope of employment, so respondeat superior usually does not apply and the employer is probably not liable, though negligent entrustment can matter.

options.t: Always liable for everything the employee does in the vehicle
options.why: Employers are not always liable; respondeat superior covers acts within the scope of employment, while a purely personal trip may fall outside it.

q: What is a joint employer?

options.t: A worker who has two names, one used at home and one used at the job
options.why: A joint employer is not a person with two names; it describes separate businesses that share control over the terms of a worker's employment.

options.t: A tax preparer who files returns for clients each spring
options.why: A tax preparer files returns for clients and is not an employer; a joint employer is a business sharing control over a worker.

options.t: A union leader who negotiates pay on behalf of its members
options.why: A union leader bargains for members and is not an employer; a joint employer is an actual business that shares control of workers.

options.t: Two or more businesses that share control over a worker's terms
options.why: Two or more businesses that share control over a worker's pay, hours or conditions are joint employers, and each can be liable for wage and hour violations.

q: What does the 'ABC test' do in some states?

options.t: Tests building codes for homes and shops in cities across the state
options.why: Building codes are set by local governments and inspected by building officials, not tested by the ABC test used for worker classification.

options.t: Tests reading skills for students in primary schools across the state overall
options.why: Reading skills for students are assessed by education tests, and the ABC test is a legal standard for classifying workers, not for schools.

options.t: Helps decide whether a worker is an employee or independent contractor
options.why: The ABC test presumes a worker is an employee unless the hiring firm proves control freedom, work outside its usual business and an independent trade.

options.t: Tests stock prices for firms listed on the exchange in each month
options.why: Stock prices are set by market trading, and the ABC test is not related to finance; it is a legal test of worker status.

q: What is a security deposit in a lease?

options.t: A fine for moving out of the rented home before the lease ends overall
options.why: A fine for early move-out is a termination or breach penalty, while a security deposit is refundable money held to cover damage or unpaid rent.

options.t: A gift to the landlord when a tenant moves into a rented flat
options.why: A security deposit is not a gift to the landlord; it is refundable money held to cover damage or unpaid rent beyond normal wear.

options.t: A tax on rent paid by the tenant to the local city government
options.why: A tax on rent is a government charge, but a security deposit is held by the landlord and is generally refundable to the tenant.

options.t: Money paid by a tenant to cover potential damage or unpaid rent
options.why: A security deposit is money a tenant pays up front to cover potential damage or unpaid rent, and it is generally returned if the unit is left in good condition.

q: A landlord keeps a tenant's entire deposit to cover normal wear and tear such as faded paint. This is generally:

options.t: Not allowed in most places
options.why: Most states let landlords deduct only for damage beyond normal wear and tear, such as unpaid rent or real damage, so keeping the full deposit for faded paint is generally not allowed.

options.t: Always allowed by the law
options.why: Landlords may deduct only for unpaid rent and damage beyond normal wear and tear, so always being allowed to keep the deposit is incorrect.

options.t: Required in every state
options.why: No state requires landlords to keep the whole deposit, and statutes generally require refunding amounts not tied to damage or unpaid rent.

options.t: A tax benefit for owners
options.why: Wrongfully retaining a deposit is not a tax benefit; it can expose the landlord to liability, including penalties in some states.

q: What is the implied warranty of habitability?

options.t: A duty to lower rent whenever the tenant asks for it
options.why: The warranty of habitability concerns safe and livable housing, not rent reductions on request, though tenants may get remedies if a landlord fails to repair.

options.t: A landlord's duty to keep rental housing safe and livable
options.why: The implied warranty of habitability requires landlords to keep rental housing safe and livable, with working heat, water, electricity and structure, and tenants cannot waive it in most states.

options.t: A landlord's duty to buy furniture for the tenants
options.why: Landlords generally need not furnish furniture unless the lease says so; the warranty covers basic safety and livability of the unit.

options.t: A tenant's duty to decorate the rental unit each year in general
options.why: The warranty places duties on landlords, not tenants to decorate, and it covers safe, livable conditions for tenants.

q: What is eviction?

options.t: The legal process of removing a tenant from rental property
options.why: Eviction is the legal process a landlord uses to remove a tenant, usually requiring notice and a court order, and self-help removal is generally unlawful.

options.t: A repair request sent by a tenant to the landlord in writing
options.why: A written repair request is a tenant's notice about maintenance and is not a process for removing a tenant from the property.

options.t: A rent increase announced by the landlord to the tenant
options.why: A rent increase is a change in lease terms, and does not remove the tenant from the property as eviction does.

options.t: A lease renewal signed by the tenant and the landlord
options.why: A lease renewal extends the tenancy, which is the opposite of eviction, which ends the tenant's right to occupy.

q: A landlord changes the locks while a tenant is at work, with no court order. This is generally called:

options.t: A lawful eviction by the landlord
options.why: A lawful eviction requires notice and a court order, so locking out a tenant without either is not lawful.

options.t: An illegal self-help eviction
options.why: Changing locks without a court order is an illegal self-help eviction in most states, and landlords may owe damages to the tenant.

options.t: A rent adjustment by the landlord
options.why: A rent adjustment changes the amount charged and does not involve excluding the tenant from the rental unit.

options.t: A routine repair by the landlord
options.why: Changing locks is not a repair; a repair fixes defects, but here the landlord is removing the tenant's access without legal process.

q: What is a deed?

options.t: A mortgage payment made to the lender each month by the owner
options.why: A mortgage payment goes to the lender to repay a loan, while a deed is the document that transfers ownership of real property.

options.t: A zoning map showing how land is used in the city and its suburbs
options.why: A zoning map shows permitted land uses, whereas a deed is the document that transfers title between owners.

options.t: A legal document that transfers ownership of real property
options.why: A deed is a written, signed legal document that transfers ownership of real property from the grantor to the grantee and is usually recorded.

options.t: A rent receipt given by the landlord to the tenant after payment
options.why: A rent receipt only proves a rent payment, while a deed transfers ownership of real estate itself.

q: What is a quitclaim deed?

options.t: A deed that guarantees clear title to the buyer, with promises about past owners
options.why: A deed guaranteeing clear title with warranties is a warranty deed, whereas a quitclaim deed gives no promises about title.

options.t: A deed that sells a car or other motor vehicle from one person to another
options.why: A car sale is transferred by a certificate of title, not a deed, and a quitclaim deed deals with real property interests.

options.t: A deed that cancels a mortgage and releases the lien on the property
options.why: Canceling a mortgage and releasing a lien is done by a satisfaction or release of mortgage, which is a different document than a quitclaim deed.

options.t: A deed that transfers whatever interest the grantor has, without warranties
options.why: A quitclaim deed transfers whatever interest the grantor has, if any, without warranties or guarantees of clear title, and is often used between family members or to clear title defects.

q: A buyer wants the strongest protection about clear ownership. Which deed should she prefer?

options.t: A general warranty deed
options.why: A general warranty deed gives the broadest protection, as the grantor promises clear title against all defects, including those arising before the grantor's ownership.

options.t: A quitclaim deed only
options.why: A quitclaim deed gives no warranties about title, so it is the weakest protection and the least suitable for a buyer wanting security.

options.t: No deed is required
options.why: A deed is needed to transfer title to real property, so skipping one would leave the buyer without legal ownership.

options.t: A lease of the land
options.why: A lease grants temporary possession rather than ownership, so it gives no protection of clear title.

q: What is title insurance?

options.t: Insurance against fire damage to the property that is owned by the buyer
options.why: Fire damage is covered by property or hazard insurance, whereas title insurance protects against defects in the title to the property.

options.t: Insurance on a car that covers damage from accidents on the road and fires every time
options.why: Auto insurance covers vehicles and has no connection to the ownership defects that title insurance covers in real estate.

options.t: Insurance protecting a buyer or lender against defects in a property's title
options.why: Title insurance protects a buyer or lender against losses from defects in a property's title, such as liens, forgery or errors in public records.

options.t: Insurance on a job that pays workers when they lose their wages at work
options.why: Lost wages from work injuries are covered by workers' compensation, which is a different insurance from title insurance on real property.

q: What is zoning?

options.t: A survey tool used to measure the size of land
options.why: Surveys measure the size and boundaries of land, while zoning is the set of local rules controlling land use.

options.t: A type of loan used to buy a home or other land
options.why: A home loan is a mortgage, while zoning is a set of local government rules on how land may be used.

options.t: A tax on land charged by the local government
options.why: A tax on land is a property tax, and zoning is instead a land use regulation that sets what may be built where.

options.t: Local rules controlling how land can be used
options.why: Zoning is a set of local government rules controlling how land can be used, such as residential, commercial or industrial zones, and what may be built.

q: A business wants to open a loud factory in a residential zone. What may it need?

options.t: A trademark registration filed for the firm
options.why: A trademark protects brand identity and does not authorize a particular land use, so it cannot allow a factory in a residential zone.

options.t: A zoning variance or rezoning approval
options.why: A factory in a residential zone breaks the zoning rules, so the business would need a variance or rezoning approval from the local authority.

options.t: Nothing, as the land is private property
options.why: Private ownership does not override zoning law, so the business cannot use the land for any purpose it wants without approval.

options.t: A patent application for the factory
options.why: A patent protects an invention and does not affect where the factory may be located or what zoning allows.

q: What is an easement?

options.t: A tax break for homeowners who pay interest on a mortgage overall
options.why: A mortgage interest deduction is a tax rule, while an easement is a right to use another's land for a limited purpose.

options.t: A type of mortgage with fixed payments for thirty years
options.why: A fixed-rate mortgage is a loan; an easement is a property right and has nothing to do with loan payments.

options.t: A right to use another person's land for a limited purpose
options.why: An easement is a right to use another person's land for a limited purpose, such as a utility line or a shared driveway, without owning it.

options.t: A building permit issued by the city for new construction
options.why: A building permit is government permission to build, while an easement is a property right to use another's land for a limited purpose.

q: What is adverse possession?

options.t: Renting land from the owner for a fixed sum paid each month under a lease
options.why: Renting under a lease is a permissive use with payments, whereas adverse possession is occupying land openly without the owner's consent.

options.t: Buying land at an auction held by the local county government
options.why: Buying land at auction transfers title by purchase, whereas adverse possession gains title through long, open occupation without consent.

options.t: Stealing a car from a parking lot in the middle of the night
options.why: Stealing a car is a crime about personal property and not adverse possession, which concerns acquiring real estate title by occupation.

options.t: Gaining title to land by openly occupying it for a statutory period
options.why: Adverse possession lets someone gain title by occupying land openly, continuously, exclusively and hostilely for the statutory period, often 10 to 20 years, depending on the state.

q: What is comparative negligence?

options.t: A rule that reduces damages by the plaintiff's share of fault
options.why: Under comparative negligence, damages are reduced by the plaintiff's percentage of fault, so a partly at-fault plaintiff recovers less but may still recover something.

options.t: A rule on rent and the amounts that landlords may charge each month
options.why: Rent rules belong to landlord-tenant law, whereas comparative negligence is a tort rule allocating fault between plaintiff and defendant.

options.t: A rule that bans suits against any firm or any person in court
options.why: Comparative negligence does not ban suits; it allows partly at-fault plaintiffs to recover reduced damages instead of being barred.

options.t: A rule that doubles damages if the plaintiff was partly at fault
options.why: Comparative negligence reduces damages for the plaintiff's fault and never doubles them, so a partly at-fault plaintiff gets less.

q: A jury finds a plaintiff 30% at fault and awards $50,000 total damages. Under comparative negligence, what does she recover?

options.why: $15,000 is 30% of $50,000, which is the amount of the reduction, not what she recovers.
Her damages are reduced by her 30% fault: $50,000 x 0.30 = $15,000, and $50,000 - $15,000 = $35,000, which she recovers.
$5,000 does not match the calculation; 30% of $50,000 is $15,000, so the recovery is $35,000.
