q: A U.S. exporter sells to a member of a trade agreement that eliminates tariffs on that product. What is the likely effect?

options.t: The product cannot be shipped, as the pact bans sales to members
options.why: The agreement removes tariffs and does not ban sales to members. Shipping remains allowed, and in fact becomes easier and cheaper.

options.t: The buyer faces lower duties and the product may be cheaper
options.why: With tariffs eliminated on that product, the buyer faces lower duties, so the landed cost falls and the product may be cheaper and more competitive.

options.t: Exports are banned for all goods sold to any member country
options.why: The pact does not ban exports. It reduces tariffs between members, so saying all goods are banned from sale to any member is wrong.

options.t: The buyer pays higher duties on all goods bought from the U.S.
options.why: Higher duties would contradict the agreement, which eliminates tariffs on this product. The buyer pays less, not more, on those goods from the U.S.

q: What is a sanction?

options.t: A tax refund that a government sends to a company after it files its return at year end
options.why: A tax refund is money returned to a taxpayer. A sanction is a penalty or restriction imposed to limit dealings, so it is the opposite of a reward.

options.t: A bonus that a company pays to staff who meet a yearly sales goal set by the board of directors
options.why: A bonus for meeting a sales goal is an incentive. A sanction is a penalty imposed by governments, so it does not reward anyone.

options.t: A penalty imposed by governments to restrict dealings with a country, entity or person
options.why: A sanction is a penalty imposed by governments to restrict dealings with a country, entity or person, such as freezing assets or banning trade and financial transactions.

options.t: A trade discount that a seller gives to customers who buy goods in bulk from the firm each year
options.why: A bulk discount is a trade reward for large purchases. A sanction is a government penalty or restriction, not a price break.

q: What is the purpose of a certificate of origin?

options.t: To list buyers of the goods and the prices that they paid
options.why: Listing buyers and prices is the job of an invoice. A certificate of origin shows where the goods were made.

options.t: To prove a seller is rich enough to sell goods abroad
options.why: A certificate of origin does not prove wealth. It states the country where goods were produced, which customs uses to apply the right duties.

options.t: To show where goods were made, which can affect duties
options.why: A certificate of origin shows where goods were made, which customs uses to decide whether preferential duty rates apply, so it can affect the duties owed.

options.t: To insure goods against loss while they travel by sea
options.why: Insuring goods against loss at sea is done with a marine insurance policy. A certificate of origin documents the country of manufacture.

q: Which document commonly serves as proof of ownership and shipment terms for goods moving by sea?

options.t: A cover letter
options.why: A cover letter introduces an application or document package and is not a shipping document. It does not prove ownership or set shipment terms.

options.t: A bill of lading
options.why: A bill of lading is issued by the carrier. It serves as a receipt for the goods, a contract of carriage and a document of title for goods shipped by sea.

options.t: A marketing plan
options.why: A marketing plan outlines promotion strategy. It has no legal role in proving ownership or shipping terms for cargo.

options.t: A zoning map
options.why: A zoning map shows permitted land uses in a locality. It is unrelated to ownership or the shipment of goods by sea.

q: What is the Bill of Rights?

options.t: The first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution
options.why: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution, protecting rights such as free speech, due process and protection from unreasonable searches.

options.t: A trade treaty between the U.S. and other nations
options.why: A trade treaty is an international agreement about commerce. The Bill of Rights is part of the Constitution and protects individual rights.

options.t: A state statute passed by a legislature each year
options.why: State statutes are passed by state legislatures. The Bill of Rights is federal and part of the Constitution, adopted in 1791.

options.t: A list of tax laws passed by Congress in the year
options.why: Tax laws are passed by Congress as statutes. The Bill of Rights consists of constitutional amendments that protect individual liberties.

q: What does due process mean?

options.t: A business license issued by the city to a shop owner for a year
options.why: A business license is a permit issued by a city. Due process is a constitutional guarantee of fair procedures, not a permit.

options.t: A speed limit that applies to drivers on public roads and highways overall
options.why: A speed limit is a traffic rule. Due process is a constitutional protection requiring fair procedures before the government takes life, liberty or property.

options.t: A tax filing made by a business owner to the state revenue office
options.why: A tax filing is a report to a revenue office. Due process is a guarantee of fair government procedures, not a filing.

options.t: Fair procedures before the government takes life, liberty or property
options.why: Due process means fair procedures, such as notice and a hearing, before the government takes life, liberty or property, as guaranteed by the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments.

q: A city seizes a business's property with no notice or hearing. Which constitutional protection is most relevant?

options.t: Third Amendment
options.why: The Third Amendment bars quartering soldiers in homes in peacetime. It does not address seizing business property without notice or hearing.

options.t: Ninth Amendment
options.why: The Ninth Amendment says listed rights do not deny other rights retained by the people. It does not directly address seizure without a hearing.

options.t: 21st Amendment
options.why: The 21st Amendment repealed Prohibition. It has no connection to seizing property without notice, so it is not the relevant protection.

options.t: Due process
options.why: Seizing property with no notice or hearing denies due process, the guarantee in the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments of fair procedures before the government takes property.

q: What is the Commerce Clause?

options.t: The rule that lets a landlord end a lease when the tenant is late on the rent
options.why: Ending a lease for late rent is a landlord tenant matter under property and contract law. The Commerce Clause is a constitutional power over trade.

options.t: The constitutional power of Congress to regulate interstate and foreign commerce
options.why: The Commerce Clause gives Congress the power to regulate commerce among the states and with foreign nations, which supports much federal business regulation.

options.t: The power of states to tax every sale that crosses their borders from other states
options.why: Taxing sales crossing state borders concerns state tax power and is limited by the Commerce Clause. The clause itself gives Congress regulatory power.

options.t: The right of citizens to trademark a name that they use in business across the nation
options.why: Trademark rights come from use and registration under federal law. The Commerce Clause is a constitutional power given to Congress over commerce.

q: The EPA issues a rule limiting emissions from factories. What type of law is this?

options.t: Contract law claims
options.why: Contract law deals with private agreements between parties. An EPA emissions rule is made by an agency, so it is not contract law.

options.t: Criminal law rules
options.why: Criminal law defines crimes and punishments enforced by the state. An agency rule limiting emissions is regulatory, so it is not criminal law.

options.t: Administrative law
options.why: Rules made by agencies such as the EPA are administrative law. Agencies create and enforce regulations under authority delegated by statutes, as with emission limits.

options.t: Common law rules
options.why: Common law is judge made law that develops through court decisions. An EPA emissions rule is written by an agency, so it is not common law.

q: What is a writ of certiorari?

options.t: An order by a higher court agreeing to review a lower court's decision
options.why: A writ of certiorari is an order by a higher court, most often the Supreme Court, agreeing to review a lower court's decision, which is granted at the higher court's discretion.

options.t: A written order from a judge freeing a person held in custody without charge
options.why: An order freeing a person held without charge is habeas corpus. Certiorari is an order to review a lower court's decision.

options.t: A document that a company files with the state to register a new business name
options.why: A document registering a business name is a filing with the state. Certiorari is a judicial order for review, not a registration.

options.t: An official warrant that lets police search a home or car for evidence
options.why: A warrant that lets police search is issued on probable cause. Certiorari is a higher court's order to review a lower court decision.

q: What is a class action?

options.t: A suit by a single customer only, filed against a firm over a faulty product last year
options.why: A class action involves many people with similar claims, not a single customer. A suit by one customer alone is an individual action.

options.t: A lawsuit brought by one or more people on behalf of a larger group with similar claims
options.why: A class action is a lawsuit brought by one or more people on behalf of a larger group with similar claims, saving costs and allowing small claims to be heard together.

options.t: A lawsuit brought by a school or a college against its pupils or students over fees
options.why: A class action is not defined by a school suing students. It means representatives bring a case for a larger group with similar claims.

options.t: A suit against a class of students filed by the school over missed lessons at the school
options.why: A class action is a group lawsuit brought on behalf of people with common claims. A school suing students for missed lessons is not one.

q: What is a legal contract's 'severability clause'?

options.t: A term that cancels the whole contract if any one part of it is found invalid
options.why: Cancelling the whole contract when one part fails is the reverse of severability. A severability clause keeps the remaining terms in force.

options.t: A term that adds extra parties to the contract after it has been signed
options.why: Adding parties after signing is an assignment or amendment matter. Severability concerns what happens when part of a contract is invalid.

options.t: A term that doubles the price if the goods are late in being delivered
options.why: Doubling the price for late delivery is a penalty or liquidated damages term. Severability deals with invalid parts of a contract.

options.t: A term saying that if one part is invalid, the rest remains enforceable
options.why: A severability clause says that if one part is found invalid or unenforceable, the rest of the contract remains in force, preserving the parties' bargain.

q: A contract has a clause a court finds illegal, but the contract includes a severability clause. What will likely happen?

options.t: The parties must restart the deal from the very beginning
options.why: Restarting the deal is unnecessary. The severability clause lets the court remove the illegal part and keep the rest, so the parties need not start over.

options.t: The entire contract is void because of one illegal clause
options.why: Without a severability clause the whole contract might fail, but this contract has one. It keeps the lawful terms in force after the illegal clause is removed.

options.t: The illegal clause is removed and the rest is enforced
options.why: With a severability clause, the court strikes the illegal clause and enforces the remaining terms, so the contract survives without the unlawful part.

options.t: The court rewrites all terms so it is fair to both sides
options.why: Courts generally do not rewrite all terms to be fair. They remove the invalid clause under the severability provision and enforce the rest as written.

q: What is a choice-of-law clause?

options.t: A term stating which state's or country's law governs the contract
options.why: A choice-of-law clause states which state's or country's law will govern the contract and its interpretation, giving the parties certainty about the rules that apply to disputes.

options.t: A clause picking a judge to hear any dispute that may arise
options.why: Picking a judge or court describes a forum clause, and even then not a particular judge. A choice-of-law clause selects governing law, not the decision maker.

options.t: A clause setting the price of goods and the date of delivery
options.why: Price and delivery date are commercial terms of the deal. A choice-of-law clause names the law that governs the contract.

options.t: A clause picking a lawyer to represent each party in a dispute in the end
options.why: Choosing a lawyer for each party is not a contract clause for governing law. Parties hire their own counsel, and the clause only picks the applicable law.

q: What is a forum-selection clause?

options.t: A term stating the price and the due date
options.why: Price and due date are payment terms. A forum-selection clause instead states where disputes must be filed, meaning the court or place for litigation.

options.t: A term on advertising by either of the parties
options.why: Advertising rules are separate commercial terms. A forum-selection clause concerns the place where disputes must be filed.

options.t: A term stating where disputes must be filed
options.why: A forum-selection clause states where disputes must be filed, such as a named state or court, which gives both parties certainty about the location of any lawsuit.

options.t: A term stating the delivery date for the goods
options.why: A delivery date is a performance term for the goods. A forum-selection clause governs the location where litigation takes place.

q: A software contract says all disputes must be filed in Delaware courts. A customer in Oregon sues in Oregon. What may happen?

options.t: The court may dismiss or transfer the case based on the forum clause
options.why: Courts usually enforce reasonable forum-selection clauses, so the Oregon court may dismiss or transfer the case to Delaware since the contract required filing there.

options.t: The contract becomes void because of the forum clause it contains
options.why: A forum clause does not void the contract. It only decides where disputes are filed, and the rest of the agreement stays valid.

options.t: The customer wins automatically, since the clause cannot be used against him
options.why: The customer does not win automatically. Courts generally enforce forum clauses, so suing in the wrong place risks dismissal or transfer rather than victory.

options.t: The clause is always ignored by the courts in every state and case
options.why: Courts do not always ignore forum clauses. Many enforce them unless unfair or unreasonable, so saying they are always ignored in every state is wrong.

q: What is whistleblower retaliation?

options.t: Rewarding workers for staying silent on wrongdoing
options.why: Rewarding silence is not retaliation. Whistleblower retaliation is punishing someone for reporting wrongdoing, and paying for silence is a different problem.

options.t: Promoting an employee who reports wrongdoing
options.why: Promoting an employee who reports wrongdoing is a reward, not retaliation. Retaliation means adverse action against the reporter.

options.t: Thanking an employee who reports wrongdoing
options.why: Thanking a reporter is a positive response. Retaliation is a negative action, such as punishment, taken because the employee reported wrongdoing.

options.t: Punishing an employee for reporting wrongdoing
options.why: Whistleblower retaliation is punishing an employee, for example by firing, demotion or cutting hours, because the employee reported wrongdoing, which is both unethical and often illegal.

q: A manager cuts an employee's hours after the employee reported unsafe wiring. What is the legal and ethical concern?

options.t: A fair scheduling choice by the manager
options.why: Cutting hours right after a safety report is not a neutral schedule choice. The timing suggests it was a response to the report.

options.t: Retaliation for protected reporting
options.why: Reducing hours because the employee reported unsafe wiring looks like retaliation for protected reporting, which is unethical and prohibited by laws such as OSHA.

options.t: A tax rule on payroll for the firm
options.why: Payroll taxes are not the issue here. The concern is that an adverse action followed a protected safety report.

options.t: A required step in the review process
options.why: A review step is a process. The concern is that the manager punished the employee for reporting a hazard, which is retaliation.

q: What is conflict minerals reporting about?

options.t: Disclosing whether products contain minerals that fund armed conflict
options.why: Conflict minerals reporting requires companies to disclose whether their products contain minerals, such as tin or gold, that fund armed conflict, so buyers can see supply chain risks.

options.t: Shipping rates that a carrier charges to move heavy cargo overseas  by sea
options.why: Shipping rates for cargo are logistics costs. Conflict minerals reporting concerns the origin of minerals in products.

options.t: Rock collecting as a hobby that people do when they visit parks
options.why: Rock collecting is a hobby. Conflict minerals reporting is a corporate disclosure rule about minerals that may fund armed groups.

options.t: Mining wages that a company pays to workers who dig for metal ore
options.why: Mining wages are a labor topic. Conflict minerals reporting concerns whether minerals in products help fund conflict.

q: What is the ethical issue with 'dark patterns' on websites?

options.t: Using night mode to cut glare on a screen after the sun goes down
options.why: Night mode reduces glare and helps users. Dark patterns are deceptive design tricks, which have nothing to do with a dark screen theme.

options.t: Design tricks that mislead users into actions they did not intend
options.why: Dark patterns are design tricks that mislead users into actions they did not intend, such as hidden fees or hard cancel buttons, and they raise ethical and legal concerns.

options.t: Using large fonts so that users with poor sight can read the text
options.why: Large fonts help users with poor sight read the text. That is good accessibility practice, not a deceptive dark pattern.

options.t: Using dark colors on a page to give it a more serious look
options.why: Dark colors are a visual choice. Dark patterns refer to manipulative design that tricks users, not the color scheme of a page.

q: A site makes it easy to sign up for a subscription but hides the cancel button. Which concern applies?

options.t: Fair pricing that treats all customers in the same way each time
options.why: Fair pricing is not the issue. Hiding the cancel button makes a deceptive design that traps customers and is unrelated to equal pricing.

options.t: Strong branding that makes the shop easy for buyers to recognize
options.why: Strong branding helps recognition. It does not explain why a hidden cancel button is a problem, which is a deceptive practice.

options.t: A deceptive design that can violate consumer protection rules
options.why: Hiding the cancel button while making sign-up easy is a deceptive dark pattern that can violate consumer protection rules, including negative option and auto renewal laws.

options.t: Good customer service that helps buyers when they have a problem
options.why: Good customer service helps buyers solve problems. Hiding the cancel button does the opposite and makes it harder for customers to leave.

q: What does corporate governance mean?

options.t: A government of cities and towns that decides how much tax each person pays
options.why: A government of towns deciding taxes is local government. Corporate governance is about how a company is directed and controlled.

options.t: A union contract between workers and the employer on pay, hours and conditions as a rule
options.why: A union contract sets pay, hours and conditions. Corporate governance is the system by which a company is directed and controlled.

options.t: A company's logo and the colors that are used in its brand on packaging
options.why: A logo and brand colors concern marketing. Corporate governance concerns the structures and rules for running and overseeing a company.

options.t: The system of rules and practices by which a company is directed and controlled
options.why: Corporate governance is the system of rules, practices and processes by which a company is directed and controlled, including the board, management and shareholder relationships.

q: What is data privacy ethics?

options.t: Collecting all data possible about every person who visits the site
options.why: Collecting all possible data is excessive and ignores data minimization. Ethical privacy practice limits collection to what is needed and justified.

options.t: Selling data secretly to firms without telling the customers
options.why: Selling data secretly without telling customers is a breach of trust and often illegal, so it is the opposite of ethical privacy practice.

options.t: Respecting how personal data is collected, used and protected
options.why: Data privacy ethics means respecting how personal data is collected, used and protected, with consent, transparency and security for the people it describes.

options.t: Ignoring consent and collecting data from people who object
options.why: Ignoring consent and collecting data from people who object violates their autonomy, so it is unethical and often unlawful.

q: A company discovers a data breach exposing customers' information. What is the most responsible response?

options.t: Promptly notify affected customers and regulators and fix the problem
options.why: Promptly notifying affected customers and regulators and fixing the problem is responsible and usually required by breach notification laws, letting people protect themselves from harm.

options.t: Delete all records of the breach and say nothing to anyone outside
options.why: Deleting records and staying silent hides the breach and destroys evidence. It breaks notification laws and leaves customers exposed to harm.

options.t: Hide the breach to avoid bad press, and quietly fix the system later overall
options.why: Hiding the breach to avoid bad press delays customer protection and breaks notification laws, so fixing the system quietly later is not responsible.

options.t: Blame customers for the breach and refuse to pay for any losses
options.why: Blaming customers is unfair and refusing losses avoids accountability. A breach is the company's failure to protect data, so it should respond openly.

q: What is an illusory promise?

options.t: A promise in writing that was signed in front of two witnesses
options.why: A written, witnessed promise can still be binding. An illusory promise is defined by lacking any real commitment, not by how it was recorded.

options.t: A promise that does not actually commit the promisor to do anything
options.why: An illusory promise appears to be a promise but leaves the promisor free to perform or not, so it does not commit them to anything and is not valid consideration.

options.t: A promise made in a dream and spoken aloud to the other party
options.why: A promise made in a dream is not a legal concept. Illusory promises are about lacking commitment, not about where they were made.

options.t: A promise made to a minor who is under the age of eighteen years as a rule
options.why: A promise to a minor raises capacity issues. An illusory promise is one that commits the promisor to nothing, regardless of the other party's age.

q: A seller promises, 'I'll sell you my laptop for $400 if I feel like it.' Why may this fail as a contract?

options.t: It involves a laptop worth far more than the price quoted
options.why: The laptop's market value does not make it illusory. The defect is that the seller can decide not to sell, so he is not bound.

options.t: The price is too low for a laptop of that kind to be sold
options.why: A low price does not defeat a contract. Courts do not weigh fairness of price, so the problem is lack of commitment by the seller.

options.t: It was spoken aloud and not written down on paper
options.why: Oral contracts for goods under $500 are generally enforceable without writing, and the sale here is $400. The defect is the seller's lack of commitment.

options.t: The promise is illusory because the seller is not bound
options.why: 'If I feel like it' leaves the seller free to refuse, so the promise is illusory and gives no binding commitment, which means no enforceable contract.

q: What is a preexisting duty rule?

options.t: Promising to do what you are already legally obligated to do is generally not valid consideration
options.why: Under the preexisting duty rule, promising to do what you are already legally obliged to do is generally not valid consideration, since nothing new is given.

options.t: Every contract needs a preexisting duty, since a promise to do what is owed forms the basis of the deal
options.why: The rule says the opposite. A promise to do what is already owed cannot form the basis of a deal because it adds nothing new.

options.t: Duties must be paid twice, once to the state and once to the other party in the deal, by law
options.why: The rule does not require duties to be paid twice. It simply holds that performing an existing duty is not new consideration.

options.t: All duties must be written down and signed by a notary before they take effect in the state
options.why: Notarized writing is not required for duties to take effect. The rule concerns whether a promise to do what is already owed counts as consideration.

q: A contractor already bound to finish a house by May says she will quit unless the owner adds $5,000, and the owner agrees. The extra promise is likely:

options.t: Fully enforceable, as a new deal
options.why: The contractor was already bound to finish by May, so the owner's extra $5,000 for the same work lacks new consideration and is not enforceable as a new deal.

options.t: Unsupported by new consideration
options.why: The contractor promised nothing beyond her existing duty to finish the house, so the owner's extra $5,000 promise lacks new consideration under the preexisting duty rule.

options.t: Required by law in all cases
options.why: No law requires such a payment. The owner's extra promise is not required in any case, since the contractor gave nothing new in return.

options.t: A gift only, with no real value
options.why: It is not a gift, because the owner agreed to pay under pressure for existing work. It is simply unsupported by new consideration, so it is unenforceable.

q: What is past consideration?

options.t: A future promise made to perform some act at a later date for the other party
options.why: A future promise to perform later is executory consideration, which is valid. Past consideration is something already done before the promise.

options.t: A payment in advance made before any work is done by the seller or provider
options.why: A payment in advance is consideration given first and is valid. Past consideration refers to acts done before the promise was made.

options.t: Something already done before a promise, which generally cannot support the promise
options.why: Past consideration is something already done before the promise was made, and it generally cannot support the promise because it was not exchanged for it.

options.t: A bonus paid to an employee for work that was done in the past by the staff member as a rule
options.why: A bonus for past work is usually past consideration, but it describes one example. The definition is any act already completed before the promise.

q: What is a quasi-contract?

options.t: A contract on land that is made between a seller and a buyer of real estate in writing
options.why: A real estate contract is an actual contract and usually requires a writing. A quasi-contract is imposed by courts without a real agreement.

options.t: A contract with a minor who is under the age of eighteen and lacks capacity to sign
options.why: A contract with a minor is a voidable contract because of capacity. A quasi-contract is not an agreement at all.

options.t: A contract signed twice by the same parties, once in May and once again in June
options.why: Signing twice does not create a quasi-contract. A quasi-contract is a court imposed obligation arising without a real agreement.

options.t: A court-imposed obligation to prevent unjust enrichment, even without a real contract
options.why: A quasi-contract is an obligation imposed by a court to prevent unjust enrichment, even though the parties made no real contract, so one who benefited must pay.

q: A plumber mistakenly fixes the wrong house, and the owner knowingly lets the work finish and benefits. What principle may require payment?

options.t: Parol evidence rule for the contract
options.why: The parol evidence rule limits outside evidence that contradicts a written contract. It does not require payment for a benefit knowingly accepted.

options.t: Statute of frauds for the written deal
options.why: The statute of frauds requires certain contracts to be in writing. It does not provide a way to pay for a benefit received.

options.t: Force majeure clause in the contract
options.why: Force majeure excuses performance during extraordinary events. It does not require the owner to pay for work from which he benefited.

options.t: Unjust enrichment under a quasi-contract
options.why: The owner knowingly accepted a benefit, so unjust enrichment under a quasi-contract can require payment of the reasonable value, even without a real contract.

q: What is reformation of a contract?

options.t: A court adds punishment to a contract term that the parties have agreed
options.why: Reformation does not add punishment. It corrects the writing so it matches the parties' real agreement, not impose a penalty.

options.t: A court forces a new contract on the parties against their stated wishes
options.why: A court does not force a new contract on unwilling parties. Reformation only fixes the document to match what they actually agreed.

options.t: A court corrects a written contract to reflect the parties' actual agreement
options.why: Reformation is a remedy in which a court corrects a written contract to reflect the parties' actual agreement, often because of mutual mistake or fraud.

options.t: A court cancels the contract and sends both parties back to where they were overall
options.why: Cancelling and restoring the parties to prior positions is rescission. Reformation instead keeps the contract and fixes its wording.

q: What is the difference between express and implied terms?

options.t: Express terms are secret and may not be shown to the other party in the deal overall
options.why: Express terms are openly stated and known to both sides. Calling them secret is wrong, because they are stated outright.

options.t: Express terms are stated outright while implied terms arise from conduct or law
options.why: Express terms are stated outright, in words, written or spoken, while implied terms arise from conduct, custom or law, even though the parties did not say them.

options.t: Implied terms are written down in full on the face of the signed contract
options.why: Implied terms are not written on the face of the contract. They are inferred from conduct or law, which is why they are called implied.

options.t: They are identical in every respect and mean exactly the same thing in law
options.why: The two differ in how they arise. Express terms are stated, and implied terms come from conduct or law, so they are not identical.

q: A restaurant serves a customer who orders a meal without discussing price. What is the customer's obligation?

options.t: To pay a reasonable price under an implied contract
options.why: The customer ordered a meal, creating an implied contract, so the customer owes a reasonable price even though no price was discussed, usually the menu price.

options.t: To pay nothing at all because the price was never stated
options.why: Silence on price does not make the meal free. The law implies a duty to pay a reasonable price for services or goods knowingly ordered.

options.t: No obligation to pay for the meal that was served
options.why: The customer ordered and received the meal, so there is a duty to pay. Having no stated price does not remove the obligation.

options.t: To pay double the menu price for the meal ordered
options.why: Nothing supports paying double. The obligation is a reasonable price, usually the menu price, not an inflated amount.

q: Why does scarcity exist?

options.t: Consumers only want the things they really need
options.why: Consumers want more than they need, so scarcity exists. Saying they only want what they need contradicts the problem of unlimited wants.

options.t: Wants are unlimited; resources are limited
options.why: Scarcity exists because human wants are unlimited while resources are limited, so choices and trade-offs must be made about how to use resources.

options.t: Governments set prices too low for most goods
options.why: Scarcity exists even without price controls. Low government prices may cause shortages, but scarcity itself is the basic limit on resources.

options.t: Firms refuse to produce enough goods for people
options.why: Scarcity arises from limited resources, not from firms refusing to produce. Even the most willing producers cannot supply unlimited wants.

q: The price of beef rises sharply. What is the most likely effect on the demand for chicken, a substitute?

options.t: Demand for chicken increases
options.why: When beef becomes more expensive, consumers shift to chicken, a substitute, so demand for chicken increases at every price.

options.t: Demand for chicken decreases
options.why: A rise in the price of a substitute increases demand for chicken, not decreases it. Decreasing demand would apply to a complement.

options.t: Demand for chicken is unaffected
options.why: Chicken is a substitute for beef, so a beef price rise changes demand for chicken. It is not unaffected.

options.t: The supply of chicken falls
options.why: The change affects demand, not supply. Supply of chicken depends on production costs and technology, so it does not fall because beef costs more.

q: Which change would shift the demand curve for a normal good to the right?

options.t: A fall in consumer confidence
options.why: A fall in consumer confidence reduces spending and shifts demand left, not right. It lowers demand for most goods.

options.t: A fall in the good's own price
options.why: A fall in the good's own price causes a movement along the demand curve, not a shift of the curve itself.

options.t: An increase in production costs
options.why: Higher production costs shift the supply curve left. They affect supply, not demand, so they do not shift demand to the right.

options.t: An increase in consumers' incomes
options.why: For a normal good, higher consumer incomes raise demand at every price, so the demand curve shifts to the right.

q: A product has elastic demand. What happens when its price rises?

options.t: Quantity demanded does not change much at all
options.why: If quantity changed little, demand would be inelastic. Elastic demand means consumers respond strongly to price changes.

options.t: Quantity demanded rises when the price is raised
options.why: Quantity demanded rises when price rises only for unusual goods. Under the law of demand, a higher price lowers quantity demanded.

options.t: Quantity falls by a larger percent than price rose
options.why: With elastic demand, a price rise causes quantity demanded to fall by a larger percentage than the price rose, so total revenue decreases.

options.t: Quantity falls by a smaller percent than price rose
options.why: A smaller percentage fall in quantity describes inelastic demand. Elastic demand means the quantity falls by a larger percentage than the price rise.

q: Where is a market in equilibrium?

options.t: Where producers earn zero revenue from sales
options.why: Zero revenue is not equilibrium. Equilibrium is where buyers and sellers agree, with sales taking place at a price that clears the market.

options.t: Where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded
options.why: Market equilibrium is where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded, so there is no shortage or surplus and the price has no pressure to change.

options.t: Where the government sets the price of goods
options.why: A government set price is a price control and can cause shortages or surpluses. Equilibrium is set by market forces.

options.t: Where the price is as high as the sellers can make it
options.why: A maximum price sellers could charge would cause a surplus because buyers would not buy. Equilibrium is where supply equals demand.

q: Which of these is a factor of production?

options.t: Inflation
options.why: Inflation is a general rise in prices, which is a macroeconomic condition and not an input used to produce goods.

options.t: Interest
options.why: Interest is the return paid for the use of money. It is a payment to capital owners, not a factor of production itself.

options.t: Tariffs
options.why: Tariffs are taxes on imports and are a government policy, not a resource used to produce goods and services.

options.t: Labor
options.why: Labor, meaning human work, is one of the four factors of production, along with land, capital and entrepreneurship, which are inputs used to produce goods.

q: What is the main purpose of a for-profit business?

options.t: To earn a profit for its owners
options.why: The main purpose of a for-profit business is to earn a profit for its owners by selling goods or services at a price above cost.

options.t: To avoid paying taxes at all
options.why: Businesses must pay taxes. Avoiding taxes entirely is illegal and is not the purpose of a for-profit firm, which exists to earn profit.

options.t: To provide services free of charge
options.why: Providing services free of charge is the mission of a nonprofit or charity. A for-profit business charges prices to earn profit.

options.t: To regulate all competition
options.why: Regulating competition is the role of governments and agencies. A for-profit business competes in the market instead of regulating its rivals.

q: Which feature is typical of a corporation?

options.t: No separate legal identity at all
options.why: A corporation is a distinct legal person, separate from its owners, so the claim of no separate legal identity at all is the opposite of the truth.

options.t: Unlimited personal liability for owners
options.why: Unlimited personal liability describes sole proprietors and general partners, whose own assets can be reached for business debts, while corporation owners are shielded from that exposure.

options.t: Limited liability for its shareholders
options.why: Shareholders risk only the money they invested, and creditors cannot go after their personal assets, which makes limited liability a defining feature of the corporate form.

options.t: A single owner who is the business
options.why: A single owner who is the business describes a sole proprietorship, since a corporation is a legal entity separate from the people who own its shares.

q: What is an advantage of a partnership over a sole proprietorship?

options.t: Profits are never shared with any partner
options.why: Partners normally share profits according to their agreement, so saying profits are never shared with any partner contradicts how a partnership is set up and run.

options.t: The partners combine their skills and funds
options.why: Two or more partners pool their skills, knowledge and money, which a one person sole proprietorship cannot do, so this is a real advantage of the partnership form.

options.t: There is only one decision maker in the firm
options.why: Having only one decision maker is a trait of a sole proprietorship, so it cannot be an advantage that a partnership has over it.

options.t: Partners avoid all personal liability for debts
options.why: General partners usually remain personally liable for the firm's debts, so avoiding all personal liability is false and is more typical of a corporation or limited partner.

q: Which business structure's profits can be taxed twice, once at the business level and again when paid out as dividends?

options.t: An LLC firm
options.why: An LLC is generally a pass through entity, so its profits are taxed once on the owners' personal returns, not twice at the business and owner levels.

options.t: Sole proprietor
options.why: A sole proprietor reports business income directly on a personal return, so it is taxed just once and there is no separate business tax level to double up.

options.t: C corporation
options.why: A C corporation pays corporate income tax on its profits and shareholders pay tax again on dividends received, which is the classic double taxation of this structure.

options.t: Partnership
options.why: Partnership income passes through to the partners, who pay tax on their shares personally, so the firm itself pays no income tax and no double taxation arises.

q: Which type of business provides services such as banking or insurance?

options.t: A farming business
options.why: Farming grows crops or raises animals, which means it produces goods and belongs to the primary sector, not the businesses that provide banking or insurance services.

options.t: A mining business
options.why: Mining extracts raw materials such as coal or metals from the ground, so it produces a tangible resource and does not provide an intangible service like insurance.

options.t: A retail business
options.why: A retail business sells finished goods to consumers, which is selling products, while banking and insurance are intangible services and fit a different category.

options.t: A service business
options.why: Banking and insurance sell intangible help and expertise rather than physical goods, which is exactly what defines a service business such as a bank or insurer.

q: How does a nonprofit organization differ from a for-profit business?

options.t: It uses surplus funds to support its mission rather than paying profits to owners
options.why: A nonprofit may earn revenue, but any surplus is reinvested in its mission and not distributed to owners, which is the key difference from a for profit firm.

options.t: It is not permitted to earn any revenue from its programs, fees or services
options.why: Nonprofits are allowed to earn revenue from programs, fees and services, and many do, so a ban on earning any revenue is false and not the real difference.

options.t: It pays no wages or salaries to any of its employees, managers or volunteers
options.why: Nonprofits can pay reasonable wages and salaries to staff and managers, so claiming they pay none to anyone is untrue and misses the real difference, which is profit distribution.

options.t: It is owned by shareholders who receive any profit it earns and pays out each year
options.why: Shareholders who collect the profits describe a for profit corporation, while a nonprofit has no owners who receive profit, so this option describes the opposite organization.

q: In a market economy, prices are mainly set by:

options.t: The state government
options.why: A state government setting prices is characteristic of a command economy, while in a market economy buyers and sellers interacting set prices without central direction.

options.t: Supply and demand
options.why: In a market economy, the interaction of what buyers want and what sellers offer moves prices up or down until the market clears, so supply and demand set prices.

options.t: A worker committee
options.why: A worker committee setting prices is not how market economies work, since prices come from the decisions of many buyers and sellers and not from any single body.

options.t: Tradition and custom
options.why: Tradition and custom guide decisions in a traditional economy, where habits are handed down, but a market economy relies on prices that respond to supply and demand.

q: In a command economy, who makes the main decisions about what to produce?

options.t: The central government
options.why: In a command economy, a central authority, usually the government, decides what goods to make, how much, and for whom, so planners hold the main decisions.

options.t: Village elders by custom
options.why: Village elders deciding by custom describes a traditional economy, where inherited practices guide production, whereas a command economy uses formal central plans.

options.t: Competing private firms
options.why: Competing private firms making production choices is the mark of a market economy, while in a command economy the state limits private firms and sets output.

options.t: Individual consumers
options.why: Individual consumers steering production through their purchases is characteristic of a market economy, not a command economy where central planners override consumer demand.

q: The economy of the United States is best described as:

options.t: A command economy
options.why: The United States is not run by central planners who dictate output, and private firms make most decisions, so labeling it a command economy is wrong.

options.t: A tradition economy
options.why: A tradition economy relies on custom and inherited methods, which does not describe the modern, technology driven United States where markets and laws guide most choices.

options.t: A mixed economy
options.why: The United States is mainly market driven but the government also regulates, taxes, and provides services such as roads and Social Security, which makes it a mixed economy.

options.t: A market economy
options.why: Calling it purely a market economy ignores the large government role in regulation, taxation and public programs, so the more accurate label is a mixed economy.

q: Which is a typical characteristic of capitalism?

options.t: Production based on tradition and custom
options.why: Production based on tradition and custom defines a traditional economy, whereas capitalism relies on private owners and market incentives rather than inherited habits.

options.t: Fixed prices set by the central planners
options.why: Fixed prices set by central planners belong to a command economy, while capitalism lets prices move freely with supply and demand instead of being decided by planners.

options.t: State ownership of all the major industries
options.why: State ownership of all major industries is a feature of socialism or communism, and it is the reverse of capitalism, in which individuals and firms own businesses.

options.t: Private ownership of businesses and resources
options.why: Capitalism rests on individuals and firms owning businesses and resources and seeking profit, so private ownership is the typical characteristic of this system.

q: Which set of questions must every economic system answer?

options.t: What to produce, how to produce it and for whom
options.why: Every society has limited resources, so each must decide what goods to make, how to make them, and who receives them, and these three questions apply to any system.

options.t: Where to advertise, when and how often to do so
options.why: Advertising decisions are business choices within a firm and are not basic questions that every economic system must settle about producing and distributing goods.

options.t: Which currency to use and which bank to join
options.why: Choosing a currency or bank is a financial detail, not one of the basic allocation questions about production and distribution that all economic systems face.

options.t: Who to tax, when to tax and why to do so each year
options.why: Taxation is a government policy matter, not one of the three core questions of what, how and for whom that every economy must answer.

q: In a traditional economy, economic decisions are mainly based on:

options.t: Government plans and rules
options.why: Government plans and rules guide a command economy, whereas a traditional economy leans on long standing customs rather than on formal directives from authorities.

options.t: International agreements
options.why: International agreements shape trade between countries but do not form the basis of a traditional economy, where local customs and inherited roles guide decisions.

options.t: Market prices and profits
options.why: Market prices and profits drive decisions in a market economy, while a traditional economy follows established practice instead of responding to price signals.

options.t: Custom and past practice
options.why: In a traditional economy, people do what their ancestors did, so decisions about producing and sharing goods follow custom and past practice from one generation to the next.

q: Which type of policy uses government taxing and spending to influence the economy?

options.t: Labor policy
options.why: Labor policy covers employment rules such as wages and working conditions, and it does not work mainly through government taxing and spending to steer the economy.

options.t: Trade policy
options.why: Trade policy deals with tariffs, quotas and agreements on imports and exports, rather than with using taxes and government spending to influence overall economic activity.

options.t: Fiscal policy
options.why: Fiscal policy is the use of government taxation and spending to influence the economy, such as cutting taxes or increasing spending to boost demand.

options.t: Monetary policy
options.why: Monetary policy is run by the central bank through interest rates and the money supply, not through government taxing and spending, so it does not fit this definition.

q: The Federal Reserve mainly carries out monetary policy by:

options.t: Setting the tax rates that all businesses must pay
options.why: Setting business tax rates is done by Congress and tax authorities under fiscal policy, not by the Federal Reserve, whose monetary tools work through interest rates.

options.t: Influencing interest rates and the money supply
options.why: The Fed carries out monetary policy by influencing interest rates and the money supply, for example through its policy rate and open market operations, to guide growth and inflation.

options.t: Passing the laws that businesses must follow
options.why: Passing laws is the job of Congress, a legislative body, whereas the Federal Reserve is a central bank that manages money and credit conditions.

options.t: Setting the prices that stores charge for most goods
options.why: The Federal Reserve does not set store prices, since prices in the economy are determined by markets, and the Fed works through interest rates and the money supply.

q: What is the purpose of antitrust laws?

options.t: To promote competition and prevent monopolies
options.why: Antitrust laws break up or block monopolies and anticompetitive practices like price fixing, which protects competition and gives consumers lower prices and more choice.

options.t: To set the minimum wage for all workers in a state
options.why: Minimum wage rules come from labor law, not antitrust law, which targets anticompetitive behavior by firms rather than the pay floor for workers.

options.t: To tax imports at the border of each country
options.why: Taxing imports is a trade policy done through tariffs and has nothing to do with antitrust laws, which deal with competition among domestic and other firms.

options.t: To guarantee steady profits for large firms
options.why: Antitrust laws do the reverse of guaranteeing profits, since they keep large firms from dominating markets and leave their success to competition.

q: During a recession, the government cuts taxes and raises spending. What is it trying to do?

options.t: Reduce the national debt and the deficit
options.why: Cutting taxes and raising spending increases the deficit and adds to debt, so reducing the national debt is not the goal; the government accepts a bigger deficit.

options.t: Stimulate demand and economic activity
options.why: Lower taxes leave households more to spend and higher government spending adds demand directly, so the aim is to stimulate demand and economic activity during the downturn.

options.t: Raise interest rates to cool the economy
options.why: Raising interest rates is a tightening monetary action that cools demand, while the government in this case is using fiscal stimulus to push demand up, not down.

options.t: Slow down inflation across the whole nation
options.why: Slowing inflation requires reducing demand, but cutting taxes and raising spending adds demand, so the policy fits a recession and not an effort to cool prices.

q: What is a subsidy?

options.t: A tax placed on goods that are brought in from other lands
options.why: A tax on goods brought in from other lands is a tariff, not a subsidy, because a subsidy is money that the government gives rather than collects.

options.t: A limit on the amount of a product that may be produced
options.why: A limit on how much of a product may be produced is a quota or production cap, which restricts supply, while a subsidy supports producers with money.

options.t: A fine charged to a company for breaking a regulation
options.why: A fine charged for breaking a regulation is a penalty paid to the government, the opposite of a subsidy, which is a payment from the government.

options.t: Government financial support to a business or industry
options.why: A subsidy is financial support from the government to a business or industry, such as a farm payment, which lowers costs or raises income for producers.

q: A government sets a price ceiling below the equilibrium price. What is the likely result?

options.t: A surplus
options.why: A ceiling below equilibrium makes the price too low, so buyers want more than sellers supply, which creates a shortage rather than a surplus of goods.

options.t: A higher price
options.why: A ceiling is a legal maximum, so it cannot push the price above equilibrium; when set below it, the controlled price is lower, not higher.

options.t: A shortage
options.why: At a capped price below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so more people want the good than producers will sell, which is a shortage.

options.t: No change
options.why: A binding price ceiling changes the market outcome by holding the price under equilibrium, so there is a gap between demand and supply and not no change.

q: How is profit calculated?

options.t: Price times the quantity sold
options.why: Price times quantity sold gives total revenue, which ignores what it cost to produce the goods, so it is not profit.

options.t: Total revenue minus total cost
options.why: Profit is what remains from sales after all costs are paid, so it equals total revenue minus total cost, positive when revenue is higher and negative otherwise.

options.t: Total revenue plus total cost
options.why: Adding revenue and cost together has no economic meaning for profit, since costs reduce what a firm keeps rather than adding to it.

options.t: Total cost minus total revenue
options.why: Subtracting revenue from cost reverses the formula, and it would show a negative number whenever the firm actually earns a profit, so it is not the right calculation.

q: Which is an example of a variable cost for a bakery?

options.t: The owner's salary
options.why: An owner's salary is fixed regardless of how many loaves are baked, so it is a fixed cost and does not change with the level of output.

options.t: Insurance premium
options.why: An insurance premium is typically a set periodic amount that does not rise or fall with how much the bakery produces, so it is a fixed cost.

options.t: Monthly rent
options.why: Monthly rent stays the same whether the bakery bakes a few loaves or thousands, which makes it a fixed cost and not a variable one.

options.t: Flour and sugar
options.why: Flour and sugar are inputs used up as more goods are made, so the amount spent rises and falls with output, which makes them variable costs.

q: A business has $6,000 in fixed costs. Each unit sells for $20 and costs $8 to make. How many units must it sell to break even?

options.t: 214 units
options.why: The figure 214 comes from dividing 6,000 by 28, adding the unit cost to the price, but break even uses the margin of 20 minus 8, which is 12.

options.t: 750 units
options.why: The number 750 comes from dividing 6,000 by the unit cost of 8, but the right divisor is the 12 dollar margin per unit, so it overshoots.

options.t: 500 units
options.why: Each unit contributes 20 minus 8, or 12 dollars, toward fixed costs, so break even is 6,000 divided by 12, which equals 500 units.

options.t: 300 units
options.why: The number 300 comes from dividing 6,000 by the price of 20, ignoring that each unit costs 8 to make; the margin of 12 gives 500 units.

q: What is marginal cost?

options.t: The cost of producing one more unit
options.why: Marginal cost is the additional cost incurred to produce one more unit of output, which helps firms decide whether expanding production adds more cost than revenue.

options.t: The average cost of all the units
options.why: The average cost of all units is average total cost, found by dividing total cost by quantity, which differs from the cost of just one extra unit.

options.t: The cost of the first unit only
options.why: The cost of the first unit alone is not marginal cost in general, because marginal cost is measured for whichever additional unit is being considered at the time.

options.t: The total of all the fixed costs
options.why: Total fixed costs are expenses that do not change with output, whereas marginal cost concerns the extra cost of one more unit, which is usually a variable cost.

q: Which of these is a fixed cost?

options.t: The annual insurance premium on a factory
options.why: An annual insurance premium on a factory is charged at the same amount however many goods are produced, so it is a fixed cost for the business.

options.t: Raw materials used in making each product
options.why: Raw materials are consumed in each product, so the total spent grows with output, which makes them a variable cost and not a fixed cost.

options.t: Sales commissions paid to sellers on each sale
options.why: Sales commissions rise as more sales are made, so the total paid changes with output, which makes this a variable cost rather than a fixed one.

options.t: Packaging supplies used to wrap each unit sold
options.why: Packaging supplies are used up with each unit sold, so total spending grows with output, which means they are variable costs and not fixed costs.

q: When do economies of scale occur?

options.t: When the total cost rises faster than the level of output
options.why: When total cost rises faster than output, the cost per unit increases, which signals diseconomies of scale, the opposite of economies of scale.

options.t: When a business produces fewer and fewer units
options.why: Producing fewer units does not lower the average cost; economies of scale involve expanding output so that the cost per unit falls, not shrinking production.

options.t: When prices are set by the government for all goods
options.why: Government set prices are unrelated to scale economies, which arise inside a firm as it grows, spreading fixed costs and gaining efficiency, not from price controls.

options.t: When the average cost per unit falls as output rises
options.why: Economies of scale occur when increasing output spreads fixed costs over more units and improves efficiency, so the average cost per unit falls as production rises.

q: What does gross domestic product (GDP) measure?

options.t: The average price of a standard basket of goods and services bought by households
options.why: The average price of a basket of goods bought by households is measured by the Consumer Price Index, not GDP, which measures production.

options.t: The number of people who have jobs in the whole economy at any given time
options.why: The count of employed people relates to employment statistics, whereas GDP measures the value of output produced and not how many individuals have jobs.

options.t: The total value of final goods and services produced in a country in a period
options.why: GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period, usually a quarter or year.

options.t: The total spending of the government over a year on all of its programs
options.why: Government spending is only one component of GDP, so total government outlays cannot be what GDP measures, since GDP covers all final output in the economy.

q: How is the unemployment rate calculated?

options.t: All adults without jobs as a share of people
options.why: Counting all adults without jobs would include retirees, students and others not looking for work, which overstates unemployment, since the labor force is the proper base.

options.t: Job seekers as a percent of the labor force
options.why: The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed job seekers divided by the labor force, expressed as a percent, so it counts only people actively seeking work.

options.t: The number of job openings divided by applicants
options.why: Job openings divided by applicants is a measure of labor market tightness and not the unemployment rate, which is based on the labor force.

options.t: The number of people who quit last year
options.why: The number of people who quit last year is a measure of job turnover, and it does not give the share of the labor force that is unemployed.

q: What is inflation?

options.t: A general rise in prices over time
options.why: Inflation is a general, sustained rise in the level of prices across the economy, which reduces what each unit of money can buy over time.

options.t: An increase in unemployment levels
options.why: A rise in unemployment is a labor market change, not inflation, which is defined by rising prices rather than the number of people without jobs.

options.t: A fall in the price of one product
options.why: A fall in the price of a single product is a relative price change, not inflation, which refers to a broad rise in prices generally.

options.t: A rise in the value of the dollar
options.why: A rise in the dollar's value would make money worth more, which is nearly the opposite of what inflation does, since inflation erodes purchasing power.

q: What does the Consumer Price Index (CPI) measure?

options.t: The total value of the goods a country sells abroad
options.why: The total value of goods a country sells abroad is its exports, a trade figure, and not the CPI, which tracks consumer prices.

options.t: The change in prices of households' goods basket
options.why: The CPI tracks how the prices of a typical basket of goods and services bought by households change over time, making it a common inflation measure.

options.t: The interest rate that lenders charge on loans
options.why: The interest rate lenders charge is the cost of borrowing and is not what the CPI measures, since the CPI follows consumer prices.

options.t: The number of businesses operating in one area
options.why: The number of businesses in an area is a count of firms and has nothing to do with the CPI, which is a price index.

q: Which best describes a recession?

options.t: A one-day fall in the value of the stock market
options.why: A one day stock market fall is a short market move and does not meet the definition of a recession, which involves broad weakness lasting months.

options.t: A period of rapid price rises across the economy
options.why: Rapid price rises across the economy describe inflation, not a recession, which is defined by a decline in output and activity rather than in prices.

options.t: A rise in the amount that the government spends
options.why: A rise in government spending is a fiscal action, often used to fight a recession, and it does not define one.

options.t: A significant decline lasting several months
options.why: A recession is a significant decline in economic activity spread across the economy and lasting several months, usually seen in falling output, employment and income.

q: What are imports?

options.t: Goods produced and sold at home to local buyers
options.why: Goods produced and sold at home are domestic goods and do not cross a border, so they cannot be imports, which come from other countries.

options.t: Goods sold to other countries by local firms
options.why: Goods sold to other countries by local firms are exports, not imports, since imports flow into the country from foreign producers.

options.t: Goods and services bought from other countries
options.why: Imports are goods and services that a country buys from producers in other countries, bringing foreign made products to domestic buyers.

options.t: Taxes on foreign goods that enter the country
options.why: Taxes on foreign goods that enter the country are tariffs, and a tariff is a charge on imports, not the imported goods themselves.

q: According to comparative advantage, a country should specialize in producing goods it can make at:

options.t: A higher opportunity cost
options.why: Producing goods at a higher opportunity cost would mean giving up more of other output, which is the opposite of what comparative advantage recommends.

options.t: The same cost as the others
options.why: Making goods at the same cost as others gives no comparative advantage and no gains from trade, since specialization pays only when costs differ.

options.t: A lower opportunity cost
options.why: Comparative advantage means a country should specialize in goods whose opportunity cost is lower than other countries', because giving up less output creates gains from trade.

options.t: The highest possible price
options.why: The highest possible price is not the test; comparative advantage is about relative opportunity cost of production, not the price at which goods are sold.

q: A country has a trade deficit when:

options.t: Its exports exceed its imports
options.why: When exports exceed imports a country has a trade surplus, not a deficit, because it sells more abroad than it buys from other countries.

options.t: Its imports exceed its exports
options.why: A trade deficit means the value of imports is greater than the value of exports, so the country buys more from abroad than it sells.

options.t: It has no trade with others
options.why: A country with no trade has balanced trade at zero and neither a surplus nor a deficit, so the situation is not a trade deficit.

options.t: Its state spends more than it gets
options.why: A government spending more than it receives has a budget deficit, which is different from a trade deficit, since that one concerns imports and exports.

q: The U.S. dollar strengthens against the euro. What is the likely effect on U.S. exports to Europe?

options.t: They become cheaper for European buyers over time
options.why: A stronger dollar raises the price of U.S. goods in euros, so exports become more expensive for European buyers and not cheaper.

options.t: They are banned automatically by the government
options.why: Exchange rate moves are market outcomes and are not banned by governments, so exports are not automatically prohibited when the dollar strengthens against the euro.

options.t: They are unaffected by the change in the dollar
options.why: When the dollar strengthens, a European buyer needs more euros to buy the same dollar priced good, so export demand is affected and not unaffected.

options.t: They become more expensive for European buyers
options.why: A stronger dollar means each euro buys fewer dollars, so U.S. goods cost more in euros and European buyers tend to purchase fewer of them.

q: What does a free trade agreement do?

options.t: Reduces tariffs and other trade barriers among member countries
options.why: A free trade agreement lowers or removes tariffs and other barriers on trade among its members, which makes it cheaper and easier to buy and sell across borders.

options.t: Sets the prices of all goods sold among the member countries in the end
options.why: Prices are still set by markets and not by the agreement, which does not fix the prices of goods traded among the member countries.

options.t: Raises tariffs on all goods that members trade between them
options.why: Raising tariffs on all goods among members would reduce trade and defeat the purpose of the agreement, which is to cut such taxes.

options.t: Bans exports of goods between the member countries entirely
options.why: Banning exports between members would end trade among them, and this is the opposite of a free trade agreement, which opens markets to more trade.

q: What is opportunity cost?

options.t: The value of the next best alternative that is given up
options.why: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up when making a choice, such as the best other use of your time or money.

options.t: The profit a business earns after paying expenses
options.why: The profit left after paying expenses is net income, which is a measure of a firm's earnings and not the value of a forgone alternative.

options.t: The extra fee charged when ordering at a store or a shop
options.why: An extra fee for ordering is a service charge, which is a money cost, whereas opportunity cost concerns the best alternative you give up.

options.t: The total dollar price paid when buying something in a store
options.why: The dollar price paid is the monetary cost, which ignores the value of the alternative given up, and that forgone alternative is what opportunity cost measures.

q: Why does scarcity force people to make choices?

options.t: Money has no value in modern economies today
options.why: Money has value in modern economies and is widely used, so claiming it has none is false, and scarcity comes from limited resources, not from worthless money.

options.t: Businesses refuse to produce enough goods
options.why: Scarcity exists because resources are limited, not because businesses refuse to produce, and even willing producers cannot satisfy every want with finite inputs.

options.t: Resources are limited while wants are unlimited
options.why: Scarcity arises because resources are limited while human wants are unlimited, so people cannot have everything and must choose among alternatives, giving up some options.

options.t: Governments ban most products so no one can buy them
options.why: Governments do not ban most products, and scarcity would still exist without such bans because resources are limited relative to the wants of consumers.

q: Which of the following is a factor of production?

options.t: Demand, which is the desire to buy goods
options.why: Demand is the desire and ability to buy goods, which describes consumers in a market and is not an input used in production.

options.t: Profit, which is money left after all costs
options.why: Profit is the money remaining after costs, a reward or result of production, and it is not one of the resources used in making goods.

options.t: Inflation, which is a general rise in prices
options.why: Inflation is a general rise in prices, which is an economic condition and not a resource that businesses combine to produce goods and services.

options.t: Labor, which is the work done by people
options.why: Labor, the work done by people, is one of the four factors of production, alongside land, capital and entrepreneurship, because it is an input used to make goods.

q: What does the factor of production called 'capital' refer to?

options.t: The money a person keeps in a savings account
options.why: Money in a savings account is financial capital, but in economics the factor called capital means physical goods used in production rather than cash held by a person.

options.t: Tools, machinery and buildings used to make goods
options.why: Capital in the factors of production means human made tools, machinery and buildings that are used to produce other goods and services.

options.t: The natural resources found beneath the ground
options.why: Natural resources found in the ground belong to the factor called land, which includes everything provided by nature, and not capital.

options.t: The skills that an entrepreneur must have in a firm
options.why: Skills of an entrepreneur are part of entrepreneurship or human capital, a separate idea from capital in economics, which means physical goods.

q: What is an entrepreneur?

options.t: A person who works for a fixed wage and has no say
options.why: A person who works for a fixed wage and has no say is an employee, not an entrepreneur, who makes decisions and bears the risk.

options.t: A person who organizes resources and takes risk
options.why: An entrepreneur brings together land, labor and capital to start a business and accepts the risk of loss in the hope of profit.

options.t: A person who lends money to businesses and banks
options.why: A person who lends money to businesses and banks is a lender or investor, not an entrepreneur, who organizes and runs the venture.

options.t: A person who collects taxes for the government
options.why: Collecting taxes is the role of a government official or tax agency and has nothing to do with an entrepreneur, who starts and runs a business.

q: Which choice best illustrates a trade-off?

options.t: Buying a gift with money found on the sidewalk today as a rule
options.why: Buying a gift with money found on the sidewalk involves no real sacrifice, since the money came free, so it does not clearly show giving up one thing for another.

options.t: Inheriting a house from a relative in another city
options.why: Inheriting a house is receiving a windfall, not choosing between alternatives, so no option is given up, which means it does not illustrate a trade off.

options.t: Receiving a prize for winning a contest at school
options.why: Receiving a prize for winning a contest is a reward with no choice among alternatives, so it does not require giving up anything and is not a trade off.

options.t: Spending an evening studying instead of working a shift
options.why: Studying for the evening means giving up the wages from a shift, so one choice is gained at the expense of another, which is exactly a trade off.

q: A student can spend Saturday either earning $80 at a job or attending a free workshop. What is the opportunity cost of attending the workshop?

options.t: The $80 that could have been earned at the job
options.why: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up, which here is the $80 that the student could have earned working on Saturday.

options.t: The $0 admission price to attend the free workshop
options.why: The workshop is free, so the admission price is $0, but opportunity cost is about the forgone earnings, not the price of attending.

options.t: The cost of the workshop's materials and books
options.why: Materials and books are out of pocket costs and are not the best alternative forgone, and the problem states the workshop is free, so the opportunity cost is the $80.

options.t: The $160 that two Saturdays would have earned
options.why: The $160 figure doubles the amount for two Saturdays, but the student gives up only one Saturday of work, so the forgone earnings are $80.

q: What does the law of demand state?

options.t: As income rises, prices must always rise
options.why: Income rising and prices rising is not what the law of demand says, which concerns the relationship between a good's own price and the quantity people buy.

options.t: As price rises, quantity demanded rises too
options.why: Saying quantity demanded rises as price rises reverses the law, since higher prices lead buyers to purchase less, not more, other things equal.

options.t: As price rises, quantity demanded falls
options.why: The law of demand says that when the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls, and when the price falls, the quantity demanded rises.

options.t: As supply rises, demand must also rise
options.why: Supply rising does not force demand to rise, and the law of demand links price and quantity demanded, not the supply and demand curves themselves.

q: What does the law of supply state?

options.t: As price rises, quantity supplied falls
options.why: Quantity supplied falling as price rises would reverse the law of supply, since higher prices give producers an incentive to sell more.

options.t: As costs rise, producers always make more
options.why: Rising costs usually discourage production or push firms to produce less, so saying producers always make more as costs rise does not match the law of supply.

options.t: As price rises, quantity supplied rises
options.why: The law of supply states that as the price of a good rises, producers are willing to supply a larger quantity, because higher prices mean more profit.

options.t: As demand falls, prices always rise
options.why: The statement mixes demand with prices, and the law of supply links a good's own price to quantity supplied, not demand falling to higher prices.

q: At the equilibrium price, what is true about the market?

options.t: Producers earn zero revenue from their sales
options.why: At equilibrium producers do sell goods and earn revenue at the market price, so claiming they earn zero revenue is not what equilibrium means.

options.t: Quantity supplied equals quantity demanded
options.why: Equilibrium is the price at which the amount buyers want to purchase equals the amount sellers want to sell, so the market clears with neither surplus nor shortage.

options.t: Consumers stop buying altogether in the market
options.why: At equilibrium consumers keep buying at the market price, and the quantity they want equals the quantity supplied, so they do not stop buying altogether.

options.t: The government has set a fixed price for it
options.why: Equilibrium arises from the interaction of buyers and sellers in a free market, not from a government fixed price, which would be a price control.

q: If the price of a product is above equilibrium, what results?

options.t: A surplus, because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
options.why: A price above equilibrium reduces the quantity people want while encouraging more production, so quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, which creates a surplus of unsold goods.

options.t: No change, because prices never affect markets in any way
options.why: Prices affect markets strongly, since they guide how much buyers want and sellers offer, so saying prices never affect markets is not accurate.

options.t: A shortage, because buyers want more than is available at that price
options.why: A shortage occurs when the price is below equilibrium and buyers want more than is available, so a price above equilibrium cannot cause it.
