options.t: A permanent monopoly for one seller of the product in the market
options.why: One seller holding a permanent monopoly is not caused by a price above equilibrium, which simply produces a surplus until the price adjusts back down.

q: If the price of a product is below equilibrium, what results?

options.t: A decrease in the number of buyers
options.why: A price below equilibrium makes the good cheaper, which attracts more buyers, not fewer, so the number of buyers does not decrease.

options.t: A surplus, because sellers have goods
options.why: A surplus occurs when the price is above equilibrium and sellers have more than buyers want, so it does not result from a price below equilibrium.

options.t: A tax refund for all of the buyers
options.why: A tax refund has nothing to do with market prices, since a price below equilibrium changes the balance of supply and demand and not taxes.

options.t: A shortage, as demand exceeds supply
options.why: When the price is below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so buyers cannot all get the product, which creates a shortage.

q: Which event would shift the demand curve for gasoline to the left?

options.t: A fall in the cost of crude oil and of gas
options.why: A fall in the cost of crude oil lowers production costs and shifts the supply curve, not demand, so it does not move the demand curve left.

options.t: A sharp rise in the popularity of electric cars
options.why: Rising popularity of electric cars reduces the desire for gasoline at every price, so the demand curve for gasoline shifts to the left.

options.t: A new refinery opening near a large city center
options.why: A new refinery increases the supply of gasoline and so shifts the supply curve, not the demand curve, so demand does not move left.

options.t: A cold winter that raises heating needs in homes
options.why: A cold winter raising heating needs would raise demand for heating fuels, shifting demand to the right if anything, and it does not reduce gasoline demand.

q: Which event would shift the supply curve for bread to the left?

options.t: A rise in consumer income levels
options.why: Higher consumer income raises demand for bread, which shifts the demand curve and not the supply curve, so it does not move supply to the left.

options.t: A new fad diet that favors bread
options.why: A fad diet favoring bread raises consumer demand, shifting the demand curve to the right, and it does not shift the supply curve left.

options.t: A drop in the price of bakery ovens
options.why: Cheaper ovens lower production costs for bakers, which increases supply and shifts the supply curve to the right, not to the left.

options.t: A rise in the price of wheat flour
options.why: Wheat flour is a key input, so a higher price raises the cost of making bread, which reduces supply and shifts the supply curve to the left.

q: What is a substitute good?

options.t: A product that can replace another when its price changes
options.why: A substitute good can replace another, so when one good's price rises, buyers switch to the other, which is the definition of a substitute.

options.t: A product used together with another and bought alongside it
options.why: A product used together with another and bought alongside it is a complement, not a substitute, because complements are consumed jointly rather than in place of each other.

options.t: A product that is only sold by one company in the market
options.why: A product sold by only one company describes a monopoly situation and says nothing about whether another good can replace it, so it is not a substitute.

options.t: A product that has no price at all attached to it in stores
options.why: Goods in stores have prices, so a product with no price attached is not a defined category and certainly not what a substitute good means.

q: What is a complementary good?

options.t: A product that can replace another in a shopper's cart
options.why: A product that can replace another is a substitute, not a complement, since complements are used together, as with printers and ink, not in place of each other.

options.t: A product that is sold only abroad and not at home
options.why: Where a product is sold does not define a complementary good, which is defined by being used together with another product, not by domestic or foreign sales.

options.t: A product that is used together with another product
options.why: Complementary goods are used together, so demand for one rises and falls with the other, as with cars and gasoline or hot dogs and buns.

options.t: A product that is given away for free to every buyer
options.why: A product given away for free is not what complementary means, since complements are paired goods that people use together, whatever their prices may be.

q: The price of hot dogs rises sharply. What is the likely effect on the demand for hot dog buns?

options.t: Demand for buns rises, because the goods are substitutes
options.why: Hot dogs and buns are used together, so they are complements, not substitutes, and a price rise for hot dogs will lower, not raise, demand for buns.

options.t: Supply of buns rises immediately after the change in price
options.why: A change in the price of hot dogs shifts the demand for buns and not supply, so saying supply of buns rises misreads the situation.

options.t: Demand for buns is unchanged, because the goods are unrelated
options.why: Hot dogs and buns are closely related goods consumed together, so the demand for buns is affected by the hot dog price and is not unchanged.

options.t: Demand for buns falls, because the two goods are complements
options.why: As hot dogs get costlier, people buy fewer of them and so need fewer buns, which means the demand for buns falls because the two are complements.

q: What is elasticity of demand?

options.t: How much a product costs to make in the factory each year
options.why: The cost of making a product is a production cost, whereas elasticity of demand concerns how buyers react to price changes, not what factories spend.

options.t: How strongly quantity demanded responds to a price change
options.why: Elasticity of demand measures how strongly the quantity demanded responds to a change in price, so a very responsive good has elastic demand and an unresponsive one is inelastic.

options.t: How quickly a business can hire new workers when sales grow
options.why: How quickly a business can hire workers relates to labor market conditions and has nothing to do with how buyers respond to a price change.

options.t: How long a product lasts before it breaks down or wears out
options.why: How long a product lasts is its durability, an unrelated product trait, whereas elasticity of demand describes how the quantity bought responds to price.

q: Which good is likely to have inelastic demand?

options.t: Insulin for a person with diabetes
options.why: Insulin is a medical necessity with no close substitute, so a patient keeps buying it even if the price rises, which makes demand inelastic.

options.t: A particular brand of potato chips
options.why: Many other chip brands exist, so shoppers can switch if one brand gets pricier, making demand for a particular brand elastic and not inelastic.

options.t: A luxury vacation package abroad
options.why: A luxury vacation is not essential and can be postponed or replaced, so buyers cut back when prices rise, which makes demand elastic.

options.t: A restaurant meal on a weeknight
options.why: A restaurant meal on a weeknight can be replaced by cooking at home, so diners respond readily to price changes, which means demand is elastic.

q: If demand for a product is elastic and its price rises, what happens to total revenue?

options.t: Total revenue stays exactly the same after the price increase
options.why: With elastic demand, a price rise changes quantity sold by a large amount, so revenue cannot stay exactly the same after the price increase.

options.t: Total revenue doubles automatically when the price goes up
options.why: Revenue does not automatically double, because a higher price also reduces quantity sold, and with elastic demand the lost sales outweigh the extra revenue per unit.

options.t: Total revenue falls, because quantity drops by a larger percentage
options.why: When demand is elastic, the percentage drop in quantity demanded exceeds the percentage rise in price, so total revenue, price times quantity, falls.

options.t: Total revenue rises, as the price increase outweighs the drop in sales
options.why: This describes inelastic demand, where the price gain outweighs the loss in sales; with elastic demand the quantity drop is larger, so revenue falls instead.

q: What is the term for the extra satisfaction from consuming one more unit of a good?

options.t: Fixed overhead
options.why: Fixed overhead is a cost that does not change with output, so it describes a business expense and not the extra satisfaction a consumer gets from another unit.

options.t: Opportunity cost
options.why: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up, not the added satisfaction from consuming one more unit of a good.

options.t: Total revenue
options.why: Total revenue is price times quantity sold, a business measure, and it does not describe a consumer's added satisfaction from consuming a further unit.

options.t: Marginal utility
options.why: Marginal utility is the additional satisfaction a consumer gets from consuming one more unit of a good, and it usually declines as more is consumed.

q: The law of diminishing marginal utility says that:

options.t: Each additional unit consumed gives less added satisfaction
options.why: The law of diminishing marginal utility states that each additional unit consumed gives less added satisfaction than the one before it, as when a third slice of pizza satisfies less.

options.t: Prices always fall as consumption rises, whatever the good
options.why: Prices do not automatically fall with consumption, and the law concerns satisfaction, not price, so this statement does not describe diminishing marginal utility.

options.t: Each additional unit consumed gives more added satisfaction
options.why: More added satisfaction from each further unit would be increasing marginal utility, the opposite of the law, which says added satisfaction declines as consumption grows.

options.t: Total satisfaction always falls with each additional unit
options.why: Total satisfaction usually keeps rising, only more slowly, while the added satisfaction falls, so saying total satisfaction always falls misreads the law of diminishing marginal utility.

q: Which is a final good for GDP purposes?

options.t: Sugar bought by a factory to make cookies
options.why: Sugar bought by a factory is used to make cookies, so it is an intermediate good, and counting it would double count its value in GDP.

options.t: Yeast bought by a bakery to make the dough
options.why: Yeast bought by a bakery for dough is an input in further production, which makes it an intermediate good that GDP excludes to avoid double counting.

options.t: A loaf of bread bought by a family for dinner
options.why: A loaf of bread bought by a family for dinner is sold to its final user, so it counts as a final good in GDP.

options.t: Flour bought by a bakery to make bread for sale
options.why: Flour bought by a bakery to make bread is an intermediate good, because its value is included later in the price of the finished bread, so GDP leaves it out.

q: Why are intermediate goods left out of GDP?

options.t: They have no economic value in the market at all
options.why: Intermediate goods do have economic value and are sold in markets, so saying they have none is false, and the reason for excluding them is double counting.

options.t: Counting them would count the same value more than once
options.why: Their value is already included in the price of the final good, so adding them separately would count the same value more than once.

options.t: Intermediate goods are always illegal to sell in the market
options.why: Intermediate goods are legal products that firms buy and sell every day, so claiming they are illegal to sell is false and is not why GDP excludes them.

options.t: They are produced abroad and never counted in the total
options.why: Intermediate goods are often produced at home, and where they are made is not the reason for exclusion; the reason is avoiding double counting.

q: What are the four components of GDP in the expenditure approach?

options.t: Wages, rent, interest and profit paid to owners
options.why: Wages, rent, interest and profit are income categories used in the income approach to GDP, not the four spending components of the expenditure approach.

options.t: Supply, demand, price and quantity in a market
options.why: Supply, demand, price and quantity are market concepts used to analyze individual markets, and they are not the components of GDP in the expenditure approach.

options.t: Land, labor, capital and enterprise in a free market
options.why: Land, labor, capital and enterprise are the factors of production, which are inputs to output, and not the spending categories that make up GDP.

options.t: Consumption, investment, government and net exports
options.why: The expenditure approach adds consumption, investment, government spending and net exports, giving GDP as the total of spending on final goods and services, often written C plus I plus G plus NX.

q: Consumption is $700, investment $150, government spending $200, exports $90 and imports $110. What is GDP?

options.why: The figure $1,090 does not follow the formula; GDP is C plus I plus G plus net exports, and net exports of 90 minus 110 equal negative 20.
GDP equals 700 plus 150 plus 200 plus net exports of 90 minus 110, which is negative 20, so 1,050 minus 20 gives $1,030.
The figure $1,250 comes from adding both exports and imports to the other components, but imports must be subtracted, so net exports are negative 20 and GDP is $1,030.
The figure $1,050 sums only consumption, investment and government spending, 700 plus 150 plus 200, and leaves out net exports of negative 20, so the correct GDP is $1,030.

q: What is the difference between nominal GDP and real GDP?

options.t: Real GDP is adjusted for inflation; nominal GDP is not
options.why: Real GDP is adjusted for inflation, so it shows output at constant prices, while nominal GDP uses current prices and can rise just because prices went up.

options.t: Nominal GDP leaves out state spending; real GDP includes it
options.why: Both nominal and real GDP include government spending, so the difference between them is about adjusting for price changes, not about leaving out state spending.

options.t: There is no difference between the two kinds of measure
options.why: There is a difference, since nominal GDP uses current prices while real GDP is adjusted for inflation, so the two can move differently when prices change.

options.t: Real GDP counts only exports; nominal GDP counts imports
options.why: Both measures count all components, including exports and imports, so real GDP does not count only exports; the distinction is the inflation adjustment.

q: Which statement describes a recession?

options.t: A short rise in stock prices over one week
options.why: A short rise in stock prices over one week is a market gain, not a recession, which is a significant decline in the economy lasting several months.

options.t: A time when the government collects extra taxes
options.why: A government collecting extra taxes is a fiscal matter and does not define a recession, which is marked by falling output, income and employment.

options.t: A significant decline lasting several months
options.why: A recession is a significant decline in economic activity spread across the economy that lasts several months, shown in falling output, jobs and incomes.

options.t: A period in which prices fall for one product
options.why: A price fall for one product is a relative price change in a single market, whereas a recession is a broad decline in economic activity.

q: What is a business cycle?

options.t: The path of money from a bank to a borrower each year
options.why: The path of money from a bank to a borrower describes lending, and it has nothing to do with the economy's pattern of expansion and decline.

options.t: The repeating pattern of expansion and contraction
options.why: The business cycle is the repeating pattern of expansion and contraction in economic activity, moving through peaks, recessions, troughs and recoveries over the years.

options.t: The steps a firm follows to make one product
options.why: The steps a firm follows to make one product describe a production process inside one company, not the economy wide fluctuations known as the business cycle.

options.t: The yearly calendar of a company's sales events
options.why: A company's yearly sales calendar is a marketing schedule and not the economy wide pattern of rising and falling activity that defines the business cycle.

q: During the expansion phase of the business cycle, what generally happens?

options.t: Output, employment and income grow
options.why: During expansion the economy grows, so output, employment and income all rise, which is the typical sign of the expansion phase of the business cycle.

options.t: The economy stops producing most goods
options.why: An economy in expansion keeps producing goods and in fact produces more, so saying it stops producing most goods describes a severe collapse, not expansion.

options.t: Output, employment and income all fall
options.why: Output, employment and income all falling describes a contraction or recession, which is the opposite of what happens during an expansion.

options.t: Prices become fixed by law for goods
options.why: Prices are not fixed by law during an expansion, because markets still set prices, so this has no link to the expansion phase.

q: What is the lowest point of a business cycle called?

options.t: The peak
options.why: The peak is the highest point of the cycle, where expansion ends and contraction begins, so it is the top, not the lowest point.

options.t: The recovery
options.why: Recovery is the phase after the lowest point, when output starts to rise again, so it follows the bottom rather than being the lowest point.

options.t: The trough
options.why: The trough is the lowest point of the business cycle, where output bottoms out after a contraction before the recovery begins.

options.t: The expansion
options.why: Expansion is the phase in which output grows, so it is a rising period and not the lowest point of the cycle.

q: What is productivity?

options.t: The total number of workers hired
options.why: The total number of workers hired is a measure of employment, not productivity, which compares how much output is produced with the inputs used.

options.t: The price at which goods are sold
options.why: The price at which goods are sold is a market price and is not productivity, which measures output in relation to the inputs used.

options.t: The wages paid to each worker
options.why: Wages paid to each worker are labor income, and they do not measure how much output each unit of input generates, which is productivity.

options.t: Output produced per unit of input
options.why: Productivity is the amount of output produced per unit of input, such as goods made per hour of labor, so higher productivity means more output from the same resources.

q: Which change would most directly increase labor productivity?

options.t: Making workers stay longer with no extra tools
options.why: Longer hours with no extra tools may add some output but not per hour, and tired workers may even produce less, so productivity is not directly raised.

options.t: Reducing the number of machines in the factory
options.why: Reducing the number of machines gives each worker less capital to use, which lowers output per worker, so it would reduce labor productivity.

options.t: Cutting worker training budgets and pay
options.why: Cutting training budgets and pay weakens skills and morale, which tends to lower output per worker, so it would not raise labor productivity.

options.t: Giving workers better equipment and training
options.why: Better equipment and training let each worker produce more in the same time, so output per hour rises and labor productivity increases directly.

q: What is specialization?

options.t: Hiring workers who have no skills for the job at hand
options.why: Hiring workers who have no skills for the job would lower efficiency and does not describe specialization, which means concentrating on what one does best.

options.t: Focusing on producing a limited range of goods or tasks
options.why: Specialization means focusing on a limited range of goods or tasks, so people and firms become more efficient at them, which raises output and gains from trade.

options.t: Making every product in one workshop so one team does the work
options.why: Making every product in a single workshop is the opposite of specialization, because it spreads effort across many products instead of concentrating on a few.

options.t: Buying goods only from foreign suppliers in other lands
options.why: Buying goods only from foreign suppliers is an import choice and not specialization, which concerns narrowing what one produces and not where goods are purchased.

q: What is division of labor?

options.t: Splitting production into tasks for different workers
options.why: Division of labor splits production into separate tasks assigned to different workers, so each becomes skilled at one step and total output rises.

options.t: Dividing the profits among all shareholders at year end
options.why: Dividing profits among shareholders is a dividend distribution and not division of labor, which concerns splitting up the tasks of production among workers.

options.t: Giving all workers identical jobs in a single firm
options.why: Giving all workers identical jobs is the opposite of division of labor, which assigns different tasks to different workers.

options.t: Splitting a large company into two firms in one year
options.why: Splitting a large company into two firms is a corporate restructuring and does not describe division of labor, which divides work tasks among workers inside production.

q: What is the main purpose of money as a medium of exchange?

options.t: To make goods hard to trade at all
options.why: Money makes trade easier, not harder, so claiming its purpose is to make goods hard to trade reverses its role as a medium of exchange.

options.t: To replace all work with leisure
options.why: Money does not replace work with leisure, and people still work to earn it, so this misstates the purpose of money as a medium of exchange.

options.t: To make trade easier than bartering
options.why: As a medium of exchange, money is accepted for goods and services, which avoids the need for a double coincidence of wants required in bartering, so trade is easier.

options.t: To ensure prices never change at all
options.why: Money cannot guarantee that prices never change, since prices move with supply and demand, and this is not what a medium of exchange does.

q: Which function of money lets people save purchasing power for later?

options.t: Medium of exchange
options.why: A medium of exchange is what people use to buy and sell goods, which is a different function from holding purchasing power to use later.

options.t: Store of value
options.why: Store of value is the function that lets people keep purchasing power, saving money today so it can be spent later on goods and services.

options.t: Deferred payment
options.why: Deferred payment lets people buy now and pay later, as with loans and credit, which is different from saving purchasing power for future use.

options.t: Unit of account
options.why: A unit of account is a common measure for stating prices and values, which is a different job from keeping purchasing power over time.

q: If prices rise by 5% in a year while a worker's pay rises by 2%, what happens to the worker's purchasing power?

options.t: It doubles, because both figures are positive
options.why: Purchasing power does not double just because both numbers are positive, and prices rising faster than pay means the worker can buy less.

options.t: It rises, because pay increased in the year
options.why: Pay rose by 2%, but prices rose 5%, a larger amount, so the worker's money buys less and purchasing power falls despite the raise.

options.t: It falls, because prices grew faster than pay
options.why: Prices rose by 5% while pay rose only 2%, so the worker can afford less than before, and real purchasing power falls by roughly 3%.

options.t: It stays the same, as both prices and wages rose
options.why: Both rose, but not by the same amount; the 5% price rise exceeds the 2% pay rise, so purchasing power does not stay the same.

q: What is deflation?

options.t: A general decline in the level of prices over time
options.why: Deflation is a general, sustained decline in the level of prices over time, so each unit of money buys more goods and services than before.

options.t: A fall in the supply of money to almost zero
options.why: A fall in the money supply to nearly zero is a monetary contraction and not the definition of deflation, which concerns falling prices in general.

options.t: A general rise in the level of prices over time
options.why: A general rise in the price level is inflation, not deflation, which is the reverse and refers to prices falling over time.

options.t: A rise in the number of unemployed workers over a year
options.why: A rise in unemployed workers is a labor market change, not a definition of deflation, which describes a general decline in prices.

q: What is unemployment?

options.t: The condition of people who choose to stay home and not look for work for a year
options.why: People who choose to stay home and not look for work are not counted as unemployed, since unemployment requires actively seeking a job.

options.t: The condition of people who work part-time by choice and are happy with the hours
options.why: People who work part-time by choice and are happy with the hours are employed and content, so they are not unemployed under the standard definition.

options.t: The condition of people who are retired and no longer wish to work for pay
options.why: Retired people who no longer wish to work are outside the labor force, so they are not counted as unemployed.

options.t: The condition of people who are able and willing to work but cannot find jobs
options.why: Unemployment describes people who are able and willing to work and are looking for jobs but cannot find them, so they count as part of the labor force.

q: A factory closes because consumers switched to a new technology and its workers must find jobs in other industries. What type of unemployment is this?

options.t: Frictional unemployment
options.why: Frictional unemployment is the short time spent between jobs or while searching, and it does not describe workers displaced when an industry shrinks because of new technology.

options.t: Cyclical unemployment
options.why: Cyclical unemployment comes from downturns in the business cycle, but this factory closed because consumers moved to a new technology, not because of a recession.

options.t: Structural unemployment
options.why: Structural unemployment arises when workers' skills no longer match available jobs because of technology or industry change, so these workers must move to other industries.

options.t: Seasonal unemployment
options.why: Seasonal unemployment follows regular yearly patterns such as holiday or summer work, but this closure came from a lasting technology shift and not from the calendar.

q: A ski instructor is out of work every summer. What type of unemployment is this?

options.t: Structural unemployment
options.why: Structural unemployment comes from lasting industry or technology changes, but a ski instructor's work disappears every summer on a predictable seasonal basis, not permanently.

options.t: Cyclical unemployment
options.why: Cyclical unemployment follows the downs of the business cycle, but this instructor loses work every summer regardless of how the overall economy is doing.

options.t: Frictional unemployment
options.why: Frictional unemployment is the short search time between jobs, but the instructor is out of work for the whole summer because skiing is seasonal.

options.t: Seasonal unemployment
options.why: Seasonal unemployment occurs when work depends on the time of year, and ski instruction is available only in winter, so the instructor is jobless each summer.

q: What is an economic system?

options.t: How a society decides what and for whom to make
options.why: An economic system is the way a society decides what to produce, how to produce it and for whom, so it answers the basic questions of scarcity.

options.t: The set of machines used in a large factory
options.why: The set of machines in a factory is part of its capital and not an economic system, which is how a whole society organizes its production.

options.t: The rules of a single company's board of directors
options.why: The rules of one company's board govern a single firm, while an economic system is the way an entire society organizes production and distribution.

options.t: The list of taxes that a country charges its citizens
options.why: A list of taxes is only one part of government policy and not an economic system, which decides what and for whom to produce.

q: Which three basic questions does every economic system answer?

options.t: When to tax, whom to fine and where to build
options.why: Deciding when to tax, whom to fine and where to build are government choices, not the three basic questions that every economic system must answer.

options.t: What to produce, how to produce it and for whom
options.why: Every economic system must decide what to produce, how to produce it and for whom, because resources are scarce and wants are not.

options.t: Which bank to use, how to save and when to retire
options.why: Which bank to use, how to save and when to retire are personal finance choices and not the basic questions that all economic systems answer.

options.t: Who to hire, where to advertise and what to charge
options.why: Who to hire, where to advertise and what to charge are business decisions within one firm and are not the three basic questions every economic system answers.

q: In a market economy, who mainly decides what gets produced?

options.t: Consumers and producers acting through prices
options.why: In a market economy, consumers and producers acting through prices decide what is made, because their buying and selling choices signal what is wanted and profitable.

options.t: A foreign trade agency in another country
options.why: A foreign trade agency in another country does not direct what a domestic market economy produces, since decisions come from local consumers and producers.

options.t: A central government office that sets all outputs
options.why: A central government office setting all outputs describes a command economy, not a market economy, where decisions are spread among buyers and sellers.

options.t: A royal family or tribal leader in each region
options.why: A royal family or tribal leader deciding for a region describes a traditional economy ruled by custom, and not a market economy driven by prices.

q: In a command economy, who makes most economic decisions?

options.t: Local families by custom
options.why: Local families following custom describes a traditional economy, whereas in a command economy the central authority, not families or custom, makes most decisions.

options.t: Individual consumers
options.why: Individual consumers guiding production through their purchases is a feature of a market economy and not a command economy, where planners decide.

options.t: The central government
options.why: In a command economy, the central government decides what to produce, how much and for whom, so it makes most economic decisions.

options.t: Competing private firms
options.why: Competing private firms making decisions is a mark of a market economy, while in a command economy the state controls most production.

q: What is a traditional economy?

options.t: An economy in which only exports are allowed by the state's law
options.why: Allowing only exports is a trade restriction and not a type of economy, so it does not describe a traditional economy based on custom.

options.t: An economy in which computers make all of the decisions for firms
options.why: Computers making all the decisions for firms is not a recognized economic system and does not describe a traditional economy, which relies on custom and habit.

options.t: An economy in which a central office sets every price and all output
options.why: A central office setting every price and all output describes a command economy, which is the opposite of a traditional economy guided by custom.

options.t: An economy in which customs and habits guide production and trade
options.why: In a traditional economy, customs and habits handed down over generations guide what is produced and traded, so decisions follow established practice.

q: What is a mixed economy?

options.t: An economy based only on bartering goods and services
options.why: An economy based only on bartering is a barter system, and it does not describe a mixed economy, which blends private choice with government involvement.

options.t: Private choice combined with government involvement
options.why: A mixed economy combines private economic choice with some government involvement, such as regulation and public services, and the United States is a common example.

options.t: An economy with no government role at all in any market
options.why: An economy with no government role at all would be a pure market economy, which is the opposite of a mixed economy.

options.t: An economy with no private firms at all in any sector
options.why: An economy with no private firms would be a pure command economy, which differs from a mixed economy that includes both private and public roles.

q: The United States is best described as which type of economic system?

options.t: A pure command economy run by the state
options.why: The United States is not a pure command economy, because private firms and consumers make most decisions, and the state does not run the economy.

options.t: A traditional economy based on custom
options.why: The modern United States relies on markets, technology and laws more than custom, so describing it as a traditional economy is wrong.

options.t: A barter economy with no money at all
options.why: The United States uses money and markets widely, so calling it a barter economy with no money at all is plainly wrong.

options.t: A mixed, mostly market-based economy
options.why: The United States is mostly market based but the government also regulates and provides services, so it is a mixed economy that leans toward the market.

q: What is capitalism?

options.t: A system in which people trade only by custom
options.why: Trading only by custom describes a traditional economy, whereas capitalism is based on private ownership and markets, with profit as a motive.

options.t: A system in which prices are set by law only
options.why: Prices set only by law would describe a controlled or command system, while in capitalism prices are mostly set by supply and demand.

options.t: Private owners control the means of production
options.why: Capitalism is a system in which private owners control the means of production, such as factories and land, and operate them to earn profit.

options.t: A system in which the government owns all property
options.why: Government ownership of all property describes communism or a pure command system, which is the opposite of capitalism, where private owners hold property.

q: What is socialism?

options.t: A system in which no taxes are collected
options.why: Socialism does not mean that no taxes are collected, and in fact such systems usually rely on taxes to fund public ownership and services.

options.t: The state or community owns major industries
options.why: In socialism the state or community owns major industries and resources and directs them for shared benefit, instead of leaving them to private owners.

options.t: A system in which individuals own all businesses
options.why: Individuals owning all businesses describes capitalism or private enterprise, which is the opposite of socialism, where major industries are collectively owned.

options.t: A system in which trade is banned by law
options.why: Socialism does not ban trade, because socialist countries still trade, and the defining feature is public or collective ownership of major industries.

q: What is the role of profit in a market economy?

options.t: It rewards risk and signals where resources are wanted
options.why: Profit rewards entrepreneurs for taking risk and signals where resources are wanted, since high profits attract producers to the goods that consumers value.

options.t: It guarantees that every business will succeed in the market
options.why: Profit does not guarantee success, because many firms lose money and fail, so it is a reward and signal and not a promise.

options.t: It is set by the government for each firm in the nation
options.why: In a market economy profit is earned by firms in the market, not set by the government for each business, so this statement is false.

options.t: It is banned by law for all firms in every state
options.why: Profit is not banned in a market economy, because it is the main motive and reward for businesses, so this option is false.

q: What is private property in a market economy?

options.t: The duty to share all goods equally with everyone around
options.why: Sharing all goods equally describes communal ownership, whereas private property is the right of individuals and firms to own and use resources for themselves.

options.t: The rule that no one may sell what they own to others
options.why: Private property includes the right to sell what you own, so a rule that no one may sell their property contradicts the idea.

options.t: The right of the government to seize any asset without paying
options.why: Private property rights protect owners from arbitrary seizure, so the government's right to take assets without paying is the opposite of the idea.

options.t: The right of individuals and firms to own and use resources
options.why: Private property means individuals and firms have the right to own, use and sell resources, which gives them an incentive to use those resources productively.

q: Which feature is typical of a market economy?

options.t: Jobs assigned by birth and tradition
options.why: Jobs assigned by birth and tradition are typical of a traditional economy and not a market economy, where people choose their work.

options.t: Competition among sellers for customers
options.why: Competition among sellers for customers is typical of a market economy, as firms try to offer better prices and quality to win buyers.

options.t: A single planner setting every price
options.why: A single planner setting every price describes a command economy, whereas in a market economy prices come from the interaction of buyers and sellers.

options.t: A ban on private businesses of any kind
options.why: A market economy allows and relies on private businesses, so a ban on them describes a command economy and is not a feature of a market.

q: What is consumer sovereignty?

options.t: Producers decide what consumers may buy from the shop
options.why: If producers decided what consumers may buy, consumers would lack power, which is the opposite of consumer sovereignty, where buyers direct production.

options.t: The government decides what consumers must buy in each market
options.why: Government deciding what consumers must buy describes central control, not consumer sovereignty, in which consumers' own choices guide the market.

options.t: Consumers' buying choices determine what producers make
options.why: Consumer sovereignty means consumers' buying choices determine what producers make, since firms must supply what people want to buy in order to earn profit.

options.t: Consumers must buy only domestic goods made at home
options.why: Consumer sovereignty lets consumers buy domestic or foreign goods, so a requirement to buy only domestic goods contradicts the idea of consumer choice.

q: What is the 'invisible hand' idea associated with Adam Smith?

options.t: Self-interested choices in markets can help society
options.why: Smith's invisible hand says that when people pursue their own self interest in markets, society can benefit, as if guided by an unseen force to good outcomes.

options.t: A secret government agency sets all prices in the nation
options.why: The invisible hand is a metaphor for market forces and not a secret agency, and Smith argued against central control of prices.

options.t: A rule that businesses must give away profits each year
options.why: The invisible hand does not require giving away profits, because it relies on people pursuing their own gain, and it is not a rule about profits.

options.t: A hidden tax that businesses pay each year to the state
options.why: The invisible hand is not a hidden tax; it is a metaphor for how self interested choices in markets can serve the wider society.

q: What is a free enterprise system?

options.t: A system in which no one may earn a profit at all
options.why: Free enterprise permits profit, since the possibility of earning profit is a key motive, so a system banning all profit is not free enterprise.

options.t: A system in which the state runs all firms and shops
options.why: A system where the state runs all firms and shops is a command economy, the opposite of free enterprise, where private businesses operate freely.

options.t: Businesses operate with limited government control
options.why: In a free enterprise system, private businesses operate with limited government control, free to choose what to make, how to make it and what to charge.

options.t: A system in which every product is free to consumers
options.why: Free enterprise refers to freedom to run a business, not to products being given away, so a system where every product is free is not what it means.

q: Which situation shows a command economy in action?

options.t: A bakery lowers prices to attract customers away from rivals overall
options.why: A bakery cutting prices to compete is a market decision made by a private firm, which is not an example of central planning in a command economy.

options.t: A central agency decides how many cars each factory must build
options.why: A central agency deciding how many cars each factory must build shows the government planning production, which is the hallmark of a command economy.

options.t: A student chooses between two job offers after graduating
options.why: A student choosing between two job offers is an individual choice made freely, which reflects market freedom and not central direction in a command economy.

options.t: A family farm follows ancestral methods season after season
options.why: A family farm following ancestral methods shows a traditional economy guided by custom, not a command economy where a central authority makes the decisions.

q: A common weakness of command economies is that:

options.t: Planners lack price signals showing wants
options.why: Without market prices, planners cannot easily tell what people want or what goods cost to make, so the command economy risks shortages and surpluses, a known weakness.

options.t: Too many firms compete for customers
options.why: Many firms competing for customers is a feature of market economies, and it is not a weakness of command economies where the state controls production.

options.t: Prices rise and fall too quickly to follow
options.why: Prices in a command economy are set by planners and do not move quickly, so rapid price changes are not its weakness.

options.t: Consumers choose too many varieties to buy
options.why: Consumers choosing among many varieties is a feature of market economies, whereas command economies often have limited choices, so this is not their weakness.

q: A common weakness of pure market economies is that:

options.t: The government owns all property in the land
options.why: Government ownership of all property describes a command economy, so it cannot be a weakness of a pure market economy, where property is privately held.

options.t: A central plan decides everything for every consumer
options.why: A central plan deciding everything for every consumer describes a command economy and not a pure market economy, which relies on individual choices.

options.t: Customs prevent change in the way goods are made
options.why: Customs preventing change is a feature of traditional economies, while market economies change quickly with competition, so this is not their weakness.

options.t: Public goods and equal access may be underprovided
options.why: Because private firms seek profit, pure markets may underprovide public goods and leave some people without access, which is a recognized weakness of market economies.

q: What is a public good?

options.t: A good that is used up by a single person at a time
options.why: A good used up by a single person at a time is a private good, whereas a public good is available to all and is not used up.

options.t: A good open to all; one's use leaves enough for others
options.why: A public good is open to everyone, and one person's use leaves enough for others, like a lighthouse or national defense, so it is nonrival and nonexcludable.

options.t: A good that only wealthy people can buy in shops
options.why: A good only wealthy people can buy is a private or luxury good, and a public good is available to everyone regardless of wealth.

options.t: A good that is sold at a store for a profit to shoppers
options.why: A good sold in stores for profit is a private good, and public goods are usually provided by government because sellers cannot easily charge users.

q: What is an externality?

options.t: A cost or benefit reaching uninvolved people
options.why: An externality is a cost or benefit that reaches people who were not involved in the transaction, such as pollution from a factory affecting neighbors.

options.t: A tax collected on imported goods at the border
options.why: A tax collected on imported goods is a tariff, not an externality, which is a side effect of an activity on uninvolved third parties.

options.t: A fee charged by a bank for services it provides
options.why: A fee charged by a bank is a direct cost paid by the customer in the transaction, and not an externality, which affects uninvolved parties.

options.t: A profit earned by a business owner each year
options.why: A profit earned by a business owner is a gain for a party in the transaction, not an externality, which falls on people uninvolved in it.

q: A factory pollutes a river and nearby residents bear the cleanup costs. This is an example of:

options.t: A public good only
options.why: Pollution harms residents rather than giving shared benefits, so it is not a public good, which is open to all and benefits everyone.

options.t: A positive externality
options.why: A positive externality gives uninvolved people a benefit, but here residents bear cleanup costs, so the spillover is harmful and is a negative externality.

options.t: A negative externality
options.why: The factory's pollution imposes cleanup costs on residents who are not part of its business, which is a cost reaching uninvolved people and so a negative externality.

options.t: Economic equilibrium
options.why: Equilibrium is where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded and it does not describe a cost imposed on uninvolved residents by a polluting factory.

q: A homeowner plants a beautiful garden that neighbors enjoy for free. This is an example of:

options.t: A monopoly position
options.why: A monopoly means one seller controls a market, and a homeowner's garden is not a business, so it does not describe this situation.

options.t: A trade deficit gap
options.why: A trade deficit means imports exceed exports between countries, and a homeowner planting a garden has nothing to do with international trade.

options.t: A negative externality
options.why: A negative externality imposes costs on others, but neighbors enjoying the garden for free receive a benefit, so this is not negative.

options.t: A positive externality
options.why: The homeowner's action gives neighbors a benefit they did not pay for, which is a benefit reaching uninvolved people, so it is a positive externality.

q: What is the free rider problem?

options.t: People benefit from a good without paying for it
options.why: The free rider problem arises when people benefit from a good without paying for it, which makes it hard for private firms to fund public goods.

options.t: People pay more than their fair share of taxes yearly
options.why: Paying more than a fair share of taxes is a fairness complaint, not the free rider problem, where people use a good without paying.

options.t: People take rides at a discount on buses and trains
options.why: Getting discounted rides on buses and trains is a price discount for riders and is not the free rider problem, where people avoid paying entirely.

options.t: People refuse to use public goods at all times
options.why: Free riders do use public goods, which is the problem, so saying people refuse to use them at all is the reverse of the issue.

q: Why does the government provide most public goods?

options.t: Citizens refuse to use goods that are provided privately
options.why: Citizens do not refuse privately provided goods, and that is not why governments provide public goods, which is a problem of payment.

options.t: Private firms cannot easily charge everyone who benefits
options.why: Because public goods benefit everyone and no one can be excluded, private firms cannot easily charge all who benefit, so the government provides them and funds them through taxes.

options.t: Public goods are always unprofitable by law in every state
options.why: Public goods are not unprofitable by law, since no law says so, and the real problem is that charging users is hard.

options.t: Private firms are banned from making goods in any state
options.why: Private firms are not banned from making goods, and the government provides public goods because firms cannot easily earn payment from them.

q: What is a fixed cost?

options.t: A cost that cannot be known in advance by the firm
options.why: A cost that cannot be known in advance is an uncertain cost, whereas a fixed cost is a known amount that does not vary with output.

options.t: A cost that is paid only when a product is sold to a customer
options.why: A cost paid only when a product is sold describes a variable cost, like a sales commission, while a fixed cost is paid whether or not anything sells.

options.t: A cost that stays the same no matter how much is produced
options.why: A fixed cost stays the same no matter how much is produced, as with rent or insurance, so it is the same at zero output as at high output.

options.t: A cost that rises with every unit produced by the firm
options.why: A cost that rises with every unit produced is a variable cost, such as materials, which is the opposite of a fixed cost that stays constant.

q: What is a variable cost?

options.t: A cost that is paid only once at start-up
options.why: A cost paid only once at start-up is a one-time fixed expense, so it does not rise or fall as the business produces more or fewer units.

options.t: A cost that stays the same at all output levels
options.why: A cost that stays the same at every output level is the definition of a fixed cost, which is the opposite of a variable cost.

options.t: A cost that the government pays instead
options.why: A cost the government pays is not a defining type of business cost, and it says nothing about how a cost responds to changes in production volume.

options.t: A cost that changes with the amount produced
options.why: A variable cost rises and falls with the quantity produced, like materials or hourly labor, so it changes whenever the business makes more or fewer units.

q: Which is an example of a fixed cost for a bakery?

options.t: The sugar used in each pastry
options.why: Sugar used in each pastry is a variable cost, because the shop buys more sugar as it bakes more pastries and less when it bakes fewer.

options.t: The flour used in each loaf
options.why: Flour used in each loaf is a variable cost, because total flour spending climbs with every extra loaf baked and falls when production drops.

options.t: The monthly rent for the shop
options.why: Monthly rent is the same whether the bakery bakes ten loaves or ten thousand, so it is a fixed cost that does not depend on output.

options.t: The boxes used for each order
options.why: Boxes used for each order are a variable cost, because the bakery needs more boxes as orders grow and fewer when orders shrink.

q: How is total cost calculated?

options.t: Fixed costs plus variable costs
options.why: Total cost combines the costs that stay constant with the costs that change with output, so adding fixed costs and variable costs gives the full total.

options.t: Fixed costs minus variable costs
options.why: Subtracting variable costs from fixed costs would shrink the result and could even turn it negative, but both cost types are real expenses that must be added.

options.t: Variable costs divided by output
options.why: Dividing variable costs by output gives variable cost per unit, an average figure, not the total cost, and it leaves out fixed costs entirely.

options.t: Revenue minus all fixed costs
options.why: Revenue minus fixed costs is a rough profit measure that ignores variable costs, and it starts from income rather than from the costs being totaled.

q: A shop has fixed costs of $2,000 and variable costs of $5 per unit. What is the total cost of 400 units?

options.why: A total of $7,000 is too high: it would need 1,000 units of variable cost at $5, but the shop made only 400 units, giving $2,000 variable cost.
A total of $2,005 adds the $5 per-unit cost only once to the fixed cost, instead of multiplying it by all 400 units produced.
A total of $2,000 counts only the fixed costs and leaves out the variable cost of $5 times 400 units, which is another $2,000.
Variable cost is $5 times 400 units, which equals $2,000, and adding the $2,000 of fixed costs gives a total cost of $4,000.

q: How is total revenue calculated?

options.t: Units sold divided by the price per unit
options.why: Dividing units sold by the price does not give money earned; it produces a meaningless ratio, since revenue is the price multiplied by the quantity sold.

options.t: Price per unit times the number of units sold
options.why: Revenue is the money brought in from sales, found by multiplying the price of each unit by the number of units the business sold.

options.t: Fixed cost plus variable cost for the year
options.why: Fixed cost plus variable cost gives total cost, which is money spent, not total revenue, which is money earned from customers buying the product.

options.t: Price per unit minus the cost to make each unit
options.why: Price minus cost to make each unit is the profit per unit, or unit margin, and it is not total revenue, which uses price times quantity.

q: A store sells 300 items at $12 each. Total costs are $2,700. What is the profit?

options.why: Revenue of $3,600 comes from 300 items at $12 each, but it is not profit because it has not yet subtracted the $2,700 of total costs.
A figure of $300 does not result from the correct calculation; revenue of $3,600 minus costs of $2,700 leaves $900, three times as much.
A figure of $6,300 results from adding revenue of $3,600 to costs of $2,700, but profit requires subtracting costs from revenue instead.
Revenue is 300 times $12, which equals $3,600, and subtracting total costs of $2,700 leaves a profit of $900.

q: What is average total cost?

options.t: Total revenue divided by the price
options.why: Total revenue divided by the price gives the number of units sold, not a cost measure, so it cannot represent the average cost of each unit.

options.t: Fixed cost multiplied by the output
options.why: Multiplying fixed cost by output makes a figure that grows without limit as production rises, while an average cost should spread costs across the units.

options.t: Total cost divided by units produced
options.why: Average total cost spreads the entire cost of production across every unit, so dividing total cost by the units produced gives the cost of each unit.

options.t: The highest cost among all products
options.why: The highest cost among products describes a maximum, not an average, and it ignores how total cost is spread over the units a firm actually makes.

q: What is marginal revenue?

options.t: The extra revenue from selling one more unit
options.why: Marginal revenue looks at one additional unit, so it equals the extra revenue earned from selling that one more unit of the product.

options.t: The revenue lost from a price cut in the year
options.why: Revenue lost from a price cut describes a possible effect of discounting, not marginal revenue, which measures the change in total revenue from one extra unit sold.

options.t: The revenue received in advance of the sale
options.why: Revenue received in advance of a sale is unearned or deposit revenue in accounting, and it has no link to the extra revenue from one more unit.

options.t: The total revenue from all of the units sold
options.why: Total revenue from all units sold covers every unit, while marginal revenue concerns only the change caused by selling one additional unit.

q: A firm maximizes profit by producing until:

options.t: Total cost equals total revenue for it
options.why: Setting total cost equal to total revenue marks the break-even point, where profit is zero, so producing only that far does not maximize profit.

options.t: Marginal revenue equals marginal cost
options.why: Producing until marginal revenue equals marginal cost works because each unit before that point adds more revenue than cost, and each unit after it loses money.

options.t: Price equals zero in the whole market
options.why: A price of zero in the whole market would mean no sales revenue at all, so it can never be the point where profit is greatest.

options.t: Fixed cost equals variable cost at all
options.why: Fixed cost equal to variable cost is a coincidence of cost levels that says nothing about revenue, so it does not identify the profit-maximizing output.

q: What is the break-even point?

options.t: The level of sales where total revenue equals total cost
options.why: Break-even occurs where total revenue exactly equals total cost, so the business earns neither a profit nor a loss at that sales level.

options.t: The date a business first opens its doors for trade
options.why: The date a business opens is a calendar event, not an output level, and it has no relation to when revenue first covers costs.

options.t: The level of output where costs are zero for a firm
options.why: Costs are never zero while a firm operates, since fixed costs continue even at zero output, so this cannot define the break-even point.

options.t: The level of sales where the profit is greatest in a period
options.why: The level of sales where profit is greatest is the profit-maximizing point, which occurs beyond break-even, where profit is only zero.

q: Fixed costs are $6,000. Price is $20 and variable cost is $8 per unit. How many units are needed to break even?

options.t: 1,200 units
options.why: A result of 1,200 units does not match the break-even formula: dividing $6,000 by the $12 contribution per unit gives 500, and 1,200 would imply only $5 per unit.

options.t: 500 units
options.why: Contribution per unit is $20 minus $8, which equals $12, and dividing fixed costs of $6,000 by $12 gives 500 units to break even.

options.t: 750 units
options.why: A result of 750 units comes from dividing $6,000 by the variable cost of $8, but break-even must divide by the $12 contribution margin.

options.t: 300 units
options.why: A result of 300 units comes from dividing $6,000 by the $20 price, which ignores variable costs, so it understates the break-even point of 500 units.

q: What is the contribution margin per unit?

options.t: Total revenue minus total cost for the year
options.why: Total revenue minus total cost is profit for the whole period, not a per-unit amount, and it does not isolate how much each unit contributes toward fixed costs.

options.t: Fixed cost divided by the total units sold
options.why: Fixed cost divided by total units sold is the fixed cost per unit, which spreads overhead and does not measure what each unit contributes.

options.t: Selling price plus variable cost per unit
options.why: Adding variable cost to the selling price produces a number higher than the price itself, which makes no sense as a margin left over per unit.

options.t: Selling price minus variable cost per unit
options.why: Contribution margin is what remains from each sale after covering its variable cost, so it equals selling price minus variable cost per unit.

q: What is economies of scale?

options.t: Higher average cost per unit as production grows
options.why: Higher average cost per unit as production grows describes diseconomies of scale, the reverse of economies of scale, where larger output makes each unit cheaper.

options.t: A tax break for large firms and big business
options.why: A tax break for large firms is a government policy and not an economic concept about costs, so it does not describe how output affects unit cost.

options.t: Lower average cost per unit as production grows
options.why: Economies of scale means average cost per unit falls as production grows, because fixed costs are spread over more units and bulk buying lowers input prices.

options.t: Equal cost per unit at every output level
options.why: Equal cost per unit at every output level describes constant returns to scale, where growth neither saves nor adds cost, which is not economies of scale.

q: A very large firm becomes so complex that its average cost per unit begins to rise. This is called:

options.t: Diseconomies of scale
options.why: When a firm grows so large and complex that average cost per unit starts to rise, it faces diseconomies of scale.

options.t: Perfect competition
options.why: Perfect competition is a market structure with many small sellers and identical products, and it does not describe average cost rising inside a large firm.

options.t: Marginal utility gain
options.why: Marginal utility gain is a consumer theory idea about satisfaction from consuming more, and it does not describe rising average unit costs for a firm.

options.t: Economies of scale
options.why: Economies of scale means average cost falls as output grows, which is the opposite of the rising unit cost this very large firm experiences.

q: What is the law of diminishing returns?

options.t: Adding more inputs always increases output equally
options.why: Adding more inputs does not always raise output equally; if it did, there would be no diminishing returns, and extra workers would be equally productive forever.

options.t: Adding more inputs always reduces output to zero
options.why: Adding more inputs does not reduce output to zero; the extra output simply grows smaller, though the total can stay positive for a long time.

options.t: Prices fall as more goods are sold each year
options.why: Falling prices as more goods are sold describes a demand effect, not the law of diminishing returns, which concerns how output responds to extra inputs.

options.t: More of one input eventually adds less output
options.why: The law of diminishing returns says that adding more of one input while holding others fixed eventually yields smaller and smaller gains in output.

q: What is gross profit?

options.t: Sales revenue minus all expenses and taxes
options.why: Revenue minus all expenses and taxes is net profit, the bottom line, and gross profit subtracts only the direct cost of goods sold.

options.t: Sales revenue minus the cost of goods sold
options.why: Gross profit is sales revenue minus the cost of goods sold, showing what remains to pay operating expenses, interest and taxes.

options.t: Sales revenue plus the cost of goods sold
options.why: Adding the cost of goods sold to revenue would inflate the figure above sales, but gross profit requires subtracting that cost.

options.t: Total assets minus total liabilities owed
options.why: Total assets minus total liabilities is owner equity from the balance sheet, a measure of net worth and not a profit figure from sales.

q: What is net profit?

options.t: The total value of everything that the business owns
options.why: The total value of everything a business owns describes its assets, a balance sheet item that says nothing about income earned over a period.

options.t: The income earned before any expense is paid out to staff
options.why: Income earned before any expense is paid describes revenue, the top line of the income statement, while net profit is what remains after costs.

options.t: The income left after all expenses and taxes are subtracted
options.why: Net profit is the income left after subtracting all expenses and taxes from revenue, which makes it the true bottom line of the income statement.

options.t: The income left after subtracting only the cost of goods sold
options.why: Income left after subtracting only the cost of goods sold is gross profit, which still has operating expenses, interest and taxes to be deducted.

q: Revenue is $90,000, cost of goods sold is $50,000 and operating expenses are $25,000. What is operating profit?

options.why: Operating profit is revenue minus cost of goods sold minus operating expenses, so $90,000 minus $50,000 minus $25,000 equals $15,000.
A figure of $40,000 is gross profit, found by subtracting only the $50,000 cost of goods sold, without deducting the $25,000 of operating expenses.
A figure of $165,000 results from adding the cost of goods sold and operating expenses to revenue, when both must be subtracted.
A figure of $65,000 subtracts only the $25,000 operating expenses from revenue and forgets the $50,000 cost of goods sold, so the profit is overstated.

q: What is markup?

options.t: The tax charged on a product at checkout in a shop or store
options.why: The tax charged at checkout is sales tax, which the government collects, while markup is an amount the business itself adds to cost to set price.

options.t: The amount a store lowers a price during a sale to attract shoppers
options.why: The amount a store lowers a price during a sale is a markdown, the reverse of a markup, which increases the price over what the item cost.

options.t: The amount added to a product's cost to set its selling price
options.why: Markup is the amount added to a product's cost to reach its selling price, which covers the business's expenses and leaves room for profit.

options.t: The cost of shipping goods to a store from a distant supplier
options.why: The cost of shipping goods to a store is a freight or delivery expense, which is part of the product's cost rather than the markup added on top.

q: A retailer buys a jacket for $40 and applies a 50% markup on cost. What is the selling price?

options.why: A price of $80 would be a 100% markup, because $40 plus another $40 doubles the cost, while the jacket has only a 50% markup.
A price of $20 is just half the cost, so it is below the $40 purchase price and would lose money instead of adding a markup.
A price of $50 adds only $10, a 25% markup on the $40 cost, but a 50% markup on cost means adding $20.
A 50% markup on a $40 cost adds $20, and $40 plus $20 gives a selling price of $60 for the jacket.

q: What is a markdown?

options.t: An addition to the cost of a product after tax
options.why: Adding to cost after tax describes a markup or a fee, which raises a price, while a markdown lowers the selling price of a product.

options.t: A reduction in the selling price of a product
options.why: A markdown is a reduction in the selling price of a product, often used for sales, clearance, or to move slow-selling inventory.

options.t: A tax on discounted goods sold in stores
options.why: A tax on discounted goods would be a government charge, but a markdown is a price decision made by the retailer itself, not a tax.

options.t: A fee charged for returns of goods to stores
options.why: A fee charged for returns is a restocking fee, which adds to what a customer pays and has nothing to do with lowering the price.

q: A $80 item is marked down 25%. What is the new price?

options.why: A 25% markdown takes off $80 times 0.25, which is $20, and $80 minus $20 leaves a new price of $60.
A price of $55 would result from subtracting $25 in dollars, which treats the 25% as $25, but 25% of $80 is only $20.
A price of $75 takes off only $5, a little over 6% of $80, so it falls well short of a full 25% markdown.
A figure of $20 is the amount of the discount, which is 25% of $80, not the new price the customer pays after the discount.

q: What does return on investment (ROI) measure?

options.t: The time it takes to earn a salary in a year
options.why: The time it takes to earn a salary describes pay periods or hours worked and has nothing to do with the return generated by an investment.

options.t: The tax paid on an investment each year
options.why: The tax paid on an investment each year is an investment tax cost, while ROI measures the gain earned compared with the money put in.

options.t: The gain from an investment relative to cost
options.why: Return on investment compares the gain from an investment with its cost, usually as a percentage, to show how efficiently money was used.

options.t: The total money put in by the owners of the firm
options.why: The total money put in by the owners is called invested capital or equity, which is the cost side, not the return that ROI measures.

q: A business invests $20,000 and earns $3,000 in profit from it. What is the ROI?

options.why: A figure of 6.7% flips the ratio: $20,000 divided by $3,000 is not a percentage return, while ROI is profit divided by cost, $3,000 over $20,000.
ROI equals profit divided by the amount invested, so $3,000 divided by $20,000 is 0.15, which is 15%.
A figure of $3,000 is the dollar profit, not the ROI, because ROI is expressed as a percentage of the investment, not as a money amount.
A figure of 60% would need a profit of $12,000 on the $20,000 investment, but the profit was only $3,000, so the return is far smaller.

q: What is overhead?

options.t: The cost of raw materials in each unit
options.why: The cost of raw materials in each unit is a direct variable cost, tied to specific products, whereas overhead is not tied to one product.

options.t: The profit paid to owners each year
options.why: Profit paid to owners each year is a distribution of earnings, not an operating cost, so it cannot be called overhead.

options.t: The wages of workers who make the product
options.why: Wages of workers who make the product are direct labor costs traced to units, while overhead covers costs that support the whole business.

options.t: Ongoing costs not tied to one product
options.why: Overhead means the ongoing costs of running a business, such as rent, utilities and administration, that cannot be tied to one specific product.

q: What is a direct cost?

options.t: A cost shared by all parts of the business
options.why: A cost shared by all parts of the business is an indirect cost or overhead, because it cannot be traced to any one specific product.

options.t: A cost paid to the government in every year
options.why: A cost paid to the government each year describes a tax, and whether it is direct or indirect depends on whether it traces to one product.

options.t: A cost that has not yet been paid by the business
options.why: A cost not yet paid is an accrued or unpaid cost, which describes timing of payment, not whether the cost can be traced to a product.

options.t: A cost that can be traced to a specific product
options.why: A direct cost, such as the wood in a chair, can be traced to a specific product, making it easy to assign to that item.

q: What is an opportunity cost for a business choosing between two projects?

options.t: The total of all costs of both projects added overall
options.why: Adding together all costs of both projects gives total expense, but opportunity cost refers to the value of the single best alternative given up.

options.t: The profit from the project that was not chosen
options.why: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative you give up, so it is the profit from the project that was not chosen.

options.t: The profit from the project that was chosen
options.why: The profit from the chosen project is the benefit gained, not the cost, because opportunity cost measures what was sacrificed by choosing it.

options.t: The tax paid on both projects by the firm
options.why: Tax paid on both projects is an actual expense and does not capture the value of the option the firm gave up by choosing between them.

q: Project A will earn $12,000 and Project B will earn $9,000, and only one can be done. The firm picks A. What is its opportunity cost?

options.why: A figure of $3,000 is the difference between the two projects, which is the net gain of choosing A, not the opportunity cost of giving up B.
A figure of $21,000 adds the earnings of both projects, but only one can be done, so the firm gives up B alone.
The firm picks A and gives up B, so the opportunity cost is the $9,000 that Project B would have earned.
A figure of $12,000 is what Project A earns, which is the benefit the firm gains, not the value of the project it gave up.

q: What is a sunk cost?

options.t: A cost already paid that cannot be recovered
options.why: A sunk cost has already been paid and cannot be recovered, so it should not influence future decisions about whether to continue a project.

options.t: A cost expected next year that can be avoided
options.why: A cost expected next year that can be avoided is a future avoidable cost, and it does matter when making decisions, unlike a sunk cost.

options.t: A cost that varies with output each month
options.why: A cost that varies with output each month is a variable cost, which is still ahead and changeable, not one that is already spent.

options.t: A cost that can be refunded fully later
options.why: A cost that can be refunded later is recoverable, so it is not sunk, because sunk costs are those that cannot be got back.

q: A company spent $50,000 on a failed product design. Which advice reflects good decision-making?

options.t: Hide the loss from the board and the owners of the firm
options.why: Hiding the loss is dishonest and harms trust in the firm, and it does nothing to help choose the best future course of action.

options.t: Ignore the $50,000 and decide using future costs and benefits
options.why: The $50,000 is a sunk cost that cannot be recovered, so a sound decision weighs only the future costs and benefits of each option.

options.t: Double the spending to try to recover the earlier loss
options.why: Doubling the spending to recover the earlier loss is the sunk cost fallacy, because it throws more good money after money already lost.

options.t: Keep spending because $50,000 was already invested in the design
options.why: Continuing only because $50,000 was already invested is the sunk cost fallacy, since the past spending is gone whichever option the firm picks.

q: What happens to the average fixed cost per unit as output rises?

options.t: It stays exactly the same for each unit made
options.why: Average fixed cost does not stay the same, because the same total fixed cost is divided by a growing number of units as output rises.

options.t: It rises, because more units are made at higher cost
options.why: Average fixed cost does not rise with output; the fixed total stays constant while units increase, so the cost per unit gets smaller, not bigger.

options.t: It becomes negative for each unit that is made
options.why: Average fixed cost cannot become negative, because both fixed cost and output are positive, so dividing one by the other always gives a positive value.

options.t: It falls as fixed costs spread over more units
options.why: Average fixed cost is total fixed cost divided by output, so as output rises the same fixed cost is spread across more units and falls.

q: What is a business?

options.t: An organization providing goods or services for profit
options.why: A business is an organization that provides goods or services to customers with the aim of earning a profit for its owners.

options.t: A group that exists only to give money to charity each year
options.why: A group that exists only to give money to charity is a charitable foundation, which does not aim for profit and so is not a business.

options.t: An agency that creates laws for a country as a whole
options.why: An agency that creates laws for a country is a legislature or government body, whose purpose is public rule making and not selling goods for profit.

options.t: A place where people live and work together in a town
options.why: A place where people live and work together is a community or neighborhood, which describes a location and not an organization that sells for profit.

q: What is a sole proprietorship?

options.t: A business owned by the government
options.why: A business owned by the government is a state-owned enterprise, whereas a sole proprietorship is owned privately by an individual.

options.t: A business owned by two or more partners
options.why: A business owned by two or more partners is a partnership, which has more than one owner, so it is not a sole proprietorship.

options.t: A business owned and run by one person
options.why: A sole proprietorship is a business owned and run by one person, who keeps the profits and is not legally separate from the business.

options.t: A business owned by many shareholders
options.why: A business owned by many shareholders is a corporation, which has numerous owners holding stock, unlike a sole proprietorship with a single owner.

q: What is a major advantage of a sole proprietorship?

options.t: It has unlimited access to investor money
options.why: A sole proprietorship has limited access to funds, since it depends on the owner's savings and loans, and cannot sell stock to investors.

options.t: The owner is shielded from business debts
options.why: The owner of a sole proprietorship is not shielded from debts, because the business and owner are legally the same, so personal assets are at risk.

options.t: It is simple and inexpensive to start
options.why: A sole proprietorship is simple and inexpensive to start, needing little paperwork or legal formality, which is its major advantage for new owners.

options.t: It continues forever after the owner dies
options.why: A sole proprietorship does not continue forever, because it ends when the owner dies or quits, since the business has no separate legal existence.

q: What is unlimited liability?

options.t: The owner pays no taxes on the firm's income
