options.why: Unlimited liability does not exempt the owner from taxes; the owner usually pays income tax on business profits, and the term concerns debts instead.

options.t: The owner is never liable for the business debts
options.why: Never being liable for business debts describes limited liability for shareholders, the reverse of unlimited liability, where the owner can be pursued for debts.

options.t: The business may never borrow money from banks
options.why: Unlimited liability says nothing about whether a business may borrow from banks; firms with this feature can borrow, and the term concerns who repays debts.

options.t: The owner is personally liable for business debts
options.why: Unlimited liability means the owner is personally responsible for all business debts, so creditors can claim personal assets like savings or a house.

q: What is a partnership?

options.t: A business owned by two or more who share profits
options.why: A partnership is a business owned by two or more people who agree to share the profits, the losses and the management responsibilities.

options.t: A business run by a union of its own workers
options.why: A business run by a union of its own workers is closer to a cooperative or labor group and does not define a partnership.

options.t: A business owned by one person only, for profit
options.why: A business owned by one person only is a sole proprietorship, whereas a partnership requires at least two owners.

options.t: A business owned by shareholders with limited liability
options.why: A business owned by shareholders with limited liability describes a corporation, while general partners usually carry personal responsibility for the firm's debts.

q: What is a corporation?

options.t: A business owned by one individual with no legal separation from them
options.why: A business owned by one individual with no legal separation from them is a sole proprietorship, not a corporation, which is a separate legal entity.

options.t: A legal entity separate from its owners, who hold shares of stock
options.why: A corporation is a legal entity separate from its owners, who hold shares of stock, so the company itself can own property and be sued.

options.t: A business that is part of the government of the state and run by it
options.why: A business that is part of the state government is a public enterprise, while a corporation is typically privately owned by its shareholders.

options.t: A business owned by a group that shares unlimited liability
options.why: A business owned by a group sharing unlimited liability describes a general partnership, whereas corporate shareholders generally risk only the money they invested.

q: What is a key advantage of a corporation?

options.t: Shareholders have limited liability for debts
options.why: A key advantage of a corporation is that shareholders have limited liability, so they can lose only what they invested, not personal assets.

options.t: Owners decide everything directly, no managers
options.why: Owners deciding everything directly with no managers is not true of corporations, where shareholders elect a board that hires professional managers to run the firm.

options.t: The business pays no taxes at all in a year
options.why: A corporation does pay taxes, on its profits, and shareholders may be taxed again on dividends, so it is not tax free.

options.t: Setup is quick and free of any cost or fees
options.why: Setting up a corporation involves legal filings, fees and paperwork, so it is neither quick nor free, and it costs more than a sole proprietorship.

q: What is a limited liability company (LLC)?

options.t: A company that cannot make any profit
options.why: A company that cannot make any profit would not be a business at all, and nothing in the LLC form prevents owners from earning a profit.

options.t: A form giving owners liability protection
options.why: An LLC is a business form that gives owners liability protection like a corporation while keeping simpler management and tax treatment.

options.t: A company owned by the state with few funds
options.why: A company owned by the state is a government enterprise, but an LLC is privately owned, and its name refers to owner liability, not funding.

options.t: A company with a cap on clients it can serve
options.why: A company with a cap on clients is not an LLC; the word limited refers to the owners' limited personal liability, not to customers served.

q: What is a franchise?

options.t: A tax paid by large companies each year
options.why: A tax paid by large companies is a corporate tax, while a franchise is a business arrangement and not a payment to the government.

options.t: A group of competing companies in a region
options.why: A group of competing companies in a region is a market cluster or industry group, but a franchise is a contract between a brand owner and an operator.

options.t: A store that sells only used goods cheaply
options.why: A store that sells only used goods is a secondhand or thrift shop, and it has nothing to do with licensing a brand.

options.t: A company licensing its brand and system
options.why: A franchise is when a company licenses its brand, products and operating system to another owner, who pays fees or royalties in return.

q: What is a nonprofit organization?

options.t: An organization that is run by the government only
options.why: An organization run by the government only is a public agency, but a nonprofit is usually a private group that is separate from government.

options.t: An organization forbidden from earning any income
options.why: A nonprofit is not forbidden from earning income; it can earn money and run fundraisers, but it must use the money for its mission and not for owners.

options.t: A group using income for a mission, not owners
options.why: A nonprofit uses its income to support a mission, such as education or charity, and does not pay profits out to owners or shareholders.

options.t: An organization owned by owners who receive profits
options.why: An organization owned by owners who receive profits is a for-profit business, which is the opposite of a nonprofit, whose income goes to its mission.

q: What is a cooperative?

options.t: A business that operates only at night time
options.why: Operating only at night describes a business's hours, which is unrelated to its ownership structure, and a cooperative can open at any time.

options.t: A business run by its members for their benefit
options.why: A cooperative is a business owned and run by its members for their shared benefit, such as farmers pooling resources or customers buying together.

options.t: A business that competes with all members in the area
options.why: A business competing against its own members would defeat the purpose of a cooperative, whose members join together to serve each other's interests.

options.t: A business owned by a single investor alone
options.why: A business owned by a single investor is a sole proprietorship, whereas a cooperative is owned jointly by many members who share control.

q: What does 'private sector' mean?

options.t: The part of the economy run by charities only
options.why: The part of the economy run by charities only is the nonprofit or voluntary sector, which is a small piece of the private sector.

options.t: The part of the economy run by the state itself
options.why: The part of the economy run by the state is the public sector, so it is the opposite of the private sector.

options.t: The part of the economy run by firms for profit
options.why: The private sector is the part of the economy made up of privately owned firms and individuals that operate to earn a profit.

options.t: The part of the economy that is hidden away
options.why: The private sector is a legitimate, visible part of the economy and is not hidden; private there means privately owned, not secret.

q: What does 'public sector' mean?

options.t: The part of the economy owned or run by governments
options.why: The public sector is the part of the economy owned or run by governments, including public schools, the military, police and public hospitals.

options.t: The part of the economy run by foreign firms only
options.why: The part of the economy run by foreign firms only is just foreign-owned business, which is part of the private sector, not the public sector.

options.t: The part of the economy run by private owners for profit
options.why: The part of the economy run by private owners for profit is the private sector, which is the opposite of the public sector.

options.t: The part of the economy that sells stock to the public
options.why: Selling stock to the public describes publicly traded companies, which are private businesses, and the term public sector instead refers to government ownership.

q: Which type of business provides intangible products?

options.t: A farm that grows apples and other fruit
options.why: A farm that grows apples produces a physical, tangible good that can be touched and stored, so its product is not intangible.

options.t: A manufacturer that makes furniture
options.why: A manufacturer making furniture produces tangible goods that customers can see and touch, so its product is not intangible.

options.t: A mine that extracts coal from the ground
options.why: A mine extracting coal supplies a physical commodity that can be handled and weighed, which makes its output tangible rather than intangible.

options.t: A service business such as a hair salon
options.why: A hair salon sells a service, such as a haircut, which cannot be touched or stored, so it is an intangible product.

q: Which action is an example of fiscal policy?

options.t: A company deciding to cut prices on its own products
options.why: A company cutting its own prices is a private business decision and not government action, while fiscal policy involves government taxing and spending.

options.t: The Federal Reserve changing the interest rate on loans as a rule
options.why: The Federal Reserve changing the interest rate is monetary policy, which works through money and credit, not through government taxes and spending.

options.t: A bank approving a mortgage for a customer who applied
options.why: A bank approving a mortgage is an ordinary private lending decision, not a government policy tool for managing the overall economy.

options.t: Congress raising or lowering taxes and government spending
options.why: Fiscal policy is the use of government taxes and spending to influence the economy, so Congress raising or lowering them is a clear example.

q: Which action is an example of monetary policy?

options.t: The president signing a spending bill into law today
options.why: A president signing a spending bill is a fiscal policy action, because it involves government spending, whereas monetary policy deals with money and interest rates.

options.t: The Fed adjusting interest rates and the money supply
options.why: Monetary policy is run by the central bank, so the Fed adjusting interest rates and the money supply is a direct example.

options.t: Congress passing a new tax law that applies to businesses
options.why: Congress passing a tax law is fiscal policy, which uses taxation, so it does not count as monetary policy managed by the central bank.

options.t: A city council approving a local budget for the year
options.why: A city council approving a local budget is local government fiscal activity, not monetary policy, which is carried out by the Federal Reserve.

q: Who conducts monetary policy in the United States?

options.t: The Securities Agency
options.why: The Securities Agency, loosely like the SEC, oversees securities markets and investors, and it does not set interest rates or the money supply.

options.t: The Commerce Department
options.why: The Commerce Department promotes trade and gathers economic data, but it does not control interest rates or the money supply.

options.t: The Federal Reserve
options.why: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States, and it conducts monetary policy by setting rates and managing the money supply.

options.t: The Internal Revenue
options.why: The Internal Revenue Service collects taxes, which is part of fiscal policy, and it has no role in controlling interest rates or credit.

q: How does the Fed typically respond to slow economic growth?

options.t: It lowers interest rates to encourage borrowing and spending
options.why: To fight slow growth the Fed lowers interest rates, which makes borrowing cheaper and encourages firms and households to spend and invest.

options.t: It raises taxes on every business in the whole country
options.why: The Fed does not have the power to levy taxes, which belongs to Congress, and higher taxes would slow growth further instead of helping.

options.t: It raises interest rates to discourage borrowing and spending
options.why: Raising interest rates makes borrowing more expensive and slows spending, which would deepen a slowdown and is the tool used against inflation.

options.t: It bans all bank lending for a year at a time in the country
options.why: Banning all bank lending for a year would freeze credit and deepen a downturn, and the Fed has no such practice as a response.

q: How does the Fed typically respond to rapidly rising inflation?

options.t: It prints more money for all citizens of the nation
options.why: Printing more money for citizens would raise the money supply and add to inflation, so it is the opposite of an anti-inflation response.

options.t: It lowers interest rates to speed up spending in the economy
options.why: Lowering interest rates speeds up spending and borrowing, which adds demand and would push prices up even faster during rapid inflation.

options.t: It raises interest rates to slow borrowing and spending
options.why: To cool rapid inflation the Fed raises interest rates, which makes loans costlier, slows borrowing and spending, and eases pressure on prices.

options.t: It cuts all taxes immediately for every household
options.why: Cutting taxes is a fiscal policy tool done by Congress, not the Fed, and it would boost spending and worsen inflation.

q: What is expansionary fiscal policy?

options.t: Increasing government spending or cutting taxes to boost the economy
options.why: Expansionary fiscal policy raises government spending or cuts taxes, which puts more money into the economy and boosts demand and output.

options.t: Banning imports to protect industries at home from foreign rivals every time
options.why: Banning imports to protect home industries is a trade policy called protectionism, not fiscal policy, which concerns government taxing and spending.

options.t: Raising taxes and cutting government spending to cool the economy
options.why: Raising taxes and cutting government spending is contractionary fiscal policy, which takes money out of the economy to cool it down.

options.t: Raising interest rates to slow lending across the whole economy
options.why: Raising interest rates to slow lending is monetary policy done by the central bank, and it is contractionary, not expansionary or fiscal.

q: What is contractionary fiscal policy?

options.t: Lowering interest rates to encourage borrowing by firms
options.why: Lowering interest rates is a monetary policy tool that encourages borrowing, and it is expansionary, so it is not contractionary fiscal policy.

options.t: Raising taxes or cutting spending to slow the economy
options.why: Contractionary fiscal policy raises taxes or cuts government spending to reduce demand and slow an overheating economy and its inflation.

options.t: Increasing government spending on roads and bridges
options.why: Increasing government spending on roads and bridges adds demand to the economy, which makes it expansionary and not contractionary.

options.t: Cutting taxes to boost spending across the economy
options.why: Cutting taxes leaves households and firms with more money to spend, so it is expansionary, which is the opposite of contractionary fiscal policy.

q: What is a budget deficit?

options.t: When imports exceed exports in the trade balance for a year
options.why: Imports exceeding exports describes a trade deficit, which is about international trade and not the government's own spending and revenue.

options.t: When government revenue exceeds its spending in a year, leaving a surplus
options.why: Government revenue exceeding spending is a budget surplus, not a deficit, since the government takes in more than it pays out.

options.t: When prices fall across the economy for a long period of time
options.why: Prices falling across the economy for a long time is deflation, which is a price level change and has nothing to do with the budget.

options.t: When government spending exceeds the revenue it collects in a year
options.why: A budget deficit occurs when government spending exceeds the revenue it collects in a year, so it must borrow to cover the gap.

q: What is the national debt?

options.t: The amount citizens owe on their credit cards each year
options.why: What citizens owe on credit cards is consumer debt, a private obligation, whereas the national debt is what the government itself owes.

options.t: The total amount the government owes from past borrowing
options.why: The national debt is the total the government owes from past borrowing, which builds up as yearly deficits are added together over time.

options.t: The amount the government spends in one year of the budget
options.why: The amount the government spends in one year is annual outlays or spending, a yearly flow, while the national debt is an accumulated total.

options.t: The amount of tax collected in a year by the state
options.why: The amount of tax collected in a year is government revenue, a yearly flow of income, and it is not the accumulated debt owed.

q: What is regulation?

options.t: Rules set by government to control how businesses operate
options.why: Regulation means rules set by government to control how businesses operate, protecting consumers, workers and the environment.

options.t: Money given by government to help businesses grow each year
options.why: Money given by government to help businesses is a subsidy or grant, which supports firms, whereas regulation sets rules they must follow.

options.t: A tax on business income paid each year to the state
options.why: A tax on business income is a corporate income tax, which raises revenue and is different from rules about how firms must operate.

options.t: A business owner's personal code of conduct at work
options.why: A business owner's personal code of conduct is private ethics, which is voluntary, while regulation is mandatory and enforced by the government.

q: Which agency enforces consumer protection and competition laws in advertising and marketing?

options.t: The Internal Revenue Service (IRS)
options.why: The IRS collects federal taxes and enforces the tax code, but it does not police advertising or competition practices.

options.t: The Federal Reserve Board of Governors
options.why: The Federal Reserve Board oversees monetary policy and banking, not advertising claims or consumer protection in marketing.

options.t: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
options.why: The FTC enforces consumer protection and competition laws, going after deceptive advertising, unfair marketing and anticompetitive business practices.

options.t: The Department of Defense and Army
options.why: The Department of Defense runs the military and national security, and it has no role in regulating advertising or marketing to consumers.

q: Which agency sets and enforces workplace safety standards?

options.t: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC)
options.why: The FCC regulates radio, television, phone and internet communications, and it does not set workplace safety standards for employees.

options.t: The Food and Drug Administration of the U.S.
options.why: The Food and Drug Administration oversees the safety of food, drugs and cosmetics, not conditions where employees work.

options.t: The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
options.why: The SEC regulates securities markets and protects investors, so it does not set rules about safety on the job.

options.t: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration
options.why: OSHA sets and enforces workplace safety and health standards, inspecting employers and fining them for hazards that endanger workers.

q: Which agency regulates the safety of food, drugs and cosmetics?

options.t: The National Labor Relations Board
options.why: The National Labor Relations Board protects workers' rights to organize and bargain, and it does not regulate food, drugs or cosmetics.

options.t: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
options.why: The EPA sets and enforces pollution and environmental standards, but it does not oversee the safety of food, drugs and cosmetics.

options.t: The Federal Reserve Board of Directors
options.why: The Federal Reserve Board guides monetary policy and supervises banks, so it has no authority over food, drug or cosmetic safety.

options.t: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
options.why: The FDA regulates the safety of food, drugs and cosmetics, approving medicines and inspecting products before and after they reach consumers.

q: Which agency sets and enforces pollution standards?

options.t: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
options.why: The EPA sets and enforces pollution standards for air, water and land, and it can fine businesses that break environmental rules.

options.t: The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
options.why: The FDIC insures bank deposits up to a legal limit, so it protects savers and does not set pollution standards.

options.t: The Social Security Administration (SSA)
options.why: The Social Security Administration pays retirement and disability benefits, and it has no authority over environmental pollution standards.

options.t: The Small Business Administration (SBA)
options.why: The SBA assists small firms with loans and counseling, but it does not set or enforce pollution standards for businesses.

q: What does the Small Business Administration (SBA) do?

options.t: Sets interest rates for banks and lenders in the nation
options.why: The SBA does not set interest rates for banks; that is done by the Federal Reserve, while the SBA supports small business lending.

options.t: Regulates the stock exchanges and the trading of shares
options.why: Regulating stock exchanges and share trading is the work of the Securities and Exchange Commission, not the SBA.

options.t: Helps small firms with loan guarantees and counseling
options.why: The SBA helps small firms by guaranteeing loans, offering counseling and training, and supporting entrepreneurs who struggle to get ordinary bank credit.

options.t: Collects taxes from small firms and checks their returns
options.why: Collecting taxes from small firms and checking returns is the job of the IRS, and the SBA exists to assist small businesses.

q: What is antitrust law designed to do?

options.t: Protect monopolies from competition in the market
options.why: Protecting monopolies from competition is the opposite of antitrust law, which exists to prevent them and the harm they do to consumers.

options.t: Promote competition and block unfair monopolies
options.why: Antitrust law is designed to promote competition and block unfair monopolies, keeping prices fair and giving consumers real choices in the market.

options.t: Set prices for all goods sold in the nation
options.why: Setting prices for all goods is central price control, which antitrust law does not do, since it relies on competition to keep prices fair.

options.t: Require every firm to merge with a rival firm
options.why: Antitrust law does not force firms to merge; it often blocks mergers that would reduce competition, which is the opposite of requiring them.

q: Two rival gas stations secretly agree to charge the same high price. Which law is most likely violated?

options.t: Minimum wage law on pay rates
options.why: Minimum wage law sets the lowest hourly pay for workers, and it has no bearing on two competitors agreeing on prices.

options.t: Truth in lending law on loans
options.why: Truth in lending law requires lenders to disclose loan terms and costs, and it does not address rival sellers agreeing on prices.

options.t: Child labor law on young workers
options.why: Child labor law limits the work young people may do, which has no connection to secret agreements between competing gas stations on pricing.

options.t: Antitrust law on price fixing
options.why: Secretly agreeing with a rival to charge the same high price is price fixing, which violates antitrust law because it removes competition.

q: What is a monopoly?

options.t: A market with one buyer only and many sellers
options.why: A market with one buyer and many sellers is a monopsony, which mirrors monopoly, because the single party is on the buying side.

options.t: A market with a few sellers who set prices
options.why: A market with a few sellers who set prices is an oligopoly, not a monopoly, which has just one seller.

options.t: One seller controls the product's supply
options.why: A monopoly exists when a single seller controls the supply of a product, so buyers have no close substitutes and little choice.

options.t: A market with many equal sellers of goods
options.why: A market with many equal sellers is perfect competition, which has the opposite structure to a monopoly, where one seller dominates.

q: What is an oligopoly?

options.t: A market with thousands of small sellers
options.why: A market with thousands of small sellers describes perfect or monopolistic competition, in which no single firm holds much power, unlike an oligopoly.

options.t: A market dominated by a few large sellers
options.why: An oligopoly is a market dominated by a few large sellers, whose pricing decisions strongly affect each other, as with airlines or car makers.

options.t: A market with no sellers at all in it
options.why: A market with no sellers has no supply or trade at all, so it cannot be an oligopoly, which needs a few active firms.

options.t: A market with only one seller present
options.why: A market with only one seller present is a monopoly, whereas an oligopoly has a handful of large competing sellers.

q: What is perfect competition?

options.t: Many sellers of identical products, easy entry
options.why: Perfect competition has many sellers of identical products with easy entry and exit, so no seller can influence the market price.

options.t: A market with government price controls only
options.why: A market with government price controls only describes regulated pricing, not a competitive market structure, since perfect competition lets supply and demand set prices.

options.t: A market with a few large sellers and high prices
options.why: A market with a few large sellers and high prices is an oligopoly, which lacks the many small sellers perfect competition needs.

options.t: A market with one dominant seller and no rivals
options.why: A market with one dominant seller and no rivals is a monopoly, the opposite of perfect competition, which has many rival sellers.

q: What is monopolistic competition?

options.t: One seller with a unique product on the market
options.why: One seller with a unique product describes a monopoly, whereas monopolistic competition has many sellers offering similar but not identical goods.

options.t: Many sellers with identical products, no price power
options.why: Many sellers with identical products and no price power describes perfect competition, not monopolistic competition, where products are differentiated and firms have some price control.

options.t: Two sellers who cooperate to set prices together
options.why: Two sellers who cooperate to set prices is a duopoly with collusion, which is an oligopoly situation and illegal in many cases.

options.t: Many sellers of similar, differentiated products
options.why: Monopolistic competition has many sellers offering similar but differentiated products, like restaurants or clothing brands, so each firm has a little pricing power.

q: What is a price ceiling?

options.t: A legal minimum price that must be charged by every seller
options.why: A legal minimum price that must be charged is a price floor, not a ceiling, because it sets the lowest allowed price.

options.t: The highest price a seller wants to receive for it
options.why: The highest price a seller wants to receive is just a seller's preference, and not a legal limit set by the government.

options.t: A legal maximum price that can be charged for a good
options.why: A price ceiling is a legal maximum price that can be charged for a good, set by the government to keep it affordable.

options.t: A tax added to a price at the point of sale by the state
options.why: A tax added to the price at the point of sale is a sales tax, which does not limit how high sellers can price.

q: If a price ceiling is set below the equilibrium price, what is the likely result?

options.t: A shortage, as demand exceeds supply
options.why: A ceiling below equilibrium holds the price down, so buyers want more than sellers will supply, and quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, causing a shortage.

options.t: A rise in the equilibrium price level
options.why: A binding price ceiling prevents the price from rising, so it cannot cause the equilibrium price to climb, which is what this option claims.

options.t: No effect, because markets ignore laws
options.why: Laws that set binding limits do affect markets, which is why a ceiling below equilibrium creates shortages and not a null result.

options.t: A surplus, as sellers produce too much
options.why: A surplus occurs when price is held above equilibrium, as with a price floor, whereas a ceiling below equilibrium produces a shortage instead.

q: What is a price floor?

options.t: The lowest price a buyer would like
options.why: The lowest price a buyer would like is only a buyer's wish or reservation price, not a legal rule set by the government.

options.t: A legal minimum price for a good
options.why: A price floor is a legal minimum price for a good, set by government so sellers cannot charge less than that amount.

options.t: A discount offered by a store
options.why: A store discount is a voluntary sale price chosen by the seller, while a price floor is a legal limit imposed by government.

options.t: A legal maximum price for a good
options.why: A legal maximum price for a good is a price ceiling, the opposite of a floor, which sets a minimum instead.

q: If a price floor is set above the equilibrium price, what is the likely result?

options.t: A shortage, because buyers want more than sellers offer
options.why: A shortage arises when price is held below equilibrium, as with a ceiling, so a floor above equilibrium produces the opposite outcome.

options.t: A fall in the equilibrium price of the good in the market
options.why: A binding floor above equilibrium keeps the price above the market level, so it cannot make the equilibrium price fall.

options.t: A surplus, because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
options.why: A floor above equilibrium raises the price, so sellers offer more while buyers purchase less, and quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, creating a surplus.

options.t: No effect, because prices adjust instantly in every market in general
options.why: A binding price floor does have an effect, because it stops the price from falling to equilibrium, so the market cannot clear and a surplus results.

q: Which is an example of a government subsidy?

options.t: A license fee for opening a restaurant in a city
options.why: A license fee for opening a restaurant is a charge paid to government by the business, so it takes money away and is not a subsidy.

options.t: A fine for polluting a river or a stream
options.why: A fine for polluting a river is a penalty collected from the polluter, so it is a payment to government and not a subsidy.

options.t: A tariff on imported steel from other countries
options.why: A tariff on imported steel is a tax on foreign goods that raises revenue and prices, so it is the opposite of a subsidy.

options.t: Payments to farmers to support crop production
options.why: A subsidy is money the government gives to support an industry, such as payments to farmers that encourage them to keep producing crops.

q: What is a tax incentive?

options.t: A rule that bans the sale of a product
options.why: A rule that bans the sale of a product is a prohibition, which forbids an activity and offers no tax benefit, so it is not a tax incentive.

options.t: A tax cut offered to encourage behavior
options.why: A tax incentive is a tax cut or credit offered to encourage a behavior, such as investing in clean energy or hiring workers.

options.t: A tax increase to punish a behavior
options.why: A tax increase to punish a behavior is a sin tax or penalty, which discourages activity, while an incentive encourages it with a reward.

options.t: A fee for using a government service
options.why: A fee for using a government service is a user fee, which is a payment to government, not a tax reduction that rewards behavior.

q: What is a licensing requirement?

options.t: Government permission to operate certain businesses
options.why: A licensing requirement means government permission is needed to operate certain businesses or professions, such as doctors, restaurants or electricians, to protect public safety.

options.t: A rule about how to advertise goods to the public
options.why: A rule about how to advertise goods is an advertising regulation, which controls marketing, whereas licensing controls who may operate a business at all.

options.t: A tax paid on business profits each year to the state
options.why: A tax paid on business profits is an income tax, a revenue measure, and not the permission to operate that licensing involves.

options.t: A subsidy paid to start-ups to help them get going
options.why: A subsidy paid to start-ups is financial support from government, while a licensing requirement is a permission, not a payment.

q: What is the effect of higher business taxes on a firm's decisions?

options.t: It guarantees much higher profits
options.why: Higher taxes take more of a firm's earnings, so they cannot guarantee higher profits; if anything they tend to reduce after-tax profit.

options.t: It can reduce investment and hiring
options.why: Higher business taxes leave the firm with less money to invest and hire, so they can reduce investment and hiring, since less cash is available.

options.t: It has no effect on any firm decisions
options.why: Taxes are a cost of doing business, and a rise in them does shape decisions about spending, expansion and employment, so they have an effect.

options.t: It always increases hiring and pay
options.why: Higher taxes do not always increase hiring and pay; they usually shrink what a firm can afford, so this claim is the opposite of the likely effect.

q: What is a tariff's effect on consumers?

options.t: Domestic producers must cut prices
options.why: A tariff protects domestic producers from foreign competition, which lets them hold or raise prices instead of being forced to cut them.

options.t: Imports become free of charge for buyers
options.why: A tariff is a tax on imports, so it makes imports more expensive, and it does not make them free of charge for buyers.

options.t: Prices of imported goods usually fall
options.why: A tariff adds a tax to imported goods, so their prices usually rise, not fall, which is the opposite of what this option claims.

options.t: Prices of imported goods usually rise
options.why: A tariff is a tax on imports, which importers pass along to buyers, so prices of imported goods usually rise for consumers.

q: Which group generally benefits most from a tariff on imported steel?

options.t: Consumers who buy products made of steel each year
options.why: Consumers who buy steel products lose out from a steel tariff, because they pay higher prices, so they are not the main beneficiaries.

options.t: Foreign steel exporters and their workers
options.why: Foreign steel exporters and their workers are hurt by a tariff, since it makes their steel costlier and cuts the amount they can sell.

options.t: Domestic steel makers, facing less competition
options.why: Domestic steel makers gain most from a steel tariff, because imports become costlier and they face less competition, allowing higher sales and prices.

options.t: Companies that use steel to make goods and cars
options.why: Companies that use steel to make goods and cars pay more for their inputs because of the tariff, so they are harmed, not helped.

q: What is the minimum wage?

options.t: The lowest hourly pay employers may offer
options.why: The minimum wage is the lowest hourly pay that employers may legally offer workers, set by law to protect workers' earnings.

options.t: The highest pay that a worker can earn
options.why: The highest pay a worker can earn describes a wage cap, which the minimum wage is not; the law sets a floor and not a ceiling.

options.t: The pay for part-time workers only in a state
options.why: The minimum wage applies to most workers, full time and part time, and is not limited to part-time work or to a state.

options.t: The average pay across all jobs in the nation
options.why: The average pay across all jobs is the mean wage, a statistic, whereas the minimum wage is a legal lowest rate of pay.

q: Why do economists often debate the minimum wage?

options.t: It has no effect on anyone in the economy
options.why: The minimum wage clearly has effects on workers and firms, which is why economists study and argue about its impact, so it is not neutral.

options.t: It is set by private firms only, not the state
options.why: The minimum wage is set by government, federal or state, rather than by private firms, so this statement is false.

options.t: It can raise some incomes but cut some hiring
options.why: Economists debate it because a higher minimum can raise incomes for some workers while it may cause employers to cut hours or hiring for others.

options.t: It always lowers inflation, so none disagree
options.why: The minimum wage does not always lower inflation; higher labor costs may even raise prices, and economists really do disagree about its effects.

q: What is the purpose of Social Security?

options.t: To provide retirement and disability income
options.why: Social Security provides retirement and disability income, along with survivor benefits, to help workers and their families stay financially secure.

options.t: To insure bank deposits up to a legal limit
options.why: Insuring bank deposits up to a legal limit is the role of the FDIC, which protects savers and is separate from Social Security.

options.t: To regulate the stock market and its traders
options.why: Regulating the stock market and its traders is the job of the SEC, whereas Social Security pays income benefits to eligible people.

options.t: To provide loans to small firms that lack credit
options.why: Providing loans to small firms that lack credit is a function of the SBA, and Social Security does not make business loans.

q: What is a transfer payment?

options.t: Money paid to a worker for a job well done
options.why: Money paid to a worker for a job well done is wages or a bonus, which is earned in exchange for work, unlike a transfer payment.

options.t: Government money given with nothing in return
options.why: A transfer payment is government money given to people with no goods or services received in return, such as Social Security or unemployment benefits.

options.t: Money paid in taxes to the federal government
options.why: Money paid in taxes flows from people to the government, the reverse direction of a transfer payment, which flows from government to individuals.

options.t: Money paid to a contractor for building a new road
options.why: Paying a contractor to build a road buys a service in return, so it is government purchasing and not a transfer payment.

q: What is an economic indicator?

options.t: A tax charged on economic activity of firms
options.why: A tax charged on economic activity is a revenue tool of government and not an economic indicator, which is a statistic used to measure performance.

options.t: A rule that sets prices in markets by law
options.why: A rule that sets prices by law is a price control, a government policy that regulates markets, not a measurement of how the economy is doing.

options.t: A company's list of products for sale online
options.why: A company's list of products for sale online is a product catalog, which describes one business and does not measure the overall economy.

options.t: A statistic showing how the economy performs
options.why: An economic indicator is a statistic, such as GDP or unemployment, that shows how the economy is performing and helps predict what comes next.

q: What does the unemployment rate measure?

options.t: The number of new jobs created last year in total
options.why: The number of new jobs created is a job growth figure, a count of jobs and not a rate, so it differs from the unemployment rate.

options.t: The percent of all people in the country with no job
options.why: The unemployment rate does not use all people in the country as its base, because children, retirees and others outside the labor force are excluded.

options.t: The average wage paid to workers in the economy
options.why: The average wage paid to workers is a measure of earnings, while the unemployment rate concerns people without jobs, not how much workers are paid.

options.t: Percent of the labor force jobless and seeking work
options.why: The unemployment rate is the percent of the labor force that is jobless and actively seeking work, so it measures labor market slack.

q: If the labor force is 200 million and 10 million are unemployed, what is the unemployment rate?

options.why: Unemployment rate is unemployed divided by labor force, so 10 million divided by 200 million equals 0.05, which is 5%.
A result of 0.5% misplaces the decimal point; 10 million out of 200 million is 5 hundredths, not 5 thousandths, so the rate is 5%.
A result of 20% would require 40 million unemployed workers, but the problem gives only 10 million out of a 200 million labor force.
A result of 10% simply repeats the 10 million figure as a percent, while the rate must divide unemployed by the labor force, giving 5%.

q: Who is counted as part of the labor force?

options.t: Only people who have a full-time job all year
options.why: The labor force includes part-time workers and those looking for work, not just full-time workers employed all year, so this definition is too narrow.

options.t: Only people who are unemployed right now
options.why: Counting only the unemployed leaves out all employed workers, who are the majority of the labor force, so this definition is incomplete.

options.t: People employed or actively seeking work
options.why: The labor force consists of people who are employed plus those who are unemployed but actively looking for work.

options.t: All people over the age of 16 in the country
options.why: All people over 16 describes the working-age population, which includes students, retirees and others who are not working or looking for work.

q: The CPI rises from 200 to 210 over a year. What is the inflation rate?

options.why: A rate of 21% mixes up the new CPI value of 210 with a percentage; inflation is the percentage change, which is only 5%.
Inflation is the percentage change in the CPI: 210 minus 200 equals 10, and 10 divided by 200 is 0.05, or 5%.
A rate of 2.1% does not match the calculation, because the CPI rose by 10 points from a base of 200, which is 5%.
A rate of 10% mistakes the 10-point rise for a percentage; the rise must be divided by the starting CPI of 200, giving 5%.

q: What does the Producer Price Index (PPI) measure?

options.t: Changes in stock prices on the exchange
options.why: Changes in stock prices on the exchange are tracked by stock market indexes like the S&P 500, not by the PPI.

options.t: Changes in worker wages in the nation
options.why: Changes in worker wages are measured by wage and earnings indexes, whereas the PPI tracks the prices of goods at the producer level.

options.t: Changes in the prices consumers pay
options.why: Changes in the prices consumers pay are measured by the Consumer Price Index, while the PPI measures prices received by producers.

options.t: Changes in prices producers receive
options.why: The Producer Price Index measures changes in the prices producers receive for their output, often giving an early signal of consumer inflation.

q: What does GDP growth rate show?

options.t: How fast output is growing or shrinking
options.why: The GDP growth rate shows how fast total output of goods and services is growing or shrinking from one period to the next.

options.t: How many jobs were lost in the year
options.why: The number of jobs lost relates to employment data and unemployment figures, not to the growth rate of total output measured by GDP.

options.t: How high interest rates are right now
options.why: How high interest rates are is shown by the federal funds rate or bond yields, and not by the growth rate of GDP.

options.t: How much the government spends in a year
options.why: Government spending is only one component of GDP, so it does not measure the speed at which total output is changing.

q: What is a recession commonly defined as in the news?

options.t: A year of rising prices for most goods
options.why: A year of rising prices describes inflation, not a recession, which is defined by falling output and not by higher prices.

options.t: One day of falling stock prices in the market
options.why: One day of falling stock prices is a market dip and does not meet the definition of a recession, which involves output falling over months.

options.t: Two consecutive quarters of declining GDP
options.why: A recession is commonly defined as two consecutive quarters of declining GDP, meaning the economy has shrunk for six months in a row.

options.t: A month of rising unemployment in a state
options.why: A month of rising unemployment in a state is a local labor change, which is too brief and narrow to qualify as a national recession.

q: What is a depression?

options.t: A drop in the price of one product
options.why: A drop in the price of one product is a normal market change for a single good, not a widespread economic downturn.

options.t: A severe, prolonged economic downturn
options.why: A depression is a severe, prolonged economic downturn, with very high unemployment and sharp falls in output, as in the 1930s Great Depression.

options.t: A mild one-quarter slowdown in output
options.why: A mild one-quarter slowdown is not even a recession, which needs two quarters of decline, and a depression is far deeper and longer.

options.t: A period of fast economic growth overall
options.why: A period of fast economic growth is an expansion or boom, which is the opposite of a depression, where output falls sharply.

q: What is the consumer confidence index?

options.t: A measure of bank interest rates for loans
options.why: Bank interest rates for loans are measured by lending rate data, not by a survey of how consumers feel about the economy.

options.t: A measure of how many goods stores sell each month
options.why: How many goods stores sell each month is retail sales, a spending figure, whereas consumer confidence measures attitudes and expectations, not actual purchases.

options.t: A measure of company profits for the year
options.why: Company profits for the year are reported in corporate earnings data, and they do not measure households' feelings about the economy.

options.t: How optimistic consumers are about the economy
options.why: The consumer confidence index gauges how optimistic consumers feel about the economy and their finances, which helps predict how much they will spend.

q: What do housing starts measure?

options.t: New residential construction projects begun
options.why: Housing starts count new residential construction projects begun in a period, which is a signal of building activity and future economic strength.

options.t: The number of renters in a city or town
options.why: The number of renters in a city is a population or housing survey statistic, not a count of new construction beginning.

options.t: The average price of a home in the nation
options.why: The average price of a home in the nation is a housing price index, not the count of new construction started.

options.t: The number of homes sold during the last year
options.why: The number of homes sold during the last year is measured by home sales data, which tracks transactions of existing or new houses.

q: Which is a leading indicator of the economy?

options.t: The unemployment rate
options.why: The unemployment rate is a lagging indicator because it tends to change after the economy has already turned, not before it does.

options.t: New building permits
options.why: New building permits are a leading indicator, because they rise or fall before construction and spending change, so they hint at where the economy is heading.

options.t: Consumer inflation rates
options.why: Consumer inflation rates are usually treated as a lagging indicator, since prices adjust after economic activity has already shifted.

options.t: Last year's GDP total
options.why: Last year's GDP total is historical data describing what already happened, so it cannot predict future conditions and is not a leading indicator.

q: Which is a lagging indicator of the economy?

options.t: Stock market prices
options.why: Stock market prices are usually a leading indicator, because investors trade on expectations and prices often move before the economy does.

options.t: Consumer confidence
options.why: Consumer confidence is usually a leading indicator, because changes in how optimistic people feel tend to show up before they change spending.

options.t: The unemployment rate
options.why: The unemployment rate is a lagging indicator, because employers cut or add jobs only after sales have already changed, so it trails the economy.

options.t: Housing starts data
options.why: Housing starts data is a leading indicator, since new construction responds early to expected demand and signals the direction the economy will take.

q: What is the federal funds rate?

options.t: The tax rate on federal income earned
options.why: The tax rate on federal income earned is the income tax rate, set by Congress, not the interest rate banks charge each other.

options.t: The rate banks charge each other overnight
options.why: The federal funds rate is the interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans, and the Fed targets it to guide the economy.

options.t: The rate of inflation in the whole economy
options.why: The rate of inflation in the whole economy is measured by price indexes like the CPI, and it differs from the federal funds rate.

options.t: The interest rate a bank charges on a mortgage
options.why: The interest rate a bank charges on a mortgage is a consumer lending rate, which is influenced by the funds rate but is not the same.

q: What does the stock market index, such as the S&P 500, measure?

options.t: The performance of a group of large stocks
options.why: A stock market index like the S&P 500 measures the performance of a group of large stocks, giving a snapshot of the market overall.

options.t: The total debt of the federal government
options.why: The total debt of the federal government is the national debt, a budget figure, and stock indexes do not measure it.

options.t: The number of jobs available in the economy
options.why: The number of jobs available in the economy is a labor market statistic, whereas a stock index tracks the share prices of companies.

options.t: The price of one company's stock on the day
options.why: The price of one company's stock is just that single share price, whereas an index like the S&P 500 combines many companies.

q: What is the trade balance?

options.t: The total amount of tariffs collected
options.why: The total amount of tariffs collected is a government revenue figure from import taxes, not the difference between exports and imports.

options.t: The number of trade agreements signed
options.why: The number of trade agreements signed is a count of policy deals, which does not measure the value of goods traded.

options.t: The gap between exports and imports
options.why: The trade balance is the gap between the value of a country's exports and imports, showing whether it runs a surplus or deficit.

options.t: The value of the currency used at home
options.why: The value of the currency used at home is the exchange rate, which compares currencies, and it is not the balance of exports and imports.

q: Why can a low unemployment rate sometimes lead to higher inflation?

options.t: Workers stop spending money on goods
options.why: If workers stop spending money, demand would fall and prices would ease, which is the opposite of how low unemployment can push inflation up.

options.t: The government bans wage increases
options.why: The government does not ban wage increases when unemployment is low; wages are free to rise, and that is part of why inflation can follow.

options.t: Businesses stop raising prices at all
options.why: Businesses do not stop raising prices when unemployment is low; strong demand and higher labor costs often lead firms to raise prices instead.

options.t: Tight labor markets can push wages up
options.why: When unemployment is low, tight labor markets can push wages up, and firms may raise prices to cover higher costs, causing inflation.

q: What is stagflation?

options.t: Zero inflation with zero unemployment
options.why: Zero inflation with zero unemployment is an ideal outcome and the opposite of stagflation, which is a painful combination of problems.

options.t: High inflation with high unemployment
options.why: Stagflation is the unusual combination of high inflation and high unemployment, with stagnant growth, as in the 1970s oil shock period.

options.t: Low inflation with fast growth overall
options.why: Low inflation with fast growth describes a healthy, strong economy, which is the opposite of stagflation, where conditions are poor on several fronts.

options.t: High growth with falling prices overall
options.why: High growth with falling prices is not stagflation, because stagflation involves weak growth and rising prices, not strong growth and falling prices.

q: What does disposable income mean?

options.t: Income earned only from stock investments
options.why: Income earned only from stock investments is investment income, a source of earnings, and it does not describe what remains after taxes.

options.t: Income spent on necessities only each month
options.why: Income spent on necessities only describes essential spending, and disposable income can be used for any purpose, whether spending or saving.

options.t: Income left after taxes, to spend or save
options.why: Disposable income is the income left after taxes are paid, which households can spend or save as they choose.

options.t: Income before any taxes are paid out of it
options.why: Income before any taxes are paid is gross income, which is larger than disposable income, since taxes have not yet been subtracted.

q: What does per capita GDP measure?

options.t: Economic output per person
options.why: Per capita GDP divides a country's total output by its population, which gives economic output per person and helps compare living standards.

options.t: Government spending per year
options.why: Government spending per year is a budget figure that is only one part of GDP, and it is not divided by population.

options.t: Total exports of a country
options.why: Total exports of a country is a trade figure covering only goods sold abroad, not output per person in the whole economy.

options.t: Total output of large firms
options.why: Total output of large firms covers only part of the economy and is not divided by population, so it is not per capita GDP.

q: What is globalization?

options.t: The ban on trading with other countries
options.why: A ban on trading with other countries is the opposite of globalization, which is defined by expanding cross-border exchange and deepening ties between nations.

options.t: The merger of all countries into one nation
options.why: Globalization does not merge countries into one nation; each keeps its own government, borders and laws while becoming more connected through trade and investment.

options.t: The growth of a single country's local market
options.why: Globalization is about links between many economies, so growth of one country's local market alone describes domestic expansion rather than any worldwide integration.

options.t: Growing links among economies through trade
options.why: Globalization means economies becoming increasingly linked through trade, investment, finance and the movement of ideas, so countries depend on one another more than before.

q: Why do countries trade with one another?

options.t: To get goods they cannot produce as cheaply
options.why: Countries trade mainly to obtain goods that other nations can make at lower cost or that they cannot produce well at home, which raises living standards.

options.t: To avoid using money at all in their trade
options.why: Trade does not avoid money; payments still happen in currencies, and barter is only a rare side case, so this is not the reason countries trade.

options.t: To prevent other nations from growing stronger
options.why: Trade is generally mutually beneficial, so preventing others from growing stronger is not its purpose, and hurting partners would also shrink the gains the country itself enjoys.

options.t: To raise their own prices at home and abroad
options.why: Countries do not trade to raise their own prices; trade usually lowers prices by adding supply and competition, so higher prices at home are not the motive.

q: What is the main benefit of specialization and trade?

options.t: Less cooperation between nations
options.why: Specialization and trade increase cooperation between nations rather than reducing it, so less cooperation is the reverse of what actually happens when countries exchange goods.

options.t: Higher import taxes for all countries
options.why: Higher import taxes are a barrier that restricts trade, and they are not a benefit of specialization, which works by letting goods cross borders more freely.

options.t: More total output and lower prices
options.why: When each producer focuses on what it does best and trades, total output rises and competition and efficiency push prices lower for buyers everywhere.

options.t: Fewer choices for consumers overall
options.why: Trade gives consumers more choices by bringing in foreign varieties, so fewer choices is backwards; the typical result is wider selection and better goods.

q: Country A can make cloth at a lower opportunity cost than Country B, while Country B can grow wheat at a lower opportunity cost. What should they do?

options.t: Neither should trade with the other country
options.why: If neither trades, each country gives up the gains from its lower opportunity cost, so both end up with less cloth and wheat than trading would give.

options.t: A makes cloth, B grows wheat, and they trade
options.why: Each country should specialize where its opportunity cost is lower: A in cloth and B in wheat, then trade, so both consume more than they could alone.

options.t: Each country should make both goods alone
options.why: Making both goods alone ignores comparative advantage, so each country wastes resources on the good it makes at higher opportunity cost, leaving both with smaller total output.

options.t: A makes wheat and B makes cloth, and they trade
options.why: A making wheat and B making cloth reverses comparative advantage, since A is better at cloth and B at wheat, so this plan would raise costs for both.

q: What is an exchange rate?

options.t: The tax on foreign goods at the border post
options.why: A tax on foreign goods at the border is a tariff, which raises the price of imports but is not what an exchange rate measures.

options.t: The interest rate on foreign loans from a bank
options.why: The interest rate on foreign loans is a borrowing cost set by lenders, whereas an exchange rate is a price that converts one currency into another.

options.t: The fee for shipping goods overseas by sea
options.why: A fee for shipping goods overseas is a transport cost added to trade, which is unrelated to the price at which currencies are swapped.

options.t: The price of one currency in terms of another
options.why: An exchange rate states how much of one currency is needed to buy a unit of another, such as dollars per euro, which links prices across countries.

q: If the U.S. dollar strengthens against the euro, imports from Europe become:

options.t: Free of all tariffs
options.why: A stronger dollar does not remove tariffs; tariffs are set by governments, and currency moves change only the dollar price of foreign goods, not the taxes on them.

options.t: Cheaper for Americans
options.why: When the dollar strengthens, each dollar buys more euros, so European goods cost fewer dollars and imports from Europe become cheaper for Americans.

options.t: Pricier for Americans
options.why: Pricier would be the result of a weaker dollar, where each dollar buys fewer euros; a stronger dollar does the opposite and lowers the dollar cost of imports.

options.t: Impossible to buy
options.why: Imports do not become impossible to buy; a stronger dollar actually makes European goods more affordable for Americans, so purchases would tend to rise rather than stop.

q: What is outsourcing?

options.t: Hiring another company, often abroad
options.why: Outsourcing means hiring another company, often in another country, to do work such as manufacturing or customer service instead of the firm doing that work itself.

options.t: Producing all goods inside the company
options.why: Producing all goods inside the company is the opposite of outsourcing, which hands tasks to outside firms, so this describes keeping work in-house.

options.t: Selling shares of stock to the public
options.why: Selling shares of stock to the public is an initial public offering or equity raise, a way of financing the firm rather than contracting out work.

options.t: Building a new factory at home now
options.why: Building a new factory at home is domestic investment in the firm's own capacity, not outsourcing, which relies on an outside company to perform tasks.

q: What is offshoring?

options.t: Moving operations to another city at home
options.why: Moving operations to another city at home is relocation within the same country, whereas offshoring specifically means shifting work across national borders to a foreign location.

options.t: Closing down a business permanently for good
options.why: Closing a business permanently is a shutdown, which ends operations altogether, while offshoring keeps the business running but moves some of its activity abroad.

options.t: Moving business operations to another country
options.why: Offshoring means a company relocates some of its business operations, such as production or services, to another country, often to cut costs like labor.

options.t: Merging with a rival firm at home to cut costs
options.why: Merging with a rival at home is a consolidation of two firms, which says nothing about moving operations abroad, so it does not match offshoring.

q: What is a trade bloc?

options.t: A group of companies that fix prices
options.why: A group of companies that fix prices is a cartel, which is an illegal or restrictive arrangement among firms and not a trade bloc of countries.

options.t: A group of banks that lend to governments
options.why: A group of banks lending to governments is a lending syndicate, a financial arrangement unrelated to countries agreeing on trade rules among themselves.

options.t: A group of workers that bargains for pay
options.why: A group of workers bargaining for pay is a labor union, which negotiates wages and conditions rather than coordinating trade policy between nations.

options.t: Countries agreeing to cut trade barriers
options.why: A trade bloc is a group of countries that agree to cut tariffs and other trade barriers among themselves, like the EU or USMCA.

q: What is the primary goal of the World Trade Organization (WTO)?

options.t: To set the price of oil each month
options.why: Setting the monthly price of oil is not the WTO's role; oil prices come from markets and producer decisions, such as those of OPEC.

options.t: To help trade flow and settle disputes
options.why: The WTO exists to keep trade flowing smoothly through agreed rules and to settle disputes between member countries, giving a forum for resolving trade conflicts.

options.t: To lend money to poor countries or firms
options.why: Lending money to poor countries is the work of institutions such as the World Bank or IMF, not the WTO, which focuses on trade rules.

options.t: To collect taxes from all nations
options.why: The WTO does not collect taxes from nations; it is funded by member contributions and has no power to tax, so this misstates its purpose.

q: What is a cartel?

options.t: A group of consumers that boycott a product
options.why: A group of consumers boycotting a product is a boycott or consumer movement, which acts on the demand side, whereas a cartel is formed by producers.

options.t: A government agency that regulates trade
options.why: A government agency regulating trade is a regulator, which enforces rules, while a cartel is a private arrangement among producers that often breaks competition laws.

options.t: Producers agreeing to control prices or output
options.why: A cartel is a group of producers that agree to restrict output or fix prices, acting like a monopoly to raise profits at buyers' expense.

options.t: A group of workers in a trade union or guild overall
options.why: A group of workers in a trade union or guild is a labor organization that bargains for pay, and it is not an agreement among producers on prices or output.

q: What is balance of payments?

options.t: A record of a company's yearly profit
options.why: A company's yearly profit is recorded on an income statement, which tracks one firm's earnings and has nothing to do with a nation's payments with the world.

options.t: A list of taxes paid by citizens
options.why: A list of taxes paid by citizens is a tax record, while the balance of payments covers all transactions between a country and the rest of the world.

options.t: A statement of government debt only
options.why: Government debt alone is a fiscal measure of public borrowing, while the balance of payments covers private and public flows of goods, services and capital with other nations.

options.t: A record of money flowing in and out
options.why: The balance of payments records all money flowing into and out of a country from trade, services, investment and transfers, over a given period.

q: Which is an example of foreign direct investment?

options.t: A car company building a factory abroad
options.why: A car company building a factory abroad is foreign direct investment because it creates lasting physical ownership and control of productive assets in another country.

options.t: A tourist buying a souvenir abroad
options.why: A tourist buying a souvenir is a small consumer purchase that creates no lasting ownership or control of business assets, so it is not direct investment.

options.t: A bank lending money for one year only
options.why: A one-year bank loan is a short-term lending flow with no ownership or control of a foreign business, so it does not count as direct investment.

options.t: A company paying a customs duty to a port
options.why: A company paying a customs duty to a port is paying a trade tax on goods, which is a cost of importing and not an investment.

q: What is a trade barrier?

options.t: A river that crosses a border or a town
options.why: A river crossing a border is a geographic feature, which might affect transport but is not a government measure and so is not a trade barrier.

options.t: A contract between two exporters on sales
options.why: A contract between two exporters is a private sales agreement that does not restrict trade between countries, so it fails to be a trade barrier.

options.t: A discount for foreign buyers of goods
options.why: A discount for foreign buyers makes foreign goods cheaper and trade easier, which is the opposite of a barrier that restricts or burdens trade.

options.t: A government measure making trade harder
options.why: A trade barrier is a government measure, such as a tariff, quota or strict standard, that makes importing or exporting goods harder or more costly.

q: Which is a non-tariff barrier to trade?

options.t: A free trade agreement among nations
options.why: A free trade agreement lowers barriers and so is the opposite of a barrier; it also works by cutting tariffs, not by adding non-tariff limits.

options.t: A strict product standard for imports
options.why: A strict product standard for imports restricts foreign sellers without using a tax, so it is a non-tariff barrier because it raises the difficulty of selling.

options.t: A lower tax for exporters, a subsidy
options.why: A subsidy lowers costs for domestic exporters and is a support payment rather than a restriction on imports, so it is not a non-tariff barrier.

options.t: A tax on imported goods at the border
options.why: A tax on imported goods at the border is a tariff, which is by definition a tariff barrier rather than a non-tariff one.

q: What is protectionism?

options.t: Policies shielding home industries from rivals
options.why: Protectionism is a set of policies, such as tariffs and quotas, that shield home industries from foreign competition by making imports costlier or harder to bring in.

options.t: Government policies that remove all trade barriers
options.why: Policies removing all trade barriers describe free trade, the opposite of protectionism, which adds barriers to defend domestic producers from foreign rivals.

options.t: Government spending on defense and security
options.why: Spending on defense and security is military policy and has no direct link to shielding home industries from import competition, so it is not protectionism.

options.t: Government rules that protect consumers from fraud
options.why: Rules protecting consumers from fraud are consumer protection laws that regulate sellers, while protectionism concerns shielding domestic producers from foreign competition.

q: What is a common argument for protectionism?

options.t: It lowers prices by keeping out cheap goods
options.why: Lower prices from keeping out cheap goods is false; blocking cheap imports raises prices, so this is not an argument that supporters of protectionism can honestly make.

options.t: It encourages more imports from abroad today
options.why: Protectionism aims to reduce imports, not encourage them, so encouraging more imports from abroad contradicts its purpose and cannot be its main argument.

options.t: It protects domestic jobs facing competition
options.why: Supporters argue that tariffs and quotas protect domestic jobs in industries that would otherwise lose business to cheaper foreign competition, which is the common case made.

options.t: It improves variety for buyers in the market
options.why: Better variety for buyers is a benefit of open trade, since imports add choices, while protectionism usually narrows the range of goods on offer.

q: What is a common argument against protectionism?

options.t: It raises prices and can invite retaliation
options.why: Critics say protectionism raises prices for consumers because competition falls, and that other countries may retaliate with their own barriers, harming exporters.

options.t: It lowers the cost of imports for buyers
options.why: Lowering the cost of imports for buyers is a benefit of free trade, so it cannot be a criticism of protectionism, which does the reverse.

options.t: It always creates more jobs for the nation
options.why: Protectionism does not always create more jobs; it may save some jobs but costs others when prices rise or exporters face retaliation, so always is false.

options.t: It increases competition abroad for local firms
options.why: Protection reduces competition from abroad for local firms, so it would not increase it, and that reduced competition is part of why critics oppose it.

q: What is a free trade agreement?

options.t: A treaty in which countries share their armies
options.why: Countries sharing armies is a defense alliance, such as a military pact, and says nothing about tariffs or the exchange of goods and services.

options.t: A treaty cutting tariffs and trade barriers
options.why: A free trade agreement is a treaty in which member countries cut or remove tariffs and other trade barriers, making goods flow more freely between them.

options.t: A treaty in which countries raise tariffs
options.why: Raising tariffs would be protectionism, the opposite of what a free trade agreement does, since these agreements are designed to lower taxes on trade.

options.t: A treaty in which countries end all trade
options.why: Ending all trade would be a total embargo, while a free trade agreement increases trade between members by lowering barriers instead of removing exchange altogether.

q: What is a currency devaluation?

options.t: A ban on using the currency in the nation
options.why: A ban on using the currency is a legal restriction on money, not a change in its official value, so it does not describe devaluation.

options.t: An increase in the official value of a currency
options.why: An increase in the official value of a currency is a revaluation, the opposite of devaluation, which means the official value is lowered by the government.

options.t: A decrease in the official value of a currency
options.why: Devaluation is a deliberate decrease in a currency's official value under a fixed or managed exchange rate, which makes exports cheaper and imports costlier.

options.t: A new design of the banknotes in a country
options.why: A new design of banknotes is a change to appearance and has no effect on the value of the currency, so it is not devaluation.

q: A bakery's price rises 10% and the quantity demanded falls 5%. What does this say about demand?

options.t: It is unit elastic
options.why: Unit elastic would need the quantity to fall by 10 percent, the same as price; here 5 divided by 10 gives 0.5, which is not 1.

options.t: It is fully elastic
options.why: Fully elastic, or perfectly elastic, means quantity falls to zero from any price rise; a 5 percent drop for a 10 percent rise is far from that.

options.t: It is elastic
options.why: Elastic demand needs an elasticity above 1, but 5 percent divided by 10 percent equals 0.5, so quantity responds less than price and demand is not elastic.

options.t: It is inelastic
options.why: Elasticity is 5 percent divided by 10 percent, which is 0.5, below 1, so quantity demanded changes proportionally less than price and demand is inelastic.

q: Price elasticity of demand is calculated by dividing the percent change in quantity demanded by:

options.t: The percent change in supply
options.why: Dividing by the percent change in supply would give a ratio between demand and supply changes, not price elasticity, which measures how demand responds to price.

options.t: The percent change in income
options.why: Dividing by the percent change in income gives income elasticity of demand, a different measure, not the price elasticity that this question asks for.

options.t: The percent change in costs
options.why: Costs affect supply, so dividing by the percent change in costs does not give price elasticity of demand, which relates quantity demanded to price.

options.t: The percent change in price
options.why: Price elasticity of demand equals the percent change in quantity demanded divided by the percent change in price, which shows how sensitive buyers are to price.

q: Quantity demanded falls 20% when price rises 10%. What is the price elasticity of demand?

options.t: 10, so demand is elastic
options.why: An elasticity of 10 would need quantity to fall 100 percent for a 10 percent price rise; the actual ratio is 20 divided by 10, which is 2.

options.t: 2, so demand is elastic
options.why: Elasticity equals 20 percent divided by 10 percent, which is 2; being above 1 means quantity falls proportionally more than price, so demand is elastic.

options.t: 1, so demand is unitary
options.why: An elasticity of 1 would need a 10 percent quantity drop for a 10 percent price rise, but the drop is 20 percent, so the ratio is 2.

options.t: 0.5, so demand is inelastic
options.why: An elasticity of 0.5 would mean a 5 percent quantity drop for a 10 percent price rise, but the stated drop is 20 percent, giving 2.

q: Which factor makes demand for a good more elastic?

options.t: The good is a basic necessity of life
options.why: A basic necessity of life tends to make demand less elastic, because people must keep buying it even when the price rises, so this lowers elasticity.

options.t: Buyers have very little time to react
options.why: Having very little time to react makes demand less elastic, since buyers cannot easily switch or change habits in the short run.

options.t: Many close substitutes are available
options.why: When many close substitutes are available, buyers can easily switch to another product if the price rises, so quantity demanded is more sensitive and demand is elastic.

options.t: The good is a tiny share of the budget
options.why: A good that is a tiny share of the budget makes buyers less sensitive to price changes, so demand is less elastic, not more.

q: What is income elasticity of demand for a normal good?

options.t: Positive, because demand rises as income rises
options.why: For a normal good, income elasticity is positive, because buyers purchase more of it as their income rises, which is the definition of a normal good.

options.t: Zero, because demand never responds to income
options.why: Zero income elasticity would mean demand does not respond to income, which describes a neutral good, not a normal good whose demand rises with income.

options.t: Negative, because demand falls as income rises
options.why: A negative income elasticity describes an inferior good, where demand falls as income rises, which is the opposite of how a normal good behaves.

options.t: Infinite, because every buyer spends all of it
options.why: Infinite elasticity is not a sensible description of a normal good; demand rises with income by a finite amount and buyers do not spend everything on it.

q: What is an inferior good?

options.t: A good whose price never changes at all for anyone
options.why: A good whose price never changes is a fixed price case and has nothing to do with income, which is what defines inferior goods.

options.t: A good that people buy more of as income rises
options.why: Buying more of a good as income rises describes a normal good, so this is the opposite of an inferior good, whose demand falls as income grows.
