options.t: A good that is of poor quality and cannot be sold
options.why: An inferior good is not defined by poor quality or being unsellable; it is defined by how demand responds to income, and inferior goods are often widely sold.

options.t: A good people buy less of as their income rises
options.why: An inferior good is one people buy less of as their income rises, because they switch to better alternatives, for example instant noodles or bus rides.

q: What is cross-price elasticity used to show?

options.t: How demand for one good responds to another good's price
options.why: Cross-price elasticity shows how demand for one good changes when the price of another good changes, revealing whether the two goods are substitutes or complements.

options.t: How prices differ between two countries over time
options.why: Differences in prices between two countries over time describe price comparisons or exchange rate effects, not cross-price elasticity, which links demand for one good to another's price.

options.t: How income affects how much people save each year
options.why: How income affects saving is a question about the savings rate and income, which cross-price elasticity does not measure; it involves two goods' prices.

options.t: How the supply of a good responds to its own price over time
options.why: Supply responding to a good's own price is price elasticity of supply, which involves one good and the supply side, not cross-price elasticity of demand.

q: The price of tea rises and demand for coffee increases. What does this suggest about tea and coffee?

options.t: They are complements
options.why: Complements would see demand for coffee fall when tea gets pricier, since goods used together move in opposite directions; here coffee demand rose, so they are not.

options.t: They are substitutes
options.why: When one good gets pricier and demand for the other rises, buyers are switching between them, which means tea and coffee are substitutes.

options.t: They are unrelated goods
options.why: Unrelated goods would show no change in coffee demand when the price of tea changes, but demand for coffee increased, so there is a link.

options.t: They are inferior goods
options.why: Inferior goods are defined by how demand reacts to income, not to another good's price, so this does not explain the rise in coffee demand.

q: What does price elasticity of supply measure?

options.t: How much profit responds to changes in taxes on firms
options.why: How profit responds to taxes on firms is a question of tax incidence and profitability, not price elasticity of supply, which links quantity supplied to price.

options.t: How much costs respond to changes in output levels
options.why: How costs respond to output describes the shape of the cost curves, which is not elasticity of supply, a measure of quantity supplied against price.

options.t: How much quantity supplied responds to a price change
options.why: Price elasticity of supply measures how much the quantity supplied changes in response to a change in price, showing how flexible producers are.

options.t: How much quantity demanded responds to a price change
options.why: How quantity demanded responds to a price change is price elasticity of demand, the buyer-side measure, while supply elasticity concerns what producers offer.

q: Why is supply usually more elastic in the long run than in the short run?

options.t: Producers have time to expand capacity
options.why: In the long run producers have time to expand capacity, build plants and hire workers, so quantity supplied can respond more strongly to a price change.

options.t: Costs fall to zero over a long period
options.why: Costs do not fall to zero over a long period; inputs always have a price, so this is not why long-run supply is more elastic.

options.t: Producers have less time to change output
options.why: Having less time to change output would make supply less elastic, which is the short-run situation, so this reverses the true explanation.

options.t: Prices stop affecting what producers do
options.why: Prices keep affecting producers in the long run, and in fact they guide entry and expansion, so this claim is false and explains nothing.

q: What is a price floor above equilibrium likely to create?

options.t: A perfect market balance
options.why: A perfect market balance exists only at the equilibrium price; a floor set above equilibrium prevents the price from falling to that balance point.

options.t: A shortage of the good
options.why: A shortage appears when price is held below equilibrium, as with a price ceiling; a floor above equilibrium has the opposite effect.

options.t: A fall in supply quantity
options.why: A fall in supply quantity is not the effect; a higher price actually raises the quantity suppliers want to sell while buyers want less.

options.t: A surplus of the good
options.why: A price floor above equilibrium raises the price so that sellers offer more than buyers will purchase, creating a surplus of the good.

q: Who bears more of a tax placed on a good when demand is inelastic and supply is elastic?

options.t: Sellers bear most of the tax
options.why: When demand is inelastic and supply is elastic, sellers can easily cut output while buyers cannot cut purchases, so sellers bear less of the tax, not most.

options.t: The government bears the cost
options.why: The government collects the tax revenue and does not bear its economic burden; the burden falls on buyers and sellers through the prices they pay and receive.

options.t: Buyers bear most of the tax
options.why: The more inelastic side bears more of the tax; with inelastic demand, buyers cannot easily cut back, so the price they pay rises most.

options.t: No one bears the tax at all
options.why: Someone always bears a tax, since the buyer's price rises or the seller's received price falls; the split depends on elasticity, but never disappears entirely.

q: What is consumer surplus?

options.t: The gap between price and the cost of making a good for sale
options.why: The gap between price and the cost of making a good is producer surplus, which belongs to sellers rather than buyers, so this describes the wrong side.

options.t: The gap between what buyers would pay and what they pay
options.why: Consumer surplus is the difference between the most buyers would be willing to pay and the price they actually pay, measuring their gain from the purchase.

options.t: The total money spent by all the buyers in a market
options.why: The total money spent by all buyers is consumer spending or total revenue to sellers, not surplus, which is a gain above what they pay.

options.t: The extra goods left unsold on shelves at the end
options.why: Extra goods left unsold on shelves describe excess supply or a surplus of goods in the market sense, not consumer surplus, which measures a buyer's benefit.

q: What is producer surplus?

options.t: The money that producers spend on materials, labor and rent
options.why: Money producers spend on materials, labor and rent is their cost of production, not a surplus, which is the benefit left over after those costs.

options.t: The unsold goods left in a warehouse at the end of the year
options.why: Unsold goods left in a warehouse are inventory or excess supply, not producer surplus, which measures the gain to sellers from the price received.

options.t: The gap between what buyers would pay and what they pay in a market
options.why: The gap between what buyers would pay and what they pay is consumer surplus, which measures the buyer side, so it is the wrong concept here.

options.t: The gap between the price received and the cost of making a good
options.why: Producer surplus is the difference between the price a seller receives and the minimum cost of making the good, showing the seller's gain from the sale.

q: A buyer would pay $12 for a meal but pays $9. What is the buyer's consumer surplus?

options.why: Nine dollars is the price the buyer pays, not the surplus; surplus is the willingness to pay minus the price, so 12 minus 9 gives a different number.
Consumer surplus equals the most the buyer would pay minus the price paid, so 12 minus 9 equals 3 dollars of gain from the meal.
Twelve dollars is the buyer's willingness to pay, not the surplus; the surplus subtracts the price actually paid, giving 12 minus 9, which is 3.
Twenty-one dollars comes from adding 12 and 9, but surplus is found by subtracting the price from willingness to pay, which gives 3 dollars.

q: Which concept says that rational people compare extra benefits with extra costs?

options.t: Thinking at the margin
options.why: Thinking at the margin means comparing the extra benefit of one more unit with its extra cost, which is how rational people decide whether to do more.

options.t: The circular income flow
options.why: The circular income flow is a model of how money moves between households and firms, and it does not describe weighing extra benefits against extra costs.

options.t: The law of large numbers
options.why: The law of large numbers is a statistics idea about averages in big samples, and it is not an economic rule for comparing extra benefits with costs.

options.t: The principle of advantage
options.why: The principle of advantage is not the standard name for this idea; comparative advantage concerns relative opportunity costs in trade, not weighing extra benefits against costs.

q: What does the circular flow model show?

options.t: How a single firm decides its output and prices each year
options.why: How a single firm decides its output and prices is a theory of the firm, while the circular flow shows the whole economy's interactions.

options.t: How taxes move in one direction only, from firms to the state
options.why: Taxes do not move in one direction only; the circular flow shows money going both ways between households, firms and the government, so this is inaccurate.

options.t: How money, goods and resources move between households and firms
options.why: The circular flow model shows how money, goods, services and resources move between households and firms through product and resource markets, in a repeating loop.

options.t: How prices rise in a spiral as wages and costs push each other up
options.why: A spiral of rising prices as wages and costs push each other up is a wage-price spiral, a feature of inflation, not the circular flow.

q: In the circular flow, what do households sell to firms?

options.t: Government bonds and notes
options.why: Government bonds and notes are financial assets sold by the government to borrowers and lenders, and are not what households sell to firms in the flow.

options.t: Labor and other resources
options.why: In the resource market households sell their labor, land and capital to firms, and in return they receive income such as wages, rent and interest.

options.t: Finished goods and services
options.why: Finished goods and services are what firms sell to households in the product market, so this is the reverse direction of the flow.

options.t: Inventory held in warehouses
options.why: Inventory held in warehouses belongs to firms and is not sold by households, so it does not describe what households sell in the circular flow.

q: What is a production possibilities frontier (PPF)?

options.t: A line showing the price of two goods over time in a market
options.why: A line showing the price of two goods over time is a price chart, which tracks costs and not the output an economy can produce.

options.t: A list of the resources a country owns and uses each year
options.why: A list of resources a country owns describes its factor endowment, not the PPF, which shows the combinations of two goods that those resources can produce.

options.t: A curve showing the most of two goods an economy can make
options.why: A PPF is a curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its resources and technology, so it illustrates scarcity and trade-offs.

options.t: A graph of a firm's yearly profit over the last decade
options.why: A graph of a firm's yearly profit over a decade is a financial chart for one company, not a model of a whole economy's output choices.

q: What does a point inside the production possibilities frontier mean?

options.t: The economy has stopped producing anything
options.why: An economy at a point inside the frontier is still producing something; it is simply producing less than it could, so stopping everything is not implied.

options.t: The economy uses resources at full capacity
options.why: Using resources at full capacity puts the economy on the frontier, not inside it, so this describes points on the curve rather than below it.

options.t: The economy has more resources than ever
options.why: A point inside the frontier does not show more resources; the frontier would shift outward for that, whereas an inside point means existing resources are not fully used.

options.t: Resources are underused or inefficient
options.why: A point inside the PPF means the economy could make more of one or both goods, so resources are idle, underused or used inefficiently.

q: What does a point outside the production possibilities frontier show?

options.t: An output level that is unattainable with current resources
options.why: A point outside the PPF shows an output level that cannot be reached with the economy's current resources and technology, though growth might make it possible later.

options.t: An output level with no opportunity cost at all for a firm
options.why: Every output choice carries an opportunity cost, so claiming a point outside the frontier has none is false; the point is simply unattainable at present.

options.t: An output level that wastes resources and labor each year
options.why: Wasting resources and labor is what a point inside the frontier shows, since output falls short of capacity, so this does not describe a point outside.

options.t: An output level that is easy to reach with the labor and machines
options.why: A point outside the frontier is not easy to reach; it exceeds what current labor and machines can produce, so it is unattainable without growth.

q: What would shift a country's production possibilities frontier outward?

options.t: A rise in the price of imports now
options.why: A rise in the price of imports affects costs and consumption but does not change how much the economy can produce with its resources, so no shift occurs.

options.t: A decision to make more of one good
options.why: Making more of one good moves the economy along the frontier rather than shifting it, since resources and technology remain the same.

options.t: A fall in the number of workers
options.why: A fall in the number of workers shrinks the resources available, which would shift the frontier inward, not outward, so this does the opposite.

options.t: Better technology or more resources
options.why: Better technology or more resources raise how much the economy can produce of both goods, so the whole production possibilities frontier shifts outward.

q: What is economic growth?

options.t: A fall in the number of jobs in the nation
options.why: A fall in the number of jobs is a rise in unemployment, which signals a weak economy and is the reverse of economic growth.

options.t: A rise in prices across the whole economy
options.why: A rise in prices across the economy is inflation, a different concept; growth is about output, not about the general price level.

options.t: An increase in an economy's output over time
options.why: Economic growth is an increase in the total output of goods and services in an economy over time, usually measured by rising real GDP.

options.t: A rise in government spending only each year
options.why: A rise in government spending only is a fiscal change that may or may not raise output, so it does not define economic growth.

q: Which factor most directly raises long-run economic growth?

options.t: Increases in productivity
options.why: Rising productivity means more output from the same inputs, which directly lifts potential output and living standards, making it the key driver of long-run growth.

options.t: Higher inflation rates
options.why: Higher inflation does not raise long-run growth; it creates uncertainty and can harm investment, so it is not a direct driver of expanding output.

options.t: A bigger trade deficit
options.why: A bigger trade deficit means imports exceed exports, which does not directly add to productive capacity and so does not drive long-run growth.

options.t: Shorter business cycles
options.why: Shorter business cycles affect the timing of ups and downs but not the underlying ability to produce, so they do not raise long-run growth directly.

q: What is human capital?

options.t: Land and natural resources of a country
options.why: Land and natural resources are a separate factor of production, not human capital, which refers to the abilities that people themselves hold.

options.t: Workers' skills, knowledge and experience
options.why: Human capital is the skills, knowledge, education and experience that workers hold, which make them more productive and raise the output of the economy.

options.t: Money that people keep in savings accounts
options.why: Money kept in savings accounts is financial capital or wealth, not human capital, since it is not a skill or ability within people.

options.t: Machines used to make goods in a factory
options.why: Machines used in a factory are physical capital, which is equipment, whereas human capital refers to qualities of the workers themselves.

q: What is physical capital?

options.t: Shares of company stock held by many investors
options.why: Shares of company stock are financial assets that represent ownership claims, and they are not tools or buildings used directly to make goods.

options.t: Workers' skills and education, called human capital
options.why: Workers' skills and education are human capital, which is a different factor from physical capital, which consists of objects used in production.

options.t: Cash held by households in their bank accounts
options.why: Cash held by households is money, a financial asset that is not itself used to produce goods, so it is not physical capital.

options.t: Tools, machines and buildings used in production
options.why: Physical capital is the tools, machines, buildings and equipment that firms use to produce goods and services, and it is made by people.

q: What is the unemployment rate formula?

options.t: Unemployed divided by the population
options.why: Dividing unemployed by the whole population is wrong, because the population includes children and others outside the labor force, so the rate would be understated.

options.t: Employed divided by the labor force
options.why: Employed divided by the labor force gives the employment share, not the unemployment rate, which looks at jobless people who are seeking work.

options.t: Unemployed divided by the labor force
options.why: The unemployment rate equals the number of unemployed people divided by the labor force, which is the employed plus those looking for work.

options.t: Labor force divided by the unemployed
options.why: The labor force divided by the unemployed turns the ratio upside down, giving a number greater than one instead of a percentage rate.

q: A discouraged worker has stopped looking for a job. How is this person counted?

options.t: As unemployed workers
options.why: A discouraged worker has stopped searching, and the unemployed must be actively looking for work, so this person is not counted as unemployed.

options.t: Not in the labor force
options.why: Because a discouraged worker has given up searching and is not working, they are counted as outside the labor force rather than as unemployed.

options.t: As employed workers
options.why: A discouraged worker has no job, so counting them as employed would be wrong; employed means currently holding paid work.

options.t: As part of the labor force
options.why: The labor force includes only those working or actively seeking work, and a discouraged worker is not seeking work, so they are excluded.

q: What is frictional unemployment?

options.t: Short-term joblessness while people move between jobs
options.why: Frictional unemployment is short-term joblessness while people search for or move between jobs, such as new graduates or workers switching careers, and it exists even in healthy economies.

options.t: Joblessness that follows the seasons of the year
options.why: Joblessness following the seasons is seasonal unemployment, found in work like farming or tourism, which is a different category from frictional unemployment.

options.t: Joblessness caused when workers' skills are not needed
options.why: Joblessness from skills no longer being needed is structural unemployment, caused by changes in technology or industries, not the brief search gap of frictional unemployment.

options.t: Joblessness caused by a recession in the economy
options.why: Joblessness caused by a recession is cyclical unemployment, tied to falling demand across the economy, which is different from frictional job-switching.

q: What is the natural rate of unemployment?

options.t: Zero unemployment at all times in every part of the economy
options.why: Zero unemployment is not realistic because frictional and structural unemployment always exist, so the natural rate is above zero even at full employment.

options.t: The rate during a deep recession, when firms lay off workers
options.why: The rate during a deep recession includes cyclical unemployment and exceeds the natural rate, so it is higher than the level at full employment.

options.t: The rate that remains when the economy is at full employment
options.why: The natural rate is the unemployment that remains at full employment, made up of frictional and structural unemployment but without cyclical joblessness from downturns.

options.t: The rate set by law and fixed in every state each year
options.why: The natural rate is not set by law; it results from labor market conditions, and no state fixes it each year.

q: What is cost-push inflation?

options.t: Falling prices caused by weak demand overall overall
options.why: Falling prices caused by weak demand is deflation or a demand shortfall, not cost-push inflation, which describes prices rising because of supply-side costs.

options.t: Rising prices caused by too much spending
options.why: Rising prices caused by too much spending is demand-pull inflation, the other main type, so it does not describe cost-push inflation.

options.t: Rising prices caused by a stronger currency
options.why: A stronger currency usually lowers import prices and eases inflation, so rising prices from a stronger currency is not how cost-push inflation arises.

options.t: Rising prices caused by higher production costs
options.why: Cost-push inflation occurs when firms face higher production costs, such as wages or raw materials, and pass them on as higher prices across the economy.

q: What is demand-pull inflation?

options.t: Prices that stay constant despite higher demand
options.why: Prices staying constant despite higher demand does not describe inflation, so it cannot be demand-pull, which involves prices rising when demand is strong.

options.t: Rising prices caused by demand that outpaces supply
options.why: Demand-pull inflation happens when total demand grows faster than the economy's ability to supply goods, so buyers bid up prices across the economy.

options.t: Rising prices caused by higher production costs at firms
options.why: Rising prices from higher production costs is cost-push inflation, which comes from the supply side, rather than demand-pull inflation.

options.t: Falling prices caused by lower demand in markets
options.why: Falling prices from lower demand describes deflation, the reverse of inflation, so it cannot be demand-pull inflation, which raises prices.

q: Who tends to lose most when inflation is unexpectedly high?

options.t: Lenders who receive fixed payments
options.why: When inflation is unexpectedly high, lenders receiving fixed payments lose most, because the money they get back buys less than they expected when lending.

options.t: Borrowers who owe fixed amounts
options.why: Borrowers who owe fixed amounts gain from unexpected inflation, because they repay with money worth less, so they are not the ones who lose.

options.t: Owners of real estate that gains value
options.why: Owners of real estate usually gain when inflation rises, since property values tend to rise with prices, so they do not lose most.

options.t: Workers whose wages are indexed
options.why: Workers whose wages are indexed receive pay raises that follow inflation, which protects their purchasing power, so they are not hurt most.

q: What is the money multiplier effect?

options.t: Bank lending expands the money supply beyond the initial deposit
options.why: The money multiplier describes how banks lend out part of each deposit, which creates new deposits and expands the money supply beyond the initial deposit.

options.t: Banks refusing to lend deposits, keeping all money in their vaults
options.why: Banks refusing to lend and keeping all money in vaults would stop money creation, which is the opposite of the multiplier effect.

options.t: Prices doubling each year for all goods and services alike
options.why: Prices doubling each year describes hyperinflation, which concerns the price level and not how lending expands the money supply.

options.t: Governments printing no new money at all in a given year
options.why: Governments printing no new money describes a fixed supply, whereas the multiplier concerns banks creating money through lending, not government printing.

q: What is a reserve requirement?

options.t: The share of loans banks must make each year to customers
options.why: The share of loans banks must make is not a reserve requirement; reserve rules limit lending by requiring part of deposits to be held back.

options.t: The fee customers pay for opening new bank accounts
options.why: The fee customers pay for opening accounts is a bank charge and has no connection to the reserves that regulators require banks to hold.

options.t: The share of deposits banks must hold rather than lend
options.why: A reserve requirement is the fraction of deposits that banks must hold in reserve rather than lend out, which limits how much money they can create.

options.t: The tax banks pay on deposits held by savers each year
options.why: The tax banks pay on deposits is a levy, not a reserve requirement, which forces banks to keep funds rather than paying them to government.

q: What is the discount rate?

options.t: The price cut on sale items in a store or a shop each day
options.why: A price cut on sale items is a retail markdown, a different meaning of discount, and it has nothing to do with central bank lending.

options.t: The interest rate the Fed charges banks that borrow from it
options.why: The discount rate is the interest rate the Federal Reserve charges commercial banks when they borrow directly from it, usually to cover short-term needs.

options.t: The interest rate on home loans from a bank to a buyer
options.why: The interest rate on home loans is a mortgage rate set by lenders, and the discount rate is a central bank rate for borrowing banks.

options.t: The interest rate banks charge each other overnight on short loans
options.why: The overnight rate that banks charge each other is the federal funds rate, a different rate from the discount rate charged by the Fed.

q: What are open market operations?

options.t: Stores extending their business hours at night
options.why: Stores extending business hours are a retail decision, and the phrase open market operations refers to central bank trading, not shop opening times.

options.t: The government selling public land to buyers
options.why: The government selling public land is a sale of assets and is not how the central bank adjusts the money supply.

options.t: Banks opening branches in new towns for customers
options.why: Banks opening branches in new towns is a business expansion; open market operations do not refer to bank locations but to central bank securities trading.

options.t: The Fed buying and selling government securities
options.why: Open market operations are the Fed's buying and selling of government securities to change bank reserves and influence the money supply and interest rates.

q: If the Fed buys government securities from banks, what happens to the money supply?

options.t: It is unchanged
options.why: The money supply does not stay unchanged, because when the Fed buys securities it pays banks, which raises their reserves and lets them lend more.

options.t: It falls to zero
options.why: The money supply does not fall to zero; Fed purchases add reserves to banks, so the supply of money grows rather than disappearing.

options.t: It increases
options.why: Buying securities puts new reserves in banks' hands, which lets them lend more, so the money supply increases through the multiplier process.

options.t: It decreases
options.why: A decrease would result if the Fed sold securities and took reserves out of the banking system, which is the opposite of buying them.

q: What is the Phillips curve about?

options.t: The trade-off between inflation and unemployment
options.why: The Phillips curve describes the short-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment, where lower unemployment tends to come with higher inflation and the reverse.

options.t: The trade-off between imports and exports overall
options.why: The trade-off between imports and exports is a trade balance idea, while the Phillips curve links inflation with unemployment rather than trade flows.

options.t: The trade-off between taxes and spending overall
options.why: The trade-off between taxes and spending is a fiscal choice, not the Phillips curve, which relates unemployment to the rate of inflation.

options.t: The trade-off between saving and borrowing each year
options.why: The trade-off between saving and borrowing is a credit and interest idea, whereas the Phillips curve concerns inflation and joblessness.

q: What is a government budget surplus?

options.t: Exports exceeding imports in value for a year
options.why: Exports exceeding imports is a trade surplus, which concerns international trade and is a different measure from the government budget.

options.t: Tax revenue exceeding government spending in a year
options.why: A budget surplus occurs when tax revenue is greater than government spending in a given year, leaving the government with money left over.

options.t: A rise in the national debt level in a given year
options.why: A rise in national debt happens with a deficit, since the government borrows more; a surplus would allow debt to fall instead.

options.t: Government spending exceeding tax revenue in a given year
options.why: Government spending exceeding tax revenue is a budget deficit, which is the opposite of a surplus, and the government must borrow to cover it.

q: What is crowding out?

options.t: Too many shoppers filling a store at the same time, so the store looks busy
options.why: Too many shoppers filling a store is simple crowding in the everyday sense, not the economic idea of government borrowing affecting private investment.

options.t: Firms forcing rivals out of the market by cutting prices below cost
options.why: Firms forcing rivals out by cutting prices below cost is predatory pricing, a competition issue, and has nothing to do with government borrowing.

options.t: Banks refusing to lend to the government for a long period of time
options.why: Banks refusing to lend to the government would limit public borrowing, which is the opposite of the demand for funds that causes crowding out.

options.t: Government borrowing raising interest rates and reducing private investment
options.why: Crowding out happens when government borrowing raises interest rates, which makes loans costlier and so reduces private investment and spending by businesses.

q: What is a progressive tax system?

options.t: Only the poor pay taxes
options.why: It is false that only the poor pay taxes; a progressive system actually asks higher earners to pay more, and everyone with taxable income contributes.

options.t: Everyone pays the same rate
options.why: Everyone paying the same rate describes a flat tax, which is a different structure from a progressive system whose rates change with income.

options.t: Rates fall as income rises
options.why: Rates falling as income rises describes a regressive tax, which takes a bigger share from low earners, the opposite of progressive.

options.t: Rates rise as income rises
options.why: In a progressive tax system the tax rate rises as income rises, so higher earners pay a larger share of their income than lower earners.

q: What is an automatic stabilizer?

options.t: A rule that bans recessions in the whole economy for good
options.why: No rule can ban recessions; automatic stabilizers soften downturns but do not prevent them, so this claim overstates what such policies can do.

options.t: A machine that fixes prices in the whole economy for firms
options.why: A machine that fixes prices is not a stabilizer; the term refers to existing fiscal policies, not to devices or price controls.

options.t: A policy that cushions the economy without new legislation
options.why: An automatic stabilizer is a policy, such as progressive taxes or unemployment benefits, that cushions the economy during swings without needing new legislation to take effect.

options.t: A law passed in each downturn by Congress to raise spending
options.why: A law passed in each downturn by Congress is discretionary fiscal policy, which needs a new vote, whereas automatic stabilizers work without any new action.

q: Why do unemployment benefits act as an automatic stabilizer?

options.t: They rise in recessions and support spending
options.why: Unemployment benefits rise in recessions as more people lose jobs, which props up household income and spending without any new law, so they stabilize the economy.

options.t: They fall in recessions and cut spending
options.why: Benefits do not fall in recessions; more people qualify when jobs are lost, so the total paid out rises, which supports spending rather than cutting it.

options.t: They end when the economy slows down a lot
options.why: Benefits do not end when the economy slows; they continue and grow as unemployment rises, so this misdescribes how the stabilizer works in downturns.

options.t: They raise taxes on workers in the economy
options.why: Unemployment benefits are payments to jobless people and do not raise taxes on workers, so this does not explain their stabilizing role.

q: Which feature marks a command economy?

options.t: Prices guide production decisions in firms
options.why: Prices guiding production decisions is a feature of a market economy, where supply and demand signals steer firms, and not of a command economy.

options.t: Central planners decide what to produce
options.why: In a command economy central planners decide what to produce, how much and for whom, replacing market signals with government plans and targets.

options.t: Consumers decide through their spending
options.why: Consumers deciding through their spending is a market economy feature, where purchases signal what firms should make, not a command economy trait.

options.t: Customs guide who does which job and why
options.why: Customs guiding who does which job is the mark of a traditional economy, where tradition rather than planners decides how work is divided.

q: What is a key advantage of a market economy?

options.t: Competition pushes efficiency and innovation
options.why: Competition pushes firms to cut costs, improve products and innovate to win customers, which is a key advantage of a market economy.

options.t: Incomes are always equal for all people
options.why: Incomes are not always equal in a market economy; rewards depend on skills and ownership, so unequal incomes are a known drawback, not an advantage.

options.t: Public goods are always supplied in full
options.why: Public goods are often under-supplied by markets because nobody can be charged for them, so supplying them in full is not guaranteed.

options.t: Central planning removes all waste in production
options.why: Central planning is a feature of command economies, and even there it does not remove all waste, so this is not a market advantage.

q: What is a key disadvantage of a pure market economy?

options.t: It has no competition at all for sellers
options.why: A pure market economy has plenty of competition among sellers, so claiming it has none misstates its main feature, which is rivalry.

options.t: It bans private property for all citizens
options.why: A pure market economy relies on private property, so saying it bans private property for all citizens reverses its basic principle.

options.t: It sets prices by central order for all goods
options.why: Setting prices by central order describes a command economy; in a market economy prices come from the interaction of buyers and sellers.

options.t: It may leave some people without basic needs
options.why: A pure market economy rewards those with money or skills and may leave people with low income without basic needs such as food or health care.

q: Which situation best fits a traditional economy?

options.t: Firms compete using prices and advertising to win sales
options.why: Firms competing with prices and advertising fits a market economy, where businesses rival each other for buyers, and not a traditional economy.

options.t: Families pass down farming methods through the generations
options.why: In a traditional economy, customs and habits decide production, so families passing down farming methods through the generations is a clear example.

options.t: A government sets quotas for every factory and what each makes
options.why: A government setting quotas for every factory is a command economy, in which central authorities direct production, not a traditional economy.

options.t: A central bank sets interest rates for the whole nation
options.why: A central bank setting interest rates is a feature of a modern monetary system and has no link to traditional economies guided by custom.

q: What is explicit cost?

options.t: A cost the firm has long since forgotten
options.why: A forgotten cost is not a defined category; explicit costs are clear, recorded payments such as wages and rent that the firm knows it makes.

options.t: A cost that never involves any cash payment
options.why: An explicit cost does involve cash payment, so a cost that never involves any is an implicit cost, which is the opposite idea.

options.t: A direct payment a firm makes to outsiders
options.why: An explicit cost is a direct payment a firm makes to outside parties, such as wages, rent, materials and interest, recorded in its accounts.

options.t: The value of the owner's own time at work
options.why: The value of the owner's own time is an implicit cost, an opportunity cost with no payment to outsiders, so it is not explicit.

q: What is implicit cost?

options.t: A cost shown on the income statement as a payment to suppliers
options.why: A payment to suppliers shown on the income statement is an explicit cost, so it is the opposite of an implicit cost, which has no payment.

options.t: A direct cash payment to suppliers, staff or lenders
options.why: A direct cash payment to suppliers, staff or lenders is an explicit cost, not implicit, because money actually leaves the firm to outsiders.

options.t: The opportunity cost of resources the firm already owns
options.why: An implicit cost is the opportunity cost of resources the firm already owns and uses, such as the owner's time or building, with no cash paid.

options.t: A cost that varies with the level of output each month
options.why: A cost that varies with output is a variable cost, which is a different classification and can be either explicit or implicit.

q: How is economic profit calculated?

options.t: Total revenue plus implicit costs and taxes
options.why: Adding implicit costs and taxes to revenue would inflate the figure instead of finding profit; costs must be subtracted from revenue, not added.

options.t: Total revenue minus explicit costs only, no owner pay
options.why: Subtracting only explicit costs gives accounting profit, which ignores the owner's opportunity costs, so it does not measure economic profit.

options.t: Explicit costs minus implicit costs for a year
options.why: Explicit costs minus implicit costs does not involve revenue at all, so it cannot be profit, which depends on what the firm earns.

options.t: Total revenue minus explicit and implicit costs
options.why: Economic profit equals total revenue minus both explicit and implicit costs, so it accounts for the opportunity cost of the owner's own resources.

q: A shop earns $90,000, pays $60,000 in cash costs and the owner gave up a $40,000 job. What is the economic profit?

options.why: Economic profit equals 90,000 minus 60,000 cash costs minus the 40,000 job given up, which is minus 10,000, so the shop earns less than the owner's best alternative.
Seventy thousand dollars could come from adding the costs, 60,000 plus 40,000 is 100,000, yet profit subtracts costs from revenue and does not add them.
Thirty thousand dollars is only revenue minus cash costs, which is accounting profit; subtracting the 40,000 opportunity cost as well gives minus 10,000.
Ten thousand dollars has the wrong sign; revenue of 90,000 is less than total costs of 100,000, so the economic result is a loss of 10,000.

q: What does a shutdown decision compare in the short run?

options.t: Price against the owner's wishes
options.why: Price against the owner's wishes is not an economic comparison; the shutdown rule is based on measurable revenue and costs rather than preferences.

options.t: Revenue against variable costs
options.why: The short-run shutdown decision compares revenue with variable costs, because if revenue cannot cover them the firm loses less by stopping production.

options.t: Profit against last year's profit
options.why: Comparing profit with last year's profit is not the rule; a firm may earn less than last year and still operate if it covers variable costs.

options.t: Revenue against fixed costs only
options.why: Fixed costs must be paid whether or not the firm produces in the short run, so comparing revenue to them alone does not guide shutdown.

q: In the short run, when should a firm shut down?

options.t: When profit is slightly lower than last year
options.why: Profit slightly lower than last year is not a shutdown trigger, since the firm could still cover its variable costs and keep operating productively.

options.t: When fixed costs are positive and large
options.why: Large fixed costs must be paid whether the firm operates or not in the short run, so they do not by themselves justify shutting down.

options.t: When price is below average total cost
options.why: Price below average total cost means losses, but if price still covers average variable cost the firm can lose less by operating than by shutting down.

options.t: When price is below average variable cost
options.why: If price is below average variable cost, each unit sold loses money even before fixed costs, so the firm minimizes losses by shutting down in the short run.

q: What is total fixed cost for a firm with $3,000 rent and $1,000 insurance?

options.why: Three thousand dollars covers the rent only; total fixed cost also includes the 1,000 of insurance, so the sum is 4,000.
Two thousand dollars is the difference between rent and insurance, but fixed costs are added together, giving 3,000 plus 1,000, which is 4,000.
Total fixed cost adds the rent of 3,000 and insurance of 1,000 to give 4,000, and these costs stay the same regardless of how much is produced.
Twelve thousand dollars would come from multiplying 3,000 by 4, yet no such calculation applies; fixed costs are simply added, giving 4,000 in total.

q: Total cost is $10,000 for 500 units. What is average total cost?

options.t: $20 per unit
options.why: Average total cost equals total cost divided by quantity, so 10,000 divided by 500 gives 20 dollars per unit.

options.t: $500 per unit
options.why: Five hundred dollars per unit is just the quantity figure used as a price; dividing 10,000 by 500 gives 20, not 500.

options.t: $50 per unit
options.why: Fifty dollars per unit would come from dividing 10,000 by 200, which is not the output given; with 500 units the answer is 20.

options.t: $5 per unit
options.why: Five dollars per unit would need 2,000 units, because 10,000 divided by 2,000 is 5; dividing by 500 units gives 20 dollars.

q: Total cost rises from $10,000 to $10,150 when output rises by 10 units. What is marginal cost?

options.t: $1,015 per unit
options.why: One thousand fifteen dollars per unit comes from dividing 10,150 by 10 and uses total cost instead of the change; marginal cost uses only the 150 increase.

options.t: $15 per unit
options.why: Marginal cost is the change in total cost divided by the change in output, so 150 divided by 10 units equals 15 dollars per unit.

options.t: $10 per unit
options.why: Ten dollars per unit would divide the units by themselves or ignore the 150 increase; the extra cost of 150 over 10 units is 15.

options.t: $150 per unit
options.why: One hundred fifty dollars is the total rise in cost, not the cost per extra unit; dividing that 150 by the 10 added units gives 15.

q: Why does the marginal cost curve eventually rise?

options.t: Output prices rise as the firm grows, which lifts costs
options.why: Marginal cost rises because of diminishing returns inside the firm, not because output prices rise as it grows, which affects revenue rather than the cost of inputs.

options.t: Diminishing returns make each extra unit cost more
options.why: Diminishing returns mean each added worker contributes less output, so every extra unit takes more input and costs more, which makes the marginal cost curve rise.

options.t: Firms forget how to produce their goods over time
options.why: Firms do not forget how to produce; marginal cost rises because of diminishing returns to inputs, so this claim has no basis in cost theory.

options.t: Fixed costs rise with each additional unit produced
options.why: Fixed costs do not change with output by definition, so they cannot rise with each additional unit and cannot explain rising marginal cost.

q: What is a perfectly competitive firm's marginal revenue equal to?

options.t: The market price
options.why: A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker that sells every extra unit at the market price, so its marginal revenue equals that price.

options.t: The firm's profit
options.why: Marginal revenue is the extra revenue from one more unit, not profit; profit also depends on costs, so the two are not equal.

options.t: A firm's fixed cost
options.why: A firm's fixed cost is a cost figure that does not change with output, whereas marginal revenue is the income earned from selling another unit.

options.t: Zero at all times
options.why: Marginal revenue is not zero at all times; a competitive firm earns the market price on each extra unit, so it is positive.

q: A perfectly competitive firm should produce where:

options.t: Fixed cost equals variable
options.why: Fixed cost equaling variable cost is not a profit-maximizing rule, since the firm decides output using marginal values, not by balancing two cost totals.

options.t: Average cost equals zero
options.why: Average cost cannot equal zero for a firm that pays for inputs, and the output decision is based on marginal cost, not average cost.

options.t: Total revenue is smallest
options.why: Producing where total revenue is smallest would give poor results, since the firm seeks maximum profit, not the lowest possible revenue.

options.t: Marginal cost equals price
options.why: A competitive firm maximizes profit by producing where marginal cost equals price, which is also its marginal revenue, because beyond that point extra units cost more than they earn.

q: What happens to a monopolist's price compared with a competitive firm's price?

options.t: A monopolist must charge the market price always
options.why: A monopolist is not a price taker; it has market power and chooses its own price rather than being forced to accept the market price.

options.t: A monopolist produces at zero profit in every case
options.why: A monopolist does not always earn zero profit; with barriers to entry it can earn positive economic profit over time, unlike competitive firms in the long run.

options.t: A monopolist usually charges more and produces less
options.why: A monopolist restricts output to raise price, so it usually charges more and produces less than a competitive firm facing the same costs.

options.t: A monopolist charges less and produces more than rivals
options.why: Charging less and producing more is what competitive firms do; a monopolist uses market power to raise price and cut quantity, so this reverses the pattern.

q: What is a barrier to entry?

options.t: A fee customers pay at a store to enter the shop floor
options.why: A fee customers pay to enter a shop floor is an admission charge, not a barrier that blocks new firms from joining a market.

options.t: Something that makes it hard for new firms to join a market
options.why: A barrier to entry is anything, such as high start-up costs, patents or legal limits, that makes it hard for new firms to join a market.

options.t: A fence around a factory site to keep out rival firms
options.why: A fence around a factory is physical security and does not affect whether rival firms can enter the market, so it is not an economic barrier.

options.t: A rule that lets any firm join freely and start selling in general
options.why: A rule letting any firm join freely describes free entry, the opposite of a barrier, which makes joining the market hard or costly.

q: What is a natural monopoly?

options.t: A market with many equal sellers and low prices for all buyers
options.why: A market with many equal sellers and low prices describes perfect competition, which is the opposite of a natural monopoly served by a single firm.

options.t: A monopoly created by hiding resources from all rival firms
options.why: Hiding resources from rival firms describes an artificial or strategic monopoly, and a natural monopoly arises from cost conditions, not from concealment.

options.t: A market best served by one firm because of very high fixed costs
options.why: A natural monopoly is a market best served by one firm because very high fixed costs make a single large producer cheaper than many small ones.

options.t: A monopoly that exists only in nature reserves owned by the state
options.why: A natural monopoly has nothing to do with nature reserves; the word natural refers to cost structure, such as in water or electricity networks.

q: What is price discrimination?

options.t: Charging different customers different prices for the same good
options.why: Price discrimination means charging different customers different prices for the same good, based on what each group is willing to pay, to raise profit.

options.t: Refusing to sell to certain groups of buyers in a market
options.why: Refusing to sell to certain groups is exclusion or unlawful discrimination in the usual sense, and not the pricing strategy of charging customers different prices.

options.t: Charging every customer the same price for the same good
options.why: Charging every customer the same price for the same good is uniform pricing, the opposite of price discrimination, which varies prices across buyers.

options.t: Lowering prices for everyone permanently, so all buyers pay less
options.why: Lowering prices for everyone permanently is a general price cut, whereas price discrimination sets different prices for different customer groups at the same time.

q: A cinema sells cheaper tickets to seniors. Which condition must hold for this to raise profit?

options.t: Resale between groups must be easy and cheap to do for buyers
options.why: Easy and cheap resale between groups would undermine price discrimination, since low-price buyers could resell to high-price buyers, so this condition would hurt profit.

options.t: The seller must have no market power, so it sets its own ticket prices
options.why: A seller must have some market power to set prices above marginal cost; with none it cannot charge groups different prices, so the claim is wrong.

options.t: All buyers must be identical in their tastes and incomes
options.why: Identical buyers would all be charged the same price, so discrimination only works when groups differ, and this condition would remove the gain.

options.t: Groups have different sensitivity to price and can be kept apart
options.why: Price discrimination raises profit when groups differ in price sensitivity and can be kept apart so no resale occurs, as with seniors and other adults at a cinema.

q: What is a loss leader?

options.t: A product sold at a loss to draw customers in
options.why: A loss leader is a product sold at a loss, or very low price, to draw customers into a store where they buy other, more profitable items.

options.t: The manager who was responsible for a loss
options.why: The manager responsible for a loss is not what the term means; it describes a pricing tactic for a product, not a person.

options.t: A product that is always unprofitable for stores
options.why: A loss leader is not always unprofitable overall; the store accepts a loss on one item to boost total sales and profit, so always is wrong.

options.t: A product given away for free forever to customers
options.why: A product given away free forever would produce losses without any aim, whereas a loss leader is priced low temporarily to attract customers.

q: What does cost-plus pricing do?

options.t: Sets prices by what buyers will pay
options.why: Setting prices by what buyers will pay is value-based pricing, which starts from demand, while cost-plus pricing starts from the cost of the product.

options.t: Adds a markup to the cost of a product
options.why: Cost-plus pricing takes the cost of making a product and adds a markup, a set percentage or amount, to arrive at the selling price.

options.t: Sets prices to the lowest possible level
options.why: Setting prices to the lowest possible level is a penetration or break-even approach, not cost-plus pricing, which includes a markup above cost.

options.t: Sets the price at what rivals charge
options.why: Setting the price at what rivals charge is competitive or going-rate pricing, which starts from the market, not from adding a markup to cost.

q: A product costs $24 to make and the firm adds a 25% markup on cost. What is the price?

options.why: Six dollars is just the 25 percent markup taken on the cost of 24; the price must be the cost plus that markup, which is 30.
Twenty-five dollars confuses the markup percent with a dollar amount; the markup is 25 percent of 24, which is 6, so the price is 30.
Forty-eight dollars doubles the cost, which would be a 100 percent markup; a 25 percent markup adds only 6 to the cost of 24.
A 25 percent markup on 24 dollars is 0.25 times 24, which is 6 dollars, so the price is 24 plus 6, giving 30 dollars.

q: What is profit margin?

options.t: Assets as a percent of equity
options.why: Assets as a percent of equity is a balance-sheet ratio of leverage, and it does not measure how much of each sale becomes profit.

options.t: Costs as a percent of assets
options.why: Costs as a percent of assets is not profit margin; margin compares profit with sales revenue, not costs with the assets that a firm holds.

options.t: Profit as a percent of revenue
options.why: Profit margin is profit divided by revenue, shown as a percent, which tells how many cents of each sales dollar remain as profit.

options.t: Revenue as a percent of costs
options.why: Revenue as a percent of costs compares sales with spending, which is not profit margin; margin puts profit, not costs, against revenue.

q: A firm earns $15,000 profit on $200,000 revenue. What is its profit margin?

options.why: Seventy-five percent would come from a misplaced decimal; 15,000 divided by 200,000 is 0.075, which is 7.5 percent, not 75.
A margin of 13.3 percent comes from dividing profit by 112,500 or a similar wrong base; the revenue is 200,000, so the margin is 7.5.
Profit margin equals profit divided by revenue, so 15,000 divided by 200,000 gives 0.075, which is 7.5 percent of each sales dollar kept as profit.
Fifteen percent would be profit over 100,000 of revenue, but this firm has 200,000 in revenue, so dividing 15,000 by 200,000 gives only 7.5 percent.

q: What is a firm's break-even quantity?

options.t: The output where revenue is zero for the firm
options.why: Revenue is not zero at break-even; a firm there sells enough to cover its costs, so revenue equals total cost, which is not a zero level.

options.t: The output that earns the largest profit for the firm
options.why: The output that earns the largest profit is the profit-maximizing quantity, which differs from break-even, where profit is exactly zero.

options.t: The output where costs are zero for the firm
options.why: Costs are never zero when a firm is producing, so break-even cannot be where costs vanish; it is where revenue matches those costs.

options.t: The output where total revenue equals total cost
options.why: Break-even quantity is the output at which total revenue equals total cost, so profit is zero, and selling any more begins to earn a profit.

q: Fixed costs are $9,000. Each unit sells for $15 and costs $6 to make. What is the break-even quantity?

options.t: 600 units
options.why: Six hundred units results from dividing 9,000 by 15, which ignores variable cost; the contribution per unit is 15 minus 6, giving 9 dollars.

options.t: 1,000 units
options.why: Break-even equals fixed costs divided by contribution per unit; each unit adds 15 minus 6, which is 9 dollars, so 9,000 divided by 9 gives 1,000 units.

options.t: 9,000 units
options.why: Nine thousand units treats the fixed cost figure as the quantity; dividing 9,000 by the contribution of 9 dollars per unit gives 1,000 units.

options.t: 1,500 units
options.why: One thousand five hundred units comes from dividing 9,000 by 6, the variable cost alone, but break-even uses the contribution of 9 dollars, giving 1,000.

q: If a firm sells above its break-even quantity, what happens?

options.t: It earns a profit
options.why: Selling above break-even means revenue exceeds total cost, so each extra unit adds to profit and the firm earns a profit.

options.t: Fixed costs vanish
options.why: Fixed costs do not vanish above break-even; they stay the same in total, but sales are large enough to cover them.

options.t: Revenue becomes zero
options.why: Revenue becomes larger, not zero, when a firm sells more units, so this contradicts what happens above the break-even quantity.

options.t: It suffers a loss
options.why: A loss happens when quantity sold is below the break-even quantity, because revenue falls short of cost, which is the opposite of this case.

q: Why do firms often use economies of scope?

options.t: Producing less to save paper and other materials
options.why: Producing less to save paper and materials is not economies of scope, which concerns producing a range of related goods rather than cutting output.

options.t: Producing related goods together lowers average cost
options.why: Economies of scope arise when producing related goods together shares inputs such as staff and equipment, which lowers the average cost per product.

options.t: Producing only one good raises cost for the firm
options.why: Producing only one good raises cost is not the concept; economies of scope come from making several related goods, not from limiting output to one.

options.t: Producing unrelated goods in different countries at once
options.why: Producing unrelated goods in different countries cannot share staff, equipment or know-how, so it does not create the savings that scope economies describe.

q: A bakery that also sells coffee uses the same staff and counters for both. Which concept explains the lower cost?

options.t: Sunk costs paid
options.why: Sunk costs are payments already made that cannot be recovered, and they have no role in explaining shared staff and counters lowering cost.

options.t: Price discrimination
options.why: Price discrimination charges different buyers different prices and has nothing to do with sharing staff and counters across two products to cut costs.

options.t: Economies of scope
options.why: Selling coffee and bread with the same staff and counters spreads inputs over related products, lowering average cost, which is an economy of scope.

options.t: Diminishing returns
options.why: Diminishing returns describe falling extra output as more input is added to a fixed amount of another input, not savings from joint production.

q: What is the long run in economics?

options.t: A period when firms cannot produce any goods
options.why: A period when firms cannot produce any goods describes no real time frame; the long run is about flexibility, and firms still produce in it.

options.t: A period longer than ten years exactly for all firms
options.why: The long run is not exactly ten years; it is defined by whether all inputs can be changed, which varies from industry to industry.

options.t: A period when prices never change at all in markets
options.why: Prices can change in the long run, and the definition rests on adjusting inputs, so a period of fixed prices is not what the term means.

options.t: A period long enough for all inputs to be varied
options.why: The long run is a period long enough for a firm to vary all its inputs, including plant size and equipment, so no inputs are fixed.

q: What is the short run in economics?

options.t: A period when at least one input is fixed
options.why: The short run is a period in which at least one input, such as plant size or equipment, is fixed, so output changes only by varying other inputs.

options.t: A period with zero production by firms
options.why: Production continues in the short run; it simply limits how much a firm can change, so a period of zero production is wrong.

options.t: A period when every input can be changed
options.why: A period when every input can be changed is the long run, so this describes the opposite of the short run.

options.t: A period lasting exactly one month in total
options.why: The short run is not a set length like one month; it depends on how long it takes a firm to change its fixed inputs.

q: What happens in a competitive industry when firms earn economic profit?

options.t: New firms enter and profit shrinks
options.why: Economic profit attracts new firms into a competitive industry, which raises supply and pushes down price until profit shrinks toward zero.

options.t: Prices rise without any limit at all
options.why: Prices do not rise without limit; extra entry increases supply, which pushes prices down, so unlimited price increases are not the result of profit.

options.t: Firms exit and profit rises for others
options.why: Firms exit when they suffer losses, not when they earn profit, so this describes the opposite of what happens in a profitable competitive industry.

options.t: Entry is blocked forever by the market
options.why: Competitive industries have no barriers to entry, so entry is not blocked forever; free entry is exactly what removes profit over time.

q: What happens in a competitive industry when firms suffer losses?

options.t: More firms enter the market
options.why: More firms entering the market happens when firms earn profit, not losses, so entry is the reverse of the response to continued losses.

options.t: Costs fall to zero for all firms
options.why: Costs do not fall to zero when firms suffer losses; firms still pay for inputs, and exit rather than lower costs removes the loss.

options.t: Some firms exit and prices rise
options.why: Losses push some firms out of a competitive industry, which cuts supply and raises prices until the remaining firms earn normal profit.

options.t: Prices fall with no limit at all
options.why: Prices rise, not fall, as firms exit and supply shrinks, and they cannot fall without limit since firms leave when they lose money.

q: What is the accounting equation for profit?

options.t: Profit equals price divided by quantity
options.why: Price divided by quantity is not the profit formula; it makes no reference to revenue or costs and would not measure what a firm keeps.

options.t: Profit equals revenue minus expenses
options.why: Profit equals total revenue minus total expenses, so a firm earns a profit when what it receives from sales is larger than what it spends.

options.t: Profit equals expenses minus revenue
options.why: Expenses minus revenue reverses the formula and gives a positive number when the firm has a loss, so it would not measure profit.

options.t: Profit equals assets minus liabilities
options.why: Assets minus liabilities gives equity or net worth on the balance sheet, which is a measure of ownership value rather than profit.

q: Which is a typical overhead cost for a retail store?

options.t: The cost of goods sold
options.why: Cost of goods sold is a direct cost tied to the products sold, not an overhead cost that stays fixed regardless of sales volume.

options.t: Commissions on sales
options.why: Commissions on sales vary with how much is sold, so they are a variable selling cost rather than a fixed overhead expense for the store.

options.t: The price buyers pay
options.why: The price buyers pay is the store's revenue, which is money coming in, so it cannot be a cost the store carries as overhead.

options.t: Utilities and rent
options.why: Utilities and rent are ongoing costs of running the store that do not depend on how much is sold, which is exactly what overhead means for a retailer.

q: Total revenue is $500,000, cost of goods sold is $300,000 and operating expenses are $120,000. What is operating profit?

options.why: Operating profit is revenue minus cost of goods sold minus operating expenses, so 500,000 minus 300,000 minus 120,000 leaves 80,000 for the business.
The figure 920,000 comes from adding all three numbers together, but costs must be subtracted from revenue, not added to it, so this is wrong.
The figure 380,000 is revenue minus operating expenses only, which forgets to subtract the 300,000 cost of goods sold from the 500,000 revenue figure.
The figure 200,000 is revenue minus cost of goods sold only, which is gross profit, and it ignores the 120,000 of operating expenses still to deduct.

q: What does a business do with the resources it takes in?

options.t: Stores them without ever using them in case prices rise
options.why: Hoarding resources unused earns nothing and wastes them, so it is not what a business does; businesses use inputs to produce something customers will pay for.

options.t: Burns them to heat the factory in the winter months
options.why: Burning resources for heat is not the purpose of taking them in; a business converts inputs into output it can sell, not simply consumes them as fuel.

options.t: Gives them away to competitors for no payment at all
options.why: Giving resources to competitors for nothing would destroy value and profit, and it is the opposite of how a business turns inputs into sellable products.

options.t: Turns them into goods or services that customers value
options.why: A business takes in inputs such as labor, materials and capital and transforms them into goods or services that customers value enough to pay for.

q: What is a limited partnership?

options.t: A partnership where no one is ever liable for debts of the firm
options.why: If no partner were ever liable for the firm's debts, that would describe a corporation style shield for everyone, whereas a limited partnership still needs at least one liable partner.

options.t: A partnership where some partners have limited liability
options.why: A limited partnership has at least one general partner with full liability and one or more limited partners whose liability stops at what they invested in the firm.

options.t: A partnership with no profit sharing among the partners
options.why: Profit sharing is normal in a limited partnership because partners agree how profits are divided, so a partnership with no sharing does not describe this form at all.

options.t: A partnership limited to two people and no one else
options.why: Limiting a partnership to two people is not what makes it limited; the word refers to limited liability for some partners, and any number of partners may join.

q: What is a general partnership?

options.t: A partnership where one partner is liable for debts, not the rest
options.why: In a general partnership every partner is personally liable for firm debts, not just one, so a single liable partner describes a limited partnership structure instead.

options.t: A partnership run by the government of the state for the public
options.why: A general partnership is a private business owned by its partners, not a government body, and nothing about it involves running a state operation for the public.

options.t: A partnership where all partners share management and liability
options.why: In a general partnership all partners share in managing the business and all carry unlimited personal liability for its debts, which is what makes it general.

options.t: A partnership with shareholders who vote on every decision
options.why: Shareholders who vote on every decision belong to a corporation; a general partnership has partners, not shareholders, and partners manage the firm directly themselves.

q: What is a partnership agreement?

options.t: A loan from a bank to a partner to fund the business
options.why: A loan from a bank is a financing contract between the lender and borrower; a partnership agreement is instead a contract among the partners themselves about running the firm.

options.t: A tax form filed with the state, listing each partner's profits
options.why: A tax form listing partner profits is a filing made with the government after the year ends, while the partnership agreement is a private contract made among the partners.

options.t: A contract stating each partner's duties, shares and rights
options.why: A partnership agreement is a written contract that sets out each partner's duties, share of profits and losses, and rights, so disputes can be settled by its terms.

options.t: A license to sell goods in the town, issued by the city
options.why: A license to sell goods in town is a permit issued by a city authority, which is a different document from the agreement signed privately among the partners.

q: What is a disadvantage of a partnership?

options.t: It pays no taxes at all in any year on its profits or income
options.why: Partnerships do pay tax on profits through the partners' personal returns, so the claim that they pay no taxes at all in any year is false.

options.t: It cannot raise any money from partners or outside lenders
options.why: Partnerships can raise money from partners' contributions and from lenders, though often less than corporations can, so saying they cannot raise any money is an overstatement.

options.t: It must be run by a single person, who decides for all partners
options.why: A partnership has two or more owners by definition, so being run by a single person who decides for all partners describes a sole proprietorship, not a partnership.

options.t: Partners can disagree and may be liable for each other's acts
options.why: Partners can disagree over decisions, and in a general partnership each partner can be held liable for debts and acts of the other partners, which is a real weakness.

q: What is double taxation?

options.t: Paying sales tax at two different stores on one purchase overall
options.why: Paying sales tax at two stores covers two separate purchases, each taxed once, which is not double taxation; the term refers to the same income taxed twice.

options.t: Corporate profit taxed at the firm and again as dividends
options.why: Double taxation happens when a corporation pays tax on its profits and shareholders then pay tax again on the dividends received from those same after tax profits.

options.t: Paying tax twice on a purchase made in one store or shop
options.why: Paying tax twice on one purchase at one store does not happen under normal sales tax rules, and double taxation is about corporate profits and dividends instead.

options.t: Filing two tax returns in one year, state and federal
options.why: Filing both state and federal returns means two different governments each tax income once, so it is not double taxation, which taxes the same corporate profit twice.

q: What is an S corporation?

options.t: A corporation taxed through its owners' returns
options.why: An S corporation passes its income, losses and credits through to its owners, who report them on their personal returns, which avoids the corporate level of tax.

options.t: A corporation that never pays tax to any government
options.why: An S corporation is still subject to tax rules because its owners pay income tax on their shares, so saying it never pays tax to any government is false.

options.t: A corporation owned by the state and run by it
options.why: State ownership describes a government enterprise, whereas an S corporation is privately owned by shareholders and is defined by its special pass through tax status.

options.t: A corporation formed only abroad in a foreign land
options.why: An S corporation is a United States tax designation for domestic firms, not a company formed abroad, and it is defined by pass through taxation instead.

q: What is a board of directors?

options.t: The employees of a corporation who work for it daily overall
options.why: Employees who work for the corporation each day are the staff, not the board; the board is a group chosen to oversee the top managers of the firm.

options.t: Customers who buy company stock in the open market
options.why: Customers who buy stock in the open market become shareholders, and only the shareholders elect the board, so customers as a group are not the board.

options.t: A bank that lends to the company and sets its rates
options.why: A bank that lends to the company is a creditor, not a board; the board of directors is elected by shareholders to guide and oversee management.

options.t: Elected leaders who oversee a corporation's management
options.why: A board of directors is a group elected by shareholders to oversee a corporation's management, set major goals and hire or replace the senior executives of the firm.

q: What is a shareholder?

options.t: A supplier of raw materials to firms
options.why: A supplier of raw materials sells inputs to firms and is a vendor, while a shareholder owns a piece of the company through its shares of stock.

options.t: A lender who holds the company's loans
options.why: A lender holding the company's loans is a creditor who is owed repayment, whereas a shareholder is an owner with a claim on profits and assets.

options.t: An owner of shares in a corporation
options.why: A shareholder owns shares of stock in a corporation, which gives a share of ownership, a claim on profits through dividends, and usually a vote on key matters.

options.t: A worker paid by the hour at a firm
options.why: A worker paid by the hour is an employee earning wages, which does not make that person an owner; shareholders hold stock and are the owners.

q: What is a stakeholder?

options.t: Only the owners of the business itself
options.why: Owners are only one group of stakeholders; the term is wider and also covers employees, customers, suppliers and communities who are affected by what a business does.

options.t: Anyone affected by a business's decisions
options.why: A stakeholder is anyone affected by or with an interest in a business's decisions, including employees, customers, suppliers, owners and the local community around it.

options.t: Only the competitors of the business as a rule
options.why: Competitors may be affected by a business, but they are only one kind of stakeholder, and the term is far broader than rivals alone.

options.t: Only the managers of the business itself
options.why: Managers are stakeholders but not the only ones, since employees, customers, suppliers, owners and communities are also affected by the firm's decisions and actions.

q: What is vertical integration?

options.t: A firm owning several stages of its supply chain
options.why: Vertical integration means a firm owns several stages of its supply chain, such as supplying inputs, making the product and selling it directly to customers.

options.t: A firm selling to many countries around the world
options.why: Selling to many countries is international expansion, which concerns where a firm sells, not whether it owns more than one stage of its supply chain.

options.t: A firm splitting into smaller units over time
options.why: A firm splitting into smaller units is a breakup or spin off, which is the reverse of integrating stages of production under one owner.

options.t: Two rivals merging at the same stage of production
options.why: Two rivals merging at the same stage of production is horizontal integration, whereas vertical integration joins different stages of the supply chain under one owner.

q: What is horizontal integration?

options.t: Selling part of the company to new outside investors
options.why: Selling part of the company to outside investors raises capital and changes ownership, but it does not combine firms at the same stage of production.

options.t: Merging with a competitor at the same stage of production
options.why: Horizontal integration is when a firm merges with or buys a competitor operating at the same stage of production, which raises market share and cuts duplicate costs.

options.t: Opening a store in a new country on another continent
options.why: Opening a store in a new country is geographic expansion, which does not involve merging with a competitor at the same stage of the supply chain.

options.t: Buying a supplier of raw materials to control early steps
options.why: Buying a supplier of raw materials to control early steps is vertical integration, since it moves backward along the supply chain rather than across to a competitor.

q: What is a merger?

options.t: Two companies combining into one
options.why: A merger is when two companies agree to combine into a single new or surviving firm, usually to gain scale, share markets or reduce costs.

options.t: A company paying a dividend out
options.why: A company paying a dividend simply distributes part of its profit to shareholders, and nothing is combined with another company in that event.

options.t: A company closing its doors for good
options.why: A company closing its doors is a shutdown or liquidation, which ends the business instead of joining it with another firm as a merger does.

options.t: One company splitting into two firms
options.why: One company splitting into two firms is a breakup or spin off, which is the opposite of a merger, where two firms join to form one.

q: What is an acquisition?
