options.t: A firm hiring a new CEO for the job
options.why: Hiring a new CEO is a management change inside one firm and does not transfer control of the company to another firm as an acquisition does.

options.t: A firm closing a branch in another city
options.why: Closing a branch is a cost cutting or restructuring step within one company, and no other company gains control of it, so it is not an acquisition.

options.t: One company buying control of another
options.why: An acquisition occurs when one company buys enough of another to take control of it, and the target usually becomes part of the buyer or its subsidiary.

options.t: Two firms agreeing to share a logo
options.why: Two firms sharing a logo might be a branding or licensing deal, but neither firm buys control of the other, so it is not an acquisition.

q: What is a hostile takeover?

options.t: A strike by employees against the company's owners
options.why: A strike by employees is a labor dispute between workers and owners and has nothing to do with another company buying control of the target.

options.t: A theft of company property by a group of staff members
options.why: Theft of company property by staff is a crime committed inside the firm and is unrelated to one company seeking to take over another firm.

options.t: An acquisition both sides welcome, with managers in favor
options.why: An acquisition that both sides welcome with managers in favor is a friendly takeover, which is the opposite of a hostile one.

options.t: An acquisition the target company's management opposes
options.why: A hostile takeover is an acquisition that the target company's management opposes, so the buyer goes straight to shareholders or buys up shares to win control.

q: What is a business plan's executive summary?

options.t: A list of every employee's pay
options.why: A list of every employee's pay would be part of a detailed payroll or staffing section, not a short summary that introduces the whole business plan.

options.t: A legal contract with investors
options.why: A legal contract with investors is a separate document, such as an investment agreement, and an executive summary is only a summary of the plan itself.

options.t: A short overview of the whole plan
options.why: The executive summary is a short overview of the whole business plan, placed first, that gives readers the key points such as the idea, market and financial needs.

options.t: A full set of financial statements
options.why: A full set of financial statements is a long, detailed section of the plan, whereas the executive summary is brief and only highlights the main financial points.

q: What is a franchisee?

options.t: The company that owns the brand and licenses it to others overall
options.why: The company that owns the brand and licenses it to others is the franchisor, not the franchisee, who is the person buying the right to use that brand.

options.t: A supplier of the brand's goods and materials to outlets
options.why: A supplier of goods and materials sells products to outlets, which is a vendor role, while a franchisee is the person who runs a branded outlet under a license.

options.t: A customer of the brand who buys its products every week
options.why: A customer buys the brand's products, while a franchisee is a business owner who pays for the right to operate an outlet under the brand's name and system.

options.t: A person who buys the right to run a business under a brand
options.why: A franchisee is a person or firm that buys the right to run a business under an established brand, paying fees and following the franchisor's methods.

q: What is a franchisor?

options.t: The company that licenses its brand and system to others
options.why: A franchisor is the company that owns a brand and licenses its name, products and business system to franchisees, who pay fees and often royalties to use them.

options.t: The bank that lends to the outlet owner for startup as a rule
options.why: A bank that lends to the outlet owner is a lender, which is a different role from the franchisor that owns the brand and licenses its system.

options.t: The person who runs the local outlet and pays a fee
options.why: The person who runs the local outlet and pays a fee is the franchisee, not the franchisor, who grants the license and receives the fee.

options.t: The customer who buys the product from the outlet
options.why: The customer who buys the product from the outlet is a consumer, and has no role in owning or licensing the brand as a franchisor does.

q: What is a royalty?

options.t: A fine for breaking a rule of the brand owner
options.why: A fine for breaking a rule is a penalty for misconduct, whereas a royalty is an agreed payment for the continuing use of someone's brand or idea.

options.t: A payment for the ongoing use of a brand or idea
options.why: A royalty is a payment made to the owner of a brand, patent or creative work for the ongoing right to use it, often a share of sales.

options.t: A tax on imported goods at the border post
options.why: A tax on imported goods at the border is a tariff or customs duty paid to the government, not a royalty paid to the owner of an idea.

options.t: A payment for one-time labor made once a job is done
options.why: A one time payment for labor after a job is done is a wage or fee, whereas a royalty keeps being paid as long as the brand or idea is used.

q: What is entrepreneurship's role in an economy?

options.t: Creating new businesses, jobs and ideas
options.why: Entrepreneurs start new businesses, which creates jobs, brings new products and ideas to market, and helps drive competition and growth in an economy.

options.t: Printing the nation's money supply
options.why: Printing the nation's money supply is done by the central bank and the treasury, not by entrepreneurs, whose role is starting and growing new businesses.

options.t: Setting official prices for all goods
options.why: Setting official prices for goods is price control by a government, while entrepreneurs operate in markets where prices come from supply and demand.

options.t: Collecting income taxes from workers
options.why: Collecting income taxes from workers is a task for tax authorities, whereas entrepreneurs create firms and jobs, which indirectly generate the income that gets taxed.

q: Which agency enforces federal rules against false advertising?

options.t: The Social Security Agency
options.why: The Social Security Agency pays retirement and disability benefits and does not police advertising claims, so it does not enforce rules against false advertising.

options.t: The Federal Reserve Board
options.why: The Federal Reserve Board sets monetary policy and supervises banks, and it has no job enforcing federal rules against deceptive advertising by businesses.

options.t: The Federal Trade Commission
options.why: The Federal Trade Commission enforces federal rules on unfair and deceptive practices, including false advertising, and can order firms to stop and pay penalties.

options.t: The Bureau of Labor Statistics
options.why: The Bureau of Labor Statistics collects data on jobs, wages and prices; it is a statistics agency with no power to enforce advertising rules.

q: What does the Securities and Exchange Commission require of public companies?

options.t: Fixed prices for their products sold
options.why: The SEC does not set product prices, because prices come from markets, and its role is to protect investors by requiring honest information from public companies.

options.t: Regular, accurate financial disclosures
options.why: The SEC requires public companies to file regular, accurate financial disclosures so investors can judge the firm, and it can punish fraud and misleading reports.

options.t: Hiring a set number of new workers
options.why: The SEC does not tell companies how many workers to hire, as hiring is a management decision, and its rules focus on investor information and fair markets.

options.t: A guaranteed profit each year for firms
options.why: No agency can guarantee a profit each year to firms, since profit depends on market conditions, and the SEC only requires honest reporting, not results.

q: What is deregulation?

options.t: Taxing an industry far more heavily than before
options.why: Taxing an industry far more heavily is a tax increase, not deregulation, which removes or relaxes government rules instead of adding financial burdens.

options.t: Taking over an industry entirely by the state
options.why: Taking over an industry entirely by the state is nationalization, which increases government control, whereas deregulation reduces the rules that apply to an industry.

options.t: Adding more rules to an industry for stricter standards
options.why: Adding more rules for stricter standards is regulation, or re-regulation, and it is the opposite of deregulation, which reduces the rules a government imposes.

options.t: Reducing government rules that apply to an industry
options.why: Deregulation means the government reduces or removes rules that apply to an industry, often to encourage competition, lower costs and give firms more freedom to operate.

q: What is a common argument for regulating pollution?

options.t: Clean air is a private good for each person
options.why: Clean air is a public good that people share and cannot be easily excluded from, not a private good, and this is why markets alone struggle to protect it.

options.t: Pollution raises company profit for everyone
options.why: Pollution does not raise profit for everyone; it imposes costs on third parties, and the harm to society is the main reason regulation is argued for.

options.t: Firms ignore costs they push onto others
options.why: Firms often ignore the costs of pollution that fall on other people, called negative externalities, so regulation makes them account for the damage they cause.

options.t: Markets always price pollution correctly
options.why: Markets do not always price pollution correctly, because polluters do not pay for the harm to others, and this market failure is what regulation targets.

q: A carbon tax is designed to:

options.t: Remove all costs from firms in the market
options.why: A carbon tax does not remove costs from firms; it adds a cost to emitting carbon so that firms have a reason to cut their emissions.

options.t: Make polluters pay for the harm they cause
options.why: A carbon tax makes polluters pay for the harm their emissions cause, turning an outside cost into a price they must weigh, which pushes them to pollute less.

options.t: Ban all production of energy for good
options.why: A carbon tax raises the cost of emitting carbon but does not ban energy production, and firms may keep producing if they pay the tax.

options.t: Reward firms that pollute with extra emissions
options.why: Rewarding polluters with extra emissions is the opposite of a carbon tax, which penalizes emissions by charging a tax on each unit of carbon released.

q: What is a tradable pollution permit?

options.t: A right to emit a set amount that can be bought and sold
options.why: A tradable pollution permit gives a firm the right to emit a set amount, and firms can buy or sell permits, so total pollution stays under a cap.

options.t: A free pass to pollute without limit whenever a firm wishes
options.why: A pass to pollute without limit would defeat the purpose, since permits set a cap on emissions and each permit allows only a fixed quantity.

options.t: A fine for emitting any pollution into the air or water
options.why: A fine for emitting pollution is a penalty, not a permit; a permit is an allowance to emit a set amount that can be traded between firms.

options.t: A ban on all emissions from any firm in the nation
options.why: A ban on all emissions would stop production completely, whereas permits allow limited pollution under a cap and let firms trade the right to emit.

q: What is a government-provided public good?

options.t: A designer jacket
options.why: A designer jacket is a private good that individuals buy for themselves, and sellers can exclude those who do not pay, so it is not a public good.

options.t: A restaurant meal
options.why: A restaurant meal is a private good that only the buyer consumes, and the restaurant can refuse service to anyone who does not pay for it.

options.t: A concert ticket
options.why: A concert ticket is a private good because only ticket holders can attend, so non payers are excluded, which means it is not a public good.

options.t: National defense
options.why: National defense is a public good that protects everyone at once; one person's protection does not reduce another's, and nobody can easily be excluded from it.

q: Why might the government give a subsidy to a positive externality such as vaccination?

options.t: Vaccines cost nothing to make, so price them low
options.why: Vaccines cost real money to make, so the claim that they cost nothing is false; the subsidy exists because society gains from vaccination beyond what buyers get.

options.t: Society gains more than the buyer alone gets
options.why: Vaccination gives benefits to others by reducing the spread of disease, so society gains more than the buyer alone, and a subsidy raises vaccination toward the best level.

options.t: Vaccines harm third parties in the market
options.why: Vaccines protect third parties by cutting disease spread, so they create benefits to others rather than harm, which is why a subsidy is used and not a tax.

options.t: Markets over-supply vaccines to all buyers
options.why: Markets tend to under supply vaccines because buyers ignore the benefit to others, so a claim of over supply gets the direction of the problem backward.

q: What is the main purpose of an excise tax on tobacco?

options.t: Lower the price for all buyers
options.why: An excise tax on tobacco raises the price for buyers, not lowers it, and the goal is to discourage use while collecting revenue.

options.t: Encourage smoking to raise revenue
options.why: Encouraging smoking is the opposite of public health goals; the tax raises the price of tobacco so that fewer people smoke while bringing in government revenue.

options.t: Raise revenue and discourage use
options.why: An excise tax on tobacco raises revenue for the government and also raises the price of cigarettes, which discourages use, especially among price sensitive buyers and young people.

options.t: Replace all income taxes soon
options.why: An excise tax on one product cannot replace all income taxes, since tobacco sales are far too small to fund the whole government budget.

q: What is a user fee?

options.t: A charge for using a government service
options.why: A user fee is a charge paid by those who use a particular government service, such as a park entrance fee or a toll, so users help fund it.

options.t: A loan from the state to a firm or person
options.why: A loan from the state to a firm or person is credit that must be repaid, and a user fee is a charge for using a service.

options.t: A fine for breaking the law or a rule
options.why: A fine for breaking the law is a penalty for wrongdoing, whereas a user fee is a price for using a government service legally.

options.t: A tax paid by every citizen each year
options.why: A tax paid by every citizen each year is a general tax, while a user fee is paid only by people who actually use a service.

q: What does the Federal Trade Commission do about mergers?

options.t: Forces all firms to merge into one company
options.why: The FTC does not force firms to merge; it checks proposed mergers and can challenge those that harm competition, which is the opposite of forcing combinations.

options.t: Sets the price of merged firms' goods each year
options.why: The FTC does not set the price of merged firms' goods, because prices are set by firms in markets, and its role is to review deals for competition effects.

options.t: Approves every merger without any review
options.why: The FTC does review mergers and may block or set conditions on them, so saying it approves every merger without any review is plainly false.

options.t: Reviews those that might reduce competition
options.why: The FTC reviews mergers that might reduce competition and can challenge or block them, so that consumers are protected from higher prices and fewer choices.

q: What was the purpose of the Sherman Antitrust Act?

options.t: Set the minimum wage for all workers
options.why: The minimum wage is set by other laws, such as the Fair Labor Standards Act, and the Sherman Act has nothing to do with worker pay.

options.t: Regulate food labels on packaged goods
options.why: Food labeling is regulated by laws such as the Food and Drug Act and later labeling laws, which came well after and differ from the Sherman Act.

options.t: Break up monopolies and ban price fixing
options.why: The Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 was passed to break up monopolies and ban price fixing and other practices that restrain trade and reduce competition.

options.t: Create the income tax for the government
options.why: The income tax was created by other laws and the Sixteenth Amendment, while the Sherman Act focused on competition and had no role in creating a tax.

q: What is a patent?

options.t: Exclusive rights to an invention for a set time
options.why: A patent gives an inventor exclusive rights to make, use and sell an invention for a set period, commonly twenty years in the United States.

options.t: Exclusive rights to a brand name or a logo
options.why: Exclusive rights to a brand name or logo are called a trademark, which is a different kind of intellectual property from a patent on an invention.

options.t: Exclusive rights to a book, song or film for life
options.why: Exclusive rights to a book, song or film are called a copyright, which lasts for the author's life plus years, and it is not a patent.

options.t: A license to open a store in a town or city
options.why: A license to open a store in a town is a local business permit, whereas a patent protects an invention and has nothing to do with store openings.

q: Why do patents sometimes create temporary monopolies?

options.t: Patents set price ceilings by law for goods
options.why: Patents do not set price ceilings; they grant exclusive rights, and the holder is free to set the price, which can be high during the protected period.

options.t: Only the holder may sell the invention for a time
options.why: A patent lets only the holder sell the invention for a set time, which gives a temporary monopoly that rewards the inventor before competitors can copy it.

options.t: Patents let any firm copy the invention at any time
options.why: If any firm could copy the invention at any time, there would be no exclusive right, so a patent does the opposite of allowing free copying.

options.t: Patents end all competition permanently in markets
options.why: Patents expire after a fixed term, so they cannot end competition permanently, and after expiry other firms may copy the invention and compete freely.

q: What is a copyright?

options.t: A guarantee of a work's quality given to the buyers
options.why: A guarantee of quality is a warranty given by a seller, while a copyright protects the creator's right to control copies of an original work.

options.t: A license to sell goods abroad for a firm or person
options.why: A license to sell goods abroad is an export license, which is a trade permit and has no link to protecting an original creative work.

options.t: A tax on creative workers such as authors and artists
options.why: A copyright is not a tax on creative workers; it is a legal protection that benefits authors and artists by controlling who may copy their work.

options.t: The legal right to control copies of an original work
options.why: A copyright is the legal right of a creator to control the copying and distribution of an original work, such as a book, song, film or software.

q: What does the Fair Labor Standards Act regulate?

options.t: Minimum wage and overtime
options.why: The Fair Labor Standards Act sets the federal minimum wage and requires overtime pay, usually one and a half times pay beyond forty hours a week.

options.t: Bank deposit insurance
options.why: Bank deposit insurance is provided by the FDIC under banking law, and it is separate from the Fair Labor Standards Act, which covers wages and hours.

options.t: Stock market trading rules
options.why: Stock market trading rules come from the securities laws and the SEC, not the Fair Labor Standards Act, which covers pay and hours of employees.

options.t: Product safety labels
options.why: Product safety labels are covered by consumer protection laws and agencies, whereas the Fair Labor Standards Act deals with employee wages, hours and child labor.

q: What does the Occupational Safety and Health Act aim to do?

options.t: Guarantee all job promotions
options.why: No law can guarantee job promotions, which depend on performance and employer decisions, and the Occupational Safety and Health Act deals with workplace safety instead.

options.t: Limit the number of workers hired
options.why: The Act does not limit how many workers a firm hires; it sets safety and health standards that apply to workplaces whatever the size of the staff.

options.t: Set the price of insurance cover
options.why: Setting the price of insurance cover is not what the Act does; its purpose is to make workplaces safe and healthy through standards and inspections.

options.t: Keep workplaces safe and healthy
options.why: The Occupational Safety and Health Act aims to keep workplaces safe and healthy by setting standards, requiring employers to fix hazards, and allowing inspections by OSHA.

q: What does the Americans with Disabilities Act require of employers?

options.t: Closing offices that lack ramps and lifts
options.why: The Americans with Disabilities Act does not close offices lacking ramps; it requires reasonable accommodations and removal of barriers where this can be done without undue hardship.

options.t: Reasonable accommodations for qualified workers
options.why: The ADA requires employers to provide reasonable accommodations for qualified workers with disabilities, such as changes to equipment or schedules, unless it causes undue hardship.

options.t: Paying disabled workers more than all others
options.why: The ADA bans discrimination and does not require paying disabled workers more than others; they must be paid on the same basis as comparable workers.

options.t: Hiring only workers with disabilities for openings
options.why: The ADA does not require hiring only workers with disabilities; it forbids discrimination against qualified people and says nothing about reserving all openings for them.

q: What is a government contract?

options.t: A license to operate a business in a state or county for a year overall
options.why: A license to operate a business in a state is a permit issued by authorities, which differs from a contract where a firm agrees to supply the government.

options.t: A subsidy paid to households to help pay for food and housing
options.why: A subsidy paid to households for food and housing is a transfer payment or welfare benefit, not an agreement for a firm to supply the government.

options.t: An agreement for a firm to supply goods or services to government
options.why: A government contract is an agreement in which a firm supplies goods or services to the government, such as building a road or providing equipment, for a set payment.

options.t: A tax form for firms that sell goods to the state each year
options.why: A tax form for firms selling to the state is a filing document, while a government contract is the agreement under which the firm supplies goods or services.

q: How do government purchases affect GDP?

options.t: They are a component of total spending
options.why: Government purchases are one component of GDP, along with consumption, investment and net exports, so they count as part of total spending on output.

options.t: They are ignored in the GDP figures
options.why: Government purchases are not ignored; they are counted in GDP as the G in the expenditure formula, since the government buys goods and services too.

options.t: They only affect imports of goods
options.why: Government purchases affect more than imports, because they are spending on domestic output, and they directly add to GDP as one part of total spending.

options.t: They are subtracted from the GDP total
options.why: Government purchases are added to GDP, not subtracted, because they are spending on newly produced goods and services, such as roads, schools and defense.

q: What is the multiplier effect of government spending?

options.t: Spending equals the tax collected, so the budget is balanced
options.why: The multiplier effect is not about balancing the budget; it describes how spending is re-spent through the economy, and it does not require taxes to equal spending.

options.t: Spending can raise total output by more than its own size
options.why: The multiplier effect means a round of government spending becomes income for others, who spend part of it again, so total output can rise by more than the original amount.

options.t: Spending has no effect on income or output at all in any year
options.why: Government spending does affect income and output, since recipients earn money and spend it, so the claim that it has no effect at all is wrong.

options.t: Spending always lowers output in the economy by the same size
options.why: Spending does not always lower output; the multiplier works in the opposite direction, raising output by more than the first round of spending would suggest.

q: What is the federal minimum wage meant to do?

options.t: Guarantee full employment for all
options.why: A minimum wage cannot guarantee full employment, because it sets a pay floor but does not create jobs, and some argue it can reduce them.

options.t: Cap how much any worker can earn
options.why: The minimum wage is a floor, not a ceiling, so it does not cap how much a worker can earn; workers may be paid more than it.

options.t: Set a floor for pay under the law
options.why: The federal minimum wage sets a legal floor under pay, so employers covered by the law cannot pay less than that hourly amount to covered workers.

options.t: Replace all collective bargaining
options.why: The minimum wage does not replace collective bargaining, because unions still negotiate pay and conditions above the legal floor for their members.

q: What is a tariff's usual effect on domestic producers?

options.t: It exposes them to more foreign competition
options.why: A tariff raises the price of imports, which lowers foreign competition for domestic producers, so saying it exposes them to more competition gets the effect backward.

options.t: It bans them from exporting goods abroad
options.why: A tariff taxes imported goods and does not restrict a country's own exports, so it does not ban domestic producers from selling goods abroad.

options.t: It sets their prices by law for each good
options.why: A tariff is a tax on imports and does not set domestic producers' prices by law, since those firms remain free to set their own prices.

options.t: It shields them from foreign competition
options.why: A tariff raises the price of imported goods, so domestic producers face less competition from abroad, which shields them and lets them sell more or charge more.

q: What is a quota's usual effect on the price of an imported good?

options.t: It tends to rise
options.why: A quota limits the quantity of an import, which reduces supply, and with demand unchanged the price of the imported good tends to rise.

options.t: It becomes zero
options.why: A quota limits supply and does not make the price zero; a price of zero would mean the good is free, which cannot result from restricting quantity.

options.t: It tends to fall
options.why: A quota cuts the supply of the imported good, and less supply with the same demand pushes the price up, not down, so falling prices is wrong.

options.t: It stays pegged
options.why: A quota does not peg the price to a fixed level; it limits quantity, and the market price still moves, rising when supply is restricted.

q: What is nationalization?

options.t: A firm selling shares to the public for the first time
options.why: A firm selling shares to the public for the first time is an initial public offering, which changes ownership but does not move a private industry into government hands.

options.t: The government taking ownership of a private industry
options.why: Nationalization is the government taking ownership of a private industry or firm, so that the state owns and often runs it, sometimes with compensation to owners.

options.t: A firm merging with a competitor from abroad to cut costs
options.why: A firm merging with a foreign competitor is an international merger between private companies, and the government does not take ownership of it.

options.t: A firm moving to another country to avoid taxes
options.why: A firm moving to another country is relocation, often called offshoring, and the government does not take ownership of any industry in doing so.

q: What is privatization?

options.t: A firm going out of business for good this year
options.why: A firm going out of business is a closure or bankruptcy, which ends the company rather than moving government owned assets into private hands.

options.t: A firm hiding its profits from the tax office
options.why: A firm hiding profits from the tax office is tax evasion, which is illegal, and it has no connection with selling government owned assets to private owners.

options.t: The state taking over a private firm and running it
options.why: The state taking over and running a private firm is nationalization, which is the opposite of privatization, where the government sells or hands over assets.

options.t: Selling government-owned assets to private owners
options.why: Privatization means selling government owned assets or enterprises to private owners, which moves ownership and often operation of a business from the state to the private sector.

q: What does real GDP adjust for?

options.t: Changes in tax rates paid
options.why: Real GDP does not adjust for tax rates; it removes the effect of price changes so that output in different years can be compared fairly.

options.t: Changes in exchange rates
options.why: Exchange rates affect trade values but real GDP does not adjust for them; it adjusts for the price level using a base year's prices.

options.t: Changes in the price level
options.why: Real GDP adjusts for changes in the price level, using constant prices from a base year, so that a rise in GDP shows more output and not just higher prices.

options.t: Changes in population size
options.why: Population size is not part of the real GDP adjustment; adjusting for population gives GDP per capita, which is a different measure from real GDP.

q: Nominal GDP rises 6% while prices rise 2%. About how much did real GDP grow?

options.why: An 8% figure comes from adding 6% and 2%, but inflation must be subtracted from nominal growth to find real growth, so 8% is wrong.
A 12% figure comes from multiplying 6% by 2, which has no meaning here; real growth is nominal growth minus inflation, not a product of the two.
A 2% figure is just the inflation rate and ignores the nominal growth, but real growth equals 6% minus 2%, which is more than 2%.
Real GDP growth is roughly nominal growth minus inflation, so 6% minus 2% gives about 4%, showing that output rose by 4% after removing the price effect.

q: What is a GDP deflator?

options.t: A device that reduces unemployment in cities
options.why: A GDP deflator is not a device that reduces unemployment; it is a statistical measure of prices and has no power to change the labor market.

options.t: A price index that covers all goods in GDP
options.why: The GDP deflator is a price index that covers all goods and services included in GDP, and it is used to convert nominal GDP into real GDP.

options.t: A rule that caps inflation at a set level
options.why: A rule capping inflation at a set level would be a policy or target, but the GDP deflator is just a measure of price changes, not a rule.

options.t: A tool that lowers a firm's taxes by a set sum
options.why: A tool that lowers a firm's taxes is a tax measure, but the GDP deflator is a price index used to measure inflation across the economy.

q: What does the Consumer Price Index track?

options.t: Wages paid to workers in all sectors of firms
options.why: Wages paid to workers are tracked by wage and earnings data, while the Consumer Price Index follows the prices households pay for a typical basket of goods.

options.t: Prices producers get for goods sold to dealers
options.why: Prices producers receive for goods sold to dealers are tracked by the Producer Price Index, which is a different measure from the Consumer Price Index.

options.t: Prices of a basket of goods households buy
options.why: The Consumer Price Index tracks the prices of a basket of goods and services that households typically buy, and it is the main gauge of inflation for consumers.

options.t: Stock market values of large firms each day
options.why: Stock market values are measured by stock indexes such as the S&P 500, whereas the CPI measures the cost of goods and services households buy.

q: The CPI was 250 last year and is 260 this year. What was the inflation rate?

options.why: Inflation is the change in CPI divided by last year's CPI, so 260 minus 250 is 10, and 10 divided by 250 gives 0.04, or 4%.
A 26% figure takes the new CPI value as a percent, but inflation is the change divided by the old CPI, which here is 10 over 250.
A 2.5% figure divides the 10 point change by 400, which is not the right base; the base should be last year's CPI of 250, giving 4%.
A 10% figure uses the 10 point change as if it were a percent, but it must be divided by the old CPI of 250 to give 4%.

q: Why is core inflation useful?

options.t: It ignores all price changes in the economy
options.why: Core inflation does not ignore all price changes; it removes only the volatile food and energy prices so that the underlying trend in other prices is easier to see.

options.t: It counts only food and energy prices today
options.why: Core inflation excludes food and energy prices instead of counting only them, so saying it counts only food and energy prices gets the definition reversed.

options.t: It predicts stock prices by removing energy
options.why: Core inflation is a measure of price trends, not a tool for predicting stock prices, and removing energy does not give it that purpose.

options.t: It leaves out volatile food and energy prices
options.why: Core inflation leaves out volatile food and energy prices, which swing with weather and oil markets, so policymakers can see the underlying inflation trend more clearly.

q: What is the labor force participation rate?

options.t: The share of jobs that are full time in the economy
options.why: The share of jobs that are full time describes job quality, not the participation rate, which looks at how many working age people are in the labor force.

options.t: The share of working-age people who are working or looking
options.why: The labor force participation rate is the share of working age people who are either working or actively looking for work, out of the total working age population.

options.t: The share of workers who are unemployed in the labor force
options.why: The share of workers who are unemployed in the labor force is the unemployment rate, which is a different measure from the participation rate.

options.t: The share of workers in unions across the whole nation
options.why: The share of workers in unions is the union membership rate, which tells us about labor organization and not about how many people are in the labor force.

q: Why might the unemployment rate fall even if no new jobs appear?

options.t: Discouraged workers leave the labor force
options.why: If discouraged workers give up and leave the labor force, they are no longer counted as unemployed, so the unemployment rate can fall even though no new jobs appeared.

options.t: Taxes rise on all workers in the nation
options.why: Tax increases on workers do not directly change how the unemployment rate is counted, and they would not make it fall without any new jobs appearing.

options.t: Prices fall across the whole economy
options.why: Falling prices across the economy do not by themselves reduce the share of people counted as unemployed, and no new jobs means no direct fall.

options.t: More people join the labor force to seek work
options.why: More people joining the labor force to seek work raises the number of job seekers, which tends to push the unemployment rate up, not make it fall.

q: What is the underemployment problem?

options.t: Workers earn more than expected, above what firms planned
options.why: Workers who earn more than expected is a positive outcome and not underemployment, which refers to people not fully using their skills or hours.

options.t: Workers have no jobs at all in the whole economy right now
options.why: Having no jobs at all describes unemployment, while underemployment means people do have jobs but those jobs are below their skills or fewer hours than wanted.

options.t: Workers hold jobs below their skills or hours wanted
options.why: Underemployment is when workers hold jobs below their skill level or work fewer hours than they want, so labor is not being fully used even though they have work.

options.t: Workers retire early by choice well before age sixty
options.why: Retiring early by choice is a decision to leave the labor force and does not describe workers who want more hours or better matched jobs.

q: What is a leading indicator?

options.t: A statistic that tends to change before the economy does
options.why: A leading indicator is a statistic that tends to change before the economy changes, such as new housing permits, so it can help forecast turning points.

options.t: A statistic that tends to change only after the economy does
options.why: A statistic that changes only after the economy does is a lagging indicator, such as the unemployment rate, and not a leading indicator.

options.t: A statistic made up by a leader of the firm each month
options.why: A leading indicator is not a number made up by a firm's leader; it is a measured economic statistic whose changes tend to come before the economy's.

options.t: A statistic that never changes over any period of time
options.why: A statistic that never changes would have no information about the economy, so it cannot be an indicator, and leading indicators do change ahead of the economy.

q: What is a coincident indicator?

options.t: A statistic that moves long after the economy does
options.why: A statistic that moves long after the economy does is a lagging indicator, so it is not a coincident indicator, which moves at the same time.

options.t: A statistic that moves before the economy does each year
options.why: A statistic that moves before the economy does is a leading indicator, whereas a coincident indicator moves at the same time as the economy does.

options.t: A statistic that moves with the economy at the same time
options.why: A coincident indicator moves with the economy at the same time, such as industrial production or employment, so it shows where the economy is now.

options.t: A statistic that has no timing link to the economy
options.why: A statistic with no timing link to the economy would not be an indicator at all, whereas a coincident indicator moves in step with the economy.

q: Which is generally a lagging indicator?

options.t: Stock prices each day
options.why: Stock prices are generally a leading indicator because they tend to move before the economy changes, as investors look ahead to future profits.

options.t: The unemployment rate
options.why: The unemployment rate is generally a lagging indicator because firms hire or lay off workers only after the economy has already turned up or down.

options.t: New housing permits
options.why: New housing permits are generally a leading indicator because builders apply for permits before construction, which happens ahead of the economy's changes in activity.

options.t: Consumer confidence
options.why: Consumer confidence is generally a leading indicator because households that feel hopeful or worried change their spending plans before the economy itself shifts.

q: What does a rising consumer confidence index suggest?

options.t: Prices will fall for certain
options.why: Rising confidence does not guarantee that prices will fall; it signals optimism about the economy, which tends to raise spending, and that can push prices up.

options.t: Unemployment must be rising
options.why: Rising consumer confidence suggests households feel secure about jobs and income, so it does not point to rising unemployment, which would lower confidence instead.

options.t: Households may spend less
options.why: When confidence rises, households feel better about the future and tend to spend more, not less, so predicting reduced spending reverses the usual relationship.

options.t: Households may spend more
options.why: A rising consumer confidence index suggests households feel better about jobs and income, so they may spend more, which can lift demand and economic growth.

q: What does the Index of Leading Economic Indicators try to do?

options.t: Count the firms in the economy each month
options.why: Counting the firms in the economy is a business census task and not the aim of the Index of Leading Economic Indicators, which forecasts changes in activity.

options.t: Measure the national debt in the economy
options.why: The national debt is measured by the Treasury from government borrowing records, and it is not what the Index of Leading Economic Indicators tries to measure.

options.t: Set the interest rate for the whole economy
options.why: Interest rates are set by the central bank and by markets, not by an index, since the Index of Leading Economic Indicators only gives forecasting signals.

options.t: Signal turning points in the business cycle
options.why: The Index of Leading Economic Indicators combines several data series to signal turning points in the business cycle, such as upcoming peaks and troughs, before they occur.

q: What is the trade deficit?

options.t: A fall in the exchange rate level
options.why: A fall in the exchange rate is a depreciation of the currency, which is different from a trade deficit, defined as imports exceeding exports.

options.t: Government spending above revenue
options.why: Government spending above revenue is a budget deficit, which is a different concept from the trade deficit that compares imports with exports.

options.t: Imports exceeding exports in value
options.why: A trade deficit occurs when the value of a country's imports is greater than the value of its exports over a period, so it buys more than it sells abroad.

options.t: Exports exceeding imports in value
options.why: Exports exceeding imports in value is a trade surplus, which is the opposite of a trade deficit, where imports are the larger amount.

q: A country exports $400 billion and imports $450 billion. What is its trade balance?

options.t: A surplus of $50 billion
options.why: A surplus needs exports to exceed imports, but here exports of 400 are below imports of 450, so the balance is negative and not a surplus.

options.t: A deficit of $50 billion
options.why: The trade balance is exports minus imports, so 400 minus 450 equals negative 50, which is a deficit of 50 billion dollars.

options.t: A zero balance, no deficit
options.why: A zero balance would require exports and imports to be equal, but 400 billion is not equal to 450 billion, so there is a gap of 50.

options.t: A deficit of $850 billion
options.why: The figure 850 billion comes from adding exports and imports together, but the trade balance is found by subtracting imports from exports, which gives a deficit of 50.

q: What does the current account measure?

options.t: A country's trade in goods and services plus income flows
options.why: The current account measures a country's trade in goods and services plus income flows and transfers with the rest of the world, so it shows its net external position.

options.t: The number of firms in the country at a given time
options.why: The number of firms in a country is a business count and has nothing to do with the current account, which tracks flows of trade and income.

options.t: The money in a person's checking account after bills are paid
options.why: Money in a person's checking account is a personal bank balance, while the current account is a national measure of trade and income flows with other countries.

options.t: The country's yearly budget for all public services
options.why: A country's yearly budget for public services is a government spending plan, not the current account, which records international trade, income and transfers.

q: What is a recession's effect on tax revenue?

options.t: It stays unchanged
options.why: Tax revenue does not stay unchanged in a recession, because incomes and spending fall and so do income and sales tax receipts for the government.

options.t: It typically falls
options.why: In a recession, incomes, profits and spending fall, so the income, corporate and sales taxes collected typically fall, and this is called an automatic stabilizer effect.

options.t: It rises sharply
options.why: A recession lowers incomes and sales, so tax revenue falls rather than rises sharply, and a sharp rise would be typical of strong growth.

options.t: It turns into zero
options.why: Tax revenue falls in a recession but does not drop to zero, since people and firms still earn income and make purchases that are taxed.

q: What does a yield curve compare?

options.t: Profits of different firms across the economy
options.why: Profits of different firms are compared in company reports, whereas a yield curve compares interest rates on bonds that differ by their time to maturity.

options.t: Wages in different cities across the country
options.why: Wages in different cities are compared in labor market data, and a yield curve has nothing to do with wages or city differences.

options.t: Interest rates on bonds with different maturities
options.why: A yield curve compares interest rates on bonds, usually government bonds, with different maturities, and its shape helps show what investors expect for the economy.

options.t: Prices of different brands of the same product overall
options.why: Prices of different brands of the same product are compared by shoppers, but a yield curve plots bond interest rates against time to maturity.

q: What does an inverted yield curve often signal?

options.t: A coming boom in output and sales
options.why: A coming boom is typically linked to a normal upward sloping yield curve, whereas an inverted curve has often come before slowdowns and not before booms.

options.t: An end to inflation as prices stop rising
options.why: An inverted curve does not mean inflation is ending; it means short term rates are above long term rates, which has often come before a recession.

options.t: No change in the economy for years
options.why: An inverted yield curve points to a possible change in the economy, because short term rates exceed long term rates, so it does not signal years of no change.

options.t: A higher chance of a coming recession
options.why: An inverted yield curve, with short term rates above long term rates, has often come before recessions, so it signals a higher chance of a coming recession.

q: What is the personal savings rate?

options.t: The share of disposable income that households save
options.why: The personal savings rate is the share of disposable income that households save instead of spend, which shows how much of their income they set aside.

options.t: The share of spending on housing and food each year
options.why: The share of spending on housing and food describes a spending pattern, whereas the savings rate measures the part of disposable income that is saved.

options.t: The share of income paid in taxes each year to the state
options.why: The share of income paid in taxes is the tax rate, but the personal savings rate looks at what households keep after taxes and do not spend.

options.t: The interest rate on savings accounts at banks
options.why: The interest rate on savings accounts is what banks pay depositors, which is different from the savings rate, the share of income households save.

q: What is retail sales data used to show?

options.t: How many stores close each year in the nation
options.why: Store closings are tracked in business closure data, but retail sales data measures the dollar value of what consumers spend at stores.

options.t: How many workers stores hire each year
options.why: How many workers stores hire is employment data, while retail sales data measures the spending that consumers do at stores.

options.t: How much stores pay in rent each month
options.why: Rent paid by stores is a cost of business, and retail sales data tracks revenue from consumer purchases, not stores' costs.

options.t: How much consumers are spending at stores
options.why: Retail sales data shows how much consumers are spending at stores, which is a key sign of consumer demand and so of the strength of the economy.

q: What does the Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) gauge?

options.t: The average wage of workers across the nation
options.why: The average wage of workers is measured in earnings data, while the PMI is a survey based index on business activity in manufacturing and services.

options.t: The number of banks in the whole country today
options.why: The number of banks in a country is a count from banking regulators, and it is not what the Purchasing Managers' Index is designed to gauge.

options.t: The health of manufacturing and service activity
options.why: The PMI is based on surveys of purchasing managers and gauges the health of manufacturing and service activity, with a reading above 50 showing expansion.

options.t: The price of homes in the whole country, on average
options.why: The price of homes is measured by house price indexes, whereas the PMI gauges business activity in manufacturing and services based on manager surveys.

q: What is the difference between a tariff and a quota?

options.t: A tariff limits imports while a quota taxes them instead
options.why: This reverses the definitions, because a tariff is a tax on imports and a quota is a limit on the quantity of imports.

options.t: A tariff taxes imports; a quota limits their amount
options.why: A tariff is a tax placed on imports, which raises their price, while a quota is a limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported.

options.t: Both mean the same thing in the law of trade and tariffs
options.why: The two are not the same, since a tariff raises government revenue through a tax and a quota caps quantities, so their effects differ.

options.t: Both pay exporters directly in cash each year of trade
options.why: Neither tariffs nor quotas pay exporters in cash; both restrict imports, and a payment to exporters would instead describe an export subsidy.

q: What is an export subsidy?

options.t: Government support that makes exports cheaper abroad
options.why: An export subsidy is government support, such as payments or tax breaks, that lowers the cost of exports, so the goods can be sold cheaper in foreign markets.

options.t: A fine for exporters who break the trade rules
options.why: A fine for exporters who break trade rules is a penalty for violations, while an export subsidy is a support payment that helps exporters.

options.t: A ban on exports of all goods and services abroad overall
options.why: A ban on exports of all goods is an export embargo, which stops exporting, whereas an export subsidy encourages more exporting by cutting the cost.

options.t: A tax on exports of all goods and services abroad
options.why: A tax on exports is an export duty, which makes exports more costly, whereas an export subsidy lowers the cost and so is the opposite.

q: Why do economists often oppose export subsidies?

options.t: They lower prices at home and help all
options.why: Export subsidies lower prices for foreign buyers, not for people at home, and taxpayers pay for them, so the claim that they help all is wrong.

options.t: They always raise efficiency in trade
options.why: Export subsidies do not always raise efficiency, because they push production toward goods that may not be made at lowest cost, so the word always is wrong.

options.t: They remove all trade barriers for good
options.why: Export subsidies add a distortion to trade and do not remove barriers, so they do not lead to freer trade and may invite retaliation.

options.t: They distort trade and cost taxpayers
options.why: Economists oppose export subsidies because they distort trade by artificially lowering export prices, and taxpayers must fund them, which wastes resources and can harm other countries.

q: What is the main benefit of comparative advantage?

options.t: Countries gain by trading what they produce at lower opportunity cost
options.why: Comparative advantage means countries gain by specializing in and trading goods they produce at lower opportunity cost, so total output and consumption can rise for all.

options.t: One country gains only at another's expense, so trade is a contest overall
options.why: Trade is not a contest where one gains only at the other's expense; comparative advantage shows both countries can gain when each specializes where its opportunity cost is lower.

options.t: All countries must make every good they use, at home and abroad
options.why: Comparative advantage says countries need not make every good at home, because they can specialize and trade, which lets them consume more than they could alone.

options.t: Trade removes the need for specialization in any country at all
options.why: Trade depends on specialization, since countries focus on goods with lower opportunity cost, so saying trade removes the need for specialization is the opposite of the truth.

q: In one hour Country X makes 4 shirts or 2 tools; Country Y makes 3 shirts or 3 tools. Who has the comparative advantage in shirts?

options.t: Country Y
options.why: Country Y gives up 1 tool per shirt, which is a higher opportunity cost than Country X, which gives up only half a tool, so Y does not hold the advantage.

options.t: Country X
options.why: Country X gives up 2 tools for 4 shirts, or 0.5 tool per shirt, while Y gives up 1 tool per shirt, so X has the lower cost.

options.t: Both equally
options.why: The two countries have different opportunity costs of 0.5 and 1 tool per shirt, so they are not equal, and one of them has the advantage.

options.t: Neither
options.why: One of the two countries must have the comparative advantage in shirts when opportunity costs differ, and here X gives up 0.5 tool per shirt and Y gives up 1.

q: What does a trade surplus imply about a country's net exports?

options.t: They are always zero
options.why: A surplus means exports exceed imports, so net exports, which are exports minus imports, are positive, not zero, in that case, and are not always zero.

options.t: They are not measured
options.why: Net exports are measured and published in national accounts as a part of GDP, so saying they are not measured is false.

options.t: They are positive
options.why: A trade surplus means exports are greater than imports, so net exports, equal to exports minus imports, are positive, which adds to a country's GDP.

options.t: They are negative
options.why: Negative net exports would mean imports exceed exports, which describes a trade deficit, not a surplus, so negative is the wrong sign for a surplus.

q: What is a floating exchange rate?

options.t: A rate set by a company or private firm in trade
options.why: A rate set by a private firm is not a floating exchange rate, because floating rates are determined by supply and demand in currency markets, not by any one company.

options.t: A rate set by supply and demand in currency markets
options.why: A floating exchange rate is set by supply and demand for currencies in the foreign exchange market, so its value moves up and down as conditions change.

options.t: A rate fixed by the government against another currency
options.why: A rate fixed by the government against another currency is a pegged or fixed exchange rate, which is the opposite of a floating rate.

options.t: A rate that never changes over any period of time
options.why: A floating exchange rate moves with supply and demand in currency markets, so it changes often, and saying it never changes is false.

q: What is a fixed (pegged) exchange rate?

options.t: A rate a government holds at a set value
options.why: A fixed or pegged exchange rate is one that a government or central bank holds at a set value against another currency, often by buying or selling currency.

options.t: A rate that changes every minute in markets
options.why: A rate that changes every minute in markets is a floating exchange rate, which responds to supply and demand, and is not fixed or pegged.

options.t: A rate set by market forces and demand
options.why: A rate set by market forces and demand is a floating rate, while a pegged rate is held at a set value by the government.

options.t: A rate set by tourists who travel abroad
options.why: Tourists do not set exchange rates, as their currency exchange is a small part of the market, and a pegged rate is set by the government.

q: If demand for the euro rises relative to supply, what happens to its value?

options.t: It becomes useless
options.why: Higher demand for the euro makes it more valuable, not useless, because buyers must bid more for it, and a currency with strong demand does not lose all value.

options.t: It depreciates
options.why: Depreciation means a currency loses value, but a rise in demand relative to supply makes the euro worth more, which is the opposite effect.

options.t: It stays frozen
options.why: In a floating system the price moves in response to supply and demand, so the euro would not stay frozen when demand rises above supply.

options.t: It appreciates
options.why: When demand for the euro rises relative to supply, buyers bid up its price against other currencies, so the euro appreciates and its value goes up.

q: A weaker home currency tends to make exports:

options.t: Impossible to sell abroad
options.why: A weaker home currency does not make exports impossible to sell; it lowers their price abroad, so they tend to sell more, not less.

options.t: Free of any tariffs abroad
options.why: Tariffs are set by importing countries and do not disappear when a currency weakens; a weaker currency changes the price in foreign currency, not tariff status.

options.t: Cheaper for foreign buyers
options.why: A weaker home currency means foreign buyers need less of their own money to buy the home country's goods, so exports become cheaper for foreign buyers.

options.t: Pricier for foreign buyers
options.why: Pricier exports would result from a stronger home currency, not a weaker one, because foreign buyers would need more of their own money to buy the goods.

q: What is the World Bank's main focus?

options.t: Financing development projects in poorer countries
options.why: The World Bank mainly finances development projects in poorer countries, such as infrastructure, health and education, through loans and grants, to help reduce poverty.

options.t: Enforcing trade rules between all nations of the world
options.why: Enforcing trade rules between nations is the job of the World Trade Organization, not the World Bank, which focuses on lending for development.

options.t: Regulating world stock markets and share prices
options.why: The World Bank does not regulate stock markets or share prices; national regulators and exchanges do that, and the Bank funds development projects instead.

options.t: Setting global interest rates for banks and firms
options.why: Setting global interest rates is not a World Bank role, since central banks set their own rates and the Bank focuses on development finance.

q: What does the International Monetary Fund do?

options.t: Builds roads and schools in poorer countries across the world each year
options.why: Building roads and schools in poorer countries is more like the work of the World Bank, which funds development, while the IMF focuses on monetary stability.

options.t: Collects tariffs for all nations and pays the money out to poorer countries
options.why: The IMF does not collect tariffs for all nations or pay money out to poorer countries; tariffs are collected by each country's own customs service.

options.t: Sets product standards for goods traded between countries and firms worldwide
options.why: Setting product standards for traded goods is work done by standards bodies and trade organizations, not the IMF, which deals with money and finance.

options.t: Supports monetary cooperation and lends to countries in financial trouble
options.why: The International Monetary Fund supports monetary cooperation among countries and lends to those in financial trouble, such as balance of payments crises, often with policy conditions attached.

q: What is the European Union's single market?

options.t: A market that is closed to all trade with other nations of the world
options.why: A single market is open, not closed to trade with other nations, and it removes barriers among member states so trade flows freely between them.

options.t: A market with no rules and no regulations of any kind for sellers
options.why: The single market has common rules and regulations that all members follow, so saying it has no rules of any kind is false.

options.t: A market allowing free movement of goods, services, people and capital
options.why: The EU single market allows the free movement of goods, services, people and capital among member states, so businesses and workers can operate across borders easily.

options.t: A market limited to one country, in which goods may not cross a border
options.why: A single market covers many member countries, not one, and goods cross borders freely within it, so a market where goods may not cross a border is wrong.

q: What is the USMCA?

options.t: A banking union among nations in Africa and the Middle East
options.why: The USMCA is not a banking union and does not involve Africa or the Middle East; its members are in North America only.

options.t: A trade agreement among the United States, Mexico and Canada
options.why: The USMCA is a trade agreement among the United States, Mexico and Canada that replaced NAFTA and sets rules for trade, labor and digital commerce.

options.t: A tax treaty with many countries in Asia and the Pacific region
options.why: The USMCA is a trade agreement within North America, not a tax treaty with Asian and Pacific countries, which are not members of the pact.

options.t: A military pact in Europe between nations for their defense
options.why: The USMCA is about trade and not defense, and its members are in North America, so a military pact among European nations is incorrect.

q: What is a customs union?

options.t: Members ban all trade among themselves and with the rest of the world
options.why: A customs union does not ban trade among its members; it removes tariffs among them, so banning all trade is the opposite of what it does.

options.t: Members keep separate tariffs for each other and set own outside rates
options.why: In a customs union members do not keep separate outside tariffs; they adopt a common external tariff, so the claim of separate outside rates is wrong.

options.t: Members share a single currency only, and nothing else about trade
options.why: A single currency is a feature of a monetary union and not the defining feature of a customs union, which concerns tariffs on trade among members.

options.t: Members drop tariffs among themselves and share one outside tariff
options.why: In a customs union, members drop tariffs on trade among themselves and apply one shared tariff on goods from outside, which keeps outside trade treatment consistent.

q: What is a trade war?

options.t: A dispute inside a single company over wages and hours
options.why: A dispute inside a single company over wages is a labor dispute, while a trade war is a conflict between countries over trade barriers.

options.t: Countries raising tariffs on each other's goods in turn
options.why: A trade war is when countries raise tariffs on each other's goods in turn, as each side retaliates, which usually raises prices and cuts trade.

options.t: A fight with weapons over trade routes between two nations
options.why: A trade war uses tariffs and trade barriers, not weapons, so a fight over trade routes with weapons is a military conflict and not a trade war.

options.t: A festival of imports and exports held each year
options.why: A festival of imports and exports is not a trade war; the term describes escalating tariffs and retaliation between countries, which harm trade and not celebrate it.

q: What is dumping?

options.t: Selling goods at a fair price abroad, the same as at home
options.why: Selling at a fair price abroad, equal to the home price, is normal trade, whereas dumping means selling below cost or below the home price.

options.t: Throwing away unsold goods at the end of the year
options.why: Throwing away unsold goods is waste disposal, and dumping in trade refers to selling goods abroad at unfairly low prices, not discarding them.

options.t: Selling goods abroad below their cost or home price
options.why: Dumping is selling goods in a foreign market below their cost or below the price charged at home, which can harm local producers and may lead to duties.

options.t: Giving products to charity at no cost to buyers
options.why: Giving products to charity is a donation, not dumping, which is a pricing practice in export markets where goods are sold below cost or home price.

q: What is the infant industry argument?

options.t: New industries need protection until they can compete
options.why: The infant industry argument says new industries need temporary protection, such as tariffs, until they grow large enough and learn enough to compete with established foreign firms.

options.t: Old industries must be shut down at once by law
options.why: The argument is about protecting new industries and not about shutting down old ones, and it does not call for old industries to be closed by law.

options.t: Babies need protection from imports of toys made abroad
options.why: The infant industry argument is about young industries in a country, not babies, and it concerns tariffs and not protection of toys or children.

options.t: All industries should be taxed more heavily each year
options.why: The infant industry argument calls for protecting new industries, not taxing all industries more heavily, so taxing all industries every year does not fit the argument.

q: What is a common criticism of the infant industry argument?

options.t: It forces firms to export more goods to many other nations
options.why: The argument calls for protecting new industries from imports and does not force firms to export more, so forcing exports is not a criticism of it.

options.t: It removes all costs for consumers, as foreign goods are kept out
options.why: Keeping out foreign goods does not remove costs for consumers; it often raises prices and narrows choice, but the claim that it removes all costs is wrong.

options.t: It always lowers prices forever for all buyers in markets
options.why: Protection does not always lower prices forever; it tends to raise them, so claiming it always lowers prices is not a true criticism of the argument.

options.t: Protection may last too long and keep inefficient firms alive
options.why: A common criticism is that protection may last too long, so the industry never has to improve and inefficient firms stay alive at consumers' expense.

q: What is a multinational enterprise?

options.t: A government trade office in the capital
options.why: A government trade office in the capital is a public agency, whereas a multinational enterprise is a private firm that runs operations in several countries.

options.t: A union of workers across borders and trades
options.why: A union of workers across borders is a labor organization, but a multinational enterprise is a business firm that operates in more than one country.

options.t: A firm that operates in several countries
options.why: A multinational enterprise is a firm that operates in several countries, with offices, factories or stores in more than one nation, and often a home base.

options.t: A firm limited to one city or one town
options.why: A firm limited to one city or one town operates locally, which is the opposite of a multinational firm that has operations in many countries.

q: What is a trade-off of globalization for workers?

options.t: No change in jobs or prices for anyone in any industry
options.why: Globalization changes prices and jobs for many people, so claiming no change in jobs or prices for anyone in any industry ignores the real trade-off.

options.t: Cheaper goods but possible job losses in some industries
options.why: Globalization often brings cheaper goods for consumers but can cause job losses in industries that cannot compete with imports, which is a real trade-off for workers.

options.t: Lower wages for every worker without exception in the nation
options.why: Globalization does not lower wages for every worker without exception, because some workers in export industries gain, so the word every makes the claim false.

options.t: Higher prices and more jobs for everyone in the nation
options.why: Globalization usually lowers prices through competition and does not give higher prices and more jobs for everyone, so that claim is the wrong way round.

q: What is a trade-off?

options.t: Giving up one thing to get another
options.why: A trade-off means giving up one thing in order to get another, since resources are limited and choosing one option usually means passing up an alternative.

options.t: Getting everything wanted at no cost
options.why: Getting everything wanted at no cost ignores scarcity, because resources are limited, and a trade-off exists exactly because choices have costs.

options.t: Trading only with other countries
options.why: A trade-off is a choice between alternatives, not trade with other countries, so trading only with other countries is a narrower idea than the term means.

options.t: Selling goods for a higher price
options.why: Selling goods for a higher price is a pricing decision, whereas a trade-off is about giving up one option to gain another.

q: A student spends Saturday studying instead of working a paid shift. What is the opportunity cost?

options.t: The cost of the textbooks bought

options.t: The time spent studying only

options.why: A tax schedule lists rates for income levels, which is a government fiscal tool, whereas the production possibilities frontier shows the output an economy can make.

options.why: A list of company profits is a financial record, and it does not show combinations of goods an economy can make, which is what the frontier shows.

q: A point inside the production possibilities frontier shows:

options.t: An impossible output for the economy
options.why: A point inside the frontier is attainable, so it is not impossible; impossible output lies outside the frontier, beyond what resources allow.

options.t: Rapid growth in the whole economy
options.why: A point inside the frontier shows output below capacity, so it does not show rapid growth, which would appear as the frontier shifting outward over time.

options.t: Full efficiency of resources
options.why: Full efficiency of resources is shown by points on the frontier, not inside it, because a point inside means resources could produce more.

options.t: Unused resources or inefficiency
options.why: A point inside the production possibilities frontier shows that the economy is not using all its resources fully, so there is unused capacity or inefficiency.

q: What does economic growth do to the production possibilities frontier?

options.t: Turns it into a line
options.why: Economic growth does not turn the frontier into a line; the frontier keeps its shape but moves outward when the economy can produce more.

options.t: Shifts it inward
options.why: Shifting the frontier inward would mean the economy can produce less, as in a loss of resources, which is the opposite of economic growth.

options.t: Shifts it outward
options.why: Economic growth increases resources or improves technology, so the economy can produce more of both goods, and the frontier shifts outward to show it.

options.t: Removes it fully
options.why: Growth does not remove the frontier; every economy still faces limits on output, and the frontier simply moves outward as the limits expand.

q: What is the law of demand?

options.t: Demand is always fixed at one level for all possible prices
options.why: Demand is not fixed at one level; the law of demand says the quantity demanded changes as the price changes, so a fixed level for all prices is wrong.

options.t: Price has no effect on demand for any good in markets
options.why: Price does affect demand, since buyers respond to price changes, and the claim of no effect for any good contradicts the law of demand.

options.t: As price rises, quantity demanded rises too, as buyers see quality
options.why: The law of demand says quantity demanded falls as price rises, not rises, and buyers seeing quality in high prices is not the general rule.

options.t: As price rises, quantity demanded falls, other things equal
options.why: The law of demand says that as price rises, quantity demanded falls, other things equal, because higher prices push buyers toward substitutes or to buy less.

q: What is the law of supply?

options.why: Supply changes with price, since the law of supply links price and quantity supplied, so supply never changing is false.

options.t: As price rises, quantity supplied rises, other things equal
options.why: The law of supply says that as price rises, quantity supplied rises, other things equal, because higher prices make producing more profitable and attract more sellers.

options.why: Producers respond to prices, since higher prices make production more profitable, so saying they ignore prices when planning output contradicts the law of supply.
